The Legacy of Nietzsche’s
Philosophy of Laughter
This book spans one hundred years of French philosophy. It investigates
the role of laughter and humor in the good life, specifically as discussed
by three prominent French philosophers who were influenced by Ni-
etzsche’s thought: Georges Bataille, Gilles Deleuze, and Clément Rosset.
Lydia Amir begins by addressing Nietzsche’s reception in France; she
explains why and how he came to be considered a “philosopher of laugh-
ter” in the French academe. Each of the subsequent three chapters focuses
on the significance of laughter or humor in the good life as advocated by
Bataille, Deleuze, and Rosset. These chapters also explore the complex
relationship between the comic and the tragic, and between laughter or
humor and irony, satire, and ridicule. Amir concludes by probing addi-
tional contributions to the philosophy of humor by French Nietzschean
and non-Nietzschean philosophers. The Legacy of Nietzsche’s Philoso-
phy of Laughter makes an invaluable contribution to recent work done
on Bataille and Deleuze, and offers further introduction to the relatively
understudied Rosset. It illuminates the philosophies of these three think-
ers, their association with Nietzsche, the contributions made to the phi-
losophy of humor by additional t wentieth-century French philosophers,
and, overall, the significant role that humor plays in philosophy.
Lydia Amir teaches philosophy at Tufts University, USA. She is the au-
thor of Humor and the Good Life in Modern P hilosophy: Shaftesbury,
Hamann, Kierkegaard (2014); Rethinking Philosophers’ Responsibility
(2017); Taking Philosophy Seriously (2018); and Philosophy,  Humor,
and the Human Condition: Taking Ridicule Seriously (2019). She is the
Founding- President of the International Association for the Philosophy
of Humor, Founding-Editor of the journal Philosophy of Humor Year-
book, and Editor of the Israeli Journal of Humor Research: An Inter-
national Journal. She is Founding-Editor of the book series, Gruyter
Studies in Philosophy of Humor, Brill series in the Human Condition,
and Lexington Series in Philosophical Practice.

The aim of this study is to investigate the role of laughter or humor in the
good life as conceived by Georges Bataille, Gilles Deleuze and Clément
Rosset. This investigation is preceded by an account of the reception of
Nietzsche in France as a philosopher of laughter, which explains the
significance of laughter and humor for twentieth-century French
­Nietzschean philosophers. This investigation ends with additional
French philosophers’ account of laughter and humor, either Nietzsche-
ans or not, and an analysis of postmodern laughter and irony.
Various disciplines such as medicine, psychology and the social sci-
ences have praised humor’s benefits for the individual and for society.
However, the question of the good life is fundamentally a philosophical
question. Thus it is important to inquire into whether philosophers have
given laughter or humor a role in the good life. This topic has been un-
derstudied as the question itself has not been formulated. The nature
of laughter or the style of writing have been put to the fore rather than
the role, explicitly formulated and defended by arguments, that laughter
may have in the good life as variously conceived by philosophers.
The studies I have undertaken to redress this neglect have disclosed
nine modern philosophers who have explicitly entrusted humor or
laughter with a role in the good life as they conceive it. They include
the third Earl of Shaftesbury, Johann Georg Hamann, Søren Kierke-
gaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, George Santayana and the ­proto-modern
philosopher Michel de Montaigne.1 The last volume which I present
here complements the former studies by engaging with the role ascribed
to laughter or humor in the good life by three French laughing followers
of Nietzsche, the twentieth-century philosophers Bataille, Deleuze and
Rosset, and complemented by additional views, which together form
a comprehensive study of the role of the comic and its cognates in one
hundred years of philosophy in France.2
The prologue addresses the French reception of Nietzsche as a phi-
losopher of laughter. That Nietzsche has been received in France as
a laughing philosopher strikes me as both important and interesting.
It is interesting, first, because it is not an obvious philosophical read-
ing of Nietzsche; second, because until recently it has mainly been a
Introduction
DOI: 10.4324/9780429506116-1


2  Introduction
French reading. It is important because of this interpretation’s pervasive-
ness in France and influence abroad, both in readings of Nietzsche and
in subsequent original philosophies that have endorsed the main themes
of laughter, comedy, parody and play. Moreover, the significance of the
French interpretation of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter extends
to the incorporation of these themes within philosophy at large due to
the influence of French philosophy outside of France.
In studying the reception of Nietzsche in France, the role played by
Bataille and Pierre Klossowki stand out in relation to the topic this study
addresses; however, the prologue also discloses the influence that Lev
Shestov’s interpretation of Nietzsche had on Bataille and Klossowki and
on many additional French philosophers of the twentieth century, such
as Albert Camus and Deleuze.
The three chapters following the prologue introduce three French
laughing followers of Nietzsche: Bataille, Deleuze and the contemporary
philosopher,3 Rosset. All three are interpreters of Nietzsche and authors
of original philosophies that entrust laughter or humor with a significant
role in their respective views of the good life. Each chapter begins with
the relevant philosopher’s view of the good life, followed, first, by his
view of the tragic and the comic, and second, by his view of the role that
his preferred cognate of the comical, laughter or humor, fulfills in the
good life. Each chapter concludes by assessing the originality and the
viability of the relevant philosopher’s views.
In the concluding remarks that close this volume, I complete the study
of the legacy of Nietzsche’s philosophy of laughter by addressing ad-
ditional French laughing followers of Nietzsche who did not explicitly
entrust laughter with a role in the good life. Either they do not argue
for, or fully develop a view of the good life; or, their view of laughter is
insufficiently developed. They include Michel Foucault, Jacques Derrida
and his followers, notably Sarah Kofman and  Jean-Luc Nancy, Jean-
François Lyotard and Luce Irigaray, and additional feminist thinkers
such as Hélène Cixous and Julia Kristeva. I compare their views with
those of French twentieth-century non-Nietzschean philosophers who
offer interesting accounts of humor, such as Vladimir Jankélévitch and
André Comte-Sponville.  Finally, I examine postmodern laughter and
irony, I analyze the former into its constituents and I criticize the latter.
Nietzsche is significant for the main thinkers this study addresses:
Bataille claims that he repeats Nietzsche’s experience and Rosset con-
siders himself Nietzsche’s sole follower. Nietzsche’s impact on Deleuze
is less explicit as early on he turns to additional philosophers, such as
Henri Bergson and Benedict Spinoza, whose presence is felt all along in
his thought.
Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset prolong their respective interpretations
of Nietzsche’s laughter into their own philosophies. Bataille interprets
Nietzsche as a mystic of laughter, a practice which he repeats and which


Introduction  3
he sees as the summum bonum. Deleuze emphasizes the practice of
laughter in Nietzsche, but uses it to service his own philosophy of differ-
ence, which he finds or projects into Nietzsche’s thought. For Deleuze,
laughter is an affirmative power of transmutation that transforms suf-
fering into joy, and an affirmative power of reflection and becoming that
affirms multiplicity and the unity of multiplicity. In the guise of humor,
it is a selective force that enables the counter- effectuation that yields
amor fati, the apex of his philosophy. Apart from the tragic laughter
that Rosset finds in Nietzsche’s thought, he emphasizes the fundamental
significance of joy which parallels his own view of joy as central for the
affirmation of life. Rosset’s innovative notion of the laughter of annihi-
lation embodies tragic laughter, yet falls short of the graced joy which is
necessary for the good life.
Nietzsche’s views of laughter, and of the tragic and the comic do not
have the same significance in these philosophers’ respective attitudes to-
ward their predecessor. All three endorse Nietzsche’s view of tragic joy
and his association of the tragic with laughter. It is the use they make
of Nietzsche’s laughter and their attitude toward it that differ. Bataille’s
strategy in defending Nietzsche after World War II was to argue that
 Nietzsche’s laughter indicates that he should not be taken seriously be-
cause his thought is no project but play: it collapses due to the inner
contradictions that structure it if we attempt to account for it in any
other way. The additional thinkers this study addresses put  Nietzschean
laughter to different uses. While acknowledging Bataille’s role in legit-
imizing Nietzsche, Deleuze is freed from this concern but takes on an-
other project, that of legitimizing Nietzsche as a philosopher; he enlists
Nietzschean laughter as a tool in a supposed discussion of Nietzsche
with Hegel and Kant, and presents it as a new way of thinking. Rosset
deems his predecessors “Hegelian philosophers,” and denounces their
use of Nietzsche’s thought as an anti-Hegelian text. He describes himself
as the sole follower of the latter’s tragic philosophy and offers an aesthet-
ics that suits such a philosophy, which includes a notion of annihilating
laughter that delights in disappearance.
Nietzsche has not theorized laughter clearly enough to evaluate if these
uses of laughter are more or less faithful to his views. Nor does this mat-
ter, as the respective views of laughter advanced by these thinkers are
meant to be used in original philosophies rather than as interpretations
of Nietzsche. To formulate their views in adequation to further forms
of laughter, such as humor and irony—terms that are almost alien to
Nietzsche who scarcely uses “humor” and explicitly dismisses “irony”—
these thinkers turn to additional French philosophers, such as Bergson
and Jankélévitch (Bergson’s student and Rosset’s teacher) in search of
definitions of the comical, h umor and irony.4 And, through the recurrent
theme of human ridiculousness, Bataille and Rosset hark back to yet
another Frenchman, Montaigne, a precursor of Nietzsche.5


4  Introduction
The three thinkers that this study addresses offer elaborate views of
the good life, in which both the tragic and the comic are interwoven, and
a sustained analysis of laughter (Bataille and Rosset) or humor (Deleuze).
Deleuze also writes a history of the comical in philosophy. The roles
Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset assign to laughter in their philosophies are
not only ethical, but also epistemological and ontological, and it is in
these later capacities that the potency of laughter within philosophy is
best disclosed.
The complexity of the philosophies of Bataille, Deleuze and Ros-
set should not mask the fact that they are conceived by their authors
as practices of philosophy, that is, as forms of life. Being arts of living,
these philosophies necessarily involve the comical, especially as humor
or self-referential laughter. Arthur Schopenhauer, who defines humor as
the incongruity between the (ideal) conception and the (lived) perception,
aptly notes that this makes the relation of thought to life comical.6 If
Deleuze is right in arguing that “Life will no longer be made to appear be-
fore the categories of thought; thought will be thrown into the categories
of life,” humor as defined by Schopenhauer will necessarily be present in
such philosophies.7
More than arts of living, however, these philosophies are theories of
liberation, which follow Nietzsche’s attempt to offer an alternative re-
demption to the Christian salvation.8 As on the path of the Nietzschean
liberation laughter plays a significant role as both a destructive and a
creative power, so does laughter or humor in the various paths to liber-
ation offered by the three philosophers who work in Nietzsche’s wake.
Laughter is the entire content of the Bataillean liberation, humor enables
the Deleuzian liberation, but for Rosset laughter is conducive to libera-
tion yet falls short of it.
The findings of this study, with its prologue, three chapters and sub-
stantive concluding remarks cannot be summed up in the introduction.
One surprising conclusion may be disclosed here, however: Deleuze
emphatically chooses humor over irony, Rosset deems the laughter he
prefers  “humor,” and the content that Bataille ascribes to “laughter,”
when it is part of the comical at all, is more akin to humor than to irony
because of the self- referential laughter that animates his thought and the
egalitarian view of human insufficiency that he embraces.
Thus, each of these thinkers opposes the supremacy of irony that has
been associated with Jacques Derrida, his followers and additional French
Nietzscheans, and has been identified with postmodernism. It is moreover
noteworthy that Derrida ignored the notion of irony and L yotard rejected
it. The significance of humor also in contrast to irony is emphasized by
additional contemporary French non-Nietzschean philosophers, such as
Jankélévitch and Comte-Sponville, who complement the scene of contem-
porary French philosophy as humorous rather than ironic.


Introduction 5
The Concluding Remarks’ carefully crafted conclusions about irony
and humor can be used to rectify an erroneous view of French post-
modernism; alternatively, they can be seen as an additional argument
against reading Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset as postmodern philoso-
phers. Ascribing postmodernism to these thinkers is problematic yet for
different reasons: Bataille has been deemed a postmodern avant la lettre,
Deleuze’s postmodernity is a matter of debate and Rosset clearly sets his
thought apart from the poststructuralists. The support that humor gets
from French philosophy can be used to strengthen the significant role it
plays in philosophy today—a role that has been eclipsed by irony’s good
press—and the important place it holds in contemporary views of the
good life.9
As few philosophers take laughter for their signature or entrust it
with a significant role in the good life they propose, a study of Bataille,
Deleuze and Rosset along these lines hopefully contributes to the under-
studied relations of philosophy with humor. I believe that it is also a sig-
nificant contribution to the commentaries of each of these philosophers
and the understanding of the relations they entertain with N
 ietzsche,
with each other and with additional French philosophers. This study
attempts to illuminate substantial interpretative issues in the respective
philosophies of these thinkers. It also assigns the understudied notions
of the comic, the tragic, humor and laughter their proper place in these
philosophers’ respective thoughts and visions of the good life.

Even laughter may yet have a future.
(Nietzsche, The Gay Science, 1)
The readers and auditors most natural to me are still Russians, Scandi-
navians and French—will they always be so?
(Nietzsche, Ecce Homo, II, WC, 3)
The French reception of Nietzsche is notable in many respects. As early
as 1929, Geneviève Bianquis’s Nietzsche en France, L’influence de Ni-
etzsche sur la pensée française exemplified the special attention this re-
ception required.1 A somewhat puzzling aspect of the French response to
Nietzsche is his interpretation as a philosopher of laugher, parody and
play.2 Despite the pervasiveness and influence of this interpretation in
France and outside of it, it did not receive the attention it merits.3 The
prologue accounts for this aspect of the French reception of Nietzsche
and assesses its interest and its significance.
1  Interest in and Significance of the French Reception
That Nietzsche has been received in France as a laughing philosopher
strikes me as both significant and interesting. It is interesting because it
is an unobvious philosophical reading of Nietzsche, and mainly a French
one. It is significant because of the pervasiveness of this interpretation
in France and the subsequent influence it had abroad: its impact is felt
not only in readings of Nietzsche, but also in original philosophies that
endorse laughter, comedy, parody and play, and most importantly in
the way that these notions were incorporated in philosophy through the
influence of French philosophy. Allow me to elaborate on these opening
remarks.
The reception that Nietzsche received in France strikes me as in-
teresting for various reasons. First, because reading Nietzsche as a
Prologue
The French Reception of Nietzsche
as a Philosopher of Laughter
DOI: 10.4324/9780429506116-2


8  Prologue
philosopher of laughter is not at all obvious. Many commentators of
Nietzsche’s works do not interpret Nietzsche along these lines, and the
alleged gaiety or funniness of his writings is not apparent to all readers.
It may even come as a surprise that Nietzsche entertains an important
relation with laughter both as a human being and as a thinker. To take
an example, John Lippitt tells us that his interest in Nietzsche’s laughter
was met with incredulity, as “a Nietzschean laughter would be some-
what manic— perhaps prompting its panicked hearers to ensure that
the steak-knives were safely locked away.”4 Along the same lines, David
Farell Krell compares Nietzsche’s thought to “laughter from a beautiful
mouth or in dancing eyes,” to the effect that “soon everyone in the room
is swept away by hilarity or hysteria, where the line that separates good
health from noxious influence is obliterated.”5
The form that Nietzsche’s laughter may take adds further difficulties
to the task of recognizing Nietzsche as a laughing philosopher: Ka

thleen
Higgins remarks, “Nietzsche’s scholarly interpreters, even if they no-
tice his frequent paeans to laughter, tend to hear more contempt that
heartiness in his sense of humor,” while Alexis Philonenko solves this
problem by categorizing Nietzsche’s laughter as sui generis.6 It is espe-
cially Nietzsche’s ability to laugh at himself that generates controversy.
According to Walter Kaufmann, who translated Nietzsche into English
and rehabilitated him after World War II, “Not Nietzsche, but most
of his interpreters, commentators, and translators, lacked the ability to
laugh at themselves.”7 To the contrary, Eric Blondel notes:
Nietzsche has no sense of humor, in the sense of showing an ability
to look at oneself critically, tongue-in-cheek, or more simply to be
able to laugh at oneself in the most serious contexts or dangerous
situations. On the one hand Nietzsche is endowed with a brilliant
sense of irony, but on the other hand as a person and in his set-
tings, he never mocks himself or laughs at his own self, never looks
at himself with this particular critical and humorous detachment
that characterized properly humor…Nietzsche only laughs at others,
never at himself.
(Blondel 1999, 171–2)
Yet Nietzsche’s laughter impacted those who knew him in his early
thirties. Malwida von Meysenburg recalls, “How cheerful he could
be, how heartily he could laugh.”8 Lawrence Hatab, one of the first
 English-speaking commentators to have recognized the significance of
laughter in Nietzsche’s thought, tells us that “Nietzsche is funny. There
are times when I laugh out loud at some of the things he says.”9 Gilles
Deleuze argues before Hatab that “those who read Nietzsche without
 laughing—without laughing often, richly, even hilariously—have, in a
sense, not read Nietzsche at all.”10


Prologue  9
Various commentators note that Nietzsche is serious about laughter:
“For Nietzsche laughter represents an attitude toward the world, toward
life, and towards oneself,” Kaufmann claims; Nietzsche’s philosophy is a
“philosophy of laughter,” for Philonenko,11 “the first and foremost rec-
ognition of the value of humour for life,” according to Greg Whitlock.12
Moreover, various scholars entrust the comic in general and laughter in
particular with significant roles in Nietzsche’s philosophy. For example,
Kaufmann remarks,
The motif sounded here [laughter] is crucial for an understanding
of The Gay Science, for an appreciation of the Prelude in rhymes
and the appendix of songs, and for much of Nietzsche’s later work,
notably Zarathustra, The Case of Wagner, and Ecce Homo.
Ran Sigad maintains that “the identity of tragedy and comedy as the
true meaning of drama is the highlight of Nietzsche’s philosophy”13;
and Hatab argues that laughter and its relation to the comic and the
tragic are the most important elements in Nietzsche’s thought. Laughter,
he claims,
is even expressed as the consummate goal to which he [Nietzsche]
is calling his readers…it is a fundamental issue in his view of the
world…the intersection of the tragic and the comic not only illu-
minates the meaning of laughter in Nietzsche, but it might also
represent the single most important element in Nietzsche’s overall
thought.
(Hatab 1988, 67–8)
If we are still surprised, it is because many have read Nietzsche without
noticing laughter or comedy in his work. Indeed, Hatab argues that “the
tragic-comic relationship is clearly significant in Nietzsche’s writings,
but it seems to have been avoided or gone unnoticed in many interpreta-
tions.”14 Along the same lines, Kaufmann notes that “Nietzsche’s early
commentators missed the laughter in Nietzsche.”15 These considerations
indicate how Nietzschean laughter and the arguments the German phi-
losopher may advance in its favor are not easily recognizable.
This first point of interest in reading Nietzsche as a philosopher of
laughter is followed by another: this unobvious reading of Nietzsche has
been until recently mostly reserved to French commentators. The com-
parison of the French reception of Nietzsche’s thought with German,
English and American responses brings some disconcerting evidence.
The German reception is solemn, apart from Thomas Mann’s personal
ironic response to Nietzsche and the rather late exception of Eugen Fink,
whose approach centers on play.16 In England, Nietzsche is received with
immediate success and is appropriated by George Bernard Shaw as a


10  Prologue
comical philosopher, an interpretation that does not find its way to the
academe. Although Kaufman sometimes mentions Nietzsche’s laughter
in the United States, one has to wait until the 1980s to find manuscripts
on this topic. Prior to 1990, if laughter is mentioned at all in English-
language philosophical books and essays on Nietzsche, its significance
is eclipsed. At best, laughter is mentioned alongside dance, as one of the
attributes of the Dionysian individual.17
Looking more closely into these receptions, Mann’s ironic response
to Nietzsche contrasts with the solemnity of the German philosophers
mainly because the irony lies in the way he approaches the work rather
than in the work itself. While Mann’s life-long interest in Nietzsche cen-
ters on the notion of irony, he explicitly notes that he does not find it in
Nietzsche; it is rather a response to Nietzsche’s work, which becomes the
cornerstone of his own work. The prologue to Reflections of a Nonpo-
litical Man (1918) discloses both Mann’s understanding of and reaction
to Nietzsche:
From an intellectual-poetic point of view, there are two brotherly
possibilities produced from experiencing Nietzsche...The other is
called irony—and here I am speaking of myself. With me, the expe-
rience of the self-denial of intellect in favor of life became irony—a
moral attitude for which I know no other description and designa-
tion than precisely this one: that it is the self-denial, the self-betrayal
of the intellect in favor of life.
(Mann 1983 [1918], 13; emphasis added)
However, the “ironic mediation between life and intellect as an appro-
priate answer to Nietzsche,” as Ernst Behler puts it, is not to be found
in Mann’s 1947 speech, “Nietzsche’s Philosophy in the Light of Recent
History.”18 There, he considers “Zarathustra with laughter’s crown…
bordering on the verge of the ludicrous.” Nietzsche’s style has “grad-
ually degenerated…into unhealthy sophisticated and feverishly gay
super- journalism, which in the end he adorned with the cap and bells
of a comic jester.”19 Irony is not in Nietzsche, but in “the spirit of man,
humanity itself assuming the form of criticism, irony and freedom, al-
lied with the judging world,” because contrary to Nietzsche’s view, life
can be judged. In the human being, “nature and life go somehow be-
yond themselves”; thus, “they lose their innocence” and acquire mind
as “life’s self- criticism.”20 Nietzsche was driven “to the snow-covered
peaks of grotesque error,” and will remain there as “a frail and honor-
able tragic figure.”21
We cannot consider Mann’s ironic response as representative of the
German reception of Nietzsche. Indeed, Nietzsche is first received in
Germany as a “poet philosopher” and as a philosopher of life by sociol-
ogists such as Georg Simmel and by philosophers such as Max Scheler,


Prologue  11
Raoul Richter, Hans Vahinger and Ludwig Klages.22 Laughter or the
comical is not a central issue in their monographs. While Karl Jaspers
and Martin Heidegger’s interpretations free Nietzsche from such clas-
sification, they remain utterly serious and humorless. As noted above,
a late yet significant exception is the contribution Fink makes to the
understanding of Nietzsche through the notion of play.23
Nietzsche’s appearance in England around 1900 has been charac-
terized as one of the greatest popular successes a modern philosopher
has ever enjoyed.24 This success is based on the challenge to Victo-
rian morals that his critique of Christianity and bourgeois morality
represents and the help he provides to those seeking to subvert this
system. The terrain for Nietzsche is well-prepared by Georges Elliot’s
human-centered morality, Walter Pater’s religion of art and Oscar
 Wilde’s project of perfection through art. In spite of his attacks on
democracy and the social movement of his time, Nietzsche finds easy
access to Fabian society, a socialist organization of intellectuals pro-
claiming the emancipation of the working class and the liberation of
women.
The most prominent member of Fabianism is Shaw, who develops
Fabian Nietzscheanism and integrates this type of Nietzscheanism in
his own “Shavian” style of life. This is a highly complex, original and
also ironic form of Nietzscheanism, which, as Behler notes, “leaves us
completely uncertain as to whether Shaw wanted to develop Nietzsche’s
thoughts or use Nietzsche to allow his own thoughts to profit from the
wave of Nietzscheanism in England.”25 The central motto of this recep-
tion of Nietzsche by a socialist consists in the word Übermensh, which
is also part of the title of Shaw’s philosophical comedy, Man and Super-
man (1903). Shaw is concerned with breeding political capacity and his
new Don Juan is a political pamphleteer inspired by the politics of the
sex question. Thus, Man and Superman looks like a highly ironic dra-
matization of a Nietzschean theme very much in vogue at the turn of the
century. None of this finds its way to the British academe.
Kaufmann translates Nietzsche’s writings into English and does much
to rehabilitate Nietzsche after World War II in America. His emphasis on
Nietzsche’s laughter varies. In the introduction to Existentialism from
Dostoevsky to Sartre, he notes “Nietzsche’s wit, his praise of laugh-
ter” in order to contrast him with German existentialists. He argues
that French existentialism is in many ways much closer to Nietzsche.
Nietzsche emphasizes “a ‘Dionysian’ joy and exultation that says Yes
to life not in a mood of dogged resolution, which is prominent in later
German existentialism, but with love and laughter.”26 In Kaufmann’s
Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist (1956), the emphasis is
not on laughter, possibly because this study’s purpose is to defend Ni-
etzsche against fascism and to establish his significance as a philosopher.
However, in the notes to the translation of Nietzsche’s Gay Science,


12  Prologue
Kaufmann contrasts the latter’s capacity for self-laughter with its ab-
sence “in most of his interpreters, commentators, and translators.”27
Although France received Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter from
the beginning of the twentieth century onward, as we will shortly see,
only recently has the English-speaking world expressed interest in this
central aspect of Nietzsche’s thought.28 Today, to use Alan Schrift’s apt
phrase, the “industry of Nietzsche’s scholarship” produces many articles
and entire books on this topic,29 while recent studies of humor written
by philosophers and non-philosophers alike almost invariably ignore
Nietzsche.30
While these considerations may indicate the initial attention the
French reception of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter, parody, com-
edy and play should draw, its significance lies elsewhere. Various factors
contribute to make it important, such as the pervasiveness of this inter-
pretation in France, its influence on further interpretations of Nietzsche
worldwide, its impact on French original philosophies and the manner in
which the notions of laughter, parody, comedy and play eventually take
part in philosophy as “a more general phenomenon of incorporating the
tenets of the comic into contemporary philosophical thinking.”31 Let me
elaborate on these factors.
A few notable exceptions aside,32 first, the pervasiveness of the in-
terpretation of Nietzsche as a laughing philosopher in French readings
is impressive. A partial list of commentators who read Nietzsche along
these lines includes Georges Bataille, Maurice Blanchot, Pierre Klos-
sowski, Michel Foucault, Jean-François Lyotard, Deleuze, Henri Birault,
Jacques Derrida, Sarah Kofman, Bernard Pautrat, Jean-Michel Rey, Eric
Blondel and Clément Rosset. Second, such readings of Nietzsche have
influenced interpretations outside of France, notably in the United States.
Schrift writes in 1995: “It bears notice that, at this historical moment,
Nietzsche’s French legacy is playing itself out more than anywhere else
in the English-speaking philosophical and critical worlds.”33Although
Schrift does not address the topic of laughter in Nietzsche’s French Leg-
acy (1995), other scholars do as entire books are now dedicated to the
topic of comedy and laughter in Nietzschean thought.34 Third, such read-
ings have influenced original philosophies: French philosophers who have
devised original thought in Nietzsche’s wake have endorsed the notions
of laughter, parody and play which served them to interpret Nietzsche.35
Finally, the French interpretation of Nietzsche as a philosopher of
laughter is significant because, independently of Nietzsche, the comical
and similar notions have exerted an influence on philosophy outside of
France. Lisa Trahair rightly notes:
Comedy, the comic, the ludic, the joke, play and laughter are terms
which pervade the works of Derrida, Baudrillard, Lyotard and
Weber—they are but better-known examples of what might be


Prologue  13
considered a more general phenomenon of incorporating the tenets
of the comic into contemporary philosophical thinking.
(Trahair 2001, 156)
One can additionally list Foucault, Deleuze, Félix Guattari, Kofman, Pau-
trat, Rey and Cixous in France, and many non-French scholars such as
Richard Rorty (1989), Alexander Nehamas (1985), Bernd Magnus, Stan-
ley Stuart and Jean-Pierre Mileur (1993). In that respect, Daniel  O’Hara’s
judgment of Nietzsche in Why Nietzsche Now is worth quoting:
Friedrich Nietzsche is not a serious writer…Nietzsche can only be
seen as the prophet of our laughter…it is as the prophet of an ironic
perception of the worthlessness at the heart of culture alone that we
laugh at and with him.
(O’Hara 1985, x)
Once the interest in and significance of this reading of Nietzsche have
been clarified, it remains to be seen how we can account for it.
2 Accounting for the French Reception
How should we understand the French reception of Nietzsche as a phi-
losopher of laughter? One option is to address the issue simply, by tak-
ing seriously Nietzsche’s conviction that his natural affinity is with the
French.36 Whatever the reasons for Nietzsche’s fondness for the French,
he often comments on feeling more at home with them than with the
Germans.37 More than once, he regrets having to write in German rather
than in a more fluid, playful, musical language like French.38 Nietzsche’s
unpublished note from Fall 1887, a draft to a preface, is revealing in this
respect:
That it is written in German is, to say the least, untimely: I wish
I had written in French, so that I might not appear to be a confir-
mation of the aspirations of the German Reich…(Formerly, I wished
I had not written Zarathustra in German).
(Nietzsche, KSA, 12, 9[188])
More than once he feels his spiritual kin to reside west of the Rhine, pre-
ferring the philosophical companionship of Michel de Montaigne, Vol-
taire and François de La Rochefoucauld to that of Gottfried W.  Leibniz,
Immanuel Kant or G. W. F. Hegel.39 He claims that he has found the
most recent Frenchmen “charming company,” noting that it would be
hard to find anywhere in past history “such inquisitive and at the same
time such delicate psychologists as in contemporary Paris.” More signifi-
cantly, perhaps, he includes the French among his most “natural readers


14  Prologue
and listeners.”40 Kofman cites and discusses several letters from late
1888 in which Nietzsche expresses his desire for two of his last books
(Nietzsche contra Wagner and Ecce Homo) to be translated into and
read in French.41
There can be little doubt that in the later part of the twentieth century,
from the sixties to the nineties to be precise, Nietzsche’s texts have been
received more enthusiastically in Parisian intellectual circles than any-
where else.42 Numerous commentators on and critics of recent French
philosophy have noted this fact, and, more than any other figure, Ni-
etzsche is cited as the philosopher who anticipates and previews the phil-
osophical topics that have dominated contemporary French thought.43
These include laughter, parody and play, not necessarily because these
notions are indeed Nietzschean, but rather because the German philoso-
pher has been received in France as a philosopher of laughter.
Taking at face value Nietzsche’s presumed affinity with the French as
an explanation of this fact would mean that the French simply under-
stood Nietzsche in the way that he expected, in this case, as a philoso-
pher of laughter. Yet unless we simply assume that the French understand
him better than their peers, which makes him a philosopher of laughter,
that aspect of the French reception of Nietzsche is in need of elucidation,
given that reading Nietzsche in that way is not an obvious reading.
The issue of Nietzsche, the philosopher of laughter, can be enlight-
ened by the background to his reception in France. Up until the 1960s,
Nietzsche appeals mainly to writers and artists in France because the
academic philosophical climate is dominated by the thought of Hegel,
Edmund Husserl and Heidegger, along with the structuralist move-
ment of the 1950s. Before the 1960s, then, the French interest in Ni-
etzsche is more literary than philosophical. It arises first around the
turn of the twentieth century and finds expression in writers such as
Paul Valery and André Gide, followed in the 1930s by Bataille and
later Blanchot.
The gist of my argument is double; it aims, first, to establish the role
that Bataille played in this reading, and, second, to unravel Lev Shes-
tov’s influence on Bataille. First, then, Nietzsche becomes a major in-
fluence in French philosophy owing to the interest later philosophers
find in the thought of Bataille and Blanchot.44 Foucault, for example,
says that he “read [Nietzsche] because of Bataille, and Bataille because
of Blanchot.”45 Klossowski’s friendship and collaboration with Bataille
and ongoing work on Nietzsche bridge generations, bringing Bataille’s
emphasis on laughter, comedy, play and parody (as well as Klossowski’s
own work on parody) to later commentators such as Deleuze. Second,
and this point is worth emphasizing, at the origin of Bataille’s acquain-
tance with philosophy in general and with Nietzsche in particular lies the
interpretation of the Russian critique, historian of philosophy and exis-
tential philosopher, Shestov or Chestov (in French).46 Bataille studied


Prologue  15
with the Russian émigré and translated into French in collaboration with
Shestov’s daughter the latter’s work on Tolstoy and Nietzsche.47 Not-
withstanding Bataille’s own interest in laughter, which antedated their
encounter, Shestov introduces Bataille to many of the notions the latter
would later endorse,48 including the main features of Nietzsche’s philos-
ophy that Bataille would extol, among them the centrality of laughter
(and tears and maledictions) in Nietzsche and in life.49 Allow me to
elaborate on these claims.
The first academics to interpret Nietzsche in France are not philoso-
phers but German Studies scholars. Unauthorized or unable to cope with
substantial philosophical issues such as metaphysics and epistemology,
they make a virtue out of necessity and read Nietzsche as a philosopher
of life, joy and laughter. They also emphasize his mysticism, his pro-
phetic philosophy and redemptive intent which significantly i nfluence
the readings of the subsequent generation.50 Moreover, as the German
Studies scholars who introduce Nietzsche to France have also to ca-
ter to the general public’s needs, Louis Pinto notes that they dwell on
 Nietzsche’s life no less than on his thought.51 Most importantly, they
take his folly seriously.
According to Angelika Schober, the French interpretation of Nietzsche
undergoes a major shift in the early 1960s, when the rejection of his work
as the product of an insane mind is superseded by the celebration of its
challenge to the limits of reason. Schober traces this reversal to the reval-
orization of madness by figures such as Foucault and Deleuze.52 Douglas
Smith stresses political developments which influenced the reception of
Nietzsche, such as the interaction between politics and philosophical
thought with specific reference to nationalism, fascism, colonialism and
theoretical questioning of the power of opposition.53
The first reactions to Nietzsche in France come from artists or G erman
Studies scholars who notice his laughter and appreciate his style but do
not consider him a philosopher.54 Next, the avant-garde and heterodox
existentialists Bataille and Klossowki play an important role in inter-
preting Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter and parody, and influ-
ence later generations of academic commentators.55 The significant role
of Bataille and Klossowki, called the “second moment” of the French
reception of Nietzsche, needs elaboration. However, at the origin of
Bataille’s Nietzsche lies Shestov’s existential and tragic reading of the
German philosopher.
Shestov’s reading of Nietzsche is all the more important, I argue, since
the orthodox existentialists Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Jean-Paul Sar-
tre almost entirely ignore Nietzsche. They prefer to follow other German
thinkers, such as Husserl and Heidegger,56 emulating the gravity that
characterizes these thinkers and emphasizing earnest topics such as au-
thenticity and ethical responsibility, which seem antithetical to laughter.
In contradistinction to these existentialists, the heterodox existentialist


16  Prologue
and novelist Bataille plays an unparalleled role in the introduction to
France of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter. The influences  exerted
on him, now unraveled, shed light on other forms of existentialism
which were brought to France by Eastern European (Jewish) émigrés.57
Bataille’s interpretation, with the help of Blanchot and Klossowski,58
influences subsequent generations of Nietzsche’s readers, as testified by
Foucault, Derrida, Lyotard and others.
Bataille’s passionate interest in laughter precedes his reading of
 Nietzsche (1922) and his first publication on his thought.59 His curi-
osity is prompted, as he repeatedly recounts, by discovering in Henri
Bergson’s Le Rire: Essai sur la signification du comique (1911)60 the
possibility of reflecting philosophically on painful personal experiences,
as well as by a mystical experience occasioned by laughter that changed
the course of his intellectual life.61 Thus, he asserts in “Conferences sur
le non-savoir,” that laughter is “the central given, the primary given, and
perhaps even the given behind philosophy,” and that insofar as he is do-
ing philosophical work, his philosophy is “a philosophy of laughter.”62
Bataille has been involved not only with Shestov, but also with the
Surrealists. The Surrealists associate tragedy and humor to create the
notion of “humour noir” (black humor)—the contribution of their
leader, André Breton, to the history of laughter.63 Shestov emphasizes
the tragic aspect of Nietzsche’s philosophy in L’Idée du bien chez Tolstoï
et Nietzsche, which Bataille translates; he associates laughter with tears
and maledictions, and promotes them at the expense of reason as the es-
sential part of life, which has been ignored by philosophy as it developed
in the West in the last 3,000 years.64 Klossowki notes how the Russian
writers and philosophers that Shestov recommended,65 and especially
Shestov himself, heavily influenced Bataille.
Bataille advances the view that laughter is tragic because in laughing
what is at stake is our unnamable death and its most “interior” or most
intimately painful and joyous experience; thus, “the tears laugh” and
“the pain is comic.”66Although in a rough draft of La Limite de l’utile
Bataille states, “it is when anguish raises its head that laughter begins,”
he is careful to differentiate himself from Heidegger. “The notable dif-
ference” between Heidegger and himself, he says, is that he takes his
“starting-point in laughter and not, as did Heidegger…in anguish.”67
As laughter is divine, for Bataille, the comical is the sovereign operation:
allowing itself to be carried away, it tumbles along with finitude into the
impossible. To “die of laughter and laugh at dying” is the title Bataille
contemplates giving to his Théorie de la religion. At the end of his life,
Bataille takes pride in having associated “the practice of the most tur-
bulent, most shocking, most scandalous, laughter with the deepest reli-
gious spirit.”68
Apart from laughter, the topics emphasized by Shestov and Ni-
etzsche’s first French readers loom large in Bataille’s work. These include


Prologue  17
Nietzsche’s mysticism, folly and redemptive intent. Bataille reads Ni-
etzsche as a mystic,69 indeed, as a mystic of laughter: the role of laughter
is to deliver the redemption that would replace the Christian salvation,
given that one yearns to be lost rather than saved. Bataille believes that
the fear of folly he shares with Nietzsche makes him uniquely capable
of understanding the German philosopher; indeed, he thinks that he is
Nietzsche insofar as he repeats his experience.
More than a theory, Bataille offers a practice of laughter which he
considers to be a necessary parody of Nietzsche: one can only be Ni-
etzsche; one cannot interpret him.70 This makes of parody a notion that
is central to Bataille’s thought; significantly, he begins Anus solaire with
the judgment that the world is thoroughly parodic, everything is a par-
ody not only of another, but of itself.71 Bataille’s interpretation favors
the acceptance of parody as a significant philosophical notion, which,
along with laughter, influences the majority of Nietzsche’s French com-
mentators and followers.72
The emergence of poststructuralism in the 1960s creates a great up-
surge of philosophical interest in Bataille. Gary Gutting notes:
The poststructuralists found the concrete without humanism in lit-
erature...they turned…to avant-garde writers such as Bataille and
Blanchot, who delineate the collapse of the concepts that structure
our conscious life, and as Derrida put it, make the limits of our lan-
guage tremble.
(Gutting 2001, 103)
Gutting emphasizes the influence of Bataille on Foucault through the
concept of transgression and on Derrida through the notion of economy,
yet he ignores laughter, comedy, parody or play.73
Klossowski’s work helps disseminate the Bataillean emphasis on laugh-
ter and parody. Klossowski goes to theology and back, translates into
French the work of Søren Kierkegaard and Johann Georg Hamann—
religious authors who assign to the comic a significant role on the way
to, and within, religion74—and collaborates with Bataille. Younger than
the latter, he influences the second wave of Nietzsche’s interpretations
by bridging the gap between them and Nietzsche’s avant-garde hetero-
dox existentialist readers. Klossowski participates in the conference in
Cerisy-la-Salle in 1972; Foucault considers him as a significant inspi-
ration and Deleuze and Felix Guattari acknowledge him as a life-long
reference.
The Bataillean notion of parody is incorporated in Klossowski’s work,
the importance of which cannot be overestimated within the reception of
Nietzsche in France.75 Klossowski formulates his view of eternal return
as parodic,76 after exploring parody in his literary production. He trans-
lates and prefaces Nietzsche’s The Gay Science (1956), where, through


18  Prologue
Bataille’s influence, parody plays an important role. This text is re-issued
in 1967 in the new Œuvres complètes of the German  Colli-Montinari
edition, prefaced by Deleuze and Foucault. Klossowski’s own criticism
of Nietzsche, translations of both his work and commentaries of his
thought, such as those of Karl Löwith and Jaspers, represent a sustained
engagement with Nietzsche thought which spans four decades, from the
1930s to the early 1970s.
Klossowski’s major contribution to the French literature on Nietzsche
is his interpretation of eternal return. Starting from a position close to
that of Bataille, he moves from an existential reading of eternal return
as the isolation and privileging of the moment to a deconstructive inter-
pretation that stresses the disintegration of the unique moment in the
course of repetition. Through recurrence, each moment loses its indi-
vidual identity as it simultaneously repeats a past moment and rehearses
a future one in a parodic cycle without beginning or end. Eternal re-
turn is thus conceived as an idea that abolishes both identity and origin.
For Klossowki, eternal return eventually becomes an idea whose own
 relentless coherence destroys the coherence of all that comes into contact
with it, from history to the individual. Eternal return makes everything
a parody of its previous and future self, a mere moment in a repeating
cycle. Nor does it spare itself in the process. Ultimately, eternal return
is just as much of a parody as everything else, a creative fiction which
challenges the very notion of truth. Klossowki’s radical interpretation
of Nietzsche’s work as both intensely critical and intensely self-critical
opens the way for much subsequent work, such as Deleuze’s two works
of the late 1960s, Difference and Repetition and Logic of Sense.77
Hub Zwart rightly notes that Klossowski’s view of eternal return is
not only parodic but also associated with laughter. The epochal events
of the disappearance of the gods and their joyful recurrence are accom-
panied by laughter.78 Bataille’s and Klossowski’s readings of Nietzsche
influence the University philosophers who form the second wave of in-
terest in Nietzsche—Foucault, Deleuze, Lyotard and Derrida.79 To those
thinkers, one should add Derrida’s followers, i.e., Kofman, Pautrat, Rey,
Nancy, and scholars such as Blondel, Hélène Cixous, Luce Irigaray and
Rosset.80 All incorporated laughter, the comic, parody and play in their
interpretation of Nietzsche and into their own philosophies.
Nietzsche becomes a necessary reference, almost an initiation rite,
in what has been known since as poststructuralist, or postmodern,
or simply “French philosophy.” While philosophers are granted an in-
credible freedom of interpretation because of the demand for new and
creative readings of Nietzsche, it is still a specific reading of Nietzsche
that is expected. For Nietzsche is played against Heidegger and against
(Alexandre Kojève’s and Jean Hyppolite’s) Hegel and shifted from the
mystical- religious-theological-redemptive setting into the more presti-
gious battlefield of structuralism.


Prologue  19
The mere fact that French avant-garde artists read Nietzsche in a cer-
tain way is not in itself an extraordinary event, since there are similar
readings in England and Germany, and after all, laughter, comedy and
parody are literary tropes and rhetorical devices that may appeal to art-
ists. That which is truly remarkable in the French reception of Nietzsche
is that these readings were embraced by the philosophical establishment,
which blurred in doing so the distinction between philosophy and liter-
ature.81 Gutting argues that Foucault and Derrida abandoned the tra-
ditional goals of philosophy such as the search for truth, meaning and
knowledge, and looked instead for alternative modes of thinking and
writing in the literary work of Bataille and Blanchot.82 Thus, the ac-
count of Nietzsche’s reception and influence in France as a philosopher
of laughter, parody, play and comedy cannot be dissociated from a study
of the relationship of the university to the avant-garde and philosophy to
literature, but also of philosophy and literature to politics.83
Nietzsche becomes especially influential in French philosophical cir-
cles during the 1960s–1980s. His declaration that “God is dead,” his
perspectivism and his emphasis on power as the real motive of and ex-
planation for actions reveal novel ways to challenge established author-
ity and launch effective social critique. Smith explains how politics in the
1960s, having to deal with colonialism, nationalism, fascism and ques-
tions about oppositional power, interacts with philosophical thought.
He further argues that Nietzsche’s thought is interpreted as a “fairly
global critique of representation, both linguistic and political, on the
grounds of its disregard for difference.” Indeed, for Nietzsche, “both
linguistic and political representation involve the substitution of one for
many, the same for the different”; yet “Nietzsche’s work remains within
this order of representation even as it criticizes it.”84
Vincent Descombes argues that the 1990s wave of philosophical Ni-
etzscheanism returns to several of the projects initiated by earlier Ni-
etzscheans. At the end of the twentieth century, the use of Nietzsche’s
critique of political and religious institutions is similar to that of earlier
Nietzscheans: it serves as a militant oppositional stance to all social and
political institutions. The result is a kind of social paralysis following the
denouncement of any form of communal political action.85
Descombes makes clear what is at stake in the politics that underlie
the third Nietzschean moment in France (1960–70). Starting from the
assumption that all social relations are power relations, the argument
of the Nietzscheans involves two steps. The first is critical: by generaliz-
ing the activity of interpretation, “truth” is reconceived as the accepted
orthodoxy, which enables to cast suspicion on all “authorized” beliefs.
The second step appeals to the sovereignty of the individual as the foun-
dation of a personal morality and a line of political conduct. Far from
being a radical innovation, Descombes notes that this principle is in fact
an expression of “the most classical French individualism,” the citizen’s


20  Prologue
fight against power. While it may actually serve as a defensible moral
principle, it is meaningless as a political principle, in contradistinction to
what the Nietzscheans believe, because it can be used as the legitimating
principle of any behavior whatsoever. A politics based on a Nietzschean
moral principle of individual sovereignty needs to be complemented with
a philosophy of law or justice; however, Nietzschean philosophers have
persistently refused to devise such a philosophy.86 Pinto has similarly
suggested that “the ‘postmodern’ is nothing but a ‘leftist’ philosophy
which is freed once again from politics,”87 and further criticisms along
these lines have been voiced by Luc Ferry and Alain Renaut in Pourquoi
nous ne sommes pas nietzschéens? (Why We Are Not Nietzscheans?).88
What is the role of laughter within this politics? Laughter serves as
a tool of criticism of both linguistic and political representations. As
argued by Mikhail Bakhtin, followed by Zwart, laughter is a weapon of
political liberation.89 According to Bakhtin’s and contrary to Bergson’s
view, laughter is a phenomenon of resistance rather than adjustment.
Using parody as its basic device, gay laughter defies (“carnivalizes”)
all  instances of authoritarianism, dogmatism, seriousness and narrow-
mindedness. It defies any pretension to absolute, extra-temporal truth,
and reveals the origin and limitation of such truth:
Although true laughter is the very opposite of government and
responsibility, it certainly is public, and even political—but in a
 bottom-up sense of the term. True laughter, Bakhtin claims, con-
cerns the entire order of life, including the prevailing truth.90 True
laughter is a moral experience of intrusion which causes the compart-
mentalization of moral life—the moral aspect of liberalism which
compartmentalizes moral life into a private and a public realm, the
public realm being identified with top-down politics (with proce-
dures, fairness, individual choices), whereas moral subjectivity is
considered the outcome of private, individual choices—to collapse.
(Zwart 1996, 207)
We laugh at “yet another moral regime that questions the admissibility
of laughter; one that laughs at yet another temporary outcome of human
history that considers itself to be permanent and final, peaceable and
lasting.”91
Jacques Bouveresse argues that a good dose of irony and skepticism
toward one’s own enterprise should be implied by this analysis; however,
there is no trace of that in the most characteristic productions of one of
the most prominent representatives of postmodernism, the deconstruc-
tion school. The derision is strangely lacking a reflexive dimension. It is
true that Nietzsche himself has not entirely escaped the fatal contami-
nation of the spirit of seriousness. For most of his disciples, however, it
should not be possible to relapse into what only they believe they have
overcome. Contemporary forms of thought which claim to be directly or


Prologue  21
indirectly Nietzschean easily preach to serious people a form of ironic
jubilation which Bouveresse, among others, claims that they are inca-
pable of practicing, with a minimum of spontaneity, naturalness and
conviction.92
Notwithstanding the translation of spontaneous self-reflexive laugh-
ter into ironic aridity, the consequences of the respectability attained by
reading Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter have had far-reaching
consequences: instead of devaluating the philosopher-poet Nietzsche
as a philosopher, philosophy was re-evaluated as literature. That the
French did this is unsettling because Nietzsche’s opinion of the French
lends prima facie validity to this reading: Nietzsche was convinced that
only the French would understand him. If the Nazi-fied Nietzsche was to
transform the world, Nietzsche as the “laughing philosopher-poet” was
to change the face of philosophy more effectively than any other modern
philosopher, including any other Nietzsche.93
3 Nietzsche as a Philosopher of Laughter
Is this reading of Nietzsche accurate? The validity of this interpretation
does not matter at this point, if we are to believe Foucault:
The only valid tribute to thought such as Nietzsche’s is precisely
to use it, to deform it, to make it groan and protest. And if the
commentators say that I am being unfaithful to Nietzsche, that is
absolutely of no interest.
(Foucault 1977, 33; quoted in Robinson 1999, 62)
Still, those of us who do not share Foucault’s view may be interested in
inquiring into the basis such a reading may have in Nietzsche’s work.
Although a fuller account of Nietzsche’s views of laughter and comedy
is given elsewhere,94 I wish to highlight here a number of points which
I deem essential to an understanding of those views.
Far from being merely one of the characteristics of the overman along
with dancing and singing, laughter in Nietzsche’s philosophy is an essen-
tial theme woven in his entire thought and intertwined in all his writings
from the Birth of Tragedy to Ecce Homo. Nietzsche may be most read-
ily remembered as encouraging philosophers to laugh: he devises a hit
parade of laughers who would be taken by laughter “out of the whole
truth”; however, his attitude toward laughter and his arguable capacity
for self-laughter should not to be taken lightly for the following reasons.
First, while Nietzsche is renowned as a fierce critic of religion, the terms
he uses to introduce laughter as his ideal are unmistakably religious:
What has so far been the greatest sin here on earth? Was it not the
word of him who said, “Woe unto those who laugh here” … for that
in laughter all that is evil comes together, but is pronounced holy


22  Prologue
and absolved by its own bliss … This crown of him who laughs, this
rose-wreath crown: to you, my brothers, I throw this crown. Laugh-
ter I have pronounced you holy; you higher men, learn to laugh!
(Nietzsche Z, IV, 13, 16; 18, 10; 13, 20)
When referring to laughter, Nietzsche uses terms which are loaded with
religious significance, such as “sin,” and “holy”; he points to laugh-
ter’s power to effectuate a cosmodicy and presents it as an analogue to
Christ’s crown.
Second, laughter in Nietzsche’s thought is not to be taken lightly. It
arguably serves a vital need in Nietzsche’s thought, the demand not to be
taken seriously. This paradoxical situation may have far-reaching conse-
quences for the status, nature and significance of his philosophy as well
as for evaluating the legitimacy of the political use to which it was put.
While I do not address the religious overtones of Nietzschean laughter
here,95 I elaborate on the possibility that Nietzsche asks not to be taken
seriously. I present two versions of it, one benign because it engages the
inward coherence of Nietzsche’s thought with no further  consequences,
and mainly addresses his epistemology; the other more consequential
because it involves the political use to which  Nietzsche’s philosophy was
subjected, and inquires whether Nietzschean laughter can shed some
light on disqualifying this politics as a genuine reading of Nietzsche.
A benign interpretation of the use of laughter in Nietzsche’s thought
may be formulated as follows: Nietzsche advances laughter as a strategy
to dismantle his thought in order to avoid irremediable contradictions
that make it incoherent. This reading entrusts laughter with an essen-
tial (epistemological) role within a philosophy which would otherwise
collapse as incoherent. Its critical and positive phases have little in com-
mon, the ideas expressed within the positive phase do not cohere and
the ideal of truth, Nietzsche’s main incentive, does not square well with
his perspectivism, which threatens to annul the whole enterprise and to
render its vehemence not only redundant but also ridiculous. According
to this reading, Nietzsche uses laughter to destroy not only the values of
 Western civilization but also of his own work.96
A more ambitious role can be given to Nietzschean laughter if it is
read through political lenses. While the very existence of Nietzschean
politics has been disputed, Nietzsche famously said that a profound
thinker prefers not to be understood.97 Yet in the 1930s aspects of Ni-
etzsche’s thought were espoused by the Nazis and the Italian Fascists,
partly due to the encouragement of Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche through
her associations with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. It was possi-
ble for the Nazi interpreters to assemble, quite selectively, various pas-
sages from Nietzsche’s writings whose juxtaposition appears to justify
war, aggression and domination for the sake of nationalistic and racial
self-glorification.


Prologue  23
If Kaufmann is correct in assessing that “not Nietzsche, but most of his
interpreters, commentators, and translators, lacked the ability to laugh
at themselves,”98 we can see in the political tribulations of Nietzsche’s
interpretations the dangers of earnestness. As recalled in Aristotle’s
Rhetoric, the sophist Gorgias maintained that “it was necessary to spoil
the seriousness of opponents by jest and their jest by seriousness.”99
It was Bataille’s strategy in defending Nietzsche after World War II to
argue that Nietzsche’s laughter indicates that he is not to be taken seri-
ously, his thought being no project but play, which collapses in contradic-
tions if we attempt to account for it in any other way. Other scholars put
Nietzschean laughter to various uses. While acknowledging Bataille’s
role in legitimizing Nietzsche, Deleuze is freed from this concern but
takes on another project, to legitimize Nietzsche as a philosopher; he
enlists Nietzschean laughter in a supposed discussion of Nietzsche with
Hegel and Kant, and presents it as a new way of thinking. Rosset deems
his predecessors “Hegelian philosophers” whose anti-Hegelian uses of
Nietzsche he denounces; he describes himself as the sole follower of the
latter’s tragic philosophy. The aesthetics such a philosophy brings about
includes a notion of tragic laughter, which describes laughter as delight
in shipwreck or engulfment.
Nietzsche has not theorized laughter clearly enough to enable to judge
the faithfulness of these uses of laughter. Nor does this matter, as the
respective views of laughter advanced by these thinkers are to be used
in original theories of the good life. To help them formulate their views
in adequation to further forms of laughter, such as humor and irony,
the three thinkers this study comprises, Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset
turn to French philosophers, such as Bergson and his student, Vladimir
Jankélévitch. Not only do they all chose humor over irony—terms that
are almost alien to Nietzsche, as he scarcely uses “humor” and explicitly
dismisses “irony”—but they all ascribe an epistemological role, some of
them, also an ontological role, to laughter, and by pointing to human
ridicule they recommend a “foolish” attitude as the content of the good
life. Through this, they hark back to another Frenchman,  Michel de
Montaigne, whose thought is a significant source for Nietzsche’s, and
may also be enlisted as precursors of the Homo risibilis (ridiculous hu-
man being) thesis, which I advocate.100
It is noteworthy that Nietzsche prophesizes that his laughter may
have a future.101 The destructive power of laughter, which for Ni-
etzsche is tantamount to courage and closely allied to contempt, makes
it a “non-discursive dismissal,” to use Lippitt’s apt characterization.102
However, Nietzsche believes that laughter not only destroys but also
enacts. The two movements are captured in the notion of the Dionysian,
being destruction and affirmation at the same time.103 Unless laugh-
ter is the affirmation of destruction within the individual in his path
to becoming who he is—a reading that postmodernists have rejected


24  Prologue
along with the notion of autonomy—the projection of this plan unto
reality which Nietzsche consciously enacts104 leaves us with destruction
alone, as a new civilization cannot be constructed on laughter alone.
This seems to be both a summary and a critique of postmodern laughter,
a topic which I address in the Concluding Remarks of this study.
The purpose of this prologue has been to trace the French reception
of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter. This reading can be traced
to his philosophy yet it is not obvious. While everywhere artists more
than philosophers did not fail to notice laughter in Nietzsche’s work, it
is in France that this reading found its way to the academic establish-
ment due to external circumstances, mostly social and political, and to
modifications of the relationship of philosophy to literature which also
enabled the work of Eastern European émigrés to impact philosophy in
France.105 The influence that French philosophy later had on other coun-
tries eventually brought legitimacy to the topics of laughter, comedy,
play and parody in the reading of Nietzsche and in philosophy at large.
New directions of philosophical thought are now possible, both within
the analytic and continental traditions.106
I turn now to an in-depth study of the three French philosophers, who,
in Nietzsche’s wake, have given to laughter an explicit and significant
role in their respective philosophies as part of the good life they endorse:
Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset. Their thought comprises the three chapters
of this study. In the Concluding Remarks, I address additional French
philosophers, both Nietzscheans and non-Nietzscheans, whose thought
further enhanced laughter into the significant philosophical topic it is,
but who do not have an encompassing philosophy, a distinct vision of
the good life or explicit arguments in favor of laughter to grant them a
lengthier discussion.
With this third and final monograph, the study of the role of laugh-
ter and humor in modern philosophy which I have undertaken, beginning
with Montaigne and finishing with postmodernism, is brought to com-
pletion.107 It may be enhanced by acquaintance with my own view of this
issue. It may be enriched by philosophy has entertained with the comic
before the ­Renaissancein in order to enlighten the classical sources that
modern philosophers rekindle and to clarify the ongoing traditions of the
comical that philosophy has salvaged for millennia.108

With a better scholarly education than previous generations of writers,

and ambiguous position between various worlds, the world of the profes-

of the political and social contemporary questions. (Pinto 1995, 46)

 66 Bataille OC, V, 341, 365.
 67 Bataille OC, VII, 218; my translation.
 68 Interview by Madeleine Chapsal, in Richardson 1998, 220. For Bataille’s
views of laughter, see Bataille (1926)1986; (1942)1973; (1943)1973;
1988a; 1988b; and 1992. See also Zwart, “Sola Experientia: Bataille,”
1996, 84–8, Borch-Jacobsen 1998; Trahair 2001; Amir 2016, and chap-
ter 1 below.
 69 Shestov is introduced as a mystic by de Gaultier’s Introduction to L’Idée
du bien chez Tolstoï et Nietzsche (1925). De Gaultier published a book
on Nietzsche, From Kant to Nietzsche (1900), and was considered “the
first great satanic philosopher (Nietzsche’s Superman is messianic), a
thinker who celebrates Evil for its dramatic and aesthetic values,” by
Benjamin Decasseres (1928), who noted: “De Gaultier says humorously
that ‘the most advanced freethinkers are almost ready to make the sign of
the cross at sight of me’” (Decasseres 1928). Because the confrontation
with truth is impossible for the human being, de Gaultier argues that
he necessitates illusion. It is this “Bovarysm” (from Gustave Flaubert’s
heroine, Emma Bovary) that creates the whole tragi-comic drama of ex-
istence. While Shestov is no stranger to this drama, his thought is darker.
The theme of folly looms large as his “philosophy of tragedy” discloses
a philosophy of despair, madness and even death (Chestov 1926, 111).
Shestov’s reading of Kierkegaard emphasizes the maddening effect of
Job’s terror, and the truth revealed to those who, tortured by anguish,
confront madness and death instead of cool and rational knowledge. He
takes issue with The Concept of Anxiety’s main thesis, however, with
Kierkegaard’s projection of anguish into the state of innocence and his
appropriation of an existentialism of anguish as the reality of liberty and
the possibility before possibility; Shestov believes that it would be better
to state that the human being in the state of innocence knows no limits in
affinity with the Kierkegaardian idea that everything is possible for God
(Chestov 1936). See also Pattison and Kirkpatrick, The Mystical Sources
of Existentialist Thought: Being, Nothingness, Love (2018), chap-
ter 3: “Mysticism in Philosophy in Early Twentieth-Century France.”
This chapter accounts for the mysticism of late nineteenth-century lit-
erature (especially in the then recently translated novels of Dostoevsky
and Tolstoy) and briefly addresses Shestov’s decisive role in shaping the
thought of Bataille.
 70 Warin 1994. This is also Shestov’s view.
 71 Bataille OC, I, 81.
 72 Mainly Klossowki 1963b, 1969; Foucault 1971; Derrida 1979.


Prologue 31
 73 For the influence of Bataille’s work on postmodern thinkers, especially on
Jean Baudrillard and Jean-François Lyotard, but also on Jacques Derrida,
see Pefanis 1991; for its influence on Foucault, who said “I read [Nietzsche]
because of Bataille, and Bataille because of Blanchot,” see Foucault, “Struc-
turalism and Post-structuralism,” interview with Gerard Raulet, in Fou-
cault (1997–99, II, 439).
 74 See Amir 2014.
 75 Douglas Smith notes, “it would, in fact, be difficult to over-estimate the
importance of the work of Pierre Klossowski within the reception of
 Nietzsche in France” (Smith 1996, 161).
 76 Published as Nietzsche et le cercle vicieux (1969).
 77 See Smith’s enlightening chronological survey of Klossowski’s views of
eternal return, from “Sur quelques thèmes fondamentaux de la ‘Gaya Sci-
enza’ de Nietzsche” (1963a [1957]) through “Nietzsche, le polythéisme et
la parodie” (1963b) and “Oubli et anamnèse dans l’expérience vécue de
l’éternel retour du même” (1967) until Nietzsche et le cercle vicieux (1969)
(Smith 1996, 150–64).
 78 Zwart 1996, 88. See Klossowski 1963b.
 79 Following in the footsteps of Nietzsche and Bataille, Foucault is a philoso-
pher of laughter, “someone who wrote in a laughing mood” (Zwart 1996,
88). Although his philosophy of laughter shares several of the features with
those of other French Nietzscheans, his philosophical laughter is of a pecu-
liar nature as it fits his remarkable views and methods. His laughter is man-
ifest in History of Madness (1961/2006), The Order of Things (1966/1973)
and his essay on Nietzsche (1971). For Foucault’s laughter, see Certeau
1994 (1986); Zwart 1996; Dreyfus and Rabinow 1982, 85–90. For Jean-
François Lyotard’s laughter, see Lyotard and Thébaut 1985, 100; Schrift
1995, 107. Gilles Deleuze writes in “Nomad Thought”:
If Nietzsche does not admit of a legitimate interpretation, there are also
completely illegitimate misinterpretations—all those that spring from
the spirit of seriousness, the spirit of gravity…The aphorism has yet a
third significant relation—in this case, to humor and irony. Those who
read Nietzsche without laughing—without laughing often, richly, even
hilariously—have, in a sense, not read Nietzsche at all.
(Deleuze 1977, 148)
Laughter is central in Nietzsche et la philosophy, and humor is significant in
his own philosophy, as is evidenced in Chapter 2 below. In Jacques Derrida’s
Spurs: Nietzsche’s Styles (1979) (Eperons: les styles de Nietzsche), the key
word is parody or simulacrum. Derrida himself acknowledges Nietzsche
for pointing the way to affirmation of the decentered play of writing that
disrupts the metaphysics of presence which guides the logocentric tradition.
Nietzschean affirmation is “the joyous affirmation of the play of the world
and of the innocence of becoming, the affirmation of a world of signs with-
out fault, without truth, and without origin which is offered to an active
interpretation” (Schrift 1995, 31). In Derrida’s call for play, we can hear
the echo of Zarathustra’s message to the higher men in the fourth book of
Thus Spoke Zarathustra, in which the recurring theme is the invitation to
dance and laugh (Z, IV, On the Higher Man, 20). Unraveling the texture of
philosophy and its obsession with a presence infinitely deferred, Derridean
deconstruction laughs at the old order, breaking the rules as it defines them,
marking the end of authority, history and the self. For Derrida on parody,
see Schrift 1995. See also Derrida 1982; Gall 1984. For all the thinkers
mentioned in this note, see the Concluding Remarks at the end of this study.

 81 Admittedly, the line between philosophy and literature has been crossed
before by Jean-Paul Sartre, but also by Shestov. A literary critic at the be-
ginning of his career, Shestov ended up as a historian of philosophy and an
existential philosopher. However, his lectures at the Sorbonne were about
Russian literature rather than philosophy. See note 83.
 82 Gutting 2001, 201.
 83 It is noteworthy that Shestov, whose interpretation of Nietzsche lies at the
origin of the second moment of Nietzscheanism in France through his in-
fluence on Bataille, was first a literary critic and only later a respected
philosopher, whose work has been translated in many languages. Shestov
addresses Nietzsche in both capacities, first in relation to Tolstoy and Dos-
toevsky, and later, as a historian of philosophy and an existential philoso-
pher, who is also the Honorary President of the German Nietzsche Society.
Shestov’s move from literature to philosophy is one more factor that could
explain Nietzsche’s acceptance as a philosopher in France. This is signifi-
cant insofar as Shestov influenced not only Bataille, but also Deleuze, who
mentioned him in two of his books (1968, 1969) and in his lectures. See
Deleuze’s What is Grounding? (2015) for Shestov’s influence on Bataille,
and Baugh 2015 for his influence on Deleuze.

Finding… in the given of laughter, the central given, the primary given,
and perhaps even the given behind philosophy…Insofar as I am doing
philosophical work, my philosophy is a philosophy of laughter.
(Georges Bataille, “Nonknowledge, Laughter,
and Tears,” 2001, 138)
The laughter of ecstasy doesn’t laugh.
(Georges Bataille, Guilty, 103)
Georges Bataille (1897–1962), “one of the most important authors of his
generation,” according to Michel Foucault,1 has been relatively  ignored
during his lifetime. He was scorned as an advocate of mysticism by
Jean-Paul Sartre, among others.2 The young philosophers Bataille col-
laborated with did not share his radical irrationalism;3 only the advent
of poststructuralism in the 1960s sparkled a philosophical interest in
his thought.4 Bataille enjoyed a considerable posthumous influence on
dominant French authors, such as Foucault, Philippe Sollers and Jacques
Derrida.5 His impact is felt also in the work of Jean Baudrillard and Jean-
François Lyotard as well as in the psychoanalytic theories of Jacques
Lacan.6 As Carolyn Bailey Gill noted a few years ago, Bataille is part
of “a number of French writers and thinkers whose potential influence
and importance, only detected in their own lifetime by a small circle of
readers, is now slowly being revealed to the English-speaking world.”7
Today, Bataille’s modernity is emphasized in contemporary French phi-
losophy and the interest in his thought in the English- speaking world is
steadily growing.8
­
The philosophical merits of Bataille’s thought may be disputed; how-
ever, a study of the French legacy of Friedrich Nietzsche’s philosophy
of laughter can only begin with Bataille. First, because of Bataille’s pio-
neering interpretation of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter and the
influence this interpretation had in France. Second, because Bataille’s
thought assigns to laughter a significance that is unprecedented in both
the philosophy and history of laughter: for Bataille, solving laughter’s
1
Georges Bataille—
The Laughter of Ecstasy
DOI: 10.4324/9780429506116-3


46  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
mystery would resolve everything. Third, because Bataille entrusts
laughter with a unique role as the key to the good life: laughter is the
very tool of the highest human operation, sovereignty, which consists in
simultaneously annihilating and preserving oneself; as there is nothing
beyond the sovereign self, the laughter that enacts it becomes divine;
and the experience of laughter for Bataille, the former Catholic, replaces
Christianity without residue.
Bataille’s view of laughter as an experience of the divine, which lies
at the heart of his philosophical project of suppressing oneself while
conserving oneself, accounts for the interest we may find in his thought.
However, Bataille’s significance lies in the primordial role he fulfills in
the reception of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter—an interpreta-
tion that would ultimately change the face of philosophy.9 As the two
aspects of his thought cannot be differentiated, Bataille’s relevance for a
study of laughter cannot be disputed nor should an account of his phi-
losophy ignore his view of laughter. Allow me to explain how these two
aspects of his work relate to each other.
Bataille is explicit about being a philosopher of laughter in his own
right; indeed, he claims that in as much as he is doing philosophical
work, his philosophy is a “philosophy of laughter”; laughter is the puzzle
which “at all costs” he “would solve (which, solved, would of itself solve
everything),” because it “is the central given, the first given, and perhaps
even the given behind philosophy”; and, following his extraordinary
experiences with laughter, in which “illuminated convulsively” he dis-
covered that “laughter was revelation, opened up the depth of things,”
Bataille declares laughter’s divinity while confessing to his fear of being
“LAUGHTER ITSELF!”10
Bataille is also a willful interpreter of Nietzsche, who initiated and
profoundly impacted, partly directly, partly through Pierre Klossowski,
the French reception of Nietzsche as a philosopher of laughter, par-
ody, chance and play.11 Bataille the philosopher and the interpreter
can hardly be differentiated. While Bataille’s view of the world as thor-
oughly parodic, which he introduces at the beginning of L’Anus solaire
(1927) could be influenced by Nietzsche, Bataille’s engagement with
laughter antedates his reading of Nietzsche, and most certainly his
writing on him.12 However, at least according to Bataille’s testimony,
it is erroneous to consider him a commentator of Nietzsche; he claims,
“I am the only one to present myself, not as an interpreter of Nietzsche,
but as being the same as he.” He explains the intimate bond his thought
shares with Nietzsche’s as follows: “Not that my thought is always loyal
to his: it is often removed from it, especially when I envisage the metic-
ulous developments of a theory. But this thought places itself within the
conditions where Nietzsche’s thought placed itself.”13
Bataille reads Nietzsche as a mystic, whose practice we should follow
if we wish to understand his thought. It is through Bataille’s repetition


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  47
or parody of Nietzsche that the latter was perceived as a philosopher of
