laughter. As Douglas Smith notes, moreover, “Bataille’s interpretation of
Nietzsche may seem willful sometimes, as he assimilates Nietzsche to his
own preoccupations…but he thereby illuminates aspects of Nietzsche’s
thought obscured or neglected by other interpretations.”14
Prior to his engagement with Nietzsche, Bataille had remarkable ex-
periences with laughter, some of them when very young. They are sig-
nificant insofar as Bataille makes these experiences the touchstone of his
philosophy by describing it as “a philosophy founded on the experience
of laughter,” which “does not even claim to go further.” Indeed, “it is
a philosophy that doesn’t concern itself with problems other than those
that have been given to me in this precise experience” (US 138). Bataille
gives us precise accounts of these experiences:
Late in night…a space constellated with laughter opened its dark
abyss before me…I became in this “Nothingness” unknown—
suddenly…I negated these gray walls which enclosed me, I rushed
into a sort of rapture. I laughed divinely…I laughed as perhaps one
had never laughed; the extreme depth of each thing opened itself
up—laid bare, as if I were dead…I was illuminated convulsively.
(IE 34)
Reflecting on this experience, he explains:
At first I had laughed, upon emerging from a long Christian piety,
my life having dissolved, with a spring-like bad faith, in laughter.
Of this laughter, I have already described the point of ecstasy but,
from the first day onward, I no longer had any doubt: laughter was
revelation, opened up the depth of things.
This experience antedates his meeting with Henri Bergson; yet it was the
lecture of Bergson’s Laughter: An Essay on the Meaning of the Comic
([1911]1999) and a disappointing encounter with the philosopher that
prompted Bataille’s interest in laughter:
I was in London (in 1920) and I was to have dinner with Bergson…I
had this curiosity—while at the British Museum I asked for Laughter
(the shortest of his books); reading it irritated me—the theory seemed
to me to fall short (for this reason, the public figure disappointed me:
this careful little man, philosopher!) but the question—the meaning
of laughter which remained hidden—was from then on in my eyes the
key question (linked to happy, infinite laughter by which I saw right
away that I was possessed), was the puzzle which at all costs I would
solve (which, solved, would of itself solve everything).
(IE 66)


48  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille’s commitment to laughter is noticeable 20 years after the
 incident related here. In 1940, he began to write L’Expérience
intérieure (published in 1943), a text that mentions “laughter” no
less than 148 times.15 Nor is this interest a passing one, as biographer
Michel Surya notes: “The discovery of laughter is attached to his
work from beginning to end, in such an indissoluble way that it will
be only slightly abusive to see in it one of keys which opened it. This
key is laughter.”16
­
Bataille admits that his thought begins with laughter: once consid-
ered by Martin Heidegger the most important contemporary thinker in
France,17 Bataille is careful to distinguish his thought from the former’s:
“I start from laughter,” he maintains, “and not, as Heidegger does in
Was ist Metaphysic? from anguish.”18 Not only does Bataille consider
laughter “the central given, the first given, and perhaps even the given
behind philosophy,”19 he restates this claim 32 years later and openly
declares when summing up his work in “Un-Knowing: Laughter and
Tears” that in as much as he is doing philosophical work, his philosophy
is a philosophy of laughter;20 in a rare interview conducted for the Ex-
press at the end of his life, in response to Madeleine Chapsal’s question,
“What do you consider the most important thing you have discovered or
contributed as a thinker?” Bataille answers that what he is most proud of
is “having associated the practice of the most turbulent, most shocking,
most scandalous, laughter with the deepest religious spirit….”21
In addition to laughter, parody plays from the very beginning a prom-
inent role in Bataille’s writings. Not only is his repetition of Nietzsche
 parodic, everything we see is a parody of another and of itself as the
opening sentence of L’Anus solaire clearly states (I 82).22
Jean Wahl, who knew Bataille, aptly compares him with the laugh-
ing philosopher, Democritus: “Bataille cherished laughter, and insisted
on laughing as Democritus of the legend.”23 Bataille corroborates this
comparison in various interesting assertions, such as “I always with-
drew from occurrence, afraid of being what I was—LAUGHTER IT-
SELF!” and “I wouldn’t give up laughing for anything!” (G 90, 54). It
is the funniness of Bataille’s texts that is controversial. Sartre finds him
comical yet unintentionally: “There [he] is in front of us, funereal and
comic, like an inconsolable widower who abandons himself, clad all in
black, to the solitary vice in memory of the deceased”; “He tells us that
he laughs,” Sartre continues; yet “he does not make us laugh.”24 Benja-
min Noys notes that Bataille’s work can be funny, whether intentionally
or not, and appropriates for it Derrida’s judgment of Heidegger: “It’s
always horribly dangerous and wildly funny, certainly grave and a bit
comical.”25 Mikkel Borch-Jacobsen maintains that what makes us laugh
is our slipping up on “all the banana peel-like passages of Bataille.”26
And Michael Richardson finds a more complex mechanism than laugh-
ter in Bataille’s texts, in that Bataille is “something like a ‘trickster,’ who


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  49
reveals the truth by embracing the path of falsehood.”27 Thus, Anca
Parvulescu rightly notes:
Most readings of Bataille, as well as second-order commentaries, do
not quite know what to make of laughter in this context. Laughter
is thought to be one of Bataille’s idiosyncrasies, an oddity that can
be safely put aside.
(Parvulescu 2010, 91)
This may be the reason why Bataille’s own laughter has been an ob-
ject of recurrent commentary by his contemporaries,28 and the topic of
a public discussion involving an assembly of philosophers and leading
French intellectuals, such as Jean Hippolyte and Sartre. Sartre had just
accused Bataille in “Un nouveau mystique” (1943) of having a “yellow
laughter,” “bitter and studied,” a laughter that is “the negative, in the
Hegelian sense.”29 Sylvère Lotringer relates: “Everyone, including Sar-
tre, noticed the gloomy outlook of Bataille’s much touted—self-touted—
laughter.”30 Bataille defended himself on spot, and later, in writing,
arguing that “a hollow laughter…is the most foreign to my own,” and
“Nothing is less characteristic of me than a bitter laughter. / I laugh in-
nocently and divinely. I don’t laugh when I am depressed—and when I
do laugh, I’m having fun.”31 Nonetheless, Sartre’s assessment created a
controversy that continues to this day. Criticizing Sartre’s view, Derrida
maintains that “laughter is not the negative, because its burst does not
maintain itself, is neither linked up to itself nor summarized in a dis-
course: it laughs at the Aufhebung”32; and Derrida’s view of Bataille’s
laughter, in turn, has been criticized for serving the former’s philosoph-
ical agenda.33
Odd as it may seem, the attention Bataille’s way of laughing has at-
tracted is relevant to an understanding of his view of laughter. Indeed,
more than a philosophy or a theory of laughter, we find in Bataille “a
practice of laughter.”34 Bataille’s own skeptical remarks on the feasibil-
ity and desirability of a theory of laughter concur with this assertion.
He argues that the “contagious nature” of laughter excludes observa-
tion (E 153), and that its main asset, liberation, transcends theoretical
analysis:
Laughing at the universe liberated my life. I escape its weight by
laughing. I refuse any intellectual translation of this laughter, since
my slavery would commence from that point on.
(G 16)
Yet Bataille does offer a comprehensive account of this practice and
attempts to explain its workings also through the use of neighboring
notions, such as the ridiculous and the comical. Taking into account


50  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille’s reservations about theorizing laughter, the nature of laughter
is not the topic this chapter addresses; rather, it inquires into the role of
laughter in the Bataillean good life.
If explaining laughter in Bataille’s thought is not an easy endeavor,
attempting to understand the inner experience that Bataille proposes as
the content of the good life is even more challenging. First, because his
contemporaries were not convinced that his writings had philosophical
content: they deemed him an egomaniac (Sartre, Gabriel Marcel, Patrick
Waldberg and Bataille himself), a madman (Sartre, André Breton, Sim-
one Weil) and a mystic (Sartre again, Nicolas Calas, Roger Caillois).35
Second, because two main ways of reading Bataille compete today.
There are those who see Bataille as a critic of systems of knowledge,
whose significance as a thinker lies in his relation to the philosophical
tradition, especially to G. W. F. Hegel and to Nietzsche. These critics
are interested in the discursive and textual dilemma occasioned by his
dismantling of metaphysical concepts and especially by his critique of
the subject of knowledge. Much of this scholarship is identified with a
poststructuralist thought and has been conducted in the wake of influ-
ential essays on Bataille by French writers. This critical tradition fol-
lowed Bataille’s death and made him famous posthumously. Rooted in
an awareness of the misunderstandings that classified Bataille as a “mys-
tic” during his lifetime, this tradition has declared with urgent sympathy
the immediate relevance of Bataille’s thought to contemporary philo-
sophical issues. Simultaneously, it has attributed to his categories a rad-
ical, violently subversive opposition to the categories of “traditional”
discourse.
Andrew Hussey explains that “the generation which posthumously
made Bataille a culture hero described the inner experience Bataille
depicts in metaphorical or metonymic terms.”36 His work of the same
name, Inner Experience, was read for the most part as a textual “trans-
gression,” the term used by Bataille to describe an erotic or philosoph-
ical violation of law or limits. Bataille’s writings on inner experience
were discussed with exclusive regard to their theoretical implications for
textual criticism, while the transgressive act of inner experience, which
undermined ordered, discursive thought with the collapse of the sub-
ject, was seen as part of a textual game. The actual experiences which
lay behind the notion of inner experience, and which were described by
Bataille with reference to the theories and experiences of religious mys-
tics were, to a large extent, overlooked or disregarded.
However, following Sartre’s characterization ([1943] 1947) and
Bataille’s classification of inner experience as being “in the line of the
mystics of all times,”37 some commentators read Bataille as a mystic.
Bataille refers abundantly to Christian as well as to non-Western mysti-
cal canonical texts. He associates mysticism with laughter and clarifies
the sort of mysticism he is advancing:


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  51
Laughter, considered as I have described it, opens a sort of general
experience that, in my opinion, is comparable to what the theolo-
gians have named “mystical theology” or “negative theology.”
(IE 34)
The purpose of reading Bataille as a mystic is not to diminish his thought.
Bataille argues that a philosophical doctrine is disclosed in mysticism
and in the sacred. Thus, Laurens ten Kate notes that Bataille makes an
effort to reconcile mystical experience and philosophical truths38; along
the same lines, Peter Connor suggests reading Bataille as both philos-
opher and mystic, because his work presents precisely the challenge of
thinking in terms of the coincidence of opposites rather than in terms
of oppositions.39 To understand Bataille, the reader should respect this
ambiguity, for any attempt to read Bataille according to one side of the
equation—as a philosopher, as a mystic or as one who oscillates between
the two—misses the point.40
Yet readers who interpret Bataille as a mystic usually fail to entrust
laughter with a special role in Bataille’s thought. This is not the case
with the poststructuralist readings of Bataille, which consider laugh-
ter central to his thought. To his thought. Lisa Trahair notes how the
scholarship exemplified in the work of Nick Land (1992), Joseph Libert-
son (1982), Arcady Plotniski (1993) and Derrida (1998) has ascribed to
Bataille’s laughter the capacity of resuscitating the Kantian noumenon,
presenting a radical alterity to philosophy, and reinscribing the Hegelian
dialectic to the point where the quest for meaning is forsaken.41
As can be gathered from this variety of interpretations, laughter is
central to the poststructuralist reading of Bataille; however, the mysti-
cal reading usually ignores the significance Bataille gives to laughter at
the expense of other notions. This presents a problem for this study, as
criticisms of the poststructuralist reading of Bataille and the mysticism
of Bataille’s writings make me lean toward the second sort of reading.42
But if Bataille deems laughter “divine,” an account of his mysticism can-
not ignore the centrality of laughter in his thought. Thus, my purpose in
this study is to explain Bataille’s mysticism of laughter, his originality as
a thinker, and the bearing of his mysticism both on philosophy and on
the understanding of laughter.
In order to successfully answer the question this chapter addresses,
what is the role of laughter in the Bataillean good life? I argue that a
new reading of Bataille is needed, one that does justice both to the signif-
icance of laughter in Bataille’s thought and to his categorizing the expe-
riences he had with laughter as mystical. Aligning myself with scholars
who consider the poststructuralist reading of Bataille problematic, I read
Bataille as he describes himself, a mystic, but I read him as a mystic of
a special, original kind, a mystic of laughter who differs from the rich
tradition that associates laughter with mysticism.


52  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille differs from this tradition in that laughter is not the after-
effect of his mystical experience. After his remarkable and repeated ex-
periences with laughter, Bataille uses laughter as the means for mystical
experience. However, as a mystical experience for Bataille is nothing
but the experience of one’s limits or a totally negative experience, there
is nothing to communicate with beyond the mystical experience; this
makes of laughter itself the sole content of the mystical experience.
Therein lies, I suggest, Bataille’s uniqueness both as laughter theorist
and mystic.
Bataille’s interest in mysticism may have been ignited when he adhered
to Catholicism as a teenager, or later, when disenchanted with it, he
trained as a medievalist. He worked as an archivist and librarian at the
same time that he published violent pornographic novels under various
pseudonyms as well as radical philosophical essays and social schemes.
He studied from 1923 to 1925 with the Russian philosopher Léon Ches-
tov (Lev Shestov, in English), deemed a mystic by Jules de Gaultier, who
prefaced the work on Tolstoy and Nietzsche which Bataille translated
into French in collaboration with Shestov’s daughter.43 As biographer
Surya notes, Shestov’s views influenced various aspects of his thought,
and in many ways Bataille’s project fits the scheme sketched by S hestov.44
However, Bataille embraced Marxism for a while, breaking with Shes-
tov before adhering to his views.45
The same pattern recurred with the Surrealists he was initially asso-
ciated with. The notion of “black humor,” which their leader Breton
contributed to the history of laughter, is of particular interest to this
study.46 Bataille fell out with Breton; he would resume cordial relations
with the Surrealists only after World War II. Bataille believed that the
significance of the irrational forces the Surrealists were trying to unleash
transcend artistic representation. A primordial experience of violence
and transgression lies at the root of society and of all that is human.
Smothered by the bourgeois society’s rationality, this experience is a
contact with the sacred.47
Bataille’s novels evoke and analyze this experience. He explores it
also through anthropological studies of primitive society together with
Roger Caillois, a classicist with strong interests in anthropology, and
with Michel Leiris, a Surrealist writer who has conducted ethnographic
work in Africa. Together, they ran the extremely influential Collège de
Sociologie (1937–39), where several renegade Surrealists studied expe-
riences of the sacred. Fascinated by human sacrifice, Bataille founded
at the same time a secret society, Acéphale (headless), the symbol of
which was a decapitated man, which attempted to stimulate ecstatic
experiences of the sacred by reviving ancient violent rituals. As legend
goes, all members agreed to be the sacrificial victim, but none agreed
to be the executioner. Although an indemnity was offered, none was
found and Acéphale was dispersed shortly before the war. The group


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  53
also published a review of the same name, which was concerned with
Nietzsche’s philosophy.
When studying Hegel at Alexandre Kojève’s seminar, Bataille was
particularly interested in the role Hegel gave to violence and destruction
 (negation) in the progress of history. In general, he was interested in
the extreme or excessive forms of modern human and social experience
which could offer a way out of Hegelian dialectic and rational consump-
tion. He saw in Nietzsche’s ideas a possible means of qualifying the as-
pects of Hegel’s work that are incompatible with the revised economics
he devised in contrast to these “closed” economies. He used laughter,
transgression, eroticism, sacrifice and death as notions that challenge
these prevailing economies.
Heavily influenced by Hegel, Sigmund Freud, Karl Marx, Marcel
Mauss, Kojève and Nietzsche, whom he defended in a notable essay
against his appropriation by the Nazis, Bataille collaborated in Acéphale
with the young philosophers Klossowski, André Masson, Roger Cail-
lois, Jules Monnerot, Jean Rollin and Jean Wahl. Sharing his fascination
with violence and transgressive action, they endorsed his rejection of
bourgeois values yet eschewed his radical irrationalism.
The controversy over the import of his philosophy and Bataille’s reluc-
tance to theorize laughter complicate the task of studying Bataille’s view
of the role of laughter in the good life. The systematic account of the role
of the tragic and the comic, of ridicule and laughter within the Bataillean
good life that this study requires is further hindered by the opacity and
unsurveyability of his writings, the embrace of paradox and contradic-
tion as a principle of thought, and the unease we feel at the oddly unde-
fined self starring in his writings. Let me detail each of these difficulties.
Bataille wrote various kinds of works, which have been justly charac-
terized as “unsurveyable and nearly impenetrable.”48 He sought a phi-
losophy that appeals more to sensibility than to intelligence because the
expression of what he has to say was more important for him than its
content. He explains that his philosophy could not express itself in a
form that would not be sensible, for nothing would remain of it.49 He
did not renounce the role of a philosopher, however uneasy as he was
about being one:
I saw myself rather as a philosopher. I have always, before all else,
leant towards philosophy… I have not quite succeeded in becoming
one … Philosophers worthy of that name must be able to link up
their thought indefinitely, but I am incapable of following mine for
very long…
(Quoted in Richardson 1998, 222)
Bataille sees himself as an existentialist, yet distances himself from
“modern existentialism and the neighboring philosophies of French


54  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
existentialism.” As “professorial philosophies,” they are “philosophies
which are the creation of professional philosophers, philosophers
qualified by the exams they had passed, and often by their profes-
sion.” Skipping modern existentialism, he relates himself directly to
the forms of philosophy from which it derives, the thought of Søren
Kierkegaard and Nietzsche which were not intended to be academic
philosophies.
Second, Bataille embraces paradox and contradiction as a principle
of thought. Revealing the truth by embracing the path of falsehood,
as Richardson argues, “it is precisely the paradoxical element of the
trickster that Bataille invokes in developing his main notions.”50 Yet
Bataille is not an inconsistent thinker. He does not endorse paradox
for its own sake but because he sees it as being the condition of human
existence. For Connor, Bataille’s work presents precisely this challenge,
to think not in terms of oppositions but in terms of the coincidence of
opposites.51
Finally, perhaps the difficulty in approaching Bataille lies in the oddly
undefined self that appears in his work. Peter Bürger explains that “it
is neither the universal self of the scientist nor the fictive one of narra-
tion not the personal self of autobiography, which could vouch for the
authenticity of what is reported.”52 Sartre was right in pinpointing the
difficulty in Bataille’s writings: the crucial content of Inner Experience
is neither philosophical nor literary, but human—“carnal” is Sartre’s
chosen term, which means that the content is Bataille himself.53 We are
fascinated, repelled, held in suspense by the “man who offers himself up
[se livre] in these pages,” Sartre tells us: “It is a man who is before us, a
man alone and naked, who disarms all deductions […], an unpleasant
and ‘absorbing’ [‘prenant’] man—like Pascal.”54 Maurice Blanchot sym-
pathetically notes that Bataille’s writings make us struggle with “this
‘I’ whose search seems still to manifest its presence at the moment when
it expresses itself.”55 As Bataille’s biographer tells us, he lived his life
disguised and died without taking off his masks56; it may then seem that
“the narrative ‘I’ of his writings remains as a testimony and a testament
to the struggle of the self with its masks.”57
Laughter may help us understand this peculiar self, as Bataille confesses
to his fear of being laughter itself (G 90).58 We may argue that laughter
is not only the key to Bataille’s work, as his biographer maintains, but
also that solely through laughter can the Bataillean good life be lived.59
Bataille lived as a tragic philosopher who sought to affirm life; he closely
associated tragedy with laughter, he saw all phenomena as comical in a
derisive rather than festive way, which points to human ridiculousness
and ultimately subsumes it under seriousness. Born of anguish, laughter
is essentially communication with each other and with death. Laughter
communicates the sacrifice of the person who is being laughed at, pro-
vided that we understand that insufficiency makes us equally ridiculous.


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  55
This view of laughter enables Bataille to use self-laughter as the experi-
ence of both collapse and triumph, and to make his voluntary symbolic
self-immolation through laughter the sovereign act par excellence, the
sole content of his meditation or mystical experience which is the pinna-
cle of the good life.
In order to explain the role of laughter in the Bataillean good life,
I explore, first, Bataille’s view of the good life; second, his view of the
tragic and the comic, and the insufficiency or ridicule that ties them
both; third, his view of laughter. In the chapter’s concluding remarks,
I position Bataille in the tradition of the mysticism of laughter in order
to assess the originality of his thought.
I The Good Life
Bataille does not decline the title “philosopher.” To the extent that he
feels uneasy about being one, it seems that lack of self-confidence rather
than doubt about the value of philosophy lies at the root of Bataille’s
reluctance to proclaim himself a philosopher.
Richardson does not believe that Bataille subverts the very notion
of what a philosopher is or that his value as a thinker is external to
the history of philosophy.60 In the interview Bataille gave to journalist
Chapsal over one year before his death, he says that he has always
“before all else, leant towards philosophy.” He admits that he has not
quite succeeded in becoming a philosopher because he cannot follow
his thought for very long.61 Elsewhere, he explains that his philosophy
is necessarily expressed in a sensible way lest nothing would remain
of it.62 He confesses, “I am not a philosopher, but a saint, maybe a
madman,”63 but he is explicit about the nature of his work: in as much
as he is doing philosophical work, his philosophy is a “philosophy of
laughter.”
The main tenor of Bataille’s philosophy lies in his view of truth as vi-
olent contradiction. This essential contradiction and the various forms
that it takes are clearly expressed and repeatedly emphasized in all of
Bataille’s works, which enable a consistent exposition of his thought.
The first part of this chapter introduces Bataille’s philosophy with the
purpose of defining his view of the good life. A fundamental contro-
versy about the best way to read Bataille’s work, as textual transgres-
sion or as lived experience, is first clarified. Then, Bataille’s criticism
of both traditional philosophy and Christianity, and his relation to
Nietzsche are explained. Finally, the main notions of his philosophy
are introduced, beginning with existence, death, communication and
eroticism, followed by religion and sacrifice, non-knowledge, play and
the impossible and concluding with sovereignty and mysticism. I begin
with taking a stand in the main controversy surrounding Bataille’s
work.


56  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
A Reading Bataille: Textuality or Experience?
Two main ways of reading Bataille compete today, one that sees Bataille
as a thinker whose primary concern is the limits of language rather
than real conceptual thought, and the other that recommends a non-
academic, supra-academic or anti-academic reading of his work. Let me
elaborate on each of these readings.
Bataille’s works have taken on an almost canonical status in the
French literary avant-garde ten years after Marguerite Duras com-
plained about the critics’ silence in 1958.64 In 1963, the journal Critique
issued a special edition in homage to Bataille; around the central figure
of Sollers, writers associated with the journal Tel Quel drew together a
generation of thinkers which saw the task of the avant-garde as match-
ing theories of language and text to the practice of cultural subver-
sion.65 According to Patrick ffrench, Bataille was the “acknowledged
hero” of Tel Quel because his work “rests on the ambiguous tension
‘between’ Nietzsche and Hegel.”66 More specifically, for the theorists
of Tel Quel and associates such as Foucault and Derrida, Bataille’s
work represented a move beyond the totalizing demands of Hegelian
philosophy toward a matrix of speculative theories which “put the sub-
ject on trial.”67Above all, Hussey argues that what brought Foucault,
Derrida and the theorists of Tel Quel together was the common belief
that there was a metaphorical parallel between the breaking of sexual
taboos and the revolt against technical constraints in writing and text.
As Roland Barthes maintains in the influential essay that he wrote on
Bataille for Critique, “La Métaphore de l’œil” (1963), aesthetic trans-
gression, the breaking with the forms and rules of language, is not only
metaphorically equivalent to sexual transgression, but indeed may well
be at the foundation of eroticism.68
This reading of Bataille was fundamental in his establishment as a
thinker whose primary concern is the limits of language rather than
real conceptual thought. As ffrench explains, the most significant aspect
of the Bataillean inner experience is its textual value for both Foucault
(1963) and Sollers (1967), and his mysticism is nothing more than a pas-
sage toward a new theory of knowledge and discourse. Unlike Foucault
or Sollers’s accounts of Bataille’s mysticism, Derrida sets out to examine
how Bataille’s thinking corresponds to the conceptual language of He-
gel,69 and argues that Bataille’s “mysticism” is a metaphor which me-
diates the demands of the Hegelian system as unrestricted negativity.70
That language precedes experience in Bataille’s work was the insight
of additional theorists in the 1960s and the 1970s, who developed in
its wake theories of reading or writing. As in the critical readings de-
scribed above, the mystical aspects of Bataille’s inner experience were ei-
ther dismissed, or discarded as analogical or symbolic forms of language
and thought with no currency beyond the allegorical value of the text.71
Thus, in “Bataille, l’experience et la pratique,” originally read at the


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  57
1972 Tel Quel conference, Julia Kristeva finds in Bataille a constitution
of nonmeaning which undermines the Cartesian subject (1977). Finally,
the translation into English of Jürgen Habermas’s influential essay, “The
French Path to Postmodernity: Bataille between Eroticism and General
Economics” (1984), establishes Bataille’s status as a precursor or even a
prophet of postmodern thought.
On the basis of these readings, Hussey argues that the prevailing view
of Bataille in France and elsewhere is of a thinker whose work has a pri-
mary textual value. Few contemporary readings of Bataille have engaged
with the language or content of mysticism in his work in relation to lived
experience.72 Yet to attribute to Bataille’s categories a radical, violently
subversive opposition to the categories of a “traditional” discourse cre-
ates serious difficulties in interpretation despite being proximate to the
exuberance of Bataille’s texts.73
Opposing the reading of Bataille as a figure in the history of ideas,
some critics have recently urged a different reading, a non-academic,
 supra-academic or anti-academic reading of his work. They deem ironic
the hyper-intellectualization of the founder of a group called Acéphale.
They view Bataille’s works as representing less a discursive or textual
dilemma than a social, erotic and religious one. Land, for example, ob-
jects to the influence of Derrida as of “a philosopher who has exercised a
hegemonic power over Bataille-reception in recent years,” and expresses
concern that Bataille’s works, which call for limitless expenditure and
liberation from the constraints of instituted knowledge, have been
“snarled up in the deconstructivist pulp industry of endless commentary
of Logocentrism.”74 Richardson recommends turning Bataille’s critique
of knowledge against those “post-modern admirers,” who “advance
their deconstruction from within secure university posts,” as most of the
authors approaching Bataille from a philosophical point of view teach
or taught at the university. To see Bataille through Foucault, Derrida or
Baudrillard, Richardson argues, is “to emasculate what is original in his
work.”75 In the same vein, Noys asserts that the recent appropriations of
Bataille are “a profound failure to read Bataille.”76
Following Sartre’s depiction of Bataille as a mystic ([1943] 1947)
and Bataille’s self-description as such, various scholars read Bataille as
a mystic. Amy Hollywood suggests that commentators have too read-
ily accepted Bataille’s assertions of the difference between his own
position and the arguments of the mystics. She rightly observes that
Bataille’s Nietzsche was a profoundly mystical Nietzsche, a view with
which Connor concurs: in Georges Bataille and the Mysticism of Sin,
he argues that Bataille read Nietzsche as a mystic, in both senses of
the sentence.77 Hussey maintains that Sartre’s attack on the sham or
false aspects of Bataille’s “mysticism” represents a closer, or at least less
partial, reading of Bataille than those which established his posthu-
mous reputation. More importantly, as Bataille himself acknowledged,


58  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Sartre’s attack inquires into many of the most important issues regard-
ing the function and meaning of inner experience.78 And, his queries
operate without reference to a context framed by the authority of textual
organization or limited to the “great irregularities of language” that is
privileged by Bataille’s postmodern critics.79
Concurring with Hussey about reading Bataille as both philosopher
and mystic, Connor argues that Bataille’s work presents precisely the
challenge to think not in terms of oppositions but in terms of the coin-
cidence of opposites. To understand Bataille, he maintains, one has to
respect this ambiguity, “for any attempt to read Bataille according to
one side of the equation, as a philosopher, as a mystic, or as one who
oscillates between the two—will miss the point.”80
The first part of this chapter attempts to understand Bataille’s phi-
losophy in order to formulate his view of the good life. It begins with
Bataille’s criticism of both philosophy and Christianity and follows with
his reading of Nietzsche. It continues with elucidating the main tenets
of Bataille’s philosophy: on existence, death, communication and erot-
icism; religion and sacrifice; non-knowledge, play and the impossible;
sovereignty and mysticism.
B Philosophy, Christianity and Nietzsche
Bataille’s work aims at substituting Christianity with Nietzscheanism,
which he considers a practice embodying the highest possibility that a hu-
man being can reach. In his attempts to account for such a life, he criticizes
philosophy for its inability to encompass the highest human experiences.
That which humankind seeks, philosophy cannot provide nor conceptual-
ize. Our human nature, our justification and significance are solely defined
by the heights we seek; yet philosophy does not conceive the peak or the su-
preme moment of human experience. As “philosophy cannot escape from
the limits of philosophy,” which are the limits of language, it uses language
in such a way that silence never follows; thus, “the supreme moment is
necessarily beyond philosophical questioning.” Given that any questioning
that means anything is elaborated by philosophy, insofar as philosophy
answers its own questions the supreme moment is beyond philosophy. Be-
cause philosophy prolongs work and taboo, it sets itself against transgres-
sion, therefore, against the peak of human experience. However,
If philosophy were to shift its ground from work and taboo with
their complementary accord to take its stand upon transgression, it
would be philosophy no longer but a mockery of itself. Compared
with work transgression is a game. In the world of play philosophy
disintegrates.
(E 274)


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  59
If, to the contrary, transgression becomes the foundation-stone of phi-
losophy, as attempted by Bataille, silent contemplation would have to be
substituted for language. At the pinnacle of being, descriptive language
is meaningless in the contemplation of being,
at the decisive instant when the stirrings of transgression itself take
over from the discursive account of transgression, and one supreme
moment follows these successive apparitions. In the hushed silence
of that one moment, that moment of death, the unity of being is
revealed through the intensity of those experiences in which truth
stands clear of life and its objects.
(E 274–5)
Bataille’s attempts to use language in order to make the supreme mo-
ment accessible to the understanding lead to a paradoxical situation.
The result is a mockery of philosophy, which disintegrates in the world
of play, in the game of transgression.
Thus, philosophy’s fault lies in its being divorced from life (E 12). The
emotions of sanctity and of eroticism are no part of the philosophical ex-
perience. The true philosopher must devote his life to philosophy; how-
ever, emotions put philosophy out of joint. The philosopher’s experience
is that of a specialist, who cannot be moved by other experiences. Philos-
ophy is studied in a vacuum because it is hard to live and to philosophize
simultaneously. Not only philosophy is no longer the sum of knowledge,
but it does not even aim at being the sum of experiences, even in the
specialist’s peculiar narrow-mindedness. However, as humanity is made
of separate experiences,
What significance can the reflections of mankind upon himself and
on being in general have, if they take no account of the intense emo-
tional states? Obviously, philosophy can only be the sum of the pos-
sibles in the sense of synthesis, or nothing.
(E 253–4)
Philosophy is nothing if it is not a disciplined effort, but it fails in its
deepest purpose if it cannot provide “the sum of the possibles seen as
a synthesizing operation.” Thus, philosophy finds itself in an impasse;
without discipline, it can accomplish nothing, and yet through discipline
and effort it cannot embrace the extremes of its subject, the extremes of
the possible, as Bataille call them, the outermost reaches of human life.
Thus, “it is doomed to failure…” There is one way out of this impasse,
that philosophy would sneer at philosophy at the summit, “loosing itself
in the final vertigo,” it would deny itself (E 259). This is what Bataille
attempts to do: to bring philosophy to its limits.


60  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Christianity is no more capable of answering the human query.
Bataille exchanges its view of original sin with another sin, which Chris-
tianity cannot address. For Bataille, the condition of existence is silence;
each time we enter into discourse, by giving form to what is formless,
we violate this silence. Writing is evil, a fundamental sinful activity; the
sense of guilt from which we suffer is a fundamental anguish of being,
the outcome of this primordial sense of violation.
In contradistinction to the Christian idea of original sin, which in-
heres in individuals, this guilt cannot be assuaged or transcended as
it is present in human existence as a whole. Insofar as Christianity
embodies a will not to be guilty, it denies the fundamental impulse
of human life and social solidarity. The basis of Bataille’s critique of
Christianity is that since redemption or salvation is impossible, the
idea that this religion instills about the possibility of not being guilty
is misleading.
If we give up the lie in the Christian promise, we can still strive toward
a state of “sovereignty,” in which we participate fully in the contingency
of the moment, expecting nothing from it and accepting it uncondition-
ally. Sovereignty represents life as its most intense, realized in fugitive
moments, such as the moment of sacrifice or laughter. It is a state of
harmony that can only be experienced, but not defined. Sovereignty is
the key concept in Bataille’s work, along with guilt and laughter. Bataille
takes these notions from Nietzsche and reads his own laughter into the
German philosopher’s experience.
To be followed, Nietzsche’s teaching requires the previous assimilation
of Christianity.81 Bataille converted to the Catholicism of his youth; yet
ten years after his conversion, his behavior is dissolute; the violent loss
of faith makes the reading of Nietzsche decisive. Bataille reads Nietzsche
as a philosopher of evil: the dead God is now replaced by Zarathus-
tra, because Zarathustra is “a seducer laughing at the responsibilities
he assumes.”82 Bataille negates God; now the flesh’s desires and human
laughter are what God was, an abyss. Bataille has found a new and more
intense religion: the Nietzschean affirmation, which he believes requires
the previous assimilation of  Christianity.83 “…my interpretation of Ni-
etzsche…may be debatable,” he writes. “I speak of community in speak-
ing of Nietzsche…” (U 96). At least according to Bataille’s testimony, it
is a mistake to see him as an interpreter of Nietzsche: “I am the only one
to present myself, not as an interpreter of Nietzsche, but as being the
same as he,” he writes. However, he admits that far from being always
loyal to Nietzsche’ thought, his own thought is often removed from it,
“but this thought places itself within the conditions where Nietzsche’s
thought placed itself.”84
According to Hollywood (1996) and Connor (2000), Bataille’s Ni-
etzsche is a profoundly mystical Nietzsche.85 Bataille reads Nietzsche as


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  61
a mystic, “in both the senses suggested by the phrasing.”86 It is through
Bataille’s repetition or parody of Nietzsche that Nietzsche is perceived as
a philosopher of laughter, an interpretation that was for many years re-
served to France.87 Bataille creates a community of likes with Nietzsche:
convinced of sharing his inner experience with him, he reads him as a
mystic, with laughter, play and parody as the content of Nietzsche’s mys-
tical states. Nietzsche, the philosopher of tragic laughter, was introduced
in France in that way.
As early as 1945, Bataille clearly states his interpretation of Nietzsche
in Nietzsche: Memorandum. In the Introduction to this collection of
texts and maxims, he writes: “Essentially, Nietzsche’s thought elevates
to the crest of the waves, TO THE POINT WHERE THE MOST
TRAGIC IS RISIBLE.” He reads Nietzsche as a mystic of laughter: the
majority of Nietzsche’s quotes on laughter (and cruelty) contained in
this little book are in the fourth part, entitled mystical states (“états
mystiques”). Everywhere in Zarathustra, morality is a mystical experi-
ence where “one climbs the crests of evil and laughter, made of disarm-
ing liberties of non-sense and empty glory.” Nietzsche wants to perish;
his roads lead nowhere, hence the anguish. Instead of an itinerary, his
morality is an invitation to a divine and solitary dance. If we dance,
we might not feel so lost, but the important thing to notice is that there
is “nothing TO DO anymore, no more issue, no more goal, no more
sense!” (M 151–2, 25–6).
Bataille’s Nietzsche is read through Kojève’s understanding of the
Hegelian end of history. This reading dismisses the goal Nietzsche
emphatically gives to humanity: creating by willing the overman. In
Bataille’s hands, to be Nietzschean is to become a nihilist, with no goal
nor project, apart from the self-destruction brought by laughter and
evil. Rather than a voluntaristic will to power, moreover, Nietzsche’s
philosophy is a will to chance for Bataille. In focusing on what he sees
as Nietzsche’s refusal of limits, ethical and otherwise, Bataille suggests
that Nietzsche’s fundamental concern is with a game of chance which
alone allows the exploration of future possibility without determining
the outcome in advance:
While the Will to Chance recognizes no limits or goals, the Will to
Power necessarily implies a voluntaristic project and can only lead
to the fragmentation of l’homme entier through his subordination
to external duty of goal.
Only a “game” had the virtue of exploring the possible in great
depth, without prejudging the results, giving to the future alone, to
its open-endedness, the power which one usually gives to a preju-
dice, which is nothing more than a form of the past.
(ON xxxi, xxvi; quoted in Smith 1996, 95)


62  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Smith notes the resemblance between Henri Lefebvre’s interpretation of
Nietzsche and Bataille’s.88 Engaging with Nietzsche’s ideas offers Bataille
a means of modifying the Hegelian framework, which he finds inade-
quate to the task of comprehending the totality of human experience. In
Sur Nietzsche, he identifies the question of human  integrity—l’homme
entier (the whole person)—as Nietzsche’s chief concern. He gives a dual
definition of the whole person: first, in terms of the renunciation of
Hegelian desire to assimilate everything other to the self, a desire which
always involves a turning away from the self; and second, in terms of a
refusal to subordinate the self to external goals or ends. One can easily
see how this interpretation serves to contradict any attempt to nazify
Nietzsche and serves Bataille’s own interests in Hegel.
Bataille’s emphasis on Nietzsche’s laughter is part of a disqualification
of any reading which attempts to put Nietzsche to political ends. I be-
lieve this is the context in which we should read Bataille’s goal of “(de)
nazifying Nietzsche,” as defined by both Smith and Gilles Deleuze.89
The emphasis on goalless freedom and the exploration of contrasting
possibilities necessarily exclude a political Nietzsche:
It is atrocious to see reduced to the level of propaganda a thought
which remains comically useless and opens a voice to those he in-
spires. Nietzsche had no political attitude: he refused, when solic-
ited, to opt for any party whatsoever, irritated that he might be
regarded as Right-wing or Left-wing. He abhorred the idea that his
thought might be subordinated to something.
(ON xxii; see also xxxi–ii)
For Bataille, Nietzsche’s philosophy is less an identifiable body of ideas
than an existential project which must be re-lived or re-enacted by the
reader:
I want to be very clear on this: not a word of Nietzsche’s work can
be understood without experiencing that dazzling dissolution into
totality, without living it out. Beyond that, this philosophy is just a
maze of contradictions. Or worse, the pretext for lies of omission…
it justifies the following definition of the entire human—human ex-
istence as the life of “unmotivated” celebration, celebration in all
meaning of the world: laughter, dancing, orgy, the ejection of subor-
dination, and sacrifice that scornfully puts aside any consideration
of ends, property, and morality.
(ON xxxii)
It is unclear if Bataille projects unto Nietzsche his own philosophy or if
he reads it in Nietzsche. If the latter, it may account for the contradic-
tions that plague the German philosopher’s thought and the difficulties


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  63
encountered when attempting to make his critical and positive philoso-
phy cohere, which some commentators address by dividing Nietzsche’s
work into distinct periods.90 However, on Bataille’s reading, Nietzsche’s
laughter is explained in a way that disavows Nietzsche’s positive philos-
ophy, whose tenets Nietzsche cherished.
“For Nietzsche, essentially, life was a game,” Bataille declares in a
radio program. Nietzsche was playing with his thoughts, and, insofar
as he wanted to play, philosophy was out of his reach. The sole reason
Nietzsche was not a philosopher, a commonplace idea in Bataille’s time,
is because he preferred to write in a way that allowed him to play with
or laugh (se jouer) at what he wrote91:
For Nietzsche the world does not have a goal and, consequently,
what is still possible for us? To laugh at what there is. But not to
laugh as it is banal to laugh, perceiving a superiority we have on
what we laugh at, but laughing a laughter that is definitive. One
cannot laugh at the world as a reality in relation to which one feels
superior, rather as a reality in front of which, to the contrary, one
feels one’s smallness and, consequently laughter in Nietzschean con-
ditions is a tragic laughter. There is no possibility of laughing from
Nietzsche’s knowledge without exhausting the possibilities of laugh-
ter, that is, to laugh tragically, to laugh as if one was laughing in
front of a crucifix.92
(LS 131–2)
Nietzsche indeed yearned for a definitive laughter, the golden laughter of
the philosophers of the future.93 A fuller account of Nietzsche’s laughter
is misplaced at this point, however. His laughter is of interest here only
because Bataille believes he emulates it. I will refer again to the tragic
laughter he believes he has found in Nietzsche below, when addressing
Bataille’s thought on the tragic and the comic.
Bataille also assimilates Nietzsche to his own preoccupations of sac-
rifice, expenditure and communication, on which I will elaborate in the
rest of this part. Bataille’s interpretation of Nietzsche seems willful but it
illuminates aspects of Nietzsche’s thought that are obscured or neglected
by other interpretations. For Smith, these aspects include the Dionysian
economy of excess and tragic intensity, the anti-teleological impulse
with its accompanying valorization of chance and the arbitrary, and the
problematic nature of both linguistic and political representations. He
argues that “the relevance of the reading is confirmed by the fact that
most of the emphases are shared by Lefebvre’s interpretation, despite
otherwise very different approaches to the subject.”94
I emphasize play, (tragic) laughter and parody, and the role that Bataille
played in initiating the poststructuralist reading of Nietzsche. This read-
ing called for a new freedom involving the notions of game, chance,


64  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
parody and laughter, and authorized to ignore without explaining Ni-
etzsche’s invitation to give a goal to humanity, to create value and to will
the overman. Whatever interest the poststructuralists may have in so
doing, it is Bataille who “read” this in Nietzsche and legitimized a way
of understanding his thought that made the non-serious, the comical and
derisory the basis for understanding this hyper-tensed and over-solemn
philosopher. Now whether it is Bataille’s philosophy that the poststruc-
turalists embrace or Nietzsche’s is something that cannot be decided
here. What is clear, however, is that Bataille has shown the way to ig-
nore the claims of Nietzsche’s positive philosophy, to dismantle as a joke
Nietzsche’s call for autonomy by emptying sovereignty of moral content
and creative values, and to brush aside the Nietzschean critical project
of liberating oneself from fear and guilt. He may have read well into the
man and his limitations because he may have shared similar experiences
of impotence and yearning; he may also have read well into Nietzsche’s
view of laughter as dismantling the philosophy he seems to enact; how-
ever, Nietzsche’s writings contradict such a reading, and Nietzsche in-
sisted that he and his writings are different things.95
In the rest of the first part of this chapter, which introduces Bataille’s
view of the good life, I explain the main notions of Bataille’s philosophy.96
C Existence, Death, Communication and Eroticism
Bataille embraces the notion of base materialism, in contradistinction
to the Marxists’ historical materialism and in opposition to any form
of idealism. He emphasizes analogies between the Gnostic doctrines (a
form of knowledge of mysteries identified with spiritual truth) and the
modern views of materialism. He argues that “it is possible to identify
as a leitmotif of gnosis the conception of matter as an active principle”
(OC, I, 223).97 This principle has “its own eternal autonomous existence
as darkness (which is not simply the absence of light, but the monstrous
archontes revealed by this absence), and as evil (which would not be the
absence of good, but a creative action)” (VE 47). Within the Gnostic
dualistic and idealistic theories, which divide the world into two, a world
of darkness in which we live and a world of light to which we aspire,
Bataille recognizes a love of darkness which he deems similar to materi-
alism. The demonic entities ruling over the material world, the archon-
tes, are described by the Gnostics as obstacles on the way of knowledge
that are supposed to awaken the mind to that which emanates from
outside this world. From a psychological point of view, Bataille argues
that the Gnostic emphasis on these powers reveals an attraction to what
is base.
Bataille is interested in showing the base in life to disconcert the
orthodox Surrealists and oppose the idealism that they endorse. He
champions an anti-idealist lucidity which incessantly points to absence,


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  65
paradoxical opposition, formlessness, gods and goddesses which are “as
crude as the matter they rule, an ecstasy that whirl us toward the in-
conceivable”98 and any possible transgression that keeps our thought
awakened by offering insomnia-provoking objects based on violence, on
eroticism meddled with guilt, anguish and death. Neither God nor social
progress can solve the basic features of the world which Bataille is so
keen to describe.
While the Surrealists wish to transfigure baseness through the pro-
duction of the marvelous, for Bataille reality is ineluctably contradic-
tory and ignoble. In his attempt to show the helplessness of superior
principles, Bataille advances a headless power (Acéphale) and makes of
baseness the principle to which we owe the most indecent respect. His
novel, Madame Edwarda, where a prostitute reveals herself as God is
the apotheosis of “base materialism.”99
Not only is Bataille attracted to the sexual philosophy of the libidi-
nous Gnostic sects, the Gnostic god reveals some similarity to his own
view of what matters in the world. Hans Jonas describes this god in the
following terms:
The Gnostic god has no positive relation to this world, he is the
totally different, the other, the different, more than the nihil than
the ens… its counterpart the acosmic Self of pneuma, otherwise
unknown, reveals itself in the negative experience of otherness, of
no-identification, and of protested indefinable freedom.
(Jonas 1958, 271; quoted in Schwartz 2000)
And so the case for a Gnostic Bataille has been made by some commen-
tators.100 Others have noted that unlike the Gnostics, Bataille is no ide-
alist but endorses a materialism which is dualistic rather than monistic.
Denis Hollier describes this Bataillean worldview as a “dualism between
morality and moral rigor which lies beyond good and evil, between the
sacred (immanent) and the profane (facing a transcendence). The sacred
confuses that which the profane keeps apart…. God is the profane world
for the sacred.” There are two worlds, “the world we live in and the
world in which we die, the world where I am and the world where I am
not.” The truth of the universe is expenditure, which cannot be grasped
and which is never fully thinkable. The opposition between thought and
expenditure is radical. Expenditure is unthinkable, and while thought is
the suspension of expenditure because it is the mode of reflection where
there is no subject left to think.101
This is as far as we can go in the attempt to describe objective re-
ality. Bataille is an (heterodox) existentialist, who argues that we can
never know existence itself, because we are only a part of something
that is greater than we are. Rather than the condition of existence it-
self, it is as a lived state that existence is for Bataille of crucial concern.


66  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
But Heidegger’s view that we come from nothing and return to nothing,
which is the basis of his interrogation of the nature of being, is alien to
Bataille. Heidegger’s assumption is unwarranted because nothingness is
a human notion with no existence outside of the human realm. It does
not inhere in existence itself because existence as a whole is marked by
continuity: we are not born from nothing. Nor are we born into some-
thing, as it is only by being born that the conditions of presence are
created by which we conceive of nothingness.102 The Bataillean essential
frame of reference is existence as a whole.
Human existence is fundamentally contingent, as we emerge in “a
chance flash of lightning, self-created through a sudden overwhelm-
ing desire to exist.” This desire is immediately frustrated, however, by
“the sense of separation we feel from the world, which becomes other
to us.”103 Richardson explains that the recognition of our presence in
the world is also the recognition of our separation from its totality. We
become aware of the difference from what surrounds us in the process
of establishing a sense of identity. We are torn from the continuity of
existence by birth, which isolates us in an alien environment. We seek
both to repair the sense of loss caused by this separation and to preserve
our autonomy as independent beings:
This is the essential tragedy of human existence. We are always
striving to satisfy contradictory impulses. And it is this that gives
our being a quality of anguish we can never elude.
(Richardson 1998, 5)
Bataille argues that we should accept that we are condemned to death,
the annihilation of our being, as it is the only truth of our existence. We
can only exist within the limits that death sets, and we should accept the
fact. The attempt to not transcend or deny death involves an intolerable
resignation. However, our death is not the death of the universe, which
continues to exist. Existence continues without us when death brings life
to an end. We then enter, or re-enter, the continuity of existence which
birth has interrupted. Our existence is now “elsewhere,” in a realm that
is inconceivable to us while we are still living, or “impossible.” That
realm is impossible because it is beyond human understanding: death
terminates our human and individual existence by putting an end to our
life. It is also impossible because we are incapable of conceiving exis-
tence outside the frame of our own existential state.
To rebel against death serves no purpose, for Bataille, because death
serves life: if there were no death, there would be no life. By itself unnec-
essary, death is made necessary by the demands of life. If we were able
to live entirely in the moment, accepting whatever is given to us for what
it is and only for what it is, that is, if we could live an entirely sovereign


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  67
existence, then death would not exist. “Death is therefore in complicity
with life to form the ‘impossible’ condition of our human existence”104:
The anguish-inspiring character of death signifies the need which
man has for anguish. Without this need, death would seem easy to
him. Man, dying poorly, distances himself from nature, engenders
an illusory, human world fashioned for art: we live in the tragic
world, in the false atmosphere of which “tragedy” is the completed
form. Nothing is tragic for the animal, which doesn’t fall into the
trap of the self.
(IE 73)
By stepping on the edge of the abyss that death represents for us, we
can engage with death. Because it frames our life, engaging with it is an
essential part of our being. Even if we know nothing of death, we can
still communicate with it, as this does not fundamentally differ from
any other communication within the world. Although we know nothing
of the “Other” while living, we intuit the existence of other conscious-
nesses in the world. We can intuit “knowledge” of what is beyond life
and death in the same way: eroticism is the most powerful intimation we
have of this.
It is separation and discontinuity that determine our existence as we
live and die detached from all others. Longing to overcome the separa-
tion from the world and from everything and everyone else in it, we still
exist as independent beings, which maintain their individuality. We are
compelled both to close the separation through identification with oth-
ers by means of communication and to widen this separation through
the assertion of our identity. The whole of our life is a balancing act in
the margin formed between the urge to independence and the longing
for communication.
Our notion of self is founded on interrelationships with other people
and the natural world. As we are contextual beings, communication lies
at the heart of human existence and takes two forms: between beings
in the world and between being itself and what surpasses being. While
the former is communication within the limits of the world, especially
within the limits of society, the latter is deemed the impossible. Com-
munication always takes place indirectly, across the gap of our mutual
 insufficiency because we realize that we are both incomplete beings.
This is how violence enters communication: because it accentuates our
difference, it institutes conflict both between us and within us as in-
dividuals. As humans begin to define themselves as a species, they in-
creasingly separate themselves, while animals being entire to themselves
do not need to communicate in anything but a rudimentary way. This
introduces a relation of subordination as we turn the world and other


68  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
persons into objects. This violence against the world is at the root of
religious sensibility and is therefore fundamental to an understanding of
human beings.
Language offers us the means to imperfectly and momentarily bridge
the breach we perceive between our individual existence and that of
others. It enables us to overcome our sense of separation. By providing
us with a means for communication, language determines human cul-
ture and mediates our lives. If we were to live outside of all discursive
patterns, as we wish, we would annihilate ourselves as human beings.
Language separates us from immediacy and prepares the alienation of
ourselves from ourselves, as we understand things now only as language
represents them rather than as they are. We now tend toward abstrac-
tion and make the world into something that is separate from us. The
distinction between ourselves and the world is predicated on our ability
to speak it. This increases the potential of communication with others
yet also restricts our thought.
The need for a fundamental communication with the reader founds
the act of writing, which intimately bounds writer and reader with each
other105 and with silence. The gap between what is written and what is
read, between human existence and the cosmos, silence is for Bataille the
only alternative to pursuing the utilitarian needs of self-interest.
The most intense communication is found in sexual intercourse. It en-
ables to glimpse the possibility of momentarily recovering “the lost unity
of the universal” before collapsing back into discontinuity. While birth
made us discontinuous beings, sexual intercourse mimics universal flow,
now encountered consciously, and enables a recovery of lost continuity.
Essential to differentiation and thus to the separation of one element
from another, sexual relations are more than a means for reproduction:
they are “a primary element in the universe.”106
However, sexuality is not essential to life. It is eroticism which mat-
ters to humans, as it differs from sexuality and differentiates us from
animals. What for other animals can be described as a simple biologi-
cal necessity, which responds to mechanical need and implies no inner
necessity, human sexual relations involve the most intimate feelings. It
makes us dizzy:
It is this dizziness that leads us to question our condition and estab-
lishes the means to effectuate a direct interpersonal communication
that attempts to bridge the gulf that we perceive to exist between us
and both other people and the world.
(Richardson 1998, 21)
Bataille explains that “our sexualized being responds integrally to
our awareness of death.” Awareness of death is also awareness of our


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  69
incompleteness, of the discontinuity of our existence. As the encounter
with otherness that sexual relations enable glimpses the continuity we
have lost and the possibility of recovering its unity, eroticism is “a de-
fining feature of the human attitude” as it is “tied in with our relation
with death.”107
But eroticism is also play, indeed its highest form, which makes it
the antithesis of work and the opposite of reproduction. An example of
pure expenditure, erotic activity does not expect return and enable us to
surrender to the moment. Thus, the erotic form of love intimates death
and glimpses a “beyond life and death” state. Between “the promise of
life implicit in eroticism and the sensuous aspect of death,” there is a
connection for Bataille (E 59), which means that eroticism and sacrifice
are clearly connected:
Eroticism performs on the individual plane what sacrifice performs
in the collective sphere. In the same way that sacrifice is the attempt
at community level to engage with what exceeds us, so eroticism
effects at individual level the longing to dissolve our own separate
personalities and consecrate ourselves in the body of another, col-
lapsing our emotional self-possession into a universal flow.
(Richardson 1998, 95)
Eroticism enables separate beings to approach the sovereign state and
may help the lover to “perceive the true depths of existence and their
simplicity” (E 21).
Bataille’s necrophilia has been the object of comments by the editor
of Bataille’s works, Hollier, and his biographer, Surya.108 Bataille’s writ-
ings obsessively reiterate that the decomposed body is excremental and
that the only sufficient answer to death is laughter. Bataille’s obsession
with “the unity of death, or of the consciousness of death, and eroti-
cism,” which he also describes as the “essential and paradoxical accord”
of death and eroticism, and “the intimate accord between life and its
violent destruction,”109 is a cohesion that finds fragmentary attestation
in the writings of Sade. Indeed, Land suggests that
Bataille’s engagement with Sade is prolonged and intense, but also
sporadic… After Nietzsche, it is Sade who comes closest and like
Nietzsche, accompanies Bataille throughout the entire length of his
textual voyage, with an intellectual solidarity so great that it touches
upon a complete erasure of distinction. Sade plays an important
role in luring Bataille’s discussion of eroticism into an abyssal (non)
sense, because his writing is baked to charcoal in the sacred. No
writer fathoms more profoundly the utter inutility of the erotic im-
pulse, nor its sacrilegious and insurrectional fury.110


70  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
This makes of Bataille a philosopher of evil, according to Land. Nietzsche
has showed that the criteria of the good originate in impulses of preser-
vation of cowardly species, which include permanence and self-identity,
benevolence and transcendent individuality. For Bataille, coming after
Nietzsche, “to defy God, in a celebration of evil, is to threaten mankind
with adventures that they have determined to outlaw.”111
D Religion and Sacrifice
The heterogeneous is the name Bataille gives to all the elements that
resist assimilation to “the bourgeois form of life and to the routines of
everyday life, just as they evade the methodical grasp of the sciences.”112
This facet of Bataille’s thought has caught the interest of Habermas in
the eighth of his “Lectures on the Discourse of Modernity.” The realm
of the heterogeneous is disclosed only in explosive moments of fasci-
nated shock. It happens when the confident interaction of the subject
with himself and with the world is disrupted because the categories that
guarantee it in everyday life fall apart. From the start, Bataille uses this
notion to qualify social groups, outcasts and marginalized persons, who
lie beyond social normality’s boundaries. As Bataille ascribes to fascist
leaders a heterogeneous existence, this aesthetic notion becomes a tool
for analyzing Italian and German fascism.
The fascist state takes over affective forces whose origin lies in a realm
that is heterogeneous in relation to normal society. Standing in the tradi-
tion of Emile Durkheim school, Bataille traces the heterogeneous aspects
of social as well as psychic and mental life back to the sacral element that
Durkheim has defined in contrast to the world of the profane. According
to Durkheim, an auratic power which simultaneously entices and at-
tracts even as it terrifies and repulses characterizes sacral objects. They
release shocking effects upon stimulation and represent a level of reality
which is not only different but also higher. They are incommensurable
with things profane; they escape any homogenizing approach that likens
the strange to the familiar, or explain the unexpected use of one knows;
they cannot be reduced to other realms.
Bataille contributes the notion of unproductive expenditure to this
Durkheimian analysis: the heterogeneous is related to the profane world
as what is superfluous. It includes excrements, dreams, erotic tempta-
tions and perversions, contaminating and subversive ideas, palpable
luxury, exuberant hopes and electrifying transcendences. In contradis-
tinction, the quotidian homogenous and conformist elements result from
profane processes of production and exchange.
The splitting off of the heterogeneous is not based on the Freud-
ian model of repression. Bataille conceives it as exclusion that enables
the stabilization of boundaries. It can only be penetrated by excess,
which means through violence.113 “By definition, excess is external to


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  71
reason”114; it is violent, as violence is a contagious element associated
with the sacred. Notwithstanding the intensely anti-Christian focus of
his work, Bataille is an intensely religious writer. His religiosity begins
in rejecting all forms of transcendence and salvation. This is what alien-
ates him from Eastern mysticism, in spite of the affinity he felt with
Buddhism.115 Moreover, he cannot accept the solitary revelation that
Christian mysticism tends to assume as the social realm is important for
Bataille. And the communication enabled through expressing his inner
experiences as well as his alleged community with Nietzsche is signifi-
cant for him.116
Therefore, askesis is not the way, but excess is; and excess is associated
with transgressing or transcending the taboo, therefore, with the sacred,
as can be seen in the notion of work. People must work to enable society
to function. A means of regulating the activity within society is needed
to protect work from violence, which is a contagious element associated
with the sacred. Taboo is instituted to found the conditions of work.
The internal necessity which the taboo is sets up prohibition and with it
a desire to violate it. Bataille considers taboo to be initially consigned to
a certain limit, defined by the idea of transgression, rather than denied,
condemned or entirely forbidden.
Thus, transgression is associated with the sacred, with the moment of
rupture which brings into focus the excluded element that is forbidden
by the taboo. Transgression was an inherent part of social life in earlier
societies. It functioned as part of the regulatory function of the taboo,
in festivals, for example, when transgression was given free play. Thus,
for Bataille, “transgression does not deny the taboo but transcends and
completes it.”117 However, the interrelation between taboo and trans-
gression breaks down in more complex societies. Taboo is associated
with what is good and with the inviolable law, which prescriptively reg-
ulates behavior.
Transgression is absolutely excluded, becoming evil and cast as the do-
main of the Devil in Christian societies. It is seen as rebellion, as refusing
to accept the taboo’s authority. It ceases to regulate the taboo within so-
ciety, and becomes instead the individual’s prerogative, who in rebellion
seeks to destroy rather than to maintain the taboo.
Bataille is fascinated by religious sacrifice. He sees it as an activ-
ity which involves a willing victim that is offered up or given away
by the whole community in order to secure its own well-being. In ar-
chaic societies, sacrifice engages with the tension of human existence
as held between life and death; it mediates our position in the cosmos.
Bataille emphasizes that death is considered a privilege in the sacrifi-
cial mode. The human being who is being sacrificed is no victim at all,
“but someone who has been privileged with the possibility of a direct
encounter with the continuity of existence, which is offered up by the
community.”118


72  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille sees sacrifice as an integral part of expenditure, indeed as its
highest form because it involves a consecration of pure loss. Sacrifice
challenges death in this pure loss because it brings life and death into
harmony by giving “death the upsurge of life, life the momentousness
and the vertigo of death opening onto the unknown” (E 91). However,
if we do look at sacrifice from the point of view of the individual victim,
we miss its meaning because sacrifice is also transgressive. Bounding
the community in harmony together, it represents a collective crime that
helps regulate its internal violence by placing it in harmony with cosmic
forms, as Richardson explains.119
Writing is associated for Bataille with sacrifice. Poetry, the highest
form of writing, may be the only possibility left in the contemporary
world for an authentic experience of the Sacred. Bataille sees writing as
an evil or sinful act, as the very condition of existence is one of guilt.
Recognizing that, the genuine writer attempts to establish a sense of har-
mony between human existence and the cosmos, much like the ancient
sacrifice. However, writing is less authentic than sacrifice. The fact of
writing precludes an immediate communication with the reader. Thus,
the impulse to write may be to establish this immediacy, which is im-
peded as the writer chooses the conditions in which the reader would
encounter the text.
Finally, it is important to emphasize that inner experience is religious
experience outside of defined religion. “Experience is ecstasy, whilst
ecstasy is communication, opposing itself to the subsidence onto one-
self.”120 The religious experience that Bataille proposes is an experience
of sacrifice, mainly of oneself. Alexander Irwin notes “Bataille’s meta-
morphosis into a perverse, provocative, spiritual figure”:
“Crucifying himself in his spare time” (OC, V, 70), Bataille both
mocked the notion of redemptive sacrifice and ambiguously mimed
the self-oblation of an abandoned God, voluntarily suffering torture
and humiliation for the sins of the world.
(Irwin 2002, xviii)
An account of Bataille’s attitude toward religion and sacrifice won’t
be complete without addressing the charge of fascism voiced by Boris
Souvarine, among others, who asserted that Bataille would have been
a collaborator would he have had the courage.121 Those claims were
fiercely contested by Bataille’s friend, Blanchot,122 and shifted from the
ad hominin domain to the level of thought by Alexander Nehamas: “A
more serious objection to Bataille concerns his intellectual relationship
to fascism. Despite his personal objection to it, there are elements in his
thought that bring him philosophically close to it.”123
The Frankfurt School has persistently made a similar claim since Wal-
ter Benjamin argued, after helping organize and attending the meetings


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  73
of the Collège de Sociology, that it displayed a “prefascist aestheticism.”
Habermas addresses the Frankfurt School’s dismissive approach to
Bataille and other thinkers; he maintains that Bataille lacks a principle
to distinguish his work from the fascism he is trying to combat.124
We should recall here that Bataille opposes the Nazi and fascist appro-
priation of Nietzsche in “Nietzsche and the Fascists” (1937). He argues
that the freedom displayed in those writings enables such appropriations;
such freedom cannot be read by Nazis and fascists as it frightens them.
He further explains that any political or philosophical reading of Ni-
etzsche is a reappropriation of a thought that resists all appropriations.
It is a thought that should not be used to a means since the experience it
conveys is of an end. The eternal recurrence of the same “unmotivates
the moment and frees life of ends—thus first of all destroys it [the end]”
(ON xxxiii), thereby involving a return to life and to existence as such.
Life has free existence of its own and does not depend on ends.
While Bataille’s view of the world as thoroughly parodic in the open-
ing line of L’Anus solaire (1927) could be influenced by Nietzsche,125
the effect of this parody is to destroy all foundations in a “circular
movement” (VE 5). Bataille makes use of the eternal return’s parodic
circulation to “depose the fascist attempts to found a community with
Nietzsche.”126
E Non-knowledge, Play and the Impossible
As we confront the world, knowledge ensues, but also “non-knowledge”
or “un-knowing.” These are significant notions in Bataille’s thought.
Bataille sees knowledge as fraudulent because in the claims made for
it, a power relation is implied. As “Knowledge is power,” Bataille seeks
to disclose how knowledge ultimately becomes empty and dishonest:
“What I bring,” he writes, is “the honesty of non-knowledge, the reduc-
tion of knowledge to what it is.”127
Surya argues that non-knowledge developed out of Socratic concerns
with self-knowledge. One of Bataille’s proposals for a seminar group
was called Collège d’Etudes Socratiques.128 It was based on the Socratic
injunction “Know Thyself” and on Bataille’s principle of non-knowledge
(“le non-savoir”), which, in turn, was inspired by Socrates’s maxim, “the
only thing I know is that I know nothing.”129
The notion of non-knowledge is used against all grand theories or
impressive projects. As knowledge is ultimately an illusion, the implica-
tion is that any claim to truth is false. The idea of non-knowledge may
be seen as targeting the Hegelian absolute. This is true to the extent that
the Hegelian absolute represents the logical conclusion of any claim to
definitive knowledge. It would be more accurate to see the notion of
non-knowledge as directed against any project whatsoever. Therefore,
Bataille’s notion discloses a profound suspicion of the world’s sturdiness


74  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
and of human affairs within it. According to Bataille, we are irrevocably
incomplete beings, caught within limits whose extent we cannot even
conceive. We can never truly know anything, because we are by defini-
tion confined to our status as separate and fragmented creatures. We can
never do anything more than delude ourselves that we know something.
As Bataille notes:
If we went beyond the quest for knowledge, to knowledge, to the
result, we would need to turn away: this is not what we are seeking.
The only reply which is not ridiculous is there is God; it is the un-
thinkable, a word, a means of forgetting the eternal absence of rest,
of the satisfaction implied in the quest of that which we are.
(“Le non-savoir”; OC, XII, 187)
This does not mean that the quest for knowledge is meaningless, or that
any form of knowledge is as good as another. Far from it, the Bataillean
idea of knowledge involves a profound moral dimension. If we wished
genuinely to know, we first had to establish the frame within which our
knowledge was being formed. This means accepting knowledge’s slip-
page. If there is real knowledge, it is not something that can be quantified
in terms of project, or in an absolute sense. Real knowledge emerges only
contingently and in relation to its own activity. It can only be measured,
therefore, by the awareness of that which it does not know. A clear influ-
ence of Nietzsche’s idea of the eternal return, when understood parodi-
cally, is disclosed here, a notion with which Bataille seems to have been
