a little uneasy but which certainly informs his own thinking.
Non-knowledge requires that we interrogate knowledge, and that we
reflect on its relation to communication. It is the underside, the shadowy
side of knowledge. Non-knowledge still abides by the codes of a scien-
tific inquiry, implying no surrender to the arbitrary or celebration of
ignorance. Rather, it is complementary to knowledge, whose value it up-
holds: “The value of knowledge, it seems, depends on its ability to make
any conclusive image of the universe impossible. Knowledge destroys
fixed notions and this continuing destruction is its greatness, or more
precisely, its truth” (G 24).
Knowledge enslaves us. Because it creates a way of life wherein each
moment has meaning only in relation to another or others that will fol-
low, at the basis of knowledge lies servility. To the contrary, Bataille
years for a situation in which, “the only object of my thought is play, and
in play my thought, the work of my thought, is annihilated” (US 129).
Bataille is ambivalent toward work. He rebels against its consequences
while recognizing its necessity. Work, which singles us out as human be-
ings, also enslaves and degrades us. Instead of consecrating existence in
the present, as play does, work enslaves humankind in view of an upcom-
ing realization; it is associated with a project. As work “subordinates all


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  75
things to the fear of dying” (US 93), it comes to represent the antithesis
of human becoming. The seriousness of work is a dead end; it means
yielding to the given conditions of existence. Although work is necessary
in order to play, work is also servile. It cannot participate in a sovereign
moment, which is “the whole being, the immediate, which has no other
end than itself and cannot exceed the moment” (US 108). Only through
play, therefore, we can begin to appreciate the need of sovereignty.
Leslie Hill explains that Bataille endorses here the idiosyncratic re-
working of Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit undertaken by Kojève in
a hugely influential series of seminars at the École pratique des hautes
études de Paris between 1933 and 1939.130 Kojève’s Hegel has achieved,
not only declared, the end of history. He has made the future course of
history superfluous. Since the serious business of human time, labor and
struggle, as well as philosophy were in principle complete, the human
being has nothing to do except to play:
In fact, the end of human Time or History, i.e. the definitive anni-
hilation of Man proper or the free historical Individual, quite sim-
ply means the cessation of Action and bloody revolution. And the
disappearance of Philosophy too; with Man himself essentially no
longer changing, there is no reason to change the (true) principles at
the basis of his knowledge of the World and self. But everything else
can be maintained indefinitely: art, love, playing, etc.; in a word,
everything that makes Man happy.131
Bataille was “racked, crushed, put to death a thousand times over” by
this news.132 His fascination with Hegel has led Allan Stoekl to main-
tain that his relationship with Nietzsche is as complex as is his relation-
ship with Hegel,133 and, according to both Hollier (1995) and Derrida
(1998), Bataille is a repetition of both Hegel and Nietzsche.
Indeed, Bataille endorses this Kojèvean idea, which describes the pur-
pose of his philosophy. In André Gillois’s 1951 radio program titled,
“Who are you, Georges Bataille?” Bataille answers, “my entire philoso-
phy consists in saying that the principal goal one could have is destroy-
ing in oneself the habit of having a goal” (LS 94). He explains:
I believe that we should shun setting a goal and holding to it. Insofar
as one has a goal, a negative look on life would ensue. First, because
the goal is limited by death. Insofar as one lives in the present, one
would see things in the most favorable way as one does not have the
leastest preoccupation about the future.
(LS 95)
He further maintains that he writes only to suppress the goal, because
writing emulates best the lack of goal.134


76  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille has an enormous faith in the potential of existence: while life
and death are but moments in the rush of existence, we know, and can
know, nothing of it. Instants of rapture intimate its wealth yet it is out of
our sensibility’s reach. “This realm—this intimation—is what Bataille
called the impossible; it is something we can sense but never grasp in
its immediacy. It is nonetheless a form of communication. All commu-
nication is with the unknown.”135 We cannot experience anything that
is beyond the confines of existence, but can still intuit something about
this condition: “Being is the absence that appearances conceal” (G 84).
Thus, Gill notes that “the central concern, the desire to experience one’s
limits and the need to feel a continuity with the totality of experience, is
unchanged” in all of Bataille’s writings.136
In Inner Experience, Bataille describes the paradoxical desire of
“wanting to be everything.” This means escaping the experience of dis-
continuous ipseity (selfhood), while maintaining its limits and integrity
in order to savor the escape from discontinuity. Alterity or “being other-
wise” is desired by ipse (the self), which at the same time fears loss in this
otherness. In a posthumous Autobiographical Note, written by Bataille
in the third person likely near the end of his life, his aim is clearly stated:
Bataille aims at a sovereign existence, which will be freed from all lim-
ited searching. His ambition targets being, and being sovereignly. He
refuses the mere implementation of means, yearning beyond them to
attain the end even at the price of disrespectful disorder. While philoso-
phy is engaged in acrobatics in its attempt to attain specific goals, rather
than attempting to attain a goal, he wishes to escape from the traps that
goals represent.137
“We are, in our essence, beings who desire to leap beyond the pos-
sible, and yet we are unable to do so without ceasing to be what we
are.”138 Against the background of the impossible, we can now address
the Bataillean notion of sovereignty.
F Sovereignty
In Richardson’s account of Bataille’s thought, sovereignty is tied with
the impossible as the central themes disclosed by his exploration of
the idea of inner experience or the sovereign operation.139 Sovereignty
is ultimately the immediate and it is Bataille’s sole ethical ideal. For-
mulated in terms of “moral goal,” “the moral of the summit” or the
“hyper-moral,”140 the imperative of sovereignty gives meaning to life
through revolt and a continuous attempt to establish the frame of one’s
own life in terms that are appropriate to oneself.
Bataille never loses sight of society, which means that he is aware of
the role of socialization in forming individuals and of their existence as
necessarily social beings. Still, he sees the individual’s struggle for what


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  77
he calls “sovereignty” as the central human existential concern. The in-
dividual is inwardly driven to oppose the subordinated forms of society
which restrict his sense of becoming. Bataille heralds the desire to ac-
cede to authentic being, to the sovereignty without which an individual
and an action have no value in themselves, but are merely useful.141 He
denies the value of work ethic—especially as it took shape in modern
industrialized societies—in which he sees less an internal necessity for
the development of society than a means of controlling the individual.
For Bataille, the acts of both writing and reading are tied up with the
sovereign operation. Writing is not a profession, still less a means of
expression. Rather, writing should be a necessity, a call. “How,” he won-
ders, “can we linger over books to which their authors have manifestly
not been driven?” (BN 157).
Libertson discloses the violence that is at work in that which Bataille
calls “communication,” which is the content of sovereignty. He notes that
Bataille’s system is structured by several dual oppositions ( “continuity”
and “discontinuity,” “prohibition” and “transgression,” “knowledge”
and “non-knowledge,” along with additional ones, such “sacred/ profane,”
“poetry/prosaim,” “sovereignty/servility,” “individual/ community,” etc.)
whose configuration is as follows. Bataille introduces the terms first as
mutually exclusive and further articulates their contamination according
to a “model of compressed intimacy or contiguity whose violence will
be described as a mise en jeu [and] simultaneously a mise en question
[bringing into play].” Bataille renounces the notion of a synthesis to re-
solve the confrontation “in favor of a space of this contamination in
which two modes of being invade each other, contaminate each other,
compromise each other, while paradoxically retaining the integrity of
their opposition.”142 This process is rendered by the notion of glissement
or sliding, and it is at this point that the intimacy that Bataille attempts
to create between these oppositions is most fully disclosed.
Libertson argues that the procedure that Bataille employs to bring
into play these opposing notions is as follows: it pits a first term that des-
ignates a form of closure, that is invoked as an ineluctable fact and that
is accompanied by a negative value judgment (“separation,” “isolation”
or “discontinuity”; “homogeneity,” “the profane vision,” “knowledge”;
“prohibition”) with another. For example, “closure,” as it is applied to
the general problem of subjectivity, is designed in various ways, the most
basic and most often repeated being “communication,” which represents
a subjectivity defined as mise en jeu.
In all cases of opposition, “closure” appears as a form of integrity
whose apparent non-violence derives from evacuating some form of
violence. For example, discontinuity is in opposition to continuity’s
violence, which is seen as “a destructive economy of life and death.” Pro-
hibition opposes transgression, considered as an excess that threatens a


78  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
subject’s integrity, and homogeneity evacuates heterogeneity. No alter-
native is given to the primary term of non-violence or integrity although
it is judged negatively, and no alternative is offered for the closure which
is “discontinuity”: although contingent, Libertson argues that closure
is presented as unavoidable; survival justifies “utility”; “prohibition” is
presented as an integral function of subjectivity.
The force that opposes violence is itself a form of violence, Libertson
explains; however, it is judged positively and is accorded a primacy over
integrity or closure by Bataille. It is at bottom as escape from closure,
which presupposes the opposing term and partakes in its violence.
Bataillean “violence” lies in the contamination of the two terms. He
prioritizes it over the second term’s professed violence, such as hetero-
geneity, or continuity, or transgression. It is in this context that Bataille
uses the notion of sliding (glissement) to designate
a subjectivity that is imprisoned between two modes of being which
constitute it simultaneously; the impossible, which designates an ip-
seity whose closure is both absolute and uncertain; inachevement
and the effort d’autonomie, which also designate this problematic
closure; the mise en jeu, etc.143
The mutual conditioning of these components is emphasized as fear and
desire which simultaneously operate within prohibition and transgres-
sion, impossibility is introduced as the “condition of possibility,” and
so on.
Libertson now carefully describes what can best be deemed a phenom-
enology of anxiety:
In the absence of a possibility of resolution to this problematic clo-
sure, the generalized concept of isolation and its “other” will have
the character of an exigency and a paradox, in Bataille’s text. This
exigency will be called “la communication,” its multiple forms in-
clude a discontinuous being that must escape its limits, and which
cannot escape its limits; a subject who must deny the constraint of
the prohibition, but whose transgression cannot be other than a
maintenance of prohibition, upon the model of a mise en jeu; an
intersubjectivity that must abolish alterity, but which cannot func-
tion as other than a mutual impenetrability. The paradigm for these
and many other forms of “communication,” in Bataille’s thought,
may be perceived in a discontinuity that contains more than it can
contain.
(Libertson [1974] 1995, 212)
Libertson does not refer explicitly to anxiety’s double bind when describing
Bataille’s explanation of the violence of communication. Communication


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  79
understood in this way is also the content of sovereignty or the higher hu-
man operation. However, Barthes’s short entry in Roland Barthes by Ro-
land Barthes, entitled “Bataille, fear,” enlightens a point about Bataille’s
experience which Libertson makes about Bataille’s “text.” Barthes con-
fesses, “Bataille, after all, affects me little enough. What do I have to do
with laughter, devotion, poetry, violence? What do I have to say about ‘the
sacred,’ about the ‘impossible’?” However, he continues:
Yet no sooner I made all this (alien) [étranger] language coincide
with the disturbance in myself which I call fear than Bataille con-
quers me all over again: then everything he inscribes describes me:
it sticks [ça colle].144
Bataille describes communication as dying and coming back. In contra-
distinction to Nietzsche, who was “helped” by madness, “the neurotic
has only a single way, and MUST RISK HIMSELF” (ON viii). Bataille
transforms Nietzsche’s “project” by completely suppressing being, some-
thing that Nietzsche was not always free to do, he argues. For Bataille,
“Nietzsche’s mistake” lies “in having poorly understood the opposition
of sovereignty to power.”145
Discarding the Nietzschean will to power and eternal return, Bataille
endorses the ecstatic revelation of the impossible which ruins the sep-
aration between object and subject.146 Morality leads nowhere. Thus,
sovereignty enables consciousness to view its own extinction, to stand
momentarily away from its own impoverished being in an empty glory
and the disarming freedom of meaninglessness.
Anguish, which the accursed share represents, is similar to the revolu-
tionary unrest: it is not progressive. “Other resist their anguish,” Bataille
writes, “I accept it.”147And nothing is offered in its place, as sovereignty
is nothing. Thus, liberation requires an ethic of abjectness, which is
achieved through a self-abnegating affirmation of anguish.148 Joy before
death causes Bataille anguish, and anguish accentuates his joy:
Gay anguish, anguished gaiety causes me absolute dismemberment,
where it is my joy that finally tears me apart, and dejection would
follow joy were I not torn all the way to the end, immeasurably.149
Bataille’s notion of liberty is thus thoroughly sacrificial, a sacred cele-
bration of the tragedy of self-loss.150 His ethics of autonomy proposes a
self that dies.151
G Mysticism
The idiosyncratic teaching of Kojève, who introduced Bataille to Hegel’s
thought, also initiated him into the history of religions. Bataille was


80  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
influenced by the teachings of Mauss and Durkheim, which led him to
believe that a philosophical doctrine lies at the root of the notion of the
sacred and of mysticism.
Bataille situates his work “in the line of the mystics of all times”152
despite Derrida’s claim that Bataille is not a mystic.153 Bataille equates
inner experience with mystical experience and argues that in the
sphere of mysticism or “the theopathic state,” we reach complete
sovereignty—the summum bonum of the Bataillean good life: “The
object of contemplation becomes equal to nothing (Christians would
say equal to God) and at the same time equal to the contemplating
subject” (E 249). Thus, the sovereign operation is inner experience or
meditation154:
I had previously designated the sovereign operation by the name in-
ner experience or extreme limit of the possible. I now designate it
by the name meditation. Changing the word indicates the nuisance
of employing any word whatsoever (sovereign operation is all of the
words the most fastidious: comic operation will be less misleading);
I prefer meditation, but it has a pious connotation.155
It is worth noting that Bataille proposes the epithet “comical” as less
misleading for defining the sovereign operation. It should be called
“comic” because the comic is precisely that which maintains an ephem-
eral appearance of sense in nonsense. As I elaborate on the comic below,
I will further explain this aspect of sovereignty.
We know that Bataille reads Nietzsche as a mystic.156 He redefines the
latter’s notion of the will to power as a will to give: “He speaks tirelessly
of power while having in mind the capacity to give,” Bataille explains;
he quotes Nietzsche’s definition of mysticism as related to giving:
The definition of a mystic: someone with enough happiness of his
own, maybe too much, seeking a language for his happiness because
he wants to give away that happiness. (The Will to Power).
(ON 166)
Bataille further explains how “the object of these ‘divine states’ known
to Nietzsche is a tragic content (time), while their dynamic is to reab-
sorb a transcendent tragic element into an immanence implied by laugh-
ter” (ON 166). Bataille sees himself as repeating Nietzsche’s experience;
thus, he claims: “Inner experience responds to the necessity in which I
find myself—and human existence with me—of challenging everything
(of putting everything into question) without rest, is to be a question, to
be a supplication without response,” which according to Bataille is “the
sole truth of man.”157


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  81
Derrida is right in asserting that Bataille is not a new mystic only in
relation to the latter’s own reluctance to be associated with the religious
overtones of the term:
Can one not free [dégager] from its religious antecedents the pos-
sibility of mystical experience—a possibility which, in spite of ap-
pearances, remains open to the non-believer? Free it from the askesis
of dogma and the atmosphere of religions? Free it, in a word, from
mysticism—to the point of linking it to the nudity of ignorance?
(IE 169; OC, V, 422)
However, Bataille makes clear that inner experience is mystical expe-
rience (IE 3): “By inner experience I understand what one usually calls
mystical experience: states of ecstasy, of rapture, at least of meditated
emotion.”158 It is also a religious experience that gives all that Christi-
anity provides, once one refuses to be saved.
Although Bataille further differentiates between inner and mystical
experiences, the writings of the mystics influence his notion of ecstasy
and their vocabulary and concerns are intimately connected with his
work. Bataille admires the texts of Dionysius the Areopagite, Jacob
Boehme, Nicolas de Cusa, Meister Eckhart, St. John of the Cross, St.
Teresa of Avila, St. Catherine of Siena, Angela of Foligno and other mys-
tics, mostly Western, who belong to the Neoplatonic schools of mysti-
cism. And even as he expresses reservations about the conclusions to
which they are led, Bataille argues throughout Inner Experience that
the content of Christianity may be lost but the framework which shapes
faith and experience remains intact.
It is the relationship between philosophy and atheology that is revealed
in the movement of inner experience. The title of the unfinished project
that Bataille initiated, La Somme athéologique,159 is borrowed from
Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologiae. This indicates how Bataille, al-
though working beyond Christianity, still uses the language and thought
of the Western tradition. Inner experience plays the same role as mys-
ticism in Aquinas’s Summa: mysticism is the central contribution of a
system which affirms that experience has a higher value than knowl-
edge. The same idea is expressed by Bataille’s teacher, Shestov, whose
“Experience of Adogmatic Thinking,” the subtitle of his Apotheosis of
Groundlessness, Bataille certainly knew.160
Hussey’s study, The Inner Scar: The Mysticism of Georges Bataille
(2000), is helpful for understanding Bataille’s mysticism in relation to
Christianity. Hussey notes the criticism of this mysticism voiced by the
Catholic existentialist thinker, Gabriel Marcel.161 In “le refus du salut et
l’exaltation de l’homme absurde” (1945), Marcel evaluates L’Expérience
intérieure from a Christian perspective and compares it with the atheist


82  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
humanism of Camus’s L’Etranger. As a Christian, Marcel is unable to
accept Bataillean mysticism because it does away with mystery, whether
it is couched in theological or philosophical terms. Marcel sees L’Expéri-
ence intérieure as self-contradictory because Bataille’s radical nihilism
concedes no summit. This criticism recalls Sartre’s reproving of Bataille
as guilty of “bad faith” because he refuses to name God.
From a phenomenological point of view, Marcel is unable to concede
the facts of Bataille’s experience as anything other than pathological,
which lead to the “grandiloquent nonsense” of Bataille’s texts.162 He
objects to Bataille placing himself in the same tradition and, in Christian
terms, on the same level, as the Church’s great mystics, such as St. John
of the Cross or Angela of Foligno; he also takes issue with Bataille’s ap-
propriation of the language of mysticism toward an end which denies the
possibility of a transcendent God.
As a “sad epigone of Nietzsche,” Bataille’s mysticism is, for Marcel
as it was for Sartre, an empty parody of experience.163 Hussey notes
that “both Sartre and Marcel couch their objections to Bataille’s inner
experience with reference to Pascal.” Pascal “posits the absence of God
as both thought and experience as that which precipitates a collapse of
absolute meaning”; “man in nature” represents “a Nothing in compar-
ison with the Infinite, an All in comparison with the Nothing, a mean
between nothing and everything.”164 For Bataille, as for Pascal,
God is an impossibility whose status cannot be defined by language
and who, not only eludes definition in the positive constitution of
meaning, but also cannot be properly defined as a negative proposi-
tion; the absence of God is not, therefore, in any sense, the same as
atheism, which posits God as a negative entity.165
(Hussey 2000, 52)
Hussey explains that inner experience, as Bataille describes it, “is an
experience which eludes all categorical possibilities and is radically op-
posed to all forms of transcendence.” However, he notes that this expe-
rience does separate “the subject from the object in a movement which
is akin to the religious ecstasy fundamental to mystical experience.”
Furthermore,
although Bataille describes inner experience as a contradiction of
the traditional meaning and function of the word mysticism, he
nonetheless persists in defining inner experience with reference to
Christian mystics such as Dionysius the Areopagite, Blessed Angela
of Foligno, St. John of the Cross, and St. Teresa of Avila, or with re-
gard to esoteric religions or practices such as Hinduism, Buddhism,
Yoga or Tantrism.
(Hussey 2000, 23)


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  83
Surya recalls the Eastern influences on Bataille, noting that he was well-
read in classical Hinduism and Buddhism. In particular, in an early text
in Documents, Bataille discloses an academic expertise not only about
Eastern topics in general but also about the “cauchemar inoubliable” of
Hindu religious experience.166 We also know that he read Alexandra
David-Neel and Mircea Eliade’s accounts of mystical practices among
the Tibetans, that he was familiar with Romain Rolland’s biographies
of Ramakrishna and Vivekananda (Essai sur la mystique et l’action de
l’Inde vivante [1929; 1930]) and possessed a heavily annotated copy of
Vivekananda’s Râja-yoga ou Conquête de la nature intérieure.167
Hussey concludes that Bataille “accedes to a state of consciousness which
is properly mystical in that it exceeds all forms of discourse, although, as
Bataille insists, it belongs to no tradition nor specific mystical idiom.”168
The inherent disorder in language characterizes mystical texts of all
times. In this respect, the mystics were modern long before the Roman-
tics. An acute awareness of this disturbance is especially pronounced in
the Neoplatonic mystical tradition to which Bataille was drawn: begin-
ning with Plotinus, and continuing through Dionysius the Areopagite,
Augustine and Cusa, the “crisis of discourse” that we like to see as spe-
cifically modern is carried through the ages into the Carmelite tradition,
and beyond.
The problem Bataille saw in the mystical and the poetic approaches
was that in most cases they offer resolution and harmonizing closure
where in reality there is only nonsense and “a voyage to the end of the
possible.” At the end of the possible is the impossible, however: inner
experience is the experience of the impossible. It is not an impossible ex-
perience; on the contrary, Bataille’s point is that everyone—“the lowliest
and least cultured human beings”—has access to this experience and
this “incomparably splendid place.”169
However, one may doubt that everyone may be interested in the kind
of experiences that Bataille describes: “Imagining myself being tor-
mented, I’m in ecstasies” (G 31); or,
I’ve just looked at two photos of torture. I’d gotten used to the
pictures, though one was so awful my heart skipped a beat. …No
sooner was I seated than I fell into some kind of trance. Unlike the
other night when I doubted it painfully, this time the fact that this
kind of state is more intense than erotic pleasure was clear to me….
I must have starting crying. I lift my empty head—empty because
of love’s strength and because of my state of being in rapture. I’m
going to tell you how I arrived at an ecstasy of such intensity. On
the wall of appearance, I threw images of explosion and of being
lacerated—ripped to pieces… I evoked every possible way there was
of my being ripped to pieces.
(G 32–3)


84  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Describing Bataille’s illumination techniques from “la pratique de la joie
devant la mort” (published in June 1939 in the last issue of Acéphale)
to the 1947 Méthode de méditation, Jean Bruno skips the torture pic-
tures.170 He argues that the persistence of these violent topics in Bataille’s
writings only seemingly indicates a sickly romanticism of pain. Espe-
cially questionable is Bruno’s eclipse of the famous picture of the tortured
 Chinese young man, which was given to Bataille by his psychoanalyst.
Circled by a crowd, a lacerated young man looks as if he is smiling (as if
he is enjoying the torture) because of the opium he was given to extend
his sufferings of the lingering death, or slow slicing, also known as death
by a thousand cuts (lingchi). Bataille explains that rather than sadistic,
his enjoyment is masochistic as he identifies with the young man’s suf-
fering, which brings about his ecstatic joy. Bruno does note that the first
time that Bataille attains full ecstasy (in the summer of 1949, during a
nocturnal walk in a forest), he has invited the menacing image of a bird
of prey, whose attack opened his throat.171 Indeed, Bruno concludes that
the upsetting images are used to open a breach in the psyche.172
Bataille has explained as early as On Nietzsche that “the neurotic has
to risk himself.” That means that he should explore the possibility of
going mad in order to repeat Nietzsche’s privileged access to madness.
Bataille often told Leiris that he wanted to go mad yet feared it. Thus,
inner experience is an exploration given in action, a journey to the end
of mankind’s possibilities that is effectuated though a plunge into the
labyrinth of lived experience. This experience is founded on rejecting
the project of future fulfillment that work promises. Rather than dealing
with the future, inner experience must be located within the experience
itself. One cannot plan it or see it from the outside:
One must live experience. It is not easily accessible […] it is only
from within, lived to the point of terror, that it appears to unify that
which discursive thought must separate.
(IE 8)
In Méthode de méditation, Bataille attempts to elucidate the processes
that constitute inner experience, which do not entail a turning away
from the world but, on the contrary, an ever-deeper penetration of it.
Bataille knows that his inclination to a certain type of mysticism
is a problematic aspect of his thought. The writings of the mystics
misrepresent his position; thus, he relates with discomfort to the mys-
tical literature, referring to it yet qualifying it and retracting from
it. The message he consistently delivers is that every human being
has access to that “place of bewilderment, of non-sense,” where the
contradictions that befall rational thought are dispelled.173 He spent
a lifetime trying to find a language to communicate an experience he
could only describe with the help of a mystical lexicon and we need


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  85
to understand the ways in which this affected how he wrote and even
why he wrote at all.
Some commentators discard readings of Bataille that are solely mys-
tical.174 They downplay the religious element that Bataille endorses and
characterize the experience he is talking about as simply an experience
that in relation to reason is excessive, beyond reason’s measure, as is
laughter, for example, or tears. Rather than the extinction of philosophy,
they argue that the mysticism without mysticism that Bataille envisages
represents the liberation of thought from the tyranny of understanding.
Along the same line, some commentators reinterpret this experience in
epistemological terms and see in it an interiorization of Hegel’s master
and slave dialectics. For Jean-Louis Baudry, inner experience is a prac-
tice of limits that enables the subject to put himself in question.175 In He-
gel, Mankind and History, Bataille specifies that the opposition between
the master and the slave can be experienced by the same individual sub-
ject.176 In this way, he introduces a contradiction that is internal to the
subject, the work of desire—an interrupted dialectic through which the
displacement of mastery into sovereignty, an entirely different matter, is
brought about.177 Along the same lines, Richardson argues:
The dialectic of mastery and servitude is a central focus in the whole
of Bataille’s work. In his earlier work, he tends towards the idea that
servitude is embedded in idealist transcendent notions, and above
all in the tendency of contemporary society to deny diversity and
heterogeneous social forms in favor of an increasing homogeneity.
Without rejecting this position, his later reflection, especially as he
thought further about Hegel’s master and slave dialectic as it has
been elucidated in Kojève’s lectures, gave his ideas a new edge.
(Richardson 1998, 119)
Richardson notes that Bataille could not accept the Hegelian view that
we could liberate ourselves through work, since the condition of work
itself is fundamentally servile for Bataille. Finding it more congenial
to think in terms of liberation through laughter, Bataille is neverthe-
less drawn to examine the issue that is raised by the Hegelian dialectic
of master and slave from the point at which it connects with his own
thinking.178
Some commentators argue that Bataille’s “religious” experience is still
a philosophical experience. Hill notes that the very thought of limits
falls into a curious, self-defeating logic. They exist only by permission of
the limitlessness they serve to repress and whose existence they are con-
strained to deny. Limitlessness as such is properly unspeakable, since it
is impossible to speak of limitlessness by adopting the very limits whose
stability is threatened by the limitlessness of which it is necessary to
speak. The problem, of which Bataille was well aware, is one with which


86  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
all negative theology has to grapple. If limits are what ground the fini-
tude of being, it is clear that limitlessness or excess, to the extent that it is
the negation of limits, cannot itself be founded. Yet it is what makes lim-
its possible. To think being at all, it is therefore necessary to think that
which is beyond the boundaries of thinking.179 The struggle to think be-
yond the limits of philosophy is itself a philosophical enterprise. This is
why the aporia cannot be resolved philosophically, according to Bataille.
There is no way out of this dilemma; philosophy must accept to be
silent about that which it cannot speak. It is death which enables philos-
ophy’s existence; yet as death is impossible, it is necessarily absent from
philosophical discourse and inconceivable within its limits. Hill notes
that it can be still addressed in fiction, provided words are willing to ac-
cept their necessary absence from truth and to countersign their ultimate
equivalence to silence. And it is on this condition, Bataille claims, that
literature is possible: as an interruption of philosophy.180
Bataille’s work has revived discussion of the topics of religiosity and
mysticism and their relation to philosophy.181 We may ask, is a project
that is beyond reason still a philosophical project? Augustine and other
religious thinkers did think so, and the poststructuralists seem to believe
it as well as long as it is not called “mysticism.”182
Sovereignty is Bataille’s answer to the content of the good life, the
highest ethical state. Whether we refer to it as mystical or epistemolog-
ical, or sadomasochist or sick, it is defined as a comic operation and is
reached through laughter. This is why, to recall the motto of this chap-
ter, the given behind philosophy is laughter: philosophy’s quest is real-
ized outside of philosophy’s scope, in laughter. “If I want, laughter is
thought, but it is a sovereign moment,” Bataille says.183 We turn now to
explaining these arguments, first, by probing the notions of the tragic
and the comic, highlighting the role of ridicule or insufficiency in bridg-
ing them, and explaining Bataille’s comprehensive theory of laughter.
II The Tragic and the Comic
Bataille sees existence as irreducibly ambiguous as it is composed of both
reason and nonsense, knowledge and non-knowledge, calculation and
excess. The irresolvable tension between these poles is a cause of anxi-
ety, which Bataille nevertheless attempts to affirm:
The ambiguity of this human life is really that of mad laughter and
of sobbing tears. It comes from the difficulty of harmonizing reason
with these tears… with this horrible laugh.
(TE 20; OC, X, 577)
Bataille’s sensitivity is essentially tragic; yet the tragic is associated with
joy and laughter. As the tragic is ultimately death, it is modulated by the


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  87
anxiety about death which is voiced in laughter, in conjunction with the
joy that Bataille associates with dying. The tears of the tragic are accom-
panied by laughter, a horrible kind of laughter which is characterized
as mad. It is the laughter at human insignificance which accounts for
the comical or derisory character of everything we do as well as for the
parody that Bataillean sovereignty is. Identifying with the executioner of
the sacrifice, Bataille laughs at the victim who is being executed, who is
none other than himself.
Wishing to be lost, and enhancing in this sacrificial act the ties of
community with violence, Bataille argues that the sacrifice which sov-
ereignty is brings joy to the victim. Bataille strives to enjoy the ecstatic
process in which he experiences his own death yet without dying by
imagining that the difference between neuroticism and sainthood is the
refusal to gasp and the will to give:
The anguish of the neurotic individual is the same as that of the
saint. The neurotic, the saint is engaged in the same battle. Their
blood flows from similar wounds. But the first one gasps and the
other one gives.184
(IE, “To Whomever Wishes Truly to Hear Me,” Section 1)
Thus, it is difficult to differentiate the tragic from the comic in Bataille’s
thought. Indeed, he makes a point of associating them as part of the
integral experience of the whole, to which he aspires; he sometimes adds
a third element that seems to balance them, such as simplicity, transpar-
ence or God. Before elaborating on the notions of tragic and the comic
separately, let me first explain how Bataille minimizes their differences.
In Méthode de méditation, Bataille reaffirms that “the essential is ab-
erration, the greatest comedy.” Meditation is both limitless comedy and
limitless tragedy; the sovereign spirit is never laughable nor tragic, but at
the same time “one and the other infinitely.”185 Thus, the totality of expe-
rience, which interests Bataille, includes both the ludicrous or ridiculous
and the painful, and cannot favorize one over the other:
If I want to realize totality in my consciousness, I have to relate
myself to an immense, ludicrous, and painful convulsion of all of
humanity… If for a single moment I forget that meaning, will I see
Shakespeare’s tragical/ridiculous sum of total awareness of an im-
manent totality becomes clear to me—but as laceration.
(ON xxix–xxx)
This is a recurring theme in Bataille, who titles Part 3 of Inner Expe-
rience “Antecedents to the Torment (or the Comedy)” (IE 63–98). He
explains that comedy is tragedy and vice versa; for example, crimes are
laughter and sacrifice, while sacrifice is “the comedy which demands


88  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
that a sole individual die in the place of others.” Another example is
that the “path of communication is in anguish,” as sacrifice or anguish
“unite men all times” (IE 98). Finally, the very contradiction which is
the sole content of truth for Bataille amounts to a contradiction between
the tragic and the absurd, which cannot be resolved. The sole possibility
open to human being is to animate this contradiction:
Each of us is as if sunken in narrow isolation. Nothing counts for
us but ourselves. … Death is the sole radical limit of this basic sol-
itude…. Everything has given me to understand that I alone mat-
tered. But death warns me that this is a lie. For I count for nothing;
it is the world only which matters. I matter insofar as I am in the
world, not as a stranger in closure and self-isolation, but as a particle
of energy blending into the light. Thus, I see that if I am to live, it
is on the following tragic condition: that, relinquishing this life of
mine, I give myself to that which knows nothing of me, to that which
is exterior to myself. At the same time, though, I feel the absurdity
of a loss which, considered from my position of inevitable solitude,
amounts to the annihilation of the entire universe….
(S 66)
It is noteworthy that Bataille adds to the opposition comedy/tragedy yet
another element. For example, describing “the state of immanence—or
the theopathic state,” he writes, “in the immanent state are united the
sense of tragic, feelings of demented comedy, and the greatest simplicity”;
and, “an entire human being is partly a clown, partly God, partly crazy…
and is transparence.”186 Here, he expresses these feelings more poetically:
Nietzsche represented the “death of god” as later provoking a return
to “a changing, fragmented, and incomprehensible reality.”
On the same level you find –
the ridiculous universe,
a naked woman,
and torment.
They make me want to lose myself.
(G 31)
The naked woman is God, as both Madame Edwarda and Story of the
Eye make clear.187 The third element that Bataille adds is God in various
guises, and this gives a special flavor to his thought and sets it apart from
the various thinkers of the tragic-comic because of the joy involved in
God’s absence:
God’s absence is no longer closure; it is the opening of the infinite.
God’s absence is greater, it is more divine than God (I am thus no


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  89
longer I, but an absence of I, I was waiting for this conjuring away
and now, beyond measure, I am gay). 188
Being oscillates between the comic and the tragic because the intuition
of the given is necessarily as risible as it is tragic. This contradiction is
lived, that is, it is only a superficial contradiction for someone who con-
siders all existence paradoxical. Thus, Bataille notes, “For us… the op-
position is not abstract, we live in it; it is the combat of our life and our
death, prodigality and greed, the conquest and gift of the self” (S 65).
The notions of the tragic and the comic still need elaboration, first,
because Bataille’s sensitivity is essentially tragic yet tied up with laughter,
and second, because the comical is not simply joyous but associated with
insufficiency and ridicule. It is Bataille’s ambivalence toward human rid-
icule which gives his philosophy its special tenor: he experiences ridicule
as painful, but also as joyful because it is painful, rather than joyful de-
spite of being painful. For Bataille, comedy is subsumed under tragedy or
suffering, as it is for Kierkegaard, who appreciates the comic but subor-
dinates it to the tragic.189 The human condition in its entirety seems to be
comedic yet in a cruel and desperate way, which he nevertheless enjoys:
“He feels a cruel joy as soon as his misery emerges,” he tells us (IE 89).
Probing further the relations between the tragic and the comic in
Bataille’s thought, I first elaborate on the tragic, I follow with the comic
and I conclude with the notion of ridicule or insufficiency, which bridges
for Bataille the comic and the tragic.
A The Tragic
Bataille’s sensitivity is fundamentally tragic as there is no possibility of
escaping the human condition. The annihilation of our being, death, is
our fate, which we should accept as the sole truth of our existence. How-
ever, it is the violence that Bataille identifies as “the element of the whole
of humanity” that gives the tenor to his view of the tragic:190 “Isn’t it
the very definition of tragedy that the human being cannot live except
by destroying, killing, absorbing,” he asks, “and not only plants and an-
imals, but other men as well?” (IE 132). But the suffocating atmosphere
in which Bataille’s texts make us abide is a violence of a certain kind,
repressed and experienced as anguish with culpability at its core because
“anguish is guilt” (C 135).
The word anguish is one of the most constant and obsessing words
in Bataille’s work. From the preface of Inner Experience to Story of the
Eye, it is always anguish which affirms itself. Around it a fundamen-
tal experience crystallizes itself, which is decisive in its extensions.191
It becomes the fleeing image of the impossible, the unbearable experi-
ence of continuous anxiety as the state he attempts to escape. To that
purpose, he deepens the anxiety, which does not enable the reader to


90  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
disengage from the asphyxiating tragic atmosphere Bataille creates, but
he also attempts to make this experience meaningful by disengaging it
from the contingency of his own personal history192 and by imagining
it not only as communal but also as communicable through the drama-
tization that writing enacts: “Using fiction, I dramatize being: I tear the
loneliness and in the tear I communicate.”193
In the interview he gave at the end of his life, he says that he attempted
to liberate himself from anguish: “I saw in the excess of anguish the
only way out of anguish… even as I took some delight in it, I fled the
anguish.”194 In “torment,” he explains that “horror can only be cancelled
out by an excess of horror,” as “an opening of consciousness pushes as
far as possible,” and “instead of avoiding it, I deepen the tear… cruelly,
I tear the tear: at this moment, I attend the point of ecstasy” (C 44). The
will to power that he makes into a will to chance fleshes out when anx-
iety metamorphoses into its opposite, ecstasy. As “the ecstasy freeing
itself with great anguish…is linked to the unknown, to non-knowledge,
he teaches “the art of turning anguish into delight” (EI 188, 49).
­
He notes that “others are rebels to anguish. They laugh and sing. They
are innocents and I am guilty” (C 74); still, he ascribes these internal tor-
tures to humanity as a whole. He generalizes this experience, claiming
that anguish and its lift, or anguish and its passing is the very foundation
of the human being.195 He argues that Christianity is mistaken insofar
as it attempts to disengage from anguish and guilt (he could not), which
is what its ideal of redemption or salvation means.
We are violently torn out from the continuity of existence by birth,
which isolates in a foreign environment. We attempt to amend the sense
of loss this separation caused at the same time that we endeavor to pre-
serve our autonomy as independent beings:
But to get from inside to outside, man must cross through that nar-
row passage whose name is anguish. The sphere is isolation is com-
parable to a prison… a narrow conduit has been contrived…but the
conduit is not really a way out; it is almost impassable. The prisoner
who tries to enter is cruelly wounded…. the bottleneck connecting
the inner being with free space is, of course, rarely death itself, but
always its adumbration or its image, its beginning.
(S 66)
Striving to satisfy contradictory impulses—“the essential tragedy of human
existence”196—our being can never elude the anguish that defines it.
We cannot deny death or attempt to transcend it; thus, death involves an
intolerable resignation. As we can only exist within the limits set by death,
we should accept the fact of death. This results in a view of the human con-
dition as fundamentally absurd. Death destroys “our world,” everything
we have built; yet we are born to grow and we grow old only in order to


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  91
die. Conscious of this absurdity—an incomplete existence between birth
and death—our fundamentally contingent existence is the product of a
sudden overwhelming desire to exist which is immediately frustrated by
the sense of separation from the world, which becomes alien to us:
Between these irreconcilable poles… a man is necessarily torn, since
he cannot decide for either direction. He can renounce neither his
isolated existence nor the exuberance of a world which cares nothing
for an existence and is prepared to annihilate him. A daily dispute
between tiny enclosure and free space goes on: first of all, between
others and one’s self, between generosity and greed.
(S 66)
Bataille went to Catholicism and back. The Christian God does not ex-
ist as a living faith in his universe, yet he is never really absent from
it.197 In terms that recall Sartre’s depiction of Bataille as an inconsolable
widower before God’s death, Blanchot explains that Bataille’s grief dif-
fers from other griefs, which is why it cannot be overcome.198 While a
missing object (which is far away or definitely gone) can create an occa-
sional grief, another kind of grief is essential for understanding Bataille.
It lies in the impossibility to perceive an opportunity for which he may
be consoled, because this grief is about an object that has never existed
nor could have existed. The state of absolute lack or a vision of absence
is what Bataille is expressing, according to Blanchot.199 The Bataillean
amorous or mystical enterprise reveals its lack of object,200 “nothing or
no-one, only a terrible absence.”201
Thus, for Bataille, the unsatisfaction tied to the human condition is
fundamental and radical, and cannot be altered by social conditions. As
human limits are unbearable and life undesirable, self-love is necessarily
self-condemnation and love is the destruction of the other.202 The essence
of the human being does not consist in an affirmation of his being but in
its reasoned denial (“seizing his divestment”). Thus, the essence of the
reel consists in its transgression; its just value should be measured not ac-
cording to what it is but in relation to all the rest that it is likely to evoke.
As existence is something we cannot know, being only a part of some-
thing bigger than ourselves, “it is a lived state, not the condition of exis-
tence itself, that is for Bataille the crucial human concern,”203 and this
lived state is tragic:
You cannot imagine that, dropped, from you don’t know where,
into this unknown immensity, abandoned to enigmatic solitude,
condemned in the end to sink into suffering, you are not seized with
anguish… from the isolation in which you grow old to the heat of
universes dedicated to your loss…
(IE 96)


92  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
The ways to avoid the tragic are much worse. The tragic human being is
essentially the individual who becomes aware of human existence. She sees
the violent and contradictory powers that agitate her: she knows herself to
be plagued by human irrationality and nature’s absurdity, but she affirms
this reality in contradistinction to “the boor who uses his weapon to vi-
olently direct outward all that agitates him, never admitting to internal
conflict, and who sees in death a source of external enjoyment.”204
In a lecture to the Collège de Sociologie in March 1938, Bataille main-
tains that there are two worlds, and both should be compared with the life
of the complacent bourgeois: a religious world, a world of tragedies and
internal conflicts, and a military world, which being radically hostile to
the spirit of tragedy constantly rejects the aggression outside by external-
izing conflicts.205 While the representatives of these worlds both oppose
the “man of law and discourse, the democratic bourgeois, the man of
comedy,”206 Bataille chooses the religious world. The tragic human being
considers as a joke the rejection on others of all that is terrifying. He inter-
nalizes his conflicts, so he exerts the true sovereignty of the one who has
renounced power. Action is still a condition of human existence. How-
ever, Bataille looks for an action which is likely to escape both the useful
and the ideal. Freed from the concern to be recognized, the tragic human
being interiorizes the conflict and lives by its tension. In a world that no
longer offers him the alibi of a credible project (history is foreclose), the
subject is led to recognize itself for what it is: an unemployed “negativity”
(freedom), and/or without a way out, or, what amounts to the same, a
“negativity empty of content.”207 Its revolt is humanely executed, tamed
by the mere demands of a sovereign, gratuitous and uninterested act.
Out of many contradictions which govern our lives, Bataille is compelled
to live forcefully one in particular, which may be best understood as the
experiential content of an acute state of anxiety: “There is a domain where
death no longer only means disappearance, but the intolerable movement
where we disappear despite ourselves, while at all costs, we should not
disappear.”208 We must live, but the movement that drives us can only be
satisfied with death. Only unfulfilled death can be a death that is lived;
only it can be the experience of the impossible.209 Dying without dying:
this is the paradox to which point the experience of the impossible and the
unexpected that constitutes for Bataille the very fact of true existence; life,
at its extreme, wants its annihilation, its own disappearance. The paradox
can be couched in moral terms: the summit is the fall; thus, the moral of
the summit is the moral of the decline.
In order to reach the tragic and attain to the dignity of existence, the
mere fact of living must engage the activity of a “sadistic consciousness.”210
The sacrifice of the individual is simultaneously his  glorification and his ex-
ecution because “joy is the same thing as pain, the same thing as death”211:
Being opened—to death, to torment, to joy—without reserve, to be
open and dying, painful and happy, already appears in the veiled


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  93
light: this light is divine. And the cry that with twisted mouth, this
being, to no avail wants to make heard is an immense halleluiah,
lost in endless silence.
(Préface de Madame Edwarda, 1956, 297; my translation)
Death is present in our lives in many ways: through sickness and anxiety,
but also through communication and laughter, eroticism and nudity.212
Death responds to the elan of all extreme passion, which is exemplified
in the confusion dead-sex, me and others: when I kill, I am destroyed,
Bataille explains. The very fact that I can ruin the self calls into question
its foundation and discloses death as the ground of being, which points
to human and life’s insufficiency.
Not only is the joy of life ultimately the joy of death, as exemplified by
the very title of Bataille’s work, “La pratique de la joie devant la mort”
(the practice of joy before death), but from Nietzsche: Memorandum
(1945) onward, the tragic is intimately connected with laughter. As we
have noted, this work is a collection of Nietzsche’s texts and  maxims,
which are assembled and presented by Bataille. In the Introduction
he writes: “Essentially, Nietzsche’s thought elevates to the crest of the
waves, TO THE POINT WHERE THE MOST TRAGIC IS RISIBLE.”
He reads Nietzsche as a mystic, who, like Bataille, wanted to perish:
For Nietzsche the world does not have a goal and, consequently,
what is still possible for us? To laugh at what there is. But not to
laugh as it is banal to laugh, perceiving a superiority we have on
what we laugh at, but laughing a laughter that is definitive. One
cannot laugh at the world as a reality in relation to which one feels
superior, rather as a reality in front of which, to the contrary, one
feels one’s smallness and, consequently laughter in Nietzschean con-
ditions is a tragic laughter. There is no possibility of laughing from
Nietzsche’s knowledge without exhausting the possibilities of laugh-
ter, that is, to laugh tragically, to laugh as if one was laughing in
front of a crucifix.
(LS 131–2)
Laughter remains joyous, Bataille notes. Paradoxically, objects of laugh-
ter are generally not joyous; thus, joy cannot be separated from a tragic
feeling. The impulse of the joy which is commonly present in laughter
easily leads to the feeling of the tragic, without decreasing the amount
of joy. He believes that this experience is “deeply consonant” with Ni-
etzsche’s experience, who was explicit about it:
It’s present, naturally and in particular, in the importance which Ni-
etzsche ascribed to laughter, and this in a great number of passages,
but mainly in a rather late, posthumously published work: “To see
the failure of tragic natures and to laugh, that is divine.” I do not


94  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
think that what I represent in general when I talk of un-knowing
and of the experience of its effects can be dissociated from an ex-
pression such as that.
(U 96)
Thus, at the beginning of World War II, Bataille sets out to re-live Ni-
etzsche’s tragedy by dramatizing his own version of it and minutely
describing its contents in Inner Experience. The pinnacle of human
life, this operation is “comical” as he mockingly puts himself to death
while watching himself die, an impossible feat were it not enabled by
laughter’s ambiguous mixture of triumph and defeat. I first address the
notion of the comical in Bataille’s thought, and follow with his view of
laughter.
B The Comic
At first, Bataille was unimpressed by Bergson’s theory of the comic,
 defended in Laughter: An Essay of the Nature of the Comic, which he
read before meeting the philosopher. However, later on, he wrote about
“the application of the mechanical to the living”:
This theory of Bergson’s, although very well known, is, I believe,
somewhat unjustifiably disparaged. … It was not very satisfying
reading, but I found it very interesting, nevertheless. And I have
continued, in my various considerations of laughter, to refer to
this theory which still seems to me one of the deepest to have been
developed.
(U 93)
When we probe the way Bataille addresses the comical, rather than
laughter, we see that he addresses it mainly as mockery. The comical is
a derisive notion, for Bataille, it means “a comedy,” that is, a sham, a
joke. To be comical is to be insufficient: indeed, these terms define the
same situation (“Comic, insufficient…,” he writes). Elsewhere, we find
that “performing in a comedy” is synonymous with “having a kind of
weakness” in one’s position.213 Thus, for Bataille the comic is equiva-
lent to ridiculousness and involves degradation. In this sense, Bataille
can write of the comedy of sacrifice, of eroticism, of impalement, even
of sovereignty. Everything solemn is also ridiculous. Let me detail these
observations.
Stoekl explains how sacrifice can be comical or ridiculous: “If ritual is
solemn there is also very often something ridiculous about it, something
that calls into question the very seriousness on which it depends.” In
“Hegel, Death, and Sacrifice,” Bataille notes the “comedy” of sacrifice,
in which “a mere vicarious experience of death, and hence only death’s


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  95
representation, is substituted for the real thing—one’s own death—
which by definition cannot be experienced.”214 Reflection on death is
much more seriously derisive than living, and “talking about death is the
most profound practical joke” (US 119). Thus, the paradoxical conclu-
sion Bataille arrives at is as follows:
The only way to express myself will be by keeping my mouth shut…
faced with non-knowledge, I have the feeling of performing in a
comedy, of having a kind of weakness in my position.
(US 115)
Commentators who take seriously Bataille’s views on eroticism often
disregard its comicality. However, the following argument will be sig-
nificant for assigning to laughter the right place in Bataille’s philosophy:
Sensuality is indeed the field of derision and imposture; it is essen-
tially a wish to lose one’s footing but without falling irrevocably,
and this could not be so without a certain fraudulence for which we
are blindly responsible but which takes us in nevertheless. To live
our sensual life, we always have to act out a naïve comedy for our
own benefit, and the most ridiculous one of the obscenity of pros-
titutes… the bitterness of the comedy or the feeling of degradation
bound up with payment add a pleasurable element for the man who
gives in to his desire to lose control.
(E 244)
Writing about “the laughable indecencies of love-making” (E 29),
Bataille does not take eroticism seriously. Another example can be found
in his 1958 preface to the new edition of Madame Edwarda, signed with
his own name, in which he undertakes to translate into philosophical
terms this text, which was published under the pseudonym Pierre An-
gelique 15 years earlier. Eroticism is referred to as a “licentious joke”
(“la plaisanterie licencieuse”) and is contrasted with “absolute laughter”
(“Le rire absolu”), which does not pull back from the extreme limit, but
pursues the extremity of that limit to the point of its limitlessness. But as
always for Bataille, this comedy is true only “in a sense”:
Eroticism, in a sense, is laughable… Allusion to the erotic is always
capable of arousing irony. Even in speaking of the tears of Eros, I
could give in to laughter. … Eros is nonetheless tragic, above all,
Eros is a tragic god.
(TE 66)
As everything else, eroticism is tragic, and its being tragic makes it
laughable. Bataille also describes as comedic a more tragic notion than


96  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
eroticism—impalement. Impalement is a ridiculous way of behaving,
he argues in Inner Experience (IE 63), and elsewhere it compares it to
laughter:
Impalement is laughter, but laughter so sharp it vanishes into thin
air. …Even the barely discernible smile on a Buddha would turn out
awkward and heavy… On an insistence on the leap, and a nimble
lightness (the essence of autonomy and freedom, give laughter its
limitless dominion. From the outset, teaching impalement as a prac-
tice is ludicrous).
(ON 64)
Finally, although there are many sovereign states, the anguished one that
Bataille explores is comical, weak and shameful:
The idea of the sovereignty of desire and anguish (or fear) isn’t so
easy for us to understand… [it] is even concealed, having only some-
thing comical and shameful to it… Human autonomy necessarily
escapes our being able to perceive it (it would be servile if it openly
declared itself). True sovereignty so conscientiously effects a mortal
destruction of itself…
(ON 99)
This makes of sovereignty itself, the content of the Bataillean good life,
a comical act215 which “is in the domain of silence.” Because by talking
about it we incriminate the silence that constitutes it, “it is always a com-
edy, a practical joke (because we spoil it as truly sovereign)” (US 126).
How does one reach sovereignty? What is the role of laughter in this
process? How does laughter bring one to the comical state that sov-
ereignty is? If it was in laughter that Bataille saw the beginnings of
liberation, it was only a beginning. The basis of liberation that laughter
founds should be explained more systematically. He writes in Méthode
de méditation:
To bring objects of thought back to sovereign moments pre-
supposes a sovereign operation, different from laughter and gener-
ally from all common effusion. It is the operation in which thought
stops the movement which subordinate it and laughing—or aban-
doning itself to some other sovereign effusion—is identified with
the rupture of the links which subordinated it […] The sovereign
operation is arbitrary and although its efforts legitimate it as far
as subordinated operations are concerned, it is indifferent to judg-
ment in this respect.
(MM; OC, V, 214; emphasis added)


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  97
Philosophy dissolves, and one’s thought identifies itself with rupture.
The means to this aim is what Bataille refers to as the sovereign or even
“comical” operation, which he variously describes as inner experience,
the extreme of the possible, or meditation.216
Kristeva explains that the sovereign operation is deemed comical be-
cause it is a passage from sense to nonsense, or as Bataille says, from the
possible to the impossible:.
The thought that comes to a halt in the face of what is sovereign
rightfully pursues its operation to the point where its object dis-
solves into NOTHING, because, ceasing to be useful, or subordi-
nate, it becomes sovereign in ceasing to be.217
In Méthode de méditation, Bataille explains that “the bottom of worlds
opened do not have any sense. But it is exactly because of this that I can
relate to it the objects of thought.” The sovereign operation is defined
as the point “where thought does not accept any subordinated object
and loosing itself in a sovereign object, destroys in it the exigency of
thought.”218 Thus, one becomes sovereign in ceasing to be:
Only by canceling, or at least neutralizing, every operation of knowl-
edge within ourselves are we in the moment without feeling it. This is
possible in the grip of strong emotions that shut up, interrupt or over-
ride the flow of thought. …It’s really the object of the laughter, or the
object of the tears, that suppresses thought, that takes all knowledge
away from us. [the comic] … the miraculous moment when antici-
pation dissolves into NOTHING, detaching us from the ground on
which we were groveling, in the concatenation of useful activity.
(Botting and Wilson 1997, 305)
Bataille describes an operation in which one brings objects of thought to
the sovereign moment and laughs at them:
In the sovereign operation, not only thought is sovereign (as when
we laugh) but its object is sovereign, and recognized as such, inde-
pendently of its insertion in the useful: what is, is not subordinated
to nothing and, revealing itself as such, makes laugh, etc.…
(MM; OC, V, 215; my translation)
It is to bring the known to the unknown; it reverses the movement of
thought, within the common domain. The less inexact image of a sov-
ereign operation is the ecstasy of saints, Bataille argues. Yet the subject
brings himself, rather than objects, into play; thus, in mediation, “the
subject contests itself… [se traque] (capriciously, often even with gaiety)”
and he is modified.219


98  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille interrogates the notions of a “transcendent beyond” and of the
“totality of what is,” and abandons them at the moment of sovereignty.
It is a sham of a sacrifice, hence comical. Fear and desire are shameful,
comical. Being is sovereignty, but sovereignty is laughter, which makes a
mockery of everything.
“As soon as I try to grasp my substance, I sense only a sliding” (S 66).
This makes philosophy laughable and especially its ambitious repre-
sentative, the all-encompassing system of Hegelian philosophy. Indeed,
various commentators note Derrida’s argument that Hegel’s system is
comic for Bataille in part because it makes itself blind to comedy and
laughter, as it makes itself blind to blind spots, including its own, and
to chance, play, poetry, ecstasy, dreams and the unconscious.220 Put
in Bataillean terms, in pursuing Hegelian mastery of lordship, Hegel’s
 system—a restricted economy—makes itself blind to sovereignty, which
always needs a general economy.221 Thus, we can see that science al-
ways needs laughter, a point which is lost on Hegel: “Nietzsche’s prin-
ciple (‘It’s false if it doesn’t make you laugh at least once’) is at the same
time associated with laughter and with ecstatic loss of knowledge”
(G 68). Derrida explains:
Laughter at the comedy of the Aufhebung, at the seriousness of He-
gel, who never laughs at himself. To laugh at philosophy (of Hege-
lianism)—such, in effect, is the form of the awakening—henceforth
calls for an entire discipline, an entire “method of meditation” …
(Derrida 1998, 252)
Trahair explains Derrida’s argument and maintains that in “Hegel,
Death, and Sacrifice” Bataille notes the general comicality of the task
Hegel sets himself. He sketches a double caricature, claiming that Hegel
usurps the sovereignty of the divine and at the same time degrades God to
the status of regent. God as eternal and unchangeable becomes “merely
a provisional end, which survives while awaiting something b etter.” It is
the Sage, Hegel, who is rightly enthroned as sovereign.  Presuming iden-
tity with Hegel, Bataille
briefly imagines the despair he might have felt on realizing that the
consequence of his insight would be that there would be nothing
else to know, but cannot fail to see the comic side of it: in order to
express adequately…one would need… the horror of tragedy. But
things will quickly take a comic appearance.222
Bataille claims that the issue of death is important to Hegel and subjects
it to various comic interpretations. It directly parodies what he identifies
as the equally comical death of Christ. “The death of Jesus partakes of


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  99
comedy to the extent that one cannot arbitrarily introduce the forget-
ting of his eternal divinity—which is his—into the consciousness of an
omnipotent and infinite God.”223 The eternal divinity of God turns the
sacrifice of Jesus into a sham—a comedy.
Similarly, Leslie Anne Boldt notes that Bataille inherits Hegel’s view in
The Phenomenology of Spirit. While Judeo-Christian doctrine situates
the realization of spirit in a transcendent “beyond,” Hegel locates such
a realization within discourse, which alone is capable of revealing the
totality of “what is.” It is the Sage at the end of history who arrives at
absolute knowledge. The Sage is fulfilled in an identity with the totality
of “what is,” not in relation to a transcendent beyond. Only completed
history and the spirit of the Sage (or Hegel)—in whom history revealed,
then revealed in full the development of being and the totality of its
becoming—occupy a sovereign position, which God only provisionally
occupies, as a regent.224
I conclude this discussion of the comical with one of Bataille’s strang-
est texts, “Beyond Seriousness.” Dating from 1955, it links up laughter
with the sovereign operation:
Beyond seriousness? Unhappiness does not reach that far! …
No one can speak beyond seriousness if he imagines that unhap-
piness would make him serious.
The beyond of the serious differs as much from the here and now
as the serious from the pleasant. It is much more serious, much more
comical—its seriousness not being mitigated by anything pleasant,
its comical side by anything serious.225
Bataille concludes that such a way of seeing renders the distress of
the condemned man stifling. While the sovereign person mocks it, he
nevertheless suffers for he cannot be released from his distress. Thus,
although being is sovereignty, because sovereignty is laughter which
makes a mockery of everything, Bataille’s last word is suffering, or the
tragic.
C Ridicule and Insufficiency: Bridging the Tragic and the Comic
Bataille combines the self’s tragic and laughable aspects. He argues
that ipse which seeks to become everything is only tragic at the summit
in its own eyes; when its impotence manifest outwardly, it is “laugh-
able” (IE 89). The notion of impotence, which means ridiculousness
or insufficiency, occupies a significant part in Bataille’s philosophy. It
is also an integral aspect of his view of the comical, which also bridges
between the tragic and comic to the point where they can hardly be
differentiated.


100  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
To explain the notion of insufficiency in Bataille’s thought, we should
recall his parodic view of the universe. Each thing is itself in a deceptive
form. Thus,
Laughter…characterizes all vacant lives as ridiculous. A kind of in-
candescent joy—the explosive and sudden revelation of the presence
of being—is liberated each time a striking appearance is contrasted
with its absence, with the human void. Laughter casts a glance,
charged with the mortal violence of being, into the void of life.
(Bataille 1985, 176)
The individual who occupies the dominant position of the summit is no
less ridiculous than those he dominates, as is ultimately revealed by his
necessity to die in order to truly be what he is—divine and sovereign,
which means mortal, for Bataille.
The desire to be everything is enhanced by a specific suffering, which
Bataille describes as “the distinguished suffering that is inflicted by the
astonishment at not being everything, at even having precise limits. A
suffering which is so difficult to acknowledge.”226 With this passage,
Bataille opens the wound of insufficiency felt by each individual who
wishes to surpass his limited existence. We cannot escape our desire to
be everything, to identify with the entirety of the universe. The desire to
communicate with what exceeds us, the nostalgia for immediacy and the
outrage that existence should be reduced to the realm of project create
chronic dissatisfaction with the attempts we make of eluding what we
are. The knowledge that we will die, that our individual existence is not
commensurate with the universe with which we seek to identify brings
about a malaise that pervades our being and inspires anguish at the in-
evitability of our disapperance.
The narcotics that are necessary to suppress the pain of our lim-
ited existence (suppressing the thought of death, postponing our ex-
istence in a frenzied yet essentially absent devotion to the world of
work, of project) never totally appease our suffering. Thus, the “self-
acknowledged suffering of the disintoxicated” is the subject of Bataille
philosophy.
It is through a suppression of discursive activity and a reinstatement of
the sacred that we cease to make an abuse of our existence. By sacrificing
our will to be everything, the sacred is reintroduced in human reality.
Boldt explains in the Introduction to Inner Experience:
In the acknowledgement of our suffering and of our limits, in our
refusal to flee the anguish inspired by the inevitability of our death,
we engage in sacrifice: we sacrifice our will to be everything, we
sacrifice the hazy illusions which were middle terms distancing us
form the experience of our limits and our eventual loss of self, and


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  101
we sacrifice the belief in a God which, like the other narcotics, was
to ensure that our presence be recuperated.
(Boldt 1998, xii)
As sacrifice is the communication of anguish, the only true sacrifice
is human sacrifice. “The victim, whom the sacrificial knife puts into
death’s power, is there for me,” Bataille argues:
in him, I was able to perceive myself destroyed by the rage to de-
stroy, or, at least, when I was afraid to look too closely, I felt my-
self to be in solidarity with the existence which fell before me into
Nothingness.
(IE 194)
Bataille generalizes this rage and construes it as the outcome of the loss
of continuity we underwent at birth. The nostalgia we feel for the con-
tinuity of being which death promises together with our dread of the
loss of our discontinuous self are expressed in the anguish and the fas-
cination which grasps us at the spectacle of death in sacrifice. Thus, we
“identify with the victim’s return to continuity without having actually
to undergo our own dissolution,” Boldt explains. And “the sacred is pre-
cisely the continuity of being revealed to those who fix their attention, in
a solemn rite, on the death of a discontinuous being.”227
Boldt points to
the individual’s struggle between, on the one hand, the desire for
continuity (which implies a loss of his discontinuous being), and, on
the other, his desire to embrace the whole (all the while maintain-
ing his discontinuity, a “narcotic” necessary to suppress the pain of
insufficiency).228
She explains that between any particular element of being and the whole
which transcends it, there arises an inevitable tension:
The isolated element seeks autonomy, yet wishes to embrace the en-
tirety of the whole: on its own, in isolation, it cannot fulfill this sec-
ond wish. To identify with the entirety of the whole, it must forego
its desire for autonomy…. The cycle in this way is renewed.229
In another passage of Inner Experience, Bataille expresses the problem
differently: the isolated individual wishes to identify with the entirety
of being, but can never satisfy this desire, given that this being is not
centralized, it is no where to be found. Rather, there is nothing but a
movement of energy passing from one temporary point of inertia to an-
other: “…where you would like to grasp your timeless substance, you


102  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
encounter only a slipping, only the poorly coordinated play of your per-
ishable elements” (IE 94). In The Accursed Share, life is described as
consisting of unending and ever-changing patterns of the accumulation
and loss of energy. In these conditions, the isolated individual cannot
realize the desire to be everything.
In Inner experience, Bataille is unequivocal: as we can neither escape
the feeling of insufficiency which leads us to desire identification with
the entirety of “being,” nor can we renounce our ambition to realize
this desire, ipse attempts to circumvent the untenable position in which
it finds itself. In wanting to possess the ungraspable whole, which is
its opposite, ipse can only “attain” the whole in a sudden negation of
 itself—in an expenditure of energy without profit which is realized when
ipse is lost in various forms of sacrifice.
As ipse has no means of identifying the whole as an entirety to be
possessed, it “grasps” the whole only for a moment for it too slips into
darkness. However, at this moment, there is communication, an opening
of the sacred:
In ipse’s renunciation of itself, there is fusion: in fusion neither ipse
nor the whole subsists. It is the annihilation of everything which is
not the ultimate “unknown,” the abyss into which one has sunk.
(IE 115–16)
Any attempt to possess the object must fail; it is only when the will
to know or possess appears as nonsense that ipse and the object (the
whole) may dissolve together: “There is no longer subject-object, but
the yawning gap” between the one and the other, and, in the gap, the
subject and the object are dissolved; there is a passage or communica-
tion but not from one to the other because the one and the other have
lost their separate existence (IE 59–60).
This is the tragic. The comic is the same:
Ridicule is what I don’t have the heart to withstand. Ridiculous are
the other men…. if I equate myself with others, I would have for
myself the contempt which ridiculous beings inspire…. the terrified
consolation which is the slave’s renunciation is laughable.
(IE 67, 68, 79)
To know oneself to be assured of insignificance is the laughter tearing
apart the fabric of which the human being is made. In Hegel’s Phenom-
enology of Spirit, the Hegelian human being—Being and God—is com-
pleted in the adequation of project. In seeking to become everything,
ipse does not fail nor does become comic or insufficient. As sufficiency is
being God, all we can find is insufficiency (IE 80, 87).


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  103
Thus, Bataille identifies at the basis of human life a principle of insuf-
ficiency. On his own, each person imagines others to be incapable or un-
worthy of “being.” The sufficiency of each being is challenged unceasingly
by those who surround him. I would like to simplify, Bataille writes, to
brave the feeling of insufficiency. However, I maintain my “pretense” by
means of the shadow in which I find myself because I really am not suffi-
cient. A burst of laughter, an expression of repugnance, these are the kinds
of shortcomings in which my profound inadequacy is betrayed (IE 81–2).
The question that surpasses understanding leaves a comical bitterness.
However, the will to be the universe is just a ridiculous challenge to the
unknowable immensity. The fate that befalls us is ridiculous because in-
evitable, yet insufficiency still exerts a cunning attraction (IE 85–6, 88).
Thus, Bataille concludes:
What counts in my eyes: to justify my foolishness (and no less that
of others), my immense vanity…Among the rights which man claims
for himself, he forgets that of being stupid; he is necessarily stupid,
but without the right to be so, and sees himself forced to dissimulate.
I would get angry at myself for wanting to hide anything.
(IE 81; emphasis added)
Bataille believes that we cannot get out of the following conundrum:
we cannot renounce ambition or escape insufficiency by any means. We
want to flee because we are afraid of being humans, which has for only
effect hypocrisy—the fact that the human being is what he is without
daring to be so. We are not entirely human beings, “in this sense, human
existence is only embryonic within us,” Bataille argues. Inevitably, the
individual must wish to be everything:
He is comical in his own eyes if he is aware of this: it is necessary,
then, for him to want to be comical, for he is so, to the extent that he
is a man (it is no longer a question of characters who are emissaries
of comedy)—without a way out.
(IE 91; emphasis added)
