This inherent ridiculousness that Bataille describes translates into a de-
finitive disharmony, a discord, an anguishing dissociation of oneself. Be-
cause we cannot palliate it, we should experience it vehemently:
Man is no longer, like an animal, the plaything of Nothingness, but
Nothingness is itself his plaything—he ruins himself in it, but illu-
minates its darkness with his laughter, which he reaches only when
intoxicated with the very void which kills him.
(IE 91–2)


104  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
What is ridicule, then? Bataille answers that ridicule is that which I don’t
have the heart to withstand. If the ridiculous would entirely qualify some-
thing, it would be bearable, he argues. But the situation is rather that the
elements of the ridiculous, which could be an easy way out of the problem,
once formulated, are revealed as useless. Thus, ridiculousness sometimes
defines the human condition in its entirety and sometimes only other per-
sons from which I wish to distinguish myself by escaping this very condi-
tion, whose ridiculousness I exemplify even more by attempting to evade it.
The latter position, the rivalry with other persons and what it brings
about is expressed as follows: “What is ridiculous, are the other men—
innumerable; in the middle; myself, inevitably, like a wave in the sea”
(IE 67). Thus,
… I want to carry my person to the pinnacle. I could, moreover, in
no way avoid it. If I had to equate myself with others, I would have
for myself the contempt which ridiculous beings inspire. In general,
we turn away terrified, from those truths without a way out: any
means of escape is good (philosophical, utilitarian, messianic). I will
perhaps find a new way out. One procedure consisted of grinding
one’s teeth, of becoming the prey of nightmares and of great suffer-
ings. Even this affectation was better, at times, than to catch oneself
in the act of climbing to the pinnacle.
(IE 68)
Bataille is aware that climbing to the pinnacle, which for him is a move
toward the whole, toward a consciousness of totality, or toward a total
friendship of humanness, is deemed unserious. This is so because this
goal discloses that which is impossible for the human being; thus, he
notes that “following this path, I become ridiculous. I acquire the incon-
sistency of all humans” (IE xxx).
This leads us to formulate the former position, which asserts the des-
perate ridiculousness of the human condition. Bataille exposes first the
ridiculousness of thought, the limitations our ignorance imposes on us:
I play the role of the jester in saying in the name of intelligence
that it refuses definitely to formulate anything whatsoever—that it
abandons not only one who speaks but one who thinks.…If I find a
thought to be ridiculous, I dismiss it. And, therefore, if all thought is
ridiculous and if it is ridiculous to think…
(IE 67)
Moreover, the impotence in front of our suffering, shared by adults and
children, is amplified by the comparison between them:
The whole human experience seems to me plunged, deeply, as a
thousand feet under the water, into an irremediable ridiculous


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  105
situation… The ridiculousness of not being children, of not scream-
ing as babies do arises most keenly in older people. Similarly, the
child who cries is ridiculous, his inanity deriving from the serenity
of the older persons.
(MM; C, V, 458; my translation; emphasis added)
Because suffering doesn’t make sense, we cannot avoid laughing at com-
mon misfortune by considering the tragic as immature. Bataille defines
the tragic as the puerile going to the end of its consequences, and thereby
confessing its awful impotence. By revealing the impossible, the puerile
or the tragic also discloses the fabric of knowledge that indefinitely sepa-
rates us by limiting us to “the fiction of a possible world.” Thus, Bataille
concludes that in the human condition, the comical is subordinated to
seriousness.230 It remains to be seen what can be the role of laughter
within earnestness.
III Laughter
Bataille’s reflection on the comical is often associated with the tragic231
and his view of human insufficiency fuels a sense of ridicule that turns
into something laughable the sham that (even) sovereignty is. The rest
of the chapter focuses on the notion of laughter in Bataille’s thought
because it is the term that is most common in his work.
I do not elaborate on humor because Bataille says very little about it,
mainly, that it is incompatible with work, and I do not address irony.
Although Bataille’s irony is “to use his own terms, a ‘black irony’ of
the absolute, cosmic variety,”232 irony in the Romantic or postmodern
stance is foreign to him. This point has not been lost on commentators:
What is singular about Bataille…is that he resisted the Romantic and
modernist twist toward ironization; he is not an ironic writer, but a
writer for whom the task of writing meant refusing the temptation—
what he would call the “consolation” —of the ironic stance.
(Connor 2000, 13)
Bataille’s reflection on laughter is both comprehensive and complex; and
as it touches on all his central notions, it is present in all of his writings.
The sociological essays concern laughter’s relation to the sacred and the
role it plays in transforming repulsive forces into attractive ones (Hollier,
College of Sociology 1937–1939), the philosophical essays concern the
intersection of laughter and philosophy (non-knowledge and Hegel) and
the mystical works deal with laughter and sovereignty (Inner Experi-
ence, Guilty).
As explained in the first part of this chapter, two readings of Bataille’s
work compete today: one disregards Bataille’s lived experience yet
does justice to the centrality of laughter in his work, while the other


106  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
adequately expresses the significance of the lived experience but usually
locates laughter at the same level as eroticism, tears and drunkenness.233
The latter reading misrepresents the supremacy of laughter in Bataille’s
thought and its culmination in the ideal and in the practice of sover-
eignty because it misses on the following argument: additional activities
that enable sovereignty are reducible to laughter as Bataille deems both
eroticism and impalement comical.
Recent commentators within the first group have given a significant
role to laughter in Bataille’s thought: Trahair mentions the work of those
who, respectively, deem Bataille’s laughter capable of resuscitating the
Kantian noumenon, presenting a radical alterity to philosophy and rein-
scribing the Hegelian dialectic to the point where the quest for meaning
is forsaken.234 However, by restricting the meaning of laughter to tex-
tuality, these readings misrepresent Bataille’s thought. Thus, the decon-
structionist does entrust Bataille’s laughter with an important role but
fails him in other respects, while those who read Bataille as a mystic
do not set laughter at the center of his thought. As the two interpreta-
tions are somewhat amiss but for different reasons, a new reading is
needed describing a mystical Bataille whose mysticism is a mysticism of
laughter.
I argue that Bataille is a mystic of laughter who uses laughter as the
means to, rather than as the result of, his operation. This is the only read-
ing which accounts for the significance Bataille gives to laughter; and,
once his peculiar mysticism is unraveled, the uniqueness of Bataille’s
position in laughter theory, philosophy and mysticism is clearly revealed.
Introducing Bataille’s comprehensive approach to, and complex thought
on, laughter requires addressing its associations with various of his cen-
tral notions. I present laughter as the most important philosophical ques-
tion for Bataille and the experience of laughter as giving way to a religion
of laughter. I examine both the cause and object of laughter that he re-
lates to non-knowing, fear and death. I probe laughter’s relation to com-
munication, to superiority and insufficiency, to ritual and self- sacrifice. I
explain the divinity of laughter, its association with sovereignty, knowl-
edge and philosophy, and finally, I account for the role of laughter in the
Bataillean good life, for the way in which laughter best fulfills the ideal
which he preaches and practices. I end this part by evaluating, first, the
contributions of other commentators; second, Bataille’s claim to repeat
Nietzsche’s experience with laughter; and third, the notion of fear as the
key to the communication that laughter is and the community within
which it operates, the sole Bataillean authority, his experience.
A Laughter: The Most Important Philosophical Problem
The significance of laughter in Bataille’s thought cannot be missed: he
deems laughter “psychology’s most complex and maddening problem”


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  107
and the central philosophical problem, on which each philosophy should
be tried.235
It was the reading of Bergson’s Laughter which prompted Bataille’s
study of philosophy. Although disappointed by the meeting with the phi-
losopher in 1920 and irritated by his theory,
The question—the meaning of laughter which remained hidden—
was from then on in my eyes the key question (linked to happy,
 infinite laughter by which I saw right away that I was possessed),
was the puzzle which at all costs I would solve (which, solved, would
of itself solve everything).
(IE 66)
Bataille believes that Bergson’s hypothesis is far from providing a solu-
tion to the mystery of laughter. The philosopher offers it not as an ex-
planation of laughter in general, but of one particular aspect of the
laughable which he terms the comic and which excludes laughter such
as “the (chance) encounter, that of tickling, that of the child’s immediate
laughter” (IE 90). Later on, he mitigated his view, if not of Bergson, at
least of Bergson’s view that the comic effect is generated by encrusting
the mechanical on the living. He ends up by considering that Bergson’s
thought on the comic is unjustifiably disparaged. Deeming it “very inter-
esting, nevertheless,” he continues in his various considerations of laugh-
ter to refer to this view as “one of the deepest to have been developed.”236
The realization that “the major problem was that of laughter” dawns
on him upon reading Bergson’s Laughter, prior to his meeting with the
philosopher. If he could manage to learn what laughter is, he “would
know everything,” he would have solved the problem that confronts the
whole philosophical enterprise: “It seemed evident to me that solving
the problem of laughter and solving the philosophical problem were the
same thing” (U 94). In Méthode de méditation, he writes:
I observed what a burst of laughter was revealing as the essence of
things, to which I acceded freely; I made no difference whatsoever
between laughing at a thing and holding its truth; I imagined not
seeing an object at which I was not laughing; that which made me
laugh were not only comical topics, but more generally, the exis-
tence of “that which is,” and my own self in particular. My laughter
engaged me, was playing me entirely and did not have limits what-
soever; I had a vague consciousness of the reversal I was making; I
thought that, laughter explained, I would know what the human
being and the universe mean: that, on the contrary, if laughter were
unexplained, knowledge was evading the essential.
I add today: That I do not see the object of which I did laugh but only
a report to the sphere of activity…In the same way in which common


108  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
knowledge reports objects to solids, that is, to the moment of subordi-
nate activity, I can report them to the sovereign moment, where I laugh.
(MM 214; my translation)
Bataille looks for explanations of laughter in philosophy because he be-
lieves it is always “extremely interesting” to attempt to test a philosophy
on the problem of laughter. The interest lies in the recognition that philos-
ophy should be able to supply the key to the problem of laughter; however,
Bataille argues that this key provides no opening at all, if it is not made
expressly for the lock in question (U 92). Elsewhere, he expresses a similar
idea, arguing that, “Every theory of laughter is integrally a philosophy
and, similarly, every integral philosophy is a theory of laughter” (ON 186).
Bataille identifies the isolation of the object of laughter as the main
mistake of most attempts to account for laughter by philosophical means.
He argues that laughter is part of a range of various possible reactions to
a given situation, whose main feature is the suppression of the character
of the known. Different reactions follow the sudden invasion of the un-
known: depending upon the case, this situation can produce laughter or
tears as well as other effects, such as poetic feelings or the sentiment of
the sacred; it can also produce anguish or ecstasy, and not only anguish
“but also, of course, the effect of terror” (U 91).
Laughter has been analyzed as a mechanism, and “in learned trea-
tises…tired scholars [treat] laughter as if it were really foreign to them;
they avoid the immediate revelation of the nature of things and of their
own lives in their own laughter” (S 69). Philosophical reflection must
bear first on laughter; however, it is impossible to discuss laughter outside
of the framework of a philosophy which goes beyond laughter, for exam-
ple, that which Bataille “might term a philosophy of un-knowing.”237
Bataille explains that we should begin with an experience of laughter
as related to the experience of sacrifice, the experience of the poetic and
so forth. His own philosophy is a philosophy founded on the experience
of laughter, and which does not even make any further claim. It is a
philosophy which casts off problems other than those provided by that
precise experience (U 91). As for Bataille, experience is the point of de-
parture of thought and is “sole value, sole authority,” let us begin with
his experiences of laughter.
B Experiences of Laughter: The Religion of Laughter
In Inner experience, Bataille describes the early experience he had with
laughter, which eventually changed his life:
Late in night…a space constellated with laughter opened its dark
abyss before me…. I became in this “Nothingness” unknown—
suddenly…I negated these gray walls which enclosed me, I rushed


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  109
into a sort of rapture. I laughed divinely…I laughed as perhaps one
had never laughed; the extreme depth of each thing opened itself
up—laid bare, as if I were dead…I was illuminated convulsively.
(IE 34)
Later, reflecting on this experience, he explains that “from the first day
onward, I no longer had any doubt: laughter was revelation, opened up
the depth of things.”238 Laughter here is a leap from the possible to the
impossible. Another experience with laughter, which Bataille describes
in Guilty, indicates that it can be the contrary:
I went to a forest at nightfall…I evoked the image of a bird of
prey going for the throat of a smaller bird. I thought of dark leafy
branches turning on me, turning on my complacency, aroused with
the anger of a predatory bird. The impression I got was of a dark
bird swooping down on me …and opening my throat. The illusion
of the senses wasn’t as successful as others I’ve had. I shrugged it
off and I think I started to laugh at that point—saved from going
overboard on horror and uncertainty. In the depth of the dark ev-
erything was clear. On the way home, I spite of being exhausted, I
walked on coarse pebbles (which normally would have twisted my
feet) light and airy as a shadow. At that instant I wasn’t expecting a
thing, but the heavens opened and I saw. I saw: what a person can
be kept from seeing only through intentional heaviness. All the use-
less fuss of the stifling day at last cracked open like an eggshell and
was volatilized in the air.
(G 39)
Bataille defines laughter as the leap of the possible into the impossible—
and of the impossible into the possible. However, he insists that it is only
a leap, as maintaining it would amount to the reduction “of the impos-
sible to the possible or its contrary” (C 139). And he tells us that in his
life, “being was lost in laughter,” his self-confidence was “un-knowing
confidence and so, a total absence of confidence.” Thus,
Unconstrained laughter leaves behind the areas that are accessible
to speech—and staring with its conditions, such laughter is an un-
definable leap. Laughter hangs suspended; it leaves you laughing in
suspense. You can’t keep up your laughter—keeping it up is ponder-
ous. Laughter hangs suspended, it doesn’t affirm anything, doesn’t
assuage anything.
(G 101)
At the time of the first experience with laughter, Bataille was deeply
religious, having converted to Catholicism at the age of 14. Wishing to


110  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
further explore the sphere of laughter, he discovers that it made a game
out of Christianity by transcending the dogma through a game of its
own. The important consequence he draws is that faith in the dogma
cannot persist, nor any faith for that matter (G 94), for laughter tran-
scends the transcendent. He would make of laughter his new religion,
ascribing it to Nietzsche, to whom he adheres henceforth as passionately
as he did to Christianity. He writes:
It very quickly became clear to me that there was nothing in my
experience of laughter which was not to be found in my former re-
ligious experience… I could recapture all the impulses of religious
experience, mingling them with the experience of laughter without
feeling that religious experience in any way impoverished… The
impulse of what I prefer to call my life rather than my work has
essentially worked toward the maintenance… of the whole religious
experience acquired within the limits of dogma.
(U 90)
Bataille maintains that unknowing, as he understands it, does not elim-
inate the possibility of an experience which he considers as equally rich
as “the religious experience present in that maximum knowledge which
is revelation.” This experience lies in considering being as problematic,
as wholly unknown, and in plunging into this non-knowledge. However,
Within the experience of un-knowing of which I speak, there re-
mains a religious experience; it is wholly detached from concern
with the future, it is wholly detached from the hold exerted by the
possible threat of suffering, it is now only play.
(U 95)
Of this laughter, Bataille has already described the point of ecstasy in
Inner Experience (IE 34). In pronouncing the word “ecstasy,” he asserts
that he limits himself to the following:
Laughter, when considered as I have done, initiates a sort of general
experience which is, in my view, comparable to what the theolo-
gians call “mystical theology” or “negative theology.” But I must
add that there is, in this respect, an essential difference to be noted:
this experience, so far as I am concerned, is not negative merely
within certain limits; it is totally negative. To this experience and
to its accompanying reflection, I would want to give the name of
“atheology,” composed of the privative prefix a and of the word
theology. It is an atheology whose fundamental consideration, let
us say, is present in the following proposition: God is an effect of


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  111
un-knowing. He can nevertheless be known as an effect of un-
knowing—like laughter, like the sacred.
I can then say the following: that this experience is, on the whole,
part of the general line of religions. In speaking as I do, I am aware
not only of adopting a basically religious attitude, but further, of
representing a kind of constituted religion.
(U 34; emphasis added)
Bataille explains that he does not aim at founding a new religion, only
at pointing to an experience. Yet this issue remains an open one, as he
adds: “Not all religions have been founded, after all; religions were able
to imply experiences constituting a more or less coherent dogma, and of-
ten less rather than more” (U 34). The experience he points to is ecstasy
and is described as follows:
In laughter, ecstasy is freed, is immanent. The laughter of ecstasy
doesn’t laugh, instead it opens me up infinitely. The light that shines
through is traversed by laughter’s arrow as it leaves mortal absence.
An opening up—deranged as this is—implies, simultaneously, love
for the arrow and a feeling of comfort deriving from an awareness
of triumph.
(G 103)
C The Cause and Object of Laughter
Bataille believes that Christianity is a pre-requisite for understand-
ing Nietzsche’s thought and that Nietzsche had a similar experience
of laughter. Laughter is an opening that reveals the ground of things
and, without being accompanied by the outward physical attributes of
laughter, brings ecstasy through simultaneous destruction and joy, or
“sovereignty.”
Laughter is communication of dispelled anguish of the unknown or,
ultimately, death. It is an ideological excrement, a leap from the impos-
sible (what cannot be grasped in any way) or the unknown (an indefinite
reality) to the possible, or the reverse. Anguish is dispelled through the
sacrifice of the victim of laughter around which the laughers gather. The
man who unwittingly falls is substituting for the victim who is put to
death, and the shared joy of laughter is that of sacred communion. Ide-
ally, one is the victim and the sacrificer at once as there is always in the
human being this necessity of suppressing himself while conserving him-
self. The unknown or the impossible is what we cannot reach without
dissolving ourselves or what is slavishly called God. Laughter dissolves
or liquidifies, thus enabling the communication—dying and coming
back—with the indefinite reality. Laughter is a religious experience by


112  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
itself, which captures without residue all that Christianity offers, once
the criticism of Christianity is accepted—that one should be lost instead
of saved: “No longer to leave outside the laughter tearing apart the fabric
of which man is made…—being itself—the fabric torn” (IE 4). This is
Bataille’s goal: “I aspire only to one thing in as much as I give myself still
goals, it is to suppress myself,” granted that “it is more amusing—maybe
more cowardly also—to attempt to suppress oneself by a gymnastic of
the spirit or by sensations” (LS 102).
Richardson notes the commonalities between sickness and laughter in
Bataille’s thought, the unity in their opposition: both bring the world into
question, by making us doubt our existence and pulling us back toward
the continuity that death represents. Sickness, coming from the outside, is
also internally generated. It challenges our mortality, signaling death as a
limit to be fought against, and forces us to engage with our powerlessness.
Like work, sickness is always serious, as it compels us to recognize death.
Since our view of the world depends on our response to the awareness of
death, if, rather than succumbing to sickness (become subservient to the
process of the world), we cure ourselves of it, we may become heroes and
saints rather than invalids: “Neurosis makes us heroes and saints when
not making us invalids.”239 Richardson explains that in laughter, “we ac-
tively participate in the absurdity of the world, turning it back upon itself.”
While sickness binds us to a discontinuous existence, the only proper re-
sponse to which is laughter, laughter frees us: “The extent to which we can
laugh at our fate is in one sense the measure of our freedom.”240
Although it is commonly believed that we laugh in order to express
our feeling of joy, Bataille emphasizes that we also laugh when we are
desperate, or for no reason at all. There is a basic connection between
laughter and fear as the two phenomena are genealogically akin. And
basically, laughter is laughter at death. There is a laughter that does
not laugh, the laughter of ecstasy, when I experience the limits of my
being, which, for Bataille, are the divine. Against philosophers such as
Thomas Hobbes and Bergson, who recognize the negative, humiliat-
ing aspect of laughter, Bataille maintains that laughter has a liberating
effect and a revealing power: it reveals the grounds of things. It is an
instance of lucidity and revelation. However, as the ground of things
is humiliating for us, Bataille’s account takes notice of the superiority
involved in enjoying another’s failure. There is something ambiguous or
even preposterous in laughter, something which defies philosophical or
scientific explanation. Bataille does not merely describe the phenome-
non of laughter but uses the language of laughter himself. He is laughter
incarnate. He is laughing, notably at Hegel, Inner Experience being
not only a phenomenology of laughter but also a parody, “a comic lit-
tle summary” (“une petite récapitulation comique” [IE 43]) of Hegel’s
phenomenology.
Laughter is Bataille’s basic “inner” experience—an experience he
claims to share with Nietzsche. Laughter is not something comical, it


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  113
is something divine, and Bataille discerns a basic truth or insight to
which laughter exposes us. Laughter is an experience of sovereignty,
which requires momentary domination rather than a real superior-
ity which it cannot achieve. Bataille’s thought on laughter is complex.
Thus, this section begins with an account of laughter’s cause followed
by an analysis of laughter’s relationship with anguish, death and
scatology.
1 The Cause of Laughter
While laughter is only one of the possible effects of non-knowing, it
remains true that its cause is non-knowing. Bataille differentiates be-
tween knowing how to provoke laughter and knowing that which really
causes laughter. The real cause of laughter has eluded the history of the
philosophical study of laughter; it is mainly the history of an insoluble
problem: “That which first seems so accessible has constantly eluded
investigation. It may even be that the domain of laughter is finally—or
so it seems to me—a closed domain, so unknown and unknowable is
the cause of laughter.” All existing explanations of laughter have never
managed to fully resolve the mystery of the meaning of laughter, that is,
of its real cause, which remains unknown (U 89–90).
Yet the answer to the problem of laughter may be disclosed by the very
failure to solve it:
There remains, perhaps, just one last theory, which has at least to its
credit, its dependence on the most outstanding and essential quality
of preceding ones: their failure. Let us suppose that that which in-
duces laughter is not only unknown, but unknowable. There is still
one possibility of be considered. That which is laughable may sim-
ply be the unknowable. In other words, the unknown nature of the
laughable would be not accidental, but essential. We would laugh,
not for some reason which, due to lack of information, or of suffi-
cient penetration, we shall never manage to know, but because the
unknown makes us laugh.
(U 90)
What is hidden in laughter must remain so, Bataille argues in Inner Ex-
perience (IE 155). What can be noticed, however, is while we thought
that everything was totally provided for, we discover that there lies con-
cealed, beneath surface appearances, “a perfect absence of response to
our expectation.” Thus, unexpectedly, there arises something unforesee-
able and overwhelming, which reveals an ultimate truth:
We perceive that finally, for all the exercise of knowledge, the world
still lies wholly outside its reach, and that not only the world, but
the being that one is lies out of reach. Within us and in the world,


114  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
something is revealed that was not given in knowledge, and whose
site is definable only as unattainable by knowledge. It is, I believe,
at this that we laugh. And, it must at once be said, in theorizing
laughter, that this is what ultimately illuminates us; this is what fills
us with joy.
(U 91; emphasis added)
Bataille readily concedes that this theory presents from the outset many
difficulties as it does not give us the specificity of laughter. That is
obviously its main defect. Even if there is in the relationship between
laughter and the unknown an element which is measurable (the less we
know of what which arises, the less we expect it, the harder we laugh),
and the suddenness with which the unknown appears also plays a role,
still, he says “it does not make a sudden catastrophe laughable” (U 91).
Throughout his work, then, Bataille sets to explain laughter’s relations
to additional reactions to the unknown, such as anguish, and to relate
anguish to death, which is ultimately the unknown or the impossible.
2 Laughter, Anguish, Death and Scatology
Laughter cannot be a direct reaction to the unknown, as the unknown
creates anguish. The preface to “Madame Edwarda” reads: “If you are
afraid of everything, read this book, but first listen to me: if you laugh,
it is because you are afraid.”241 Laughter and fear are genealogically
akin. Laughter, as well as orgasm and sacrifice, all “failures tearing the
heart,” are manifestations of anguish (C 86). Shared laughter assumes
the absence of true anguish, and yet it has no other source than anguish
(IE 96). Obviously, anguish does not release laughter, but anguish in
some form is necessary: “When anguish arises, then laughter begins” (S
70). Thus, laughter is an impulse by which anguish is dispelled.
All anguish is ultimately of death. “Die of laughter and laugh at dy-
ing” is a title Bataille contemplated for his Théorie de la religion. All
laughter is ultimately laughter at death, he says in the interview he gave
to journalist Chapsal over one year before his death:
Death is what seems to the most ridiculous thing in the world… I
am even inclined to think that laughter, on the philosophical and
paraphilosophical plan, is laughter at death. And the human ambiv-
alence is that we cry at death, but when we laugh, we do not know
that we are laughing at death… People could rather easily develop
an idea of death that is close to the grotesque… It is really a question
there of something atheistic, because one cannot laugh at death in
the presence of God who is a judge.
(Richardson 1998, 223)


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  115
Bataille’s biographer notes that Bataille begun by positing laughter as a
denial of death. Only later (1922–23), Bataille ascribes to laughter an-
other sense altogether: that of affirming death, not denying it.242 Land
explains that “laughter is a communion with the dead, since death is
not the object of laughter: it is death itself that finds voice when we
laugh.”243 Thus, when laughing, we have a sense of falling rather than
of elevation. And such laughter, as Surya notes, dissolves.244
But laughter is also associated with scatology: Bataille’s poem “Rire”
(“Laughter”), which Land studies, introduces three of the most signif-
icant topics of Bataille’s work: laughter, excrement and death: “Laugh
and laugh/ At the sun/At the nettles/At the stones/At the ducks/At the
rain/At the pee-pee of the pope/At mummy/At a coffin full of shit.”245
Laughter’s exceeds rationality by momentarily affirming life, contin-
gency and the body. It breaks with thought and effects a rupture within
ideality. In his criticism of the Surrealists, Bataille deems laughter scato-
logical even though it is a nonmaterial, and thus an ideological, mode of
excretion. As scatology is equivalent to heterology, it marks the elimina-
tion, dissimulation and even repression of excessive, wasteful and non-
productive elements. A pure elimination and waste, laughter is a mode
of non-knowledge, the adequate but meaningless sign of an incommuni-
cable inner experience. As such, it defies rationality:
As soon as the effort at rational comprehension ends in contra-
diction, the practice of intellectual scatology requires the excretion
of inassimilable elements, which is another way of stating vulgarly
that a burst of laughter is the only imaginable and definitely termi-
nal result—and not the means—of philosophical speculation. And
then one must indicate that a reaction as insignificant as a burst of
laughter derives from the extremely vague and distant character of
the intellectual domain, and that it suffices to go from a speculation
resting on abstract facts to a practice whose mechanism is not differ-
ent, but which immediately reaches concrete heterogeneity, in order
to arrive at ecstatic trances and orgasm.
(Bataille, “The use-value of D.A.F. de Sade,”
in Botting and Wilson 1997, 155)
Bataille’s texts obsessively reiterate that the decomposed body is excre-
mental, and that the only sufficient response to death is laughter:
To him who is, in this sort of crisis, unrooted from his very life, the
possibility of worlds unlimited opens to the point that he dies. For
in that kind of beyond into which he now emerges—into which,
against his will only, he can enter—he can no longer distinguish
himself from that which is most fearful to him; he is no longer


116  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
separable from death, from that which is mortal to him, since by
an inextinguishable, rending laugh he has crossed the threshold, en-
tered into this dreadful unison.
(S 70)
The idea that laughter is an opening can also be found in Claude Lévi-
Strauss. He sees an interplay between laughter and other bodily open-
ings in the topic of opening/shutting in American myths:
Laughter is an opening. It can cause opening: or the opening itself
is represented as a combinative variant of laughter. It is therefore
not surprising that tickling, the physical cause of laughter, may be
replaced by other similarly physical causes of bodily opening.
(Levi-Strauss 1970, 125)
According to Lévi-Strauss, the dialectic of opening and shutting is
characteristic of laughter but not restricted to laughter. The myths of
laughter pertain to a greater group of myths which use the dialectic
of opening and shutting: this dialectic operates on two levels, “that of
upper orifices (mouth, ear), and that of the lower (anus, urinary canal,
vagina).”246
As for Bataille the community is bound by the inter-attractive force of
laughter which encloses the sacred nucleus of death, the specific form of
human inter-attraction is laughter (ARI 108).
D Laughter as Communication
The specificity of Bataillean laughter is best formulated in the essays
“Attraction and Repulsion I” and “Attraction and Repulsion II” in
the College of Sociology (1988a, 1988b). There, the social communi-
cative function of laughter as it develops from unmediated to mediated
laughter discloses the latter’s relation to failure and death. Laughter
cannot be studied from the outside because if I laugh, I necessarily
participate in it. Thus, laughing can be approached only through
experience.
The first essay begins to unfold a relationship between psychological
and social mechanisms and addresses the issue of communication. On
the one hand, we have something like a mechanical understanding of
communication or contagion, in which laughter is almost the equivalent
to instinctive reactions of societies such as shawls of fish, which move—
or are convulsed automatically—which explains communication. On the
other hand, we have the psychic component in which laugher is mediated
or unmediated. Human laughter is unmediated only at the very begin-
ning: a child responding to its mother’s face. Mediated laughter is the
product of displacement and distortion in the Freudian sense. However,


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  117
laughter is abortive and is also contagious—“contagious contagion,”
Bataille says—hence the communication between human beings which
are convulsed.
To witness a classical example of unmediated laughter, we could watch
a few weeks old child who responds to an adult’s laughter. The laugh of
satisfaction that follows appeasement, such as taking nourishment or a
warm bath, comes before the laugh of recognition (ARI 109). In a row
state, laughter is first the expression of an intense joy and does not repre-
sent a simple current of communication that is established between two
people or several people laughing together. “What is communicated is
joy” (ARI 110).
Later comes the laughter of recognition in the child, to which laugh-
ter in general is reducible. This calls to mind Vergil’s line: incipe, parve
puer, risu cognoscere matrem (“Begin, young man, to recognize your
mother by your laughter,” or “by her laughter”)247:
All of a sudden, what controlled the child falls into its field. This
isn’t an authorization but a fusion. It’s not a question of welcom-
ing the triumph of man over deteriorated forms, but of intimacy
communicated throughout. Essentially, the laugh comes from com-
munication…. Conversely, intimate communication doesn’t utilize
exterior forms of language but sly glimmerings analogous to laugh-
ter (erotic raptures, sacrificial anguish, or—in poetry—evocation).
(G 140–1)
Apart from this kind of example, natural laughter is denatured or me-
diated. Natural laughter could be no more than a very contagious vital
exuberance. This simple exuberance would be formed with depressing
images, with images of failure or death, comparable to just so many
emissions from a sort of central nucleus in which social energy would be
charged and concentrated (ARII 113). Bataille insists that “only to the
extent that a silence laden with a certain tragic horror weighs down on
life that this life is profoundly human” (ARI 112). But it is precisely this
excess that makes the example significant: it emphasizes something that
usually is barely mentioned. Laughter about failing is already in some
manner laughter about death, but since the distress involved is minimal,
it does not prevent a communicative laughter. Here, it is clear that what
is revealing is the anomaly where inhibition is lacking (ARI 110).
Bataille notes that at this point we must bring into question the ex-
istence of a sacred nucleus around which the joyful round of human
communication is formed. He argues that human nature as a whole, in
each group agglomerated around each sacred nucleus, has, to a large ex-
tent, by participating in the activity of this nucleus, acquired the faculty
of transforming the left into the right (in other words, the impure into
the pure, the unlucky into the lucky [ARII 121]), distress into strength,


118  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
which takes place in laughter in common. If in a communicative reaction
of exuberance and general joy a third term interferes, one partaking of
the nature of death, it is to the extent that every dark, repulsive nucleus,
around which all turbulence revolves, has created the principle of life out
of the category death, aspiring out of falling (ARI 111).
Bataille emphasizes the automatic, incontrollable nature of these re-
actions as they develop. That which we control, which we can modify
at will, has, relatively speaking, little meaning. If we could no longer
consider our reactions of open laughter as inferior, our state will be
changed; we could construct another world. But we lack the strength;
we are bound. We can neither eliminate the weight of gravity nor modify
the conditions under which we laugh. The rules are so clearly defined
that if anyone would happen to modify them, we could no longer quite
say that he is a human being.
Thus, we should distinguish between communication linking up
two beings (laughter of a child to its mother, tickling, etc.), for exam-
ple, “laughing, I am back again, back with other human beings,” and
communication, through death, with our beyond (essentially through
sacrifice)—
not with nothingness, still less with a supernatural being, but with
an indefinite reality (which I sometimes call the impossible, that is:
what can’t be grasped (begreift) in any way, what we can’t reach
without dissolving ourselves, what’s slavishly called God…
(G 60)
Failure and death lead to the issue of communication. Communication
is a will to lose oneself; thus, although necessary, it is destructive and
self-destructive. Communication is transgression and anguish. A daily
dispute between tiny enclosure and free space goes on: first of all, be-
tween others and one’s self, between generosity and greed. But to get
from inside to outside, the human being must cross through that narrow
passage whose name is anguish. Thus we find in moments of communi-
cation which unite us with our own kind a slow, conscious and mortal
anguish. It is most acute when the communication brings all of existence
into play, when the life of people and the presence of the universe are
associated with these moments (S 67). However, the contagious nature
of laughter excludes the possibility of observation:
Seeing laughter, hearing laughter, I participate from within in the
emotion of the one who laughs. It is this emotion experienced from
within which, communicating itself to me, laughs within me. What
we know through participation (through communication) is what
we know intimately: we immediately apprehend the laughter of


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  119
the other by laughing ourselves, or his excitement by sharing the
excitement.
(E 153)
Which is also to say, by identifying with the other, and the two of
us together with this third who makes us laugh. We lose ourselves in
another, and with another in this great panic laughter which gathers
us together around our own loss, our own death. All of this cannot
take place unless we let ourselves go, unless we ourselves burst out in
 laughter. Thus, “there is no theory of laughter, there is only an expe-
rience,” the experience of “the dizziness of the gulf that separates us
together” (E 13, 150).
Everything is anguish; therefore, everything becomes laughter. Sacri-
fice is the ultimate question, but laughter is sacrifice, and self-laughter
the ultimate sacrifice:
There is an assuaging need to lose one’s self; ecstasy is attainable
only through loss of self. Nothing sublime can exist in man without
its necessarily evoking laughter. By laughter, a major sort of commu-
nication, everything is violently called into question. Sublime forms
of communication have isolating effect.
(S 68)
In laughter, Bataille finds a tool of self-suppression that enables him
 simultaneously to preserve himself. When asked, “what is the purpose
of laughter?” he answers: “There is in the fact of laughing at oneself a
radiance whose foundation is on the whole a collapse. It is sometimes
difficult to express.”248 Or, “that which is revealed in our laughter: a
fundamental accord between our joy and an impulse to self-destruction.
[And] the difficulty of that accord” (S 70). However, this is “a moment
of infinite laughter or ecstasy” (G 139), which cannot be maintained.
E Superiority and Insufficiency
Bataille disparages Marcel Pagnol’s view of laughter as superiority249;
yet his own position bears similarity to this view as well as to other
theories of laughter as superiority, because for Bataille one laughs from
a state of dominance: “I believe that the nature of laughter as one of the
group of effects which I relate to un-knowing lies in its link to a position
of dominance.” At least, “to laugh, it is necessary that one not risk losing
one’s position of dominance” (IE 97).
Laughter is associated with a position of dominance in which we
laugh at the unjustified pretense of sufficiency (IE 90). We laugh at in-
sufficiency, which means that we laugh at insignificance. Laughter arises


120  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
out of difference in level, of depressions suddenly produced and of fail-
ure enjoyed at the same time that one’s sufficiency is untarnished:
If I pull the rug out from under… the sufficiency of a solemn figure
is followed suddenly by the revelation of an ultimate insufficiency
(one pulls the rug out from under pretentious beings). I am happy,
no matter what, by failure experienced. And I lose my seriousness
by laughing. As if it were a relief to escape the concern for my suf-
ficiency. I cannot, it is true, abandon my concern forever. I discard
it only if I can do so without danger. I laugh at a man whose failure
does not tarnish my effort at sufficiency, at a peripheral figure who
had pretentious and compromised authentic existence (by mimick-
ing its outward appearance). The happiest laughter is that whose
source is a child. For he must grow up, and I know that the insuffi-
ciency which he reveals, at which I laugh, will be followed by a suf-
ficiency of the adult…The child is the opportunity to learn—without
deep anxiety—over an abyss of insufficiency.
(IE 89)
But the child grows up and so does laughter. In its innocent form, laugh-
ter follows the constitution of society: laughter guaranties and reinforces
the movement in which society throws weak forms off toward the pe-
riphery: laughter puts those which it assembles into “unanimous con-
vulsions.” But laugher does not reach merely the peripheral regions of
existence; its object are not only fools or children (those who became
empty or who still are empty [of sufficiency] by a necessary reversal);
rather, laughter returns from the child to the father, from the periphery
to the center, each time that the father or the center betrays, in their
turn, their insufficiency.
Bataille notes that in both cases we laugh at the same situation: the un-
justified pretense of sufficiency. He notes that “the necessity for reversal is
so important that it had, at one time, its consecration… the saturnalias or
festivals of madmen reversed the roles” (IE 90). As laughter closely follows
the structure of society, we can see now that laughter can go in two oppo-
site directions which still keep intact the hierarchy of society:
If we now compare the constitution of society to a pyramid…the
summit incessantly throws the foundation off into insignificance
and, in this sense, waves of laughter traverse the pyramid by grad-
ually contexting the pretense of sufficiency of the beings placed at
the lower level. But the first pattern of these waves issued from the
summit flows back and the second pattern traverses the pyramid
from the bottom to the top: the flowing back this time contexts the
sufficiency of beings placed at a higher level.
(IE 90)


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  121
What seems to be of significance here is that beyond its relationship with
the social, laughter is most deeply connected with an existential truth
about our inanity, which Bataille associates with his initial description
of the human condition as a contradictory situation of impossible yet
necessary desire. One would expect that the consciousness of this ex-
istential situation as reflected in laughter will sober us up and deliver
additional transforming insights,250 but Bataille insists that being aware
of our inanity does not change anything:
Laughter intuits the truth which the rupture at the summit lays  bare:
that our will to arrest being is damned. Laughter slips on the sur-
face, the whole length of slight depressions: rupture opens the abyss.
Abyss and depressions are together a same void: the inanity of being
which we are. Being within us is elusive—we are lacking it, since
we enclose it within ipse and since it is desire—necessity—to em-
brace everything. And the act of grasping clearly the comedy of this
changes nothing.
(IE 90–1; emphasis added)
Bataille can now explain both laughter at the slipping on a banana peel
and the communion created by the contagion of laughter in stand-up
comedy, where the comedian lampoons one person of the audience.
Thus, the individual who unwittingly falls is substituting for the victim
who is put to death, and the shared joy of laughter is that of sacred com-
munion. When we laugh as one, we penetrate together into “the secret
places of things” in a voluptuous inner harmony of laughter and vertigo:
The spellbinding spark of roaring laughter came to mean, in a way
that was crucial, a kind of dawn, a strange promise of glory (he
who wishes to keep his attention focused upon this sliding, dizzying
point needs great strength).
(S 69)
When laughter breaks up, the separation of the withdrawn individual
from a world of sudden flashing movement instantly ceases; for example,
in tickling, I am released of my withdrawal by my belly being tickled
(S 69). When laughing together, barriers collapse:
An individual’s fall has only to reveal the illusory nature of stability,
and the witnesses of that fall pass, with him, from a world in which
all is stable to one of slips and slides. Barriers collapse…Not only
does each man participate in the limitless streaming of the universe
but his laughter mixes with that of others, so that a room… con-
tains…a single wave of hilarity (both communications).
(S 69)


122  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
All are aware that their condition is, in its strangest and most exciting
aspect, linked to the unfortunate fall. It is an expressible intimacy, other
than that achieved by a man and a woman alone together; there exists no
other form of harmony so visibly authentic. Moreover, laughter is conta-
gious; it has the quality of provoking laughter in return, an invitation to
relief that can hardly be refused:
Hilarity discloses the fall… or some equivalent cause of joy, the cer-
tain presence of prospects of the spirit’s release. This invitation is
difficult to resist. Isolation is always the effect of gloom, of fatigue,
or heaviness; when invited to join in the “mad dance of release,” the
spirit rushes in heedlessly.
(S 69)
Thus, we laugh in mutual recognition, in sudden release from solitude,
in communication. A tension close to anguish has arisen, as sacrifice
is the communication of anguish (S 73). Obviously, anguish does not
release laughter, but for Bataille anguish in some form is necessary; as
noted above, when anguish arises, then laughter begins (S 69–70). How-
ever, when I laugh, what is communicated to me by the laughter of oth-
ers is the cancelling of anguish (S 73). Thus, laughter is an impulse by
which anguish is dispelled.
The superiority involved in laughter is explained by Bataille’s theory
of release from anguish: the child who witnesses a fall gains in seeing
himself as superior, for he remains upright. This helps to dispel the
anguish that arises from noting the resemblance between the falling
man and himself, and of the possibility of his own fall. Endorsing Berg-
son’s view of the anaesthesia of the heart required for laughing, Bataille
notes that indifference or hostility are required, or an evident absence
of gravity in the fall (S 70). The person falling does not laugh for he
gains nothing in it: when a convulsion entailing loss of some kind be-
gins, the presence of some profit—the sense of superiority—is required.
Thus, Bataille concludes, “To laugh at something is to see it as an in-
ferior mode of being” (S 73). Bataille talks also of “the disparaged world
of the comic” (S 72), which means that to be comical is to be worthy of
derision, that is, of mockery.
If Bataille’s account of superiority recalls Hobbes and Pagnol’s theo-
ries of laughter as well as Bergson’s, the notion of release he uses asso-
ciates him with Immanuel Kant on two counts. First, in requiring that
the change that brings up laughter be sudden (this was also required
by Hobbes’s theory); and second, in the view that laughter is about an
expectation that resolves into nothing. While Bataille refers to a sudden
change, he makes this requirement his own by defining it as a change of
knowledge into non-knowledge:


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  123
In laughter, in particular, there is knowledge given of a common ob-
ject… This object is always known, but normally from the outside.
A difficult analysis is required if inner knowledge of it is attempted.
This change makes me laugh under two conditions: 1) that it’s
sudden; 2) that no inhibition is involved… In any kind of joking, a
system that’s given as isolate liquefies, falls suddenly into another…
(G 141)
And Bataille reformulates Kant’s definition of laughter in the third Cri-
tique, “an affection arising from a strained expectation being suddenly
transformed into nothing.”251 Bataille quotes without reference Berg-
son’s translation, which reformulates it: “the object of laughter…is al-
ways NOTHING, substituted for the anticipation of a given object; the
miraculous moment is the moment in which the anticipation is resolved
in NOTHING.”252 We need to elaborate on this “nothing,” which Sar-
tre’s criticism of L’ Expérience intérieure in “A New Mystic” illuminates
(1943). Bataille acquiesces to Sartre’s description of his philosophy and
quotes it at the end of On Nietzsche, in “Appendix IV: Reply to Jean-
Paul Sartre (Defense of Inner Experience)”:
Bataille has hypostasized pure nothingness, sometimes he gives and
sometimes withholds the name of God. Knowledge is what creates
an object as over against a subject. Non-knowledge is “a cancel-
lation of subject and object, the only means of not ending up in a
possession of an object by means of a subject.” There remains “com-
munication.” Which is to say, the night absorbs everything. To give
oneself to night is rapturous. It is a certain way of dissolving oneself
into nothing. I dissolve into myself.
(ON 171–2)
Tony Corn argues that laughter leads to that nothing, which Bataille
hypostasizes. This nothing is death. Leslie Anne Irons-Boldt explains
that Bataille’s notion is a singular meditation upon the Hegelian moment
of “unemployed negativity.” While it is marked by Hegelian discourse,
it extends the latter by imagining, in désœuvrement, the culmination of
productivity at the end of history.253
For a study of laughter, however, the interest lies in Bataille’s alter-
ations of Kant’s definition to suit his own philosophy. He identifies
the nothing we laugh at as death and the expectation violated as
revealing a truth about reality that cannot be otherwise disclosed.
This gives to laughter an epistemological role that does not follow
from Kant’s definition. Similarly, the existential nature of human suf-
ficiency or insufficiency which Bataille grounds in the slippery nature
of human existence and knowledge transforms the superiority theory,
as defined by Hobbes, Pagnol or Bergson, justifying in this case as in


124  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
the previous one Bataille’s assertion that the nature of laughter can be
disclosed only within a philosophy that goes beyond it.
F Ritual, Self-Sacrifice and Laughter
Bataille is preoccupied, even obsessed with sacrifice. In Bataille’s
 fictional, discursive and confessional writings alike, sacrifice becomes
the first and last question. Literature, philosophy, religion are rooted
in it, as sacrifice was there at the dawn of time and would be present
as its end.254 Like a puzzle, sacrifice, once unlocked, would reveal the
founding secrets of humanity itself, as well as the fundamental economy
of religion, poetry and philosophy.255 These notions recall those used
to emphasize laughter’s significance, the sacrificial aspects of laughter
and self-laughter. This section follows Bataille’s thought in its movement
from sacrifice to self-sacrifice and describes how these notions relate to
laughter.
Stoekl notes that in “Hegel, Death, and Sacrifice,” Bataille refers to
the “comedy” of sacrifice where “a mere vicarious experience of death,
and hence only death’s representation, is substituted for the real thing—
one’s own death—which by definition cannot be experienced.” Stoekl
explains that “ritual, for all its solemnity, includes often something ri-
diculous about it, which calls into question the very seriousness on which
it depends.” At the end of the story, Stoekl concludes, “laughter is rec-
ognized as ritually substitutable for reverential and silent homage.”256
For Bataille, dying and coming back is “communication” itself. He
wished to die without dying from it.257 He yearned for sharing a crime
in a ritual sacrifice, which will destroy the limits of being. Eventually, he
interiorized his violence, by defining the moral summit as (self-)sacrifice.
As the vulgar morality of good and evil is inadequate to express intense
experiences that tear beings apart, Bataille turns its intimate suffering
into a triumphant affirmation of guilt. He turned himself into a means:
To summon all of man’s tendencies into a point, all of the “possible”
which he is, to draw from them at the same time the harmonies and
violent oppositions, No longer to leave outside the laughter tearing
apart the fabric of which man is made…—being itself—the fabric
torn.
(IE 4)
Bataille’s criticism of Christianity amounts to the will to be saved
rather than lost. The sense of guilt that plagues us because we violate
the continuity of being by being born manifests itself by a fundamen-
tal anguish of being. We cannot assuage or transcend this guilt be-
cause it does not inhere in us individuals; thus, the notion of personal


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  125
salvation  makes no sense as guilt is present in human existence as a
whole. Recalling his former conversion to Catholicism, he says, “inside
this Catholic belief, I remember that I managed to imagine that paradise
is one’s suppression.”258
The Christian will to not be guilty denies the fundamental impulse
of human life and social solidarity. As there is no possibility of redemp-
tion or salvation, we can only strive toward “sovereignty,” the state in
which we accept the contingency of the moment unconditionally, partic-
ipating fully in it yet expecting nothing from it. Bataille frequently re-
peats his criticism of Christianity, whose “impoverishment lies in its will
(through asceticism) to escape a state in which fragility or non-substance
is painful” (G 23). He proposes to go beyond Christianity, rather than
turning one’s back on it, as Nietzsche has done. By creating a “hyper-
Christianity,” an “atheology,” Bataille believes that he gives meaning to
the experience of life as it is really lived.
Richardson explains that “despite Christianity’s attempt to foist guilt
onto the individual, the nature of collective guilt remains at the heart of
our definitions of ourselves as a species.” This raises issues that we need
to confront if we are to rebuild a sense of collective values.259 Thus,
Bataille defines his goal as suppressing himself. He acknowledges that
reaching this goal in a mock way, through mental gymnastics, is more
cowardly as one stays alive, but it is also more amusing. He thus gener-
alizes this “necessity” to all individuals, who “always” wish this para-
doxical goal:
I aspire only to one thing in as much as I give myself still goals, it
is to suppress myself… It is more amusing—maybe more cowardly
also—to attempt to suppress oneself by a gymnastic of the spirit or
by sensations. …there is always, I think, in man, this necessity of
suppress himself while conserving himself. 260
The self-sacrifice toward which Bataille’s thought consistently leads
makes him emphasize the significance of self-laughter: “One who laughs
is himself laughable and, in a profound sense, is more so than his vic-
tim…” (IE 97). It remains to be seen how this shared ridicule is trans-
formed by the divinity ascribed to laughter.
G  The Divinity of Laughter: Becoming Divine through
Self-Laughter
Bataille may seem to be interested in laughter in general, but he clarifies
that he is mainly interested in what laughter can do in relation to his
most cherished aspirations. Reflection on laughter should focus on that
particular experience that Bataille had with laughter:


126  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
What matters to me insofar as I speak of laughter is situating it at
that point of slippage which leads to that particular experience, the
laughter which becomes divine insofar as it can be one’s laughter at
witnessing the failure of a tragic nature.
(U 97)
I believe that laughter’s divinity is attained mainly through self-laughter
in Bataille’s thought; at least, this view is intimated by the following
comment: “I cannot imagine someone so cruel that, from the shore, he
could observe someone dismasted with a joyous laughter.” Interestingly,
Bataille further alludes to both Lucretius and Arthur Schopenhauer,
who note the pleasure brought by looking from shore at a sinking boat.
Clément Rosset will make the analysis of such pleasure the cornerstone
of his tragic philosophy of laughter, the laughter of annihilation, as we
shall see in Chapter 3. Bataille then adds, “the act of sinking, however,
is something else: one can give oneself fully to this experience with a
joyful heart.”261
The divinity of laughter is the title of a substantial part of Guilty
(“La Divinité du rire” in Le Coupable). We should first recall Bataille’s
view of the divine in order to account for laughter’s divinity as the en-
tire laughing atheology of Bataille is summed up in the following quote:
“God is not the limit of man, but the limit of man is divine. In other
words, man is divine in the experience of his limits.”262 The experience
Bataille refers to is an “incursion into the sphere of the divine, his dying
unto himself.”
The dying unto himself gets its full significance insofar as he who
laughs no longer belongs to the world of seriousness: he is no more seri-
ous than the objects at which he laughs. These operations are considered
in advance inferior, Bataille explains, as they will be null and void for
the serious individual that the laughing person will again become. How-
ever, in the moments when laughter intensifies, a person may feel that he
becomes God; he can never capture these moments and believing that he
does is mere delusion: “We have to keep laughing at laughter: Laughter
is lightness, and we miss it insofar as we cease to laugh at it.” “To laugh
and to be serious at the same time is impossible. We may cease to con-
sider laughter as an inferior mode of being only if we take it seriously”
(S 72–3; emphasis added). Thus:
From the moment that we clarify the experience of what is specifi-
cally tragic, so that we are able to laugh at it, everything is lightened,
everything is simple, and everything can be said with no tone of
misery whatsoever, with appeal to no emotions that have not been
surmounted… What characterizes laughter… is that it is linked to a
dominant position.263


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  127
In “Le Rire de Nietzsche,” Bataille is more radical in his emphasis of
identificatory passion: sympathizing with the one who founders tragi-
cally, the divine laugher dies of laughter and laughs at dying, bent con-
vulsively over the impossible abyss of his own finitude:
Usually, laughter is the reaction that the impossible produces when
sympathy does not involve us personally. Whether the impossible
reaches those who are indifferent [to me], or whether it reaches be-
ings to whom sympathy assimilates me, but without really endan-
gering them, I can laugh at the impossible as a human being: in this
case the impossible leaves the core of the possible intact. Laughing
at the impossible which reaches me, laughing with the knowledge
that I am foundering, I am a god, who makes jest of the possible
that he is.
(OC, VI, 311)
Thus, I am divine only on the condition that I laugh at myself—that is, at
this other self (at this “fellow-being,” as Bataille often says) who found-
ers divinely, tragically. Laughter is not divine and sovereign because it
hovers over miserable human finitude, but rather because it allows itself
to be carried away and falls along with that finitude into the impossible;
this, in turn, presupposes that sovereignty resides within the fall.
I laugh at the passer-by who slips on a banana peel not because I am
what the other is not—superior, sovereign or sufficient. On the contrary,
I laugh by participating joyously in his fall, by slipping with him into this
sudden and sovereign nullity. In short, by losing “my seriousness my-
self.”264 The “incandescent joy” of laughter stems from the sudden reve-
lation of my being as slipping away in the disappearance of the other. It
is the brutal toppling of the other into insignificance and perhaps death
which reveals to me, through laughter, my ultimate and sovereign being,
“the inanity of the being that we are.”265
H Sovereignty and Laughter
Sovereignty is one’s personal transcendence. However, in order to de-
stroy transcendence, as Bataille wishes, there has to be laughter because
immanence is nothing else than the laughter that liberates us from time
and utilitarian action.266 Transcendence has to be destroyed as it sym-
bolizes the feudal and capitalist dominations in the sphere of activity
that Bataille urges us to give up. This destruction has to be effectuated
every time and as soon as human entirety can recognize itself outside
of action, by seeing that every transcendent possibility is a trap which
is a loss of its totality. To liberate time, it is sufficient to appeal to the
immanence of laughter:


128  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
To see tragic natures go under and be able to laugh… In freedom,
abandon, and the immanence of laughter, Nietzsche was among the
first to eliminate what still linked him… to vulgar forms of tran-
scendence, which remain freedom still in chains. To choose evil is to
choose freedom. — “freedom, emancipation from all constraints.”
(ON xxxiv)
In an appendix to On Nietzsche titled “inner experience and Zen” (ON
177–8), Bataille equates the “method of laughter” described in Inner
Experience with Zen methods. He tells us that the method of laugh-
ter is “the ecstatic experience of the meaning of nonmeaning again be-
coming the nonmeaning of meaning and then again… with no possible
outcome…” He argues that a closer look at the methods used in Zen Bud-
dhism enables to find that they imply this movement. “Satori is sought
via concrete nonmeaning substituted for the sensed reality, as revelatory
of deeper reality. This is the method of laughter…” (ON 141). However,
there is a difference, as in Zen satori is addressed only “through comic
subtleties, since it is the pure immanence of the return to self,” while
the difference between his method and Zen is that he does not “imagine
attaining satori without first being overwhelmed by suffering.”267
Bataille is not mistaken about the relationship that Zen entertains
with laughter as modern scholarship has amply exemplified. Because
Zen identifies the ideal with the empirical, at its core lies the deflation of
pretensions, an expectancy that resolves in nothing, that is, in laughter.
In Zen, the masters and the monks are described with thick bellies and
open mouths roaring with laughter:268
Zen writing abounds in anecdotes that stimulate the diaphragm.
Enlightenment is frequently accompanied by laughing of a transcen-
dental kind, which may further be described as a laughter of sur-
prised approval. The approval is continuous, it will even increase,
but the surprise, though it may not disappear, subsides…269
“Since the master kicked me, I have not been able to stop laughing,”
replied Shuilao, when asked what his enlightenment was.270
In his study of laughter in Zen, Reginald Blyth notes that the essence
of Zen is humor; it is an odd and deeply significant thing that “Zen be-
gins (or is supposed to begin) with a smile,” as it is “the only religion in
which laughter is not merely permitted but necessary.”271
Blyth lists the main characteristics of the Zen enlightenment accord-
ing to Daisetsu T. Suzuki. They are irrationality, intuitive insight, author-
itativeness, affirmativeness, a sense of the beyond, an impersonal tone, a
feeling of exaltation and momentariness.272 In the explanation given by
Blyth, one can recognize many of the topics that Bataille cherishes. Laugh-
ter is breaking through the intellectual barrier; at the moment of laughing,


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  129
something is understood; it needs no proof of itself; it is in no sense de-
structive or pessimistic nor concerned with sin or punishment. Laughter
is a state of being here and also everywhere, an infinite and timeless ex-
pansion of one’s own nevertheless unamiable being. When we laugh, we
are free of all oppression of our personality, or that of others, and even of
God, who is indeed laughed away. The one who laughs is master of his
fate and captain of his soul, because, and here Blyth differs from Bataille,
“Weep, and the world weeps with you;/ Laugh, and you laugh alone.”273
In The Inner Scar: The Mysticism of Georges Bataille, Hussey ex-
plains that “like many of his generation, Bataille was widely read in the
texts of Oriental mysticism.” Moreover, he argues that
In his mystical experiences during late 1930s, he sought to enact a
movement in which the subject would be subsumed or literally dis-
solved into the movement of the cosmos, as does the participant in
mystical experience in the Oriental tradition, rather than to aim at a
summit which would be a point of encounter with God.274
(Hussey 2000, 5)
Hussey further claims that Bataille uses techniques of Buddhist media-
tions to enact this movement in real experience. However, other schol-
ars point to techniques taken from Shamanism (Richardson) or from
Tantrism (Foljambe), among other possibilities.275 While the shamanic
experience has interesting associations with Bataille’s experience, it does
not have a historical relation to laughter. Zen is both explicitly compared
by Bataille with his inner experience and has by itself a privileged rela-
tionship with laughter as does the Bataillean experience. In this chapter’s
concluding remarks, I relate Bataille to additional currents of thought
and more modern forms of spiritual exercises to which I believe Bataille
would have felt some kindship.
I Laughter, Knowledge and Philosophy
Laughter fulfills an epistemological role in Bataille’s philosophy. It is
not laughter’s physical aspect with its benefits, such as emphasized by
the yoga of laughter, which is of interest to Bataille. Rather, “laughter is
thought” (EI 213), “to laugh is to think” (US 90). This kind of laughter
is not necessarily related to its bodily manifestation, which he describes
as follows:
We are suddenly invaded when our habitual foundation is upset,
producing in us that “sudden widening of the face,” those “explosive
sounds of the larynx,” and those “rhythmic spasms of the thorax
and of abdomen” described by medical men.
(U 90)


130  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
The experience Bataille talks about is quite detached from the move-
ments that “medical men” describe as it is always possible not to widen
one’s face without fundamentally changing anything in the experience of
laughter (U 96). Thus, Bataille can say, “the laughter of ecstasy doesn’t
laugh, instead it opens me up infinitely” (G 103). It is the complex rela-
tions that this experience of laughter entertains with thought that I wish
to explore in this section through five points of interest. I follow with
some consequences that this analysis of laughter holds for philosophy
and philosophers.
First, Bataille begins with the early intuition he got from his encoun-
ter with Bergson in 1920, the association of laughter with thought and
thought with laughter: “Thought without laughter seemed to me mu-
tilated, laughter without thought was reduced to this insignificance
which is commonly granted to it, and which Bergson had so poorly de-
scribed.”276 Bataille later argues that laughter presents the possibility of
uniting two sorts of knowledge at a precise point, communal and dis-
ciplined emotional knowledge, on the one hand, and discursive knowl-
edge, on the other, which have until now been unknown to one another
or only roughly brought together. He discovers that the contents of var-
ious forms of expenditure, such as laughter, flow into one another and
define a law of communication which regulates the play of the isolation
and the dissolution of beings. Bataille argues that the analysis of laugh-
ter has given “this ontology its unhoped-for consistency: thought dis-
solved in its entirety but was rediscovered again at a point where laughs
the unanimous throng” (IE xxxiii).
Second, he argues that in laughing, knowledge is suspended rather
than abolished. Laughter may be the effect of unknowing, but when
laughing one does not accept the idea that one knows nothing. Some-
thing unexpected occurs, instead, which is in contradiction to the knowl-
edge that we have: the position of him who laughs implies “the refusal
to accept that which, deep within ourselves, we know”; he who laughs
does not reject his knowledge but refuses for a limited time to accept it.
While allowing himself to be overcome by the impulse to laugh, so that
what he knows is destroyed, he retains deep within the conviction that it
is not destroyed after all. Thus, “when we laugh, we retain deep within
us that which is suppressed by laughter, but it has been only artificially
suppressed.” For example, laughter has the power to suspend strict logic,
to enable us to retain faith, but also to know that which we simultane-
ously destroy as known (U 97).
Third, thinking for Bataille is a passage to the limit, an exposure to
the outside. He relates laughter to knowledge, indeed, to the limits of our
knowledge or the impossible, that is, to our limits. Laughter is transgres-
sion, as eroticism is. Because Bataille argues that laughter is the limit of
our known world and a means to transgress that limit, his arguments
about laughter enable us to read him as a mystic. Indeed, he describes


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  131
ecstasy as differing little from the death of thought and as a new domain
that is opened to consciousness from that death. From non-knowledge,
a new knowledge is possible, he argues. The consciousness of non-
knowledge is a consciousness of the absence of consciousness. A study of
sovereign moments follows from the death of thought. As St. John of the
Cross exemplifies, the study of the mystical moment is in fact a study of
the sovereign moment (US 124, 129).
Fourth, in his essay “Un-Knowing: Laughter and Tears,” Bataille
openly declares that as much as he is a philosopher, he is a philosopher
of laughter.277 To make laughter the very basis of philosophy may be
construed as an attempt to further perturb the happy marriage of phi-
losophy and reason that was, until Nietzsche, “still in its honeymoon pe-
riod,” as Trahair notes.278 “That which is laughable may simply be the
‘unknowable,’” Bataille argues, and it is this very unknowability which
is essential as he holds that “the unknown makes us laugh.”279 In his
attempt to produce a philosophy of laughter, which means a philosophy
of the unknowable, Bataille questions the conventional understanding of
the philosopher as lover of wisdom, knowledge, learning and erudition,
and soundness of judgment:
We perceive that finally, for all the exercise of knowledge, the world
still lies wholly outside its reach, and that not only the world, but
the being that one is lies out of reach. Within us and in the world,
something is revealed that was not given in knowledge, and whose
site is definable only as unattainable by knowledge. It is, I believe,
at this that we laugh. And, it must at once be said, in theorizing
laughter, that this is what ultimately illuminates us; this is what fills
us with joy.
(U 91; emphasis added; quoted in Sanders 1995, 192)
Fifth, Bataille emphasizes the philosophical character of his attempt to
understand the nature of laughter. Despite its negative character, he in-
sists that “this way of seeing” is necessarily linked to a positive philoso-
phy insofar that one recognizes that “positive philosophy itself is not…a
sort of ineluctable necessity; it is rather, suspended, as I have suggested
that dogma might been within laughter” (US 99–100). Yet this view of
positive philosophy comes with a criticism of the regular philosopher
who “renounces being a whole man.” The philosopher, insofar as he
wants to be a whole human being, wants it as a philosopher. But in
proportion to his pretension, he must immediately see that philosophy is
only a specialized activity:
The “whole man” only justifies his character when it is lost in imme-
diacy; he loses it each time when, if [in] view of an ulterior motive,
he is limited to a determined activity. It is the philosopher’s misery


132  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
to be brought to confuse a miserable instrument with the totality of
being. This is his contradiction and also his misery. To such a degree
that he is held in a profound way to this laughable attitude.
(US 108)
The criticism of philosophy along these lines is not original and was
already made by Kierkegaard, as Bataille probably knew.280 Kierke-
gaard considers the philosopher a fool for living in abstractions. His
conclusion resembles Bataille’s in that the former argues for the neces-
sity of incorporating humor within philosophy. Humor, as the highest
form of the comical for Kierkegaard, becomes the necessary corrector
of pre-Kierkegaardian philosophy because reflection should incorporate
the irrational in the form of doubt about its own certainty. Paraphrasing
Shakespeare’s melancholic Dane Prince, who claims that “there are more
things in heaven and earth, / Horatio, / than are dreamt of in your phi-
losophy,”281 the philosopher known as “the melancholy Dane” writes:
Danish Philosophy—if there ever comes to be such a thing—will be
different from German philosophy in that it definitely will not begin
with nothing or without any presuppositions whatsoever or explain
everything by mediating, because, on the contrary, it begins with the
proposition that there are many things between heaven and earth
that no philosophy has explained. By being incorporated in philos-
ophy, this proposition will provide the necessary corrective and will
also cast a humorous-defying warmth over the whole.
(Kierkegaard 1967–78, vol. 3, 3299)
From now on, the philosopher should learn to laugh, as well as keep
silent when the knight of faith laughs at him: according to Kierkegaard’s
ethics of the comic, the most earnest has the last laugh.
Humor, for Kierkegaard, is the highest philosophical position one can
reach, topped only by religion. Similarly, as far as philosophy is involved,
laughter is primordial for Bataille: it is philosophy’s first and central
given because laughter is the problem to be solved; it is also the given
behind philosophy because the radical recognition of sovereignty is the
collapse of the intellectual in laughter, which is the religious experience.
This happens when “at the summit philosophy denies philosophy and
sneers at philosophy” (E 259). Philosophy along with the philosopher
is dissolved in laughter, in the laughter that Bataille believes he shares
with Nietzsche.282 When we disengage ourselves from knowledge and
laugh at unknowing, a new form of thought is possible that indicates
that laughter is thought:
In sum, the discipline I am dreaming of will be to philosophy what
the whole man is to the philosopher, or even, if you will, if he were a


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  133
theologian—to God himself! This proposition gives raise, of course,
to the jest: the best thing is a silent, angelic, feeling of divine mock-
ery. The inaccessible nature of the totality of the instant motivates
less remorse than humor (simultaneously angelic and black).
(US 108)
J Laughter and the Goal of the Bataillean Good Life
