Only laughter can fulfill the Bataillean goal as described in this chap-
ter, once we concede that which he grants, that “this experience of
laughter is rather remote from the common experience of it” (G 90).
Let me show that this is the case in two steps, first, by explaining how
laughter fulfills the goal of the Bataillean good life, and second, by
recalling how every other notion that Bataille offers as the content of
sovereignty is reduced to laughter: Bataille eventually deems alterna-
tive sovereign experiences either comical (as eroticism is) or laughable
(as impalement is). Thus, laughter is not only Bataille’s first word, as
we have seen, but as it trumps all his additional notions it is also his
last word.
First, let’s recall Bataille’s explicit goal. He tells us that he remembers
that even as a Catholic, he imagined that paradise was one’s suppression;
His desire has not changed:
I aspire only to one thing in as much as I give myself still goals, it
is to suppress myself… [It is more amusing—maybe more cowardly
also—to attempt to suppress oneself by a gymnastic of the spirit or
by sensations.] …there is always, I think, in man, this necessity of
suppress himself while conserving himself.283
As dying and coming back is what Bataille believes “communication” is
about, Bataille wants to die yet without dying from it. He seeks a ritual
sacrifice where the crime is shared. As he failed in creating these circum-
stances through the many associations he founded, he turned outer vio-
lence inward, seeking to continue the destruction of the limits of being
that his anguish operates. He defines the moral summit as sacrifice, and
specifies that destruction is ultimately self-destruction.
As far as laughter is concerned, Bataille notes that “the one who laughs
is himself laughable and, in a profound sense, is more so than his vic-
tim” (IE 97). He internalizes destruction through laughter, “no longer to
leave outside the laughter tearing apart the fabric and its object— being
itself—the fabric torn” (IE 4). As the next passage explains, laughter
exactly fulfills his desire to die yet without dying from it. Thus,
Laughter is at the root of everything. On one condition, which is
that it may be a matter of laughing at oneself, and never of believing


134  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
that that one gets rid of what is intolerable by laughing at another.
To laugh at another because we naively condemn something about
it is not to get on top of the problem. We never get rid of anything,
and in laughing at another, in fact we do not suppress the profound
complicity there is between the one who laughs and the one who is
the object of laughter…. There is in the fact of laughing at oneself
a radiance whose foundation is on the whole a collapse. It is some-
times difficult to express.
(“Interview,” Richardson 1998, 223; emphasis added)
Bataille finds in laughter a means for self-suppression which still enables
him to preserve himself: “That which is revealed in our laughter: a fun-
damental accord between our joy and an impulse to self- destruction.
[And] the difficulty of that accord” (S 70). This can be so because, as
noted above, one of the characteristics of laughter is retaining deep
within us that which has been only artificially suppressed by laughter
(U 97). The paradoxical goal of dying while not dying, which is the pur-
pose of reaching ecstasy, is best attained through laughter:
When I laugh, I celebrate defeat’s marriage to power. The feeling
of power is a tribute to the success of a natural element against
 nature—an element that questions nature. Nature would prevail
nonetheless—it would elude being questioned—if the element, when
it prevailed over nature, would justify nature by its success in pre-
vailing. And that would be nature’s triumph, instead of a way for
nature to be questioned. To be questioned still means defeat. It
means that defeat is success (that defeat succeeds), and pure lucidity
cannot, in this sense, go all the way. It cannot succeed at laceration!
Being, when questioned, slips into indecisiveness, turns into interfer-
ence, splits apart—like laughter…
(G 103; first emphasis added)
In the aftermath of his meeting with Bergson, when he decided that
laughter is not limited to the former’s “shabby comical,” laughter for
Bataille amounted to God in terms of lived experience.284 Laughter pre-
cipitates “God’s agony into the dark night,” because being a dissolving
power, laughter also dissolves God: “In infinite laughter, the divine form
melts like sugar in water.”285
But every additional sovereign state available to the human being
slides into laughter, as the degradation that ridicule involves accurately
describes Bataille’s evaluation of the act. Thus, Bataille describes sacri-
fice, eroticism, impalement and even sovereignty as comedic, “bestowing
on the operation of the comic nothing less than the status of sover-
eignty.”286 Eroticism, although tragic, is also laughable as “the field of
derision and imposture” (E 244); suffering is puerile; talking about


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  135
death is ridiculous; impalement is laughter and so is everything else that
fulfills the condition of sovereignty, as we have seen in the description
of the comic above, because “the essence of autonomy and freedom give
laughter its limitless dominion” (ON 64).
Most commentators do not draw from Bataille’s utterances on laughter
this last conclusion and conceive of the various means to sovereignty as
being on the same level, all alternative ways of reaching sovereignty. By
doing so, they disregard the fact that each time it is the incongruity be-
tween the attempt and the outcome that is the content of sovereignty.287
Only recent studies undertaken by very young scholars (students) refer
to or argue for the privilege of laughter over additional sovereign mo-
ments.288 Indeed, hardly nothing rivals the epistemological, ontological
and  ethical roles that laughter fulfills in Bataille’s philosophy, and at
least in relation to sovereignty, the summum bonum of the Bataillean
good life, the role of laughter is clearly explained.
Nothing is grand, except witnessing one’s self-annihilation: because it
is necessarily a comedy, a parody of death and a mockery of ethics, any
operation that leads to it, such as eroticism or impalement, always in-
duces (self-)laughter as does the puerility of the tragic. But self- laughter
in itself suffices to enjoy one’s downfall, to witness one’s failure, to peak
while sinking, to “celebrate defeat’s marriage to power.” Laughter is the
essence of “true sovereignty,” which “conscientiously effects a mortal
destruction of itself” (ON 99) because its sudden glory slides into de-
jection and so satisfies the urge to enjoy the anguish involved in dying
without dying.
K Laughter, Nietzsche, Fear
In the last section of the discussion of Bataillean laughter and just before
the concluding remarks that end this chapter, I wish, first, to comment
on the main interpretations of Bataillean laughter; second, to assess his
repetition of Nietzsche by probing the latter’s view of laughter; and third,
to explore the fear that animates Bataille’s work, as initially noted by
Barthes in the entry “Bataille, fear,”289 because fear’s association with
communication and community enlightens Bataille’s need for laughter.
1 Interpretations of Bataille’s Laughter
No interpreter can miss the prominent role of laughter in Bataille’s
work.290 However, few do it with full justice, maybe also because few
take it as the sole topic of their study. I have gathered here additional
comments on laughter than those I have used, which may enhance its
significance in Bataille’s thought.
For Derrida, whose influence on the reception of Bataille has
been  deemed by Lang as “hegemonic,”291 laughter is an interruption


136  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
of the philosophical discourse. It originates with Bataille as a reader of
that discourse because laughter is the modality of Bataille’s reading of
philosophy. It is the functioning of his concept as an interruption of phi-
losophy’s repression. In the case of Hegel, Bataille’s laughter appears
when the Master’s embrace of death is adequated with a philosophical
need to continue living: “Burst of laughter from Bataille. Through a use
of life, that is, of reason, life has thus stayed alive.”292 The rire interrupts
the conservative, profane motivation of thought. What is laughable? For
Derrida’s Bataille,
What is laughable, is the submission to the self-evidence of mean-
ing, to the force of this imperative: that there must be meaning,
that nothing must be definitely lost in death, or further, that death
should receive the signification of “abstract negativity,” that a work
must always be possible which, because it defers enjoyment, confers
meaning, seriousness, and truth upon the “putting at stake.” This
submission is the essence and element of philosophy…
(Derrida 1998, 256–7)
Where Derrida writes of an “irruption of discourse” effected by Bataille’s
laughter, Libertson sees laughter as conditioning philosophy’s very dis-
course.293 He quotes Bataille:
Human life is linked to lucidity—which is not given from without,
acquired in opposite conditions—a lucidity comprised of unceas-
ing contestations of itself, dissolving ultimately into laughter (into
non-knowledge). Lucidity, contestation, cannot fail to attain the
consciousness of limits—where the results vacillate, where being is
the putting into question of oneself.
(C 347)
Libertson explains how knowledge is motivated by a relation to the
limit: as a willful conduct, knowledge leads to the limit. The illusory
oppositions which govern Bataille’s thought reveal a hidden accord
between knowledge and non-knowledge. Rather than rational, the de-
sire to know is violent, an exigency conditioned by survival and death.
Through its privileged illusion of objectivity and the possession of truth,
it leads inevitably to its limit, the experience of which is non-knowledge.
As laughter, non-knowledge is the dissolution of lucidity, the greater vi-
olence toward which the contestation of lucidity leads. Allow me to ex-
plain these assertions.
Knowledge leads to non-knowledge as anguish gives way to rapture.
Knowledge is a temporary and illusory moment, which depends on
non-knowledge. As the condition for the illusion of the possible, which
means utility, survival or accomplishment, is the impossible, it is also


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  137
the experience of limits, that “which cannot avoid its limits, and cannot
hold to them either” (C 261).
Libertson argues that “knowledge leads, through a certain apprehen-
sion of the illusory nature of the ‘possible,’ to a violent awareness of the
fact that discontinuous man is the im-possible.” Thus, thought leads in-
evitably to non-knowledge, which may take the form of a certain burst of
laughter: lucidity made of incessant contestations itself, ultimately dissolv-
ing in laughter (in non-knowledge). This laughter represents the moment
of the impossible and of communication, as “essentially, it is from com-
munication that laughter proceeds” (C 390). The structure of this laughter
is that of transgression, the inner experience or communication, in the
human sense: the anguish of discontinuity at the extreme of the possible,
faced with the limit, and awareness that this situation is the impossible.
In Bataille’s eyes, laughter would not be an interruption of the servil-
ity of knowledge, but rather an anguish at the heart of that servility, an
anguish that immediately compromises the very term of servility. In the
temporality of discontinuity, laughter would not supervene, but would
condition submission from the beginning. Philosophy would be not only
the laughable, but laughter itself. Thus, “laughter is thought” (EI 213),
and “it is in the failure of questioning that we laugh” (SN 63).294
Borch-Jacobsen (1998) explains how in Bataille’s thought one ends
up laughing at the philosopher in oneself (Eroticism 1986d, 149). It is
by uniting to the bitter end the experience of laughter, right up to that
volatile borderline where “the object of thought vanishes” (OC, VII,
259) with reflection upon the same laughter. The philosopher cannot
reach laughter, which is the “final given of philosophy,” except on the
condition of ceasing to be a philosopher. “And of ceasing to be, period,”
Borch-Jacobsen adds, quoting Bataille: “I am in fact nothing more than
the laughter which takes hold of me” (OC, V, 364).
Borch-Jacobsen quotes Bataille on sovereignty, and argues that being
is sovereignty, but sovereignty is laughter, which makes a mockery of
everything:
Laughter…characterizes all vacant lives as ridiculous. A kind of in-
candescent joy—the explosive and sudden revelation of the presence
of being—is liberated each time a striking appearance is contrasted
with its absence, with the human void. Laughter casts a glance,
charged with the mortal violence of being, into the void of life.
(VE 176)
Borch-Jacobsen notes that to be at the summit is no less ridiculous than
are those one dominates because at the end one must die in order to be
truly what one is—divine, sovereign, that is to say, mortal.
Borch-Jacobsen associates laughter with the sublime, but as its con-
trary. The frankest mirth is that which provokes the degradation, as


138  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Alexander Bain says, of the sublime into the ridiculous. Because then
I am greater than what is “absolutely great,” according to the Kantian
definition of the sublime (“Sublime is the name given to what is abso-
lutely great”). Borsh-Jacobson notes how this definition can be alterna-
tively formulated as, “that is sublime in comparison with which all else
is small.”295 This makes of laughter a sort of inverted sentiment of the
sublime in as much as it places one in the position that “in comparison
of which everything is small,” that is, in the sublime. Formulated differ-
ently, laughter is the tragic overturned or overcome; it is finitude seen
from the bright side, the side of the infinite or God.296
For Bürger (2002), the particularity of Bataille’s gesture lies in his
maintenance of a double determination of the self. He knows himself to
be nothing and to be “all reality” at the same time. And he knows him-
self to be one and other simultaneously. When Bataille defines himself as
“useless negativity” in a 1937 letter to Kojève (OC, V, 396), he presents
himself in Hegelian terms as a self doubly determined: as negativity, he
coincides with that which moves everything; yet as one for whom no
historical perspective remains available (sans emploi), he must accept his
irrevocable meaninglessness.
The double determination of the self tears the subject asunder. It disin-
tegrates into a small contemptible ego and a grandiose self. Nothing sep-
arates the former from the world of the many, which, as the grandiose,
disdains that ego, since its life passes on in subjection to the imperative
of the useful. The grandiose self, which imagines itself as the master,
stands, however, at the border of madness. It knows only unbridled ex-
penditure. The unity of the two and the knowledge of that impossibility
is uniquely captured by Bataille in “laughter,” Bürger argues, “the ges-
ture that radically places his thought in question without stripping it of
its deadly seriousness.”297
It is significant to notice that Bataille’s point, as captured by Bürger, is
evidenced in publications on humor. For example, in The Senses of Humor:
Self and Laughter in Modern America (1998), Daniel Wickberg comments
on William M. Marston’s study of humor (1937). Martson argues that to
have a sense of humor is to enlarge the self by adopting the perspective of
others toward the self, that is to say, by diminishing it. Wickberg explains
that Martson, like his contemporaries, seemed uninterested in following
this contradiction through its final affirmation of the self as both all and
nothing. Instead, he opted for a characteristic view of the self as possessing
a sense of proportion that rendered it both big and small at the same time.
The self must be large in order to be small, and vice versa. Bürger’s com-
ments help us see Bataille as inhabiting Martson’s contradiction in being
both all and nothing in the laughter that enacts sovereignty.298
In An Intimate Destruction: Tantric Buddhism, Desire and the Body
in Surrealism and Georges Bataille, Alan Foljambe (2008) indicates that
the point sought by Bataille is also looked for by Tantra, Buddhism and


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  139
Surrealism. In the sixth chapter, called “S(laughterhouse): The Reso-
lution of Duality,” Foljambe explains how all these theories associate
laughter with desire. First, desire, paradox and helplessness together cre-
ate “the moment,” which is freed from the illusions of past and future.
As desire depends on the belief in a future moment, it collapses into
itself when it realizes the totality of the present and one’s unchangeable
place within it. When desire is simultaneously attained, surrendered to
and overcome, this paradoxical situation merges with “the helplessness
of singularity in the present moment.” Foljambe recognizes this as “the
state of ecstasy in which the separate self is dissolved in laughter, irre-
spective of its source.” In Bataille’s words:
If I possessed within me musical resources to communicate my
feelings, what would eventuate would be a (quite probably feeble)
 explosion—an explosion that, at one and the same time, would be
both a languorous demented wave of sound and the expression of
wild joy—a joy so untamed, however, that listening to it there would
be no way of knowing if it came from my laughing or dying.
(ON 86)
As the inevitability of both laughing and dying is clarified, they become in-
distinguishable. The “victim of time” realizes the certainty of extinction,
and transcends what would be seen as tragic were it not for perceiving its
avoidance as an impossible illusion. When the absence of alternative is
fully grasped, the sting of death collapses into “an absurd parody of itself,
and the idea of life is abdicated in favor of an all-encompassing existence
within the present instant.” This happens when “the dependence of eter-
nity on its own impossibility is revealed, and the single, present moment
regains its primacy over illusions of past and future.” This is what Fol-
jambe refers to as the laughter in life’s slaughterhouse.299
Foljambe further notes that laughter is a psycho-physical reaction to
paradox, which depends on the body:
Like death, it is a phenomenon of incarnated existence, and a reac-
tion to the helplessness inherent in such an existence. The body is the
worldly medium of both humor and suffering, the crucible where the
two are joined. When suffering is viewed as opportunity, and laugh-
ter as the transcendence of tragedy, one is on the path to a fusing of
duality and a demolition of the chasm between laughter and slaugh-
ter. The body can be known as that which suffers, and that which
laughs, the paradoxical alliance of these two functions brought fully
into consciousness by moving outside of the profane realm and into
the sacred, through ascetic practices such as meditation, or through
the exalted excess advocated by Bataille.
(Foljambe 2008, 235)


140  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
The pursuit of the sacred is the denial of profane absurdity, Foljambe
argues, and thus also the implicit confirmation of its existence. He sees
the necessary illusion of God as the only sensible alternative to an absurd
universe: a world in which religion makes sense would be the only world
in which it is not needed.
In many of the systems of thought that Foljambe explores, the body
is associated with the alienated ego, which simultaneously deifies and
demonizes as the driving force of creativity and the barrier between the
self and the divine. He mentions the Tantric use of corpses, the frenzied
self-erasure of Artaud and the Bataillean fascination with the “acéphale”
where one can see “the tormented and paradoxical groping of the hu-
man towards some level of resolution with the impossible fact of our
separate physical existences.”
This “resolution” is the intimate destruction that is private and exclu-
sive, but also infinitely small yet all-encompassing:
It is not a damaging of self at the level of self, but an absolute anni-
hilation at a level beyond the cellular, beyond the molecular, beyond
the atomic; a destruction at the level of memory and possibility, a
destruction beyond mourning and illusion, turning full circle and
coming to rest at the place of a greater creation.
(Foljambe 2008, 235–6)
Whether born of lack or of excess, Foljambe argues that desire is fu-
eled by the courageous existence of joy in the face of death. Systems
of thought such as Tantric Buddhism, Surrealism and “the oeuvres of
Artaud, Masson and Bataille” are the children of this hazardous desire:
In laughter, in joy, in the identity of torment and ecstasy, unity lies
hidden like a numinous pearl between the dualistic hemispheres of
reason’s brain: the opportunity to experience the impossible coex-
istence of sovereignty’s rebellion with the dissolution of absolute
surrender.
(Foljambe 2008, 236)
I further elaborate on this topic in the concluding remarks of the chap-
ter. There I introduce additional views to those that Foljambe analyzes,
which I take from various mystical theories in order to find out whether
Bataille’s views of laughter and sovereignty are original.
Let me conclude this sub-section with Drew Wright’s recent study, the
sole to privilege (because of laughter’s epistemological status) the expe-
rience of laughter, rather than its textuality, over additional sovereign
states. Wright writes about “the meteoric ‘intimacy’ of atheological con-
sciousness, of this highly contingent ‘awakening’ of consciousness to the
‘sovereign instant’ of its rifting,” which “finds its privileged presentation


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  141
and performance in Bataille’s meditations on the ‘lived experience’ of
laughter and, more specifically, in Bataille’s fervent efforts to engage this
‘lived experience’ at the level of epistemology (AS III 202).”300 He notes the
coincidence of laughter and thought, and Bataille’s self- characterization
of his thought as a “philosophy of laughter,” a form of thought which
never proceeds independently of the experience of laughter.
As I have chosen in this sub-section to illuminate aspects of laughter
that may have been insufficiently emphasized in this study, many addi-
tional commentators were left out of this short account,301 and many
more were only partially evoked during this study. We should consider
now Bataille’s work as he saw it, as repeating the laughter of Nietzsche.
2 Repeating Nietzsche’s Laughter
Bataille is convinced that he shares Nietzsche’s experience, with whom
he creates a community of likes.302 He reads him as a mystic: Nietzsche’s
quotes on laughter and cruelty, game and parody are described as his
mystical states (“états mystiques”) in the fourth part of Nietzsche:
 Memorandum. Everywhere in Zarathustra, Bataille sees morality as a
mystical experience in which “one climbs the crests of evil and laughter,
made of disarming liberties of non-sense and empty glory.” Bataille ar-
gues that Nietzsche wants to perish; his roads lead nowhere, hence the
anguish. Rather than a path to be followed, Nietzsche’s morality is an
invitation to a divine and solitary dance. Dancing, we might not feel so
lost, but the significant thing is that there is “nothing TO DO anymore,
no more issue, no more goal, no more sense!” (M 151–2; 25–6).
This is Nietzsche read through Kojève’s reading of Hegel’s end of
history, as we noted, which dismisses the goal that Nietzsche emphat-
ically gives to humanity: creating by willing the overman. In Bataille’s
hands, Nietzsche becomes a nihilist, with no goal nor project, apart
from self-destruction to which laughter and evil serve as instruments.
This is also the profoundly mystical Nietzsche that Shestov introduced
to Bataille in relation to Dostoevsky, confounding in this way Russian
and German nihilism into one thought of the impossible.
Nietzsche as a philosopher of tragic laughter has been introduced in
France in that manner. Bataille gives weight to this view by asserting the
sole authority of experience, which he claims to share with Nietzsche by
repeating it. He notes that this experience of laughter is different from
more common ones: “I am naturally led to lay stress upon the fact that
this experience of laughter is rather remote from the common experience
of it” (U 90). Bataille is interested in “the laughter of ecstasy,” which
“doesn’t laugh,” but rather opens him up “infinitely” (G 103), a laughter
that is an ontological experience.
We need not take Bataille’s assertion of repeating Nietzsche as a key
to Nietzsche’s own views. We can inquire and find out if this is so. The


142  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
goal of the Bataillean good life is described as fulfilling the essence of
the human being, which does not consist in an affirmation of his being
but in its reasoned denial, a “seizing [of] his divestment.” The way it was
presented in the previous section bears some resemblance to the Nietzs-
chean ideal of the autonomous individual: “It [the living] must become
the judge, the avenger, and the victim of his own law”:
Can you give yourself your own evil and your own good and hang
your own will over yourself as a law? Can you be your own judge
and avenger of your law? Terrible it is to be alone with the judge and
avenger of one’s own law.303
We may further question the similarity of Bataille’s view of laughter
as enabling sovereignty to Nietzsche’s own views, as well as the addi-
tional opinions he holds by comparing them to Nietzsche’s views. Since
Bataille ascribes all of his experiences to Nietzsche, boasting that he is
Nietzsche rather than his interpreter, and disclosing rightly or wrongly
the association of the tragic with laughter in Nietzsche’s thought, I pro-
pose to restate here some of my arguments on Nietzsche’s laughter in
order to see if they can be at the origin of Bataille’s.304
In contradistinction to Bataille, Nietzsche hardly defines laughter,
nor does he explore it at length. One Nietzschean definition associates
 laughter with Schadenfreude or rejoicing at someone’s else expense:
“Laughter means: Being schadenfroh, but with a good conscience.”305
Walter Kaufmann explains that “the word is famous for being untrans-
latable: it signifies taking a mischievous delight in the discomfort of
 another person” (GS 207n51). The second definition locates the origin
of laughter in release from fear:
Whenever something sudden and unexpected in word and deed hap-
pens without occasioning danger or injury man becomes wanton,
passes over into the opposite of fear: the anxious, crouching crea-
ture springs up, greatly expands—man laughs. This transition from
momentary anxiety to short-lived exuberance is called the comic. In
the phenomenon of the tragic, on the other hand, man passes swiftly
from great, enduring wantonness and high spirits into great fear
and anguish; since, however, great, enduring wantonness and high
spirits is much rarer among mortals than occasions for fear, there is
much more of the comic than the tragic in the world; we laugh much
more often than we are profoundly shaken.
(Nietzsche HH I, 169)
The relation of fear and laughter is endorsed by Bataille, and so is
Nietzsche’s reference to Kant’s description of laughter as a sudden re-
lease from tension that Friedrich Schelling repeats and Schopenhauer


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  143
intelligibly alters and develops.306 As we have seen, Kant defines laugh-
ter as “an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained
expectation into nothing.”307 In a note from 1879, Nietzsche’s leaning
on Kant is obvious: “Everything sudden pleases if it does not harm;
hence wit… For a tension is thus released.”308
Laughter is also one of the characteristics of the Nietzschean redeemed
person.309 However, a comprehensive account of laughter in Nietzsche’s
thought should not take into consideration only its role in the redeemed
state, as Zarathustra announces. While the Dionysian arts of dancing,
singing and silence characterize solely the redeemed person,310 laughter
accompanies the entire path toward liberation that Nietzsche describes.
Both destructive and regenerative, laughter kills, but is also the sign of a
radical freedom, a rebirth.311
Nietzsche looks for a synthesis of destructive and regenerative laugh-
ter which will simultaneously destroy the foundations of Western civi-
lization and establish the overman.312 This synthesis is realized in the
idea of self-overcoming, which is destructive at the same time that it
establishes a new freedom. The higher men of the future will learn the
art of destructive and creative laughter that is missing today.313
Nietzsche was a philologist; I believe the origin of both these uses of
laughter can be found in Ancient Greece. In Laughing Gods, Weeping Vir-
gins: Laughter in the History of Religion, Ingvild Gilhus explains that in
the Near Eastern mythology, when divine laughter is used in a purposeful
way, its contact with the irrational is kept under control. But as we move to
Greek sources, laughter becomes a prominent and alarming vehicle for the
unthought and a force that transcends the limits of culture and society.314
Because of its violent, eruptive character, laughter tends to be perceived as
powerful, either destructive or life-giving force. Laughter does not point
to one ultimate meaning but has various meanings, which in religion are
often clustered into two opposing phenomenological fields. These fields
are constituted, on the one hand, by creation and birth, joy, sexuality and
eroticism; food and intoxicating drinks; feasts and comedies; dancing; ec-
stasy, madness and wisdom; and, on the other hand, by destruction and
death; derision and shame; ridicule and blasphemy; and tragedy.315
In Greece, the god of laughter was Dionysus. Beside the mythology of
Hesiod and Homer and the cult of Demeter, Dionysus’s cult is the third
great context of religious laughter in Ancient Greece. Not only regenera-
tive laughter of the erotic and comic variety, but also derisive and tragic
laughter found their special forms in his cult.316 Nietzsche uses laughter
in all those various meanings. Particularly, the two kinds of laughter
identified in ancient religions and in the cult of Dionysus parallel exactly
the two main uses of laughter in Nietzsche’s thought.317 “The laughter
of derision” characterizes his critical philosophy and the means of de-
struction it uses, while “the laughter of regeneration” characterizes his
positive philosophy.


144  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille uses both aspects of laughter at once, as a means of attaining
to being more than one is and less at the same time, something that
laughter can indeed do.318 Yet he interprets this capacity of laughter as
enabling him to be simultaneously high (sovereignty) and low (suppres-
sion of self). The identity of the judge and the victim that one simultane-
ously is at the autonomous stage, which is the pinnacle of Nietzschean
morality, sums up Bataillean sovereignty. However, this procedure is not
a means to establishing one’s values as Nietzsche intended autonomy to
be; because Bataille uses laughter to reach sovereignty, the means lead
to nothing and become the end; thus, when laughter is the means, by
becoming the end it is seen as divine.
The difference between this view and Nietzsche’s is that in the latter’s
thought laughter first destroys and then enacts a liberated state. The
laughs Nietzsche refers to differ from each other, the laugh of scorn that
serves “the lion” of the destructive stage differs from the liberated laugh
that characterizes the “child” of the regenerate state. Bataille’s original-
ity lies in disclosing in laughter itself the two simultaneous movements
of glory and dejection. But because he does not differentiate between
these movements, his laughter does not free itself from the destruction it
entails, which is exactly the reason Bataille chooses it as the means and
as the end.
Because laughter originates in release from fear for Nietzsche, it is
helpful in freeing us from fear. An understudied topic in Nietzsche’s
philosophy, fear is a central notion that is at the origin of all values
that inhabit the false consciousness that Nietzsche wishes to abolish.319
Courage is needed to overcome fear, and laughter, for Nietzsche, is a
form of courage. Nietzsche claims that insofar as “courage wants to
kill,” “courage wants laughter” (Z, I, 7). The courage that needs laugh-
ter appears in contexts of cruelty and self-cruelty, which are necessary
for self-overcoming. Nietzsche endorses ancient views of laughter that
associate it with cruelty. Moreover, the amorality which is characteristic
of laughter320 serves the Nietzschean ideal of living beyond good and
evil:
You that have seen man/ As god and sheep/ Tearing to pieces the
god in man/ No less than the sheep in man, / And laughing while
tearing—/This, this is your bliss! / A panther’s and eagle’s bliss/ A
poet’s and fool’s bliss!
(Z, IV, 14, 3)
The same idea is repeated elsewhere, “To see higher nature perish and to
laugh at it…this belongs to greatness!”321
For Bataille too, the origin of laughter is fear, although the com-
plex relationship that laughter entertains with anguish is much more
elaborated than it is in Nietzsche, as is the notion of anguish itself.


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  145
However, one may wonder if the Bataillean equation of divine ecstasy
with extreme horror as exemplifying the “impossible” identity of perfect
contraries322 indeed highlights Nietzsche’s thought. If it were so, Ni-
etzsche would not need the constructive part of his philosophy.
Bataille is also honest about his lack of courage in affronting his own
insufficiency; thus, he makes sure that if laughter is enlisted as a means
to climbing to the summit, it also enacts nothing but his own destruc-
tion. However, Bataille’s reliance on a version of “original sin,” his basic
assumption that guilt and anguish are the fact of all humanity with no
way out is exactly what Nietzsche’s critical philosophy seeks to reject as
the offspring of Christianity. Nietzsche’s thought attempts to liberate the
individual from fear and guilt and the autonomous person who crowns
it, the child, is the one who succeeds in regaining his innocence. Thus,
laughter is used as a tool of liberation in Nietzsche’s thought rather than
as an ambivalent tool that traps you in the very liberation that it offers.
Nietzsche also goes beyond the autonomous individual in yearning
for the overman, which Bataille may see as a confession that Nietzsche’s
philosophy cannot be of use for the human, all-too-human being that
we are. As there are internal tensions among the notions advanced in
 Nietzsche’s late positive philosophy, such as eternal return, amor fati
and the overman, and between these notions and those used in his criti-
cal philosophy, in ignoring Nietzsche’s positive philosophy Bataille may
be seen as a keen observer of Nietzsche’s difficulty in providing a coher-
ent philosophy.
A significant commonality between Bataille and Nietzsche is often
eclipsed, as few notice the religious terms in which Nietzsche describes
laughter:
What has so far been the greatest sin here on earth? Was it not the
word of him who said, Woe unto those who laugh here…For that in
laughter all that is evil comes together, but is pronounced holy and
absolved by its own bliss…This crown of him who laughs, this rose-
wreath crown: to you, my brothers, I throw this crown. Laughter I
have pronounced you holy; you higher men, learn to laugh!
(Z, IV, 13, 16; 18, 10; 13, 20)
Stanley Rosen interprets Zarathustra’s laughter as the reversal of Pla-
tonism and Christianity, and his crown of roses as the opposite of the
weeping Christ’s crown of thorns.323 To avoid all doubt, Zarathustra
prides himself on sanctifying laughter:
This crown of him who laughs, this rose-wreath crown: I myself
have put on this crown, I myself have pronounced my laughter holy.
Nobody else have I found strong enough for this today.
(Z, IV, 12, 18)


146  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Like Nietzsche, who, signing his letters as “The Crucified,” took the
place of God at the end of this life (“son dio, ho fatto questa carica-
tura”), Bataille follows Zarathustra in taking the place of the laughing,
agnostic Christ, but to another purpose: he imagines himself being sac-
rificed for the benefit of humanity, for the community which communi-
cates religiously with death through the victim that he is.
Irwin concludes Saints of the Imagination (2002) with the assertion
that Sartre’s description of Bataille in “A New Mystic” (1943) is exact.
Bataille’s writings describe the man that he is, a mock victim, akin to
Dianus324 and similar to the mutilated and helpless Christ, the mute cri-
tique of power that Bataille describes in one of his lectures.325 Bataille
makes a point of outdoing Christ in being absurd, tragic yet also comi-
cal, and “lubricious, cruel, and mocking” rather than innocent.326
Zarathustra is an embarrassment to many Nietzsche scholars, who
see in him a sad epigone of Nietzsche, which Marcel sees in Bataille. I
let the reader decide if Bataille is Nietzsche’s last man, who prefers to
want nothingness rather than desire nothing, or if he points to the true
meaning of Nietzschean autonomy and discloses the emptiness of the
latter’s positive philosophy, or again, if between these two extremes,
Bataille’s experience of Nietzsche teaches us something significant about
Nietzsche himself.
3 “Bataille, Fear”
Hollier endows Bataille’s anxiety with political meaning: “It frees
the modern self out of his cage” though self-laceration, self-loss, self-
annihilation and ultimately, self-sacrifice; Bataille’s anguish conjures a
state of abject loss, which banishes the left-wing fantasies of progress
toward a “better” future.327 It is significant to note that Bataille refuses
to consider his anxiety a personal matter. The idea that anxiety is “po-
litical” is endorsed by Foucault in The History of Madness (1961/2006),
where he argues that instead of the free terror and the laughter that
characterize the insane in the Renaissance, the insane’s sufferings have
been reinterpreted in the modern period as anxiety and interiorized as
guilt and shame.
While not insane, Bataille suffers from the change of mores which
denies the once socially acceptable outlet for his desires, such as the
religious (public) display of sacred human sacrifice, which was enacted
in the past in various cultures. By endowing his sufferings with meaning
(recall Nietzsche’s similar attempts formulated as “thus suffers a god!”),
Bataille consciously aestheticizes them, making them bearable by a styl-
ized staging that betrays his exhibitionism.
“Such melodrama comes rapidly to amuse,” says Land about
Bataille,328 were it not from the terror that animates Bataille’s writings,
let me add. Michael Mocatta maintains that Bataille’s writings span the


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  147
gamut of anguish, agony and annihilation of self.329 Barthes’s entry,
“Bataille, fear,” notes that only through the disturbance he calls fear, he
can relate to Bataille:
Yet no sooner I made all this (alien) [étranger] language coincide
with the disturbance in myself which I call fear than Bataille con-
quers me all over again: then everything he inscribes describes me:
it sticks [ça colle].330
It is important to note that Barthes refers to fear as a “disturbance.”
Only on this condition can Bataille’s description be inscribed in Barthes.
Yet Bataille sees his thought as offering a path for all who aim high,
predicated on a definition of human essence, and describing an ethical
goal to be followed at all times. He does not consider fear to be a dis-
turbance, robbing it of the capacity to serve as a yardstick for regular
human life, because fear is a constant in Bataille’s life and work. It is
the notion of fear that I propose to examine in closing the exposition of
Bataille’s thought in order to see how it is related to laughter as commu-
nication and community in Bataille’s sole authority, his experience.
“What forces me to write, I imagine, is the fear of going mad.” These
are Bataille’s final words in On Nietzsche. Bataille identifies as fear his
need for communication through writing or dramatization. The imag-
ined community with Nietzsche comes from a similar fear he diagnoses
in the German philosopher: “It is from a feeling of community linking
me with Nietzsche and not from an isolated originality that the desire to
communicate arises in me.”331 The prohibition to exist as an indepen-
dent being tends to be resolved by shunning individuality as “nothing
is more foreign to me than a personal way of thinking; my hatred for
individual thought…attains calmness, simplicity: when I put forward a
word, I play upon the thought of others…”332 This may be the reason
for Bataille’s reinterpretation of anxiety as the mark of sainthood of a
yet to be discovered religion, which sanctifies through communion the
communication with death.
The background to such an activity or the drive behind Bataille’s liter-
ary work has been called by Jean Durançon “Bataille’s little secret.”333 It
is the biographical evidence of Bataille’s breakdowns, repeated anxiety
attacks and pathological guilt, which give rise to obsessive themes in
his work such as death, sacrifice, ecstasy and expenditure.334 Nor does
Bataille hide these facts; to the contrary, he talked openly about his pre-
dicament.335 However, we owe to Bataille’s contemporary, the French
philosopher Gilbert Simondon, the clarification of anxiety’s relation to
communication and community. Simondon explains that the risk of the
individual’s dissolution which is experienced as anguish necessarily cre-
ates the need for communicating with others and thereby founds the
communal feeling of society.336


148  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
“I imagine myself… and in imagining it, I weep,” Bataille writes. Out
of the maddening loneliness of fear, Bataille imagines himself or “dra-
matizes.” Bataille tells us that dramatization is a Christian technique
used by St. Ignatius de Loyola that enables to emulate the sufferings of
Christ. However, both Hollier and Bataille associate dramatization with
laughter: “Dramatization makes presence burst forth,” Hollier explains,
“it makes it burst out laughing.” Bataille argues that “if we hadn’t
known how to dramatize, we would not know how to laugh.” Bataille
further maintains that ecstasy depends on dramatization because “if we
didn’t know how to dramatize, we wouldn’t be able to leave ourselves…
One only attains states of ecstasy or of rapture by dramatizing existence
in general.”337
Dramatization itself, as the play of one’s parody, necessarily leads to
laughter, which, in turn, leads to the knowledge of one’s limits and the
revelation of the ultimate nature of things. Because laughter is “a state
of communication” (IE 112), an opening, even in loneliness, especially
in loneliness, Bataille begins with laughter rather than with anguish as
Heidegger does.338
Plagued by terrible anxiety attacks and anguished by the fear of
 becoming mad, Bataille could not stand the gratuity, the expendi-
ture of his solitary suffering and unnecessary immolation. To endow
his martyrdom with meaning, he communicated it by laughing and
through a dense meditation on/of laughter. He saw laughter as the
 sacred light that irradiates the digging of his grave in the dark, opening
up the ground of things to enable his joyful participation in his own
engulfment:
If someday, I had the occasion to write with my blood my last words,
I would write this: “All that I have lived, said, written, […] I imag-
ined it communicated. Without that, I could not have lived it.”
(ON; quoted in Irwin 2002, 213)
IV Concluding Remarks
The purpose of the concluding remarks is to assess the originality of
Bataille’s views of laughter, especially the association of laughter and
mysticism which constitutes the pinnacle of the Bataillean good life. Let
me explain the choice of this association as the most relevant topic of
evaluation. Bataille associates laughter with fear and death, the comic
with weakness, and ridicule with insufficiency. For his view of the
comic and laughter, he leans on Nietzsche and Bergson, and ultimately
on Michel de Montaigne. A similar view of ridicule will be found in
Rosset, among other traces of Bataille’s view of the comic and laughter
that mark the thought of both Deleuze and Rosset as unfolded in the
next chapters. I wish to await the final chapter where Rosset’s view of
­


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  149
ridicule is introduced before I assess Bataille’s, as both adumbrate Homo
risibilis or the ridiculous human being, the worldview I advance.339 The
themes of fear and death are so common in laughter theory that Bataille
won’t fare well in originality if judged according to them; and the asso-
ciation of fear and laughter is ultimately derived from Nietzsche.
What strikes me as potentially original, then, is what Bataille con-
siders his main thesis, in which he takes pride yet which he ascribes to
Nietzsche: the relationship between mysticism and laughter. This par-
adoxical situation can be clarified as follows: Nietzsche undoubtedly
speaks of laughter in religious terms, sanctifying it and introducing it
as an equivalent to Christianity; however, whether Nietzsche’s laughter
is mystical or not is of no relevance for assessing Bataille’s original-
ity for the following reason.340 In the Western tradition, Bataille is
the sole explicit proponent of the well-attested relationship of laughter
with mysticism, the sole that argues for laughter’s role in mysticism
rather than merely recommending laughter. This may be due to the
singular place that Bataille explicitly holds, as mystic and philosopher,
between religion and philosophy. Thus, it is this aspect of this thought
that I wish to illuminate in these concluding remarks, first, by inserting
Bataille within the rich tradition that unites mysticism and laughter,
hoping that the arguments advanced here will further clarify Bataille’s
ideas and practices; second, by indicating how Bataille is to be dis-
tinguished from this tradition, and hopefully pointing thereby to the
potential originality of his thought.
In “Les techniques d’illumination chez Georges Bataille,” Bruno
(1963) asserts that Bataille yearned for a community of mystical re-
searchers. I believe that, would he lived longer, he would have found this
community in the New Age movement, especially in Zen Buddhism and
Taoism practices which make ample use of laughter.341 Laughter is no
foreign to other mystical movements, however. To the contrary, in the
mystical tradition, “laughter transcends language and is frequently used
as a characteristic of the divine.”342 This is so because,
To abandon oneself to laughter means the temporary unmaking of
one’s traditional self and the letting loose of a violence that sweeps
the outlived away, makes the world vibrate with life. But in the dark
depths of laughter, life-giving and destructive values meet and in-
termingle, and ultimately these depths are impenetrable for human
thought.
(Gilhus 1991, 139)
We see in Gilhus’s account various themes that recall the main ideas
of Bataille. I propose to introduce the reader to the rich tradition that
unites mysticism and laughter in order to see if Bataille innovates in his
mysticism of laughter. The more original the theory and the practice, the


150  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
more idiosyncratic; thus, we should not expect feasibility and desirabil-
ity to follow from an assessment of the originality of Bataille’s view.
A Laughter in Mysticism
In the Introduction to the chapter, we have noted that Wahl compared
Bataille to Democritus, the laughing philosopher.343 Influenced by an-
other philosopher of laughter, George Santayana, Horace Kallen writes
of Democritus, who
laugh at them both—at the invincible nature of things and at de-
luded mankind waging its foredoomed war against the invincible
nature of things; the laugher frees himself also from the suffering of
its coercion and hurt, and he laughs again, his laughter at once his
liberation and his liberty.
Such laughter is transcendent. It is beyond words. It is a mys-
tic experience. It is expression which supervenes when words have
been used up and serve no longer to utter the events that laughter
appraises. It is what one or another Taoist painter labored to signal-
ize on the faces of Taoist sages. It is immanent in the smile of the
Buddha; and audible in the voices of some of his disciples. It is the
promise in the smile of Erasmus’s Dame Folly.
(Kallen 1968, 64)
Studies of laughter in religions commonly stress that laughter and mys-
ticism go hand in hand,344 that “laughter is the greatest spiritual phe-
nomenon”345 and that humor is one of the essences of mysticism.346
Mysticism has established powerful and stable pacts with paths of flight
from suffering, such as creativity, love and humor.347 The pact with hu-
mor is surprising for the usual tactics of humor and mysticism are con-
tradictory. The mystic is persuaded that he has to escape from the outer
world because it is painful, misleading and alien to his essential being,
whereas the person with a sense of humor turns the outer world, includ-
ing all the painful in it, into a source of pleasure. Thus, the humorist
…laughs at his torturers, at his hunger, inanity and failures. Because
he finds life, with all its sufferings, so pleasurable, he is sure of his
power when he encounters them and he has no need of escaping. He
is strong, because humor allows him a sure but effective rebellion
against all that which is no object of his suffering; he is also lucid
because humor requires the comparison of illusion with reality.
(Scharfstein 1972, 181; my translation)
Humor and mysticism are only apparently opposed to each other. In his
groundbreaking philosophical study of mysticism, Ben-Ami Scharfstein


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  151
gives as examples the books of Chuang Tzu and Lao Tzu, which recom-
mend being a mystic but with a light laughter; he also references Zen
Buddhism because it conflates the ideal with the empirical, which makes
the expectation of nirvana end in nothing, that is, following Kant’s defi-
nition, in laughter.
In the last section of her 1991 article, titled “Mysterium Tremendum
and Ridiculum,” Gilhus asks whether there is a connection between
the transcending function of mystical and ludicrous experiences. She
answers:
The experience of the ludicrous is always triggered off by external
stimuli, but the moment of laughter there is a feeling of having direct
access to the world and not being filtered through the ideological
filter.
(Gilhus 1991, 272–3)
Mary Douglas has aptly suggested that the joker “should be classed as
a kind of minor mystic.”348 It is no accident that mysticism often exists
in company with a rich sub stream of humor, jokes and laughter. The
joker and the fool often appear in religious movements which lay stress
on personal and direct experience. Wise-fools (oqala-ye majnum), with
Mulla Nasreddin as their most famous representative, are part of Islamic
Sufism.349 Masters of the Zen Buddhism tradition appear as complete
fools and even exhort to such behavior, as does Harada Sogaku:
My admonition, then: Be a great fool! You know don’t you, that
there was a master who was himself just that (Ryokan)? Now, a
petty fool is nothing but a wording, but a Great Fool is a Buddha.
Shakyamuni and Amitabha are themselves Great Fools, are they
not?350
Fools for Christ’s sake (salos in Greek, jurodivyj in Russian) were part
of the Orthodox Church. These are persons who were considered as holy
because they acted eccentrically and transcended the law and morality,
very often with a comical result.351
In many traditions, religious reality is considered as ultimately inex-
pressible. When the mystics wish to describe the direct experience that
they have of this reality, their desire clashes with the explicit feeling of
its impossibility. In general, mystics have a great need to express mystical
experience. The jokers and the fools share with the mystics an awareness
of the partiality of categories and genres in relation to the whole of re-
ality and of the possibility of alternative ways of expression. The jokers
and the fools’ knowledge are implicit and remain so. The ludicrous is
expressed through a joke or a comical situation; it does not exert any
pressure on its protagonists to be described. Its source is not a profound


152  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
experience similar to the one the mystic has. The direction of the two
types of experience (the ludicrous and the mystical) is invariably oppo-
site: the direction of the mystic’s experience tends to point away from the
carnal man, while the fool tends to bring him to the foreground. Never-
theless, “because of their common characteristic—that is, a knowledge
of the relativity of all ideologies, religious or otherwise—the mystic and
the clown often appear together.”352
Some of Bataille’s ideas on laugher appear to be an integral part of
these mystical traditions. For example, Blyth points to the “Chinese
 understanding of the fact that death is the great subject for laughter as it
is for tears,” while Conrad Hyers notes that
to take oneself seriously, therefore, as a human being, and as a hu-
man being in relation to the sacred, is to laugh; for it is the serious-
ness of one who is awkward and often contradictory in his finiteness,
his fallibility, and his folly.353
Especially relevant for Bataille, who took Gnosticism seriously, is Gil-
hus’s description of the Gnostics’ laughter of insight:
In Gnosticism, the soul’s salvation was dependent on Gnosis, or
knowledge. The process of acquiring salvific knowledge in Gnos-
ticism was akin to solving a riddle or seeing the point of a joke. In
opposition to the wisdom tradition, which had a more static concep-
tion of knowledge, the Gnostic approach was dynamic and incorpo-
rated the laughter of insight or understanding.
(Gilhus 1997, 70)
It may be of interest to point out that Jesus laughs in the Gnostic tradi-
tion,354 especially since laughter relates less to the mystical traditions of
the West than to those of the East. Sociologist Peter Berger notes that
some religions are more humorous than others, and some gods laugh
more than others. In East Asia in particular, “Zen monks and Taoist
sages seem to be helplessly in the grip of mirth much of the time, and
every souvenir store…offers a variegated line of laughing Buddhas.”355
One new religious movement that systematically includes techniques
of laughter and develops a jocular and playful attitude is that of Bhag-
wan Shree Rajneesh (1931–90), later called Osho. He is an extreme ex-
ample of how Indian religion has been reinvented and transformed in
a Western context.356 And in his practice, Bataille would have found a
mysticism of excess rather than of askesis. The following description will
bring Bataille to mind:
Laughing meditation was… taught and encouraged. Consisting of
five minutes of pure laughter with the purpose of losing oneself…


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  153
For Bhagwan, like many of his predecessors in the history of reli-
gions, laughter was an opening up of the body… an early strategy
of Bhagwan was to open it up by means of sex. But after the threat
from AIDS, this procedure became dubious. Laughter was a safer
option, causing the same operation, but giving the body only a mi-
nor shock, without risking death.
(Quoted in Gilhus 1997, 229, 133, 134)
For Osho, to be a sannyasin, a holy man, clearly meant to be in a festive
mood. Bhagwan saw laughter as a primary state of the holy nature and it
was therefore encouraged and cultivated. People smiled and laughed a lot
in Bhagwan’s ashram, and he had special joking relationships with several
of his disciples. One of them said that “laughter is the greatest spiritual
phenomenon.”357 Instances of unquenchable laughter are recorded by his
disciples, even in solemn occasions such as initiation into the community:
Ma satya Bharti laughed herself to pieces when she was initiated to be a
sannyasin and received the mala. She began to laugh and laugh uncontrol-
lably. She continued to laugh for hours, as she also did on later occasions.358
Bharti was not satisfied with making people laugh. The experience
of laughter was a symbol that he used in the mystical-poetic discourse
on cosmology. That cosmology embraced the individual and the world.
Bharti formulates this cosmological thinking of laughter more expres-
sively as follows:
Life is unendingly funny. Do you see it; do you feel it? I suffer, there-
fore I am. I laugh; therefore, I am not. When “you” are not, then
the ego dies, only laughter exists. Existence is a big belly laugh, a
beautiful joke. The stars are laughing, the Buddhas, the Christs and
the Bhagwans are all laughing. Only we sit, locked inside our condi-
tioning, with unsmiling faces.
(Bharti 1981, 24)
The power of laughter can for a moment stop the individual from think-
ing rationally and thus be an awakening:
It is possible, when you have a hearty laugh, mind stops, because
mind cannot laugh. It is structured seriously; its function is to be
serious, miserable, sick. The moment you laugh—it does not come
from your mind, it comes from the beyond, from your inner spirit.359
As clowns and mystics have always gone well together, probably be-
cause they share knowledge of the relativity of all ideologies, Gilhus
adds that it is no coincidence that several of Bhagwan’s books comment
on mystical wisdom traditions, such as Zen Buddhism, Taoism, Sufism
and Gnosticism.360


154  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Because laughter is placed at the heart of his religion as its very es-
sence, Rajneesh also uses laughter to explain the difference between the
religiosity he advances and additional religions. He claims that the Bud-
dha, Jesus and Lao Tzu never laughed, “they were serious people and
were doing serious work.” He argues that all religions have missed a
dimension of great importance, the sense of humor, and have made the
entire world unnecessarily serious.361
B Conclusion: A Mysticism of Laughter
Bataille considered himself a mystic of laughter, and, in so far as he
was a philosopher, a philosopher of laughter. Although the later claim
has not been ignored by poststructuralist commentators of Bataillean
thought, these interpretations make of laughter a textual affair, thus
emasculating the French thinker’s experience of laughter and ignoring
his self-confessed mysticism.362
There is another way of reading Bataille. Following Sartre’s depiction
of Bataille as a mystic (1943), Bataille’s situating his writing “in the line
of the mystics of all times,”363 and his abundant references to Christian as
well as to non-Western mystical canonical texts, there are commentators
who read Bataille as a mystic.364 Although Bataille is clear about the kind
of mysticism he is advancing (“Laughter, considered as I have described
it, opens a sort of general experience that, in my opinion, is compara-
ble to what the theologians have named ‘mystical theology’ or ‘negative
theology’” [IE 34]), commentators who respect Bataille’s religiosity are
reluctant to reduce it to the phenomenon of laughter. More specifically,
they do not single out laughter among other transgressive states, such as
eroticism, tears and drunkenness,365 although Bataille does.
Thus, those who interpret Bataille as a mystic usually consider laughter
too thin to represent the whole subject of Bataillean atheology and too
light to be the sole content of its religiosity. On these readings, as well as
on those who read Bataille as both mystic and philosopher,366 the Batail-
lean experience of laughter—the content of his entire inner ex
 perience—
is usually ignored as too idiosyncratic to be taken seriously.367
This is why a new reading of Bataille was needed, a reading that does
justice both to the significance of laughter in Bataille’s thought and to
his characterization of his experience with laughter as mystical: align-
ing myself with scholars who consider the poststructuralist reading of
Bataille problematic,368 I read Bataille as he describes himself, a mystic,
but I read him as a mystic of a special, an original kind, a mystic of
laughter who differs from the rich tradition that associates laughter with
mysticism. The difference lies in that laughter is not the after-effect of a
mystical experience for Bataille; rather, after his remarkable and repeated
experiences with laughter, Bataille uses laughter as the means for mys-
tical experience, but as mystical experience for Bataille is nothing but


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy  155
the experience of one’s limits, or a totally negative experience, there is
nothing to communicate with beyond the mystical experience; this makes
laughter itself, granted that we understand what laughter represents for
Bataille, the sole content of the mystical experience. Therein lies, I sug-
gest, Bataille’s uniqueness both as a laughter theorist and as a mystic.
We have seen that Bataille is explicit about the relation between mys-
ticism and laughter: “Laughter, considered as I have described it, opens
a sort of general experience that, in my opinion, is comparable to what
the theologians have named ‘mystical theology’ or ‘negative theology’”;
only this experience is totally negative (IE 34). Bataille christens this
experience, together with its accompanying reflection, with the name
of “atheology,” and presents its fundamental idea as follows: “God is
an effect of un-knowing. He can nevertheless be known as an effect of
un-knowing—like laughter, like the sacred.” The entire laughing atheol-
ogy of Bataille is summed up in the following statement: “God is not the
limit of man, but the limit of man is divine. In other words, man is divine
in the experience of his limits,” because the “incursion into the sphere of
the divine” is “his dying unto himself,” his sacrifice.369
Bataille uses a quote from Nietzsche’s Nachlass (1882–84) published
in the French translation of the Will to Power, “To see the failure of
tragic natures and to laugh, that is divine,”370 in order to explain that
the failure or insufficiency at which we laugh is an intimation of death,
and this is why it always makes us happy:
Born of anguish, laughter is communication with each other and with
death:
... which is also to say, by identifying with the other, and the two of
us together with this third who makes us laugh. We lose ourselves
in another, and, with him, in this great panic laughter which gath-
ers us together around our own loss, our own death. All of which,
cannot take place unless we let ourselves go, unless we ourselves
burst out in laughter. There is no theory of laughter, there is only an
experience.
(IE 150)
We can approach community through the “experience” of the void, even
if this cannot be retained, so it does not have to be with other people that
the communication occurs—it can be with all that is “other.”371
Laughter communicates the dispelling of anguish through the sacri-
fice of the person who is being laughed at. Yet, “the one who laughs
is himself laughable and, in a profound sense, is more so than his vic-
tim…” (IE 97). As Borch-Jacobsen explains, “it is the brutal toppling
of the other into insignificance and perhaps death which reveals to me,
through laughter, my most ultimate and sovereign being, ‘the inanity of
the being that we are.’”372


156  Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
Bataille uses self-laughter as the experience of both collapse and tri-
umph, and makes of his voluntary symbolic self-immolation through
laughter the sovereign act par excellence, the sole content of his medita-
tion or mystical experience which represents for him the pinnacle of the
good life. Bataille deems the sovereign operation comical, that is, derisory,
because real sovereignty does not exist, except as failure. We become sov-
ereign in (apparently) ceasing to be. The radical recognition of sovereignty
is the collapse of the intellectual in laughter, which is the religious expe-
rience. But the religious experience is nothing else than laughing itself,
which explains how laughter is deemed “divine.” And this, I suggest, is an
unprecedented and unfollowed view of laughter, as well as of the divine.
Yet Bataille reads this philosophy into Nietzsche, with whom he believes
he has created a community—a communication—founded on a shared fear
of going mad.373 Bataille reads Nietzsche as a profoundly mystical thinker,
whose mysticism of laughter Bataille repeats. The tragic is intimately related
to laughter, that is, to joy; to laugh tragically is all that is left for us, now that
we have no purpose, no “project,” no “work.” This Bataillean Nietzsche,
read through the eyes of Kojève’s Hegel, but also through Shestov’s associa-
tion of Nietzsche with Dostoevsky, is at the origin of the laughing Nietzsche
that influenced all subsequent French philosophers, a laughing Nietzsche
that never took complete hold of the Academic English-reading public.374
Bataille appropriates what he sees as Nietzsche’s goal, emasculating Ni-
etzsche’s own vision of autonomy and freedom by reducing Nietzsche’s proj-
ect to a sham of sovereignty: in the Nietzschean highest moral goal—to be
the creator of one’s values or an autonomous individual who is at once the
“judge, the avenger, and the victim of [his] its own law”375—Bataille sees
only a will for self-destruction which is best accomplished through laughter.
Bataille also points to the difference between his method and Zen
Buddhism: he does not “imagine attaining satori without first being
overwhelmed by suffering.”376 It is this aspect of Bataille’s thought on
laughter, I suggest, the sacrificial pain involved in laughter, that seems to
make his mysticism of laughter unique.
But can laughter as we know it fulfill the role Bataille assigns to it?
Gilhus suggests that destruction and regeneration are intimately linked
in laughter:
To abandon oneself to laughter means the temporary unmaking of
one’s traditional self and the letting loose of a violence that sweeps
the outlived away, makes the body blaze and makes the world v ibrate
with life. But in the dark depths of laughter, life-giving and destruc-
tive values meet and intermingle, and ultimately these depths are
impenetrable for human thought.
(Gilhus 1997, 149; emphasis added)
I have found these two aspects of laughter helpful in illuminating Ni-
etzsche’s manifold use of laughter, first, as a destructive force in the


Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy 157
critical part of his philosophy, and later, as a regenerative force in his
positive philosophy.13 But Bataille uses these two aspects at once because
for him “divine ecstasy and extreme horror is the same: the identity of
perfect contraries.”377 Indeed, as Catherine Cusset explains, Bataille’s
writings attempt to express the “coincidence of life and death…the ab-
ject and the divine, ugliness and beauty, horror and sanctity, disgust
and veneration.”378 In the same vein, Connor sees the coincidence of
opposites as the key to Bataille’s thought and Richardson considers par-
adoxicality a reason to deem Bataille a trickster.379 As I have shown
elsewhere, laughter is a means for holding opposites together.380
Bataille differs from Zen Buddhism in one more important aspect.
Laughter for him is the sole means and the sole content of the mystical
experience. Though laughing techniques are used in one form of Zen
Buddhism as a way to quicken satori, they are preceded and followed
by years of long daily hours of meditation within the walls of a mon-
astery. Bataille’s meditation techniques do not attempt to emulate that;
he concentrates on augmenting the horror of anxiety through pictures
of torture in order to let the meaninglessness of the impalement flow
into a laughterless laughter that is ecstatic.381 Thus, laughter is not the
after- effect of a mystical experience for Bataille as it is for the laughing
Buddhas; rather, Bataille uses laughter as the sole means for his project;
and, as mystical experience for Bataille is nothing but the experience
of one’s limits, there is nothing to communicate with beyond the mys-
tical experience, thus, it is laughter itself which provides the content
of the mystical experience. Rather than a laughing mysticism, Bataille
experiences and conceptualizes a mysticism of laughter. The religious
experience is nothing but the laugh itself, and there, I suggest, is the
origin of the uniqueness of Bataille’s conception of both laughter and
the divine.382

Maurice de Gandillac: “We’re not talking about the laughter in

Platon était ce que j’avais besoin d’entendre.
(OC, VIII, 563)
 44 Shestov’s ideas can be found in Bataille’s thought. The latter’s biographer,
Michel Surya, argues that they represent the entirety of the Bataillean project.
Before meeting with Shestov, Bataille read no philosophy; he may have read
Nietzsche ideally, as a poet; yet he needed an intercessor (Surya 2002, 57).
Among the similarities between Shestov and Bataille that Surya lists, we can
find the notions of the abyss, the tragic and the impossible as well as the very
idea that one has to become Nietzsche-Zarathustra to understand Nietzsche.
These are the backbones of the differences with Shestov that Bataille would
later list. Moreover, Shestov imbued Nietzsche with significance by presenting
it in the context of the philosophies of Plotinus, Tertullian and Pascal: Shes-
tov’s Nietzsche was not only tragic, but thoroughly Christian and imbued
with Pascal, albeit a Nietzschean Pascal. Furthermore, Shestov introduced
Bataille to Dostoevsky, whom Bataille recommended to Leiris; the hero of
Dostoevsky’s Notes of the Underground had such an impact on Bataille that
he became an “impossible man, ridiculous and odious beyond limit” (Surya
2002, 61), gambling his money and life. For Shestov’s influence on Bataille,
see Surya 2002, 57–61, and Surya 1995. See also next note.

 45 Of special relevance to Bataille’s thought, see the publications of Shestov
(Chestov) on the following topics: death (1923a), Pascal (1923b), Dosto-
evsky and Nietzsche as philosophers of tragedy (1926), Kierkegaard and
existential philosophy (1936) and adogmatic thought (1927). See also the
letter he wrote to his daughters (13.04.1921) that prefaces Sur la balance de
Job: Pérégrinations à travers les âmes (1929), where he writes:
L’essentiel, précisément, consiste à ne pas déduire. C’est-à-dire à savoir
prendre la vie dans sa totalité avec toutes ses inconciliables contradic-
tions…. Aussi la révélation de la mort n’est pas une négation de la vie,
mais, au contraire, plutôt une affirmation—mais une affirmation d’autre
chose que de cet habituel remue-ménage de souris par lequel se laissent
prendre les hommes.
For the influence of Shestov on existentialism and French philosophy, see
Weingrad 2002; Vorozhikhina 2017.
 46 André Breton (1896–1966) is the poet and theoretician of Surrealism. He
introduces the notion of “black humor” in Anthologie de l' humour noir
(1940). It is a complex notion which makes use of the Surrealists’ “ob-
jective hazard,” G.W.F. Hegel’s “objective humor” and Sigmund Freud’s
views of humor and the unconscious. Through “objective hazard,” Breton
purports to understand the relationship between natural and human neces-
sities, correlatively between necessity and liberty. Objective hazard is the
encounter between external causality and internal finality. This category
enables the Surrealists to see the world as a vast network of signs and hi-
eroglyphs, to endow with sense and arguably to explain the occurrences
of these coincidences, these marvelous, strange facts and these encounters



Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy 163
of which the Surrealist poet or artist is the witness, the interpreter, or the
medium through which they manifest themselves. Breton reflects about the
latter in Freudian terms and talks about objective hazard as the form of
manifestation of external necessity which enters the unconscious. Breton
also uses Hegel’s concept of “objective humor,” broached in a few remarks
at the end of Hegel’s discussion of Romantic art. According to Hegel, Ro-
mantic art risks to stumble on two pitfalls. On the one hand, a realist con-
ception of art, which will content itself of imitating nature in its accidental
forms; on the other, humor, understood as a manifestation of the highest
degree of the personality’s need of independence. This “subjective humor”
is Romantic irony, which Hegel criticizes in Jean Paul (Richter)’s humor.
The resolution of these two tendencies is what Hegel calls objective humor.
Objective humor reaffirms the substantive, spirit absorbs itself in exter-
nal contemplation, and humor, which conserves its subjective and reflected
character, lets itself be captivated by the object. By means of “deep feel-
ing, a felicitous witticism, an ingenious reflection, and an intelligent move-
ment of the imagination, objective humor attempts to vivify and expand
the smallest details of its subject rather than destroy it.” Even so, Hegel
does not hold much hope for this type of humor, for unlike its subjective
counterpart, it becomes boring rather quickly. Divorced from “negation,”
the comic loses its charm. (For Hegel’s concepts of subjective and objective
humors, see Pillow 2000, 224–8.)
For Breton, black humor is the dialectical synthesis of objective hazard
and objective humor. Objective humor discovers in objective hazard an ex-
alting and unsettling manifestation of the external world which creates a
contradiction. In order to overcome it, and in accordance with Freud’s views
of humor, a defense mechanism is put in place which preserves the invulner-
ability of the ego. It is one of the means with which the spirit defends itself
against the ineluctable absurdity of the universe in refusing the universe any
pretension to impose itself on him. It is, for the Surrealist Belgium poet,
Achille Chavée (1906–69), the politeness of despair.
 47 Gutting 2001, 103. Albert Camus’s description of Surrealism in L’Homme
révolté (1951, 118–27) reveals its affinities with Bataille’s thought:
Absolute revolt, total insubordination, lawful sabotage, humor et the
cult of the absurd… the first intent of surrealism is defined as the trial of
everything, which has to be repeated… as Breton said rather superbly:
“Incapable of accepting the fate destined for me, affected in my highest
consciousness by this denial of justice, I am careful not to adapt my ex-
istence to the ridiculous conditions of life in this earthly existence.” He
disputes death and the “derisory duration” of a precarious condition.
(Camus 1951, 118–19; my translation)
Camus adds that Surrealism is really about love without object, the love of
broken souls (1951, 121). Anyone can transform the real into the marvel-
ous, a splendid revenge of human imagination. The marvelous occupies for
Breton the place that the rational holds for Hegel (1951, 124). The Surreal-
ists attempt to conciliate Karl Marx’s call to transform the world and the
poet Arthur Rimbaud’s call to change one’s life (1951, 125). The surreal for
Breton is a fusion of dream and reality, a sublimation of the ancient contra-
diction between the ideal and the real (1951, 126).
Especially Bataillean is the following idea, “one of fundamental the-
ses of surrealism,” that there is no redemption. Thus, the revolution, for
Breton, should purify and clarify our tragic condition in order to preclude


164 Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
the entirely artificial precarity of the social condition from masking the real
precarity of the human condition (1951, 124). The following “surrealist
solution” is Bataillean as well:
Concrete irrationality… The search for the summit-abyss (sommet-abime),
with which the mystics are familiar. In fact, it is a mysticism without God
which quenches and illustrates the absolute thirst of revolt. The main en-
emy of surrealism is rationalism. … Indeed, it is about melting the con-
tradictions in the flame of desire and love, bringing down the walls of
death. Not a politic, nor a religion, surrealism may be only an impossible
wisdom. But it’s the very proof that there is no comfortable wisdom.
(Camus 1951, 126; my translation)
As close as the Surrealists and Bataille may seem, their respective projects
explore different territories: the Surrealists explore spirit, the imaginary
and especially the unconscious; in contradistinction, Bataille grounds his
thought in an aggressive materialism, which prioritizes the body and its con-
straints as living matter.
 48 ten Kate 2000, 250.

 49 10 July 1954, in Pierre Barbier’s program “la vie des lettres,” aired on the 17
(Surya 2000, 107). While Sartre attacked Bataille, Martin Heidegger praised
him; yet, for Michael Richardson, Bataille is not an existentialist. If he is an
existentialist, he is certainly closer to precursors such as Friedrich Nietzsche
and Søren Kierkegaard for their appreciation of laughter and humor, and to
the theater of absurd, and quite different from the contemporary existen-
tialists, such as Sartre, Camus, Heidegger, whose shunning of laughter is
noteworthy. Sartre denounces the spirit of seriousness, whose traces can be
found in his notion of bad faith; yet on laughter, he has this sole comment:
“Laughter is proper to the human because he is the only animal that takes
itself seriously: hilarity denounces false earnestness in the name of genuine
true earnestness” (Sartre 1971, 821; my translation); Camus complains in a
personal conversation, related by Clément Rosset, that his sense of humor is
overlooked by readers and critics (Polac and Rosset 2003, 83). Interestingly,
philosophers of the absurd have no humor: Sartre has been deemed “among
contemporary philosophers the most obvious candidate for the title ‘Least
Humorous’” (Davenport 1976, 170). There is hardly any humor in other
existential philosophers, such as Heidegger or Karl Jaspers.
