 57 Champagne 1998, 23–4. Champagne further notes that at the same time
Bataille’s creative writings allowed him to expose “the masks of guilt, anxi-
ety, desire, frustration, joy, mysticism, and loneliness.” He explains the sig-
nificance of masks for Bataille. Mentioning Descartes’s motto, which was
later endorsed by Roland Barthes, “I advance pointing to my mask” (lar-
vatus prodeo), Bataille believed that “the mask allows the individual to dis-
place the individuation of personal death and the anguish of the proximity
of the abyss” (Champagne 1998, 101). A key element in such stories as Ma
Mère, the mask is commented on in “L’Alleliuah: le catéchisme de Dianus”:



Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy 165
“What appears to be desirable is masked; the mask falls one day or another
when what is unmasked is anguish, death, and the annihilation of the per-
ishable being” (OC, V, 402). Necessary to disguise insecurity, “the mask
retains the force of appearing on the threshold of this clear and reassuring
world of anxiety as an indistinct incarnation of chaos” (OC, II, 403); both
quotations are translated by Champagne (1998, 82–3).
 58 Referring to “the subject of Bataillean thought,” Drew Wright gives a
compelling description of what being laughter itself may mean. He makes
use of Foucault’s endorsement of the Bataillean notion of transgression,
which posits “a curious intersection of beings that have no other life be-
yond this moment where they totally exchange their beings” (1998, 34),
and argues:

The subject of Bataillean thought is the subject caught in the “difluvial
flood” of laughter’s spell, a subject which, in bursting (into laughter) and
therein becoming suddenly disengaged from the “profane” world of la-
bor, reason, and discourse, is nothing but this oceanic torrent of lightness
in whose high tide of consumption the subject is awash… The Bataillean
subject, as such, is the contagion of “communication,” and its essential
epistemological gesture is to fall into the excess of laughter. Head thrown
back and mouth irrepressibly agape, the subject of Bataille’s “impossible
thought” is the spitting image of impropriety: a subject which is, in a
sense, nothing but the sputtering opening of a mouth that insists on itself
(i.e. its opening), a subject vehemently exposing its own excesses like the
exuberant parting of lips exhibiting fluids, teeth, and tongue. The subject
shaken in the spell of Bataillean thought would thus appear a body bound
by alterity, held together by a gesticulating choreography of fragments,
an unrecognizable voice, full of sound and fury, acousmatically rupturing
the soundscape while disfiguring the ordered austerity of the face, body
and voice doubling over each other in rabid, ejaculatory waves that foam
over the exorbitantly exposed buccal recesses, signifying nothing.
(Wright 2017, 9–10)

on the margins of the World War II” (Irwin 2002, xviii; emphasis added).

 214 Stoekl 1995, 79. See the illuminating account Irwin gives of the “comedy”
of the “religious suicide” that Bataille describes, his own and the one in-
volved in the mediation on death of the Tibetan monk (2002, 259). The
hermit “gives himself over to a ‘comedy’ of sacrifice” (OC, VIII, 258–90).
Through the sacrificial “comedy,” the “Tibetan ascetic” lives his own
death: “He dies in seeing himself die—that is, consciously—and even, in
a certain way, by his own will” (HDS 19). This “comedy” or “simulacra”
(2002, 258) are the way to a deeper truth, Irvin notes, because they initiate
a genuine accord with death. Bataille was also fascinated by Vincent van
Gogh’s tendency to self-immolate and the sun’s influence on it, as well as
Aztec sacrifices to the sun-god and the classical Greek model of Icarus
(Champagne 1998, 63).

233 See, for example, Andrew Hussey’s alignment of laughter with eroticism
and tears: “The ‘alleluia,’ or ‘awakening to laughter,’ or eroticism, or tears,

172 Georges Bataille—The Laughter of Ecstasy
of philosophy as well as being the ‘trial by death’” (Hussey 2000, 159); or
Alexander Irwin, who by listing on equal terms laughter as well as tears,
drunkenness and sexuality does not single out laughter as the main feature
of inner experience or meditation:
The new avatars of sacrifice include all behaviors that unleash the affec-
tive power of communication, dissolving rigid boundaries and catalyzing
a compenetration of object and subject, self and other: Bataille’s lists of
such comportments include laughter, tears, drunkenness, sexuality (OC,
V, 391). Yet the most crucial modes of contemporary sacrifice, inexplica-
bly interwoven, are inner experience (mediation) and writing.
(Irwin 2002, 32)
See also the Editor’s Introduction to the useful anthology of Bataille’s
writings, The Unfinished System of Nonknowledge: “Laughter is one
among many such distinctly human ‘inner experiences,’… ‘one among
many effusions, one among many deliriums, one among many means to
the impossible’—alongside erotic ecstasy, tears, art, sacrifice—that attests
to immediacy as that which is ‘essential to experience’” (Kendall 2001,
xxxix). Only in more recent studies, such as Frédéric-Charles Baitinger’s
article and Drew Wright’s Master’s thesis did I find an explicit reference in
the former and an argument in the latter to the privilege of laughter over
other sovereign moments (Baitinger 2015, 224; Wright 2017).

 238 It is significant that the passage continues less joyously:

For a long time I knew nothing other than chaotic euphoria. After only
a few years, I felt the chaos—an accurate image of various beings in
a state of incoherence—gradually becoming suffocating. I was broken,
undone, from having laughed too much, such that, depressed, I found
myself: the inconsistent monster which I was, empty of sense and of will,
frightened me.
(IE 66)
This quote comes from the third part of Inner Experience, tellingly titled,
“Antecedents to the Torment (or the Comedy).”

To interpret a text, I believe, always amounts to evaluating its humor. A
great author is somebody who laughs a lot.
Gilles Deleuze, “Proust Round Table,” Two Regimes of Madness.
In truth, there are never contradictions, apparent or real, but only de-
grees of humour.
(Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, Anti-Oedipus 1983, 68)
Humor is inseparable from a selective force: in that which occurs (an
accident), it selects the pure event… Bousquet listed the characteristics
of the humor-actor (“l’humour-acteur”): …to liberate for each thing “its
immaculate portion,” language and will, Amor Fati…This is the solu-
tion of humor, quite different from the romantic irony of the person still
founded upon the identity of contraries.
(Gilles Deleuze, Logic of Sense, 151, 157)
Gilles Deleuze (1925–95) describes himself as “a classic philosopher,” a
“pure metaphysician,” who is doing “philosophy, nothing but philoso-
phy, in the traditional sense of the word.”1 He ignores the proclamation
of philosophy’s death and devises a metaphysics that corresponds to the
findings of contemporary science and mathematics; it is a process meta-
physics, whose notions of multiplicity, event and virtuality replace the
more conventional terms of substance, essence and possibility.2
Deleuze is renowned for a number of important monographs on the
history of philosophy and for his writings on the various arts which
introduce concepts that correspond to the artistic practices of paint-
ers, filmmakers and writers.3 Félix Guattari, the radical psychoanalyst
and political activist, collaborated with Deleuze from 1968 onward.
Together, they wrote several works which are significant for the devel-
opment of Deleuze’s ethical and political thought.4 Antedating these
contributions, Deleuze’s interest in novel thought is exemplified by his
early publications, which he later requested to remove from his official
bibliography.5 His first article, “Description of Woman: For a Philoso-
phy of the Sexed Other,” is a pastiche on Jean-Paul Sartre.6
2
Gilles Deleuze—The Humor
of Affirmation
DOI: 10.4324/9780429506116-4


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  191
Deleuze knew both Georges Bataille and Clément Rosset, disliking
the former and befriending the latter for reasons that would be clarified
below.7 Michel Foucault thought highly of Deleuze, believing that “one
day, perhaps, this century will be known as Deleuzian.”8 Deleuze’s work
has already enjoyed a considerable influence both inside and outside the
academe as well as a growing influence in philosophy.9
To answer the question that this chapter addresses, what is the role
of humor in the Deleuzian good life? we need to comprehend Deleuze’s
thought. This task is challenging for various interconnected reasons. Let
me begin with those which are the most relevant to this study, such as
Deleuze’s characteristic sense of humor, the unusual way in which he
uses the notions of the comic and its cognates, and the paucity of ac-
counts of humor in Deleuze’s studies despite the centrality of this notion
in his thought.
First, Deleuze’s friends, colleagues and students noted his char-
acteristic sense of humor. Reflected in his works, and noticeable in
his lectures and the sole videotaped interview he left,10 his humor
often obscures rather than clarifies the content of his thought. Yet it
pervades his work, as both Deleuze and his commentators acknowl-
edge. The Logic of Sense, for example, is described by Deleuze as “a
cheerful book”11 and by scholars as artistic and humorous; some of
them see humor and creative experimentation as necessary for get-
ting the work’s deepest insights.12 Similarly, Manfred Frank notes
the “consciously Dadaist and carnivalesque style” of the two volumes
that Deleuze wrote with Guattari, Capitalism and Schizophrenia; and
commenting on the performative effect of humor in Anti-Oedipus,
Daniel Smith and John Protevi remark on how “very few philosophy
books contain as many jokes, puns, and double entendres.”13 Deleuze
and Guattari claim that “together” they would like to be “the Humpty
Dumpty of Philosophy” or its “Laurel and Hardy,” and maintain
that the circular form they give to A Thousand Plateaux is “only for
laughs.”14 Finally, in relation to his work as a whole, Deleuze discloses
that he aims at creating “a counter-philosophy of the schizophrenic
laughter and revolutionary joy of the great books,” a philosophy
which “gets the giggles, which wipe away its tears” at the competing
commercial concepts.15
Second, Deleuze’s contribution to the study of the comic, laughter and
humor lies in the central roles he assigns to these terms within his phi-
losophy, once he redefines them to fit its goal or conceptualizes some of
them as characters or “conceptual personae.”16 For example, his dis-
cussion of cinematic comedy does not contain an explicit account of the
role of the comic or the comedic, as Lisa Trahair notes; still, Russell Ford
shows how comedy is intrinsically associated with Deleuze’s philosoph-
ical project: it “facilitates a morally relevant experience” for the French
philosopher, “an experience of wonder at a world that is not organized
by the concepts and judgments of subjectivity.”17 This is no small feat,


192  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
as the scope of the Deleuzian comic is enriched by his view of the tragic,
which is partly converted into the comical: the tragic is first categorized
as sad or joyous; the former is discarded on account of its sadness, and
the latter is transformed into the comical owing to the Nietzschean as-
sociation of joy and laughter with the tragic.
Deleuze does not use often the term “laughter,” except when account-
ing for the thought of (the Deleuzian) Nietzsche and the ensuing associ-
ation of laughter with the tragic. He quickly reverts to irony and humor,
as defined by Henri Bergson in Laughter: An Essay on the Meaning of
the Comic, in order to introduce these notions as necessary forms of
thought. Briefly adding satire to the discussion of comical forms, he nev-
ertheless rejects both satire and irony in favor of humor. Thus, Deleuze’s
preferred form of laughter is always humor—an explicit and emphatic
position he holds in all of his writings and interviews, and a virtue he
ascribes to almost all the philosophers and writers he likes.18 However,
the role of humor in Deleuze’s work is uncharted territory. Humor is
rarely addressed in the extensive critical literature on Deleuze;19 it is not
indexed in the English translation of Logique du sens as an indepen-
dent topic (despite its explicit presence in a text which includes a series
called “Humor”). Yet on the topic of humor, Deleuze’s significance is
unmistakable: not only does it play a crucial role in Deleuze’s philoso-
phy, as Giorgio Baruchello argues, it may be further qualified, accord-
ing to Jean-Claude Dumoncel, as an attitude that animates the whole
of Deleuze’s philosophy and “which can be compared to the role irony
plays in Socratic thought.”20
Additional hurdles to understanding Deleuze’s view of the good life,
in relation to content as well as style, could be listed. These include
his frequent references to additional fields, the multiple versions of his
philosophy, the changes of terminology in each work, the problem of
differentiating between the historical interpretations he offers and the
philosophy he advances, the resistance to common sense his metaphysics
displays, the opacity of his ethics and politics, and the allusiveness of his
style. Let me elaborate on these hurdles.
The extent of Deleuze’s references to additional fields should be noted
first. These include differential calculus, thermodynamics, geology, mo-
lecular biology, population genetics, etiology, embryology, anthropol-
ogy, psychoanalysis, economics, linguistics and esoteric thought.21 Far
from being mere references, moreover, Deleuze’s excursions into various
fields and many philosophical systems enable Deleuze to present multiple
versions of his philosophy. To that purpose, he appropriates the philo-
sophical vocabularies of Humean empiricism and Foucaultian archaeol-
ogy, mathematical terminologies of set theory and differential geometry,
and aesthetic expressions derived from the novels of Marcel Proust and
the paintings of Francis Bacon, among other works. As Deleuze assumes
that the reader is familiar with literary and philosophical works, both


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  193
ancient and modern, he does not necessarily elaborate on the views he
uses, such as the scholastic philosophy of John Dun Scotus.
Furthermore, Deleuze changes his terminology in every book he
 authors,22 at times borrowing terms from, or ascribing them to other
philosophers. Thus, the question of the content of this philosophy, or
what is being asserted, is further complicated by the question of the
authorship, or who is asserting it. Indeed, Deleuze’s career begun with a
variety of historical studies, which indicate in retrospect the adumbra-
tion of his own standpoint through his reflection on classical themes.
The Stoics, Lucretius, David Hume, Bergson, Nietzsche, Benedict Spi-
noza and Immanuel Kant provide much of the materials Deleuze em-
ploys. While publishing carefully crafted, systematic and sympathetic23
accounts of these philosophers’ thought, he uses an imperative tone in
guiding the reader through these theories24 while altering them in more
than one way. Not only does he emphasize selected themes at the ex-
pense of others, even at the price of ignoring vital aspects of the philos-
ophy he presents, but his account also diverges from the philosophy at
hand: he either reads it through the lenses of another philosopher,25 or
presents it as directed against other philosophers,26 or uses it to formu-
late his own agenda without explicitly acknowledging his alterations or
contributions.27
This recurring procedure has been denounced at the outset by aca-
demic philosophers, yielding reactions ranging from unease to indig-
nation.28 Nor does Deleuze deny that he indeed proceeds in that way;
to the contrary, he acknowledges it as a deliberate attempt to create a
“monstrous child” by taking these philosophers “from behind”; this en-
abled him to innovate despite being compelled to write on the history of
philosophy as the philosophical establishment required.29 An account
of Deleuze’s thought should begin by clarifying this procedure, which
bears both on the methodology Deleuze uses and on our reading of his
philosophy. As this topic exceeds the introduction’s purpose, I clarify
it below, at the beginning of my elaboration of Deleuze’s philosophy.30
Even if we use the historical studies to understand Deleuze’s thought
rather than the philosophers he portrays, Deleuze does not clarify how
his thought progresses from one work to another. Thus, Michael Hardt
rightly notes that “Deleuze’s explanations appear incomplete,”31 be-
cause he takes the results of previous research for granted.
Additional barriers to understanding Deleuze’s thought involve con-
tent as well as style. Deleuze’s metaphysics has been diagnosed by James
Williams as offering a “profound resistance to common sense” and “to
the association of reality with representations based on the empirical
sciences.”32 Not only is the very existence of Deleuzian ethics and pol-
itics a matter of controversy, those who recognize such dimensions in
his thought point to their opacity.33 Finally, Deleuze’s allusive style,
which uses neologisms and additional terminological innovations that


194  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
shift from one work to the other, is yet another barrier for mainstream
philosophers.34
Claire Colebrook argues that the difficulty of Deleuze’s texts is tac-
tical as “his works attempt to capture (but not completely) the chaos of
life”:
Instead of providing yet one more system of terms and ideas Deleuze
wanted to express the dynamism and instability of thought. He re-
invented his style and vocabulary with each project. No term in his
work is capable of being defined in itself; any single term makes
sense only in its relation to the whole which it helps to create. For
this reason, reading Deleuze is not an easy task.
(Colebrook 2002a, 4)
However arduous the reading of Deleuze may be for the various reasons
listed above, it is not possible to make sense of the Deleuzian view of hu-
mor outside the manifold aspects of his complex philosophy as variously
exposed in all of his works, including lectures and interviews. As we
shall see, humor is intertwined with every topic that Deleuze holds dear
and is itself transformed into a Deleuzian creative concept which is part
of the characters or conceptual personae his philosophy enacts. I argue
that Deleuze uses humor as a philosophical concept, which side-steps
all the innovations his philosophy offers. He explicitly entrusts humor
with a unique role in the good life he proposes, which is to enable the
transformation that defines that life. In this capacity, humor’s role can
hardly be differentiated from philosophy itself, conceived by Deleuze
as a paradoxical endeavor aiming at emancipation, transformation and
affirmation; humor constitutes the Deleuzian-specific contribution to
the tradition of amor fati that he endorses.35 Thus, humor cannot be
dissociated from the aim of Deleuze’s ethics, which is also the purpose
of his philosophy. The Deleuzian affirmation of life is effectuated by
self-directed laughter that transmutes suffering into joy; the affirmation
of multiplicity is signified by roars of laughter; humor is the main tool of
vice-diction in Difference and Repetition and of counter-actualization
in The Logic of Sense, these notions being the key to Deleuze’s ethics
of amor fati, as that which enables the selection necessary for eternal
return.
In order to answer the question this chapter addresses, what is the
role of humor in the Deleuzian good life? I introduce Deleuze’s view
of the good life, followed by his views of the comic also in relation to
the tragic, and of humor, along with irony and satire. I emphasize his
rejection of irony and satire in favor of humor, and elaborate on the role
Deleuze gives to the latter in his philosophy of mind, his aesthetics and
politics, and especially in his ethics. In the concluding remarks that end


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  195
this chapter, I evaluate the viability of Deleuze’s notion of humor and the
originality of his partiality for humor over irony.
I The Good Life
Deleuze is party to the general theme of difference which is fundamen-
tal for all poststructuralists, who are in principle wary of thought that
reduces diverse elements to the sameness of unifying concepts or theo-
ries. His philosophy develops out of two fundamental convictions, one
of being, the other of the thinking whereby being is grasped. The first
conviction is that being is radically diverse; the second is that, corre-
spondingly, thought is a recognition of ontological diversity rather than
a reduction to unity.
Deleuze changes his terminology in every book he authors.36 One of
his most significant and prevalent notions, multiplicity, a group of diverse
elements, emerges from the historical studies he has undertaken which
indicate in retrospect the adumbration of his own thought through his
reflection on classical themes. Deleuze draws on the Stoics, Lucretius,
Hume, Bergson, Nietzsche, Spinoza and Kant to get the materials he
needs to enact his vision of reality as a flux of irreducible plurality.
Paul Patton courteously refers to “the dual and paradoxical relation-
ship which characterizes all of Deleuze’s accounts of other philosophers,
and which involves both faithful rendering and deliberate forcing of the
original text.”37 This attitude is described by Deleuze in less elegant
terms: he conceives of his relationship with the main figures of the his-
tory of philosophy as a kind of “buggery” or “immaculate conception”
in which he imagines himself “taking an author from behind and giving
him a child that would be his offspring, yet monstrous.” Deleuze ex-
plains that it mattered that it should be the author’s child, “because the
author had to actually say all I had him saying.” However, “the child
was bound to be monstrous too, because it resulted from all sorts of
shifting, slipping, dislocations, and hidden emissions that I really en-
joyed.”38 The context may explain this shocking confession. Accused of
“being stuck,” and specializing in the history of philosophy as French
professors were expected to, Deleuze defends himself by qualifying his
attitude to the thought of others as perverse.39
The nature of Deleuze’s attitude toward philosophers becomes the fo-
cus of David Lapoujade’s study. In Deleuze, les mouvements abérrants
(Deleuze: The Aberrant Movements, 2014), Lapoujade argues that the
aberrant movement is the defining characteristic of Deleuzian philos-
ophy as a whole.40 Deleuze prides himself on this procedure, singling
out his book on Bergson as exemplary.41 He notes, however, that since
with Nietzsche such a procedure is impossible, his encounter with the
German philosopher changed the manner in which he engages with the


196  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
history of philosophy.42 Yet such dislocations as Deleuze admits are eas-
ily perceived in his studies not only of Bergson,43 but also of Nietzsche44
and Spinoza.45
The question is, why would a commentator take such liberties? This
is all the more puzzling as Deleuze prides himself on bringing joy to the
philosophers of the past:
My ideal, when I write about an author, would be to write nothing
that could give him sadness, or if he dead, that might make him
weep in his grave. Think of the author you are writing about. Think
of him so hard that he can no longer be an object, and equally so
that you cannot identify with him. Avoid the double shame of the
scholar and the familiar. Give back to an author a little of the joy,
the energy, the life of love and politics that he knew how to give and
invent.
(D 119)
This recommendation is coupled with Deleuze’s view that there are no
genuine “difficulties” in an author; interpretations and criticisms should
be rejected.46 Thus, the commentary of the history of philosophy is an
activity that is fundamentally protective if not repairing.47
Deleuze’s devise “Experiment, don’t interpret!”  is not advanced in
the introductions to the books on the history of philosophy he penned;
on the contrary, these are written in the authoritative voice of a guide,
in the imperative tense of showing the right way and a dismissive atti-
tude toward (other) interpretations.49 One can also doubt the joy the
philosophers would feel in witnessing the avowed violation of their
thought.50
48
Deleuze addresses in an interview the procedure he uses with figures
of the philosophical canon. He gives the following explanation, which
a few scholars report: in the same way that a painter, obsessed with
colors, is wary of using them, a philosopher does not dare to express
his philosophy; instead of creating his own concepts he portrays the
concepts of others.51 The contradictions between the above statements,
Deleuze’s good intentions and apparent honesty, on the one hand, and
acknowledged results, on the other, are resolved by most commentators
as follows: Deleuze always reflects with other philosophers rather than
about them; his commentaries on philosophers are as much an account
of his own thought as an exposition of theirs.52 Moreover, the historical
texts are important for understanding Deleuze’s thought; each of these
texts is a fragment of his philosophy, which can also be read as a tool
for understanding one of philosophy’s possible becomings, hidden under
the names of Hume, Nietzsche or Spinoza.53 Furthermore, some com-
mentators avail themselves to Deleuzian terms to describe his utilization
of the concepts of other philosophers as “re-actualizations rather than


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  197
re-presentations,” or as “a systematic virtualization of the history of
philosophy as a mode of actualizing that is infinitely variable.”54
Hardt frankly asserts that “Deleuze’s early work constructs an odd
sort of history of philosophy in which the connecting links depend not
on actual philosophical historiography but on the evolution of Deleuze’s
own thought.”55 Thus, in his commentary on Deleuze’s early philosophy
(1993), Hardt always qualifies as “Deleuzian” all references to (the lat-
ter’s accounts of) Nietzsche, Spinoza, Bergson or any other philosopher
Deleuze addresses.56
The more positive statement that can be gathered from Deleuze’s ac-
count of his relationship with the history of philosophy is the following:
he loves the philosophers who opposed the rationalist tradition. Between
Lucretius, Hume, Spinoza and Nietzsche he denotes “a secret link con-
stituted by the criticism of the negative, the culture of joy, the hatred of
interiority, the exteriority of forces and of relations, the denunciation
of power, etc.”57 He does not mention Bergson, the philosopher of joy,
from whom he draws his ontology. Most importantly, he reveals that
what he detests above all is Hegelianism and the dialectic.
At the end of 1960s, in Difference and Repetition and The Logic of
Sense, Deleuze turned from historical adumbrations to full-blown expo-
sitions of his philosophy on its own terms. Although Deleuze does not
entirely abandon the language of multiplicity that he used in his former
books, two parallel terms, difference (in Difference and Repetition) and
event (in The Logic of Sense) take on a dominant role. Deleuze’s “dif-
ference” is the key to his radical reformulation of the classical problem
of the one and the many. He objects to the assumption that there must
be principles of unity or forms, whatever their ontological status, which
constitute the essential nature of concrete realities. His positive ontolog-
ical project is to develop concepts and language that express the view
that “the thing differs with itself first, immediately,” that to be is to be
different.58
In The Logic of Sense, he appropriates the anti-Platonic Stoic distinc-
tion of bodies and events, according to which events are the locus of
incorporeal meanings that do not exist in a separate Platonic realm but
instead “float” on the surfaces of substantial bodies, of which they are
the epiphenomenal effects. Understanding events in this way, The Logic
of Sense continues, in another key, the metaphysics of intensities and
ideas developed in Difference and Repetition.
Of special importance for the development of Deleuze’s ethical and
political thought are his two major collaborative works with Guattari,
L’Anti-Œdipe (1972) and Mille plateaux (1980), presented as the two
parts of an overall project entitled Capitalisme et schizophrénie. The
focus on social and political issues corresponds to Deleuze’s turn to mil-
itant political activism, particularly in Foucault’s Groupe d’Information
Prison and in support of Palestinian rights.59


198  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
In order to understand Deleuze’s view of the good life, I first introduce
his ontology, followed by an account of the main notions he is known for,
difference and repetition. I then examine his attitude toward Nietzsche
and compare it with Bataille’s, I elaborate on further notions, such as
thinking and sense, and I end this part with an account of Deleuze’s
ethics which culminates in a version of amor fati that is indissociable
from humor.
A Ontology
Deleuze develops in Difference and Repetition and The Logic of Sense
a process metaphysics of events, intensities and ideas. Process philoso-
phy reflects a line of thought that can be traced back in the history of
philosophy to the days of the pre-Socratics. Its leading exponents are
Heraclitus, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Henri Bergson, Charles Pierce,
William James, Alfred North Whitehead and his school (Charles Harts-
horne, Paul Weiss), but also additional philosophers such as Samuel
Alexander and C. Lloyd Morgan. This variant line of thought contra-
dicts the marked bias of Western metaphysics from Aristotle on, which
concentrates on perduring physical things as existents in nature. This
prejudiced focus slights the equally good claims of another ontological
category, namely, processes, events, occurrences—items better indicated
by verbs than nouns—which are the object of process metaphysics.60
The “profound resistance to common sense and to the association
of reality with representations based on the empirical sciences,” which
Williams finds in Deleuze’s philosophy may partly explain why the task
of clarifying his philosophy is so arduous.61 In what follows, I rely on
Williams’s enlightening guides to Deleuze’s ontology.62
The key to Deleuze’s ontology, according to Williams, is the reality of
two intertwining flows—the one virtual, the other actual—that make
up processes. There is no sense of speaking of the virtual without the ac-
tual or the reverse. “For Deleuze, the things that operate in the processes
that bring us about and make us into individuals are not actual objects
and the knowledge we may gain of them”; rather, “they are the sensual
variations and the variations in ideas that take place in order for actual
things to gain a living significance for us.” Moreover, individuals are not
necessarily well-defined human individuals: the individual is
A series of processes that connect actual things, thoughts, and sen-
sations to the pure intensities and ideas implied by them…. A pure
difference is transferable through very different actual things, and
depends on them only for its expression, not for its essence. A pure
difference has to be actualized, but it is not the only thing that be-
comes actualized.
(Williams 2003, 7)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  199
This realm of pure becomings Deleuze calls the virtual, while becomings
are referred to as “intensities” and “ideas.” Ideas are not contained in
the mind; they are rather relations between things in the virtual, which
are the conditions for the evolution of actual things. They should be
distinguished from our common perception of ideas as any identifiable
thought about something. Deleuze defines an idea as an “n- dimensional
well-defined and continuous multiplicity,” where the dimension is the
number of variations and where the variations are continuous, that is,
involve no discrete steps. The multiplicity is, therefore, a structure of
elements defined as things in continuous variation that are resistant
to identification: relations between those elements; relations between
those relations and actual relations; and relations between the elements
and actual forms and terms. Finally, the elements of ideas are pure
differences.
Virtual ideas are the conditions for changes in actual ideas; however,
they should not be confused with them. The idea cannot be known,
only sensed and known partially as it is expressed. The idea is resis-
tant to identification as an object of knowledge because its elements are
pure differences that cannot be identified; they can only be deduced on
the basis of sensations. All ideas “coexist,” but this co-existence is a
differentiated one. Deleuze uses “differentiated” in a highly specialized
manner: it does not mean “different,” in the sense of “opposed”; rather,
it involves various or different degrees with respect to pure difference or
variations. Clarity and obscurity or light and shadow are the metaphors
which are used to convey differences in degree in a whole that cannot be
separated into distinct zones. Ideas are differentiated because they are
differently lit versions of the whole of ideas. Deleuze calls this interrela-
tion of ideas their perplication, which is explained in terms of the way in
which intensities envelop one another.
This sense of folding avoids possible misinterpretations of the light and
shadow metaphor: that which is left obscure in an idea is neither unimport-
ant nor intrinsically threatening—it is merely combined in a less intense
way. Things can be only more or less obscure or they can be more or less
clear, they cannot be distinct, according to Deleuze. Those things which
are necessarily connected to a clearly appearing thing are condemned to
obscurity. Therefore, as Williams explains, a truthful understanding of any
one thing is beyond our reach. Coming to the fore for a thing depends on
the fading into the background of many other things. Moreover, that which
is left obscure by an idea is more important that that which is made clear.
For example, the connectedness of one idea with other ideas is hidden while
the well-marked difference from other ideas comes to the fore:
The virtual is made up of Ideas and intensities, the actual consists of
actual things, or actualities. The only things that can be considered
real are both actual and virtual, made up of Ideas, intensities, and


200  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
actual things; these are individuals and signs, where signs prompt
the evolution of individuals
(Williams 2013, 242)
Deleuze’s notion of ideas and intensities seems to preclude precise defi-
nitions; yet it is presupposed by actual things. They are necessary and
well-determined only as relations.
An idea is a multiplicity of relations between pure variations. The
relation between ideas is one of clarity and obscurity—that is, ideas can
be differentiated according to the different clarity and obscurity of their
elements, where clarity comes from being at the center, in the sense of
greatest number of connections, of a nexus of relations and obscurity
from a peripheral position.
Intensities are determined by relations of envelopment with other in-
tensities. “Intensities envelop or cover one another—that is, intensities
can be differentiated according to the way in which some take the fore-
ground whilst others move to the background, but without in themselves
changing in intensity.”63 These relations of envelopment bring different
virtual ideas into greater clarity and obscurity.
Williams concludes that Deleuze argues for the reality of things which
we cannot identify and which are not actual. We need intensities of pure
becomings to explain both significance and sensations in the realm of
actual things; however, these intensities should be outside that realm.
Sensation and significance would be secondary to external structures of
measurement and value if intensities were measurable and comparable,
that is, identifiable. As Deleuze believes that sensation and significance
are uniquely significant to individuals, or incomparable events, he resists
such moves. As Williams explains:
Intensities are a necessary condition for explanations of why life is
significant but uniquely so for each individual. As such, intensities
could not be identifiable as comparable qualities of actual experi-
ences and objects.
(Williams 2013, 8)
Actual things cause one another to change, but that causal explanation
is not sufficient for understanding reality and evolution. Any actual
event is significant because it is the expression of a change in the envel-
opment of intensities and in the clarity and obscurity of ideas. Deleuze
exemplifies this two-sided structure of reality in relation to death, which
is an important theme in his philosophy.64 Death has two faces, an ac-
tual death, the ceasing of the heartbeat or of activity in the brain, but
also a series of virtual deaths, the way in which our becomings lead us
to change irrevocably.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  201
Deleuze insists that being is univocal. That is, no event or phenomenon
is more real than any other. There is only one being, so that perceptions,
anticipations, memories and fictions are as real as atoms, universals,
concepts or bodies. Deleuze claims that only with univocity there can
be real difference. In Difference and Repetition, Deleuze describes an
alternative history of philosophy comprising those philosophers daring
enough to think of being as univocal, such as John Duns Scotus, Spinoza
and Nietzsche.65 If philosophy has been dominated by Platonism, this
is because being has been understood as equivocal. Equivocity means
that only one being truly is, while other beings are dependent, second-
ary, either not truly substances or different types of substance. Mind
is elevated above matter, original is elevated above copy, the actual is
the privileged and proper locus of the potential, only the actual is real
or proper being, while the potential cannot be said to exist in the same
sense. Against this equivocity, Deleuze argues for univocity:
Being is univocal, equal. In other words, every entity is equally be-
ing, in the sense that each actualizes its power in immediate vicinity
with the first cause. The distant cause is no more: rocks, flowers,
animals, and humans equally celebrate the glory of God in a kind of
sovereign an-archy.
(TRM 261)
Once univocity’s work was done, Deleuze moved on.66 This exemplifies
that which Daniel Smith identifies as the “dynamic nature of Deleuze’s
thought, which must be defined and comprehended in terms of its move-
ment.”67 I address now the notions of difference and repetition, which
have made Deleuze famous and which are indissociable from his reading
of Nietzsche.
B Difference and Repetition
Deleuze believes that only Nietzsche overcomes the equivocal definition
of being and its relation to judgment by insisting that being is only in
the modes. To be is to become, and things only acquire identity because
they become, because they express pure variations. Deleuze believes that
Nietzsche prepares the way for the revelation of the eternal return but
that due to lack of time he does not disclose the revelation itself.68
According to Deleuze, the idea of eternal return is that repetition and
difference are the same thing; what is repeated is difference.69 He sees
Nietzsche’s work as fundamentally anti-dialectical and argues that it
cannot be fully understood outside the context of its vehement opposition
to Hegel: anti-Hegelianism runs through the Deleuzian Nietzsche’s work
like a thread of aggressiveness.70 Hegelian dialectic operates through


202  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
a process of negation and assimilation, as its thesis is contradicted by
an antithesis, both of which are sublated into a synthesis. According to
Deleuze, Nietzsche proposes the affirmation of difference over against
its Hegelian assimilation through negation and contradiction: “For the
speculative element of negation, opposition or contradiction, Nietzsche
substitutes the practical element of difference: object of affirmation and
pleasure.”71
The ultimate goal of Nietzsche’s philosophy is, for Deleuze, the lib-
eration of thought from nihilism as represented within dialectic by the
reactive categories of identity and negation. Since traditional thought in
philosophy and science is largely predicated upon nihilism, the primacy
of identity and negation, this project implies the elaboration of a new
way of thinking and inquiring which affirms difference and expels the
negative.
Before this philosophy of the future can be fully realized, however,
a radical break with tradition is required. The means of achieving this
break is the thought of eternal return. For Deleuze, eternal return chal-
lenges the notions of teleology and identity which are central to tradi-
tional metaphysics. First, by substituting cyclical for linear time, eternal
return abolishes all goals. This is essentially a re-statement of the po-
sition articulated by Bataille in the 1930s and 1940s.72 Second, for
Deleuze, eternal return does not mean the eternal return of the same.
This is the innovative aspect of his reading of this doctrine in his 1962
publication, Nietzsche et la philosophie, where Deleuze interprets eter-
nal return as the principle of the reproduction of diversity and of the
repetition of difference.73
Such a reading rests on the proposition that eternal return is selective,
and that it eliminates the negative and reactive because they lack the
strength to repeat themselves, while at the same time it preserves that
which actively affirms and differentiates.74 This affirming and differ-
entiating principle is the will to power. Thus, because it promotes will
to power eternal return affords us with the means of transforming hu-
manity into the Übermensch. Such an understanding of eternal return
is highly indebted to Klossowski interpretation and also represents a
Deleuzian reading of the Bergsonian ideal of going beyond the human
condition.75
In spite of the innovative interpretation of eternal return, the aspect of
Nietzsche’s work which Deleuze isolates as its crux in 1962 is the account
of the relationship between active and reactive forces—in Nietzsche’s ter-
minology, between the aristocratic and slave moralities explored in On
the Genealogy of Morals. The main reason for this emphasis is that it is
in this work that Nietzsche offers an alternative analysis of the master-
slave relation to the one associated with Hegel. In contrast to Hegel’s
account of this relation as dialectical, a reciprocal and reversible rela-
tionship in which positions may be exchanged, Nietzsche appears to in-
sist on the difference between the master and the slave as a difference


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  203
of essence rather than one of position—the master is deemed essentially
different from the slave. The two are definitely separated by what Ni-
etzsche calls the “pathos of distance” (Pathos der Distanz).76
In the lecture at the 1964 Royaumont conference on Nietzsche,
Deleuze emphasizes how in Nietzsche’s work the conflict of differential
forces, active and reactive, dissolves the notion of individual identity. In
the same conference, Klossowski indicates how eternal return works to
the same end, not by relentlessly subdividing the “indivisible” individual
but by introducing difference into identity through its repetition over
time.77 Extending this interpretation, Deleuze goes on to suggest that
eternal return does not presuppose a prior identity on the part of what is
to return, but in fact produces identity as an affect of that very return.78
Thus, it is in returning that the different resembles itself or acquires an
identity. Difference precedes and is prior to the identity it reproduces
through repetition: the world of eternal return is a world of intensity, a
world of differences, which presupposes neither the One nor the Same,
but is constructed on the tomb of one God as on the ruins of the identi-
cal self. Eternal return itself is the sole unity of this world which is only
unified through “recurrence,” the sole identity of a world which is only
the “same” through “repetition.”79
This view of difference and repetition finds expression in Difference
and Repetition, which extends the anti-Hegelian project of Deleuze’s
earlier work. Continuing his critique of the concept of dialectical nega-
tion, this critique is now supplemented by another attack on the philo-
sophical tradition, specifically on the order of identity and representation
which Deleuze associates with Plato. Reversing Platonism is therefore a
matter of rehabilitating the simulacrum, thereby subverting the world of
representation. As in his Royaumont closing statement of 1964, Deleuze
identifies this reversal of priority and consequent loss of grounding as
a Nietzschean moment and associates it closely with the idea of eternal
return.80According to Deleuze, the idea of eternal return has both a
manifest and a latent content. Its manifest content is its capacity to or-
ganize chance and give form to the arbitrary, while its latent content is
its tendency to affirm chance and the arbitrary even as it simulates order
and necessity. For Deleuze, eternal return reverses the premises of the
order of representation by excluding everything which presupposes iden-
tity and resemblance and including anything which promotes difference
and divergence.81
In Difference and Repetition, Deleuze expands on the relationship
between eternal return and the collapse of representation and identity.
For Deleuze, the Nietzschean declaration of the death of God is short-
hand for this very collapse.82 The death of God creates a vacuum in the
place of the absolute values he stood for, and leaves the individual with-
out any transcendental guarantee to back him or her up, thus preparing
the dissolution of his or her identity, in turn. What replaces the single
stable identity of both God and the individual is the endless repetition


204  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
of eternal return. In a similar fashion to the death of God, eternal re-
turn destroys all grounding—everything is already a copy or parody of
its previous and future self. Thus, there is no end or origin, simply an
ongoing cycle. Deleuze even goes so far as to state that this abolition of
the origin is the fundamental meaning of eternal return: “Eternal return
has no other meaning that this: the absence of any assignable origin.”83
Williams explains:
Deleuze’s interpretation of the doctrine of eternal return, that only
becoming returns and not identity, is the culmination of his dialectic
opposing univocal definitions of being. When he says that to be is
said of all things in the same way, he means that all things are as the
return of pure differences and only as pure differences. There are no
attributes and there is no substance independent of them.
(Williams 2003, 68)
It is the same pure becoming that returns but one has no identity other
than in its repetitions. This will have repercussions in Deleuze’s eth-
ics: if the eternal return were about actual bodies, qualities and their
mixtures, repetition would be the recycling of the Same, and the only
ethics possible would then be the morality of resignation. But the eternal
return Deleuze advances is “the theory of pure events and their linear
condensation on the surface.”84 Only in their case repetition can be im-
posed as the task of freedom. Repetition, says Deleuze, is like a festival
that repeats that which cannot begin again, not in order to multiply the
original by so many festivals, but rather in order to take the first time to
the nth power, “once and for all” and “for all times.”85
Things acquire an actual identity, that is, fixity and boundaries
through repetition. Parts or boundaries then allow us to see the indi-
vidual as a member of a class or species. Repetition allows us to explain
the relation of virtual events to actual events and vice versa. Existence is
not characterized primarily by unities, but rather by a continual sense of
movement and change. That is, being is becoming. In turn, the unities
and structures that we find in life are therefore the result of organizing
this fundamental movement, and not the other way around. Rather than
seeing difference as a difference between two things, difference must be
thought of as the continual movement of self-differing, like the continual
variation of a sound rising and lowering in pitch without stopping at
notes in a scale. In other words, difference is a continuous variation.86
C The Deleuzian Nietzsche
Before elaborating on Deleuze’s theory of individuation, it is helpful to
recall the main innovations that Deleuze prides himself in bringing to
the reading of Nietzsche.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  205
The first point concerns the will to power. For Deleuze, it is paramount
to avoid interpreting the will to power as “wanting to dominate” or
“wanting power.”87 Bataille had already argued that the fascist will to
dominate is antithetical to the will to power. But Deleuze turns the will to
power inside out88: “Power, as a will to power, is not that which the will
wants, but that which wants in the will (Dionysus himself).”89 And he
adds, “The will to power is the differential element from which derive the
forces at work, as well as their respective quality in a complex whole.”90
The second point concerns strength and weakness. It is equally im-
portant to reject the belief that “the most powerful in a social regime are
thereby the strong.”91 Deleuze attempts to explain Nietzsche’s view of
strength by emphasizing that
The weak, the slaves, triumph not by adding up their forces but by
subtracting those of the other: they separate the strong from what
they can do. They triumph not because of the composition of their
power but because of the power of their contagion.92
The third point concerns the eternal return, on which I elaborated
above. It is crucial to avoid interpreting the eternal return as “an old
idea, borrowed from the Greeks, the Hindus, the Babylonians,” or as
“a cycle, or a return of the same.”93 Rather, it confirms becoming over
being.94 In Nietzsche et la philosophie, Deleuze reads it in ethical terms:
the eternal return is the equivalent of a Kantian maxim that helps guide
our actions. Rather than the categorical imperative, it is the threat of
recurrence: act so that you would be willing to always have your action
recur. Deleuze in fact states that eternal return gives to the will a law
that is as rigorous as the Kantian law.95 As an ethical thought, eternal
return is the new formulation of the practical synthesis: whatever you
will, will it in such a way that you also will its eternal return.96 Deleuze
points to Nietzsche’s formulation of the eternal return in The Will to
Power: “If, in all that you will you begin by asking yourself: is it certain
that I will to do it an infinite number of times? This should be your most
solid center of gravity.”97
A fourth point involves rescuing the last works of Nietzsche from his
later madness and including them in the reconstruction of his thought.
The central themes that emerge from Deleuze’s reading of Nietzsche
are chance, multiplicities and becoming. Some of them Bataille adum-
brated. Bataille has subtitled On Nietzsche, “the will to chance,” a
theme that recurs in Deleuze’s Nietzsche along with the dice and ran-
domness.98 However, Deleuze mainly rejects Bataille’s and Klossowski’s
approach to Nietzsche, whose thought may have served as a spur to
Deleuze’s own contribution to Nietzsche studies.
Indeed, when still in high school, Deleuze was exposed to representa-
tives of the marginal pole of the philosophical field, and particularly to


206  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
members of Acéphale et the Collège de sociologie, such as Bataille and
Klossowski, whose reading of Nietzsche in the 1930s helped to oppose the
fascist appropriation of Nietzsche, and more generally, contributed to his
political restoration. From his first book on Nietzsche onward,  Nietzsche
et la philosophie (1962), Deleuze circumvents the reception of the German
philosopher by these readers; he does not criticize, yet he ignores the texts of
Acéphale and in fact implicitly opposes some of them. While Deleuze recog-
nizes the importance of Bataille’s role in rehabilitating Nietzsche from asso-
ciations with fascism, he does not appreciate his interpretation of Nietzsche.
Deleuze’s task in relation to Nietzsche is different than it was for
Bataille and Klossowski; the challenge now is to habilitate him as a
philosopher. The Deleuzian means to Nietzsche’s habilitation are listed
by Bruno Meziane (2019): Deleuze singles out a conceptual systema-
ticity in Nietzsche’s thought that has been ignored so far, he forcefully
inscribes Nietzsche’s theoretical perspective within the history of phi-
losophy and establishes Nietzsche’s philosophy as a new perspective
within it. Therein lies the implicit opposition to Bataille. While Bataille
assumed in L’Expérience intérieure the profound ignorance Nietzsche
had of Hegel, Deleuze constructs a Nietzsche who is a resolute adversary
of Hegel and Hegelianism, whose theory of culture opposes head-on the
dialectical schema of alienation and reappropriation, whose incentive
for his genealogical problematization of sense and value is the critical
evaluation of the master and slave Hegelian dialectic, who defines the
dialectician as a “type” to be opposed by another “type,” the “geneal-
ogist” as a different intellectual sensibility, characterized as a different
relation to culture, another ethos, another style and another method.
Moreover, this form of philosophical legitimation contrasts with the
interpretation of the members of Acéphale and especially with the one
given by Bataille since the originality of Nietzsche is not perceived as a
function of an essential relation between thought and life but is rather
attached to the genealogical method. This method is itself irreduc-
ible to an exploration given in “inner experience”—at the limit of the
 ineffable—of the death of God, of extasy and joy. Joy, jouissance and
laughter are not the “remainders” of discursive thought invested by neg-
ativity without employ, as they are for Bataille: in Deleuze’s Nietzsche,
these are values that are immanent to a new type of thinker and thought
whose systematic dimension should be explained.
Thus, the systematic perspective that Deleuze defends so forcefully
in the 1962 work has at least a double consequence: it enables to reveal
in Nietzsche’s thought an autonomous problematique along its creation
of concepts, and is consequently irreducible to a simple “response” to
the rationalistic tradition in philosophy. This perspective objectifies a
Nietzschean philosophy that is irreducible to the person of Nietzsche, a
philosophy whose requirements can be pursued beyond the “case” Ni-
etzsche and reinvested in new philosophical problems.99


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  207
D Individuation
Deleuze uses Nietzsche to explain that being is becoming and difference
is continuous variation, as noted above. Deleuze’s theory of individu-
ation addresses—in the process of virtual, continuous (intensive) mul-
tiplicities becoming (extended) discrete—the apparently contradictory
co- existence of the continuum and the discrete. Constantin Boundas
explains that “the process of individuation is called ‘differenciation’
with respect to the continuum, and ‘differentiation’ with respect to the
discrete.”100 The differentiated virtual is difference itself or difference
differenciating itself. The modulating process of individuation is the
transduction101 of the virtual continuum of intensities to the discrete ex-
tended actual, all the while remembering that the actual is never totally
devoid of the dynamism of the pre-individual virtual. Thus, the actual
is capable of being reabsorbed by the virtual. Intensity is what makes
the passage from the virtual to the actual possible. The modulation is in
a state of permanent variation—a promise of becomings—disallowing
predictions of what an individuation is capable of. Williams explains:
Ideas become determined when they are expressed in actual things,
in a sensation that accompanies an actual event, and when that sen-
sation is accompanied by a change in the relation of envelopment of
intensities. This is the process of differenciation where actual dif-
ferences allow for ideas to become determined in terms of clarity
and obscurity… The process of differentiation, however, shows how
actual events go beyond actual identities when intensities and ideas
are expressed in the actual. Any actual event is significant because it
is the expression of a change in the envelopment of intensities and in
the clarity and obscurity of ideas.
(Williams 2013, 242–3)
Thus there is no differenciation without differentiation: ideas and actual
things determine each other. But this relation must be mediated through
the expression of intensities in actual sensations. Deleuze calls this me-
diating process dramatization.102
Dramatization explains Deleuze’s interest in the concept of expres-
sion. Actual things express ideas but are not caused by them. As opposed
to cause, expression is not regular; each expression is one off and cannot
be repeated or guaranteed to behave in the same way at another time.
This is because any expression changes the relations of envelopment of
intensities and of clarity and obscurity of ideas, in such a way as to
make each new relation of actual to virtual different from the former.
Thus, we can have signs as to how to express anew but never knowledge.
Expression associates radically different entities. Actual things have an
identity, but virtual ones do not; they are pure variations. An actual
thing must change or become something different in order to express


208  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
something. While the expressed virtual thing does not change, only its
relation to other virtual things, other intensities and ideas do. Deleuze
has to introduce the concepts of multiplicities of pure differences and of
envelopments of intensities in order to escape ways of thinking of change
in terms of causal changes in parts that effect a whole. He introduces
these concepts through the dramatizations of ideas and intensities and
through a critique of positions based on identity.
Dramatizations are ways of expressing sensations rather than true
representations of them. This may or may not be sensations we share
with many others or positions we think are important.103 The role of
sensation in dramatization, and its association with a singular relation
of envelopment among intensities and clarity and obscurity among ideas,
focuses Deleuze’s philosophy on individuals. Individuals are the singular
relation of ideas, intensities and sensations, set in motion by signs or
changes in the relation through an interaction with other individuals.
Individuals are no subjects or selves. The self and the subject are mo-
ments in the processes associated with the individual. The haecceity is
the inessential event that defines an individual or a world.104 Deleuze
understands “haecceities” as degrees of intensity (a degree of heat, a
certain time of the day) that, in combination with other degrees of inten-
sity, bring about individuals. The individuals they bring about retain the
anonymity of the pre-individual real. First, haecceities consist entirely
of movement and rest (longitude) between non-formed molecules and
particles. Second, they have the capacity to affect and be affected (lati-
tude). Haecceities co-exist on a plane of consistency, each one of which is
compossible with, and responsible for, the generation of others. In order
to accentuate their impersonality, Deleuze argues that we need a new
language by which to refer to them, one that consists of proper names,
verbs in the infinitive, and indefinite articles and pronouns.105
There can be no universal apodictic ground because all thought and
all reality must begin with individuals that have nothing identifiable
in common. Deleuze’s philosophy begins with the singular rather than
the universal: there are individuals determined by questions that they
cannot avoid and which are driven by sensation rather than intellectual
deductions. Deleuze does not attempt to show that these questions are
necessary or universal. They find no ground in either the questioner or
what which is questioned. Questions have no ground in the object nor in
the subject—they arise with and for contingent individuals. How do we
know that such questions, whatever they may be, really arise for individ-
uals? Deleuze resists here phenomenological or scientific approaches to
an experience. He does not seek universal phenomena through a process
of reduction—he seeks rather universal conditions on the ground of the
sensations of individuals.
Individuals must connect to the changes that things may undergo.
We must connect to the increases and decreases that flow through us,
through our thoughts and sensations, when we are in presence of things.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  209
Deleuze wants us to connect to the pure variations that ideas and sensa-
tions may connect to: becoming harder, softer, pricklier, spongier. Pure
variations must not be confused with actual things. In order for these
variations to enrich the way we may live with them in the future, we must
leave behind the urge to identify the intensity of sensations and the power
of creation with actual things and only those things. We should be open
to unpredictable and apparently small-scale events: events and cracks106
that run through and disrupt lives and things in The Logic of Sense.
E Thinking
Thinking is not a shared universal faculty; rather, it exemplifies partic-
ular characteristics in each of us. Our thought reflects the physical and
biological but also the virtual repetition that have made us individual
thinkers, as opposed to identical subjects and selves defined by right.
Due to the effect of an “image of thought,” a particular set of proposi-
tions about the form thought should take, thinking has been damagingly
restricted. This is why we have missed, Deleuze believes, the essence of
difference and repetition.
This image of thought is neither represented directly in a given phi-
losophy or scientific theory, nor is it the object of empirical research.
Deleuze’s point is that the construction of philosophy takes place against
a background defined by the postulates. The image is in the everyday
common sense and good sense that philosophies can seem to support
and give rise to. Thought is in principle sharable and good; it unites
different faculties through the transcendent faculty of recognition, and
recognition depends on representation. Representation unites all fac-
ulties through judgments based on identity and the exclusion of that
which cannot be identified. True difference and repetition are excluded
by representation.
Deleuze opposes this image of thought with a novel view, which Wil-
liams explains as follows:
The difference between Deleuze’s position and the postulates he
wishes to oppose come out in his demand to give form to the ground.
The refusal to accept the reality of the ground as difference and rep-
etition allows it to work violently within our very attempts to escape
it. We must express and work with the repetitions that become con-
centrated in us and come to make us since to repress them or to treat
them as something external is to redouble their force.
(Williams 2013, 135)
The authentic role of philosophy is to forgo the image of thought and
connect to what Deleuze calls ideas, the transcendental condition for
thinking and that which vivifies actual lives through intensities, through
difference in itself. Rather than being contained in the mind, ideas are


210  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
relations between things in the virtual which are the conditions for the
evolution of actual things. They should be distinguished from our com-
mon perception of ideas as any identifiable thought about something.
The virtual ideas are the conditions for changes in our actual ideas and
must not be confused with them. The idea cannot be known, only sensed
and known partially as it is expressed. The idea is resistant to identifica-
tion as an object of knowledge because its elements are pure differences
that cannot be identified but only deduced on the basis of sensations. All
ideas “coexist” but this co-existence is a differentiated one.
The way Deleuze uses “differentiated” is different from its common
usage. Rather than meaning “different,” or opposed in some way, it in-
volves different degrees with respect to pure difference, or variations.
Clarity and obscurity, light and shadow are the metaphors Deleuze uses
to convey differences in degree within a whole that cannot be separated
into distinct zones. Thus, ideas are differentiated because they are differ-
ently lit versions of the whole of ideas. Deleuze deems this interrelation
of ideas their “perplication,” which is explained, in turn, in terms of the
way in which intensities envelop one another. Rather than misinterpret-
ing the light and shadow metaphor, this sense of folding indicates that
that which is left obscure in an idea is neither unimportant nor intrinsi-
cally threatening—but merely combined in a less intense way.
Rather than distinct, recall, things for Deleuze are either more or less
obscure or more or less clear. Since a thing is always connected with
other things, the more clearly it appears, the more the other things it
is associated with fade into obscurity. Thus, a true understanding of a
thing evades us. The cause of clarity of some things is the obscurity of
others, since coming to the fore is predicated on other things falling into
the background. The connection with other ideas, left obscure by an
idea, is nevertheless more significant than the clear-cut difference from
other ideas which is highlighted by its clarity.
We should not confuse the virtual with the possible. Actual things
are not the expressions of other things, which they may express or not.
They are not the possible yet not actual outcomes of a thing. The dif-
ferentiation of ideas is not done in terms of existence or non-existence;
only in terms of relations of clarity and obscurity is the whole of ideas
differentiated. The role played by very obscure and distant ideas is a real
one, rather than a possible one, in relation to the more clearly expressed
ideas. As Williams further explains:
That other life is not simply possible for you. The intensities and
Ideas that made it live for you once still exist, though the intensi-
ties do not envelop others and the Ideas are not clear in the current
actualization.
(Williams 2013, 176)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  211
Deleuze’s view of thinking should be complemented with his view of
sense, before we can address his ethics.
F Sense
While Difference and Repetition ranges over a wide field of philosoph-
ical topics, The Logic of Sense focuses on two aspects of a single issue,
the structure and genesis of sense. The latter work introduces the con-
cept of series. A series is a disjunctive synthesis running in different ways
across two independent but irreducible sides of reality—sense and ex-
pression, virtual and actual, surface and depth. A disjunctive synthesis
is not a reduction through abstraction but a transforming addition that
connects by creating differences (“both, and”). Events are such disjunc-
tive syntheses. The synthesis is carried by “aleatory points,” mobile fac-
tors running along the series, which are either empty places or elements
without a place. Deleuze thus avoids the critique that these synthesizing
factors introduce an external identity into the concept of disjunctive syn-
thesis. The Logic of Sense is an answer to the question of how are series
determined with no external reference point.107
Deleuze is opposed to rules or laws which prior to series determine
what can be a valid series. He criticizes logical validity and grammatical
rules: series are not defined by a logical function or a grammatical defi-
nition. They are processes to be observed and lived through. They are
sensed and expressed.
In The Logic of Sense, Deleuze first develops the paradoxes that result
from the structure of sense and then sketches a theory of the genesis of
sense. He does this by using resources from analytic philosophy and
the Stoics in the course of reading Lewis Carroll. His analysis of the
structure of sense reveals three types of relation within propositions:
first, designation or denotation, which is the relation of a proposition
to an external state of affairs (theory of reference, with its criterion of
truth or falsity). Second, manifestation, which marks the relation of the
proposition to the beliefs and desires of the person who is speaking (with
its values of veracity or illusion). Third, signification or demonstration,
which is the relation of the proposition to other propositions (the do-
main of logic, with its relations of implication and assertion). Sense,
then, would be a fourth dimension of propositions, for which Deleuze
reserves the term expression. As for Gottlob Frege, sense for Deleuze
is what is expressed in a proposition; the two senses of “morning star”
and “evening star” are two ways in which the same denotatum may be
expressed in propositions.
Deleuze’s contribution to the philosophy of sense lies in his showing
that the attempt to make this fourth dimension evident is akin to Car-
roll’s Hunt for the Snark, or to unraveling a Möbius strip, since sense


212  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
has neither a physical nor a mental existence. Deleuze suggests that it
was the Stoics who first discovered the dimension of sense when they
distinguished between corporeal mixtures and incorporeal events.108
I can attribute the proper name “Battle of Waterloo” to a particular state
of affairs, but the battle itself is an incorporeal event (or sense) with no
other reality than that of the expression of my proposition; what we
find in the state of affairs are bodies mixing with one another—spears
stabbing flesh, bullets flying through the air, cannons firing, bodies be-
ing ripped apart—and the battle itself is the effect or the result of this
intermingling of bodies. Sense thus has a complex status. While it does
not exist outside the proposition that expresses it, it still cannot be con-
fused with the proposition: it has a distinct “objectity” of its own, which
means that it does not exist, but rather “subsists” or “insists.” It is also
attributed to states of affairs or things, however, it cannot be confused
or identified with the state of affairs or with a quality or relation of these
states:
Sense is both the expressible or the expressed of the proposition, and
the attribute of the state of affairs. It turns one side toward things,
and another side toward propositions. But it cannot be confused
with the proposition which expressed it any more than with the state
of affairs or the quality which the proposition denotes. It is exactly
the boundary between propositions and things.
(LS 22)
The structure of sense generates a number of paradoxes, which Deleuze
distinguishes from the paradoxes of signification discovered by Bertrand
Russell in set theory (the set of all sets, and the “barber of the regi-
ment”). The first is the paradox of regress, or indefinite proliferation:
I can never state the sense of what I am saying, but I can take the sense
of what I am saying as the object of another proposition, whose sense,
in turn, I cannot state, ad infinitum. This first paradox points both to
the impotence of the speaker (my inability to state the sense of what
I am saying) and to the highest power of language (its infinite capability
to speak about words). The second paradox is that of sterile reiteration
or doubling: one can avoid the infinite regress by extracting sense as the
mere double of a proposition, but at the price of catapulting us into a
third paradox of neutrality or sterility—sense is necessarily neutral with
regard to the various modes of the proposition: quality (affirmation, ne-
gation), quantity (all, some, none), relation and modality (possibility,
reality, necessity).
Extracted from the proposition in this way, Deleuze argues that sense
has the status of a pure ideational event, irreducible to propositions and
their three dimensions: first, the states of affairs the propositions denote;
second, the experiences or mental activities (beliefs, desires, images,


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  213
representations) of persons who express themselves in the proposition;
and, third, universals or general concepts. But how can sense be said
to engender the other dimension of the proposition? This is the second
task of a logic of sense: “To combine the sterility of sense in relation to
the proposition from which it was extracted with its power of genesis in
relation to the dimensions of the proposition.”109
The domain of sense is necessarily subject to a fundamental fragil-
ity, capable of toppling over into nonsense: the ground gives way to a
groundlessness, a sans-fond. The reason for this is clear. Sense is never
a principle or an origin; rather, it is an effect and it is produced and it is
produced out of elements that do not, in themselves, have a sense. Sense,
in other words, has a determinate relation with nonsense. Deleuze, how-
ever, distinguishes between two very different types of nonsense. The
first is that of Carroll’s, which remains at the surface of sense, and, like
children, makes use of the non-signifying elements of language in order
to construct the portmanteau words (snark = shark + snake; frumious =
furious + fuming) and nonsensical phrases (“‘Twas brillig, and the slithy
toves did gyre and gimble in the wabe”) that populate his writing. If The
Logic of Sense is in part a reading of Carroll’s work, it is because no
one knew better than Carroll about the conditions for the production of
sense, which Deleuze elucidates in detail: the extraction of differential
elements or pure event, their organization in multiple series, and most
importantly, the aleatory point or paradoxical element that links the
series (the ideal “quasi-cause” that produces the effect of sense out of
nonsense).
But there is a second type of nonsense, which is more profound than
the surface nonsense found in Carroll. This is the terrifying nonsense
of the primary order of schizophrenia, which found expression in the
writings of the French playwright, Antonin Artaud. Sense is what pre-
vents the sonorous language from being confused with the physical body
(noise). But in the primary order of schizophrenia experienced by Ar-
taud, there is no longer anything to prevent propositions from falling
back onto bodies, which mingle their sonorous elements with the olfac-
tory, gustatory and digestive effects of the body (Artaud’s cris-souffles:
“ratara ratara ratara Atara tatara rana Otara otara katara”).
G Ethics
Todd May suggests that the question of how to live is the cornerstone
of Deleuze’s philosophy.110 Deleuze repeatedly endorses Foucault’s and
Nietzsche’s conviction that life has to be lived as a work of art or as a
“life-style.”111 Thus, Deleuze draws a clear distinction between morality
and ethics throughout his work. While morality implies that we judge
ourselves and others on the basis of what we may become, ethics for
Deleuze is inherently tied up with the notion of becoming:


214  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Ethics, which is to say, a typology of immanent modes of existence,
replaces Morality, which always refers existence to transcendent val-
ues. Morality is the judgment of God, the system of values (Good-
Evil) is supplanted by the qualitative difference of modes of existence
(good-bad).
(SPP 23)
Life cannot be measured against transcendent values, but constitutes its
own immanent ethics. For the sake of clarity, I divide this section into
two parts, one that addresses Deleuze’s view of ethics and the other that
inquires into the impact that Deleuze’s collaboration with Guattari may
have had on his ethics.
1 Deleuze
Nietzsche’s and Spinoza’s ethical thoughts are the two main influences
on Deleuzian ethics.112 Referring to their similarities as the Nietzsche-
Spinoza identity, he endorses what he takes to be their common view of
ethics, a form of evaluation and affirmation.113 For Deleuze, the world
is neither true nor real, but should be accepted as “living.” The notion of
becoming makes the question of truth or untruth irrelevant as it applies
to being rather than becoming. Here, Deleuze departs from Spinoza,
but also from Nietzsche. The tension we find in Nietzsche between the
notion of truth, in the name of which he undertakes his critique, and the
perspectivism which he advances, is not fully resolved.114 In France, it
is Shestov who presented Nietzsche’s thought as being not solely beyond
good and evil, as indeed Nietzsche claims it is, but also beyond truth and
falsity.115 Thus, the supposed identity between Spinoza and Nietzsche is
constructed by Deleuze as an axiological attitude: affirming life is eval-
uating it with the view of setting free that which lives, ethics innovates
by creating affirmative values in order to make life active and light to the
contrary of morality which burdens life with higher values.116
According to Deleuze, the great ethical thinker is Spinoza. Four “dis-
ciples,” Nietzsche, D. H. Lawrence, Franz Kafka and Artaud, follow
his break with the Judeo-Christian tradition and develop his ethical
approach by criticizing the psychology of the priest. In particular, Ni-
etzsche denounces the judgment that subjects us to an infinite debt that
cannot be paid. Contrary to appearances, moral and juridical judgment
is not more moderate than a system of “cruelty.” Being a system of debt,
it is inscribed on the body, measured in blood and “condemns us to in-
finite restitution and servitude.”117
Deleuze further shows how these four “disciples” elaborate a system
of “cruelty” that is opposed to moral judgment and which constitutes the
basics for an ethics. These thinkers developed the notion of unconscious
thought and Spinoza emphasized the unfamiliarity of the body, which


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  215
together may ground an ethics if we exchange good and evil with good
and bad. Ronald Bogue’s Deleuze’s Way: Essays in Transverse Ethics
and Aesthetics (2007; 2016) is helpful for understanding the Deleuzian
ethics that is expressed in these works.
Bogue explains that in Nietzsche and Philosophy (1962), Deleuze ar-
gues that Nietzsche’s view of amor fati (love of fate) is an alternative to
Kant’s categorical imperative: whatever you will, also will its eternal
return. That means that a good player in the game of life rolls the dice
once, affirms whatever the result is and wills its eternal result. Thus,
a good player genuinely affirms the play of the world and avoids the
resentment of finding the world guilty of frustrating his desires. Amor
fati is a Stoic notion, however, which Deleuze introduces in The Logic of
