Sense within the context of the Stoic philosophy of the event:
The virtual eludes our commonsense understanding but it impinges
on us in moments of vertigo when rational spatiotemporal coordi-
nates are scrambled and a pure “event” emerges.
(Bogue 2016, 8)
Everywhere, the virtual is passing into the actual while remaining im-
manent within it. Nietzsche’s amor fati is endorsed by Deleuze as an
ethics of willing the virtual event, “which is immanent within the actual
and impinges on us in moments of disequilibrium and disorientation.”118
The quintessential event is an infinitive, elusive, anonymous occurrence,
which is outside conventional time. Deleuze’s ethics consists of being
worthy of that which happens, in other words, of willing the event that
is immanent within my ongoing actualization of the world. It is to will
the difference, multiplicity and chance of the virtual, and thereby avoid
ressentiment and affirm the past events which have shaped one’s pres-
ent.119 Williams explains the main crux of Deleuze’s ethics:
Deleuze believes that we have to find the right ways of acting in
terms of underlying processes of repetition that we cannot fully con-
trol or understand. He calls these acts the vice-diction, doubling, or
counter-actualization of virtual events. There is a way of repeating
well with respect to the pure differences that give life its intensity.
(Williams 2008, 85)
Deleuze’s ethics of affirming the present goes by the name of vice- diction
instead of contradiction in Difference and Repetition and counter-
actualization in The Logic of Sense.120 He uses the term “vice-diction”
to avoid the Hegelian notion of (the dialectic as) “contradiction,” which
he derives from the ancient Indo-European linguistic roots of “vice.”
The etymology of “vice” is “to bend,” “to change,” “to become,” i.e., a
“vice-president” is one who “becomes” president in the case of absence.


216  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
To counter-actualize the virtual is to identify and engage with the
virtual event which is immanent in my world. This is what is meant by
vice-diction, whose purpose is transforming the virtual differences at
work, experimenting with them once I enter into their play. Vice-diction
undoes and constructs connections among differences; it alters the situa-
tion by experimenting with metamorphosis.121 Creators, such as artists,
philosophers and scientists, experiment on the virtuous immanent lines
of continual variations, and thus affirm the creative potential immanent
within the real. As Williams explains:
The concept of vice-diction is Deleuze’s answer to the question of
how to live with the way virtual ideas, and therefore, pure differ-
ences condition our actions. This leads to answers to the question to
how to act. The concept is, therefore, central to Deleuzian ethics and
politics and to the question of how to live well.122
(Williams 2003, 157)
The rigidity embodied in ideas and actual things should be obliterated
by vice-diction.123 Counter-actualizing or vice-dicting events means
playing with them. There are several ways to do this. “After the event
occurs, we have to be like actors or mimes who replay the event in the
series it has occurred in. It means that we have to transform the event in
the same way an actor transforming a part,” Williams explains.124 The
event sets off punctures, clashes and wounds, which are its depth aspect;
however, if we do not add an individuating sense of it, the event’s mean-
ing is incomplete. Taking his inspiration from the Stoics, Deleuze argues
that we should replay the events in such a way that we do not deny them
nor the truths they hold for us. Translated in a more practical language,
this means that although life is determined through structural patterns
running through series, individuating paths are not fully determined by
those patterns; moreover, when not determined by individuating paths,
the patterns are still hollow and incomplete. Individuating paths are de-
termined by events; however, the sense of the event only emerges as the
individuating path replays the event by acting it anew. Thus, this deter-
mination is a two-way process.125
Finally, in the case an event is a wound, that is, a deep-seated fac-
tor that makes a given individual path different in positive and negative
ways, these patterns governing it only explain the general “how” of a
wound and not the way of a wound, its significance and its “wherefrom”
and “where to” (its destiny). A wound is a rare event and a form of des-
tiny, rather than the many injuries that assail life without determining
it (including deadly ones). “In order to be an event, a wound must be
worked through creatively in an individuating path, that is change and
be changed by the path,” Williams explains.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  217
Thus, events are both necessary and offer a potential for open and
reviving transformations. Things are naturally determined; however,
things are also individuated; thus, the commitment to sense avoids the
reductive aspects of such natural explanations. Things are not individual
through dependence on godly intervention or human freedom, but rather
through the following two-way relations: the way events determine indi-
viduals and the way different individuals replay their determining events.
Deleuze sees in the latter aspect the locus of resisting determination as
the event makes sense only when transformed and affirmed. It can be
affirmed on the condition that it is not denied, or blamed on external
necessity, or on free acts. To be worthy of the event is not to negate it,
but rather, by working with it, to replay it differently in all series, that is,
to redouble or counter-actualize it. Thus,
When struck by a moral challenge, a challenge about how to live, we
might ask: 1. How does a problematic series of emotional, ideal and
physical tensions determine the situation? 2. How is the situation
still open to reinvigorating change? 3. Which events trigger sense or
value here? 4. How shall these events be replayed?
(Williams 2008, 12)
The ethics of the event is not the ethics of the state of affairs. The event
intended in the formula of (Stoic) ethics is virtual, and, to the extent that
virtual events are still-future and always-past, the ethics of the event pre-
supposed a will that seeks in states of affairs the eternal truth of the pure,
virtual event which is actualized in them. True amor fati is not the accep-
tance of the actual state of affairs but rather the counter- actualization of
the actual in order for the virtual, pure event to be thought and willed.126
Consequently, the mime to whom Deleuze entrusts the ethical task is not
the hero of the representation of the same (the Kantian who “repeats” a
maxim until the categorical imperative acquires the extension of a law of
nature). The Deleuzian mime is given the twin obligation to unmask the
pretension of the actual to be the only player in the field and to re-enact
the virtual in its infinite process of differing from itself.127 In the com-
prehensive anthology edited by Boundas, Columbia Companion to 20th
Century Philosophies (2007), Boundas attempts in “Different/ciations:
The Case of Deleuze” to explain Deleuze’s ethics:
In the imperative of the eternal return and in the accompanying in-
vitation that we measure up to the event, we may find the elements
of an ethics. Obligation, in order to be admitted, must be measured,
in the first place, by men and women whose souls have been tried
and proven noble in the fire of the eternal return. These men and
women are not all that far from Aristotle’s megalopsychoi. They are


218  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
the ones worthy of the event, the actors and dancers—the mimes of
the counter-actualization.
(Boundas 2007c, 498)
However, in an introductory essay of the same book, “How to Rec-
ognize Continental European Philosophy,” Boundas acknowledges that
“Deleuze’s becoming worthy of the event, despite the dash of Spinoza’s
joyful wisdom, remains enigmatic.”128
Deleuze’s Stoic commitment to the ethics of the event—our becom-
ing worthy of the event through the process of counter-actualization
of that which is happening to us—involves embracing an ethics of joy,
the articulation of which is the result of his encounter with Spinoza.129
“The nodal point that represents the linkage of this commitment is the
Nietzschean affirmation of the eternal return—the lynchpin of Deleuze’s
ontology and the indispensable imperative of his ethics.”130
Nietzsche’s imperative, which Deleuze often makes his own belongs
here: whatever you will, will it in such a way that you also will its eternal
return. The influence of Nietzsche on Deleuze’s ethics of joy lies in that
the pedagogy for the formulation of adequate ideas becomes the process
of the counter-actualization of that which happens to us. It is no longer
the generality of the common notion that stands for the cogitandum of
practical reason; it is the event that must be grasped though the process
of counter-actualization. The sadness in the state of affairs passively af-
fecting us is transformed into a joyful affirmation of the event. Passive
affections are turned into active ones that are capable of transvaluing
and transforming states of affairs.131
Throughout all of Deleuze’s work, there is an ethics of the event that
owes much to Spinoza and Nietzsche as it does to the Stoics. It is a
question of willing the event in such a manner or to such an extent that
the quality of the will itself is transformed and becomes affirmation.
Moreover, it is by means of the concept that this transmutation in the
quality of the will is achieved. Ultimately, the purpose served by the
creation of concepts is ethical rather than epistemological. Philosophy
extracts events from bodies and states of affairs and in doing so enables
us to affirm the sense of what happens. “There is a dignity of the event
that has always been inseparable from philosophy as amor fati”; hence,
“Philosophy’s sole aim is to become worthy of the event.”132
The notion of immanence is a constant in Deleuze’s thought. He reads
the entire history of philosophy as an attempt to establish a plane of im-
manence. The sole philosopher who does not make compromises with
transcendence is Spinoza, this is why he is the prince of philosophers
for Deleuze.133 Deleuze claims Spinoza’s legacy with the difference that
he detaches immanence from substance.134 He creates “an immanence
which is immanent in nothing,” pure immanence, and identifies it with
life. In his last published essay, “Immanence: A Life,”135 he describes life


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  219
as the immanence of immanence, or absolute immanence, and asserts
that it is “complete power, complete beatitude”136:
What is immanence? A life…No one has described what a life is better
than Charles Dickens […]. Between Riderhood’s137 life and his death,
there is a moment that is only that of a life playing with death. The life
of the individual gives way to an impersonal and yet singular life that
releases a pure event freed from the accidents of internal and external
life, that is, from the subjectivity and objectivity of what comes to pass:
a “homo tantum” with whom everyone sympathizes and who attains
a kind of beatitude; or an ecceity, which is no longer an individuation,
but a singularization, a life of pure immanence, neutral, beyond good
and evil, since only the subject that incarnated it in the midst of things
made it good or bad. The life of such individuality is eclipsed by the
singular immanent life of a man who no longer has a name, though he
can be mistaken for no other. A singular essence, a life…
(TRM 386–7)
However, Deleuze generalizes this claim as true even when life does not
confront death. As a life is everywhere, this indefinite life does not arrive
or come after; rather, it “presents the immensity of an empty time where
one sees the event to come and already past, in the absolute of an imme-
diate consciousness.”138 Although a life contains only virtuals, that is, it
is made of virtualities, events and singularities, it does not lack reality as
the plane of immanence gives virtual events their full reality. Thus, the
event considered as non-actualized indefinitely lacks nothing at all.139 In
his way, a life can be described in terms of power and beatitude.
Thus, Deleuze’s philosophy of life rejects the reduction of life to con-
sciousness and, beyond that, to the person, the subject and the human
being himself. Immanence and life know neither a sovereign subject (a
transcendence) nor a person or an organic individual. “It is organisms
that die, not life…All I have written, has been vitalist, at least I hope so,”
he writes in assessing his contribution.140
2 Deleuze and Guattari
In his preface to Anti-Oedipus, Foucault notes that it is “a book of ethics,
the first book of ethics to be written in France in quite a long time.”141
Foucault points to the connection between the immanent theory of eth-
ics that Deleuze developed in his monographs on Nietzsche and Spinoza
and the theory of desire exposed in Anti-Oedipus. Deleuze’s collabora-
tion with Guattari issued in the two-volume Capitalism and Schizophre-
nia comprising Anti-Oedipus (1972) and A Thousand Plateaus (1980),
and their final joint work, What Is Philosophy? (1991). We may ask,
what has this collaboration added to Deleuze’s view of ethics?142


220  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
The overall goal of Capitalism and Schizophrenia seems to be a Ni-
etzschean synthesis of psychoanalysis and Marxism, a synthesis that
also combines Deleuze’s metaphysics with Guattari’s psycho-social theo-
rizing. The leading notion is that of desire, which can be construed as a
psycho-social expression of Deleuzian difference, since desire is precisely
the impetus for becoming other (differing). Traditionally, however, from
Plato through Sigmund Freud, desire has been constructed as subordi-
nated to the lack that it is striving to fulfill. This contradicts Deleuze’s
intuition of the primacy of difference by deriving it from an anterior
need. Deleuze and Guattari instead propose a view of desire that, like the
Nietzschean will to power, is a pure affirmation of difference for its own
sake. Such desire is “deterritorialized,” that is, not rooted in any pre-given
nature of institution. So construed, desire corresponds to modern capital-
ism’s model of individuals as autonomous choosers of goods valued only
because they are desired, not in virtue of any intrinsic worth (e.g., ethical,
religious, cultural). Deleuze and Guattari have no problem with this model;
their criticism of capitalism is rather that it goes on to accord general (pub-
lic) value to desires only on the basis of their market value, relegating in
that way any non-economic modes of valuation to the private sphere.
The project of Anti-Oedipus is to reformulate psychoanalysis and
Marxism in ways that avoid the above deficiencies and, combined with a
Deleuzian (Nietzschean) theory of desire, that will be able to launch an
effective critique of capitalism.
The debate about the grand narratives and their subsequent atrophy
did not cause the disappearance of the emancipatory interest from the
agendas of the postmodern philosophers. A rearticulation of this interest
also runs through Deleuze and Guattari’s work, which is best considered
as an ethics.143 In what follows, I rely on Boundas’s account of nomad-
ism. Their contribution is better understood by taking into account the
simultaneous presence in their texts of two attitudes—subversion and
perversion.144 Their subversive tendencies tend to cluster around the
concepts minority/majority and nomad/sedentary, developed in A Thou-
sand Plateaus (1987), in an attempt to rally together those in a position
to stand against the state’s capturing forces. It was in this context that
Deleuze and Guattari issued an appeal to minor, transformative forces
(of life, politics, thought, artistic creation) and to their capacity to escape
the sedentarism and stratification that are dear to majorities. Nomads,
having portable roots, were granted the ability to reterritorialize upon
the line and the trajectory of their own deterritorialization. Boundas
explains:
In the nomadology that emerges from Deleuze and Guattari’s writ-
ings, one can still hear the echo of the Marxists’ reading of the
state as the “capturing apparatus” in the hands of the ruling class,
being maintained for the sake of that class’ interests. The seden-
taries, that is, the majority or the majoritarians, are the state or the


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  221
state- apparatus or the state-form; the nomads, that is, the multi-
tudes or masses or minorities, are those whose investments of desire
do not coincide with the interests of the state—but with a difference:
in Deleuze and Guattari’s post- Marxist context, the nomads do not
want to become the state or to take over the state-apparatus—not
even temporarily; rather, they strive to dismantle it or to flee from it.
When all is said and done, the nomad is the one who tries to prevent
the social sedimentation of desire from blocking the connective pro-
cess of the production of desire. Nomadic lines of flight are lines of
subversion and transformation of the well-organized and smoothly
functioning institutions of sedentarism.
(Boundas 2017a, 19)145
In Deleuze and Guattari’s terminology, “schizophrenia” refers to the
deterritorialized desire that is generated by capitalism and endorsed
by Deleuzian philosophy of difference. Rather than an illness, it is a
value to be nurtured. Deleuze and Guattari characterize human be-
ings in terms of desiring-machines. Gary Gutting explains how the
“desires constituting an existence are creative achievements in their
own rights, not responses to lacks determined by factors (the world,
human nature) outside of desires.” A desiring-machine synthesizes
Freudian desire with Marxist’s production, “a synthesis that simul-
taneously makes desire part of the Marxist infrastructure and gives
socio-economic significance to Freudian desire (libido).146
Deleuze and Guattari hope for a becoming-democratic, a politics of
a universal brotherhood. although they have reservations in relation to
actual democracies. In the Deleuzian story, the people to whom the po-
litical theorist appeals are missing; Boundas notes how “a new people
and a new earth à venir” give Deleuze and Guattari’s political posture
“a purposefulness without purpose.” He adds that the clarion for new
people and a new earth should not be understood as a teleological antic-
ipation with messianic aspirations. Deleuze and Guattari did not desig-
nate or name the people to come or the new earth; they did say, though,
that the new “race” exists only as an oppressed race, and it suffers only
in the name of the oppression. They did claim that race is always inferior
and minoritarian and that “race” is not defined by its purity, but rather
by the impurity conferred upon it by a system of domination. Verena
Conley explains that
While minoritarian is seen as potential (puissance), creative and in
becoming, a majority is linked to a state of power and domination.
Domination always translates into hegemony, while a determination
which differs from the constant is considered minoritarian. Blacks,
Jews, Arabs or women can only create by making possible a becom-
ing, but never through ownership.
(Conley in Parr [2005] 2010, 166)


222  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Deleuze states clearly that a majority is never a becoming. Our age is
becoming the age of minorities. Becoming is creation, and the invention
of people to come is the goal of philosophy: this is minoritarian people
with humor.
The notion of “minoritarian” is often used in relation to postcolonial
theory and the concept of minor literature, Conley explains.147 A person
(that is, a subject, but also a creative and active individual) has to deterri-
torialize the major language rather than reterritorialize herself within an
inherited dialect. Recourse to a minor language puts the major language
into flight. Minoritarian authors are those who are foreigners in their
own language. The primary function of language is not to communicate
but to impose power relations, which by contributing to shape the world
transforms language into a mode of action. A minor literature is not a
literature written from the perspective of an oppressed group, nor is it
a secondary or neglected literature in Deleuze’s view. Minor literature,
such as Kafka’s takes the language of the dominant culture and warps it
to new purposes, creating what Deleuze calls “lines of flight.” As Bogue
notes, for Deleuze, this creation involves a certain kind of becoming,
becoming-imperceptible:
Becoming-imperceptible is a process of elimination whereby one di-
vests oneself of all coded identity and engages in the abstract lines of
a nonorganic life, the immanent, virtual lines of continuous varia-
tion that play through discursive regimes of signs and nondiscursive
machinic assemblages alike.
(Bogue 1989, 73)
In short, minor literature creates a type of living that is not merely a rep-
lication of dominant motifs but a process of touching on what Deleuze
calls “the virtual.”
A Thousand Plateaus maintains the tripartite ontological scheme of
all of Deleuze’s work, but, as the title indicates, with geological terms of
reference. Deleuze and Guattari call the virtual “the Earth,” the intensive
is called “consistency” and the actual is called “the system of the strata.”
As the latter term indicates, one of the foci of their investigations is the
tendency of some systems to head toward congealment or stratification.
More precisely, any concrete system is composed of intensive processes
tending toward the (virtual) plane of consistency and/or toward (actual)
stratification. We can say that all that exists is the intensive, tending
toward the limits of virtuality and actuality; these last two ontological
registers do not “exist,” but they do “insist,” to use one of Deleuze’s
terms. Nothing ever instantiates the sheer frozen stasis of the actual nor
the sheer differential dispersion of the virtual; rather, natural or worldly
processes are always and only actualizations, that is, they are processes
of actualization structured by virtual multiplicities and heading toward


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  223
an actual state they never quite attain. More precisely, systems also con-
tain tendencies moving in the other direction, toward virtuality; systems
are more or less stable sets of processes moving in different directions,
toward actuality and toward virtuality. Chapter 10 addresses again in-
tensive experimentation through the notion of “becoming,” in which an
emergent system or “assemblage” is created from at least two systems
that come together.
To sum up Deleuze’s view of the good life as imbedded in his ontol-
ogy, it may be interesting to evaluate Alain Badiou’s interpretation of it.
 Badiou maintains that, contrary to the dominant perception, Deleuze is
not so much a philosopher of the multiple as of the One. Whence the sub-
title of Badiou’s book, The Clamor of Being, which refers to Deleuze’s
reading of the tradition of univocity in metaphysics: “A single and same
voice for the whole thousand-voiced multiple, a single and same Ocean
for all the drops, a single clamour of Being for all beings.”148
However, Peter Hallward, a Badiou scholar, characterizes Badiou as
painting Deleuze as a “poet of a living cosmos,” who nonetheless es-
tablishes a philosophy that is “indistinguishable from a philosophy of
death”; in this, Badiou “goes perhaps a little too far.”149 For Hallward,
Deleuze’s singular logic of Being can be seen as analogous to the tra-
dition of theophanic thinkers, whereby the divine spark of creation is
entombed in creatures; the task of the creature is to redeem that divine
spark from its creatural prison.150 Although counter-effectuation—or
the “extraction of the event”—is not an annihilation of the creature, it is
its “self-transcendence,” so that it may become “an adequate vehicle for
the creating which sustains and transforms it.” Counter-effectuation is a
“redemptive” move, Hallward claims, taking us “out of this world.”151
The Deleuzian joy of creation and the humor of counter-effectuation
intervene here, as we shall shortly see. I hope that the account of the
Deleuzian good life has helped to elucidate what counter-effectuation
means for Deleuze, as well as to identify the unclarity that still plagues
it. This elaborate explanation was necessary in order to consider whether
the good life that Deleuze describes is tragic or comical, before address-
ing the role that laughter, humor, irony and satire play in such a life.
I now turn to these topics.
II The Tragic and the Comic
Deleuze differentiates between the comical and the tragic, and chooses
the former over the latter in all of his writings. The tragic is either aban-
doned or its suffering transmuted in Deleuze’s thought. He uses the fol-
lowing argument: the tragic can be differentiated into the sad tragic and
the joyful tragic; the former is discarded because it is sad, while the
joyful tragic, because joyful, is tragic no more. The role of laughter,
along with play and dance, is to transmute suffering into joy. Thus, the


224  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
comic replaces the tragic in Deleuze’s philosophy, given that the comic is
compatible not only with seriousness, but also with terror, atrocity and
cruelty. In order to clarify Deleuze’s unorthodox views, let me elaborate
first on the tragic and then on the comic.
A The Tragic
Deleuze differentiates between two kinds of tragic: one is joyful while
the other is sad. The joyful tragic can be transmuted through laughter,
as well as through play and dance, into joy, while the sad tragic should
be renounced. Deleuze believes that the Nietzschean idea of the tragic
has been misunderstood: being a joyful tragic, it is not tragic, but joyful;
the sense of the tragic is joy; for Deleuze’s Nietzsche, thus, it is joy that is
tragic. Tragic verily means joyful, as it is a dynamic gaiety.
Affirming life is tragic because it affirms chance, and through chance,
being or the multiple, and through the multiple, the one:
Every Nietzschean concept lies at the crossing of two unequal ge-
netic lines. Not only the eternal return and the Overman, but laugh-
ter, play and dance. In relation to Zarathustra laughter, play and
dance are affirmative powers of transmutation: dance transmutes
heavy into light, laughter transmutes suffering into joy and the play
of throwing (the dice) transmutes low into high. But in relation to
Dionysus dance, laughter and play are affirmative powers of reflec-
tion and development. Dance affirms becoming and the being of be-
coming; laughter, roars of laughter, affirm multiplicity and the unity
of multiplicity; play affirms chance and the necessity of chance.
(NP 193–4)
Multiplicity is affirmed as multiplicity and becoming is affirmed as be-
coming. That means that affirmation is itself multiple, that it becomes
itself and that becoming and multiplicity are themselves affirmations.152
Multiplicity is no longer answerable to the One, nor is becoming an-
swerable to Being. Being and the One not only lose their meaning but
take on new meanings: now the One refers to the multiple as the mul-
tiple, as splinters of fragments; Being refers to becoming as becoming.
Thus, becoming is no longer opposed to Being, nor is the multiple op-
posed to the One and with the disappearance of these oppositions, the
category of nihilism disappears as well:
What is affirmed is the One of multiplicity, the Being of becom-
ing. Or, as Nietzsche puts it, he affirms the necessity of chance.
Dionysus is a player. The real player makes of chance an object of
affirmation: he affirms the fragments, the elements of chance; from
the affirmation is born the necessary number, which brings back


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  225
the throw of dice…the play of the eternal return. This return is pre-
cisely the Being of becoming, the one of multiplicity, the necessity
of chance.
(NP 86–7)
Thus, only affirmation comes back, only what is affirmed comes back,
only joy returns.153 Repetition saves: this is the prodigious secret of a
repetition that is liberating and selecting.154
In contradistinction to the tragic that is transmuted into joy through
laughter, dance and play, the sad tragic is nothing but a “caricature
of the tragic, a comedy of false consciousness.”155 One of the things
that reflects our decadence is the manner in which we need to express
our anguish, solitude and guilt, to dramatize encounters, “in short,
the whole tragedy of interiority.” If Nietzsche admits of no legitimate
interpretation, Deleuze argues, “there are also completely illegitimate
 misinterpretations—all those that spring from the spirit of seriousness,
the spirit of gravity, Zarathustra’s ape—that is, the cult of interiority.”156
Nietzsche should be differentiated from other tragic thinkers such as
Blaise Pascal, Søren Kierkegaard and Lev Shestov, for whom tragedy
means the ills of interiority: anguish, sights, guilt, bad conscience, all
the forms of discontentment. The troubles of interiority associated with
the majority of the tragic thinkers should be discarded as should the
Hegelian vision of the tragic as burden.157 Philosophy incarnated in He-
gel is the enterprise to “burden” life, that is, to overwhelm it with ev-
ery weight, to reconcile life with the state and with religion, to inscribe
death in life—“the monstrous enterprise to submit life to negativity, the
enterprise of resentment and unhappy consciousness.” One of the princi-
ples of the Hegelian dialectic is the valorization of sadness and suffering,
of sad passions as a practical principle which manifests itself in division
and tearing apart.158 With this dialectic of negativity and contradiction,
Hegel has inspired all the languages of betrayal, on the right as well as
on the left.159 Hence, as we have seen, Deleuze affirms that that which
he detests more than anything is Hegelianism and its dialectic.160
­
Instead of Hegelianism, Deleuze sides with the naturalists. He argues
that between Lucretius, Hume, Spinoza and Nietzsche, there is a secret
connection founded on the criticism of the negative, the cultivation of
joy, the hatred of interiority, the exteriority of forces and relations, and
the denunciation of power. One of the most profound constants of nat-
uralism is the condemnation of all sadness, including everything that
causes it and anything that needs sadness for exercising power. From
Lucretius to Nietzsche, the same end is pursued and attained: natural-
ism affirms life with the assistance of thought and sensibility. Natural-
ism directs its attack against the prestige of the negative, depriving it
of its power by denying the spirit of negativity the right to speak in
 philosophy’s name. For naturalists,


226  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
The multiple as multiple is the object of affirmation, just as the
diverse as diverse is the object of joy. Lucretius established for
a long time to come the implications of Naturalism: the posi-
tivity of nature; Naturalism as the philosophy of affirmation;
pluralism linked with multiple affirmation; sensualism con-
nected with the joy of the diverse; and the practical critique of all
mystifications.161
(WP 279)
Discarding the tragic is not tantamount to denying cruelty and terror.
“Entity=event, this is terror, but also a lot of joy,” Deleuze affirms.162
Moreover, Deleuze sees terror as fundamentally associated with modes
of the comic:
You asked me whether dramatization in general is related to the
tragic. I don’t see there being any privileged relation between them.
The tragic and the comic are still categories of representation,
whereas there is a more fundamental relation between dramatiza-
tion and a certain mode of terror, which can entail a maximum of
clownishness as well as grotesque.
(DI 98)
Deleuze expresses his interest in cruelty in various works.163 Difference
as chaos is necessary, and it compels acts of determination to essential
cruelty. Cruelty is the generation of emotion and change as things are
determined in relation to an indifferent background. Individual things
are animated with pain, fear and lust against an indistinct ground. In
order to tame difference, philosophy has posited an original happy state
free of cruelty. On the contrary, Williams explains:
Difference in itself is vivifying, in the sense that to live is to be deter-
minate, but that living intensity has an indistinct ground as its con-
dition. To live is to live in horror of the ground—difference is cruel.
(Williams 2003, 59)
Deleuze’s world is a chaos dramatized or actualized as a theater of cru-
elty, like the world of the Stoics, Nietzsche, Leibniz and Artaud, whose
notion of a theater of cruelty Deleuze endorses. We can note the role of
cruelty in various aspects of Deleuze’s thought. First, Deleuze tells us
that he has chosen the Stoics in The Logic of Sense because none has
described a world more agitated and obscure—one has only to think
of Seneca’s tragedies.164 Second, he asserts that the world of Leibniz is
perhaps the cruelest of all worlds.165 Third, he argues that Nietzsche
brought theater into philosophy, and with it, new means of expression
that enabled the transformation of philosophy. Indeed, since the Ger-
man philosopher introduces “a theatre of cruelty, a theatre of the will


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  227
to power and the eternal return,”166 Nietzsche’s philosophical theater
anticipates Artaud’s. Finally, Deleuze notes that Artaud perceived the
world as a theater of cruelty, “a strange theatre comprised of pure deter-
minations, agitating time and space, directly affecting the soul, whose
actors are larva.”167
Deleuze is not an optimistic philosopher, as his teacher Maurice de
Gandillac rightly points out.168 Toni Negri detects “a tragic note” in
Deleuze, who does not deny it.169 Elsewhere, Deleuze says that if he had
not been a philosopher, he would have been a wailer.170 Yet in Theatrum
Philosophicum, Foucault describes Deleuze’s philosophy in the follow-
ing terms:
This is philosophy not as thought, but as theatre: a theatre of mime
with multiple, fugitive, and instantaneous scenes in which blind ges-
tures signal to each other. This is the theatre where the explosive
laughter of the Sophists tears through the mask of Socrates; where
Spinoza’s methods conduct a wild dance in a decentered circle while
substance revolves about it like a mad planet…In the sentry box of
the Luxembourg Gardens, Duns Scotus places his head through the
circular window; he is sporting an impressive moustache; it belongs
to Nietzsche, disguised as Klossowski.
(Foucault 1977, 196)
Foucault describes Deleuze’s philosophy as a gag comedy, in which dis-
guise is the law. If the comical replaces the tragic in Deleuze’s philos-
ophy, we should address the Deleuzian view of the comic in order to
understand the tragic.
B The Comic
Far from being a monolithic notion, the tragic that Deleuze endorses is
either sad or joyful. His rejection of sadness suffices for discarding the
tragic that saddens; as the result is joy, that which remains of the tragic
is not tragic anymore. The comical takes the place of the tragic if we note
its compatibility in Deleuze’s philosophy with seriousness and with the
terror, the atrocity and the cruelty involved in the comical.
Here are two examples. In his work on Foucault, Deleuze introduces
Discipline and Punish thus:
The Divine Comedy of punishment means we can retain the basic
right to collapse in fits of laughter in the face of a dazzling array of
perverse inventions, cynical discourses and meticulous horrors. A
whole chain of phenomena, from anti-masturbation machines for
children to the mechanics of prison for adults, sets off an unex-
pected laughter which shame, suffering or death cannot silence.
(Deleuze 1988, 23)


228  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Outside events may affect us, but will not fully subsume us. Expressing
laughter is “a great joy which is not the ambivalent joy of hatred, but the
joy of wanting to destroy whatever mutilates life.”171
Another example is the provocation of Nietzsche’s laughter in “No-
madic Thought.”172 Coming “face to face with something sickening, ig-
noble, disgusting” results in laughter, which expresses the unbounded
joy of revolution for Deleuze. This kind of laughter is positive and cre-
ative, according to Deleuze, an uncontrollable escape from restraints of
imposed logic and morality.
Deleuze affirms that the essence of all great work lies in comicality; to
rest satisfied with tragic first impressions is to misread the text:
This pseudo-sense of the tragic makes us stupid. How many authors
we deface by substituting a puerile, tragic feeling for the aggressive,
comic power of the thought which animates their work? A “burst of
laughter” is undifferentiated from artistic joy.
(P 130)
There can be no tragic work of art because joy is essential for creation:
since it necessarily liberates, art makes everything explode, first and
foremost the tragic. There is no unhappy creation; it is always in the vis
comica that art is to be found.173
We risk to misjudge a great writer in the following ways: we may
fail to recognize the profound logic or the systematic character of his
work, or we may fail to recognize his comical genius and power, from
which the work generally draws the greater part of its anti- conformist
efficiency. We prefer to relate the anguish of the author and the tragic
features of the work.174 However, the comical is the mark of all great
writers and self-parody is the mark of the genius175: “In all great writers
one encounters a humorous or comic level along additional levels, which
are not merely serious but atrocious.”176
Max Brod recounts how the audience went wild with laughter when
Kafka read The Trial.177 Deleuze maintains that one can hardly read
Samuel Beckett without laughing, without passing from one moment of
delight to another:
Laughter—and not meaning. Schizophrenic laughter or revolution-
ary joy, this is what emerged from the great book; not the anguish
of petty narcissism, the dread of guilt. We could call it superhuman
comedy, a divine jest. An indescribable delight always springs forth
from the great books, even when they present things that are ugly,
desperate, or terrifying. As it is, all great books bring about a trans-
mutation; they give tomorrow’s health. One cannot help but laugh
when the codes are confounded.
(NT 148)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  229
Foucault exemplifies for Deleuze the alliance of cruelty and laughter
which can be found in all great writers. Not only does he have a diabol-
ical humor, his work on infamous men, which is a master-piece of com-
icality and beauty infused with discrete gaiety, exemplifies how funny
philosophical analysis can be.178
Nor does Deleuze settle for the mixture that the tragi-comic rep-
resents. Analyzing the work of its most renowned representative, Charlie
Chaplin, he rejects the tragic:
Chaplin knew how to select gestures which were close to each other
and corresponding situations which were far apart, so as to make
their relationship produce a particularly intense emotion at the same
time as laughter, and to redouble the laughter through this emo-
tion…No case can be made for a tragic Chaplin. There is certainly
no case for saying that we laugh, whereas we should cry.
(MI 170–71; quoted in Baruchello 2002, 463)
Deleuze interprets even Chaplin’s art as non-tragic. Once the tragic is
discarded, the comic is analyzed into its constituents, mainly humor and
irony, but also satire. This analysis is important, as not all the forms
of the comical express the power of the free person. Only strength en-
ables the destruction that the comic enacts to be also a construction, as
only the free person destroys that which is worth destroying.
III Humor
Humor and irony are the main constituents of the comic in Deleuze’s early
writings. Parody and satire are briefly addressed: subsumed under humor,
parody is deemed “the highest humour”179; satire is not introduced before
The Logic of Sense, where it is briefly discussed only to be brushed aside.
Deleuze conceives of both irony and humor as necessary in various
works, such as Difference and Repetition, Masochism, and Nomad
Thought. In The Logic of Sense, Deleuze adds satire to the comical
terms he examines, only to reject it along with irony in favor of humor.
It is noteworthy that Deleuze rejects irony in all of his writings and in-
terviews since The Logic of Sense onward. The term “laughter” is used
in Nietzsche and Philosophy but abandoned afterward.
Deleuze’s manifold references to the comic in the history of  philosophy
constitute an alternative history of laughter, and an alternative history of
philosophy. Before further elaboration, let me indicate the main points
of interest of the Deleuzian notion of humor.
First, humor is often qualified within Deleuze’s writings and lectures,
either by quotes (“Humour”), or by epithets, such as “black,”180 “dia-
bolical,” “Jewish” and “Ethical.” These qualifications are usually not
clarified, nor do they always seem justified.


230  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Second, Deleuze ascribes humor not only to the novelists he likes (such
as Kafka and Proust), but to all the philosophers he admires, such as
Hume, Rousseau, Kant, Leibniz, Foucault, among others, as well as
to his teacher, de Gandillac. Only Bergson is exempted, and reference
to Bergson’s Laughter is strangely missing from Deleuze’s Bergsonism
(1966).181 However, Deleuze appropriates Bergson’s definitions of humor
and irony from Difference and Repetition on. Spinoza, hardly a humor-
ist, is deemed anti-satirical and ascribed a form of humor that Deleuze
characterizes as “Jewish,” “ethical” and “diabolical.” The latter epithet
also qualifies the humor of Leibniz and Foucault, while “Jewish” quali-
fies the humor ascribed to Proust. In Difference and Repetition, Deleuze
renders accurately Kierkegaard’s view humor by noting its limitations,
as Kierkegaard goes beyond humor; and Deleuze carefully and rightly
avoids ascribing humor to Nietzsche, replacing it with parody and irony:
parody as “the highest form of humor” for Deleuze qualifies Nietzsche’s
use of the comic, together with irony, the counterpart of humor, despite
Nietzsche’s emphatic rejection irony, which Deleuze choses to ignore.182
Third, Deleuze’s use of irony and humor follows the definitions Berg-
son gives to these terms at the end of the second chapter of Laughter. For
Bergson, irony and humor are related to the most common of contrasts,
the contrast between the real and the ideal, between what is and what
ought to be:
When we state what ought to be done, and pretend to believe that
this is actually being done, we have Irony. When, on the contrary,
we describe with scrupulous minuteness what is being done, and pre-
tend to believe that this is what ought to be done, we have Humour.
(Bergson 1956, 143)
Humor, thus defined, is the counterpart of irony. The higher we allow
ourselves to be uplifted by the idea of the good that ought to be, the
more irony is emphasized: thus, “irony may grow so hot within us that it
becomes a kind of high-pressure eloquence. However, the deeper we go
down into an evil that actually is, in order to set down its details in the
most cold-blooded indifference, the more humor is emphasized.” Hence,
both are forms of satire for Bergson, but irony is oratorical in its nature,
while humor partakes of the scientific:
Several authors, Jean Paul amongst them, have noticed that humour
delights in concrete terms, technical details, definite facts. If our
analysis is correct, this is not an accidental trait of humour, it is its
very essence. A humourist is a moralist disguised as a scientist, some-
thing like an anatomist who practices dissection with the sole object
of filling us with disgust; so that humour, in the restricted sense in


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  231
which we are here regarding the word, is really a transposition from
the moral to the scientific.
(Bergson 1956, 143)
Irony goes up and humor goes down, for Bergson and Deleuze. Irony is
lofty, humor is concrete and both are considered necessary in Deleuze’s
early works.
The new element that Deleuze adds to Bergson’s view of humor is guilt:
guilt is indistinguishable from humor, as Kierkegaard maintained.183
This feature is exemplified in masochistic humor: we can appreciate the
pervasiveness of guilt or humor once masochism is understood as “a
fundamental human disposition with profound religious and philosoph-
ical implications.”184 Guilt before the law, in which we all partake, is
nothing but anxiety that discharges itself in laughter, as in the public
readings of Kafka’s novels.
As Deleuze’s thought evolves, Deleuze variously qualifies various sorts
of humor. However, they have this in common: they are always opposed
to irony, sometimes also to satire, and are systematically elected by
Deleuze over their ironic counterparts. Thus, British, Jewish, Stoic and
Zen “humor,” which oppose various forms of irony, are to be preferred
to their respective ironic counterparts. Masochistic humor is to be cho-
sen over Sadean irony, both being ways of confronting the law. Humor
is to be preferred as it deals with individuals, with solutions, even par-
tial, and constitutes the art of surfaces, in contradiction both to ironic
alternatives, the art of the heights, and to satiric alternatives, the art of
the depth.
Fourth, the notion of humor is interwoven in all the main concepts
of Deleuzian philosophy, on which I elaborated in the first part of this
chapter. One can hardly find an idea he advances or a proposition he
endorses, beginning with his philosophy of mind, continuing with his
aesthetics and his politics and ending in his ethics that is not somehow
associated with humor.
Fifth, humor cannot be dissociated from the aim of Deleuzian ethics,
which is also the purpose of his philosophy. The Deleuzian affirmation
of life is effectuated by self-directed laughter that transmutes suffering
into joy; the affirmation of multiplicity is signified by roars of laughter;
humor is the main tool of vice-diction in Difference and Repetition and
of counter-actualization in The Logic of Sense, these notions being the
key to Deleuze’s ethics of amor fati as that which enables the selection
necessary for eternal return.
Finally, the person who implements this ethics, called humor-actor
or mime, is also referred to as “idiot,” as “playing the idiot” is an in-
trinsic part of the new figure of philosophy and politics that Deleuze
proposes.


232  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Following these introductory remarks, I elaborate in this part on the
use of humor and irony as essential aspects of Deleuze’s method in his
early writings, his later rejection of irony along with satire in favor of
humor, which he ascribes to all the philosophers and writers he likes,
and the role humor plays in various aspects of Deleuze’s philosophy be-
ginning with his philosophy of mind, continuing with his aesthetics and
politics and ending with his ethics. I conclude this part with a discussion
of actors, mimes and idiots in attempting to clarify the significance that
“playing the idiot” has in Deleuze’s philosophy and politics.
A The Need for Humor and Irony
Humor and irony are essential aspects of Deleuze’s method inasmuch
as they apply the principles of connection he advances. Deleuze is “de-
termined to forget, destroy and move beyond established truths be-
cause they obscure deeper truths about reality.” As Williams explains,
humor and irony combine connection with a constructive or creative
destruction.185
To this purpose, Deleuze appropriates Bergson’s definitions of humor
and irony and invests them with new meanings: they are now seen as
two ways of overturning the moral law, which is the Kantian approach
to morality. The Marquis de Sade and Leopold von Sacher-Masoch ex-
emplify for Deleuze the two main attempts at subverting the moral law
by responding to it through irony and humor, respectively.
Deleuze consistently rejects the moral law, which he sees as abstract,
moralizing and limiting. The argument against the role of laws in mo-
rality focuses on the rational decision to lead a life according to laws
or rules. Deleuze opposes this decision for the following reasons: living
according to rules perpetuates the illusion that life can be thought as
repetitive, as a repetition of the same; moreover, in perpetuating this il-
lusion, living according to rules diverts us from the genuine source of in-
tensity in our lives, that is, the creative experimentation with simulacra
as individuals caught in a process of change. This means that we should
consciously adopt a law according to which we never repeat. Indeed, if
repetition were possible, it would be due to a miracle rather than a law.
Repetition opposes the law on both counts, the similarity of the form
and the equivalence of its content. Moreover, if repetition were possible,
it would be opposed not only to moral law but to natural law as well.
Natural law is the unconscious acquisition of habits. However, habit
cannot be understood in terms of generality; rather, it should be un-
derstood in terms of a constantly altering scene, where an action has to
change in order to reinforce the intention to acquire a habit, or where the
action remains the same but in a different context. Difference in itself is
a necessary condition for repetition and for habit.
In every respect, then, repetition is a transgression. It puts the law into
question by denouncing “its nominal or general character in favour of a


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  233
more profound and more artistic existence.”186 There are two ways of
overturning the moral law, for Deleuze. One way is
by ascending towards the principles: challenging the law as second-
ary, derived, borrowed or “general”; denouncing it as involving a
second-hand principle which diverts an original force or usurps an
original power. The other way, by contrast, is to overturn the law
by descending towards the consequences, to which one submits with
a too-perfect attention to detail… The first way of overturning the
law is ironic, where irony appears as an art of principles, of ascent
toward towards the principles and of overturning principles. The
second is humor, which is an art of consequences and descents, of
suspensions and falls.
(DR 5)
Irony and humor either show the sources of the law that run counter to
it, as irony does, or ridicule the law by too great an obedience, as humor
does. Thus, both irony and humor transgress the law. Repetition ap-
pears in the suspense (humor) and the ascent (irony), as though existence
recommenced and “reiterated” itself once no longer constrained by laws.
Thus, Deleuze argues that “repetition belongs to humor and irony”; be-
ing by nature a transgression or exception, repetition always reveals a
singularity that is opposed to the particulars subsumed under laws, a
universal that is opposed to the generalities which give rise to laws.187
Rather than oppose and replace the moral law, humor and irony work
within it. They transform the law and our relation to it; however, they
are not simply against it. They satisfy the Deleuzian principle of seeking
completeness by following the law, rather than avoiding it or replacing
it with something different. Thus, the law remains but its status has
changed and the context within which it is applied has been enhanced.
Moreover, humor functions by discarding a significant property of
the law: it undermines its claims to purity and universality. Thus, humor
also satisfies the Deleuzian principle of forgetting or constructive de-
struction, and combines in this way connection with destruction.
In Masochism’s seventh chapter, “Humor, Irony and the Law,” Deleuze
relates a history of humor and irony. Beginning with Plato, it continues
with Kant and Nietzsche up to Kafka.188 From Plato onward, humor and
irony are associated with the law and enable politics. As Bogue explains,
Before Kant, law has been conceived along Platonic lines as subsidi-
ary to both a higher principle of the Good and a consideration of the
consequences of the application of law (which Deleuze labels “the
Best”). Inherent in Plato’s notion of law is an ironic recognition of
the law’s imperfection, when viewed from the perspective of the
Good, and a humorous attitude toward the law’s inadequacy, when
seen as flawed but necessary for the maintenance of societal order


234  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
(as when Socrates, amidst the laughter of his disciples, decides that
it is best to observe the law and drink the hemlock).
Deleuze further explains in Masochism that:
The disciples present at the death of Socrates could not help laugh-
ing. Irony and humor are the essential forms through which we ap-
prehend the law. It is in this essential relation to the law that they
acquire their function and their significance. Irony is the process of
thought whereby the law is made to depend on an infinitely superior
Good, just as humor is the attempt to sanction the law by recourse
to an infinitely more righteous Best.
(M 85)
In the Critique of Practical Reason, Kant articulates a new conception
of the law as a pure form, which is independent of the Good and the
Best. The moral imperative cannot be grounded in something external,
by taking into consideration the consequences of observing it. The Good
itself is made to depend on the law rather than the other way round. The
object of the law becomes by definition unknowable and elusive as the
law becomes an ultimate ground.189
Thus, despite their domination in the reflection on the law, Plato’s classi-
cal irony and humor are turned upside down. The superior principle of the
Good and the sanction of the righteous in the light of the Best, or the upper
and lower limits of the law, are now reduced to nothingness. Unwittingly
elucidating the principles portrayed in The Trial and In the Penal Colony,
Kant’s Law becomes Kafka’s Law: a law that reveals itself through the
execution of its sentences, whose indeterminacy makes us all guilty. As all
that remains is the indeterminate character of the law and the specificity of
the punishment, irony and humor take on a modern aspect. Reconceived in
terms of the indeterminacy of its content and of the guilt of the person who
submits to it, the law is still represented by irony and humor; yet,
Kafka gives to humor and irony their full modern significance in
agreement with the transformed character of the law. Max Brod re-
calls that when Kafka gave a reading of The Trial, everyone present,
including Kafka himself, was overcome by laughter—as mysterious
a phenomenon as the laughter that greeted the death of Socrates. A
spurious sense of tragedy dulls our intelligence; how many authors
are distorted by placing a childishly tragic construction on what is
more often the expression of an aggressively comic force! The comic
is the only possible mode of conceiving the law, in a peculiar combi-
nation of irony and humor.
(M 85–6)
Irony and humor are directed in modern thought at the subversion of the
law. The two main attempts at subversion are Sade and Sacher-Masoch’s


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  235
respective ironic and humorist responses to the law. Unlike Plato, they
use irony and humor to turn the law upside down.
Deleuze’s discussion of Sacher-Masoch aims at reviving the reputation
of the celebrated and prolific nineteenth-century novelist, who is cur-
rently remembered solely as the paradigmatic exemplar of masochism.190
He attempts to show that Sacher-Masoch is an astute psychologist and
a profound thinker whose works, along with those of Sade, articulate a
perverse idealism aimed at the subversion of the Kantian notion of law.
Deleuze sees Sacher-Masoch as a Nietzschean philosopher; rather than
a sick man, he is a doctor of civilization:
The great artists…are not sick but on the contrary, they are rather
special doctors. Why Masoch gives his name to a perversion as old
as the world? Not because he “suffers” from it, but because it ren-
ovates the symptoms, he paints an original picture in making of
the contract the principal sign, and also in linking the masochist
conducts to the situation of minorities: masochism becomes an act
of resistance, inseparable from a humour of minorities. Masoch is
a grand symptomologist… Nietzsche was saying, the artist or the
philosopher are doctors of civilization.
(P 195)
The modern conception of law enunciated by Kant in the second critique
elicits responses from both Sacher-Masoch and Sade. Irony aims at tran-
scending the law toward a higher principle; thus, the Sadean hero sub-
verts the law. However, the masochist should not be regarded as gladly
submitting to it; rather, his submission contains elements of contempt,
criticism and provocation. The masochist also attacks the law, but in
a downward movement from the law to its consequences, in contradis-
tinction to the upward movement of irony toward a transcendent higher
principle that overrides it. The downward movement of humor, which
seeks to reduce the law to its farthest consequences, indicates the law’s
absurdity; it can be detected through a closer examination of the mas-
ochistic behavior:
The essence of masochistic humor lies in this, that the very law
which forbids the satisfaction of desire under threat of subsequent
punishment is converted into one which demands the punishment
first and then orders that the satisfaction of the desire should nec-
essarily follow upon the punishment…The same process is reflected
in the other features of masochism, such as disavowal, suspense and
fantasy, which should be regarded as so many forms or aspects of
humor. The masochist is insolent in his obsequiousness, rebellious
in his submission; in short, he is a humorist, a logician of conse-
quences, just as the ironic sadist is a logician of principles.
(M 88–9)


236  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
A falsely submissive soul manages to evade the law by adopting it, tasting
pleasures and mocking by submission. The world of masochism contains
elements of humor and provocation, of parody (the highest humor) and
ridicule.191 Following Kierkegaard, Deleuze argues that guilt is indis-
tinguishable from humor. Thus, in the very intensity of the masochist’s
sense of guilt and in the severity of his punishment, the humor that char-
acterizes the masochist’s predicament is already at work, “for it is the
father who is guilty in the son, not the son in relation to the father.”192
This means that sadism does not turn into masochism or masoch-
ism into sadism, contrary to Freud’s analysis of sadomasochism in the
wake of Richard von Krafft-Ebing.193 Rather, each is a paradoxical by-
product of the other: sadism is the humorous outcome of masochism,
and masochism is the ironic outcome of sadism.194
Deleuze emphasizes the political insight inherent to Sade’s view of the
revolutionary republic of 1789 as an institution opposed to both con-
tract and law. Because of the sexual and sexualized context of this view,
however, it is entirely ironic, “as if deliberately to challenge any attempt
to think of politics in legalistic or contractual terms.”195 Sacher-Masoch
presents us with a comparable tour de force, which is the humorous con-
verse of Sade’s, this time in the context of the 1848 Revolution.
Deleuze assigns irony and humor also to Kierkegaard and Nietzsche.
They also resist constructively moral laws and generality by using irony
and humor in repetition, an attitude which Deleuze associates with
theater and drama. For Kierkegaard, Job’s infinite contestation and
Abraham’s infinite resignation are one and the same thing. While Job
challenges the law in an ironic manner, Abraham submits humorously to
the law. The former refuses all second-hand explanations and dismisses
the general in order to reach the most singular as principle or as univer-
sal. The latter finds in that submission precisely the singularity of his
only son whom the law commanded him to sacrifice.196
For Nietzsche, everything is mask. The tone changes in his work,
bringing a new violence or a new humor as exemplified by the comedy
of the Overman.197 When the masks are conflated into that of a dunce
and a buffoon under the effect of some organic process, the illness itself
becomes inseparable from the last writings. Madness is the “comic solu-
tion,” the final farce that Nietzsche spoke of.198
Nietzsche and Kierkegaard give rise to Deleuze’s view of philosophy
and metaphysics as theater. The Deleuzian notion of theater responds to
the problem of how to create without representing. Hegel’s logic moves
from one representation to another that negates it, and on to a synthesis
of both, whereas representation has no place in the theater that Nietzsche
and Kierkegaard enact: the movement is not from one thing to another,
but within one changing individual. Thus, Deleuze argues that Kierke-
gaard and Nietzsche inaugurate something new. Rather than theorizing
theater, they enact it in philosophy, creating in this way a theater of real


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  237
movement and actual repetition. By inventing “an incredible equivalent
of theatre within philosophy,” they found “simultaneously this theatre
of the future and a new philosophy.”199
Kierkegaard creates a theater of humor and faith,200 which ends as
a theater of faith; he opposes the spiritual movement or the movement
of faith to the movement of logic. He invites us to go beyond aesthetic
repetition, beyond irony and even beyond humor, in full awareness
that only the aesthetic, the ironic and the humoristic images of such a
 going-beyond can be offered.201 Therefore,
In Kierkegaard…there is an adventure of faith, according to which
one is always the clown of one’s own faith, the comedian of one’s
ideal…the believer does not lead his life only as a tragic sinner in so
far as he is deprived of the condition, but as a comedian and clown,
a simulacrum of himself is so far as he is doubled in the condition.
Two believers cannot observe each other without laughing. Grace
excludes no less when it is given that when it is lacking. Indeed, Ki-
erkegaard said that he was a poet of the faith rather than a knight—
in short, a “humorist.” This was not his fault but that of the concept
of faith; and Gogol’s terrible adventure is perhaps more exemplary
still. How could faith not be its own habit and its own reminiscence,
and how could the repetition it takes for its object—a repetition
which, paradoxically, takes place once and for all—not be comical?
(DR 96)
Zarathustra exemplifies for Nietzsche the “incredible equivalent of the-
atre within philosophy,” which founds simultaneously his theater of the
future and a new philosophy. Conceived entirely within philosophy, but
also entirely for the stage, Zarathustra enacts “a comic opera about ter-
rible things.” Thus, Deleuze notes, “it is not by chance that Nietzsche
speaks of the comic character of the Overman.”202 Deleuze qualifies the
drama that Nietzsche enacts as a theater of unbelief, a theater of cruelty,
and humor and irony as indispensable and fundamental operations of
nature within this philosophy.203 Thus,
The eternal return is not a faith, but the truth of faith: it has isolated
the double or the simulacrum, it has liberated the comic in order
to make this an element of the superhuman. This is why—again as
Klossowski says—it is not a doctrine but the simulacrum of every
doctrine (the highest irony); it is not a belief but the parody of ev-
ery belief (the highest humor): a belief and a doctrine eternally yet
to come. We have too often been invited to judge the atheist from
the viewpoint of the belief or the faith that we suppose still droves
him—in short, from the viewpoint of grace.204
(DR 95–6)


238  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Both Kierkegaard and Nietzsche’s works call for a reading that has to
re-enact them. This means that the reader is an actor following Kierke-
gaard’s and Nietzsche’s script and stage directions. As Williams ex-
plains, re-enacting becomes a central notion in Deleuze’s philosophy
through vice-diction and counter-effectuation. “To vice-dict or counter-
effectuate the script is to say it in a different way by expressing how it
works on us.”205 To do so is also to change the script, and this is enabled
by the script’s looseness with respect to the specification of characters in
Kierkegaard and Nietzsche—they are merely layers of masks that need
to be fleshed out. The texts force the reader to put new voices and feel-
ings and new contexts and thoughts into them. In that sense, the reading
is not a literal repetition, but a way of playing Kierkegaard’s aesthetic life
or Nietzsche’s overman:
In the theatre of repetition, we experience pure forces, dynamic lines
in space which act without intermediary upon the spirit, and link
it directly with nature and history, with a language which speaks
before word, with gestures which develop before organized bod-
ies, with masks before faces, with specters and phantoms before
 characters—the whole apparatus of repetition as a “terrible power.”
(DR 19; quoted in William 2013, 48)
Deleuze suggests a role for death in the play of masks and disguises. The
death-drive is the condition for actual repetition and not the other way
around:
Death has nothing to do with a material model. On the contrary, the
death instinct may be understood in relation to masks and costumes.
Repetition is truly that which disguises itself in constituting itself,
that which constitutes itself only by disguising itself.
(DR 28; quoted in Williams 2013, 51)
We repeat because as masks or combinations of actual things, sensations,
virtual ideas and the intensities that light them up, we are repeatedly
driven to play various aspects of ourselves in different ways. The motiva-
tion behind this play is not to return to our origin or to renew the plea-
sure that destruction affords because it resolves tensions in our character.
Rather, this play follows from our being a necessarily unstable combina-
tion of actual things and pure differences. Thus, the Deleuzian definition
of a mask is something that represents nothing, but which instead puts
significant components of other masks into play again in ever new ways.
Nietzsche introduces in philosophy two kinds of expression, the aph-
orism and poetry, which imply a new conception of philosophy, a new
image of both thought and thinker. Interpretation and evaluation re-
place the discovery of the truth as the ideal of knowledge. Interpretation


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  239
establishes the “meaning” of a phenomenon, which is always fragmentary
and incomplete, while evaluation determines the hierarchical “value” of
the meanings and totalizes the fragments without diminishing or elim-
inating their plurality. The aphorism is both the art of interpreting and
what must be interpreted, while poetry is both the art of evaluating and
what must be evaluated. The interpreter is the physiologist or doctor, the
one who sees phenomena as symptoms and speaks through aphorisms.
The evaluator is the artist who considers and creates “perspectives” and
speaks through poetry. The philosopher of the future is both artist and
doctor—in one word, he is a legislator. Moreover, the aphorism is asso-
ciated with humor and irony, and Nietzsche’s philosophy with laughter:
The aphorism has yet a third significant relation—in this case, to
humor and irony. Those who read Nietzsche without laughing—
without laughing often, richly, even hilariously—have, in a sense,
not read Nietzsche at all. This is not only true for Nietzsche but
for all the other authors who belong to the same horizon of our
counterculture.
(NT 147)
For Nietzsche, laughter always refers to an exterior movement of irony
and humor, a movement of intensities or intensive qualities, as Klos-
sowski and Jean-François Lyotard have noted. Deleuze notes the free
play between low and high intensities: a low intensity can undermine the
highest; it may even become as high as the highest. Not only does this
play on scales of intensity affect the ebb and flow of irony and humor in
Nietzsche, but it also qualifies experience from without:
An aphorism is a matter of laughter and joy. If we have not discov-
ered what it is in the aphorism that makes us laugh, what the distri-
bution of humor and irony is, what the division of intensities is, then
we have not found anything.
(NT 148–9)
In his annotation to Deleuze’s “Nomad Thought,” Mal Ahern notes that
aphorisms oppose the law and are seen through “embarkation,” which
means a deterritorializing experience of intensity. Their mobility draws
attention both to the way they are framed and to the exterior of the
frame, that is, the boundaries between the text and reality. The line of
the frame of an aphorism originates outside it, rather than beginning
inside the text or within the limits of the frame; thus, the aphorism’s
argument both begins outside the frame and traverses the frame.206
Summing up this analysis of irony and humor, we can see how hu-
mor and irony are essential aspects of Deleuze’s method as displayed
in his early works. Both notions are necessary to repetition and to the


240  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
subversion of the law under its Kantian or Kafkian guise, as exemplified
by Sade and Sacher-Masoch, or to the opposition to the law as general-
ity, as exemplified by Kierkegaard and Nietzsche.
As Deleuze’s thought evolves, satire enters the discussion to be re-
jected along with irony in favor of humor. Humor emerges as the form
of the comical Deleuze consistently and explicitly prefers. Let’s see how
this is done.
B Discarding Irony and Satire
Irony and humor are both necessary in Difference and Repetition
(1968), Masochism (1967) and Nomad Thought (1973). Already in Dif-
ference and Repetition, however, radical humor is considered a “supe-
rior irony,”207 and since The Logic of Sense onward (1969), Deleuze
consistently rejects irony in his writings and interviews.
Deleuze’s most significant criticism of irony can be found in Dialogues
and The Logic of Sense.208 Deleuze sees irony as a tendency of thought
to posit beyond difference an ultimate point of view rather than to rest
with the world’s flux of differences. Irony entails the elimination of dif-
ference, an inability to admit what is beyond its point of view. The ironic
ascent, which has dominated Western thinking, as Colebrook notes,209
is explained by Deleuze as follows:
An ironist is someone who discusses principles; he is seeking a first
principle, a principle which comes even before the one that was
thought to be first, he finds a course which is even more primary
than the others. He constantly goes up and down. This is why he
proceeds by questioning, he is a man of conversation, of dialogue,
he has a particular tone, always of the signifier.
(D 68)
Irony appears to resist foundations and therefore it seems to remain open
to events by avoiding the trap of forcing them into a pre-given frame; its
skeptical power depends on taking up a proposed foundational truth
prior to leading it to a nonsensical conclusion. However, this strategy
is flawed. When faced with the question “Who speaks?” irony returns
to a form of ground in the individual. Philosophical irony, that is the
skeptical dismantling of claims to certainty from Socrates through Kant
and on the post-Kantian romantics, depends on the ironist as an indivis-
ible and unique source: the individual who speaks or plays. This source
takes different forms. With Socrates, it is the individual thinker, named
and characterized; with Michel de Montaigne and then developed in
Kant, it is the person, any and all subjects, the “I” as a class; with the
romantics, it is a poetic creativity, capable of taking up all expressive
possibilities, of playing any role, as Kierkegaard noticed. The flaw here


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  241
is that, unlike humor, “irony encloses singularity within the limits of
the individual or person.”210 With the individual, there is still a form of
identity- restricting thought and inhibiting its openness to events. This
can be a character or a human (Socrates), a form (the “I”) or a power
(the romantic poet). In each, it leads to the following consequences:
openness is merely an appearance, the individual remains stuck with its
commanding identity; and each figure of the individual is threatened by a
terrible “undifferentiated ground,” a bottomless and terrifying chaos.211
By attacking the history of subjectivism, which posits a ground behind
acts and forces, Deleuze provides a history of time and history which is
anti-ironic. Irony steps above the events and flows of time to ask about
what is in general: “The whole destiny of irony is linked to representa-
tion, irony ensures the individuation of the represented or the subjectiva-
tion of the representor,” he writes. Thus, “irony contains an insufferable
claim: that of belonging to a superior race, of being the preserve of the
masters…” (D 68–9). Differentiating between classical and romantic iro-
nies, Deleuze condemns both. While romantic irony discovers the sub-
jectivity of the principle of all possible representations, classical irony
consists in showing that what is most universal in representation
is the same as the extreme individuality of the represented which
serves as its principles (classical irony culminates in the theological
affirmation according to which “the whole of the possible” is at the
same time the reality of God as singular being).
(D 68–9)
Deleuze’s criticism of the subject, the signifier and negativity are issued
as a critique of irony, also in Anti-Oedipus.212 Along the same lines, in
The Logic of Sense, he commends the Stoics and the Cynics for their
refusal of irony, which is by the same token a rejection of the tragic,
because irony is related to the tragic213:
Height, however, prepares new values for language and affirms in it
its independence and its radical difference from depth. Irony appears
each time language deploys itself in accordance with relations of
eminence, equivocity, or analogy. These three great concepts of the
tradition are the source from which all the figures of rhetoric pro-
ceed. Thus, irony will find a natural application in the tertiary order
of language, in the case of the analogy of significations, the equiv-
ocity of denotations, and the eminence of the one who manifests
himself—the whole comparative play of the self, world, and God, in
the relation of being and the individual, representation and person,
which constitute the classical and romantic forms of irony. But even
in the primary process, the voice from high above liberates prop-
erly ironic values; it withdraws behind its eminent unity and utilizes


242  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
the equivocity of its tone and the analogy of its objects. In short,
it has at its disposal the dimensions of a language before having at
its disposal the corresponding principle of organization. There is,
for example, a primordial form of Platonic irony, redressing height,
disengaging it from depth, repressing and hemming in satire or the
satirist, and employing all its “irony” in asking whether, by chance,
there could be an Idea of mud, hair, filth, or excrement.
(LS 247)
Deleuze disavows all the ironic figures of the individual in favor of an
individuation. The answer to the question “Who speaks?” are the vir-
tual conditions of the movement for the dramatic changes and events.
These conditions are Deleuze’s “sense”; they are prior to anything ac-
tual, even if they must be in relation to it. Sense speaks and not indi-
viduals. Against the elevation of the signifier and irony to a universal
and inescapable principle, Deleuze argues later, with Guattari, that the
logic of the signifier and the idea of a necessarily imposed structure are
strictly modern. Not only can we think of the emergence of signification,
subjectivity and structure, we can also think beyond the logic of irony.
Irony relies on the logic of the signifier: in order for a sign to mean, it
must have a lawfulness that transcends any specific speech act.
Both in The Logic of Sense and in his writings with Guattari, Deleuze
attempts to free sense from the system of language, by arguing that hu-
man signification and the production of a speaking “I” are effects of a
“milieu” of sense which goes well beyond the system of speech. Before I
utter a proposition, for example, I must have a perception of this world
and a desire to act in this world; there are problems, perceptions, desires
or “planes” of sense that enable some system of logic to emerge. Deleuze
and Guattari insist that there was a history and a politics before the
logic of the signifier, before the notion of a necessary system, structure,
subjectivity or law to which “we” are all necessarily submitted:
Nevertheless, what silences irony is not a return of satiric values
in the manner of an ascent from bottomless depths. Besides, noth-
ing ascends except to the surface—in which case a surface is still
necessary. Once height makes the constitution of surfaces possible,
along with the corresponding release of sexual drives, we believe
that something happens, something capable of vanquishing irony
on its own terrain—that is, on the terrain of equivocity, eminence,
and analogy. It is as if there were an eminence in excess, and exag-
gerated equivocation, and a supernumerary analogy which, rather
than being added to the others, would on the contrary ensure their
closure. An equivocation such that “afterward” there can be no
other  equivocation—this is the sense of the expression “there is also
sexuality.”
(LS 247)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  243
Colebrook examines humor and irony in the light of Deleuze and Guat-
tari’s thought: while irony steps above the events and flows of time to
ask about what is in general, Deleuze begins with the counter-tendency
of humor.214
Deleuze sees laughter and humor as a distraction of subjective posi-
tions. Whichever direction we go, either in irony or in humor, Deleuze
insists that both tendencies bring us to an ultimately inhuman unity: ei-
ther that which lies beyond us or the impersonal molecular singularities
from which we move.
As traditional irony has always seen the ultimate unity of existence as
an already given absolute within which we are located, Deleuze prefers
humor. Humor, by contrast, descends to the depths of life, disclosing
forces or powers that can never be exhausted by representation.215
In The Logic of Sense, satire is introduced as an alternative to irony;
it pertains in literature to comic poets, and in philosophy to the pre-
Socratics’ concern with depth216:
This strict combination of obscene and abusive words testifies to
the properly satiric values of language. We call “satiric” the pro-
cess by which regression regresses itself; that is, it is never a sexual
regression at the surface without its also being a digestive alimen-
tary regression in depth, stopping only at the cesspool and pursuing
the withdrawn voice as it uncovers the excremental soil that this
voice leaves behind. Making a thousand noises and withdrawing his
voice, the satiric poet, or the great pre-Socratic of one and the same
movement of the world, pursues God with insults and sinks into the
