excrement. Satire is a prodigious art of regressions.
(LS 246)
Marked by insults and obscenity, satire occupies a marginal place in The
Logic of Sense. Like irony but for different reasons, satire is discarded in
favor of humor, which is the form capable of thinking with events.
Spinoza is credited with criticizing satire, of writing his Ethics to
counteract the satirist’s sad view of human nature, as does Deleuze at the
end of The Logic of Sense. For Deleuze, Spinoza’s geometrical method
is not a method of intellectual exposition, but an inventive method of
vital and optical rectification, which gets its full sense in the Ethics when
viewed as opposed to all that which Spinoza calls satire.217
Whether indignant or railing, that is, when laughing a bad laughter,
the satirist is saddened by the human condition and by human passions.
He is one of the three individuals Spinoza denounces: the other two are
the person with sad passions, and the person who exploits these pas-
sions to gain power over others. Satire is condemned as is any thing that
takes pleasure in human impotence and sorrow, that scorns and mocks,
everything that feeds on accusation, malevolence, depreciation and base
interpretation, in short, anything that breaks one’s soul.218 That kind of


244  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
satirical laughter, as the lectures on Spinoza make clear, is not different
from irony.219
Deleuze suggests that moving away from irony with the “subject” it
creates is ethically affirmative.220 Both irony and satire are rejected in
favor of humor, which is described as the art of the surface, that is, of
immanence and naturalism, as the form capable of thinking with events.
Thus, Deleuze and Guattari’s task may be characterized as anti-ironic
and in Colebrook’s apt characterization, this talk “is not to produce a
point of view above and beyond life, but to see life itself as a humorous
or joyous multiplicity of incommensurable perceptions.”221 We need to
specify now the role of humor in Deleuze’s thought.
C Ascribing and Choosing Humor
In a series of oppositions between irony and humor that runs throughout
Deleuze’s writings and interviews, Deleuze systematically chooses hu-
mor. For example, in the sadist versus the masochist controversy, or the
ironic versus the humorous overcoming of the law, Deleuze sides with
masochistic humor. More significantly, perhaps, this process of selec-
tion begins by ascribing humor to all the philosophers he admires, who
“seemed to be part of the history of philosophy, but who escaped from it
in one respect or altogether.”222 Describing these authors as humorous,
sometimes in opposition to evidence, seems as important to Deleuze as
ascribing to them views that they do not endorse. As we have seen above,
Deleuze acknowledges that, “the author had to actually say all I had him
saying. But…it resulted from all sorts of shifting, slipping, dislocations,
and hidden emissions that I really enjoyed,” and which created in this
way a “monstrous child.”223
Thus, the highly idiosyncratic rendering of other philosophers’ thought
includes their alleged sense of humor. Zen Buddhists, the Cynics, the
Stoics, Leibniz, Spinoza, Hume, Rousseau, Kant, Nietzsche, Foucault
and even Deleuze’s teacher, de Gandillac, are all credited with humor. In
many cases, Deleuze’s observations are true and reveal his keen under-
standing of the history of humor in philosophy. In some cases, however,
the attribution of humor may surprise us; it may require us to reconsider
our understanding of humor or reject as inappropriate Deleuze’s charac-
terization without further evaluation.
I quote at length Deleuze’s arguments for ascribing humor to vari-
ous philosophers, so that the reader may see what counts for humor for
Deleuze and judge for herself the viability of his characterizations of the
humorous.
Already in Difference and Repetition, Leibniz’s alleged humor is pre-
ferred to Hegel’s alleged irony: humor is aligned both with finite rep-
resentation and with the thought of Leibniz in contrast to the infinite
representation of Hegelian dialectic.224 Deleuze favors Leibniz over
Hegel, descent over ascent and the infinitely small over the infinitely


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  245
large.225 Moreover, in The Logic of Sense, humor corresponds to Leib-
niz’s alogical incompatibility:
There is something which does not allow itself to be reduced to a
logical contradiction between predicates and which is nevertheless
an incompatibility; but it is an alogical incompatibility, an incom-
patibility of “humor” to which Leibniz’s original criteria must be
applied. The person, such as we have defined it in its difference from
the individual, pretends to amuse itself ironically with these incom-
patibilities, precisely because they are alogical.
(LS 157)
Furthermore, Leibniz is credited with “a kind of diabolical humor,”226
which Gregg Lambert justifies thusly: “One can stress the profound and
‘diabolical’ humor in Leibniz by noticing that the principal characteristic
of the monad is an extreme vertigo, or dizziness, brought on by extreme
heights even though it lives in a room located on the second floor, one
without any windows.”227
“A kind of diabolical humor” is also ascribed to Spinoza.228 While
Deleuze does not mention Spinoza’s theory of laughter, he notes his gai-
ety, the humorous procedure by which Spinoza derives shocking conse-
quences from Descartes’s geometrical method, and the comical passages
in the Ethics at which it is philosophically appropriate to laugh.229
Deleuze additionally points to Spinoza’s “Jewish humor,” on which he
does not elaborate, and to his “Ethical laughter,” which he contrasts
with both the buffoonery of the slave and the satirical laughter of the ty-
rant and the priest.230 Deleuze rejects satirical laughter along with irony,
as both are kinds of laughter that judge and condemn:
There are some very comical pages in Spinoza’s Ethics…When Spi-
noza laughs…it is a completely different laughter. I would say that
it is much more Jewish humor. It is very Spinozist…It is a very par-
ticular kind of laughter and Spinoza is one of the most cheerful au-
thors in the world… it is to this [the slave, the man of remorse,
and the satyr man] that Spinoza opposes the conception of a strong
man a powerful man, whose laughter is not the same. It is a kind of
very benevolent laughter, the laughter of the man said to be free or
strong. He says: if this is what you want, then go on, it is funny, yes
it is funny! It is the opposite of the satyr. It is Ethical laughter!231
Hume is credited with humor as well. Deleuze argues that Hume’s skep-
ticism is expressed through humor, which he contrasts with the irony of
the Platonic Socrates:
Hume goes on to apply the same critical method not simply to
revealed religion but also to so-called natural religion and to the


246  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
teleological arguments on which it is based. Here, Hume is at his
most humorous: beliefs, he says, all the more form part of our na-
ture as they are completely illegitimate from the point of view of
the principles of human nature. …If everything is belief, including
knowledge, everything is a question of degrees of belief, even the
delirium of non-knowledge. Humor, the modern skeptical view of
Hume, against irony, the ancient dogmatic virtue of the Socrates of
Plato.
(PI 44–5)
Further refereeing to Hume’s Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion,
“perhaps the only case of real dialogues in philosophy,” Deleuze points
to Philo, the skeptic, one of the three characters there who plays various
parts. Thus,
Hume-Philo’s humor is not simply a way of bringing everyone to
agreement in the name of skepticism that distributes “degrees” but
also a way of breaking with the dominant trends of the eighteenth
century and of anticipating a philosophy of the future.232
Finally, in David Hume, the work Deleuze co-authors with David Cres-
son, skepticism is described as inspiring Hume with an amicable smile
against the Pyrrhonist’s ridiculous exaggerations and absurd position.233
Rousseau has humor too. In the same context where Deleuze notes,
“whoever does not laugh out loud while reading Kafka does not truly
admire Kafka,” he articulates the two rules of thumbs we should fol-
low to avoid misjudging a great writer: they concern failures to recog-
nize “the profound logic or the systematic character of his work” or
“his comic genius and power, from which the work generally draws the
greater part of its anti-conformist efficacy (we prefer to speak of his an-
guish and tragic aspect).” Deleuze notes how these rules “are especially
invaluable for Rousseau.”234 How so? He explains:
To find oneself in impossible situations is the destiny of the beautiful
soul. This extraordinary comedy of situations is the source of all
Rousseau’s gusto. If Rousseau’s Confessions end up being a tragic
and hallucinatory book, they begin as one of the most joyful books
in literature. He loves virtue more than he is virtuous… he will
therefore require subtle devices of another kind to avoid tempting
situations or to get himself out of them. He plays on everything,
including his bad health, to keep his virtuous aspirations intact. ….
Illness inspires him, like a sense of humor (Rousseau tells of his ear
trouble with a gusto similar to Céline’s much later). But humor is
the flip-side of morality: he would sooner be a music-copyist than a
pensioner of the king.
(DI 54)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  247
Even Kant has humor: “Kant’s humour makes God into the master of a
syllogism.” This is the consequence drawn from “the Kantian definition
which posits God as the a priori principle of the disjunctive syllogism,
so that all things derive from it by a restriction of a larger reality (omi-
nitudo realitas).”235
Malebranche has some very comical, very powerful pages, according
to Deleuze.236 And we have seen that Foucault has a sense of humor:
There’s a general outlandishness [drôlerie] in Foucault: not only out-
landish punishments, which produce the great comic passages in Dis-
cipline and Punish, but the outlandishness of things, and of words.
There was a lot of laughter in Foucault, in his life as well as his books.
And Foucault’s book of 1963 on Roussel is already, so to speak, the
poetic and comic version of the theory of utterance set out in the Ar-
chaeology of 1969. To be an infamous man was a sort of dream for
Foucault, his comic dream, his way of laughing: “am I infamous?”237
(N 107)
It is significant that Deleuze begins by ascribing humor to all the philos-
ophers he admires. As his arguments sometimes disdain evidence drawn
from the philosopher’s writings or from his life, I quoted them at length
in order to let the reader judge their cogency. Deleuze’s arguments ig-
nore the views of laughter these philosophers advance, which could have
strengthened the case he makes for Kant and Spinoza, and disregard
testimony of the philosopher’s sense of humor.238 Deleuze’s arguments
have this in common: they are premised on identifying the comical with
strength (as the tragic is deemed weak and neurotic) and on identifying
a form of humor that stands out within the conventions of philosophy:
“Philosophy has its humour as well.”239
The process of ascribing humor to some philosophers and irony to
others is followed by systematically selecting the humorous philosophers
as preferable, and this for the very reason that humor is ascribed to
them. Thus, when summing his views on humor and irony in Dialogues,
and in the process of referring to many of his works on literature and
desire, Deleuze opposes Jewish humor to Greek irony, Job’s humor to
Oedipus’s irony, British humor to Continental irony, Stoic humor to Pla-
tonic irony, Zen humor to Buddhist irony, masochist humor to sadistic
irony, Proust’s humor to André Gide’s irony.240
This “Litany of Humor,” to use Dumoncel’s apt characterization,
shows us that humor can decide between schools of thought, for example,
between Platonism and Stoicism. Dumoncel argues that the difference
between irony and humor discloses a genuine procedure of philosophical
decision where humor is the touchtone, indicating every time the right
choice to make. Deleuze discloses humor as a genuine transcendental no-
tion, according to Dumoncel, because the choice of humor is predicated
on humor’s ability to provide an affirmative criticism.241


248  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
It is significant that irony is discarded in favor of humor. Deleuze
explicitly states that radical humor is a “superior irony,”242 echoing
the views formulated by Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard and Bergson’s
student, Vladimir Jankélévitch. Schopenhauer deems humor “the
 double counterpoint of irony,” the young Kierkegaard refers to  humor
as “mastered irony” and Jankélévitch proposes to call humor “an
irony of the second power,” where the “allegorical” relation appears
 doubly indirect, thus creating an “irony, which is finally serious” or a
 “humorous irony.”243 But the arguments that Deleuze uses in fa
 vor of
choosing humor over irony differ from those that these philosophers
use.  Williams explains:
Irony is a valuable but a closed and tragic intellectual art, while hu-
mor is an open and affirmative physical one. The openness is af-
forded by a refusal to separate sense from nonsense, whereas irony
deploys the promise of a higher sense against a failed lower one.
Affirmation in humor is achieved by avoiding the security of self-
identity and the power of representation—the same aware swagger
and descriptive verve of the ironic stance—in favor of mobile and
disjointed series synthesized briefly when a point runs through them.
(Williams 2008, 18)
The role of humor in Deleuze’s thought is best summarized in the fol-
lowing quotes, both from The Logic of Sense:
The values of humor are distinguished from those of irony: humor
is the art of the surfaces and of the complex relation between the
two surfaces. Beginning with one excessive equivocation, humor
constructs all univocity; beginning with the properly sexual equiv-
ocation which ends all equivocity, humor releases a desexualized
 Univocity—a speculative univocity of Being and language—the en-
tire secondary organization in one word.
(LS 248n5)
In “the Nineteenth Series of Humor” in The Logic of Sense, Deleuze
defines humor as “the co-extensiveness of sense with non-sense” and
characterizes it as follows:
Humor is the art of the surfaces and of the doubles, of nomad sin-
gularities and of the always displaced aleatory point; it is the art of
the static genesis, the savoir-faire of the pure event, and the “fourth
person singular”—with every signification, denotation, and mani-
festation suspended, all height and depth abolished.
(LS 141)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  249
Let us now probe in more detail the role Deleuze ascribes to humor, first,
in his philosophy of mind, then his aesthetics and politics, followed by
its role in the ethics which constitutes the Deleuzian good life.
D Humor in Deleuze’s Philosophy of Mind
Humor is significant in Deleuze’s philosophy for various reasons. First,
Deleuze rejects common sense and good sense in favor of original
thought, and humor is always the outcome of the latter. Deleuze’s work
treats humor as a type of creative thought, which is perverse and trans-
gressive, as is all genuine thought for Deleuze. This makes of humor a
form of thinking. Thought is defined as creating new situations through
an original and perverse destruction which is allied to intensive affects.
One affect of this kind is laughter. The destruction involved is allied also
to all the other physical activities captured in movements and the body,
and in language when it stutters and fails.
Second, and relatedly, Deleuze reserves an important place for par-
adox in his philosophy, since “paradox is the pathos or the passion of
philosophy.”244 There are several kinds of paradox, all of which are op-
posed to the complementary forms of orthodoxy—namely, good sense
and common sense. Philosophy is revealed not by good sense but by
paradox. If philosophy is paradoxical by nature, this is not because phi-
losophy sides with the least plausible opinion or because it maintains
contradictory opinions; rather, because philosophy uses sentences of a
standard language to express something that does not belong to the or-
der of opinion or even of the proposition.245
Moreover, a theory of pure becoming and transformation such as
Deleuze is advocating can only be a theory of paradoxes and of series-
formation: “It is at the same moment that one becomes larger than one
was and smaller than one becomes.”246 Predicative logic is not equipped
to handle pure becoming. The discussion of Carroll’s Alice in Wonderland
in The Logic of Sense reflects the significance of humor and paradoxical
series in freeing sense from its more common contexts and meanings.
Nonsense is not the absence of sense but rather the presence of an
important kind of sense that can only operate through nonsense. Par-
adoxes are not puzzling and detrimental contradictions that are gen-
erated within logical systems. Rather, they are forms that reveal how
contradiction is generated. They reveal in that way the limits of com-
mon sense and good sense. They also create space for a different sense
located in language and in things, one that embraces impossibility
against common and good sense. Nonsense has the dual function of
breaking with the demands of denotation, manifestation and signifi-
cation, and opening up an additional realm of sense: nonsense words
articulate their own sense.


250  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
Paradoxes and contradictions can make sense in spite of logical inva-
lidity. Their role in thought should be defended.247 Williams explains:
The difference between a world conditioned by sense and by dis-
junctive syntheses, and a world conditioned by the principle of
non-contradiction, as well as other resolutions of paradoxes, is mir-
rored in two further differences: first, a distinction drawn between
conscious cogitation and thinking with the unconscious; second,
a distinction drawn between a thought that assigns categories or
enclosures (common sense) and then assigns beings to these cate-
gories (good sense), and thinking in relation to events before and
free of such assignations. These oppositions are consistent themes
in Deleuze’s thought.
(Williams 2008, 72)
Those oppositions are further developed in two texts. In the third chap-
ter of Difference and Repetition, they are used to criticize common sense
and good sense. In A Thousand Plateaus, they serve the criticism of spa-
tial assignment; and, in the distinction Deleuze draws between smooth
and striated spaces, he opposes the latter to flow free of boundaries.
Humor expresses paradox. While paradox is the tool the Cynics use
against Plato, the Stoics, who enjoy paradoxes and invent many of them,
introduce paradox into philosophy and turn humor into a philosophical
concept. Deleuze equates Cynic and Stoic humor with nonsense humor
and Zen humor248 in The Logic of Sense, and opposes humor to the
Socratic-Platonic irony:
The Stoics are amateurs and inventors of paradoxes…the only equiv-
alent of which are to be found in Zen Buddhism on the one hand and
in English or American nonsense on the other…Paradox appears as
a dismissal of depth, a display of events at the surface, and a deploy-
ment of language along this limit. Humor is the art of the surface,
which is opposed to the old irony, the art of depths and heights.
The sophists and Cynics had already made humor a philosophical
weapon against Socratic irony; but with the Stoics, humor found its
dialectics, its dialectical principle or its natural place and its pure
philosophical concept. Lewis Carroll carries out this operation, in-
augurated by the Stoics, or rather, he takes it up again.
(LS 8–9)
Fourth, therefore, Deleuze conceives of humor as a new “solution,”
which he advances as an alternative to the Socratic-Platonic, Kantian or
Romantic forms of irony.
Contrary to most contemporary philosophers, Deleuze has a very
good mastery of the history of philosophy. In order to clarify Deleuze’s
claims on satire, irony and humor, I assess his arguments by introducing


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  251
the reader to what we know of the various schools of thought he ad-
dresses, such as the Sophists, the Cynics, the Stoics and Zen Buddhism
and to their influence on later philosophical uses of satire, paradoxes
and humor. I believe that this detour will be helpful for understanding
additional Deleuzian arguments about the comical.249
1 The Sophists
Beginning with the Sophist Gorgias Leontinus (fifth century BC) and
recorded approvingly by Aristotle, the Sophists recommend laughter as
a rhetorical device to destroy the opponent’s argument, which led to a
whole branch of Greco-Roman rhetoric. Aristotle records that “Gorgias
said it was necessary to spoil the seriousness of opponents by jest and
their jest by seriousness.”250 The mocking Sophist had an immense in-
fluence on Western civilization. Aristotle begins a serious study of “wit”
that reappears in treatises on stylistics and discourse through the twenti-
eth century, as associated principally to concerns of ethos (the nature and
character of the rhetor as portrayed in the speech) and pathos (an appeal
made to alter the judgment of an audience). The rhetor’s treatment of
wit is further involved in the practice of “dissimulating,” “understating”
or “hiding” his underlying intensions, called eironeia. Aristotle uses the
word to describe a kind of intelligent “mock modesty,” which is deviant
from the truth but which is preferable to a boisterous character.
Aside from Aristotle’s references to understatement and mockery,
antiquity left us with two prominent treatments of humor in oratory
 situations—Marcus Tullius Cicero’s dialogical de Oratore (c. 46 BC)
and Quintilian’s Institutio Oratoria (c. 95 AD). Although rhetoricians in
the Middle Ages and the Renaissance are advised to cut on their wit lest
their character be damaged,251 through Cicero and Quintilian’s influ-
ence on later generations, wit becomes a weapon in modern rhetoric.252
Since Plato’s Socrates, most philosophers denigrate rhetorical wit253;
John Locke and Immanuel Kant’s objections to wit are representative
of philosophers’ willingness of differentiating themselves from rhetori-
cians.254 The latter circumvent reason by addressing the emotions, while
philosophers address reason.
However, Thomas Hobbes, who taught rhetoric, availed himself to it
in his writings.255 Hobbes defines laughter as “nothyng else but a sud-
daine Glory arising from suddaine Conception of some Eminency in our
selves by Comparison with the Infirmityes of others, or with our owne
formerly.”256 Hobbes declares his theory original,257 but apart from the
element of surprise that Hobbes adds following others in the Renaissance,
his theory is overwhelmingly indebted to ancient theories: as Quentin
Skinner notes in Reason and Rhetoric in the Philosophy of Hobbes, it
amounts to little more than a summary of Quintilian’s argument.258
Hobbes follows the Roman rhetoricians, whose body of thought is
adopted without alteration by the rhetoricians of the Renaissance. It is


252  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
this part of Aristotle’s view of laughter and this part only, however, that,
through its impact on further rhetoricians, is taught at the seventeenth-
century English grammar schools that Hobbes attended, and which in-
fluenced him.259 On this view, the talent for provoking laughter is a
lethal weapon of debate.
There is a certain tension between Hobbes’s precepts about the provo-
cation of laughter and his own rhetorical practice, however. As Hobbes
becomes more and more convinced of the need for rhetoric to supplement
reason, the tone of Leviathan correspondingly differs in comparison
with the studiously scientific neutrality of his earlier works. Following
the Renaissance’s list of vices worthy of attacks (vainglory, avarice and
hypocrisy), Hobbes makes extensive use of satire in his attack on clerical
avarice, on the Church’s hypocrisy and on the egregious Schoolmen.260
So much so that Hobbes’s contemporaries object to the style of the En-
glish version of Leviathan (1651) that Skinner deems “a masterpiece of
satire and invective, embodying as it does a systematic application of the
techniques evolved by the theorists of rhetoric for speaking with ridicule
and contempt.”261
Indeed, Hobbes is deemed a dangerous scoffer.262 But his sense of hu-
mor is much more varied than his use of satire and invective shows. John
Aubrey tells us that he possessed an exceptionally quick wit, not only
being “of a cheerful and pleasant humour,” but “marvellous happy and
ready in his replies,” so much so that “if trueth (uncommon) delivered
clearly and wittily may goe for a saying, his common discourse was full
of them.”263 Hobbes himself tells us that he liked to joke in company.264
2 The Cynics
The tradition of ridiculing academic philosophers begins with Heracli-
tus laughing at his predecessors, followed by Diogenes the Cynic scorn-
ing Plato. Heraclitus is part of the iambic tradition that Deleuze alludes
to when refereeing to the comic poets.265 With the Cynics, we witness
the beginning of the use of paradox in Western philosophy as well as the
serio-comic genre that would change in Roman times into the satire that
Deleuze reproves.
Philosophy is comedic for the Cynics of the fifth century BC. Laughter
in various forms (irony, wit, sarcasm, humor) is an important means for
conveying philosophical ideas that seem paradoxical and are at odds
with society’s values, as well as for attracting attention, overcoming re-
sistance and prompting change in listeners or readers by enabling them
to contemplate both sets of values—society’s and philosophy’s—with the
quick cognitive shifts and reduced anxiety levels produced by laughter.
The Cynics justify the comic on moral grounds by integrating into
philosophy the promising alliance between humor and moral teaching
used by Aristophanes and other comic poets and playwrights. Their


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  253
philosophy begins as physical comedy: tradition is unanimous on the
remarkable powers of ridicule and repartee of the Cynic Diogenes and
the notorious eccentricities undertaken to expose the artificiality of
 convention—entering a theater when everyone else is leaving it, going
about in broad daylight with a lighted lantern, looking for an honest
man. The philosophical wit introduced by Diogenes is further devel-
oped by Crates, who, purporting to cure human confusion with gentle
discourse accompanied by much joking, laughter and merriment and
the example of his life, “passed his whole life jesting and laughing, as
though on perpetual holiday.”266
Cynic comedy is literary as well: for the purpose of furthering phil-
osophical education, the Cynics invent a literary genre, the serio-comic
(spoudaiogeloion), which, based on a paradox, is primarily an attempt
to adapt the “Socratic” forms of popular philosophical propaganda
to the requirements of the Hellenistic age.267 The Romans give the
serio-comic its own genre in the form of satire, notably in the poets
Horace and Juvenal, the former explicitly arguing in Ars poetica that the
best ethical instruction (the utile) is mixed with pleasure (the dulce).268
The paradoxicality of the serio-comic had a long history in philosophy
after the Middle Ages: although late antiquity and the Middle Ages are
fond of the antithesis between jest and earnestness, they nevertheless
lose their ability to conceive of the two in synthesis. Desiderius Erasmus,
an important figure in the serio-comic tradition, retrieves Lucian’s ca-
pacity for using humor to provoke the audience into considering a sub-
ject simultaneously from divergent points of view. Because his books are
translated and read all over Europe, he is considered largely responsible
for the ironic smile curling so many sixteenth-century lips.269 Pascal
says that eloquence “requires the pleasant and the real,” but the pleasant
must “itself be drawn from the true”; Christian laughter is thus a saintly
ridicule of human mistakes, and derisive laughter should be praised for
awaking us to the earnestness of existence.270
With the Cynics’ influence on all Hellenistic schools271 and the in-
fluence of these schools on the Renaissance and the Enlightenment, the
serio-comic becomes the main form of exoteric writing in philosophy. It
is used, among others, by the Stoics, Lucian, Erasmus, Montaigne, the
third earl of Shaftesbury, Nietzsche, Kierkegaard and George Santayana.
3 The Stoics
It is the Stoics, as the Cynics’ heirs, who significantly explore the role of
laughter in attaining to the good life. The eminent Hellenistic scholar,
Martha Nussbaum, notes that in Epictetus’s brusqueness, “we glimpse
a sense of humor” that follows the practice of the founder of Stoicism,
Zeno and his student, Cleanthes.272 The humor of the latter Stoic is more
easily evidenced, for example, in Seneca’s arguments in favor of laughter


254  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
as a tool for fighting against anger and in Marcus Aurelius’s smile that
shines through his Meditations. Laughter “is a well-developed practice
in Roman Stoicism,” Nussbaum further explains, as “Stoic writers often
deliberately cultivate in their reader a type of laughter that promotes
detachment from the sources of anger, fear, grief.”273
Stoic laughter arises from the contrast between a Stoic perspective of
detachment, which distances the laugher from ordinary valuations, and
the fear and anger these valuations nonetheless entail. It is about coming
to terms, gently or harshly, with the real values in things, and the reality
of one’s condition. It is a laughter of acknowledgment not distraction.
It represents a progress beyond the grief, fear, or anger that would oth-
erwise have been the person’s response to the tragic or ominous events
described.274 Apart from the comedies of Plautus, Seneca writes the fun-
niest work in the Latin language, the Apocolocyntosis or Pumpkinifica-
tion of the Divine Claudius.275
In his philosophical writings, however, Seneca recommends self-
directed humor “in order that man may not have to live his life in dis-
quietude, fearing everybody’s laughter, everybody’s tongue”276; “and so
sneerers and those who point their wit with insult,” he explains, “are
robbed of an excuse if you anticipate it with a move on your part. No
one becomes a laughing-stock who laughs at himself.”277 Seneca takes as
examples Socrates and Antisthenes, Socrates’s student and the founder
of Cynicism, whose use of laughter as a means to secure or express en-
durance Seneca admires.278 He follows their example in recommending
laughter as a means to “bringing composure to the mind; it either does
not feel anger, or is superior to it”: “With what laughter should we at-
tend the things that now draw tears from our eyes!” he exclaims; we
should “step back quite far and laugh! (recede longius et ride!),” in or-
der to secure detachment both from slights to one’s own reputation and
from the serious public crimes and injustices that Seneca enumerates.279
The dichotomy humor/anger is known in philosophy since the first
century. We know through Stobaeus that Sotion used it, and it was made
famous through Seneca, the latter’s renowned student. Seneca contrasts
laughter and anger several times in his work: initially, he prefers laugh-
ter or tears to anger280, but Seneca’s sympathies, like those of his fellow
Stoics, lay ultimately with Democritus and laughter, while the weeping
philosopher, Heraclitus, is gently ridiculed for his tearful response to the
human condition. As in Horace,281 it is the spectacle of the world that is
the source of Democritus’s laughter. Seneca urges us to imitate Democri-
tus rather than Heraclitus, for it is kinder to laugh at life than to weep
over it282: “Laughter, and a lot of it, is the right response to the things
which drive us to tears!”283
“When you laugh, you are not just expressing a Stoic revaluation al-
ready formed; you are advancing toward the goals of Stoic therapy,”
Nussbaum explains.284 It is not the sage already detached from ordinary


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  255
valuations who laughs, but the person making progress. Seneca laughs at
himself precisely because he catches himself out in a non-Stoic moment,
and the laughter emerges from the juxtaposition of his residual ordinary
valuations and those that Stoicism would recommend. The laugh is a
kind of movement away, and it relies for its genesis on the fact that the
personality is still to some degree in movement. The laugh is itself a
separative movement: “Step back and laugh” does not denote two dis-
tinct stages; it is one stage, because in laughing one changes perspective
and steps back.285
This sort of distancing laughter is frequently in evidence in Stoic texts,
often with a strong satirical side, mocking the pretensions of worldly
goods. Epictetus, who is closer to the Cynics than Seneca, employs it
constantly. Yet Stoic laughter comes in two different varieties, the harsh
and the gentle, Epictetus being harsher and Seneca gentler. The differ-
ence is made to some extent by the personality of the writer (Seneca
believes that mercy is appropriate for all-too-human failings), but also
by the nature of the object: if the object of laughter is a fool, the laughter
may be harsh. If it is the philosopher himself, or some earnest progress-
ing person, the laughter is often gentler.
Following the practices of the founder of Stoicism, Zeno, and of his
follower, Cleanthes, Epictetus typically addresses fools, real or fictional.
Seneca’s letters address both himself and Lucilius, a serious student of
philosophy.286 For example, Letter 12 is a very rich case of Stoic laugh-
ter: the theme of the letter is old age; the laugh concerns the discrepancy
between Seneca’s proud irascible denial of age and the real facts; the
laughter is a gentle mockery of Seneca’s vanity and irascibility, and his
reluctance to accept age in a properly Stoic spirit, which then becomes
the theme of the rest of the letter.
Stoic laughter is a remedy that helps achieve firmness of mind, liberty
and tranquility. Since Democritus’s admonition, however, it is expected
that laughing philosophers laugh at themselves: “No one is a laughing-
stock who laughs first at himself,” says Seneca.287 Seneca has an enor-
mous influence on the Renaissance, notably on the laughing philosophers
Montaigne and Erasmus, and on the neo-Stoic Justus Lipsius.
The early Stoics’ humor is exemplified in their paradoxes, however,
rather than in self-referential laughter. As the context de Deleuze’s com-
ments on the Stoics is the introduction of humor in philosophy, Deleuze
must refer to the early Stoics, to whom I now turn.288
The Stoics offered an extensive treatment of the entire range of the par-
adoxes known in antiquity.289 Especially the most ancient Stoics studied
paradoxes very closely. Chrysippus’s interest in “things signified” other
than propositions and arguments is evidenced by several brief fragments
dealing with opposites and paradoxes.290 The influence of the Megarian
school, which was interested in logical paradox, can be detected here.
The Stoics’ appreciation for logic probably originated with the school’s


256  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
founder. Zeno studied with Stilpo the Megarian, and Megara was the
home of a number of important philosophers engaging in a discipline
that we would today call logic. Without question, Chrysippus is the phi-
losopher most responsible for the logic associated with the Stoics.
The paradoxes evolve out of the Stoics’ requirements of rational co-
herence. Examples of such paradoxes are following the well-known Stoic
affirmations: only the sage is free and sovereign, even in slavery; the
slave in prison is the freest of all human beings (Epictetus); all vices are
equal, he who strangled an unneeded rooster or his father.  Conscious
and constant paradoxical discourse is used by Zeno, Hecaton and
 Chrysippus.291 Many of these paradoxes are presented in Cicero’s The
Paradoxes of the Stoics, a series of six essays in which Cicero sets out the
essential doctrines of the Stoics.
Philo of Alexandria gives the following brief and notoriously cryptic
account of a puzzle about personal identity created by the Stoic philos-
opher Chrysippus:
Chrysippus, the most distinguished member of their school, in his
work On the Growing [Argument], creates a freak of the follow-
ing kind. Having first established that it is impossible for two pecu-
liarly qualified individuals to occupy the same substance jointly, he
says: “For the sake of argument, let one individual be thought of as
whole-limbed, the other as minus one foot. Let the whole-limbed
one be called Dion, the defective one Theon. Then let one of Dion’s
feet be amputated.” The question arises which one of them has per-
ished, and his claim is that Theon is the stronger candidate. These
are the words of a paradox-monger rather than of a speaker of truth.
For how can it be that Theon, who has had no part chopped off, has
been snatched away, while Dion, whose foot has been amputated,
has not perished? “Necessarily,” says Chrysippus. “For Dion, the
one whose foot has been cut off, has collapsed into the defective
substance of Theon. And two peculiarly qualified individuals can-
not occupy the same substrate. Therefore, it is necessary that Dion
remains while Theon has perished.”292
John Bowin explains that although this is not the way that the man in the
street thinks about identity, the man in the street is often wrong. When
the Stoic talks of “common conceptions,” he does not mean “common
opinions,” and indeed, the common opinion that matter is the sole prin-
ciple of identity is, on this showing, incoherent. The Academics set out to
show that the very notion of personal identity is incoherent. By exposing
a conflict between two venerable items of common opinion—that matter
is the sole principle of identity and that identity is continuous over time,
what Chrysippus’s puzzle shows, is that one of those common opinions
is incoherent by itself, and this resolves the Academic aporia.293


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  257
4 Zen Buddhism and Nonsense
The adventure of the Stoic sage is the first instance of the two-fold
dismissal of height and depth to the advantage of the surface, which
Deleuze names the adventure of humor. Later on, yet in another con-
text, it will also be the adventure of Zen—against the Brahman depths
and the Buddhist heights. Deleuze takes the famous problem-tests, the
questions- answers or koans to demonstrate the absurdity of significa-
tions and indicate the nonsense of denotations. With the staff as the
universal instrument and the master of questions, mimicry and con-
sumption seem to be the response. Coming back to the surface, the sage
discovers objects-events which communicate in the void that constitutes
their substance. The void is the site of sense, or of the event, which har-
monizes with its nonsense, across the abolished significations and the
lost denotations “in the place where the place only takes place.”294
Indeed, Zen Buddhism is one of the rare traditions of wisdom that
holds as its ideal a laughing sage; another Eastern tradition that influ-
enced it is Taoism.295 In one of the forms of Zen, the paradoxical koans
are the main learning device.296 An example of koan is, what is the
sound of the clapping of one hand? By looking for rational answers, the
student is “losing his mind,” which is exactly what the master needs
him to understand, that rationality should be abandoned. Only when
the student understands that what he looks for, nirvana or satori, is
identical to real life when approached differently, does he laugh. His
laughter signals his liberation from the conundrum and his affirmation
of existence as it is.
Thus, in the 19th series of The Logic of Sense, Deleuze argues for
the significance of humor in thought and life as a central aspect of phil-
osophical teaching and learning. Some things can only be learned by
humor because they are resistant to rational demonstration and to prop-
ositional understanding. Humor helps us sense that conveying meaning
may not be the aim of certain forms of communication; moreover, when
creating humor, the meaning reason uses does not define clear borders
on the other side of which lie nonsense and absurdity, but use a different
kind of sense allied to “non-sense” and to paradox.
In order to point in that way, however, humor cannot simply appeal to
rational demonstration and to straightforward sense. Both in Cynicism
and Zen Buddhism bewilderment, physicality, unrest and laughter are
essential to the lesson taught: they encourage the apprentices to look
for their own responses; they teach them that the question was in some
ways unanswerable and fell besides the problem; they introduce a strong
discomfort; and they trigger a life-affirming physical and emotional
reaction.
Finally, building on what he considers as the Stoic philosophy of super-
ficies in contradistinction to the pre-Socratics’ philosophy of profundities


258  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
and the Platonic philosophy of heights, Deleuze proposes a metaphysics
of events, of which humor is the art. He finds this art expressed in “En-
glish humour (?), Jewish humour, Stoic humour, Zen humour.” Noting
this “strange broken line” in Dialogues, he further explains the working
of humor as follows:
In Humour principles count for little, everything is taken literally,
the consequences are expected of you (this is why humour is not
transmitted through plays on words, puns, which are of the signi-
fier, and like a principle within the principle). Humour is the art of
consequences, of effects: OK, fine, you give me this? You’ll see what
happens. Humour is treacherous, it is treason. Humour is atonal,
absolutely imperceptible, it makes something shoot off. It never
goes up or down, it is on the surface: surface effects. Humour is
the art of pure events. The arts of Zen, archery, gardening or tak-
ing tea, are exercises to make the event surge forth and dazzle on a
pure surface. Jewish humor versus Greek irony, Job-humour versus
Oedipus-irony, insular humour versus continental irony, Stoic humour
versus Platonic irony, Zen humour versus Buddhist irony, masochist
humour versus sadistic irony, Proust-humour versus Gide-irony, etc.
(D 68)
Novelty and creation, intensity and value, can come only from sense and
nonsense, as humor is the co-extensiveness of sense with nonsense.297
Christel Stalpaert further explains how
the alternative image, of thought as creative, exceeds “pat” images of
the real and instead tackles the unrepresentable and a-presentative.
It is a matter of invoking a rhizomatic view of reality, of encoun-
tering multiplicities and open-ended systems of multiple differential
elements.
(Stalpaert 2007, 120)
As humor has always undermined games of principles or causes in favor
of the event and games of individuations or subjectivation in favor of
multiplicities,298 Baruchello notes:
This undifferentiated multiplicity, this surface of being resting on a
void subtending substance, is the place where humor is supposed to
guide us. Humor “descends” from the One to the multiple by break-
ing down the unity of sense, annihilating any umbrella-concept ca-
pable of circumscribing all the possible instances of a phenomenon
that, once disappeared the unifying bound of that concept, explodes
in a myriad of independent scattered phenomena.
(Baruchello 2002, 451)


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  259
Now that the role of humor in Deleuze’s philosophy of mind has been
explained, and his claims about humor checked in the history of phi-
losophy, it remains to be seen how humor becomes the main notion in
Deleuze’s aesthetics, and how it fulfills the significant role Deleuze as-
signs to it in his politics and ethics.
E Humor in Deleuze’s Aesthetics
In Nomad Thought, irony and humor are both the key to intensities.
At the end of Difference and Repetition, however, Deleuze entrusts this
role to humor alone by associating irony with dialectic and humor with
aesthetics or intensity:
A whole flow of exchange occurs between intensive quantities and
Ideas, as though between two corresponding figures of difference…
The aesthetics of intensities thus develops each of its moments in
correspondence with the dialectic of Ideas: the power of intensity
(depth) is grounded in the potentiality of the Idea…The unconscious
of little perceptions or intensive quantities refers to the unconscious
of Ideas, and the art of the aesthetic echoes that of the dialectic.
The latter is irony, understood as the art of problems and questions
which is expressed in the handling of differential relations and in the
distribution of the ordinary and the singular. By contrast, the art of
the aesthetic is humour, a physical art of signals and signs determin-
ing the partial solutions or cases of solution—in short, an implicated
art of intensive qualities.
(DR 244–5)
Deleuze continues the comparison of irony with humor in relation to
the individual: while irony is unaware of the individual, humor plays
upon the individual and individuating factors. It is true that irony as
the art of differential idea is certainly aware of singularity. As such,
it plays upon the distribution of ordinary and distinctive points but
these are pre- individual singularities distributed within the idea. While
irony proceeds to “the differentiations necessary within the calculation
of problems or the determinations of their conditions,” humor “bears
witness to the play of individuals as cases of solutions, in relation to
the differentiations it determines.”299 It is because humor is the art of
intensive quantities that it plays on individuating factors and on the
individual.
Stalpaert explains how for Deleuze classical representation was es-
tablished by Aristotle, whose main concern was the recognition of the
identical rather than the distinction of the different. Thus, difference
disappears in the representative model, which grounds classical dra-
matic aesthetics. In contradistinction to the classical model, however,


260  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
there is a right way to experience difference as one can ground an
aesthetic of difference that escapes representation. To that purpose,
Deleuze proposes an aesthetic of intensities. This is an open-ended
post- representational mode of thinking, where connections are not
limited to the relations fixed identities hold. Deleuze considers that
the energetic or intensive connections that constitute this “plane of
immanence” signal the triumph of “becoming” over “being.” His aes-
thetics of intensities establishes an energetic connection that develops
relations of speed and rest. It denies the representative value accorded
to ideas in favor of the value of the affects to explain the state of
the body in relation to surrounding bodies. It places the emphasis on
the production generated by the contact and intermixing of different
bodies.
A limiting image of the self and the body is generated by common
sense. The surrender to continuous metamorphoses that creative or
nomadic thinking effectuates constantly rises above any grounding of
bodily images. The ideal of statuesque “being,” Stalpaert explains, is ex-
changed for a here and now materiality. Because it is the “contemporain
par excellence,” humor is its art. As the multiplication of destabilizing
perspectives which we call humor can affirm difference without hav-
ing to depend on representation, humor is the Deleuzian aesthetics of
difference.300
Far from being merely the content of aesthetics, humor plays a signif-
icant role in Deleuze’s politics and ethics as well.
F Humor in Deleuze’s Politics
The political implications of masochism and sadism drawn by Deleuze
and his association of humor with the notion of minorities enable humor
to hold a significant part in Deleuzian politics. Sade’s ironic attitude
to the 1789 Revolution is expressed in his opinion that the Revolution
will be unproductive unless it gives up making laws and setting up in-
stitutions of perpetual motion. This attitude is paralleled by Sacher-
Masoch’s humorous attitude to the 1848 Revolutions and the Pan Slavic
movement. Sacher-Masoch suggests that “contracts should be drawn up
with a terrible Tsarina, thus ensuring the most sentimental but at the
same time the coldest and severest law.”301
The political implications of masochism and sadism are reprised in
Deleuze and Guattari’s views of the political, which, as François Zoura-
bichvili argues, has also a posture qualified as “perverse”: “Politics is a
posture, a matter of perception, the result of a conversion that allows the
development of a mechanics of resistance to the present.”302
Zourabichvili further explains that, with respect to Deleuze and
Guattari’s subversive tendencies, emancipation is reduced to the ques-
tion “how best to flee,” without being deprived of weapons or of the


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  261
artifices that will be needed on the line of deterritorialization. The ques-
tion of the best means available for fleeing, in turn, leads to Deleuze and
Guattari’s “perversion.” However,
The true bearer of the emancipatory interest is not the sadist, for
steeped in the language of the law, and contesting the fiction of
the deduction of the law from an alleged principle of the law, he
chooses to subvert the old law ironically by maintaining its form,
while, at the same time, replacing its content with precepts deduced
from a “principle of evil.” Rather, the true bearer of the eman-
cipatory interest is, according to Deleuze and Guattari, the mas-
ochist, because he chooses to pervert the law by submitting to it
humorously in order to savor pleasures that the law prohibits and
punishes.303
(Boundas 2007a, 19)
Humor is associated with the significant notion of minorities: “Hu-
mour, on the other hand, claims kinship with a minority, with a
minority- becoming.”304
Deleuze states clearly that a majority is never a becoming. However,
our epoch belongs to minorities. As becoming is creation, the invention
of people to come is the goal of philosophy, and its successful outcome is
minoritarian people with humor.
A minor literature is not, in Deleuze’s view, a literature written from
the perspective of an oppressed group; nor is it secondary or neglected
literature. Minor literature, such as Kafka’s work, uses the language of
the dominant culture for new purposes and in this way creates “lines
of flight.” Creation of this sort involves becoming- imperceptible, as we
have seen above. Thus, minor literature creates a type of living that is
not merely a replication of dominant motifs but a process of touching on
what Deleuze calls “the virtual”:
It is humour which makes a language stammer, which imposes on
it a minor usage, or which constitutes a complete bilingual system
within the same language. And, indeed, it never involves plays
on words (there is not a single play on words in Lewis  Carroll),
but events of language, a minoritarian language, which has it-
self become creator of events. Or else, might there be “indefi-
nite” plays on words which would be like a becoming instead of
a completion?
(D 68–9)
Baruchello has written an important article on Deleuze’s humor, in which
he emphasizes (1) the iconoclastic force of humor; (2) its capacity to break
any boundary or law, either logico-linguistic or ethico- psychological; (3)


262  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
its casting light onto the surface of being, the surface of singular events;
and (4) its practical co-extensiveness with nonsense or the absurd.305 We
have seen all these features in this part of the chapter; it remains to be
seen how these capacities of humor bear on the Deleuzian ethics, which
constitutes his view of the good life.
G Humor in Deleuze’s Ethics
Deleuze builds on Spinoza and Nietzsche’s views of ethics as a form of
affirmation and evaluation. Such an ethics implies the acceptance that
the world is neither true nor real, but “living.” To affirm is to evaluate
life in order to set free that which lives. Rather than weighing down life
with the burden of higher values, it seeks to make life light and active,
and to create new values that are life-affirming. To laugh is to affirm
life.306
The influence of Spinoza on Deleuze’s ethics of joy is as follows: the
process of formulating adequate ideas, for the former, becomes the pro-
cess of the counter-actualization of that which happens to us, for the
latter:
It is no longer the generality of the common notion that stands for
the cogitandum of practical reason; it is the event that must be
grasped though the process of counter-actualization. The sadness in
the state of affairs passively affecting us is transformed into a joyful
affirmation of the event. Passive affections are turned into active
ones that are capable of transvaluating and transforming states of
affairs.
(Boundas 2010b, 267)
Although counter-actualization is accomplished through humor in
The Logic of Sense, the influence of Nietzsche’s view of laughter as
interpreted by Deleuze in the last chapter of Nietzsche and Philos-
ophy is noticeable here. Already in relation to Zarathustra, Deleuze
emphasizes that laughter is an affirmative power of transmutation:
laughter transmutes suffering into joy. In relation to Dionysus, how-
ever, dance, laughter and play are affirmative powers of reflection and
development. Roars of laughter affirm multiplicity and the unity of
multiplicity.
Thus, the key to understanding humor in Deleuze’s ethics is given
in Nietzsche and Philosophy. Humor is the mark of an aristocratic
thought that respects the causes of one’s misfortune at the same time
that it cannot take seriously one’s misfortunes. These two aspects of
the same thought coincide, for Deleuze, and should be compared with
“the seriousness with which the slave takes his misfortunes.”307 This


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  263
restricts the aristocratic reaction to self-laughter (“auto-derision”).
Contrary to common opinion, to think is not to take something seri-
ously: it is not to be weighed by it, but rather to affirm it. While the
negated is weighty, affirmation is light. In Immanence: A Life, Deleuze
explains how,
The life of the individual gives way to an impersonal and yet singu-
lar life that releases a pure event freed from the accidents of internal
and external life, that is, from the subjectivity and objectivity of
what happens: a “Homo tantum” with whom everyone empathizes
and who attains a sort of beatitude. It is a haecceity no longer of
individuation but of singularization: a life of pure immanence, neu-
tral, beyond good and evil, for it was only the subject that incar-
nated it in the midst of things that made it good or bad. The life of
such individuality fades away in favor of the singular life immanent
to a man who no longer has a name, though he can be mistaken for
no other. A singular essence, a life…
(TRM 386–7)
The content of this passage needs to be explained as is its relation to hu-
mor. Immanence, A Life… returns to a topic that Deleuze has addressed
in various works, the counter-effectuation or counter-actualization of
the event and its relation with eternal return. This will be the focus of
our interest now, while the Deleuzian notions of actors and mimes, who
counter-effectuate the event, and of idiots, who redefine philosophy and
politics, will occupy us next.
1 Humor in Counter-actualization
Humor enables the distancing and the doubling that counter- actualization
or counter-effectuation requires. Inseparable from a selective force, hu-
mor selects the pure event, that is, the eternal in the event, given that
eternal return is a theory of pure events. The free man enacts the actor,
which enables the distancing required. He is a mime, an actor-humor,
Deleuze says. We accompany ourselves with humor, which enables the
liberation that counter-actualization effects when one selects oneself or
universal freedom. This liberation amounts to amor fati, the ethics of
philosophy, according to Deleuze. Thus, humor helps us reach philoso-
phy’s goal. This is what Deleuze refers to as the solution of humor. Let
me elaborate on these opening remarks.
In The Logic of Sense, Deleuze endorses the Stoics’ ethics of amor
fati. In his account, amor fati appears as indissociable from a humorous
acceptance. Humor is a selective force which discloses the pure event:
Deleuze uses the writings of the poet Joë Bousquet (1897–1950) to


264  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
explain how the “actor-humor” counter-actualizes the event. In What
Is Philosophy? written with Guattari, the same idea is reprised; how-
ever, it is philosophy itself which is now tending toward amor fati, and
whose conceptual personae are now the actors who counter- actualize
events.
In The Logic of Sense, humor is introduced as the opposite of resigna-
tion, which is yet another form of ressentiment. Humor is the acceptance
that reveals the glory or the sense of the event. It is presented both as
that which enables amor fati and as that which constitutes it. We accom-
pany ourselves through humor as we are doubling ourselves constantly:
myself is another for Deleuze, and an event, including death, as Maurice
Blanchot has shown, has two faces, an ambiguity that Deleuze argues is
necessary; thus, the painful actualization of the event, such as one’s sin-
gular death, is accompanied by a counter-actualization which liberates
the individual by uniting him with a pre-individual field, an impersonal
“one” who dies. What Is Philosophy? does not refer directly to humor;
however, it endorses the Zen Buddhist’s silencing of logic. Recall that in
The Logic of Sense, Zen Buddhism is associated with nonsense humor
and the paradoxes of the Stoics, and in Dialogues, with humor as the art
of pure event.308
Allow me to elaborate on the association that Deleuze establishes be-
tween humor and amor fati. Deleuze explains that an entity is an event,
which creates panic but also much joy; the most delicate thing in the
world, as Dialogues characterizes it, excludes drama or histrionics. Amor
fati is described as willing the event: far from resignation, it also differs
from acting as a buffoon or being hysterical. Its art is humor: humor is
associated with amor fati through the notion of counter- actualization,
as Deleuze explains in the “Twenty-First Series of the Event” of The
Logic of Sense. A counter-weight to terror and to resentment, “Humor
is inseparable from a selective force: in that which occurs (an accident),
it selects the pure event,”309 that is, the eternal in the event. As eter-
nal return is “the theory of pure events and their linear and superficial
condensation,” which “has a sense of selection and remains tied to an
incompatibility—with the forms which hinder its constitution and its
functioning,”310 it follows that humor enables us to effectuate eternal re-
turn. Through counter-actualization of each event, the actor-dancer se-
lects universal freedom and cosmopolitanism, which Deleuze describes
in terms of spiritual liberation. This is the content of amor fati, the sole
ethics of philosophy. This is also the role of philosophy, which extracts
events from bodies and states of affairs and in doing so enables us to
affirm the sense of what happens. “There is a dignity of the event that
has always been inseparable from philosophy as amor fati”; hence, “Phi-
losophy’s sole aim is to become worthy of the event.”311 By enabling us
to reach philosophy’s goal, “the solution of humor” to which Deleuze’s
philosophy points is finally clarified.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  265
To explain how we can become worthy of the event, Deleuze refers
to Bousquet in The Logic of Sense’s remarkable “Twenty-First Series of
the Event”:
Bousquet listed the characteristics of the humor-actor (“l’humour-
acteur”): to annihilate his or her tracks whenever necessary; “to
hold up among men and works their being before bitterness,”
“to assign to plagues, tyrannies, and the most frightful wars the
comic possibility of having reigned for nothing”; in short, to lib-
erate for each thing “its immaculate portion,” language and will,
Amor Fati.
(Bousquet 1955, 103; LS 151)
In this passage, humor and actor are presented as identical. The hyphen
links humor and actor as it does in “Job-humour…Proust-humour [and
Gide-irony].”312 This means that humor qualifies here the actor. If we
look for another indication that humor is not accidental here, we may
note that it is followed by “the comic.” Yet commentators who address
this part of Deleuze’s thought do not explain the humor, only the actor.
Let me attempt to explain that series, beginning with Bousquet and the
significance he holds for Deleuze’s thought.
Wounded in 1918 at the end of World War I, Bousquet was par-
alyzed for the rest of his life. He lived a life largely bedridden, sur-
rounded by his books. His physical incapacity and constant pain led
to his retreat from the world but also to an extensive body of poetry
and writing. His work was admired by many twentieth-century French
writers, including René Char, Louis Aragon, André Breton, Gide and
Valéry. Deleuze expresses a profound interest in Bousquet’s Les Capi-
tales, which he quotes in the passage from The Logic of Sense above.
His interest in that work lies in the problem of language it raises in
relation to the univocity of Being, which begins with a meditation on
Duns Scotus.
Deleuze sees Bousquet’s work in its entirety as a meditation of the
wound, the event and language.313 He takes Bousquet as a living ex-
ample of the version of the Stoic ethics of amor fati he advances: “Joë
Bousquet must be called a Stoic…Either ethics makes no sense at all,
or this is what it means and has nothing else to say: not to be unwor-
thy of what happens to us.” However, what does it mean to will the
event? “Is it to accept war, wounds, and death when they occur?” He
asks. Not at all. Rather, willing the event is to release its eternal truth.
Thus:
We are faced with a volitional intuition and a transmutation. “To
my inclination for death,” said Bousquet, “which was a failure of
the will, I will substitute a longing for death which would be the


266  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
apotheosis of the will.” From this inclination to this longing there is,
in a certain respect, no change except a change of the will, a sort of
leaping in place of the whole body which exchanges its organic will
for a spiritual will. It wills now not exactly what occurs, but some-
thing in that which occurs, something yet to come which would
be consistent with what occurs, in accordance with the laws of an
obscure, humorous conformity: The Event. It is in this sense that the
Amor fati is one with the struggle of free men.
(LS 149; first emphasis added).
Amir fati is the love of that obscure conformity, which he qualifies as
“humorous.” This redoubling that the actor effectuates is further de-
scribed as “superficial,”314 making it consistent with the superficiality
of humor as the art of the surfaces. The significance of this redoubling
should not be minimized:
Nothing more can be said, and no more has ever been said: to be-
come worthy of what happens to us, and in this to will and re-
lease the event, to become the offspring of one’s own events, and
thereby to be reborn, to have one more birth, and to break with
one’s carnal birth—to become the offspring to one’s events and not
of one’s actions, for the action is itself produced by the offspring of
the event.
(LS 149–50, emphasis added)
Deleuze argues that the misfortune that strikes him is present in all
events, but so are a splendor and a brightness which dry up misfortune
and enable the event, once willed, to be actualized in its most con-
tracted point. All this is the effect of the “static genesis” and of “the
immaculate conception.” The splendor and magnificence of the event is
sense; however, the event is not what occurs, such as an accident; it is
rather inside what occurs, the purely expressed. It signals and awaits
us: it is what must be understood, willed and represented in that which
occurs.
It may be helpful to repeat the difference between actualization and
counter-actualization. In Gilles Deleuze: Affirmation in Philosophy, Jay
Conway explains that the actor actualizes the event, but in a manner
that is entirely different from the actualization of the event in the depth
of things. The actor redoubles this cosmic or physical actualization in
his own way, which may be superficial but also more distinct, trenchant
and pure. Thus, Deleuze emphasizes that the actor delimits the original,
disengages from it an abstract line and keeps from the event only its con-
tour and its splendor, becoming thereby the actor of one’s own events,
which he deems counter-actualization.315


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  267
Another explanation makes counter-actualization’s relevance to
wounds and death salient. There is a double structure of every event: the
present moment of its actualization, the moment in which the event is
embodied in a state of affairs, an individual or a person; when an event
occurs, the future and the past of the event are evaluated only with re-
spect to this definitive present, and from the point of view of that which
embodies it. However, there is also the future and the past of the event
considered in itself, which by side-stepping each present is free of the
limitations of state of affairs. This is an impersonal and pre-individual
event, a neutral, neither general nor particular, an eventum tantum. It
has no other present than that of the mobile instant which represents it,
which is always divided into past-future and which forms what must be
called counter-actualization.
How can we make this difference relevant to my life? Deleuze here
relies on Blanchot’s description of an ambiguity which Deleuze sees
as describing the mortal wound, that is, the wound and death. 316 For
Blanchot, death is a double event, which Deleuze describes as two ac-
complishments, akin to actualization and counter-actualization: in one
case, my life seems too weak for me and slips away at a point which, in
a determined relation to me, has become present. In the other case, I am
too weak for life, which overwhelms me and scatters its singularities all
about in no relation to me and in no relation to a moment that can be
determinable as the present; rather, it is an impersonal instant which is
divided into still-future and already-past.
However, and here lies the significance of the detour through death,
Deleuze generalizes Blanchot’s argument to describe all events: every
event is like death, double and impersonal in its double. Deleuze empha-
sizes the impersonal aspect by noting the “they” (die) or “on” (meurt),
grammatically, the “fourth person,” whose splendor is the splendor of
the event itself.317 He explains that in contradistinction to any form of
psychological or linguistic personalism, events
lead to promoting a third person or even a fourth person singular,
the non-person or It, in which we recognize ourselves and our com-
munity better than in the empty I-You exchanges. We believe that
the motion of subject has lost much of its interest in favor of pre-
individual singularities and non-personal individuations.
(TRM 2007, 351)318
This is why in The Logic of Sense, Deleuze argues that there are no
private or collective events, no more than there are individuals and uni-
versals, particularities and generalities. Everything is singular, and thus
both collective and private, particular and general, neither individual
nor universal.319


268  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
At the mobile and precise points where all events gather together in
one, Deleuze argues, transmutation happens. It means that “death turns
against death.” However, dying, here, is the negation of death. Thus,
“death turned on itself would be willed against all deaths.”320 Most
importantly,
The impersonality of dying no longer indicates only the moment
when I disappear outside of myself, but rather the moment when
death loses itself in me, and also the figure which the most singular
life takes on in order to substitute itself for me.321
The physical mixture is exact only at the level of the whole, in the full cir-
cle of the divine present. But with respect to each part, there are many in-
justices and ignominies, many parasitic and cannibalistic processes which
bring about terror of that which happens to us and resentment at what
which occurs. This is when humor can act as will, in that it selects and that
which it selects is affirmed: “Humor is inseparable from a selective force:
in that which occurs (an accident), it selects the pure event.”322 Thus, eth-
ics is amor fati, love of pure becoming. If we want, Deleuze argues, “the
intolerable returns against itself and transmutes (counter- effectuate) in
resistance.” The volitive intuition or transmutation enables the actor to
want as comical and light the greatest atrocity.323 When life is being too
feeble for me and I too weak for it at the same time, these two elements of
the same event, which is both too small and too big for me, are the place
of the fiercest tragic and of the subtlest humor. Every event has a double
structure like death does. In this structure, the subject disappears because,
as Blanchot says, “I do not die, one dies.” Amor fati is liberty; it is the hu-
morous art of becoming greater than what is too great for me.
Counter-actualization is a transmutation which enables liberation,
a new birth, a “leap in place” of the individual who “transcends his
form and its syntactical link with a world.”324 It depends, first, from
a certain orientation in relation to events, which enables us to see that
they are excessive in relation to their actualization, with respect to their
material cause, as Jon Roffe notes.325 If we abstain from doing this, we
act with ressentiment; insofar as we grasp what happens as unjust and
unwarranted, our sores are repugnant.326 Thus, the event should not be
reduced to the order of causes, which is also the order of blame because
“what is really immoral is to use moral notions such as just or unjust,
merit or fault.”327 The second aspect of counter-actualization is an act
of will, where the leap in place means disengaging myself from my own
body, which is subject to the casual nexus, in order to identify with the
event that is my genetic condition. Roffe explains:
I sidestep my place in the causal order, and begin miming or
acting (I become a humour-actor, Deleuze says, referring to Joë


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  269
Bousquet) of the event, no longer invested in what is here and
now, but instead with what in what is here and now that could
be the locus of an otherwise. To counter-actualize is… a matter
of changing the locus of my actions from immediate (… efficient)
causality to the quasi-causal event, or from a causal agent to an
agent of potential energy. This, in turn, furnishes an entire pano-
ply of motivations, orientations; in short, an entirely new nature.
(Roffe 2011, 121)
Grasping myself as the paradoxical locus of the difference that inhabits
me in the form of the event is the single ethical maxim of The Logic of
Sense.
2 Humor and Eternal Return
In order to explain how humor is associated with eternal return, by
choosing the pure event against terror and resentment, we should turn
to the Twenty-Fifth Series of The Logique of Sense. Deleuze argues that
we cannot limit ourselves to the counter-actualization of an event—to
the actor or dancer’s simple, flat representation—while taking care to
prevent the full actualization which characterizes the victim or the true
patient, as abstract thought would prefer. “The ridiculousness of the
thinker” lies in suggesting counter-actualization without actualization.
Yet this is impossible as there are always two aspects to an event and the
two processes differ in nature328:
The eternal truth of the event is grasped only if the event is also
inscribed in the flesh. But each time we must double this painful
actualization by a counter-actualization which limits, moves, and
transfigures it. We must accompany ourselves—first, in order to sur-
vive, but then even when we must die. Counter-actualization is noth-
ing, it belongs to a buffoon when it operates alone and pretends to
have the value of what could have happened. But, to be the mime of
what effectively occurs, to double the actualization with a counter-
actualization, the identification with a distance, like the true actor
and dancer, is to give to the truth of the event the only chance of
not being confused with its inevitable actualization… It is, finally,
to give us the chance to go farther than we have believed possible.
To the extent that the pure event is each time imprisoned forever in
its actualization, counter-actualization liberates it, always for other
times. (LS 161; emphasis added)
Humor is the very mode which enables to perceive the metaphysics that
Deleuze devises. This is so on account of the way in which Deleuze
conceives of contradictions. Events are not concepts; identity and


270  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
contradiction do not apply to them; they should rather be seen as com-
patible or incompatible. Contradiction is defined in the space between
the principle and the negation of the consequence. Contradiction always
results from a process of a different nature. Thus, the alleged contradic-
tion pertains to concepts and should, at the level of events, be seen as
merely an alogical incompatibility.
While the Stoics did not resist the temptation to revert to contradic-
tion in their extant (“surviving, partial and deceiving”) writings,329 it
is Leibniz who should be seen as the first theoretician of alogical in-
compatibilities, therefore, as the first important theoretician of the
event. Rather than identical or contradictory, events are compossi-
ble and incompossible as a consequence of convergence or divergence
of series; thus, this topic is an essential component of the theory
of sense:
There is something which does not allow itself to be reduced to a
logical contradiction between predicates and which is nevertheless
an incompatibility; but it is an alogical incompatibility, an incom-
patibility of “humor” to which Leibniz’s original criteria must be
applied. (AO, 1983, 68; emphasis added)
This alogical incompatibility can be called an incongruity, which ex-
plains why Deleuze refers to it as “an incompatibility of ‘humor,’”
using the well-known incongruity theory to explain humor. Arthur
Koestler suggested in the first chapter of The Act of Creation that
humor is the paradigm of all creative acts in that it bi-sociates two
logics, or two series of “events.”330 However, and here lies Deleuze’s
innovation, freed from theological concerns, with which Leibniz was
preoccupied: incompatibility does not exclude, but “divergence and
disjunction are, on the contrary, affirmed as such.” They are affirmed
simultaneously because difference itself is affirmed and is itself affir-
mation. Rather than an identity of contraries, they are not identified
but their distance is affirmed. Positive distance belongs to topology
and to the surface, while depth and elevation restore the negative and
identity.
Disjunction is no longer a means of separation and incompatibility
is now a means of communication. Either/or becomes pure affirmation
as “the communication of events replaces the exclusion of predicates.”
We should talk now of resonance and displacement rather than iden-
tity or contradiction. This means that all events, even contraries, are
 compatible—“they are inter-expressive.”331
Deleuze turns to Nietzsche’s perspectivism to explain this point: health
and sickness are vantage-points from which one examines the other;
when Nietzsche could no more do so, he was definitely sick. Deleuze also


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  271
turns to Klossowski’s interpretation of eternal return and to its use of
the comical and of parody to explain his own view of eternal return and
to associate it with counter-effectuation:
The problem is therefore one of knowing how the individual would
be able to transcend his form and his syntactical link with a world,
in order to attain to the universal communication of events, that
is, to the affirmation of a disjunctive synthesis beyond logical con-
tradictions, and even beyond alogical compatibilities. It would be
necessary for the individual to grasp herself as event; and that she
grasps the event actualized within her as another individual grafted
onto her. In this case, she would not understand, want, or repre-
sent this event without also understanding and wanting all other
events as individuals, and without representing all other individuals
as events. Each individual would be like a mirror for the condensa-
tion of singularities and each world a distance in the mirror. This is
the ultimate sense of counter-actualization. This, moreover, is the
Nietzschean discovery of the individual as the fortuitous case, as
Klossowski takes it up and restores it, in an essential relation of the
eternal return. (LS 208-9)
Klossowski describes Nietzsche’s work as an attempt to teach the
 unteachable, that is, to pinpoint and communicate the moments when
 existence reveals its fortuitousness, the moments when it can no longer
be rationalized and thus taught.332
Klossowski suggests that, in the course of this paradoxical attempt
to teach the unteachable, Nietzsche’s arguments are often torn between
two poles of argument which imply very different attitudes to existence:
on the one hand, the artistic or religious apprehension of life through
simulacra or fictions, and, on the other hand, the scientific investigation
and explanation of phenomena.333 This tension between scientific and
fictional accounts of the world poses a particularly acute problem with
respect to the central idea of eternal return—an idea which resists ratio-
nal elucidation and can only be expressed thorough song and image.334
Klossowski argues that Nietzsche ultimately tended to resolve this ten-
sion by implicitly privileging the aesthetic over the scientific dimension
of his own work.
For Klossowski, this privileging of the aesthetic is clearly articulated in
the section of Twilight of the Idols entitled “How the True World finally
became a fable.”335 Klossowski argues that Nietzsche’s dissolution of
the scientific in the aesthetic as evidenced here results from his suspicion
of the operations of rational consciousness. Much of Nietzsche’s work,
for him, takes the form of a critique of consciousness and rationality,
designed to rehabilitate the unconscious impulsive forces or drives which


272  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
they distort or repress. Conscious thought and communication are linear
and teleological and so standardize and falsify the unconscious life of
impulses which recognize no goals.336 As a result, what is not essential
to the self remains incommunicable through language.337
Klossowski argues that, as an alternative to language, Nietzsche en-
visages laughter and crying as a more adequate expression and satisfac-
tion of the needs of the unconscious life, offering access to the essential
aspects of the self—its fragmentary and fortuitous nature as an intersec-
