tion of unconscious forces. (“And it is as fragment, enigma, chance that
I remain in relation to what is most essential in me, which perhaps has
just expressed itself through this unmotivated laughter and tears.”)338
Accordingly, Nietzsche seeks to substitute for conscious thought a new
mode of parodic understanding and knowing.339 His strategy thus be-
comes one of using the elements of conscious thought and its teleology
against itself.340 This accounts for the manner in which science is par-
odied in the “scientific” accounts of eternal return. For Nietzsche, art
and science are both errors, but while scientific truth is an unconscious
error due to the distortions imposed by consciousness, art is a willed
error, and therefore superior.341 It is the willed error—the fiction, the
 simulacrum—which is ultimately better able to take account of an ex-
istence whose essence is a truth which absents itself.342 This account of
truth is obviously derived from the Heideggerian notion of truth as ale-
theia or unveiling, according to which the truth of Being (Sein) is always
withheld behind entities or beings (Seiende) which obscure it as much as
they reveal it.343
Klossowski now suggests that eternal return is, in fact, a simulacrum
of a doctrine rather than a serious proposition. It is a parody induced by
and inducing laughter, laughter being one of the means of access to what
is essential in the self—its fortuitous character as a coincidence of im-
pulses and drives: “The doctrine of Eternal Return is conceived […] as a
simulacrum of a doctrine whose very parodic character takes account of
hilarity as an attribute of self-sufficient existence when laughter bursts
out from the depths of the whole truth.”344 This laughter, as a revelation
of fortuitousness, marks not only the death of the monotheistic God and
the loss of individual identity, but also the simultaneous inauguration
of an order of polytheism and plural identities. The pluralizing effects
of eternal return thus remove the old God only in order to replace Him
with a panoply of vying deities. In this sense, the polytheistic parody of
monotheism enacted by eternal return is also a self-parody, a parody of
its own supposedly radical, but actually limited, impact on monotheism
it could only replace rather than remove:
Zarathustra, from the moment he willed the Eternal Return of all
things, chose in advance to see his own doctrine ridiculed, as if
laughter, this infallible assassin, were not also the best inspiration,


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  273
as well as the best denigrator of this same doctrine; thus the Eternal
Return of all things also wills the return of the gods. (SFD 227)
Starting from a position close to that of Bataille, Klossowski has
changed his existential reading of eternal return for a deconstructive
interpretation. He read eternal return as the isolation and the privi-
leging of the moment and exchanged it for a reading that stresses the
disintegration of the unique moment in the course of repetition. Each
individual moment loses its individual identity through recurrence. At
the same time, it repeats a past moment and rehearses a future one in a
parodic cycle without beginning or end. Eternal return is seen now as
abolishing both identity and origin, and it is this idea that is considered
Klossowski’s main contribution to the scholarship on Nietzsche. Thus,
Deleuze notes:
Witness the vehement oscillations which upset the individual as long
as he seeks only his own center and does not see the circle of which
he himself is a part; for if these oscillations upset him, it is because
each corresponds to an individuality other than that which he takes
as his own from the point of view of the undiscoverable center.
Hence, an identity is essentially fortuitous and a series of individual-
ities must be traversed by each, in order that the fortuity make them
completely necessary. (LS 178)
As the individual affirms the distance with respect to every other event,
which means raising “each event to the power of the eternal return,” he
follows and joins it, passing through all the other individuals implied
by the other events, and extracts from it a unique event which is once
again himself, or rather the universal freedom. Thus, the eternal re-
turn is not a theory of qualities and their circular transformations, but
rather the theory of pure events and their linear and superficial conden-
sation. The eternal return has a sense of selection and remains tied to
an  incompatibility—with the forms which hinder its constitution and
its functioning.345 Deleuze explains:
We do not raise contrary qualities to infinity in order to affirm their
identity; we raise each event to the power of the eternal return in
order that the individual, born of that which comes to pass, affirm
her distance with respect to every other event.346
Counter-actualizing each event, the actor-dancer makes of the disjunction
a synthesis which affirms the disjunct as such and makes each series
resonate inside the other. Each series returns to itself as the other
series returns to it, and returns outside of itself as the other series


274  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
returns to itself: to explore all distances, but over a single line; to run
very fast in order to remain in the same place.347
Thus, counter-actualization comes about when an individual considers
herself as an event and that event as “another individual grafted onto
her.” This double affirmation extends to treating other individuals as
events and their events as individuals—it is this affirmation that brings
events “to the power of the eternal return.”348 The power of the eternal
return is that which allows for an affirmation of the disjunctive synthe-
sis; in other words, the divergence of two series (individuals with respect
to the distance of other individuals or events) is not only affirmative but
it necessarily alters the other series by resonating in it and vice versa. It
is the conjunction of Leibnizian monads and counter-actualization that
allows Deleuze to talk of a unique event. It is this unique event that the
univocity of Being is: “If Being is the unique event in which all events
communicate with one another, univocity refers both to what occurs
and to what is said.”349
The eternal return is only of pure events.350 At this level, there is no
incompatibility between their acosmic, impersonal and pre-individual
singularities. While the ironist in its various guises (Deleuze follows Ki-
erkegaard’s typology from Socratic irony to Romantic irony in listing
various ironists) amuses himself with these alogical incompatibilities,
the task of the individual is to liberate himself and all other events by
releasing them at the level of pure events. His thought must be capable to
embrace this humorous worldview to affirm reality through its alleged
contradictions. Humor is the art of the surfaces and unless it is prac-
ticed, the higher level of pure events cannot be attained. The capacity to
identify with a distance, on which counter-actualization is predicated, is
best done though humor. As Nathan Widder notes, “the ethical trans-
mutation of the eternal return, therefore, is not meant to secure an ‘I’
who wills. On the contrary, the condition of this ethical affirmation is
that the ‘I,’ the ego, must be taken far less seriously.”351
Humor was used in this way by the Stoics: “Step back and laugh,”
said Seneca, where the stepping back and the laughing are not sepa-
rate steps, as Nussbaum explains.352 The identification with a distance
“permits us to go farther than we have believed possible.” It liberates
the pure event. Consequently, the mime to whom Deleuze entrusts the
ethical task is not the hero of the representation of the same (the Kan-
tian who “repeats” a maxim until the categorical imperative acquires
the extension of a law of nature). The Deleuzian mime is given the twin
obligation to unmask the pretension of the actual to be the only player
in the field and to re-enact the virtual in its infinite process of differing
from itself.353
The actor, sometimes in itself (the mime), sometimes associated with
the dancer (actor-dancer), sometimes with humor (humor-actor), is


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  275
deemed an “anti-god” (contradieu).354 To see how these various person-
ages (actor, dancer, mime, humorist) are related, we should see how they
parallel the end of Nietzsche and Philosophy, where they are deemed
powerful powers of transmutation, as affirmation takes place though
play, dance and laughter:
In relation to Zarathustra laughter, play and dance are affirmative
powers of transmutation: dance transmutes heavy into light, laugh-
ter transmutes suffering into joy and the play of throwing (the dice)
transmutes low into high. But in relation to Dionysus dance, laugh-
ter and play are affirmative powers of reflection and development.
Dance affirms becoming and the being of becoming; laughter, roars
of laughter, affirm multiplicity and the unity of multiplicity; play
affirms chance and the necessity of chance. (NP 193–4)
In The Logic of Sense, Deleuze describes the actor or Stoic sage as some-
one able to evoke an instant with a taut intensity that is expressive of an
unlimited future and past, and thereby embody the incorporeal effects of
a state of affairs rather than merely its spatio-temporal actualization.355
Such actors do more than merely portray a character’s hope and regrets;
they attempt to “represent” a pure instant at the point at which it divides
into future and past, thus embodying in their performance an intimation
of virtual relations beyond those actualized in the situation portrayed. If
one wills to be just in the manner of a Stoic sage, one wills that is not the
repetition of past acts of justice, but a justice that has always been and
has yet to be—the incorporeal effect of justice that is never made fully
manifest in any concrete situation.356
We should turn to the Twentieth-Fifth Series of Univocity to see that
Deleuze refers to the amor fati expressed in counter-actualization, and
when systematically effectuated for each event, to its outcome, eternal
return, as “the solution of humor”:
My love is an exploration of distance, a long journey which affirms
my hate for the friend in another world and with another individ-
ual. It causes the bifurcating and ramified series to resonate within
one another. But this is the solution of humor, quite different from
the romantic irony of the person still founded upon the identity of
contraries.357
Now, this is not a solution that holds only for The Logic of Sense. In or-
der to see that, we should recall that Deleuze and Guattari maintain in
Anti-Oedipus that “in truth, there are never contradictions, apparent or
real, but only degrees of humour.”358 Incompatibility is born only with
individuals, persons and worlds in which events are actualized but not
between events themselves or between their acosmic singularities. The


276  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
self merges with the disjunction which he liberates. The self, the world
and God share, as Klossowski has shown, a common dissipation at the
surface of things:
We do not raise contrary qualities to infinity in order to affirm their
identity; we raise each event to the power of eternal return in order
that the individual, born of that which comes to pass, affirm her dis-
tance with respect to every other event. As the individual affirms the
distance, she follows and joins it, passing through all the other in-
dividuals implied by the other events, and extracts from it a unique
Event which is once again herself, or rather the universal freedom.
(LS 178)
“Philosophy merges with ontology, but ontology merges with the univoc-
ity of Being,” and as beings are always produced by a disjunctive synthesis,
“the Univocity of Being merges with the positive use of the disjunctive syn-
thesis which is the highest affirmation. It is the eternal return itself…”359
But for philosophy to merge with ontology, it has to embrace the frame of
thought that enables to conceive of Deleuzian ontology. In order to “make
of the disjunction a synthesis,” one needs humor. Simultaneously being
too weak for my life and too strong (when my life is too weak for me), the
ambiguity which is present in every wound and necessarily in death, the
mortal wound, requires a form of thought that can comprehend ambigu-
ities without collapsing them. Only humor can do this.
The essential part of The Logic of Sense, which identifies amor fati
and humor, is reprised in What Is Philosophy, without allusion to humor
but with reference to Zen Buddhism. In the latter work, the right attitude
toward logic is silencing it as Zen Buddhism does. But Zen Buddhism is
always associated with humor in all of Deleuze’s works: in The Logic of
Sense, Zen Buddhism is related to the Stoics, as amateurs and inventors
of paradoxes, and to English or American nonsense.360 In Dialogues,
Deleuze writes:
English humour (?), Jewish humour, Stoic humour, Zen humour:
what a strange broken line… humour is the art of pure events. The
arts of Zen, archery, gardening or taking tea, are exercises to make
the event surge forth and dazzle on a pure surface…Zen humour
versus Buddhist irony.
(D 68)
The only difference between the counter-effectuation described in The
Logic of Sense and the one described in What Is Philosophy? is that
the mime of The Logic of Sense is replaced by the conceptual persona:
“The event is actualized or effectuated whenever it is inserted, willy- nilly,


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  277
into a state of affairs; but it is counter-effectuated whenever it is ab-
stracted from states of affairs so as to isolate its concept.” Thus,
There is a dignity of the event that has always been inseparable from
philosophy as amor fati: being equal to the event, or becoming the
offspring of one’s own events—“my wound existed before me; I was
born to embody it.”361 I was born to embody it as event because
I was able to disembody it as state of affairs or lived situa-
tion. There is no other ethic than the amor fati of philosophy.
(WP 157)
3 Mimes, Perceptual Personae and Idiots
In The Logic of Sense, Deleuze uses Stéphane Mallarmé’s notion,
“mime,” to explain the counter-effectuation of the event which he de-
scribes. The writer chooses that term for this action because it side-steps
the state of affairs and “confines itself to perpetual allusion without
breaking the ice.”362 The mime is a particularly interesting notion
for Deleuze because the repetition which he effectuates is indebted to
Jacques Lacan’s view of repetition, which ties it with mimicry. Rather
than mere reproduction or passive adaptation or copying, repetition is
an active inscription of the subject into a picture, for Lacan. Mimicry
involves “disguise, camouflage, and masquerade,” as Widder notes.363
Such a mime neither reproduces the state of affairs nor imitates the lived
situation.
Deleuze and Guattari eventually replace this “ambiguous name” with
“conceptual persona.”364 We are told now that the “mime” does not
give an image but constructs the concept. It does not look for the func-
tion of what happens but extracts the event from it, or that part that
does not let itself be actualized, the reality of the concept. Rather than
willing what happens with a false will that actually complains, defends
itself and loses itself in gesticulations, Deleuze and Guattari suggest that
we take the complaint and rage to the point where we turn against what
happens so as to set up the event, to isolate it, to extract it in the living
concept:
Philosophy’s sole aim is to become worthy of the event, and it
is precisely the conceptual persona who counter-effectuates the
event. Mime is an ambiguous name. It is he or she, the conceptual
persona carrying out the infinite movement. Willing war against
past and future wars, the pangs of death against all deaths, and
the wound against all scars, in the name of becoming and not of
the eternal: it is only in this sense that the concept gathers together.
(WP 199)


278  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
It is thus imperative that we understand what a conceptual persona is.
Deleuze argues that concepts are spiritual signatures, which dwell not
only in one’s mind because they are also ways of living. They are not
brought about by choice or reflection as the philosopher reflects no more
than do the painter or the musician. Creative activity rather than a re-
flexive dimension defines actions. Deleuze dreams of a quantification
which would count how many concepts philosophers have signed or
invented.
He further explains that aesthetic figures are not the same as concep-
tual personae. They do not share the same becoming: conceptual becom-
ing is the action by which the common event eludes what it is. Events are
the reality of the virtual, forms of a thought-Nature that survey every
possible universe. With its concepts, philosophy brings forth events.365
Moreover, the conceptual persona is not the philosopher’s represen-
tative, rather, the reverse: the philosopher is only the envelope of his
principal conceptual persona and of all the other personae who are the
intercessors, the real subjects of his philosophy. Conceptual personae are
the philosopher’s “heteronyms,” and the philosopher’s name is the sim-
ple pseudonym of his personae. I am no longer myself but thought’s at-
titude for finding itself and spreading across a plane that passes through
me at several personae.366 Vital anecdotes recount a conceptual perso-
na’s relationship with animals, plants or rocks, “a relationship accord-
ing to which philosophers themselves become something unexpected
and take on a tragic and comic dimension that they could not have by
themselves.”367
Philosophy is the “counter-effectuation of the event,” abstracting an
event or change of pattern from bodies and states of affairs and thereby
laying out the transformative potentials inherent in things, the roads
not taken that co-exist as compossibles or as inclusive disjunctions (dif-
ferentiation, in the terms of Difference and Repetition). Humor seems
to be Deleuze’s perceptual persona, which effectuates in the concrete-
ness of life that which philosophy effectuates in the abstract: humor is
a selective force that selects affirmation; it enables to hold together the
alogical contradictions that constitute reality for Deleuze and Guattari,
and the “I” which is a “multiplicity of subjects living different tempo-
ralities within the same, not very unified being.”368 By identifying philos-
ophy as the new actor of counter-effectuation, Deleuze identifies humor
as that which enables to select the pure event with creative philosophical
thought.369
A final Deleuzian notion that should be clarified is the “idiot.” Deleuze
asserts in one of his lectures on Spinoza that to philosophize is to act
the idiot.370 Referencing the work of Nicholas de Cusa, as explained
by his teacher, de Gandillac (1941), he uses the former’s notion of the
idiot as representative of the true thinker.371 For Deleuze, the idiot is a


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  279
conceptual persona or a key esthetic figure. In contradistinction to the
public philosopher, the idiot is a private thinker, who wants to think by
himself using the natural light of his reason.372 To his students, Deleuze
first introduces the idiot as the ignorant philosopher tending toward
truth or God, a private thinker whose thought is exemplified by Socra-
tes’s  ignorance or Descartes’s doubt. As the Deleuzian image of thought
cannot keep the relation to truth or God, however, in What Is Philoso-
phy? Deleuze and Guattari present an image of thought that embodies
the new idiot. This conceptual persona is related to the notion of ethical
humor.373
The difference with the former idiot is as follows: the idiot is still the
singular or the private thinker, but his singularity has changed. While the
former idiot aspired to self-found evidence, the new one does not want
evidence at all. He wants the absurd. The former idiot wanted truth;
this one wants to make of the absurd the highest power of thought, that
is, creation. While the two idiots are not the same personae, these two
concepts are linked: the former idiot who is related to the traditional
image of thought had to lose his reason so that the latter, which Deleuze
and Guattari introduce, would find what the former had lost in finding
reason.374
The new idiot is the thinker who aspires to realize the task of philos-
ophy, which is to create new concepts, cases of solution to a problem.
Thought can get there by turning toward the absurd, the incomprehen-
sible, the paradoxical, rather than toward the limits of orthodox think-
ing. Here, Deleuze and Guattari follow not only Kierkegaard, who made
these notions the key of internal change, but also Shestov and his disciple
Benjamin Fondane. However, for Deleuze, the new idiot opens thought
to what transcends it without reference to God or to the Immutable
Ideas. He is in contact with the Other of thought, which is nevertheless
real and immanent. He represents the essence of thought through which
philosophy manages to keep contact with the indeterminate and its in-
finite movement.
From Dostoyevsky’s prince Mychkine to Melville’s Bartleby and the
majority of Beckett’s characters, the idiots are Deleuzian heroes in-
asmuch as they exhibit a fundamental indetermination. The Russian
idiot comes from the long tradition of the Holy Fool and Orthodox
Christianity originating in Russian medieval culture. Taking him as
an example, Deleuze and Guattari hold that to raise the absurd to its
higher level is to create, which is the task of philosophy. This is also
the task of the ethical humorist, as Jean-François Lyotard argues when
referring to Deleuze in order to explain humor.375 Rather than at-
tempting to create a series of laughs, the inanity of the humorist-idiot
is a necessary condition for seizing the opportunity, for being able to
grasp that which presents itself in the breaches of rigidified quotidian


280  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
life, Jérôme Cotte explains. The inhibited cheerfulness the humorist
creates bursts from the inside the lawful generalities. His eccentric
discourse may be marginalized by common sense, but it is still the
humorist that sees something else. Its art is to construe new problems;
its treachery, atonality and freedom are the reverse of the “dirty little
secret of sexuality,” of the “Oedipus-irony,”376 and of the ready-made
ironic answer.
Thus, the association between deterritorialization, idiotism, ethical
humor and philosophy as rethought by Deleuze and Guattari becomes
obvious. Jean-Michel Counet (2016) emphasizes the essential role that
the idiot plays in Deleuze’s philosophy: it is at the core of the image of
thought that the philosopher invokes and implicitly presupposes, and
of the creation of concepts that he explicitly forms. In Faire l’idiot: La
politique de Deleuze (To Act the Idiot: The Politics of Deleuze [2013]),
Philippe Mengue emphasizes the primordial role of the perceptual per-
sona of “the idiot” in Deleuzian philosophy as well, as that which gives
coherence to its system but also orientation for its politics. He specu-
lates an idiosyncratic politics out of the figure of the idiot taken from
Deleuze’s metaphysics. While Mengue’s argument has not been left un-
criticized,377 I delineate its main argument to show how far the figure of
the idiot may be taken, when he is designated as the counter-actualizer
of the Deleuzian event.
Mengue admits that Deleuze does not offer a counter-politics in the
traditional sense of a direct confrontation, which diminishes his contri-
bution to democratic politics. And yet his micropolitics of “becoming”
or “playing” the idiot does offer an alternative form of resistance. It
points to a way of escaping control by carving out the “smooth” space
of indiscernibility and non-communication within the “striated” space
of institutions.
For Deleuze, Mengue argues, the figure of the idiot emblematizes the
encounter with the pure event and the primary state of being. It brings
forward the disruptive force of the virtual into the symbolic domain.
Thus, the idiots are the emblems of counter-actualization or counter-
effectuation as presented in this chapter. All famous Deleuzian idiots
are immersed in the plane of immanence and express their Otherness
as new intensities of impersonal life. Even though such idiotic figures
do not produce or actualize the event in social reality, their obstinate
persistence in their own alterity enables its appearance. Mengue de-
scribes such characters as intercessors between the plane of virtualities
of becomings and that of social where their suspension between the
empty zone of indetermination and the actual state of affairs operates
according to the Deleuzian principle of the disjunctive synthesis378; in
the context of Kant’s metaphysics, this reflects their epistemological
lingering on the border or passage between sensible intuitions and the
concept.379


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  281
Thus, to philosophize, as well as to act and to think politically, ac-
cording to Mengue, is always a way of playing the idiot. Leaving aside
politics, we can see that since philosophy is a paradoxical enterprise,
which thrives on creativity, Deleuzian humor merges with it. The philos-
opher presents itself as the idiot, as did Socrates in relation to the Soph-
ists, Descartes in relation to Aristotle, the entire Christian tradition with
de Cusa in relation to philosophy, and the Russians, either as Orthodox
Christians, Dostoevsky or Shestov in relation to reason and logic. By
Deleuze’s account, in Différence et répétition, the idiot is the pedant’s
polar opposite. Accepting his share of ridicule in relation to common
sense, the philosopher-humorist or Deleuzian hero counter-actualizes
quotidian life by bringing it to the level of the pure event, problematiz-
ing it conceptually while liberating himself practically whether as actor-
humor, mime or idiot.
Humor opens us to what is impersonal, pre-individual, to the no-
madic and free singularities, Deleuze says in The Logic of Sense.380
Humor seems to be the selective force of eternal return. After all,
eternal return is called “parodic,”381 and parody is deemed the high-
est humor.382 Willing the humorous necessity, which is amor fati,
yields eternal return, which is the task of the free man, the revolution-
ary, the philosopher. The same idea is put forth in exalting terms in
The Logic of Sense and more soberly in What Is Philosophy? Humor
as creative, paradoxical and affirmative thought is hardly differen-
tiable from philosophy when it fulfills its role as the creator of new
concepts, and from the philosopher as embodying the sole ethics of
amor fati.
IV Concluding Remarks
The primordial role that laughter plays in Deleuzian philosophy has
been established by now. Deleuze appears as a philosopher of humor,
as indeed the philosopher who has so far given the most extensive role
to humor in philosophy. To conclude this chapter, an evaluation of
the originality of these contributions is in order, beginning with the
idiosyncratic notion of humor that Deleuze systematically advances
and following with the no less systematic rejection of irony in favor of
humor.
A Deleuzian Humor
Although at first sight in conformity with Bergson’s definition of humor,
Deleuze’s own view of humor is highly idiosyncratic in that he ascribes
it to everyone he likes or whose thought he admires. I have quoted at
length his rendering of the humor of various philosophers so that the
reader may have a direct impression of this process, which divests humor


282  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
of any particularity that is generally associated with it. This point was
not missed by the few critical studies of Deleuzian humor, such as Ba-
ruchello’s excellent essay (2002). Baruchello takes issue with Deleuze’s
use of “humor” and his ostracism of the tragic figure involved in the
humorous, to the effect that “not only Deleuze’s notion of humor is too
broad and counterintuitive, but also too poor.”383
Deleuze uses “humor” in a counterintuitive way, even when there
is no comical or hilarious component. When dealing directly with the
issue of humor, Deleuze does not seem to be interested in the amuse-
ment that humor is supposed to give us. Baruchello notes that Deleuze
rather focuses on the iconoclastic force of humor, its capacity to break
any boundary or law, both logico-linguistic and ethico-psychological,
its casting light onto the surface of being or the surface of singular
events and its practical co-extensiveness with nonsense or the absurd.
“These four features become so crucial in his view,” Baruchello notes,
“that he ends up neglecting the point that they could have nothing
funny at all.”384
Deleuze’s humor is often a humorless humor, at least according to
“the commonsensical notion of humor” to which Baruchello appeals,
which “requires that being funny, producing laughter, possessing some-
thing comical, amusing, hilarious, is given as necessary condition for
something to be humorous.”385 This explains why Deleuze’s view of hu-
mor is too narrow.
But it is also too broad, Baruchello further maintains, because Deleuze
includes as humorous authors, insights and experiences that no one
would consider humorous. Baruchello asks, why does Deleuze make use
of such atypical meaning of humor? Doesn’t he realize that not even all
of Diogenes or Chrysippus’s “monstrations” were humorous?
Another significant criticism is that Deleuze “ostracizes the tragic fig-
ure involved in the humorous,”386 by turning tragedy into comedy, or
into a partial secondary feature of the work at issue, without recogniz-
ing the co-existence, co-determination and mutual need of the tragic and
the comic. Thus, not only Deleuze’s notion of humor is too broad and
counterintuitive, but it is also too poor.387
Baruchello’s critique is justified; yet I believe that an attempt to ex-
plain Deleuze’s use of humor should take into consideration the follow-
ing observation: humor in philosophy is never very funny, nor is often
humor itself, according to the contemporary French philosopher, André
Comte-Sponville, who defines it in his Dictionnaire philosophique as
follows: “Humor is a form of the comic, but which makes us laugh espe-
cially at that which is not funny.”388 Moreover, as “humor” ranks as a
philosophical concept for Deleuze, it is opposed, as such, to good sense
and common sense, that is, also to the common sensical understanding
and use of the concept.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation  283
We may say, then, that “humor” itself is a conceptual persona in
Deleuze’s philosophy, which makes it into something that can be eval-
uated only within this particular philosophy. I have striven to show
that, contrary to many Deleuzian concepts, humor is a constant in
all of Deleuze’s works. The right way to evaluate it, then, is to find
its role in the Deleuzian good life, as I have attempted to do, rather
than find out whether it fits our accepted use of humor. Most philo-
sophical uses of humor can be evaluated only in this way, as Bataille
notes, because accounts of laughter depend on the philosophies that
create them.
Once the role of humor in Deleuze’s thought has been explained,
and the divergence of his views, both from usual uses of humor and
from the normal relationship of tragedy and comedy, has been high-
lighted, what could be further evaluated in Deleuze’s account? An-
other topic of interest is the sustained Deleuzian choice of humor
over irony.
B Humor rather than Irony
I propose to assess the originality of Deleuze’s systematic choice of
humor over irony. Recall that he first establishes the necessity of both
notions early in his writings, pitting the irony of the heights (asso-
ciated with  transcendence and truth) with the humor of the surface
(associated with immanence). Later on, however, he chooses humor
over irony. In order to evaluate the originality of this choice, I put
Deleuze in relation to philosophers’ attitude toward irony since this
notion surfaced on the philosophical agenda. Following the Romantic
and postmodern endorsements of irony, we are often ignorant of the
attitude toward irony in the history of philosophy prior to the nine-
teenth century. I wish to fill this lacuna by showing that, contrary
to the common view that philosophers prefer irony to humor or to
additional forms of laughter, the rejection of irony is the attitude most
philosophers embrace after Plato, except for the Romantics and their
followers, the postmodernists, who use irony in highly idiosyncratic,
yet differing, ways.
­
Deleuze’s criticism of irony echoes Hegel’s.389 In rejecting irony,
Deleuze joins a long list of philosophers, who, beginning in Ancient
Greece, disliked this attitude. It is mainly Plato who presents Socrates
as ironic, not only in the sense it had in Greek culture, as a form of dis-
honesty, but in a new sense which serves the diffident teacher that Plato
is.390 We should add to this consideration Plato’s own irony, which is
directed toward the reader rather than used in the portrayal of Socra-
tes’s attitude: each reader believes that if he were to confront Socrates,
he would have behaved differently than Socrates’s interlocutor, which


284  Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
of course is unwarranted. Additional authors wrote Socratic dialogues,
at that time a fashionable genre, and in other accounts Socrates is por-
trayed as more jocular and humorous than ironic.
Irony has been identified with Socrates, and rejected already by Aris-
totle391 and his follower Theophrastus.392 The Aristotelian discussion
of irony’s merits and defaults is undertaken in the context of truth, not
of the comical. The Peripatetics were not the only ones to distance them-
selves from irony, however, as all philosophical schools which chrono-
logically followed Aristotle rejected it: the Cynics, the Epicureans, the
Stoics and even the Platonists, who endorsed from the first century
AD Aristotle’s view that irony is a vice.393 The Cynics preferred sar-
donic laughter to irony.394 The Epicureans rejected Socrates as a model,
together with (his) irony and rhetoric as unsuitable for the search of
truth.395 The Stoics, who venerated Socrates, nevertheless considered
irony as unworthy of the manly and earnest person.396 So practically, all
Greek and Hellenistic philosophical schools shunned irony.
In medieval times, irony was not associated with the comical.397 In
the Renaissance, texts that were lost in the West reemerged, allowing
to reappropriate this association and to write, as Erasmus did, about
Socrates’s “habitual irony” in the sense of comical irony. However, var-
ious scholars argue that it is only since Romanticism’s interest in irony
that we value it.398 It is during the nineteenth century that the ironic
Socrates replaces the comical Socrates, fueling our imagination to this
day. Indeed, Alexander Nehamas maintains that because we appreciate
irony, we value Plato’s account of Socrates more than other accounts.399
It is noteworthy that in Xenophon’s account, for example, Socrates is
presented as jocular or humorous, rather than ironic, a point that Karl
Popper emphasized when criticizing Plato.400 How Socrates’s comicality
should be characterized and his irony understood are still controversial
issues which are debated among contemporary prominent scholars, such
as  Nehamas, Gregory Vlastos and Paul Woodruff.401
Not only Hegel, but Nietzsche, Bataille, Lyotard and Theodor Adorno
reject irony.402 Deleuze’s choice of humor over irony is echoed by the
French philosophers Vladimir Jankélévitch, André Comte- Sponville and
Clément Rosset.403 Humor was characterized as modern in contradis-
tinction to ancient irony by Arthur Schopenhauer, and many nineteenth-
century German thinkers, who partake in the tragic tradition, extol
humor.404
Deleuze’s criticism of irony places him in respectable company. Yet
his arguments for rejecting irony may prove more original than his
mere rejection of it. The superiority exercised by the ironist is disap-
proved by most critics; yet the philosophy of irony itself, the worldview
that it presupposes, is emphasized by Deleuze as worthy of rejection
and indeed as the target of his, and his and Guattari’s philosophy, so
much so that their whole project may be characterized as anti-ironic.
Yet this denial is not one in favor of earnestness (Stoics) or genuineness


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation 285
(Aristotle), but more in line with the Cynics, who favored another form
of comicality, although the form Deleuze chose differs from theirs.
Deleuze’s criticism of irony puts him at odds with postmodern irony,
and with postmodernity itself. Indeed, Colebrook echoes many authors
in her identification of irony and postmodernity. She notes that the hu-
mor beyond irony, or the “superior irony” that radical humor is for
Deleuze,405 “is opposed to the politics of capitalism, communication
and subjectivity and to the poetics of ‘post-modern’ irony.”406
The next and last philosopher this study addresses, Deleuze’s contem-
porary, Clément Rosset—the focus of the next chapter—rejects irony in
favor of humor, as do Deleuze and Bataille, among many others. This
is one additional indication that the three thinkers this study addresses
are not postmodern. Rosset will satisfy our need to enlighten laugh-
ter, however, as commonly experienced. To this purpose, he offers an
innovative view of the laughter of annihilation, which, in its guise as
“brief laughter” or humor, attempts to explain one of our experiences
of mirthful laughter, which is not yet adequately elucidated. Shocking as
his explanation may be, and embedded in his tragic philosophy, which
originates and monopolizes it, it will be of a phenomenon we will rec-
ognize as laughter, if we only dare to admit it, rather than a conceptual
persona that enacts the very reality it wishes to explain.

of humor, which would make Rosset puff of laughter (Rosset also noted
Deleuze’s theatricality, intellectualism, nomadism or instinct of liberty,
and hatred of the medias). Charles Stivale notes that throughout the sole
videotaped interview we have of Deleuze, L’Abécédaire (a dialogue with
his former student Claire Parnet [Deleuze and Parnet 1996]), Deleuze
laughs profusely on various occasions “at Parnet questions, through-
out his own answers, sometimes at the expense of others, sometimes at
his own expense, and most frequently, in the interstices of his insights
and comments” (Stivale 2008, 118; see chapter 7: “Deleuze’s Laugh”).
Deleuze accepted the interview on the condition that it will be released
posthumously.
 11 TRM 2007, 63.
 12 E.g. Williams 2008, 14.
 13 Frank 1987, 316; Smith and Protevi 2011.
 14 The first quote is from Deleuze, who adds “A philosophy-cinema” (Deleuze
2007, 66); the second is from Deleuze and Guattari’s Introduction to A
Thousand Plateaux (TP 22).
 15 Deleuze 1977, 147; WP 11.
 16 A conceptual persona is defined in What Is Philosophy? as a type of subject
that operates with concepts. Conceptual personae are the real subjects of
a philosopher, his “heteronyms.” The philosopher’s own name is a pseud-
onym, “an idiosyncrasy” of his conceptual personae. Thus, “the destiny of
the philosopher is to become his personal persona or personae at the same
time that they become other than what they are historically, mythologically
and commonly…” (WP 64). This also explains the uncommon use Deleuze
makes of the notions of the comic, laughter and humor.
 17 Trahair 2007, 61; Ford 2016.


288 Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
 18 The only exception is Bergson, whose book on laughter Deleuze surpris-
ingly does not mention in Bergsonism, but whose definitions of irony and
humor he endorses from Difference and Repetition onward.
 19 Notable exceptions are Baruchello 2002; Colebrook 2004, chapter 7; Wil-
liams 2008, 17–20, 85–6; Dumoncel 2009; Ford 2016; Cotte 2018. See
also Cherniavsky 2007, and Garnett 2010.
 20 Baruchello 2002; the second quote is from Jean-Claude Dumoncel’s “Pre-

 21 Smith and Protevi 2011. In her biography of Deleuze (2017), Frida Beck-
man notes his early interest in esoteric thought. Among the works prior
to 1953, which Deleuze indicated to leave out of his authorized publica-
tions, one can find the Introduction he was invited to write to Jean Mai-
fatti de Monterreggio’s Études sur la mathèse ou anarchie et hiérarchie de
la science (1946). Deleuze was attracted to Maifatti’s view of mathesis,
which states that the individual and the universe are one. For an account
of Deleuze’s interest in esoteric thought, sorcery and magic, and theories of
the unconscious that Sigmund Freud either discarded or neglected, such as
Carl Jung’s theory of the unconscious and Ludwig Binswanger’s approach
to schizophrenia, see Kerslake 2007. For an attempt to read Deleuze within
the hermetic tradition, see Ramey 2012. For a more extensive biography of
the lives and thought of both Deleuze and Guattari, see Dosse 2007, 2010.
 22 For a helpful attempt at listing synonyms and mapping the connection be-
tween Deleuze’s differing terminologies, see DeLanda 2002, Appendix:
Deleuze’s Words, 157–80; also useful is Parr’s The Deleuze Dictionary
2005, 2010. For Deleuze and Guattari’s terms, see Patton 2001a.
 23 May 2002.
 24 Ramond 2011.
 25 Bergson is read through Duns Scotus and Nietzsche, but also through Spi-
noza, Leibniz and Hume; Nietzsche is read through Bergson and Spinoza,
and Spinoza through Nietzsche and Duns Scotus, for example. Alberto
Toscano describes the outcome thus: “A Bergsonized Spinoza accompanies
a Spinozistic Nietzsche and a Nietzschean Bergson” (Toscano 2009, 380).
Conway puts it differently:
Implicitly or explicitly, Deleuze’s readings engineer and draw attention
to a series of becomings within philosophic systems. The portrait of
Bergson includes a becoming Spinoza, a becoming Leibniz, and a be-
coming Hume; the portrait of Nietzsche includes a becoming Spinoza
and becoming Bergson; the portrait of Spinoza includes a becoming
Nietzsche.
(Conway 2010, 178)
 26 Hume and Bergson against Kant, Nietzsche against Hegel and Kant, Spi-
noza against Descartes, etc.
 27 Deleuze sometimes points to his contributions; for example, when he notes
in Nietzsche and Philosophy, “It is difficult to deny a Spinozist interpre-
tation here” (NP 62). Conway argues in an optimistic vein that in other
cases, “it is simply familiarity with the second portrait which enables the
reader to detect the fold” (2010, 178). The way Deleuze subtly differs from
the views he ascribes to the Stoics, without acknowledging it (Johnson
2017), and the accounts of the Deleuzian Bergson, the Deleuzian Nietzsche
and the Deleuzian Spinoza in the notes below are good examples of this
procedure.
 28 In an article called “the ‘bad boy’ of the history of philosophy,” Frédéric
Streicher notes:


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation 289
betraying an author whilst respecting him, using his concepts without
endorsing the whole of his thought, the practice of Gilles Deleuze in the
history of philosophy is at least singular and innovative. Before produc-
ing the post-68 disturbing and atypical works… [between 1960 and
1969] Gilles Deleuze dedicated himself to the history of philosophy and
wrote diverse monographs about illustrious philosophers…The content
of this work seems at first sight to be simply and banally “honest” in its
scholarly and didactic objectives … (moreover, he publishes his books
in series that are accessible to students). It seems as if it simply aimed, as
any work of a studious commentator, at making accessible to the gen-
eral public the thought of an author, which had impacted the history of
philosophy, by explaining it consciously and meticulously.
(Streicher 2005; my translation)
The reservations about Deleuze’s Nietzsche and Philosophy voiced by Jean
Wahl (1962) and Rosset (1985), among others, are also worth noticing.
In an important review that Wahl wrote about Deleuze’s work in Revue
de métaphysique et de morale, he did not hide the “mixture of admira-
tion and malaise” he felt when reading it (Wahl 1962; quoted by Meziane
2019). Wahl deems Deleuze’s work too scholastic because of the philo-
sophical qualities that the Deleuzian Nietzsche possesses, which cannot
be found in Nietzsche. Yet Deleuze interprets him with the same concep-
tual rigor that is applied to some of the most prestigious representatives
of philosophical rationalism. Rosset diagnoses the French Nietzscheans,
and Deleuze among them, as disappointed yet persevering Hegelians, who
“advance without recoiling, in the name of Nietzsche, views that are most
evidently opposite to those Nietzsche held” (1985, 81; my translation). As
far as Bergson is concerned, Madeleine Barthélemy-Madaule contests “Mr.
Deleuze’s use of Bergsonism as the title of his study” (Barthélemy-Madaule
1968, 120; quoted in Hardt 1993, 24) and Alexandre Lefebvre qualifies
Deleuze’s “bold opening move” at the beginning of Bergsonism, which is
reiterated in the concluding paragraph, as “a highly—an incredibly!—anti-
Bergsonian gambit” (Lefebvre 2015, xviii). For Deleuze’s Spinoza and ad-
ditional reactions to the Deleuzian Nietzsche and the Deleuzian Bergson,
see the notes below.
 29 “Lettre à Cressole” ([Cressole 1973]; reedited as “Lettre à un critique
sévère” in Deleuze’s Pourparlers 1972–1990, 1990, 14–15). This proce-
dure recalls the Deleuzian description of the masochist’s subversive accep-
tance of the law which is described below in this chapter.
 30 See below, the opening paragraph of the section “The Good Life.”
 31 Hardt 1993, xix. The example given by Michael Hardt is the following:
“Many of Deleuze’s claims for Nietzsche’s attack on the dialectic remain
obscure unless we read into them a Bergsonian critique of a negative
movement.”
 32 Williams 2003, 4.
 33 In “How to Recognize Continental European Philosophy,” in the anthology
he edited for Columbia Press (2007), Boundas notes: “Deleuze’s becoming
worthy of the event, despite the dash of Spinoza’s joyful wisdom, remains
enigmatic” (Boundas 2007b, 393). Doubts about the viability of an ethics and
a non-utopian politics in Deleuze’s writings are common. See, for example,
Slavoj Žižek’s assertion that “‘in himself,’ Deleuze is a highly elitist author,
indifferent toward politics,” in contradistinction to the political “Guatta-
rized” Deleuze brought to the fore by the Anglo-Saxon reception: “It is cru-
cial to note that not a single one of Deleuze’s own texts is in any way directly
political” (Žižek 2003, 20). Conway notes this point and mentions several


290 Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
additional points that disparage the political import of Deleuze’s thought
(2010, 222), including Badiou and Peter Hallward’s claims (Badiou 2000,
10; Hallward 2006, 162). On Deleuze’s relevance for contemporary political
problems, see Pachilla 2015. However, many commentators, beginning with
Foucault’s Introduction to Anti-Oedipus (Foucault 1977, xiii; Deleuze and
Guattari 1983, xv), emphasize the ethical significance of Deleuze’s philos-
ophy (see, for example, Todd May [2005, 3]), and some works take as their
explicit objective the formulation of his engagement with normative political
issues that is largely absent in those he penned with Guattari (Patton 2010,
7). Indeed, Paul Patton argues that Deleuze’s “conception of philosophy was
political from start to finish” (Patton 2010, 1).
 34 For Deleuze’s style, see Bogue 2004, 9–26; interestingly, Bogue refers to
Rosset’s description of Deleuze’s style as “dry” (sec) (Rosset 1980 [1972]).
We should note here that Rosset distances himself from Deleuze at the
beginning of the latter’s collaboration with Guattari, from Anti- Oedipus
onward. In the Introduction to Deleuze’s letters, he explains: We “no lon-
ger wrote in the same language” (Rosset 2013).
 35 Not everyone seems to think so. Claire Colebrook, who has penned two
monographs on irony, does not mention irony or humor in Deleuze and the
Meaning of Life (2010). Published in the same year, Jay Conway’s Gilles
Deleuze: Affirmation in Philosophy mentions Deleuze’s typology of hu-
mor, including irony, only once (2010, 82; the index points also to page
104, but this seems to be a mistake). Conway also identifies irony with ge-
nealogy (107; and other places, as noted in the index). Although Conway’s
study spans all of Deleuze’s writings he writes rather laconically in the
notes: “The discussion of humor and irony is found in Deleuze, Difference
and Repetition, p. 5. Black humor is employed and defined in Deleuze and
Guattari, Anti-Oedipus, p. 11” (2010, 234n111). The few sentences on
humor (and irony) his study contains are the following:
For Deleuze, philosophical discourse contains distinct forms of comedic
criticism: humor (overturning a law through over-conformity), black
humor (the combining of radical, noncontradictory differences) and
irony (presenting ‘noble,’ ‘original’ principles as derivative of base or-
igins). The best way to understand the anti-phenomenological message
of What Is Philosophy? is as an ironic, genealogical assault on the con-
servative tendencies within the phenomenological tradition.
(Conway, 2010, 82)
Although not indexed, Conway addresses Deleuze’s laugh (132–9), but only
at the death of philosophy (“I have never been worried about going beyond
metaphysics or about the death of philosophy”; “philosophy will only die
chocking with laughter” (Conway 2010, 13; WP 9; N 136; D 1). Although
Conway recognizes that Deleuzian philosophy deserves the names “differ-
ence,” “desire” and “creativity” (136), he misses on the opportunity to asso-
ciate some of these terms with humor, as Deleuze has done. I hope to show in
this study that both the Deleuzian meaning of life that Colebrook addresses
and the Deleuzian affirmation of philosophy and affirmation tout court that
Conway analyzes are deeply conditioned by what Deleuze terms “humor.”
 36 For a helpful attempt at listing synonyms and mapping the connection be-
tween the different terminologies, see DeLanda 2002, Appendix: “Deleuze’s
Words,” 157–80; also useful is Parr’s The Deleuze Dictionary (2005; re-
vised edition 2010). For Deleuze and Guattari’s terms, see Patton 2001a.


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation 291
 37 Patton 1996, 3.
 38 “Que ce soit bien le sien, c’est très important, parce qu’il fallait que l’au-
teur dise effectivement tout ce que je lui faisais dire. Mais que l’enfant soit
monstrueux, c’était nécessaire aussi, parce qu’il fallait passer par toutes
sortes de décentrements, glissements, cassements, émissions secrètes qui
m’ont fait bien plaisir” (P 14–15; “Letter to a Harsh Critic,” N 6).
 39 14–15; “Letter to a Harsh Critic,” N 6; see also D 17.
 40 David Lapoujade argues that the thought of Deleuze and of Deleuze and
Guattari can be defined as an encyclopedia of aberrant movements which
philosophy should describe; moreover, their irrational logics should be ac-
counted for, as this is one of the great novelties of Deleuze and Guattari’s
work (2014).
 41 “Mon livre sur Bergson est pour moi exemplaire en ce genre” (P 14–15).
 42 “C’est Nietzsche que j’ai lu tard et qui m’a sorti de tout ça. Car c’est impossi-
ble de lui faire subir à lui un pareil traitement. Des enfants dans le dos, c’est
lui qui vous en fait” (P 14–15; Deleuze, “Letter to a Harsh Critic,” N 6).
 43 While Guy Lardreau argues that Bergson is the only philosopher that avoids
“falsification” in Deleuze’s work because “Deleuze is Bergson ill-written”
(Lardreau 2006, 60–2), this view is not shared by many Deleuze and Berg-
son’s scholars. For example, as we have seen above, Lefebvre notes that
Deleuze’s mention of stages and progress in Bergson’s philosophy, the “bold
opening move” he makes at the beginning of Bergsonism and reiterates in
the concluding paragraph, is “a highly—an incredibly!—anti-Bergsonian
gambit.” Lefebvre explains:
At the outset of his interpretation of Bergson, Deleuze avowedly (I am
tempted to say, brazenly) occupies the very standpoint that Bergson had
spent a lifetime problematizing: a retrospective vision that sees move-
ment only in terms of the destination it reaches.
(Lefebvre 2015, xviii)
Lefebvre maintains that “Bergsonism is an indisputably powerful work of
interpretation. It is tremendously systematic, tightly presented, and speaks
in a commanding no-nonsense tone”; however, he also notes, “for all its
strengths, balance is not one of them. Deleuze is highly selective in the
concepts he chooses to exposit. And he is determined to demonstrate a
clear-cut progression in Bergson’s thought” (xvii–xviii). “No doubt, it buys
Deleuze a sharp and systematic presentation; but it comes at the price of
faithfulness,” Lefebvre explains. For example, Deleuze “systematically un-
derpins the subjectivist, spiritualist and phenomenological dimensions of
Bergson’s thought” and pushes “Bergson’s analysis of subjective experience
toward an ontological—or, as he puts it, an ‘inhuman’ or ‘superhuman’—
register of duration.” Thus, the Two Sources of Morality and Religion gets
barely seven pages because it does not sit well with Deleuze’s account of
Bergson as progressively moving away from a theory of subjective expe-
rience toward an ontological account of duration: this is a book on the
emotions, which has at its centerpiece an account of the pressure and pull
of obligation and the aspiration to love. In qualifying “the New Bergson,”
Suzanne Guerlac notes along the same lines that Deleuze seems to have
“carefully edited those features of Bergson’s thought that might appear
as ‘metaphysical’… the features that might distinguish the human being
from the machine” (Guerlac 2006, 179–80). Barthélemy-Madaule argues
that Deleuze tries to read the Two Sources of Morality and Religion as


292 Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
a Nietzschean and anti-humanist text when it actually discloses the pro-
foundly religious character of Bergson’s thought: “The principal conclu-
sion that we take from this interpretation is that Bergson is not Nietzsche”
(Barthélemy-Madaule 1968, 120). She explains how “interpreting a doc-
trine supposes that one has accounted for all the terms of the ensemble”;
as it does not seem to her that this is the case, she “would contest Mr.
Deleuze’s use of Bergsonism as the title of his study.” Many years later, this
point is not lost on Christian Kerslake (2007, 8).
 44 For Deleuze’s interpretation of Nietzsche as differing from that which was
accepted in academic circles, see Meziane 2019. Let me elaborate here on
the initial responses I noted above (note 28) of Deleuze’s protégé, Ros-
set, and Deleuze’s much admired teacher, Wahl, and add the objections of
a sympathetic reader such as Hardt. While Rosset’s specific criticisms to
Deleuzian Nietzscheanism are better appreciated in light of his own Nietzs-
chean philosophy (see chapter 3, note 18 below), a general comment, which
also targets Deleuze, is relevant here: “Most French Nietzscheans advance
without recoiling, in the name of Nietzsche, views which are most evi-
dently opposite to those that Nietzsche held” (Rosset 1985, 81; my transla-
tion). See also Wahl’s early response revieweing Nietzsche et la philosophie
in Revue de métaphysique et de morale (Wahl 1962), which is interest-
ing on various counts. In Dialogues, Deleuze heralds Wahl, his teacher
at the university, as a philosopher who is no less significant and original
than Sartre. However, Wahl expresses his dissatisfaction with the work, a
mixture of admiration and unease in relation to its scholastic exposition
of Nietzsche: the Deleuzian Nietzsche has philosophical qualities that Ni-
etzsche does not always possess. He is interpreted with the same concep-
tual rigor that is applied to some of the most prestigious representatives
of philosophical rationalism. Moreover, contrary to the interpretations of
Bataille and Wahl, Nietzsche is presented as a consequent reader of He-
gel (or of Kant), in dialogue with them, and answering them intentionally.
Deleuze’s Nietzsche is a thinker who is integrated in the traditional history
of philosophy, an “irrationalist,” undoubtedly, who nevertheless created a
conceptual method. In this sense, Deleuze’s Nietzsche is at the same time
too much of a philosopher and too scholarly for Wahl, who, following Karl
Jaspers, sees Nietzsche first as an educator and a poet, whose thought is
far from being stable, and particularly, far from being stabilizable. More-
over, two years before Deleuze, Wahl has published his courses on Ni-
etzsche at the Sorbonne. His long series of commentaries of Nietzsche’s
quotes attempt to display the tensions and contradictions that inhere in
Nietzschean thought. These disappear in Deleuze’s exposé and are replaced
with forcing maneuvers whose purpose is disclosed by Wahl as presenting
a much more philosophical Nietzsche than he actually is. Finally, even a
sympathetic reader such as Hardt comments on the strain that Deleuze puts
on Nietzsche by selecting the “impersonal” in Nietzsche. Commenting on
Deleuze’s insistence on the impersonal nature of the question “Qui?” in
Nietzsche— the most personalist philosopher—Hardt objects:
It is often a strain to read Nietzsche without adopting personalist ref-
erences. Not only is there a long tradition of reading Nietzsche in this
way, but also it would not be difficult to cite several passages in which
we cannot help but read Nietzsche “personally.” Here, we have a very
clear idea of Deleuze’s selectivity. In effect, Deleuze brings a Bergso-
nian approach to Nietzsche so as to read him in logical terms, that is,
as a logic of the will and value that animates the field of pre- subjective


Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation 293
forces… The “impersonal” interpretative strategy can also be seen as a
political selection. In fact, Deleuze’s reading has made such a profound
impression on Nietzsche studies partly because it succeeds in making
so much of Nietzsche’s thought while avoiding or effectively diffusing
the force of arguments about Nietzsche’s individualism and reactionary
politics, nearly all of which are centered around a “personalist” inter-
pretation and selection.
(Hardt 1993, 31)
This is obviously not Nietzsche. Even Hardt seems to acknowledge this:
“Although this selection may be necessary for Deleuze, it is effectively this
‘impersonal’ aspect that marks the limit of Deleuze’s development of ethi-
cal and political veins in Nietzsche” (Hardt 1993, 31).
 45 The great identity between Nietzsche and Spinoza (toward which everything
tended, according to Deleuze) does not exist, but is rather a production, as
Jonathan Phillippe argues (2003). See also Amir, Redemptive Philosophies:
Spinoza versus Nietzsche. For Deleuze’s interpretation of Spinoza, see the
notes below. In chapter 3 of What Is Philosophy? Deleuze and Guattari
may be read as legitimizing the liberties that Deleuze avails himself with
the names and views of other philosophers: taking Plato’s Socrates or Ni-
etzsche’s Zarathustra as examples of “conceptual personae,” they may be
understood as legitimizing Deleuze’s Nietzsche and Deleuze’s Spinoza (see
Phillippe 2003, 183nn2 and 5). With Spinoza Deleuze is more careful than
with other philosophers: immanence appears only in the last chapter of his
second book on Spinoza; he openly states elsewhere that his interpretation
turns more on modes than substance and in the late 1980s translation of
Expressionism into English, he confides his aspiration to read Spinoza ac-
cording to the two criteria a plane of immanence denotes, which are the ex-
pressive character of individuals and an immanence of being (the last point
is mentioned in Lefebvre 2008, 242). For the impact of Spinoza on Deleuze,
see Macherey 1996; for the relations that hold between the philosophies of
Deleuze and Spinoza, see Sauvagnargues and Sévérac 2016.
 46 One should not argue with philosophers because they are always right, and
one should not argue with interpreters because they are always wrong. In
the two works on Spinoza, the highly significant and very rich secondary
literature on Spinoza and the critical commentaries are treated with osten-
sible disdain, Charles Ramond notes
Il n’y a pas à discuter les auteurs, parce qu’ils ont toujours raison, et il
n’y a pas à discuter les interprètes, parce qu’ils ont toujours tort. Dans
les deux ouvrages sur Spinoza, la très importante et très riche littéra-
ture secondaire, ou critique, sur Spinoza, est traitée avec un dédain
ostensible.
(Ramond 2011)
Deleuze is generally hostile to any form of “interpretation” of a text. The
commentaries on Spinoza are no exception; nor are those on Bergson (see
Lefebvre 2015, xix, and note 49 below).

read it (Lefebvre 2015, xix); Ramond notes his dismissive attitude toward

Nietzsche takes liberties in his publication on the Pre-Platonic Philosophers

freely with Pre-Socratics and Socrates. In this text, scholarship is wanting
(Whitlock 2001) as well as arguments (Thomson 2003) and contradictions

brags about it in Ecce Homo (1979).

phy, he had to conquer his inhibitions regarding creation by clarifying his
relation to the history of philosophy, if only to be able to take upon himself
or carry the weight of tradition” (Streicher 2005; my translation; quoted
in French in Lemieux 2007, 15). Along the same lines, Lardreau argues
that Deleuze avails himself to one of the strategies open to a historian of
philosophy: amending or rectifying a system in order to temporarily avoid

mieux gives of this topic (2007).

contradistinction of what Deleuze explicitly maintains, Badiou replied that
it would not be the first time that Deleuze would have been accused of such

traiture (WP-F 55) which uses conceptual personae as constituent elements

 56 As doing the same in this chapter would be cumbersome, I do not follow

 59 Deleuze and Guattari also published together “La synthèse disjunctive”
(1970), Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1986), and What Is Philoso-
phy? (1991).
 60 For process philosophy, see Rescher 1996.
 61 Williams 2003, 4. For a construction of Deleuze’s ontology, see DeLanda
2002. Although this volume describes becoming-actual in detail, DeLanda
spends considerably less time on the reverse problem of becoming-virtual,
or how the actual becomes virtual. James Williams has written critical in-
troductions and guides to Difference and Repetition ([2003] 2013) and The
Logic of Sense (2008). Both of Williams’s works are invaluable for under-
standing Deleuze’s philosophy, and in what follows I rely on those texts.

on Bogue’s and Boundas’s numerous publications, as listed in the references.
 63 Williams 2008, 199.
 64 DR 112–14.
 65 Univocity was first introduced by Duns Scotus; Deleuze uses this term to
interpret Spinoza’s philosophy, criticize orthodox theology and confront
Aristotle with Heidegger’s problem of ontological difference.
 66 Daniel Smith notes that in A Thousand Plateaus the logic of “is” gives
way to a conjunctive logic of “and.” This overthrows ontology and places
relations “outside everything which could be determined as Being, One,
or Whole” (ATP 25; see 98). The same is true for simulacrum: “It seems
to me that I have totally abandoned the notion of simulacrum, which is all
but worthless” (“Letter-Preface to Jean-Clet Martin,” TRM 362). Since

 129 The thought of Spinoza permeates all of Deleuze’s works, including those
that he authored with Guattari. Deleuze acknowledges that he worked
harder on Spinoza than on any other philosopher. Deemed in What Is Phi-
losophy? (1991) the “Prince” and the “Christ” of philosophers, Spinoza is
approached in the two works Deleuze penned on him with the utmost re-
spect and with less familiarity than the other philosophers whose thought
he forces. However, Deleuze’s use of Spinoza, as of other philosophers, is
selective. First, as Hardt indicates, Spinoza is approached through Bergson,



Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation 299
whose metaphysics he uses to bear on the Dutch philosopher, while their
commonalities, the religious or theological concerns that they share, are
neglected because they are not part of Deleuze’s interest (Hardt 1993, 56).
Spinoza is deemed an enigma by Hardt, following Deleuze’s note that he,
as everybody else, has not understood Spinoza (D 15; 57). Second, Lefebvre
explains how the criticism of Spinoza and the reworking of his thought has
already been undertaken by Bergson (Lefebvre 2008, 252), how Deleuze’s
reading exchanges the immutability and eternity of Spinoza’s substance for
the modes, for creativity and duration at the same time that he disregards
that the notions of duration, the new and the experimental are foreign to
Spinoza. On common notions, Lefebvre notes that “Deleuze’s interpreta-
tion of Spinoza is original” (222); finally, in Spinoza’s work expression
is rarely used and the parallelism of body and mind is never mentioned
(2008, 218–51). May explains in a book review that addresses the relations
between Deleuze and Spinoza that in Difference and Repetition (1994, 40),
published the same year as Expressionism in Philosophy, Deleuze writes:
Spinoza’s substance appears independent of the modes, while the modes
are dependent on substance…Substance must itself be said of the modes
and only of the modes. Such a condition can be satisfied only at the
price of a more general categorical reversal according to which being
is said of becoming, identity of that which is different, the one of the
multiple, etc.
In this area, May explains, Deleuze’s thought is characterized not by the
tripartite division into substance, attributes and modes, but into the bi-
partite division into the virtual and the actual. He notes that the example
he discussed is only one indication that Expressionism in Philosophy is
not a statement of Deleuze’s philosophy but rather an attempt to read Spi-
noza as sympathetically as possible. Another example is that Deleuze is
not committed to necessitarianism, unlike Spinoza. His discussion of the
dice-throw in Nietzsche and Philosophy and his embrace of the scientific
work of Jacques Monod and Ilya Prigogine show that chance plays a role in
Deleuze’s ontology that has no equivalent in Spinoza. May concludes that
“it is impossible to offer an assessment of Deleuze’s thought through this
single work, or through any single work of Deleuze’s (although admittedly
certain texts, Difference and Repetition among them, are more crucial to
that task)” (May 2002). Moreover, as other scholars have noted, Spinoza’s
rationalism is downplayed in Deleuze’s interpretation, and while Spinoza
was critical of State power, he cannot easily be made to share the same
theoretical premises as the anarcho-Marxism of Deleuze and Guattari. As
far as ethics is concerned, Deleuze’s Spinoza is Spinoza read through the
eyes of Nietzsche, and especially through Deleuze’s interpretation of the
Nietzschean doctrine of eternal return (see Surin 1989, 261).

 134 There are numerous Spinozian legacies in Deleuze, but one of the most
important is certainly the ontological notion of univocity. Univocity, as
opposed to equivocity and analogy, is the key to developing a “philosophy
of difference” (Deleuze’s term for his project in Difference and Repetition),
in which difference would no longer be subordinated to identity. The result
is a Spinozism minus substance or a purely modal or differential universe.
In univocity, as Deleuze reads Spinoza, the single sense of Being frees a
charge of difference throughout all that exists. In univocal ontology, Being
is said of difference itself. That is, difference is difference in degrees of
“power,” given that we distinguish the two French words puissance and
pouvoir. In social terms, puissance is immanent power, the power to act
rather than the power to dominate another. Deleuze develops a notion of
puissance as the ability to affect and to be affected, to form assemblages or
consistencies, that is, to form emergent unities that nonetheless respect the
heterogeneity of their components.

 161 Deleuze recalls Karl Marx’s theory of historical repetition, as it appears
notably in the Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1960 [1852], “all
great events and historical personages occur, as it were, twice…The first
time as tragedy, the second as farce”, and describes it as follows in Differ-
ence and Repetition: “Repetition is comic when it falls short—when in-
stead of leading to metamorphosis and the production of something new, it
forms a kind of involution, the opposite of an authentic creation. Travesty
replaces tragic metamorphosis” (DR 91–2). However, Deleuze disputes the
order that Marx assumes: “It appears that for Marx this comic or gro-
tesque repetition necessarily comes after the tragic… This temporal order
does not, however, seem to be absolutely justified.” The two moments are
not independent (they exist for Marx only for the third moment beyond
the comic and the tragic, which is “the production of something new” that
“entails a dramatic repetition which excludes even the hero” (DR 92). At
the beginning of Difference and Repetition, Deleuze has explained that
when Marx also criticizes the abstract false movement of mediation of
the Hegelians, he finds himself drawn to an idea, which he indicates
rather than develops, an essentially “theatrical” idea: to the extent that
history is theatre, then repetition, along with the tragic and the comic
within repetition, forms a condition of movement under which the
“actors” or the “heroes” produce something effectively new in history.
(DR 10)

Deleuze wishes to disengage the comic from its intermediary role between
the tragic and the absolutely new by arguing that, “Once the two elements
acquire an abstract independence or become genres, then the comic suc-
ceeds the tragic as though the failure or metamorphosis, raised to the ab-
solute, presupposed an earlier metamorphosis already completed” (DR 92).

 167 DI 107, 108. Antoine Marie Joseph Artaud, better known as Antonin Ar-
taud (1896–1948), was a French playwright, poet, actor and theater di-
rector. Along with Roger Votrac, Artaud ran the Alfred Jarry Theater in
1926–28. 1938 saw the publication of The Theatre and Its Double, his
most well-known work. This book contains the two manifestos of the the-
ater of cruelty, essential texts for understanding his artistic project. Cruelty
does not refer solely to sadism or the causation of pain, but just as often to a
violent, physical determination to shatter the false reality. He believes that
the text has tyrannized meaning, and advocates, instead, a theater made
up of a unique language, halfway between thought and gesture. Artaud
describes the spiritual in physical terms, and believes that all theater is
physical expression in space:

The Theatre of Cruelty has been created in order to restore to the the-
atre a passionate and convulsive conception of life, and it is in this sense
of violent rigor and extreme condensation of scenic elements that the
cruelty on which it is based must be understood.
(Artaud 1968, 66)
For Artaud’s theater of cruelty, see Artaud 1964, 1968; Dumoulié 1992.

 194 M 39–40. A true sadist would not tolerate a willing masochist as an accom-
plice, according to Deleuze, and the punisher will be seduced and educated
by the masochist into a “quasi-sadistic” behavior, which is distinct from
sadism. For Deleuze’s psychological understanding of Sade and Sacher-
Masoch, see Deleuze’s preface to Masochism (1991) and Bogue 1989,  45–54.
Jack  Reynolds remarks:

It is not just Freud who is being targeted here, but also the Hegelian
master-slave dialectic, as well as Sartre’s reinvention of it (1996, 257),
in which we are envisaged to be thrown back and forth between the
attitudes of sadism and masochism in an ultimately impossible attempt
to control how we are seen by others, and to eliminate the prospect of
shame and alienation before the look of the other.
(Reynolds 2006, 90)
Because Deleuze sees Freud’s clinical experience as flawed, being based on
young neurotics’ reminiscences, and his therapy as efficient for hysterical,
obsessional and anxiety-ridden patients but not for masochists, Deleuze
recommends studying Sacher-Masoch’s novel to educate ourselves about
the phenomena. The novelty of the literary approach to masochism is


304 Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation
challenged by David Sigler, who finds fictional base for understanding mas-
ochism both in Jacques Lacan and in Freud himself (Sigler 2011). Deleuze
criticizes all Freudian approaches to the unconscious, including Reik’s, as
expressed in Masochism and Modern Man (1941), for being too limited to
account for the kinds of neurosis that verge on psychosis, the so-called per-
sonality disorders. In these cases, Jung’s view of the unconscious is more
efficient, as the images that haunt the subject cannot be reduced to his
own history but recall the Platonic reminiscence of a pure past, that has
never been. The therapy in these cases should enhance those parts of the
personality that are underdeveloped due to the law or to social constraints.
Deleuze’s contemporaries studied Sade rather than Masoch. In Sade My
Neighbour, Klossowski argues that Sade has a system as developed as that
of Hegel, but it can never be realized as it is always against (Klossowski
1992, 18–19), and we have seen in Chapter 1 that Bataille has defended
the Marquis.

 204 A number of explicit references testify to Deleuze’s acquaintance with
Klossowski’s accounts of eternal return (DR 312–13; LS 264). Moreover,
there is a general consonance in their readings of Nietzsche. The concept
of the simulacrum, with its abolition of the origin and identity, is intro-
duced first by Klossowki. He brings the old notion of bad or parodic copy,
the simulacrum, into relation with the modern psychoanalytic notion of
the phantasm, an imaginary scenario generated by unconscious drives and
subject to compulsive repetition. This is a conjunction which Deleuze takes
up in The Logic of Sense, with reference to the representation of histori-
cal events (LS 100, 210–16). Deleuze also gets the idea of intensity which
governs the plateau from Klossowki, who is responsible for refurnishing
intensities with philosophical and theological depth. Klossowki develops
a whole semiology out of intensities. Still active in medieval physics and
philosophy, the notion of intensity has been more or less obscured by the
privilege granted to extensive qualities and the geometry of extended space.

240 D 68. In Proust and Signs, Deleuze contrasts again Proustian with Socratic
intelligence, Jewish humor to Socratic irony:



The Socratic demon, irony, consists in anticipating the encounters. In
Socrates, the intelligence comes still before the encounters. Proust’s hu-
mor is of another nature: Jewish humor as opposed to Greek irony. One

C’est la Litanie de l’Humour. Puisque l’humour peut y trancher, par
example, entre Platon et le Portique, on voit que dans la litanie la dif-
férence entre ironie et humour donne une véritable procédure de de-
cision philosophique où l’humour est la pierre de touche, indiquant à
chaque fois le bon choix. Autrement dit Deleuze découvre dans l’hu-
mour un veritable transcendental.
Dumoncel further explains the role of humor in Deleuze’s philosophy as
affirmative criticism:
Mais comment l’apologiste de la pensée affirmative peut-il être l’auteur
d’un Anti-OEdipe? La réponse est dans le distinguo deleuzien entre
fausse et vraie Critique (L’Île déserte et autres textes: textes et entre-
tiens 1953–1974, 191). Ce distinguo prend la forme d’une Critique au
Carré: la fausse critique est la critique des faux contenus (fausse religion,
“erreurs” du capitalisme ou de l’impérialisme, etc.), la vraie critique est
la critique des vraies formes de ce qu’elle critique (de la vraie religion,
du capitalisme triomphant, etc.). Deleuze en énumère quelques maîtres:
Vallès, Tati, Jerry Lewis. Ainsi, même la critique peut être affirmative.
(Dumoncel 2010, 210)

 301 M 93. The term “law” is ambiguous. Deleuze is interested in jurisprudence
and the internalization of subjection that psychoanalysis terms repression. In
a conversation with Toni Negri, Deleuze says: “I was initially more interested
in law than politics. Even with Sacher-Masoch and Sade what I liked was
the thoroughly twisted conception of contracts in Sacher- Masoch, and of
institutions in Sade, as these come out in relation to sexuality” (Deleuze and
Negri, 1990). “La loi,” “les lois,” translated as “the law” and “laws,” cor-
respond to a judicial system of positive laws enacted in a legal code (such as
the Civil Code in France). By contrast, in a 1988 interview, Deleuze remarks
that “rights aren’t created by codes and pronouncements but by jurispru-
dence. Jurisprudence is the philosophy of law, and deals with s ingularities, it
advances by working out from singularities” (Deleuze 1995, 153).

 302 Zourabichvili 1998, 357; in Boundas 2007a, 19.
303 In the conversation with Negri mentioned above, Deleuze distinguishes crit-
ically between law and jurisprudence: “What interests me isn’t the law [la
loi] or laws [les lois] but jurisprudence.” Elsewhere, Deleuze is interested
in repression as the internalization of subjection. Freud’s Oedipus complex
seeks to explain why and how we are repressed—how it is that we submit
to law and renounce our enjoyment. Psychoanalysis explains our repression
by arguing that we all desired our mothers but had to abandon incest for the
sake of social and cultural development. In Anti-Œdipe, Deleuze and Guat-
tari argue that the repressive idea of renunciation and submission is rather a
historical and political development. Desire, they insist, is not the desire for
some forbidden object, a desire that we must necessarily repress. Rather, all
life is positive—it is expansion, connection and creation (1972, 240). The late
modern understanding of the self or subject as necessarily subjected to law is
the outcome of a history of political development that has covered over the
originally expansive, excessive and constructive movements of desire. A num-
ber of philosophical movements, including psychoanalysis, have explained
life from the point of view of the already repressed subject, the bourgeois in-
dividual who has submitted his desires to the system of polity and the market.

308 Let me repeat here what I noted above: “The Stoics are amateurs and inventors
of paradoxes… the only equivalent of which are to be found in Zen Buddhism
on the one hand and in English or American nonsense on the other” (LS 8).
Summing up his views on humor and irony in reference to many of his works
on literature and desire, Deleuze opposes in Dialogues Zen humor to Bud-
dhist irony, and put the former in relation with other forms of humor (“En-
glish humour (?), Jewish humour, Stoic humour, Zen humour: what a strange
broken line…”) with the assertion that “humour is the art of pure events,”
which makes the event “surge forth and dazzle on a pure surface” (D 68).



 309
Deleuze writes: The physical mixture is exact only at the level of the
whole, in the full circle of the divine present. But with respect to each



Deleuze—The Humor of Affirmation 309
part, there are many injustices and ignominies, many parasitic and can-
nibalistic processes which inspire our terror at what happens to us, and
our resentment at what which occurs. Humor is inseparable from a se-
lective force: in that which occurs (an accident), it selects the pure event.
(LS 151)
