 351 Widder 2008, 99. Philippe Sergeant argues for the role of humor in the
Nietzschean eternal return by offering an account in the last chapter of his
work (2010), which is actually a Deleuzian reading according to Juliette
Feyel (2011). Sergeant argues that “when the three times—Cronos, Aiôn,
Kaïros—are taken in the nets of Nietzschean dancing, laughing and play-
ing, eternal return discloses its lightness, its secret: creating life rather than
assuming it. Here is the dangerous ground of humor” (Sergeant 2010, 26;
my translation). Sergeant presents humor as a transgressive element which
enables the philosopher to move from one line of time to another, Feyel
notes (2011). Humor enables a movement of deconstruction of being, a
“de-ontology,” as the author calls it (2011). I did not take this work into
account as it is a reading of Nietzsche rather than of Deleuze.

 352 “When you laugh, you are not just expressing a Stoic revaluation already
formed; you are advancing toward the goals of Stoic therapy,” Nussbaum
explains (2009, 88). The laugh is itself a separative movement: “Step back
and laugh” do not denote two distinct stages; it is one stage, because in
laughing, one changes perspective and steps back (89). This sort of distanc-
ing laughter is frequently in evidence in Stoic texts.

Laughter is the only power that enables a fair fight against the damages
caused by knowing the horrifying and unbearable in life. Those who do
not have a sense of humor have received the poison without the antidote.
(Michel Polac and Clément Rosset, Franchise Postale: Courrier mai
2002—décembre 2002, 81–2)
One has to choose between the clown, which is tragic, and divertissement
that masquerades as earnestness. There is no other alternative; for there is
only one genuine earnestness, the clown, and only one profound frivolity,
the spirit of seriousness… Whoever wishes to be in earnest is a clown.
(Clément Rosset, Le Monde et ses remèdes, 144–5)
Clément Rosset (1939–2018) is an eminent contemporary French philos-
opher who has attracted a cultish group of fans in Europe. His philos-
ophy may be characterized as a reflection on the principal Nietzschean
themes, which results in a personal and highly original reflection that
prides itself on its independence from contemporary currents.
Rosset reads Nietzsche as a tragic thinker, and considers his own
thought as the sole that is loyal to Nietzsche’s philosophy.1 Reprov-
ing the betrayal of reality of which we are all guilty, his thought of-
fers an alliance between lucidity and joy, in which laughter fulfills the
epistemological role of accessing to otherwise unreachable layers of
reality. Moreover, his tragic philosophy defines a “laughter of annihi-
lation,” a unique way of laughing that rejoices in destruction. Finally,
it advances a view of existence that grounds the comical ontologically,
and therefore enables to single out humor as an indispensable tool for
survival.
Rosset rejects most philosophical theories of laughter in favor of his
own view, which deems laughter tragic because it laughs at annihilation.
Tragic philosophy both originates and monopolizes this sort of laughter,
he argues. Grounded in laughter’s love of the real—the notion Rosset uses
to denote “the world” or “reality”—tragic philosophy defines laughter as
3
Clément Rosset—The
Laughter of Annihilation
DOI: 10.4324/9780429506116-5


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  329
expressing the enjoyment of engulfment, a delight in the elimination of
that which is unreal. Not only is the comical inseparable from the tragic
in Rosset’s philosophy, but humor as “brief laughter” (“rire court”) is
favored as a form of knowledge and affirmation of reality.
Hardly any philosophy has entrusted the comical, laughter and humor
with significant roles such as those ascribed to them by Rosset. To him,
“laughter is the most important thing, it is above everything else.”2 Its
significance is due to the fact that a sense of humor is absolutely critical
for survival: the human being, and only him, needs laughter because he
is the only being that cannot bear nor process the knowledge he has of
certain aspects of existence, without the necessary additional assistance
and distancing that laughter affords. As one of the knowledges of real-
ity, laughter fulfills an epistemological role in the good life, which leads
to the affirmation of unvarnished reality. Rosset is also one of the few
philosophers who assert that the comical is ontologically grounded; as
existence is predicated on hazard, appearance and disappearance, life
and death are equally comical.
­


However significant the role Rosset ascribes to laughter in the good
life, laughter’s capacity for affirming and knowing the real is surpassed
by the power of the graced joy of life. As joy enables further affirmation,
joy is a more significant epistemological tool than laughter, for affirma-
tion alone enables a full encounter with the real. Joy is a graced state
because its advent in our lives does not depend on us. Thus, laughter
does not have an active role to play in the occurrence of graced joy or in
the fuller affirmation of the real that joy enables.
Rosset has been deemed “one of the rare philosophers to practice
humor,” one who makes successful use of a “comic verve that is un-
conceivable in philosophy,” and the only follower of Nietzsche who
has incorporated insouciance into his own philosophy.3 Spiced up with
amusing stories, Rosset’s philosophy is humorous and witty, an “omni-
referential system in which film, literature and comic strips all operate
on the same level.”4 It possesses an element of burlesque, which is es-
pecially prominent in his description of many of the renowned philoso-
phies it undertakes.5 In a recent interview, Rosset confesses:
If it’s funny, I can’t help myself…If there’s a way to point out some-
thing comical in any situation, I cannot resist it. Of course, I apply
the same principle to myself—in Les Matinées structuralistes, I too
appear as a grotesque character.
(Polac and Rosset 2003, 78–9; my translation)
Self-referential laughter is notable also in Rosset’s sole non-philosophical
book (Route de nuit, 1999), in which he describes the depression that
plagued him in the final years of his life. Deeming his dramatic mood
­


330  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
swings “very funny,” he published the manuscript on account of its “fan-
tastical and comical quality.”6
Apart from a few exceptions, such as Nietzsche in La Force ma-
jeure and Parmenides in Principes de sagesse et de folie, Rosset does
not take philosophers seriously. He refers to them only to make fun of
them:  incapable of reflecting upon that which exists, they ponder about
 everything else, that is, about nothing. Rosset ridicules the false confi-
dence the great philosophies exude; for all their appearance as rational
masterpieces, they are made of absurdities and shipwreck unexpectedly,
like the  Titanic. Avant-garde authors, such as Georges Bataille, Michel
Foucault, Pierre Klossowki, Jacques Lacan, Louis Althusser, Jacques
Derrida and Gilles Deleuze are especially prone to extreme comicality.7
Rosset ridicules the prevailing themes of the French intelligentsia in
Lettre sur les Chimpanzés (which Deleuze read and appreciated),8 and
pokes fun at both contemporary intellectual trends and philosophical
luminaries in a pseudonymous play, Les Matinées structuralistes.9 He
argues that contemporary philosophers take themselves too seriously
and welcome all ordeals except insouciance.10 Rosset distinguishes him-
self from contemporary French philosophers by rejecting the style,11 the
methods of interpretation, the erroneous reading of Nietzsche and the
implicit ideology found in the work and in the views of the comical of
the poststructuralists.
Rosset’s criticism targets both Bataille and Deleuze. Like “most
French Nietzscheans,” he writes, they “do not recoil from asserting, in
Nietzsche’s name, opinions that are most certainly opposite to those
Nietzsche held.”12 Rosset diagnoses the French Nietzscheans as disap-
pointed, yet persevering, Hegelians, a view that is echoed by commenta-
tors of both Bataille and Deleuze.13
Though Rosset acknowledges Bataille’s modernity in deeming de-
sire insatiable, he sees as problematic the latter’s view of desire as lack,
both in eroticism and mysticism.14 Rosset’s criticism ultimately bears on
Bataille’s view of the world as parodic: desire is never this or that, but
always close to this or that, as the Story of the Eye exemplifies.15
More importantly for this study, Rosset denounces Bataille’s inter-
pretation of Nietzsche as inaugurating the tragic, and of the tragic as
the province of a few gifted intellectuals. While acknowledging that
Bataille’s work announces the genuine beginning of Nietzsche studies,
Rosset first points to Bataille’s faulty assessment of Nietzsche’s historical
significance: contrary to Bataille’s view, Nietzsche is not the first phi-
losopher to free the world’s representation of rationalistic, finalistic or
theological thinking by founding a philosophy on “no-sense” or hazard.
Rosset then attacks Bataille’s assertion that the tragic, as life founded
on no-sense, is ignored by all except by a few brilliant intellectuals who
can bear the tragic. To the contrary, Rosset argues, the tragic in life
is common knowledge, shared by many and expressed by the popular


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  331
adage “this is life” (ç’ est la vie); only a few intellectuals, such as philos-
ophers and theologians, refuse to acknowledge the tragic, preferring to
put their faith in reason or in some other order that transcends the tragic.
While it is true that the common view of the tragic is rarely expressed,
only intellectuals can believe that what is not expressed does not exist.16
Nor is Deleuze exempted from reproach. Following his discovery in
the library of Rosset’s first book, Philosophy of the Tragic, while do-
ing research for his own Nietzsche et la philosophy, Deleuze initiated
a meeting with the young man, whom he befriended and counseled.
Deleuze often invited Rosset, had dinner with him at home, and kept
reading and commenting on his publications.17 Rosset distanced himself
from Deleuze when the latter began cooperating with Guattari; yet he
continued to refer to him while disapproving of his reading of Nietzsche,
which emphasizes the critical at the expense of joy and misrepresents the
eternal return, and his view of humor, which is predicated on sense and
its contraries.18
Rosset’s writings have been translated into many languages, rarely into
English.19 Not much has been written about Rosset in any language.20
There are no studies of Rosset’s view of laughter, thus no studies of the
role that laughter plays in his view of the good life.
I would like to fill this gap by introducing Rosset’s view of the good
life, followed by his thoughts on the comic also in relation to the tragic,
and on the role laughter fulfills in such a life; I examine Rosset’s charac-
terizations of laughter as rejoicing in annihilation, ironic and humorous,
transcending sense and nonsense, disclosing the derisory in all existence,
and as different from joy but close to anxiety and death. I c onclude by
assessing the originality of Rosset’s views of the ontological dimension
of the comical, the laughter of annihilation he introduces as the aesthet-
ics of tragic philosophy, the significance of playing the clown and the
enigmatic joy his philosophy advances, by comparing these views with
other thinkers’, including those of Bataille, Deleuze and my own philos-
ophy of Homo risibilis, or the ridiculous human being.
I The Good Life
Rosset believes that he is Nietzsche’s sole disciple insofar as he devises a
tragic philosophy based on affirming reality through the irrational joy of
life. He grounds his thought on a critique of the majority of philosophical
theories, especially of non-naturalist, poststructuralist and postmodern
approaches to reality. He argues that philosophy’s role is to prepare us
to confront the real rather than to resort to its illusory doubles,  address
irrelevant issues or comment on philosophical texts. In order to explain
the Rossetian good life, an understanding of his tragic philosophy is
required. It is followed by describing the place that joy holds in such a
vision, and the role philosophy can fulfill in attaining to joy.


332  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
A Tragic Philosophy
The “real” (le réel) or “reality” (la réalité) and its betrayal are at the
center of Rosset’s work. The “real” refers to everything that exists as a
function of the principle of identity, which states that A is A. In describ-
ing the real, Rosset uses idiocy in its etymological sense, idiôtès, which
means “simple.” The real is simple, particular and unique; it excludes
all double. Every existing thing is absolutely singular, unique and unre-
peatable; yet the singular nature of existence makes it at once infinitely
precious and fated to insignificant oblivion. The world—the “real” or
“reality,” as Rosset indifferently refers to it—is meaningless and free
from any underlying order, necessity or logic. It is pure hazard, thus
chaotic and cruel, in one word, unbearable.21
Most philosophers betray the real by formulating a worldview that
dismisses, occults and replaces reality with a fictional representation of
a higher truth. The history of philosophy is ultimately divided into two
noticeable leanings. A speculative trend, on the one hand, which origi-
nates in Platonic philosophy and has been dominant from the very be-
ginning. Another more or less suppressed movement, on the other hand,
contests the illusions perpetrated by the speculative tradition and at-
tempts to bring humanity face to face with the brutal and chaotic nature
of the real, with its lack of meaning and order. The latter trend emerged
twice in the history of philosophy, first with the pre-Socratics and later
in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
In addition, isolated and marginalized figures in the history of phi-
losophy, such as Lucretius, Michel de Montaigne, Blaise Pascal and Ni-
etzsche surface as effective representatives of the second movement. As
speculative philosophy cannot allow such incursions, it has usually rele-
gated them to domains which do not partake in the noble philosophical
tradition: Montaigne writes essays, Pascal produces only fragments and
Nietzsche is no more than a literary figure who prefers aphorisms to
arguments, and so on.
The speculative tradition led philosophy astray by offering consola-
tion. However, the world, or that which exists, holds absolutely no con-
solation for human beings. Faced with the meaninglessness of the world,
the individual most often quakes and turns away. The experience of the
real is literally unbearable, for reality surpasses the human faculty of
understanding. More importantly, it exasperates human tolerance. In
the case of serious conflict with the real, the individual who instinctively
feels that the recognition of reality would exceed his power and endan-
ger his very existence is forced to decide instantly to opt for the real or
for his own self. As granting preference to the real leads to suicide, either
psychological or physical, the individual is inclined to choose himself
and condemn the real.22


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  333
Tragic philosophy favors the real, to the contrary. It encourages
“thinking the worst,” the utter inexistence of any underlying order, ne-
cessity or logic to being. Any such logic or order amounts to the rejection
of that which exists—which by (and as) itself is without reason—thus
conveying depreciation, however subtle, of existence. Tragic philosophy
seeks to enunciate this silent intuition of that which is sufficient to itself,
that which lacks nothing. It does this in order to enable immediate and
unconditional affirmation: “Affirmative thought is terroristic because it
sees in terror the philosophical condition of any affirmative thought.”23
Rosset invariably attempts to provoke an encounter with the real, to
trigger a moment in which his reader may suddenly come to realize that
the real is all we have. Such a confrontation implies the recognition of a
world free of mediation, and also necessarily intimates that philosophy
cannot pretend to interpret the confrontation by interceding or mitigat-
ing its effects. A philosophy that could fulfill such a draconian requisite
for effacement would be perilously close to silence: “Logically, tragic
discourse could, even should, stop here—in silence.”24
Rosset describes being as tragic, hence illogical, amoral and contra-
dictory. We cannot conciliate ourselves to, nor are we responsible for,
the tension that defines it. The individual is tragic in a tragic world
 “solitary, thus without love, base, therefore without value, and mortal,
hence without life.”25 The tragic is a mystery which we can only no-
tice.26 The human being has ventured into an encounter with a truth
that he cannot face, which constitutes his contradictory and tragic
 destiny—tragic in the sense that Rosset’s former teacher, the philosopher
Vladimir Jankélévitch, understands it, “the alliance of the necessary and
the impossible.”27
Rosset mentions approvingly Lucretius, who repeatedly notes the dif-
ficulty of aligning thoughts with desires. This difficulty is for the latter
the principal source of the tragic and pitiful character of the human
being, condemned to live on the condition that he does not think, or to
think on the condition that he does not live. Hence the seemingly para-
doxical yet perfectly logical double consequence: reduced to the inability
to think and fully understand that which he knows, the individual must
distance himself from his own knowledge in order to continue living. He
must regard his knowledge as valid, on the one hand, and as null and in-
consequent, on the other. In order to survive, homo sapiens must double
himself as homo non sapiens, sapiens when salvaging his material life
and nonsapiens when preserving his mental health.28
B Joy
Our highest and most difficult task is to accept the real, to find satis-
faction in the sensual and perishable world.29 Accepting reality


334  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
presupposes a consciousness that is capable of both knowing the worst
and being unaffected by this knowledge. The capacity to know without
mortal damage exceeds human faculties, unless some extraordinary as-
sistance is provided, which Pascal calls grace and Rosset joy30:
This wisdom is not evident and supposes, in order to be efficacious,
the extra-help of an extraordinary, not to say supernatural, force
which I call the joy of life, which alone enables the fulfillment of
Rimbaud’s wish as expressed in the last line of his Season in Hell:
“To possess truth in body and soul.” In other terms: to finally ac-
cord the faculty of knowing with the faculty of living.
(Rosset 2001a, 85; my translation)
We cannot turn to philosophy to interpret the real; we have no other
recourse than to confront it and to recognize its brutal nature. Yet we
are not condemned to a bleak pessimistic outlook on life: we can live
this life even if there is no meaning to it, without succumbing to pessi-
mism. Indeed, nothing could be more foreign to Rosset’s approach than
pessimism. In fact, he sees in pessimism a surreptitious affirmation of
the optimistic view to life, the approach that suggests the existence of
meaning and of an ordering pattern to the real. The pessimist rejects
the real not simply because it is too cruel but also, and more funda-
mentally, because she believes that there could be something better,
something other than the real. This something other never material-
izes, of course. It is simply one of the many illusions of potential order
and signification manipulated by those who refuse to face the fact of
meaninglessness.
If neither optimism nor pessimism is permissible, which attitude is
recommended, what is viable when we finally face the real? The attitude
that Rosset endorses is comparable to the cruelty mixed with gaiety to
which Nietzsche alludes to when he writes about Georges Bizet’s Car-
men: “This music is cheerful…fate hangs over it; its happiness is brief,
sudden, without pardon.”31 Rosset calls such a healthy reaction to the
real, joy.
Because joy is not a simple emotion, it can never be fully explained as
a reaction to a particular object or a specific event as it always contains
some additional content. It overshoots its mark and somehow puts the
person who experiences it in contact with a general affirmation of the
real, with the entirety of its chaotic and cruel presence. The reasons for
being joyous or depressed have this surprising, and apparently paradox-
ical, feature—they are rigorously the same. Sadness is but the other face
of a coin whose tail is joy. Real joy is no different from either a lucid
vision of the human condition, which is presupposed or argued. Sadness
is the same vision yet dismayed. Joy is what Benedict Spinoza calls an
“active mode” of sadness, while sadness is a “passive mode” of joy.32


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  335
Joy is related to the Nietzschean embrace of life and to the Pascalian
intervention of divine grace. When there seems to be no possible means
of surviving the confrontation with the real, affirmation emerges as joy.
As a moral reaction to affirmation, joy reaches beyond emotions. It orig-
inates in the awareness that follows the laying aside of all mediation
between oneself and the real. It is both a tool and an epistemological
requirement. Without the joyful affirmation of the real, no one can ulti-
mately know reality because those who have not experienced that joyful
affirmation have necessarily turned away from reality, pulling back in
horror and misery. Thus, they cannot fully experience reality because
they cannot bear the suffering it brings along. One’s understanding of
the real is limited to the extent of joy’s intervention, which keeps an
individual focused on the real alone, on the world as it is, not as it may
be yet never will.
All joy consists of “the joy of life and of that alone.”33 The central
paradox of joy is that it expresses unconditional delight in existence,
although existence itself is anything but joyful when examined through
the sober lucidity that characterizes rationality. Rational thought is
continually inclined toward condemning existence because of the lat-
ter’s unjustifiable and undesirable character. What comes into existence
cannot possibly last, nor has it any chance of occupying a substantial
place in infinite space. Philosophy’s painful role amounts to realizing the
nothingness to which everything is necessarily reduced.34 The paradox
of joy—the incompatibility between joy and its rational justification—
reveals that joy consists of an unthinkable delight. Though it is possible
to experience this joy, it is impossible to conceive it because it eludes ex-
planation or rigorous argumentation.35 Simultaneously real and uncon-
ceivable, this experience raises the most serious question that philosophy
has ever addressed:
Either joy consists of an ephemeral illusion of having gotten rid of
the tragic nature of existence, in which case joy is not paradoxical
but illusory, or it consists of an affirmation of existence which is
held to be irremediably tragic, in which case joy is paradoxical, but
not illusory.
(OF 17)
Rosset opts for the second case; not only does joy manage to accom-
modate the tragic, but it exists because of, and only in this paradoxical
agreement with, the tragic. It is joy’s privilege to remain simultaneously
aware of and perfectly indifferent to the misfortunes that constitute ex-
istence. This also explains joy’s unique sense of contentment without
reservation. What Rosset means by joy’s indifference to misfortune is
neither its lack of attentiveness to, or ignorance of, misfortune. On the
contrary, it is eminently attentive to calamity precisely because of the


336  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
power of affirmation, which enables further and better knowledge of
reality. This is why Rosset notes, “there is no true joy unless it is also
thwarted, in contradiction with itself. Joy is paradoxical or is not.”36
Three main consequences follow from the paradoxical character of
joy, which Rosset outlines in “The Overwhelming Force.”37 First, by its
very definition, joy is illogical and irrational. Second, joy is necessarily
cruel by virtue of its carefree attitude in the face of destiny and the most
tragic of circumstances. Not only is joy not a psychological affair, which
by affecting the ego would produce a sensation of personal happiness;
it seems indifferent to all feelings and provokes a sort of general insen-
sitivity that may be compared to the “anesthesia of the heart,” to which
Henri Bergson alludes in his analysis of laughter.38
Nonetheless, the insouciance of joy is not entirely naïve; rather, this
view has to be taken with a pitch of salt and as a last resort, as a “sec-
ond naivety,” that is, once everything is known and has been felt. The
original alliance between joy and cruelty is corroborated by the harsh
and relentless quality that characterizes all profound gaiety. Rosset adds
that cruelty is in every case a mark of distinction, and this is true in all
domains—provided, of course, we understand cruelty not as a pleasure
taken in cultivating suffering but as a refusal to be complacent toward
any object, whatever it may be.
The third and last consequence of the paradoxical nature of joy is that
joy is the necessary condition, if not of life in general, then at least of life
lived consciously, in full awareness. The act of taking reality into con-
sideration, the simple exercise of reflection suffices here to discourage all
effort—unless joy somehow comes to one’s assistance, a joy which, like
the Pascalian God, steps in when all forces are failing and brings about,
in extremis and against all odds, the triumph of the weakest cause. Pas-
cal defines this act in the final apology of the second of the Provincial
Letters precisely as an extraordinary intervention (“secours extraordi-
naire”). The intervention of joy is forever mysterious, impenetrable even
for those who feel its beneficent effects:
In the final analysis, nothing has changed for them, and they under-
stand no more than before. They have no new argument to invoke in
favor of existence and they are still perfectly incapable of saying why
or for what they are living. And yet from this moment forth they
value life as indisputable and eternally desirable. This is the mystery
inherent to the zest of life.
(OF 19)
As mysterious as joy is, its bolstering effect is necessary for life, when life
is conceived as awareness of reality.39
Rosset criticizes the majority of the “French Nietzscheans” for being
disloyal to Nietzsche’s thought. He reformulates the latter’s philosophy


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  337
by concentrating on what he deems to be its fundamental notion, beat-
itude,40 though other words would do just as well, “joie de vivre, glad-
ness, jubilation, pleasure of living, affirming reality, and still others.”41
Beatitude is another way of expressing the affirmation of the real, the re-
fusal to entertain the idea of a truer world beyond the one that exists here
and now. According to Rosset, everything in Nietzsche follows from this
principle, which is an epistemological attitude. The gay science, blessed-
ness, joy: these descriptions of the perspective that a philosopher must
adopt toward the real are characteristic of Rosset’s thought. The les-
son that Nietzsche’s philosophy teaches is one of attitude and approach:
it goes beyond the Nietzschean critique of the philosophical tradition.
Thought should begin out of the beatitude of unconditional affirmation.
This is the meaning of the gay science. Affirmation is not stance to be
attained through a process that divests existence of negativity. A tragic
consciousness, according to Rosset, declares the death of happiness and
the triumph of the tragic. Neither conflicted nor anguished, it has the
serenity of the tragic certitude.42
However, Rosset later changes his view about happiness, deeming it
good, whatever its name, be it gladness, gaiety or joy, and apologizes for
his youthful dismissive attitude toward it. Repeating Nietzsche’s use of
happiness as the unique and unconditional principle of all philosophical
evaluation, Rosset also mentions Nicholas de Cusa, who credits divine
providence for this extraordinary privilege of happiness and Jorge Luis
Borges, who opposes it to the confused thing that life is: “Only happi-
ness is without mystery, because it justifies itself.”43
B The Role of Philosophy
Philosophy has traditionally come to the rescue of humanity from mean-
inglessness, through fashioning the illusion of truth which would take
us away from the suffering that necessarily ensues from encountering
the real. Speculative philosophies have regularly triumphed since the
Greeks because of the consolation they offer in the face of the desolation
of the real. The invention of doubles and the recourse to moral catego-
ries are both ways of denying reality, of turning away from tragedy. The
double and morality are two aspects of the same problem. Whenever re-
ality seems unpleasant, people find extraordinarily imaginative ways of
creating a substitute for it, which acts as a veil that hides whatever might
be raw, unpalatable or otherwise intolerable about the real. Instead of
the world as it is, we invent a duplicate or a double, a parallel universe
which functions as a phantom rival to the existing world, a desperate
compensation for the acceptance of reality. This duplicate takes on all
kinds of forms, from the cuckolded husband who, because he cannot
bear the truth, persuades himself that his wife is faithful, to the critic of
globalization who believes in the possibility of a different world and the


338  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
metaphysical philosopher who proves that reality is always somewhere
else.44
Every double is an illusion, less of an error than an embodiment of
wishful thinking. Rather than being blind, illusion sees double. In its
rejection of the real, illusion doubles it and chooses the double, that is,
nothing.45 In his monograph on Rosset’s philosophy (2001), Rafael del
Hierro Oliva lists the various functions that the double fulfills46: the
practical function of distancing the real, the metaphysical function of
interpreting it and the fantastic function of constituting the absent object
or the desire for nothing. In serving its metaphysical function, the dou-
ble bestows meaning upon reality, which then ceases to be idiotic and
unique. One of the most representative doubles is the concept of nature:
The idea of nature—by whatever names it goes—… seems to be one
of the major screens that separates the human being from the real,
by substituting the ordered complication of a world for the chaotic
simplicity of existence.
(Rosset 1973, 5; my translation)
Any philosophy is naturalist insofar as it uses the idea of nature to tran-
scend material hazard and human artifice. Nature is neither matter nor
human, but belongs to another category that requires body from the
former and soul from the latter. To humans’ effects and the effects of
hazard, we can add nature’s effects, which are explained not through
the spontaneous inertia of matter or through the calculated action of
human artifice, but through “natural” force and “natural” necessity. In
the history of philosophy, natural philosophies prevailed in two periods,
one in which ancient naturalism, as developed by Plato, Aristotle and
the Cynics, continued toll the crisis of scholasticism, and the other in
which modern naturalism, as reconstructed by René Descartes, John
Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, is kept alive today by myth, religion,
morality, reason, scientism, historicism and political intolerance.
Rosset sets himself against the dominant trends of post-war phi-
losophy, which are variants of what he refers to as “naturalism.” At
first glance, as David Bell notes, it may be tempting to consider Ros-
set’s thought as characteristic in some ways of familiar poststructural-
ist modes of approaching meaning.47 The poststructuralist strategy in
criticizing structuralism is undertaken as a series of attempts to undo
representation. The reason is the conviction that the stability of repre-
sentation, along with a traditional faith in meaning and truth, can be
located at the heart of even the most iconoclastic acts of the structuralist
enterprise. But Rosset claims that this attempt to destabilize representa-
tion and the structures of meaning that it implies is not radical enough.
The notion of deferral, whether in the image of the labyrinth or in the
“illusionism” of those whom Rosset calls “modern Hegelians” (Bataille,


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  339
Derrida and others), retains a logic of meaning, which suggests that if
we accomplish a sufficiently thorough working through this concept,
we might find an ultimate signification after all. Nor is the more ironic
postmodern perspective on meaning, the celebration of its demise in a
mixing of styles and metaphors, in a rediscovery of classical represen-
tational styles that are no longer attached to their contexts and become
empty rhetorical figures playing endlessly and eclectically with one an-
other, radical enough.
Bell believes that in the minimalist approach toward what exists, the
effort to encounter the real in the absence of all mediation precludes the
kind of rhetorical trifling common in postmodern thought. He sees it as
demanding a simple approach toward the real and an affirmation of the
real that seems particularly difficult for postmodern thought to imagine
or accept.48 Moreover, Rosset believes that one of the fundamental prob-
lems of postmodern attempts to radicalize philosophy is that they take
the philosophical tradition too seriously. In a strange twist, postmodern
thinkers take the foremost texts of the tradition even more seriously than
did those who produced them. Thus, contemporary  philosophy often
appears to produce endless interpretations, critical of, yet always rev-
erential toward classical philosophical texts. Reveling in exegesis, it is
totally oblivious of existence.
Rosset’s disapproval of this way of thinking follows from another vi-
sion of philosophy’s purpose: philosophy prepares us to confront that
which exists; it is an activity that should under no circumstances alle-
viate that confrontation. Anyone who fundamentally believes that real-
ity is all that matters should also understand that philosophical activity
cannot replace the real; it cannot pretend to position itself in a hierarchy
above that which actually exists in the world.
Morality for Rosset is a powerful illusion. It is essentially the product
of the Enlightenment as theorized by Rousseau and Immanuel Kant,
with many heirs as well as illustrious predecessors such as Plato.49 Moral
discourse has always deliberated about what should and should not be,
without paying attention to what actually is.50 The human and philo-
sophical propensity for morality imposes a fantastic realm of “should
be” to the sovereign and confining reign of being. What morality fights
against is not the immoral, the unjust, the scandalous, but indeed the
real—the sole and true source of scandal.51 Thus, moral reflection and
tragic thought are adversaries.
Like the texts of Lucretius, Montaigne, Pascal and Nietzsche, Rosset’s
writings reach out to those who are healthy enough to eschew illusion
and to live this life. He supports their embrace of the world and all of
its aspects, and the sober refusal of all semblances of reality that mask
its true character. Bell rightly assesses Rosset’s diagnosis as “therapeu-
tic only for the strongest at heart.”52 Rosset never experiences the re-
volt against existence, however, the feeling that the Romanian-French


340  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
philosopher Emil Cioran traces back to “the inconvenience of being
born.”53 Contrary to Cioran’s extreme dissatisfaction, the experience of
the real itself motivates the joy of life since “for life to have a meaning
it is enough that it be tragic.”54 In a recent interview, Rosset expresses
his belief that “it is possible to marry lucidity—awareness of the fact
that life is absurd, ridiculous—and happiness [allégresse]. Despite every-
thing, happiness is still happiness.”55
From a tragic perspective of life, actions are undertaken not with pur-
pose but haphazardly. Nevertheless, a tragic philosophy has practical
implications—it is at the root of certain disastrous behaviors that follow
uniquely from subscripting to this philosophy.56 The logic of the worst
attempts to explain such outcomes. One of these behaviors is tolerance
as a morality of the worst. Since the philosopher knows that that there is
no ultimate meaning to the world, any tentative description of meaning
is not to be taken entirely seriously and should be left to coexist with
other uncertain propositions about the experience of life. The casual
reformer is one who has not gone through the ordeal of the real. Re-
fusing to accept the cruelty of its unmediated disorder, he has turned
away from it to build another world although this one is all we will ever
have. This tolerance is predicated on deriding all non-tragic endeavors:
“Their oppositions seem petty, byzantine, grotesque. If they knew how
we laugh at their seriousness! … Do they ignore their union, their con-
federation against the tragic?”57
Only the peculiar combination of joy, affirmation and insouciance al-
lows access to that which exists and is thus recommended as an authen-
tic way of life. Tragic philosophy also originates and monopolizes two
aesthetics of the worst, a creative aptitude and a kind of laughter. Since
original creation is impossible because it seeks necessity in hazard, thus
adding hazard to hazard,58 the second form of aesthetics may be more
auspicious. Indeed, the real is no less comical than it is tragic for Rosset,
and the tragic laughter of annihilation plays an important role in the
good life conceived as knowledge and affirmation of the real.
II The Tragic and the Comic
The comic and the tragic are identical for Rosset insofar as they describe
the same reality and consider laughter as the adequate response to the
tragic. The comic is ontologically rooted; unless one plays the clown to
indicate the ultimate insignificance of everything, one betrays reality by
being too serious. The tragic approach to reality that animates the comic
differs from the absurd; Rosset differentiates his thought from the lat-
ter’s pessimism in order to make place for the gaiety that the tragic view
of life brings about through either tragedy or comedy.


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  341
A The Tragic
Rosset’s view of the tragic cannot be the object of a separate discussion
because it is the very content of his tragic philosophy. We have seen
that Rosset describes being itself as tragic, by which he means illogical,
amoral and contradictory. As we cannot accept the tension that defines
it, we are tragic in a tragic world: we are lonely, base and mortal, which
means that we are loveless, valueless and lifeless. As the tragic is a mys-
tery which we can only notice, facing its truth is beyond our powers, in-
deed, this is what constitutes our contradictory and tragic destiny; tragic
is the sense of allying the necessary with the impossible.
The intimate relationship that the tragic shares with joy has been out-
lined above, as only the joy of life enables us to withstand the tragic.
However, the source of this joy, which is not caused by identifiable rea-
sons, is akin to grace; it is a gift whose origin we do not know. As the
description of the Rossetian good life is entirely about the tragic, there
is no need to further elaborate on it except to explain its profound sim-
ilarity with laughter.
The essence of laughter is tragic, according to Rosset, for laughter is
joy, or enthusiasm, in response to the tragic purely affirmed. Laughter
expresses an enthusiastic consent to, and a satisfaction with the tragic.
Laughter is enamored with that which it laughs at, including the tragic.
Rosset repeats Deleuze’s example of the relationship between the
tragic and laughter: Kafka was laughing when reading aloud his manu-
scripts to his friends.59 Thus, comedy cannot exclude despair or cruelty:
Probably no sound thought is possible—and likewise, no artistic
work, irrespective of genre, even comedy or opéra bouffe—outside
the register of the pitiless or the desperate…Anything that aims at
reducing the cruelty of truth, at diminishing the harshness of the
real suffers the inevitable consequence of discrediting the most bril-
liant of endeavors or the worthiest of causes—the proof of this can
be found, for example, in Charlie Chaplin’s movies.
(CP 1993a, 70)
Tragic communion is similar in comedy or in tragedy, for in both, the
veil is torn and the inessential abolished. The tragic and the comic agree
on the fundamental lack of human freedom, both shedding light on
necessity. The essence of the tragic is always automatism, whether it
is perceived as “comic” or “tragic.” A joyous consent to automatism,
a collective enthusiasm, even in solitude, for the intoxicating idea that
freedom and its dullness are only illusions is present both in comedy and
in tragedy. These are two aspects of the same situation, the sublime and
the happy.


342  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
The god’s imposition of the tragic situates the human being in the sub-
lime, while his generous consent to this inevitable situation endows his
laughter with meaning and abundance.60 These are two aspects, rather
than two interpretations, of the same situation, for there is one joy, pow-
erful, irresistible and tragic. Whether we laugh or tremble, we are de-
livered from the nightmare that a free finality represents. We are now
joyous, grave and light at the same time; much more than free, we are
liberated from freedom in order to fight against necessity, our adversary.
The tragic may be our enemy, but we are an even greater enemy of the
tragic. This enmity reveals our fathomless power and opens up infinite
horizons. This is why we are grave in the midst of laughter:
Any burst of laughter implies: that I accept and note the tragic, with
its three main characteristics of irreconcilability, irresponsibility,
and indispensability…I discover my finality, my true path; my very
laughter is the proof of my victory and my power over this tragic
with which I measure myself. Because at last I laugh at the specter
of the absurd, tragic automatism and necessity. Doesn’t the fact that
this anti-human absurd makes me laugh signify the affirmation of
my own finality: I am capable of laughing at and of appreciating in
the sublime the conclusive and definitive spectacle of the horror of
the absurd. I am at least as strong as this destiny which overwhelms
and enthuses me at the same time… Hence my joy, my confidence in
my strength, in my value, my raison d’être.
(Rosset 1991, 63–64; my translation)
Rosset sees the comic and the tragic as complementary because the con-
flict or coexistence of rigidity and liberty, of death and life, partakes of
both comedy and tragedy. For example, the tragic essence of passion re-
sults from encrusting a rigid and automatic principle on a free and living
being—as if it were death which seizes life yet without killing it. Bergson
used the same sense of encrusting to define the comic in Laughter: An
Essay on the Meaning of the Comic: something mechanical encrusted
on the living.61 Thus, the stereotyped attitude of a passion leads some-
times to laughter, sometimes to tragedy.
Both the comic and tragic rely on two complementary aspects of the
same human reality in the intuition of necessity. This perpetual oscilla-
tion between the comic and the tragic seems to conform to rather myste-
rious laws, if it follows laws at all. It is difficult to detect what is it that
orients our sentiments toward laughter rather than toward the tragic.
This affinity between the comic and the tragic shows that the intuition
of the given is generally as risible as it is tragic, and that consequently,
the spirit of seriousness that rebels against this intuition is always as
frivolous regarding its tragic reality as it is stuffed regarding its relentless
risible facet.


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  343
Thus, the oscillation between tragedy and comedy at the heart of exis-
tence explains the persisting ambivalence of the moral person: incapable
of embracing existence given the comic and tragic evidence of the human
condition, the moral person seems to be at the same time ridiculously
serious and ridiculously frivolous.62 All moral attempts, without excep-
tion, share the common motivation to restore a bit of seriousness in a life
that is tragic, or fundamentally lacking in gravity and significance. The
common specter which horrifies the moralists is the clown (guignol),63
which expresses the gratuity of being as being. For Rosset, what is at
stake in philosophy is accepting the clown that we are, and embodying
the clown as the one who probes the anguish and desperation of living.
The rest is hypocrisy, as is any belief in the significance of anything
whatsoever:
One has to choose between the clown, which is tragic, and divertisse-
ment that masks itself as earnestness. There is no other alternative;
for there is only one genuine earnestness, which is the clown, and
only one profound frivolity, which is the spirit of seriousness…“The
human being is neither an angel nor a brute, and the unfortunate
thing is that he who would act the angel acts the brute.”64 Who-
ever wants to be earnest is a clown…He who plays the clown like
Céline has more chances of disclosing himself as a tragic and prolific
thinker, instead of he, who, like Sartre, ascending to the chair to
debate important affairs is promised right from the start the destiny
of a bad buffoon (bateleur).
(Rosset 1964, 144–5; my translation)
The purpose of morality is to shelter us from the real; it is a divertisse-
ment in the Pascalian sense: getting busy in order to deviate one’s gaze
from suffering and death, from the hazardous and derisory in life. It
boils down to an inversion of earnestness and frivolity: taking care of
life in the face of its tragically gratuitous, derisory and foolish aspects
is not earnest enough for the moralist. For tragic philosophy, morality
along with optimistic humanism are deemed hallucinations from which
philosophers suffer, which should be denounced as a sham.
The relationship that tragic philosophy and a philosophy of the absurd
entertain with the comic differs. The two philosophies should not to be
confused as the absurd need not have a relation to the tragic. Rosset
substantiates this claim with Arthur Schopenhauer, whose thought he
sees as the philosophy of the absurd par excellence.65 The human being’s
double bind—as an individual unwillingly chained to the sole interests
of the species, who unknowingly participates through the illusion of a
free finality in an immovable absence of finality—dooms him to a tragi-
comic situation. The absolute absurd, as Schopenhauer describes it, par-
ticipates more in the risible than in the tragic. The human condition is


344  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
more akin to a tragi-comedy than a tragedy, as Schopenhauer always
keeps in mind the comical aspect of life while cursing it. In the midst
of determinism, human beings consider themselves free, active and liv-
ing, while they are passive and dead. To use Bergson’s language, the
individual appears in Schopenhauer’s philosophy as a finality encrusted
on an absence of ends. This is his destiny, which is absurd at the same
time that it is ridiculous.66 Due to the comicality of repetition, tragedy
when repeated becomes a tragi-comedy. While this is necessarily the way
the human condition is portrayed in Schopenhauer’s philosophy, it also
frames Rosset’s own view of life.67
B The Comic
Rosset uses “the comic” to refer to that which makes us laugh. He en-
dorses Bergson’s definition of the comic but inverses it, privileging the
living placated on the mechanical rather than the opposite. Rosset’s
application of the definition exceeds Bergson’s use, because he argues
that before becoming comical through misinterpretations, everything is
comical and rejoicing in nature first and foremost, simply by virtue of
existing. The right attitude toward life is to be a clown which expresses
the gratuity of being as being.
The main term of the comic is invariably laughter for Rosset. The
experience of laughter and the rather enigmatic pleasure it occasions is
common but resistant to analysis. Theories of laughter usually connect
the real with its representation and rightly so. Laughter introduces the
space of a contrast in favor of which the real confounds the idea we had
of it (or that we maliciously proposed). This is the classical definition of
the comic, which is accepted notwithstanding notable variants by phi-
losophers like Kant, G. W. F. Hegel, Schopenhauer, and psychologists
like Sigmund Freud. Hence, for example, Schopenhauer’s formulation:
The origin of the ludicrous is always in the paradoxical, and thus
unexpected, subsumption of an object under a concept which is
in other respects heterogeneous. Accordingly, the phenomenon of
laughter always signifies the sudden apprehension of an incongruity
between such a concept and the real object thought through it, and
hence between what is abstract and what is perceptive.
(Schopenhauer 1966, vol. II, chapter 8, 91)
This definition remains valid even for Bergson, notwithstanding the in-
novations he brought to the understanding of the comic. The rupture
between the living and the mechanical which grounds the theory of
Laughter can also be considered a way the real has (as living) to make
itself known to human beings, by contradicting all representation (as
far as the latter necessarily implies a beginning of “mechanization” in
relation to life).


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  345
Rosset considers that the various philosophers’ theories of laughter
are accurate and profound. He sees them as perfectly accounting for
both the occasional absurdity in the representation of the real and the
pleasure that the comic affords. It is a pleasure we take in perceiving
the real, as delineated back-stage and furtively appearing through the
downfall of that which pretends to represent it. It is a profound rejoicing,
which is a distant relative of the joy that is sometimes born out of the
simple sentiment of existing, but whose principle nevertheless remains
mysterious (since it implies a congruity with the real which is not ob-
vious, as repeatedly noted in the philosophy of Schopenhauer). Though
these theories rightly insist on possible discrepancies between the real
and its representation, they do not address the status of the real itself as
perceived in the comic operation. It is as if the comical essence exhausted
itself when confronted with the relationship between the real and its
representation, unable to affect the terms of this relationship, that is,
the real itself (or its representation). In other words, according to these
theories, the real can never be “funny” in itself.
Most theories of laughter identify the laughable as expressing the gap
between reality and representation. Representations may appear absurd,
but the real itself when perceived without its representations, without
meaning, Grund or “principle of reason” is disclosed as absurd. Ac-
cording to the principle of sufficient reason, everything that exists has a
cause, with no exception. If this principle is renounced as Rosset’s phi-
losophy requires, the assimilation of the real and the singular strips real-
ity of any external foundation. It follows that all reality is “singular” in
the two senses of the word (single and remarkable) and that all that ex-
ists is foolish. Thus, the comic has its origin in a universal and profound
ontological source. Before becoming comical through its misrepresen-
tations, everything is comical; therefore, everything rejoices primarily
and merely because it exists. The nature of this comical effect, which
is a particular form of the real’s upshot, is rather obscure because the
emotions elicited by the real are as incomprehensible as they are intense.
But the obscurity of laughter indicates a profundity, arguably the
greatest profundity of the comical, which is to approach the singularity
of the real—its defining mystery. Implicit in all the theories of the com-
ical is this mysterious presence of the real along with the emotion it cre-
ates, often against the will of the person which it addresses in the most
discrete way possible, as it offers itself as inconsequentially laughable.
Finally, the only criticism of classical theories of the comic that one
can offer is that they are too clear and overly analytical. Such clarity
masks the realization that an obscure and fundamental element, the con-
tact with the real, remains unknown; however, without it, the comical
effect has no efficiency nor raison d’être.68 As Rosset explains:
It is the fate of all reality to exist…necessarily and by itself some-
what bizarre and crazy (loufoque)…it is the fate of any object to


346  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
find itself doted, by the simple fact that it exists, of a certain com-
ical (cocasse) virtue, in the sense of the French dictionary Robert:
“which is of a buffoon strangeness, which astonishes and makes us
laugh”….existence is…strange (insolite) by nature…the only thing
in the world that one cannot get used to.
(Rosset 1991, 54, 59; my translation)
Rosset therefore subscribes to the view, shared by few philosophers, that
existence is comical. This assertion is reinforced by the following argu-
ment: when something is necessary and not necessary at the same time,
it is sometimes laughable and most of the time irritating. But this is true
of any reality, since everything is a coincidence of necessity and hazard.
In most of the cases, if this does not make us laugh or irritate us it is
because we do not perceive it as we bury it under meaning:
All reality is necessarily some or other, or indifferent and plain
(quelconque), at the same time determined and fortuitous, hence
insignificant. Except the fact of reality itself, which is the enigma
par excellence, that is, the contrary of some or other (quelconque).
(Rosset 1977, 40; my translation)
By bestowing meaning on the real, we lend it an imaginary value, since
hazard suffices to explain everything. No worldly object is exempt from
being revealed as laughable and unworthy of attention under a lucid ex-
amination from the point of view of its fragile constitution, of its simul-
taneously ephemeral and miniscule position in infinite time and space.69
The comic has an ontological foundation for Rosset. Applying Berg-
son’s view of the comic to his own view of the human condition, Rosset
concludes that automatism is at the root of both the tragic and the comic.
Existence oscillates between the comic and the tragic, as the conditions
and circumstances that it is grounded upon are generally as ridiculous as
they are tragic. Thus, the clown, which represents the gratuity of being,
is the most serious subject, while the earnest man who denies this fact is
the most ridiculous. Becoming the clown is the right thing to do in order
to resist the mirage of significance. Lucidity, as the awareness of life’s
ridiculousness and absurdity, partners with joy.70
The resulting evaluation is that Rosset’s tragic philosophy is a tragi-
comedy as much as Schopenhauer’s philosophy is, notwithstanding
their differences as philosophies of the tragic (Rosset) and of the absurd
(Schopenhauer).
III Laughter
Following Bergson, Rosset does not differentiate between his investi-
gation into the comical and into laughter. The discussion of that which


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  347
makes us laugh, or the comical, continues in Rosset’s analysis of laugh-
ter, as the main term of the comic is invariably “laughter” for Rosset.
Laughter is a quotidian experience for human beings, no less than
death and desire; however, “nothing testifies better to the fragility of
the naturalist design which serves as a backdrop to everyday represen-
tation.”71 Thus, one of the behaviors that tragic philosophy both causes
and monopolizes is a certain way of laughing. Its aesthetics of the worst
yields a kind of laughter that delights in destruction, which Rosset chris-
tens the laughter of annihilation.
Joy is caused by the destruction of the real’s double and the percep-
tion of the real’s existence as itself comical. This realization has escaped
theorists of laughter: concerned with the relation of the real to its repre-
sentation, they have failed to engage with the ontology of the comic, its
grounding in reality that laughter reveals.
Tragic laughter signifies that hazard is appreciated, and that its oc-
currence is celebrated by laughter. Sense, significations and counter-
significations which are used by other forms of laughter are entirely alien
to it. Its indifference to nonsense is the defining characteristic that sets it
apart from other forms of laughter. Every time we laugh,
a little spot of necessity gives way to this corrosive which has no
cure, which complacently reveals the presence of hazard and the
unusual under all the disguises which it touches. There is no produc-
tion, whatever its appearance of necessity, which does not dissolve
instantaneously through the effect of laughter that lets nothing re-
main but the arbitrary.
(Rosset 1995b [1973], 86–7; my translation)
Rosset further explains that laughter directly attacks the underlying
framework, the skeleton of what it dislocates, thus leaving intact the
elements while dissolving the principle of their assembling. Therefore,
After the passage of laughter reality remains, but in a stripped con-
dition: it lacks the ensemble of the articulations that would have
made it seem necessary. As a perpetual advent of the artifice on the
background of nature, laughter assimilates the necessary to hazard
in comical instances where order loses itself in disorder, exactly as,
according to Bergson’s analysis, the autonomous loses itself in the
automatic, and life in death.
(Rosset 1995b [1973], 87; my translation)
From the point of view of tragic thought, the formula that the l aughter of
annihilation follows is the inversion of Bergson’s definition of the comi-
cal. Recall, Bergson defined the laughter that arises from the  comical as
a reaction to something living encrusted on the mechanical. In Rosset’s


348  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
terms, laughter means that finality is superimposed on hazard, which,
due to a coincidence made possible by laughter, volatizes at its contact.
Laughing at annihilation signifies, therefore, the victory of underlying
chaos over the appearance of order, the recognition of hazard as the
“truth” of “that which exists.”
As laughter is associated with death and with the anxiety it creates in
life, laughter’s destructiveness is best expressed through humor rather
than irony. Rosset argues that the pessimism of humor and the reach of
its attack as an ephemeral form of laughter, which destroys sense with
neither a rational nor moral reason, are more destructive than the moral
optimism of prolonged laughter (irony).
It is the derisory, the laughable or ridiculous, which is disclosed in
insignificance that is pregnant with consequences for philosophy. First,
it establishes de Cusa’s “learned ignorance” instead of Socrates’s “Know
Thyself”; second, it discloses happiness as the sole criterion of value in
anything human. Laughter, along with additional artistic creations,
should be evaluated in relation to the happiness it grants; but laughter
has an additional value which other creations lack: in destroying mean-
ing it gets an intrinsic value.
Laughter, however, is not happiness. It is joy, and as all joy it partakes
in the joy of living. Laughter as knowledge and affirmation of the real
falls short of the joy of living, which is a gift akin to grace; nor is laugh-
ter a means to it. Rather than assigning absurdity or nonsense to the de-
naturalized world, laughter helps us get its insignificance; it thus enables
the dis-apprenticeship of the various “meanings,” an exercise of intrinsic
value for Rosset. Such a procedure is not, nor does Rosset wishes it to
be, an entrance to a transcendent reality, a mystical access to the essence
of being, as de Cusa or Pascal attempted to find; however, as laughter
reveals the doubly derisory aspect of all existence, both insignificant and
provisory in relation to the infinite, it does constitute a philosophical
alternative to negative theology and its main philosophical spokesmen.72
And in so doing, laughter grants us a few moments of happiness, as all
artistic creation does, which in the end is laughter’s sole purpose and
raison d’être.
Rosset uses the expression “a sense of humor” only once. In an inter-
view, he argues that those who do not have a sense of humor lack the
weapon required for the serene and amiable confrontation with reality.
That laughter is the mark of the human being, as the Homo ridens tradi-
tion has emphasized since Aristotle, does not merely mean that laughter
pertains only to humanity. It also means that laughter is necessary to
the human being and only to him, because as far as we know, he is the
only being who knows things that he can bear and process only with the
additional help and distance that laughter provides.73
Individuals without a sense of humor are imperfect creatures in the Ar-
istotelian sense of the word, beings who did not attain to the perfection


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  349
of their form: they may perfect knowledge and expand consciousness;
yet they lack the virtue that enables them to bear the contents that are
revealed. Laughter is the only power that enables a fair fight against the
damages caused by knowing that which is horrible and unbearable in
life. Those who do not have a sense of humor have received the poison
without the antidote. They should be pitied but also feared in as much
as they find the principal remedy to their suffering in the nuisance they
create for their peers, whom they can stand only if contaminated by their
own suffering. This is true both for the domestic tyrant and the Chief of
States who dreams of universal happiness for humanity.74
At the other end, we find the professional comedian, who is question-
able too because he does not challenge the social and moral norms. Con-
trary to the spontaneous humorist, he reinforces the accepted order.75
Rosset does not recommend scorn, although he believes that the path
leading to the love of life passes through a phase of ridiculing and scorn-
ing life. This is done in order to gain a sense of self-esteem and a feeling
of being worthier and stronger than life, which is eventually replaced by
a love of life, however tragic. Through this love, one can accept oneself
as tragic without feeling that one is unordinary. One is redeemed from
one’s solitude in a universe that once seemed incongruous, but now ap-
pears to have been made just for oneself.76 This is accompanied by a
kind of laughter that Rosset deems the laughter of annihilation, best
expressed through humor because it transcends sense and nonsense. As-
sociated with anxiety and death, it falls short of the joy of living. In what
follows, I elaborate on each of its characteristics.
A The Laughter of Annihilation
One of the behaviors that tragic philosophy both causes and monopo-
lizes is a certain way of laughing, a laughter of annihilation that con-
stitutes an aesthetic of the worst.77 In the Titanic disaster, one can find
various tragi-comic circumstances, which do not exhaust the profound
laughter that may burst out at the very mention of disaster. The Titanic
exemplifies a certain way of laughing which properly pertains to the
tragic vision, for, according to the tragic perspective, the very fact of
engulfment possesses a comic virtue.78
Engulfment is annihilation without residue, a disappearing that is not
compensated by any appearance, a pure and simple cessation of being.
In the passage from being to non-being, which no necessary factor mo-
tivates, lies laughter’s proper motivation as related to the tragic perspec-
tive. Laughter is born out of the disappearance of something without
reason, either because the disappearance reveals the strangeness of the
appearance that preceded it, or the hazardous nature of existence. It is
a gratuitous laughter of annihilation. Defeating without justification, it
destroys without inscribing this destruction in an explanatory, finalistic


350  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
or compensatory perspective. It laughs without saying why it laughs or
what it laughs at. If we would insist in interrogating it, it would have to
say that contrary to common occasions of laughter, it laughs at nothing79:
It is a laughter that may appear paradoxical and devoid of any true
comical efficacy, for it dissolves without affecting that which is dis-
solved with a coefficient of risibility or of ridicule that would justify
the dissolution.
(Rosset 1993b, 173)
Rosset differentiates between irony and humor along the lines estab-
lished by his former teacher, Bergson’s student, Jankélévitch, and follows
him in preferring humor over irony.
B Humor and Irony
Rosset distinguishes between two sorts of destructive laughter, an
ephemeral and fleeting laughter (“rire court”) or “humor,” which is pes-
simistic, tragic and outrageous, and a prolonged laughter (“rire long”)
or “irony,” which is optimistic, ethical and honest. The comic effect that
extends to the implicit consequences of laughter does not exhaust the
efficacy of prolonged laughter. Destruction is compensated by the a con-
trario affirmation of the principles that have contributed to establishing
comic aggression. Not only did we laugh but we were right to laugh: this
reason discloses a stable instance that floats in the shipwreck of what it
has engulfed. Thus, the ironist, for example, may destroy whatever she
pleases, but on the condition that she reveals principles she embodies
and champions in order to proceed with her act. She may make the
grotesque surface in the name of the reasonable, instigate scandal in
the name of the tolerable and endorse nonsense in the name of a certain
sense.
The second form of laughter is a brief, ephemeral laughter that is usu-
ally called humor. When the comic effect passes, reflection cannot jus-
tify the laugh: the mind is left without an insight of the significance and
the impact of the destruction. A brief or quick laughter, therefore, begets
no perspective, takes away yet gives nothing in exchange and appears
often frivolous and inconsequential. It attacks everything indifferently,
without organizing its attacks on systems that assist the recognition of
the themes being attacked, and consequently, of those being defended.
Rosset believes that to his contemporaries, who are more particularly
focused on one target or another, such laughter would appear to aim at
nothing.
Rosset follows the characterization of humor and irony given by
Jankélévitch in L’Ironie ou la bonne conscience (“Irony or Good Con-
science,” 1964). In finding both irony and humor invested with the same


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  351
destructive function but to a different degree, Rosset’s analysis keeps
intact the unity of the comic, that is, the general nature of the pleasure
gained in laughing.
Timid in his attack, the ironist destroys locally and alludes to a pos-
sible reconstruction. By attacking everything, the humorist appears to
attack nothing at all. The humorist’s pleasure lies in the total devastation
that humor brings. It takes time to appreciate its corrosive efficacy; yet
this brief laughter has long-term consequences both from a chronologi-
cal and from a philosophical point of view. From a chronological point
of view, humor doesn’t require references to values or truths that vanish
with time; and from a philosophical point of view, humor constitutes a
more violent aggression toward sense than any prolonged laughter, re-
fusing any interpretation of destruction, that is, any reinvestment in less
exposed territories of destroyed meanings. Indeed, humor or ephemeral
laughter does not believe in the existence of safe territories in which
sense can be located. Thus, it engulfs sense immediately and once and
for all, just as the waves of the Atlantic engulfed the Titanic. There is
nothing to be said afterward, and laughter naturally comes to an end.
C Sense and Nonsense
Tragic laughter, which manifests a destructive pleasure that is indif-
ferent to all that is destroyed, is made possible through the notion of
hazard. Tragic laughter indicates that one takes pleasure in hazard and
celebrates its appearance through laughter. It is therefore completely
foreign to the idea of sense, of significations and counter-significations
which are being played in other forms of laughter. It is also indifferent to
nonsense, and in this it differs from all other laughters.
The majority of philosophers describe laughter as an effect of the
 contrast between sense and its contrarieties. All of Deleuze’s laughters
partake of this weakness, according to Rosset, for instance, the Stoic
 humor that Deleuze assimilates into the English humor of nonsense
(Chrysippus’s chariot and Lewis Carroll’s dining table), as well as the
humor of the Cynics and of Zen.80 Foucault’s laughter in The Order
of Things in relation to Borges’s unthinkable catalogue shares the same
fate.81 The great weakness of the humor of the Stoic, the Cynic, and the
nonsense and Zen kinds, as eulogized by Deleuze in Logic of Sense, is
that it is conditioned on a requirement of order that is seen both as evi-
dent and necessary.
However, such a view of laughter is incapable of attaining to the
notion of hazard. If disorder is taken to be the contrary of order, this
view confesses that it does and will always ignore the notions of haz-
ard and chaos. Moreover, laughing at the contrarieties of sense does
not signify the ruin of sense, but rather its affirmation in extremis and
a contrario. Many examples of Anglo-Saxon nonsense—a model of


352  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
moral respectability—merely celebrate implicitly an established order
through the very fact that its contrary, nonsense, is reputed as hilarious
and unthinkable.
Although foreign to the games of sense and nonsense, the laughter of
annihilation as conceived and practiced by tragic thought conforms to
the scheme of the comic that Bergson proposed in Laughter, something
mechanical encrusted upon the living.82 A tragic perspective accepts the
truth of this Bergsonian schema only on the condition of inversing its
terms. The “living” that Bergson refers to indeed implies teleological
assumptions (a biological finalism) that the comic has the effect to elimi-
nate. From the point of view of tragic thought, the formula of the laugh-
ter of annihilation is something living encrusted on the mechanical, or
finality superimposed on hazard. Laughter makes this finality disappear.
Thus, the laughter of annihilation signifies the triumph of the chaotic
on the seemingly ordered, the acknowledgment of hazard as the truth of
existence. This acknowledgment is also an affirmation, since laughter
is accompanied by pleasure, which necessarily signifies acceptance as
Freud has shown in Jokes and Their Relations with the Unconscious.83
We laugh when that which was pretending to double the real disap-
pears. Nothing rejoices us more than the collapse of that which assumes
gravity and importance. This explains the intensity of laughter that the
theater, the movies and the comics elicit. Sense burdens us daily. The
burlesque of life, which the arts know how to represent, somewhat re-
lieves us: it is “a holiday from sense, or simply a holiday.”84
The emergences of the “natural” on the background of the “artifice”
are frequently evoked as explanations of the comical. If the real in its
entirety is reputed as artificial, however, and the idea of nature is con-
sidered a mask whose role is to dissimulate this reality, the terms of the
problem are inversed: it is rather the emergences of the artificial over the
natural which seem to indicate the victory of the real over the fictive and
the failure of the disguise of artifice in nature. Yet this failure of the nat-
uralist imagery is a typical experience, even more significant because it
intervenes often in the course of circumstances that naturalism precisely
considers the most “natural”: in desire, death and laughter, in all experi-
ences in which the naturalist scenery suddenly (and temporarily) cracks.
Undoubtedly, these momentary total collapses of naturalism do not
mark the emergence of truth over illusion or the authentic on the fabri-
cated. They signal only the passing elimination of an imagery, to which
no imagery substitutes itself in those decisive instants. The emergences
of the artifice dissipate the naturalist illusion without proposing a spare
truth. The real which they signal is too talkative to integrate itself in a
new intellectual interpretation: “The mask falls, reality remains,” says
Lucretius.85 Only the thing (res) remains, which is no more accompanied
in these critical instances of a signification which enables to refer to it as
truth or error.86


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  353
Rosset maintains that Bergson’s views of laughter are valid whether
his philosophy is true or not, and especially if it is not. In a text on vis
comica appended to Le Choix des mots, suivi de La Joie et son para-
doxe, Rosset sums up his ideas on the comic power: it is a force that
attacks and destroys, which is incapable of pitying that which it crushes
because of the momentary anesthesia of the heart Bergson alludes to at
the beginning of Laughter.87 The comic reveals the clownish nature of
all certitude, of all sentiment of the infallible.
Tragic laughter celebrates hazard, and has no relation to sense or non-
sense. From the point of view of tragic thought, the formula of the laugh-
ter of annihilation is the inversion of Bergson’s. It is something living
encrusted on the mechanical or finality superimposed on hazard. This
finality is destroyed by laughter because hazard or the mechanism of life
is disclosed.
D Death and Anxiety
Laughter as an instance that affirms the real should be distinguished
from affirmation itself. The former is only a clue of the latter. Laughter
offers to testify to the possibility of such an affirmation—since hazard
here is the source of laughter, hence of pleasure, but not of affirmation.
Indeed, an incommensurable distance separates affirmative laughter
from affirmation itself:
In a Plotinian perspective, the laughter of annihilation is only the
hypostasis of affirmation, which derives its existence from affirma-
tion, but is not identical with it.
(Rosset 1979, 37; my translation)
Rather than laughter at death, affirmation is celebration in front of
death. Tragic philosophy did not begin when human beings learned
how to laugh at their cadavers, but rather on that mysterious day, as
Nietzsche recognizes in the Birth of Tragedy, when the Greeks con-
founded in one celebration the cult of the dead, from which tragedy
was born, and the cult of the god symbolizing wine and drunken-
ness: the Great Dionysia, which celebrates the games of life, death and
hazard.
I repeatedly mentioned Bergson’s formula that laughter occurs when
something mechanical is encrusted upon the living. This condition is
never so well nor so totally realized as in death, Rosset maintains. By
transforming the living body into a cadaver, death “brings to a hun-
dred percent coefficient of inertia that which, during life, hovers around
a more modest percentage.” The moment of death, which submits the
totality of the body to the laws of mechanics, and, to repeat Bergson’s
terms, makes of the human being a pure “thing,” is therefore necessarily


354  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
the comical moment par excellence. And it is so, in effect, if one ab-
stracts the sentiment of desolation, which almost always mingles with
the pure receptivity of the phenomenon. More precisely, in accordance
with the Bergsonian principle, death is eminently comical if one persists
in the attempt to match the living and the mechanical. That is, if one
decides to treat the dead body as a living thing affected by a considerable
coefficient of inertia, taking for granted the material identity of a living
being and its corpse.88
Rosset adds another argument in view of the conclusion that death
is funny. He differentiates between the natural and the artificial; the
natural embodies the ensemble of non-existing laws, while the artificial
indicates an ensemble of existing facts. Applying these definitions to
death, Rosset argues that there is nothing more artificial than death.
This is established by the following syllogism: death is a fact; given
the designations of the natural and the artificial, death pertains not
to nature, but to artifice.89 This is so because the order of nature is
rebellious to any factual concretization. Nature’s order is impervious to
artifice; it is perfect in itself, at the condition of remaining an idea (or
rather a pseudo- idea). If it pretends to double the facts and to take its
foot in the real, it is immediately rejected as inadmissible and ludicrous.
Precisely, the factual character makes it inadmissible: death is a fact
which transgresses all rights and which ignores all the desiderata of the
persons interested in this very fact. Death is buffoon in its pretention to
disguise itself in a rule: as if it could invoke some necessity in the name
of which it could deprive the living from a permanent duration. In this
sense, nothing is as funny as death. It is the irruption of the factual
in the rule, the unexpected in the order, symbolizing thus a victory of
opacity on spirituality in which Bergson recognized one of the principal
competences of the comic.90
The obscurity of laughter is the clue of the greatest profundity of the
comic: to approach the singularity of the real, that is, its proper mys-
tery. Like laughter, anxiety which is sometimes accompanied by a panic
reaction defies analysis.91 The terrifying object is identical to the laugh-
able. In laughter, the real is comical and rejoicing, while in anxiety, it is
dramatic, an undesirable effect of the real. What terrifies is the real, not
only as singular, but also as when it is terrifying through its very singu-
larity, when it is perceived as a threat without appeal.92
E The Derisory
Folly or foolishness characterizes existence itself, but also human rea-
son. This gives the derisory a special status in Rosset’s philosophy:
The human being defines itself by reason, but reason is mad or fool-
ish: while it can measure, it cannot “commensurate” (“mesurer sans


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  355
‘commensurer’”), that is, evaluate in relation to the infinitely small
and the infinitely big. When one realizes this paradox, insignificance
becomes not only intrinsic (due to hazard) but also extrinsic. Thus,
