everything is doubly derisory, first in itself because it is just circum-
stance (hazard), but also because it is devoid of any conceivable
evaluation due to its incommensurability with the indefinite sum of
circumstances.
(Rosset 1995b [1973], 76; my translation)
The access to the double derisory aspect of everything yields two con-
sequences. First, a learned ignorance of the kind that de Cusa proposed
replaces the Socratic injunction, “Know Thyself”; and second, happiness
is revealed as the sole object of philosophical interest and knowledge.
First, then, learned ignorance offers an alternative to philosophy. It
opposes the injunction, “Renounce to Know Thyself,” to the Socratic
call for self-knowledge. But this ignorance is learned because it also com-
prehends its ignorance, which somewhat resolves anguish by succeeding
in formulating it; and because it attempts measuring in the incommen-
surable by welcoming its insignificant powers, a partial and provisory
knowledge, which the Sophists endorsed in contradiction to the cer-
tainty of Platonic knowledge. As it is psychologically harder to give up
most things than to give up everything, more economical to renounce
everything than almost everything, Plato denigrated this insignificant
knowledge and renounced all possible knowledges to adhere to the only
true one. 93
The other consequence of this approach is that happiness is disclosed
as the only object of philosophical knowledge and interest, as it is the
only “value” that eludes insignificance because it denotes the ensemble
of events that are indifferent to measurement and evaluation. Only hap-
piness, insofar as it manifests the recognition of satisfaction which is
independent of all external consideration, is indifferent to the mystery
of its constitution and to its condition in relation to the infinite. This is
why happiness is the only experience that is relatively serious and the
sole that is relatively noble. Serious because it does not lie outside of the
register of insignificance, noble because it is the only experience which
necessarily implies the assumption of hazard and finitude. Contrary to
what Pascal believed, the entire dignity of the human being consists not
in his thought, but in his capacity for happiness.94
Happiness is disclosed as a criterion of choice, not because it enables
to evaluate but because it is the sole experience that needs no evaluation.
This is why a philosophy that focuses on insignificance should pay atten-
tion in all human creations only to the coefficient of happiness toward
which the work of art gestures through its precarity. Aesthetic creation
need not protect us from the passing and the frivolous, but should only
testify to a few moments of happiness.95 And, among human creations,


356  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
laughter provides us abundantly with such moments; it should be evalu-
ated accordingly.
F Laughter and Joy
Joy is a knowledge of the real, but there are a number of acquaintances
with the real that are very different from the experience of joy. These
are the experiences of boredom, drunkenness and fear, as described by
Schopenhauer, Charles Baudelaire and Roland Barthes, respectively, and
of laughter as described by Rosset.96
Contrary to fear, which is a forced and panicked recognition of the
real without any jubilation, laughter is an immediate and forced recog-
nition of the real, but without panic or sadness, even if, properly speak-
ing, laughter is not the same as jubilation. In contradistinction to fear,
the trial of the comic is marked principally by an intense and specific
pleasure. It is the pleasure of seeing the imaginary disappear, that is,
anything that exists only in representation or convention, which enables
to confront the real wherein the comic effect culminates. Laughter thus
takes pleasure in the somewhat public and official elimination of that
which does not exist anyway.
To assess laughter’s value, we should specify its attitude toward the
real. However, it is difficult to determine which is more enjoyable in
laughter, the triumph of the real or the defeat of the unreal:
Laughter is indeed a way of affirming the real, though it is associ-
ated with the particular case in which the real contradicts immod-
erate manifestations of the unreal. The fact that the condemnation
of the real in the comic experience is accompanied by pleasure is
certainly an important point in favor of the real, but not a decisive
one. Applauding the elimination of the unreal is different from con-
gratulating its replacement by the real.
(Rosset 1979, 103–4; my translation)
It seems, therefore, that joy is not only a knowledge of the real, but also
an implied affirmation of that which this knowledge discloses. Joy is a
loving knowledge that is more affirming of the real than the comic’s mere
recognition of the real. The comic is satisfied with disclosing the real and
with finding in the gap between reality and representation a reason for
rejoicing. Joy appears to proceed not so much from the eruption of true
existence, however, but rather from the vanishing of the appearances
displaced by true existence. The comic takes its leave from that which
is not and does so with pleasure. Although it implies an a priori favor-
able disposition toward that which exists, this pleasure does not warrant
by itself an unreserved attachment to the real that replaced the dissi-
pated representation. Abandoning the false does not necessarily imply


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  357
endorsing the true. Indeed, the comic effect consists essentially in dam-
aging the erroneous; rather than disclosing the real, the comic discloses
all that the real is not. This explains why one feels “lighter but necessar-
ily also hungry, more relieved than seduced,” after a burst of laughter.97
Still, the pleasure that the comic takes in dissipating the non-real in-
dicates a strong attachment to the real. With good reason one finds in
humor and in the comic in general, as one usually does, the mark of con-
tentment with, and affirmation of, the real. But this comic affirmation
is merely a benevolent disposition in principle, which implies no formal
engagement with that which actually exists, when the real is perceived
more precisely:
Both the comical and joy intend to protect the real, to make it their
unique favorite: but the former functions as if it were the beginning
of a friendship, the latter as if it were a confirmed love.
(Rosset 1979, 103–4; my translation)
To conclude, laughter is necessary to the human being and only to the
human being, because as far as we know, he is the only creature who
knows things that he can tolerate and process only with the extra help
and distancing that laughter provides. Laughter is tragic; it is a celebra-
tion in the face of death, because the real produces either anxiety or
laughter. Death is funny; it answers directly to Bergson’s definition of
the comical, the mechanical encrusted upon the living. Tragic philoso-
phy originates and monopolizes a certain way of laughing, the laughter
of annihilation, which exemplifies that the very fact of engulfment pos-
sesses a comic virtue.
The notions of humor and irony as defined by Jankélévitch help Rosset
decide that humor or brief laughter is more efficacious as the laughter
of annihilation than is irony or prolonged laughter. Laughter is one of
the knowledges of the real. Although laughter is joy, it differs from the
graced joy of life in that the latter is also an affirmation of what it re-
veals. Laughter as an approving instance of the real is merely the sign
of affirmation. Since affirmation is the main epistemological tool which
enables a full encounter with the real, joy is more significant as an epis-
temological tool than laughter. Because joy is a graced state, it is an
intervention that is beyond our power. Thus, laughter has no active role
to play in the advent of graced joy.98
IV Concluding Remarks
Rosset maintains that a sense of humor is essential for one’s survival,
that the comic is ontologically grounded and that laughter fulfills an
epistemological role in the good life because laughter is one way of
knowing the real. However, laughter falls short of joy. As the good life


358  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
is affirmation and only affirmation enables knowing reality, the good
life cannot be attained without joy. Yet the joy of life that enables af-
firming and knowing reality is beyond our power. It is a mysterious phe-
nomenon, akin to the Pascalian Godly grace. Laughter is not a means
to the graced joy that Rosset presents as the necessary condition for
embracing life. The laughter of annihilation, however, which Rosset’s
tragic philosophy defines and whose role is best fulfilled by humor,
delights in the disappearance of all that is unreal. By fighting actively
against illusions, one can prepare the ground for the advent of the joy
of life, or alternatively, one can enjoy the more limited cheerfulness that
humor affords us.
Like Kierkegaard and Deleuze and maybe because of Jankélévitch,
whose views will be introduced in this study’s Concluding Remarks,
Rosset chooses humor over irony. I do not elaborate on this aspect of his
thought here as I have discussed at length the status of irony in relation
to humor in philosophy (when concluding Deleuze’s views in Chapter 2),
and I address this topic again in the Concluding Remarks of this study.
We will see that irony is rejected by additional French philosophers, by
non-Nietzscheans but also by postmodern philosophers, such as Der-
rida. This fact first challenges the ascription of irony to postmodernism
but also further enables to conduct a thorough criticism of irony.
I do not address the irony-humor controversy here for another reason:
the study of the role of laughter in the good life as defined by Rosset has
revealed various challenging views whose assessment is more pressing.
These views include the ontology of the comic, the laughter of annihi-
lation, the earnestness of the clown and the priority of joy. In assess-
ing these views, I introduce additional philosophers that are relevant
to Rosset’s thought: to assess Rosset’s claim about the ontology of the
comic, I introduce the views held by Hegel, Søren Kierkegaard and the
Spanish- American philosopher, George Santayana (1863–1952); to ap-
praise Rosset’s views of the laughter of annihilation and the earnestness
of the clown, I recall their differences from Bataille’s; finally, to evaluate
his recommendations to play the clown and to be joyful, given that the
latter state cannot be attained by one’s powers, I briefly introduce a the-
sis which I defend elsewhere at length,99 Homo risibilis or the ridiculous
human being.
A The Ontology of the Comic
The view that the comic is ontologically rooted is intimated by Hegel
and Kierkegaard and endorsed by Santayana. I begin with the latter’s
view as it is similar to Rosset’s significant assertion that the comic is
valuable because the very existence of all things is comical.100 Indeed,
Santayana sees all existence as comical; however, he sees existence itself
as merely one aspect of reality. “Everything in nature” is “comic in its


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  359
existence,” he maintains, but also “lyrical in its ideal essence, tragic in
its fate.”101 He emphasizes that the tragic is also “a true aspect of exis-
tence in one relation and on a certain view an important feature of life,”
which is not to be denied or explained away, “as is sometimes attempted
in cowardly and mincing philosophies.” The tragic is “this aspect of
vanity and self-annihilation, which existence wears when we consider
its destiny”; and it is significant because “we cannot take a long view
without finding life sad, and all things tragic.”102
The comic is the truest expression of the inherently anarchic reality
of existence,
a conjunction of things mutually irrelevant, a chapter of accidents,
a medley improvised here and now for no reason, to the exclusion
of myriad other forces which, so far as their ideal structure is con-
cerned, might have been performed just well.103
“All reality is comic,” he says, “and especially a phase of it where illu-
sion, jollity, conceit, mishap, and chagrin follow one another in such
quick alternation.”104 Existence itself fails to fit within a fully rational
conception of the world; it is “radically comic,” he says, “because this
world is contingency and absurdity incarnate” and “to be irrational and
unintelligible is the character proper to existence.” Existence should be
met on its own terms; according to Santayana, the adequate response
is one that involves joy and amusement. In being “something joyful,
hearty, and merry,” we should find “all things vivid and comic.”105
In contradistinction to Santayana, Rosset does not qualify existence
as absurd; he rather emphasizes the opposition between a tragic philos-
ophy and an absurd one. Nor can Rosset counsel us to be amused or
joyful in encountering reality, as joy is outside of our control. However,
joy plays an epistemological role in Rosset’s philosophy, which it does
not play in Santayana’s: it is the pre-condition of all knowledge of reality
for the former, while the latter’s epistemology allows us to know reality
regardless of our state of mind, be it joyous or not.
Antedating Santayana and Rosset, Hegel, later followed by Kierke-
gaard, defines the comical as ontologically based in yet another sense
than both twentieth-century philosophers found. Hegel asserts that the
discrepancy between an assumption and reality, which produces laugh-
ter, is grounded in reality itself. Thus, the comic in all cases displays an
ontological dimension because it tells us something about the being of
its object and, in a sense, about being itself. This follows from Hegel’s
conception of dialectics, according to which the truth is never affixed,
but is rather articulated and realized in contradictory ways. The comic
is precisely an awareness of this contradiction.106
Kierkegaard too ties the comic to contradictions or incongruities that
are objective because they are constitutive of the human self. These


360  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
incongruities are to be found when we juxtapose the finite and the in-
finite, singularity and generality, reality and ideality—in short, the hu-
man being’s bodily time-limited existence and his aspirations toward the
eternal. The discrepancy between reality and ideality calls for either a
tragic interpretation or a comic one. The discrepancy is objective because
it refers to a general human predisposition or ideality, to a framework of
existence that is pre-given in an objective way. The comic or the tragic
are points of view that are generated by considering the discrepancy
from ideality to reality and from reality to ideality, respectively. Due
to the reflexive aspect of the comic, however, the comic contradiction
is “objective,” in the sense that it is discernible to the detached, “self-
less” eye. The comic has an objective basis in reality insofar as there is
an objective truth (Christianity) that determines the hierarchy of forms
of life according to their distance from it. Whoever misrepresents this
hierarchy, laughing as if he were superior while he is actually inferior, is
comical. That which counts as legitimately comic is grounded in reality
as a feature of the world, regardless of a particular person’s capacity to
appreciate it.107
Apart from the examples spanned here, very few philosophers endorse
the view that existence or reality is comical. Benjamin Fuller suggests
in his essay, “Is Reality Really Comic?” (1946), that most philosophers
have disdained the aid of the comic value in exploring the nature of
reality because they adhere to the philosophical assumption that the
universe is amenable to explanation. To admit that the comic value
may have a cosmic significance and that it may be utilized as a possible
guide to the nature of things is to admit that reality itself may possibly
be irrational and unintelligible at heart, or at least that undetermined,
unpredictable, spontaneous and capricious elements may enter into its
essential structure.
Rosset prides himself on being one of those few, and indeed as far as
he knows, the only one to ascribe reality to the comical, probing in this
way not only the relationship between the real and its representation,
as others do, but also the nature of reality and its relationship with the
comical. This is certainly a substantial contribution; if it is to be rejected
for the view of reality it advances, it should still be considered for the
question it raises in relation to the comical.
B The Laughter of Annihilation
Rosset’s view of laughter bears some similitude to Bataille’s. Both em-
phasize the relationship of laughter with anxiety and death. But while
Bataille identifies laughter with the joy of living and gives laughter an
epistemological role within the good life he proposes, Rosset reserves
this role to joy, which he differentiates from laughter. Laughter does not
lead to happiness nor is it identical to it, Rosset says in the interview


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  361
titled “Despite Everything Happiness Is Still Happiness,” 108 whereas
Bataille seems to subordinate even happiness to laughter: “It seems to
me that happiness is a sort of secret which one seeks out in order to be
indifferent to misfortune, in other words that one could laugh about
it.”109 This raises the question of the viability of joy, which I address
below.
As far as laughter’s theory is concerned, Rosset’s sizable contribu-
tion is the laughter of annihilation, the aesthetics of his tragic philos-
ophy. While Rosset believes that his philosophy both originates this
kind of laugher and monopolizes it, I believe that they can be sepa-
rated, if needed. Indeed, the laughter of annihilation explains why
we take pleasure in the fact of engulfment or disappearance itself, as
Kant’s definition points to, in “the sudden transformation of a height-
ened expectation into nothing,”110 which theories of incongruities have
difficulty  explaining.111 Unless we assume that the “nothing” fulfills
another expectation, a deeper level of knowledge which is revealed and
recognized as such, we never get rid of difficulties in explaining various
kinds of laughter. Thus, this kind of laughter indicates that we enjoy
glimpsing at death and the disappearance it brings about, maybe be-
cause being taboo in most civilizations, visions of death or enjoyment of
its prospect are denied.
C The Earnestness of the Clown
Rosset emphasizes the human being’s inherent ridiculousness, its de-
risory and insignificant nature, and considers this feature the most
serious element of the human condition. He reminds us again of
Bataille’s view of the insignificance or insufficiency of human reality.
While Bataille restricts his discussion to humanity’s lived experience,
Rosset develops a full-fledged philosophy of the real which carries
this argument to existence as a whole. Rosset’s argument is that as
Being oscillates between the comic and the tragic, the intuition of the
given is necessarily as risible as it is tragic. Thus, the clown, which
represents the gratuity of being, is the most serious thing, and the
serious person who denies it, the most ridiculous. Acting as the clown
is the right thing to do in order to never succumb to the mirage of
significance. Lucidity as awareness of life’s ridiculous absurdity can
be allied to joy.
For Rosset, what is at stake in philosophy is accepting the clown that
we are and embodying the clown as the one who probes the anguish and
desperation of living. The rest is hypocrisy, as is any belief in the signifi-
cance of anything whatsoever.
The view that the human being is inherently laughable or ridiculous
(Homo risibilis) does not originate with Bataille or Rosset. It has been
rarely endorsed, especially in comparison to Homo ridens, the view that


362  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
humans are the only animals that laugh. Let me briefly introduce the two
views and highlight their differences. Homo ridens has been introduced
in Western thought by Aristotle; Homo risibilis, a notable variant of it,
can first be found in a commentary on Aristotle’s Categories penned by
Notker Labeo, an eleventh-century monk.112 Following Aristotle, many
thinkers (including Boethius, Alcuin, Rabelais, Montaigne, Voltaire and
Baudelaire) have characterized the human being as homo ridens or the
laughing species. Few, however, have characterized him as homo risibilis
or the laughable animal.
Though the characteristic of the human as the laughable animal does
not escape Plato’s keen eye in his discussion of laughter in the Philebus
(48–50), Plato does not apply it to all but only to those persons who are
lacking in both self-knowledge and power. A few centuries later, Labeo
innovates with his claim that the human being is not only the sole crea-
ture capable of laughter but also the sole laughable creature: we laugh
only at that which is human or at that which reminds us of the human
(quia quidquid risibile est, homo est). Montaigne revives this view by
maintaining that we are both homo ridens and homo risibilis, as “our
own specific property is to be equally laughable and able to laugh.”113
Bergson draws attention to this defining characteristic at the very begin-
ning of his book on laughter: “Several have defined man as ‘an animal
which laughs.’ They might equally well have defined him as an animal
which is laughed at.”114 More recently, Simon Critchley has reprised
both characterizations:
Homo sapiens is therefore not so much homo ludens as Johan Huiz-
inga famously argued, where humanity would be identified with the
capacity to play. Rather, we are homo ridens, laughing beings, or
indeed, homo risibilis, which suggests both “the risible or ridiculous
being,” and “the being gifted with laughter.”
(Critchley 2002, 41)
Bergson’s idea has also been echoed in Maurice Charney’s observation
that “to be human is to be inherently comic.”115 Bergson rightly wonders
why “so important a fact, and such a simple one too, has not attracted to
a greater degree the attention of philosophers.”116
The view that we are laughable beings does not necessarily imply
that we laugh at ourselves. Because Bergson considers laughter a social
punishment, he emphasizes in his study the laughter that targets others
rather than oneself. By giving priority to the self-mocking ridicule found
at the core of Freud’s paper “Der Humor,” Critchley takes the argument
one step further; he sees humor as essentially self-mocking ridicule and
argues, “In humour I find myself ridiculous and I acknowledge this in
laughter or simply in a smile.”117


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  363
Helmut Plessner advances a similar view in his characterization of
the human being as the eccentric animal and in viewing laughter as con-
firming the eccentric position of the human being in the world of na-
ture.118 Plessner’s thesis is that the life of animals is centered, that is, the
animal simply lives and experiences. By contrast, the human being not
only lives and experiences, but also experiences those experiences. In
other words, the human being has a reflective attitude toward its experi-
ences and toward itself. This is why humans are eccentric, because they
live beyond the limits set for them by nature by distancing themselves
from their immediate experience. In living outside of themselves, the re-
flective activity of human beings achieves a break with nature. Plessner
further maintains that the human being is this break, this h iatus, this
gap between the physical and the psychical. Working out of the conse-
quences of the human-eccentric position is the main task of a philosoph-
ical anthropology. This is why laughter occupies such a central role in
Plessner’s work.
With the exception of Labeo, Montaigne, Critchley and arguably
Plessner, who uses the term “eccentric” rather than “ridiculous,” the
view that human beings are ridiculous has rarely been advanced; even
less so in order to recommend self-mocking ridicule, except in religious
or mystical doctrines both Western and Eastern. These spiritual an-
tecedents are more widespread than their secular counterparts. In the
West, the Orthodox Church endorsed the view that we should be fools
for Christ’s sake, an attitude that can be found (without reference to
Christ) in the East as well, in Taoism, and later, through the influence it
had, in Ch’an (Zen) Buddhism as well.119
Rosset and Bataille both make human ridiculousness an essential trait
of the human condition. Both also recommend embodying this feature
by playing the clown. But none of them believe that doing so would
change anything in our condition or in the way we approach it. This is
where I disagree, but let me first further clarify the arguments advanced
by Bataille and Rosset.
Bataille hardly differentiates between the tragic and the comic. His
view of human ridicule follows from noting the puerility of the tragic.
This view is repeated by playwrights of the theater of the absurd: the
tragedy of the human being lies in its ridicule; “by reveling his absurdity
one can achieve a sort of tragedy,” Eugène Ionescu notes in referring to
The Chairs as a “tragic farce.”120 While the comical in Rosset’s philoso-
phy is also identified with the tragic, and the latter is associated with joy
and laughter as it is in Bataille’s thought, Rosset’s vision is paradoxically
more cheerful because it is tragic rather than absurd.
Let me then first address Bataille’s view of this matter and then
generalize my argument to apply it to Rosset as well. Theories of
the absurd have forgotten that the absurd is a category of the comic.


364  Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
Although Bataille assigns sovereignty to the comical, his view of it is still
serious (and tragic): there is no way out of the tragic. However, if reality
is comical and tragic at the same time, something that is both tragic and
comic cannot be solely tragic, as the tragic cannot hold these contradic-
tory tendencies; the comical can, I argue.
The worldview that obtains from the combination of the tragic and
the comic is necessarily a comical view, of a more encompassing nature,
yet still comical. The comical is inclusive, also of the tragic, in a way that
the tragic cannot be in relation to anything, especially not in relation to
the comic. This is referred to as “comic inclusivism, in contrast to the ex-
clusivism of the tragic view.”121 Similarly, John Crossan maintains that
“tragedy is swallowed up in comedy” because the fact that “the same
world can be interpreted in these opposite ways is itself comical.”122
This argument is valid for both Bataille and Rosset. The higher vision
that obtains may be better called a humorous vision, which holds the
two aspects, the tragic and the comic at once. It is true that the ridicu-
lousness that follows from pitting the two together represents well the
human condition. The awareness that takes place, I suggest, is ridic-
ulousness as a defining characteristic of the human condition: Homo
risibilis. However, by playing the clown, one embodies this condition
and cannot do it unless one embraces it. This self-acceptance transforms
one’s attitude toward oneself, others and life: the embrace of ridicule
liberates us from its sting, and from the tragic and the comic at the same
time. Ridiculous are those who do not know themselves to be so; it arises
out of ignorance of one’s condition. By assuming our identity, we regain
our dignity and our innocence in embracing our unwilled ridiculousness
at the same time that we disengage ourselves from the dramas of the
comic, the tragic and the ridiculous. The joke may be on us, but once we
get it, we are no longer its butt.
Homo risibilis brings about a stable joy and thus offers a viable alter-
native to Rosset’s view that makes of joy a mystery. I address now this
further problem in Rosset’s philosophy.
D Joy
Laughter cannot bring about the joy of life; Rosset affirms that such joy
is akin to “Pascalian grace.” Deep down, he tells us, he considers joy to
be out of reach: as soon as a spoon hits your foot at the age of two, joy
is impossible.123 While referring to the “salvation through joy,” Rosset’s
philosophy deems it a miracle akin to grace, a sort of supernatural assis-
tance which he cannot explain. And, maybe because of this incapacity,
he does not indicate a way that leads to it.124
Moreover, Rosset has explicitly maintained that the use of alcohol
or drugs is not opposed to the lucidity his philosophy recommends; he


Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation  365
himself was often drunk.125 And, insofar as ad hominem arguments
are permitted, Rosset sunk into a long depression a few years before his
death.126 He has been accused of offering a philosophy which can be
stomached only at the price of evading it by using various substances or
by being incapacitated by it. These considerations weight on the viability
of the joy that Rosset proposes.
Laughter falls short of the graced joy of life, as noted, but we have no
positive indication of how to make this miracle happen. We should cou-
ple this conclusion with Roxanne Breton’s observation that Rosset’s phi-
losophy is an inquiry about an object which resists all conceptualization;
moreover, we should note “the evanescent character of the notion of the
tragic, which remind us of the sinuousness of negative theology, enabling
only a diffuse perception of its nature, whose definition constraints us to
an elliptic, even apophatic, language.”127 When the tragic is defined in
such a mystical way and is coupled with “the salvation through joy,” on
which Rosset refuses to talk for being too intimate, we may ask if Rosset
does not recuperate here the religious Nietzsche which Lev Shestov has
found and transmitted to Bataille.128
Even if we resist this conclusion and state that Rosset attempts an
original reading of Nietzsche, with joy as the main idea their philos-
ophies share, it is still a “tragic joy,” a “paradoxical accord with” the
tragic,129 which Breton and others emphasize.130 Given that tragic joy
in introduced only in the philosophies of Nietzsche, Bataille and Rosset
(and the artists Richard Wagner and William Butler Yeats), and given its
irrationality as differently defined in these philosophies, we may doubt
its existence. The tragic is never coupled with joy before Wagner and
after Rosset.
Moreover, if we accept the existence of tragic joy as the paradoxi-
cal accord with the tragic, isn’t it, at least in Rosset’s case, the perfect
double? It certainly functions as a double to the tragic, with suffering
doubling itself as joy in much the same way that anxiety doubles itself
as laughter, and death as life. The moral function of joy, then, is similar
to any double: it exchanges metaphysics and false views of sense and
value with the irrationality of a graced joy whose function is to bear the
tragic. It would then be an instinctual doubling of the tragic that would
enable its knowledge. Wouldn’t then the edifice of Rosset’s philosophy,
as a criticism of the double, collapse?
There may be paths which ground joy less miraculously, establish it
more methodically and indicate a more systematic way to reach it. In
concluding this chapter, the last of this study, let me point out that I have
advanced such a path to joy, which, moreover, can be reached with the
sole use of self-referential laughter.131 Not only is the joy that is attained
a stable joy, the worldview on which it rests is epistemologically less de-
manding than Rosset’s. While it is not predicated on any visions of the


366 Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
real, whether known or negatively approached, it also prides itself in es-
chewing any kind of mysticism or personal experience of the evanescent
aid of grace that Rosset may have had.132

ce qu’il pense, je le pense aussi, et ses idées me passent tout le temps dans la
tête)” (Lejeune 2012, 252).
 2 Polac and Rosset 2003, 81; my translation.

duces in philosophy from the publication of Le réel et son double (1976)
onward (Tellez 2009, 10), and both Jacques Bouveresse and David Bell
deem him nonchalant (“insouciant”) (Bouveresse 1984, 119; Bell 1993,
xiv). His humor is evident in the collection of intimate stories Rosset wished
to publish posthumously, as editor Santiago Espinoza notes in the Intro-
duction to Ecrits intimes: Quatre esquisses biographiques (Rosset 2019a).
Finally, in the Introduction to his interviews of Rosset (2019b), Alexandre
Lacroix notes the mordant irony with which Rosset treats his contempo-
raries (“you cannot deride Derrida,” he used to say), his open mockery of
Jacques Lacan’s hermetic thought and the way Rosset uses humor to deflate
criticism: instead of defending his views, Rosset laughingly annihilates his
opponents’ objections.

published under the pseudonym Roger Crémant and reedited in 2008 un-

that this anthology of stupidity gives satirical definitions of philosophical
terms. It is a pastiche of handbooks of philosophy which calls for laughter
rather than reflection. It nevertheless attempts to show that the transmis-
sion of knowledge, through works of pedagogical vocation, is often con-
fused with the transmission of imbecility. Thus, the reader’s immediate
reaction is perplexity, as he doesn’t know whether this book was written
by a madman, an idiot or a swindler. Using the same pseudonym, Rosset
published in 1969–70 a series of chronicles in the Nouvel Observateur,
which infuriated the readers. These chronicles have since been gathered in

cism and mysticism, as “mystical experience reveals the absence of any ob-
jects (Bataille 1957, 30, my translation; quoted in Rosset 1985, 81). Sense is
always displaced, first in Stéphane Mallarmé’s work, then in Bataille’s and
finally in Derrida’s unhappy Hegelianism. In Bataille, the hope to reach the
thing in itself which is never attained is a remarkable illustration of Hegelian
nostalgia and of a refined illusionism of sense—sense being always else-
where. Bataille represents the modern sensibility which is a state of lack—
lack of object—one consequence of which is to link the destiny of lovable
objects to that of missing ones. It is a vision of what is in principle invisible,
the imaging of that which no image can represent (Rosset 1985, 82).

 18 Rosset distances himself from Deleuze at the beginning the latter’s collab-
oration with Félix Guattari, from Anti-Oedipus onward: “We hardly saw
each other in the last part of his life… we no longer spoke—and no longer
wrote in the same language,” he writes in the Introduction to Deleuze’s let-
ters (Rosset 2013). For Rosset’s view of Deleuze, see his article on Deleuze
(Rosset 1980 [1972]). Rosset voices two main criticisms of Deleuze’s view
of Nietzsche: first, he reproaches him the emphasis on the critical Nietzsche
instead of noting the primacy of joy in his work. Thus, Nietzsche did not
reach affirmation through a negation of negativity as Deleuze’s reading im-
plies (Deleuze 1983, 74–5). Second, Rosset’s view of eternal return reveals
his implicit criticism of the Deleuzian interpretation. Did Deleuze under-
stand eternal return in making it an attribute of becoming, as a pure form
of time which is a fortiori selective? Is a differential and selective repeti-
tion even thinkable for Nietzsche? Deleuze believes that only difference re-
peats itself, repetition being different things for different persons: to the
nihilist corresponds the repetition-old tune, and to the affirming person—
differential repetition. Rosset rejects Deleuze’s reading (which he had pre-
viously endorsed), and provides a radical reinterpretation of eternal return.
Basing himself only on Nietzsche’s published writings, Rosset reintegrates
in his “Notes on Nietzsche” the cosmic interpretations of eternal return
rejected by Deleuze and reestablishes the theory’s doctrinal and psycho-
logical character (Rosset 1993a). In a Letter to Rosset from 28 November
1983, which Rosset published, Deleuze refers to this new interpretation:

criticism of Deleuze’s view of humor, see below, section 4.

 21 In order to designate nothing, or “to make silence talk,” as Rosset says, the
French language disposes of a word that is missing in current usage in all
other European languages—“hasard” (hazard). The Englishman says al-
most always chance, the German Zufall, the Italian caso, the Spanish casu-
alidad, all words deriving from the Latin idea or word casu, accident (from
cadere, to fall). But this notion of casu does not cover precisely the idea of
“hazard.” Using etymological and epistemological points of view, Rosset
distinguishes among four levels in the genesis of the ideas of hazard. These
levels span the more specific, the more extended and the more talkative to
the less extended and less talkative—that is, the less hazardous to the more
hazardous, if “hazard” indeed designates a concept which, if it is not quiet,
at least tends infinitely toward silence. Thus, he differentiates between the
notions of fate, encounter, contingency and hazard. For Rosset’s view of
hazard, see Rosset 1993b, 73–6.

 44 Rosset’s preoccupation with the double begins with Le Réel et son double
(1976) and continues through Impressions fugitives (2004), which treats
such doubles as the shadow, reflection and the echo. While the double is the
major symptom of the rejection of the real and the main factor of illusion,
as Rosset continuously maintains, some doubles are to the contrary marks
of the real, which warrant its identity. These are the doubles of proximity,
such as the shadow, reflection and the echo. They are necessary comple-
ments of the real; they are inconsistent, yet real (Rosset 2004).
 45 The emphasis on illusions recalls “the will to illusion,” which another great
French Nietzschean, Jules de Gaultier (Jules Achille de Gaultier de Lagu-
ionie 1858–1942), christened “Boravysm,” after the illusions that beset Ma-
dame Bovary, Gustave Flaubert’s heroine (de Gaultier 1921). Flaubert has
famously stated that “Madame Bovary ç’est moi” (I am Madame  Bovary)
and that he wrote this novel “in hatred of realism” (Clark 2001, xiii). Bora-
vysm denotes a conceited or romantic conception of one’s own importance.
De Gaultier argues that Flaubert invested most of his characters with this
trait; however, he de-medicalizes and generalizes this capacity by diagnosing
all of us as suffering from it. The human being has to power to conceive him-
self as different from what he is; to the difference of one’s real self, the image
of oneself that one creates and projects is a parody; yet the gap between the
imaginary and the real, between what we think we are and what we actu-
ally are, cannot be bridged. Therein lies all the comic and all the drama of
human life. The degree of the energy being used to display the imaginary
decides whether it is a tragedy or a comedy. Our power to deform does not
reach external reality and we cannot make things be otherwise than what
they are (de Gaultier 1921, 8, 13–16). De Gaultier’s view of the comic and
the tragic as well as their dependence of the quantity of energy invested
recalls Plato’s view of the comic as due to a lack of self-knowledge in those
who are not powerful, as formulated in the Philebus (48–50): the comic
originates in non-powerful persons’ self- ignorance. Through de Gaultier, we
can understand that powerful persons can actually deform external reality
in ways that are not funny anymore. For his view of laughter, however, de
Gaultier refers to Schopenhauer’s view of the discrepancy between the con-
cept and reality, and asserts that all comic writers build on the disproportion
between the general concept and the individual energy, resulting in a lack of
balance and equilibrium (1921, 71). Thus, he maintains that
tout le rire human tient dans l’intervalle due de l’angle bovaryque, dans
l’écard qui se forme entre la réalite de quelque personage et la fausse
conception de lui-même à laquelle il s’attache. C’est dans cet intervalle
qu’il trébuche et donne le spectacle plaisant de ce qui perd l’équillibre.
(all instances of human laughter originate in the interval the Bovarian
angle creates, in the gap between a person’s reality and his cherished


370 Rosset—The Laughter of Annihilation
yet false self-conception. It is in this interval that he slips and gives the
 pleasant spectacle of that which loses balance.) (de Gaultier 1921, 69–70)
However, de Gaultier does not explain why losing one’s balance is a pleasant
spectacle. Roland Jaccard relates in his autobiography how a friend com-
pared Rosset unfavorably to Gaultier, feeling that the two are close but that
the former is lacking both the depth and style of the latter (Jaccard 2013,
21). Rosset, who did not read de Gaultier, has another view of the comical
as rooted in the hazard of reality, and of the laughter of annihilation, which
also explains why it is pleasant to witness a loss of balance. Apart from
personally emulating Nietzsche, de Gaultier gave us a valuable interpreta-
tion of Nietzsche, which include theses such as the difference between the
instinct to live and the instinct to know (see de Gaultier 1904, 1922, 1) and
the emphasis on artifice. These ideas are found in Rosset as well. However,
de Gaultier differs from Rosset in that, as many others, he follows the ideal-
ists in seeing the real itself as a construction, a view that Rosset rejects (for
the difference between Rosset on this point and many other thinkers, such
as Martial Gueroult, see the Introduction to Stéphane Vinolo’s study [2012]
that Charles Ramond penned). De Gaultier thus went in another direction,
a more Montaignian one, which delights in illusions as the enjoyable ne-
cessity of human reality. Rosset, however, went in the opposite direction,
chasing each illusion in an attempt to get to the real, which for him precedes
all illusion and exists independently of any idea we may have of it. Thus, de
Gaultier, despite his numerable publications on Nietzsche, seems to follow
more closely Schopenhauer than Nietzsche; indeed, his thought constitutes
an alternative to the Nietzschean answer to Schopenhauer rather than an
interpretation of Nietzsche, and an embodiment of a Nietzschean person,
which he represented for many. We also owe to de Gaultier the Introduction
to Lev Shestov’s (Léon Chestov) L’Idée du bien chez Tolstoï et Nietzsche
(1925), and his balanced view of Shestov as both skeptic and mystic. On de
 Gaultier, see, among others, Benjamin De Casseres 1913.

was first published in Le Monde de l’Education in November 1999 as
“Etre heureux, c’est toujours être heureux malgré tout.” Reprinted in Le
Monde de l’Education 294 (July 2001), 29–32, it was translated into En-
glish and published in 2003 in Angelaki. The English text mistranslates
Rosset’s notion of “allégresse”: notwithstanding the interview’s title in
French, which is indeed about happiness (heureux), the rest of the text
refers to “allégresse,” which means cheerfulness, not happiness. However,
Rosset notes in various interviews that in his first book, written at the age
of 20 and published at the age of 21, La Philosophie tragique, he trashed
happiness and opted in favor of tragic joy. Later on, he came to endorse any
kind of joy, whether called cheerfulness or happiness. And in his last work,
published fifteen days after his death, he affirms that heaven is on earth,
given that the cruel and laughing reality, the one thing one does not entirely
get used to is the domain of happiness: “Happiness can only be human:
the gods must sometimes regret that they are not human so that they could
join the party” (“Il n’est de bonheur qu’ humain: les dieux doivent regretter
parfois de n’être pas des hommes pour pouvoir être de la fête” [2018a; my
translation]).

would be a mistake or rather a superfluous creation. God would suffice”

real is indifferent. It is reassuring if the real is threatening, and threatening
if the real is reassuring.

 73 It follows that the less we know ourselves, the better we feel. Self- knowledge
is both unnecessary and unattractive. Those who often examine themselves
do not much advance in self-knowledge (“La connaissance de soi est à la
fois inutile et inappétissante. Qui souvent s’examine n’avance guère dans
la connaissance de lui-même. Et moins on se connaît, mieux on se porte”
[Rosset 1999b]). Much like Montaigne and Hume, Rosset rejects the notion
of a “natural” identity, which would be different from the social one. He
thus titles his work on self-identity Loin de moi (“Far from Me” [1999b]).
Rosset explains that it also evokes “a way of distancing oneself: the self is
something that I keep at a distance from myself, I am ‘far from myself’”
(Rosset 2003, 82; my translation). In the same vein, he argues in L’Invisi-
ble that one never recognizes oneself, one is always invisible to oneself (“Il
est une personne qu’on ne reconnaît jamais parce qu’elle est constamment
invisible, et c’est évidemment soi-même” [2011]).

This is where he adds the sentence I translated above:
Deep down I think that joy is impossible. As soon as a spoon hits your
foot at the age of two, joy becomes impossible. Consequently, it is mi-
raculous. (Ma pensée profonde est que la joie est impossible. Dès qu’on
a reçu une cueillère sur le pied à deux ans, la joie devient impossible.
Donc, elle est l’effet d’un miracle).
However,
I would point out that this miracle can be found again in Lucretius:
there is a miracle of materialism and a miracle of sensuality… This is
why all things have very little metaphysical value, everything is rather
ultimately inherent to the things themselves (Je ferais d’ailleurs remar-
quer que ce miracle se retrouve chez Lucrèce: Il y a également un miracle
du matérialisme and un miracle de la sensualité… C’est pour cette rai-
son que tout est si peu métaphysique, tout est finalement inherent aux
choses mêmes).
(Rosset, in Lejeune 2012, 257)

Perhaps, even if nothing else today has any future, our laughter may yet
have a future.
(Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, 223)
If they learned to laugh from me, it still is not my laughter that they have
learned.
(Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, IV, 16, 1)
I begin the Concluding Remarks by comparing the insights into the
comical and into laughter or humor, which I gathered from the philos-
ophers addressed so far, Georges Bataille, Gilles Deleuze and Clément
Rosset. To complete this study, I introduce additional views of laughter
held by twentieth-century French philosophers and developed both in
 Nietzsche’s wake and independently of him.
I Concluding Previous Chapters
Nietzsche is significant for the three thinkers addressed in the previous
chapters, less so for Deleuze than for Bataille and Rosset. Early in his
career, Deleuze turned to other philosophers, such as Henri Bergson and
Benedict Spinoza, who may have proved to be all along more significant
for his thought than Nietzsche has been. For the other two thinkers that
this study addresses Nietzsche’s significance is predominant: Bataille
claims that he repeats Nietzsche’s experience and Rosset considers him-
self Nietzsche’s sole follower.
What is the role of Nietzschean laughter and Nietzsche’s views of the
tragic and the comic in the three philosophers’ thought? All three en-
dorse his view of tragic joy and his association of the tragic with laughter.
But the use they make of Nietzsche’s laughter and their attitude toward
it differ. It was Bataille’s strategy in defending Nietzsche after World
War II to argue that Nietzsche’s laughter indicates that he is not to be
taken seriously, his thought being no project but play, which collapses in
Concluding Remarks
Additional Twentieth-Century
French Views of Laughter
DOI: 10.4324/9780429506116-6


Concluding Remarks  381
contradictions if we attempt to account for it in any other way. The other
two philosophers (and as we will see below, additional scholars as well)
put Nietzschean laughter to differing uses.
While acknowledging Bataille’s role in legitimizing Nietzsche, Deleuze
is freed from this concern but takes on another project, to legitimize Ni-
etzsche as a philosopher; he enlists Nietzschean laughter in a supposed
discussion between Nietzsche and Hegel and Kant, and introduces this
laughter as a new way of thinking. Rosset deems his predecessors “Hege-
lian philosophers” whose anti-Hegelian uses of Nietzsche he denounces;
he describes himself as the sole follower of the latter’s tragic philosophy.
The aesthetics such a philosophy brings about includes a notion of tragic
laughter, which describes laughter as delight in engulfment or annihilation.
Nietzsche has not theorized laughter clearly enough to enable to judge
these uses of laughter in terms of faithfulness to his views. Nor does this
matter, as the respective views of laughter advanced by these thinkers are
part of original philosophies of the good life. To formulate their views in
adequation to further forms of laughter, such as humor and irony—terms
that are almost alien to Nietzsche, who scarcely uses “humor” and ex-
plicitly dismisses “irony”—two of these thinkers turn to French philoso-
phers, such as Bergson and his student Vladimir Jankélévitch. As humor
and irony hardly play a role in Bataille’s thought, he turns to Bergson
(and Kant) for additional input on the comic and on laughter. However,
the self-referential laughter that animates his thought and the egalitarian
view of human insufficiency point more to humor than to irony.
It is significant that irony hardly plays a role in Bataille’s thought and
is emphatically discarded in favor of humor by Deleuze and Rosset. The
anti-ironic project may even be called the touchstone of Deleuze’s philos-
ophy, after an initial phase in which irony occupies an equally significant
role as humor does. These considerations should make us pause as we
tend to assume philosophy’s predilection for irony, a view that seems
mistaken when we look at twentieth-century French thinkers, but also
when we consider it in a historical perspective. Irony seems to be the
defining feature of a short period, Romanticism; Nietzsche’s criticism
of irony should make us reconsider his alignment with the Romantics.
When used in another sense than in Romanticism, irony is also descrip-
tive of another form of thought, postmodernism, which also reads it
back in other periods and various authors, but as we shall see, irony is
usually ascribed to, rather than endorsed by most postmodernists. The
reason that we often err in assigning irony a significant role in philoso-
phy seems to be that the study of art or aesthetics, the philosophic field
to which irony belongs, originates in Romanticism, the sole period that
explicitly endorses irony wholeheartedly.
Irony is inconsequential in the philosophy of the three authors we
studied; yet it is so only from a certain point on for Deleuze. This
may be the reason why later on he rejects it more emphatically than


382  Concluding Remarks
the two other thinkers do. Deleuze also takes satire as his target indi-
cating in this way that he does eventually rejects Nietzsche’s scornful
laughter in order to endorse Spinoza’s laughter of pure joy.
The Deleuzian notion of the comic may derive from the same Spino-
zian source as he sees in it a moral force, the laughter of the ethical man;
for Bataille the comic is reduced, it is meant as a joke or sham, similar to
the laughter at misfortune which he believes animates comedies. Rosset’s
use of the comic, is out of three philosophers, more in tune with our
common intuition of the comical as that which makes laugh (gaily), that
which produces mirth.
The Deleuzian notion of the comical enables him to ascribe it to various
authors, whose writings do not produce mirth but strength and a sense of
elation. Many authors are comical, as he explicitly asserts that this is what
defines a great author. One is tempted to say that he means that the work
of such author adds to the general joy of living; however, he also means
that such an author laughs a lot. Thus, we should not easily dismiss the
Deleuzian notion of the comic as completely foreign to common usage.
However, this may not be so with Deleuze’s and Deleuze and Guattari’s
notion of humor. Humor comes to replace contradictions in the ontology
these authors propose and becomes indistinguishable from difference it-
self. For Deleuze, humor becomes a conceptual persona, a notion or an
idea that he creates as part of his philosophy; once generated, however, it
is ascribed to others; it becomes the yardstick which evaluates the thought
of others: only those who are identified as humorous are further “cho-
sen,” while those who lack it are rejected. Humor fulfills in Deleuze’s phi-
losophy a similar role, a “selective force,” as he calls it, which enables the
eternal return and the (im)personal solution of amor fati in the counter-
effectuation of the event.
Thus, Deleuze rewrites the history of laughter and the history of phi-
losophy through his notions of humor and the comical. His view of
humor discloses a philosophical “humor,” or “the humor of the philos-
ophers” which is different from regular humor (as is the God of philos-
ophers from the personal God of the faithful). It is a humor that does
not necessarily laugh and whose smile may sometimes be imperceptible
upon encountering an alogical contradiction or facing the incongruity of
one’s extinction. But as part of the aesthetics of the surface, it is meant
to be the leading mode of the comical and resonates with what common
sense calls humor.
Bataille attempts an in-depth analysis of laughter in utter contradiction
to his assertion that he refuses any theoretical analysis as it would mean
the end of his freedom. He turns the tables on previous philosophers’ at-
tempts to understand the cause of laughter and uses Sigmund Freud’s as-
sertion to the effect that what one laughs at may better remain unknown
(if one is to laugh) in order to argue that the unknown itself makes us
laugh. The communication that laughter is, the sign that anguish is off,


Concluding Remarks  383
enables him to associate laughter with fear and with death. Identify-
ing the marriage of defeat with triumph in laughter and the masochism
that inheres in self-laughter, he creates his religion of laughter on these
grounds. The singular mysticism of laughter that Bataille advances is
original when compared with the well documented laughter of the mys-
tics. Its benefits are partially used in yoga laughter and partially missed
because the goal of suppressing oneself while preserving oneself is not as
broadly endorsed as Bataille believes it should be. Bataille is original also
in defining the comical as sovereign and in pointing to the insufficiency
of human ridicule as that which associates and eventually identifies the
tragic with the comic.
Rosset’s careful differenciation of joy from laughter is notable on the
background of the abrasiveness of his colleagues, who conflate the tragic
with joy or laughter. He also preserves the tragic, which disappears in
Deleuze’s thought into the joy and laughter of the tragic, and into the
comical. Rosset’s capacity to delineate both joy from laughter and the
comical align with our intuitions of what these notions mean; it also en-
ables him to illuminate aspects of our (common) laughter which were
unresolved till now. This is why he says that his philosophy originates and
monopolizes the notion of the laughter of annihilation, the pleasure we
take in objects that disappear. However, Bataille also addresses this issue
as it is ultimately an explanation of Nietzsche’s quote, “To see higher na-
tures perish and to laugh at it…this belongs to greatness!”1
It is notable that many Bataillean ideas about laughter and the
 comical, especially human ridiculousness and the significance of playing
the clown, can be found in Rosset. The idiot and the clown play a role
in Deleuze’s thought as well, although a lesser one. By pointing to hu-
man ridiculousness, these authors recommend humor or self- referential
laughter, sometimes a “foolish” attitude as the content of the good life.
In this, they hark back to another Frenchman, Michel de Montaigne,
whose thought is a significant source for Nietzsche, and may also be
enlisted as precursors of the Homo risibilis (ridiculous human being)
thesis, which I advocate.2
All three philosophers ascribe an epistemological role to laughter. The
Rossetian idea that laughter is a knowledge of reality can be found in
Bataille, who sees laughter as thought and as leading to ultimate reality.
For Deleuze, humor is a new form of thought which enables to grasp the
alogical contradictions of reality.
The ontological status of laughter follows the epistemological role
of laughter or humor as ascribed by the three thinkers. Not only does
laughter open up the ground of things for Bataille; the sliding or glisse-
ment between the worlds that he describes is expressed by our insuffi-
ciency, which points to our inherent failure and necessary fall into the
gulf that opens before us. Deleuze sees humor as enabling access to the
world’s real constitution; but if it is a world of alogical contradictions to


384  Concluding Remarks
which humor is the solution, humor seems to be more than an epistemo-
logical principle; it seems to have an ontological basis in reality. While
Rosset ascribes an epistemological role to laughter, it is in a further elu-
cidation of reality itself that we can see most explicitly the ontological
basis of the comical, on whose revelation he prides himself: he is the sole
philosopher, he argues, to have ascribed a comic quality to the real itself,
to existence, which uniquely explains why we enjoy the comical at all.
Finally, from an ethical point of view, laughter is everything for
Bataille, humor as the affirmative “solution” of amor fati is much for
Deleuze, and laughter is insufficient for Rosset. The Bataillean good life
is laughter itself, humor enables Deleuze to attain to the good life that
he proposes, while laughter, which prepares the path for encountering
the real for Rosset, does not provide the joy necessary for sustaining
this encounter. The graced joy of life that enables living lucidly without
evading the tragic knowledge of reality, which constitutes the Rossetian
good life, does not depend on laughter.
The elaborate philosophies of Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset should not
mask the fact that they are presented by their authors as practices of phi-
losophy, that is, as forms of life. This is clearly formulated by Bataille,
who reads this back in Nietzsche, Eastern philosophies and various mys-
tics. One can mistake Deleuze’s work for an elaborate metaphysics and
miss out on his emphasis on ethics as a style or art of life.3 He harks back
to the Stoics, revealing their humor, but also to Lewis Carroll and to Zen
Buddhism. Rosset prides himself on being Nietzsche’s sole true follower
and entrusts philosophy with a new role of preparing the encounter with
reality.
Being arts of living, these philosophies necessarily involve the comical,
especially humor or self-referential laughter. Arthur Schopenhauer, who
defines humor as the incongruity between the (ideal) conception and the
(lived) perception, aptly notes that this makes the relation of thought to
life comical. If Deleuze is right in arguing that “Life will no longer be
made to appear before the categories of thought; thought will be thrown
into the categories of life,” humor as defined by Schopenhauer will nec-
essarily be present.4
Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset are not the only French philosophers of
their generation who were interested in laughter. Anca Parvulescu notes
that “the philosophical avant-garde of the second part of the twentieth-
century” formed a community “with a common passion for laughter”
as a means of reflecting about “temporality, action, and gender.”5 Ju-
lia Kristeva does not strictly refer to the philosophical avant-garde and
the postmodern philosophers when she notes “the centrality of laughter
to the thought of her generation.”6 Thus, the interest in laughter’s sig-
nificance is not restricted to Nietzschean philosophers. I address now
those twentieth-century French thinkers, both Nietzscheans and non-
Nietzscheans, who were not studied in previous chapters.


Concluding Remarks  385
II  Additional Twentieth-century French
Views of Laughter
I introduce twentieth-century French philosophers, both Nietzscheans
and non-Nietzscheans, who elaborate on laughter yet do not offer full-
fledged visions of the good life or do not explicitly argue for laughter’s
role in such a life. I begin with the non-Nietzschean philosophers, Vlad-
imir Jankélévitch and André Comte-Sponville. Among Nietzschean
philosophers, I focus on Michel Foucault, Jacques Derrida and his fol-
lowers, notably Sarah Kofman and Jean-Luc Nancy, on Jean-François
Lyotard and Luce Irigaray, and on additional feminist thinkers such as
Hélène Cixous and Julia Kristeva. I conclude with general comments on
postmodern laughter and irony.
A Non-Nietzschean Philosophies of Humor
Laughter is a popular topic among French philosophers regardless of
their relation to Nietzscheanism. Vladimir Jankélévitch and André
Comte-Sponville exemplify the interest in laughter of non-postmodern
French philosophers. They offer valuable contributions to the topic this
study addresses, and interestingly, reject irony in fa
 vor of humor as do
Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset.7 They precede and follow Rosset, respec-
tively, as Jankélévitch was Rosset’s doctoral advisor and Comte- Sponville
endorses much of Rosset’s thought on the comical. These philosophers
do not elaborate systems of thought, however, in which laughter or hu-
mor may have an explicit role to play in the good life.
1  Vladimir Jankélévitch: The Smile of
Reason—Humor as Serious Irony
Vladimir Jankélévitch (1903–85) maintains his agnostic reflection at the
limits of the intelligibility of human experience. He rejects the idea of
a systematic philosophy, and focuses instead on the “je-ne-sais-quoi” (a
quality that cannot be described or named easily) and the “presque-rien”
(almost nothing), which define philosophy as he sees it.8 At the limits of
intelligibility, reflection breaks in paradoxes, the articulation of which
forms the bulk of Jankélévitch’s subtle ethical thought. A son of Russian
émigrés, Jankélévitch exemplifies in this predilection the thought of an-
other émigré, Lev Shestov.9 However, it is to the ideas of Bergson, his
teacher, that he adheres. His fame was first built on Henri Bergson, one
of the two works that Bergson authorized as genuinely descriptive of his
philosophy.10
Much like Bergson’s, Jankélévitch’s thought tends toward earnest-
ness.11 Apart from his contributions to moral philosophy, he makes
notable contributions to aesthetics. He oscillates between the tragic


386  Concluding Remarks
and irony, between seriousness and levity, and allocates a significant
place for humor as “the only earnest thing down here.”12 Although
Jankélévitch focuses on irony rather than on humor in L’Ironie ou la
bonne conscience (Irony or Good Conscience [1964]), it is humor, de-
fined as open irony, an “irony that is finally serious,” which concludes
this work.13 The interest the current study has in Jankélévitch lies in this
innovation: defining humor as open irony, he differs from the custom-
ary approach which merely opposes the two notions instead of associat-
ing them by making one a species of the other.
However, Jankélévitch begins, as many do, by differentiating between
irony and humor: while misanthropic irony maintains a polemical atti-
tude toward human beings, humor is sympathetic. Humor differs from
blame and sarcasm; it empathies with the butt of its attack; secretly an
accomplice of ridicule, it connives with it.
As the “smile of reason,” humor is defined as open irony. However,
the difference between closed and open ironies is vast: while closed irony
does not attempt to instruct, open irony is ultimately a principle of mu-
tual understanding and spiritual community. While closed irony cannot
transcend the pessimism of satire, humoristic irony is always somewhat
humble. Free from bitterness, it pacifies by mediating, by conciliating
the cruel antitheses of sarcasm; humor has a tender spot for what it rails.
The humorist’s stance is a comeback to educated naivety. Humoristic
irony is characterized by an additional subtlety that is missing in the
abusing form of irony. This is why Schopenhauer deems humor “the
double counterpoint of irony,” according to Jankélévitch.14 The latter
proposes to call it, more simply, an irony to the second power, where the
“allegorical” relation appears as doubly indirect:
The humorist too plays, only his earnestness is infinitely remote, it is
an evanescent grace. To humorize is to ironize by looking afar and
beyond; through this complex path, consciousness is led back to its
ungraspable truth…
(Jankélévitch 1964, 173; my translation)
Thus, humor is a supreme reflection of consciousness. The flight of the
bird that Nietzsche alludes to in Beyond Good and Evil requires not
only detaching from attachments, but also detaching from detachment
itself.15 Jankélévitch notes the dogmatism involved in irony: unconscious
as are all forms of absolutism, it freezes in a ridiculous affirmation of its
own frivolity. In order to remain in a transient state, to be truly humoris-
tic and genuinely self-conscious, irony should avoid self-consciousness—
it should be ironic in order to know how to be serious, complicated
in order to know how to be simple. Neither can irony be systematic:
humoristic irony cannot abide anywhere. And, this nomad irony cannot
be a profession; much like freedom, it is an inspiration and a vocation.16


Concluding Remarks  387
Affected irony becomes inadvertently naive, while humoristic irony
reaches the profound earnestness of life by remaining alert, supple and
infinitely conscious. The result of both penetrating consciousness and
infinite lucidity, humoristic irony turns out to be innocent again as a
creature in the world’s first morning. Whence its airy and ever ambigu-
ous character: in contradistinction to wit, humor is a sort of evanescent
grace.
Between the beyond of pride and the down here of humility lies the
virtue of the mixt and earnest human being. This is the modest and
earnest virtue of “neither angel nor brute,” the virtue of the person who
maintains herself in the truth of her condition. If it is not a tragedy,
that intermediary situation is defined as truth itself by Jankélévitch.
At work in irony and humor lies one principle: the awareness that be-
cause nothing is worthwhile, everything is too serious. In contradistinc-
tion to the temptation that both extremes represent, either playing the
brute or playing the angel—either orgiastic forms of drunkenness or
puritanism— humoristic seriousness inculcates disenchantment, taking
us back to prosaism or the sobering and disappointing truth of work
and hope.17
Earnestness is not an aesthetic category; it lies among the comic, the
frivolous and the tragic. The earnest man is the metaphysical man, who,
through an interior vibration, willingly turns himself into a mediator be-
tween the finite and the infinite. It is earnestness that founds the genuine
insouciance which is truly philosophic. One should not take absurdity
tragically or lightly, but simply seriously.18 Jankélévitch thus concludes,
“this irony, which is finally serious, is what with Höffding we could call
Humour.”19
2  André Comte-Sponville: The Virtue of Joyful
Disillusion—Humor Laughs at That Which Is Not Funny
André Comte-Sponville (1952–) attempts to overcome the materialism
which has been associated with traditional atheism. The philosophy he
proposes spiritualizes atheism20 and embraces humor.21 He defines him-
self as a non-Nietzschean who aims at the rehabilitating morality once it
is differentiated from politics.
Comte-Sponville’s criticism of Nietzscheanism targets the views
of laughter of both Nietzsche and his followers. First, he objects to
 Nietzsche’s call to sanctify laughter. In response to Nietzsche’s claims,
“I myself have pronounced my laughter holy,” and “Laughter I have
pronounced you holy,”22 Comte-Sponville exclaims: “We, who did not
sanctify our laughter, and laugh better because of that!”23 Second, he
distances himself from French Nietzscheanism, this “philosophy of chat-
terers,” excepting Deleuze from this charge24 and singling out Rosset
as one of the few contemporary philosophers who have influenced him.


388  Concluding Remarks
Comte-Sponville endorses Rosset’s view of reality as idiôtès, mean-
ing “simple,” senseless and contingent. He approves of the latter’s re-
versal of the Bergsonian definition of the comical25: Bergson’s formula
is always true because we continuously laugh at sense inlaid into non-
sense; however, as sense is permanently inlaid into nonsense, all sense
is de jure laughable. The laughable is almost always the ridiculous: the
unwarranted pretension to sense, either in its authentic version, such
as in life or satire, or in its artificial version, such as in burlesque or
humor. As Thomas Hobbes has argued, laughter originates when one
guesses or unmasks this pretension: laughter is the triumph of the spirit
on the ridiculous that threatens it, that perhaps defines it. One laughs
at this prodigious lack of sense, which is as common as truth yet rarely
acknowledged because its law is ridiculousness.26 More specifically,
Comte-Sponville argues that humor laughs at the sense whose absence
humor notes, when sense volatilizes at its contact. This is why laughter
is so rare: the resistance of sense is earnestness itself, as Comte- Sponville
explains:
Humor always dwells in the in-between, in the abrupt movement…
between sense et non-sense: too much sense and it is not yet hu-
mor (often, it is still irony), too little, it is only the absurd. We find
here a quasi-Aristotelian mean: humor is not earnestness (for which
everything makes sense) nor is it frivolity (for which nothing has
sense). Rather, it is an unstable or equivocal or contradictory mean,
which reveals the frivolous in all earnestness and the serious in all
frivolity.
(Comte-Sponville 1995, 286–7; my translation)
Following Rosset, but also Deleuze and Jankélévitch, Comte-Sponville
considers humor superior to irony; yet unlike the argument that serves
Rosset, Comte-Sponville’s reasons for doing so are ethical: humor is
associated with love and derives its superiority from this association.
Humor should be contrasted with religion (“the contrary of prayer
is laughter”), and Bataille’s views seemed to be echoed when Comte-
Sponville deems laughter an a-theological virtue, an “anti-religion.”27
However, it is the anti-religious Epicurus’s affirmation of humor, rather
than Bataille, that Comte-Sponville quotes in this context: “At the
same time, we must philosophize, laugh, and manage our household
and other business, while never ceasing to proclaim the words of true
philosophy.”28
Humor belongs to the materialistic, the anti-religious faction; the
comical is legitimately of our time, as Gilles Lopovsky notices.29 The
comical destroys all idols by mocking the gods, one’s fetishes and one’s
self. It is not only destructive, however; it is also salutary for it creates


Concluding Remarks  389
space for truth. The comical is the bereavement of sense, which makes
joy possible again by forcing it to face the absurd or the real. This is
the comic of despair, because “the contrary of belief is knowledge; the
 opposite of prayer is laughter.”30
At this point, only laughter remains, the “pure joy”31 that Spinoza
 defines, which defies sense and nothingness for Comte- Sponville.
 Following Spinoza, he distinguishes at all times between various forms
of laughter, especially humor and irony. He choses humor: equating
mockery with irony, he follows Spinoza in rejecting the former.32 Rainer
Maria Rilke advises in his Letters to a Young Poet, “Search into the
depths of things: there, irony never descends…”33 Comte- Sponville con-
cludes that this is a first difference between humor and irony.34 The
second, more significant difference lies in humor’s reflexivity, interiority
or immanence. Irony laughs at the other (or as in self- mockery, at the
self as another); humor laughs at one’s self, at the other as oneself and al-
ways includes itself in the nonsense it generates or reveals. This does not
mean that the humorist does not take things seriously, as humor is no
frivolity. He simply refuses to take himself, his laughter or his anxiety
seriously. Humor puts the ego at a distance; it forgives or understands,
while irony despises, excludes and condemns; irony hurts, humor heals
or appeases.
Let me elaborate on these differences. Irony is a weapon that is al-
most always used against another. It is a wicked laughter, a sarcastic
laughter; it is the laughter of scorn, the laughter that wounds and may
kill, the laughter that Spinoza denounces.35 In Spinoza’s Ethics, laugh-
ter and jest are embraced as “pure joy,” but it is another kind of laugh-
ter, which Spinoza explicitly distinguishes from mockery.36 Mockery
is the laughter of hatred, the laughter of contest. When needed, it is
effective, as most weapons are; however, no weapon is peaceful as no
irony is humor:
How sad it would be if we could only laugh against! And what se-
riousness, if we could only laugh at others! Irony is exactly that: it
is a laughter that takes itself seriously, that mocks, but not itself…
If I use it against myself (in self-mockery), it remains exterior and
harmful… irony scorns, accuses, condemns … it takes itself seri-
ously and suspects only the other’s seriousness—even if it means
speaking of oneself as of another, as Kierkegaard saw (1977, XI,
189). This broke or bridled more than one spirit. Irony is not hum-
ble, as one has to take oneself very seriously to mock others. How
proud one must be to despise oneself! Irony is this seriousness in
whose eyes everything is ridiculous. Irony is this smallness in whose
eyes everything is small….
(Comte-Sponville 1995, 280; my translation)


390  Concluding Remarks
As Kierkegaard notes, irony seeks to stand out; to the contrary, humor
seeks to obliterate itself; this is why Comte-Sponville prefers humor over
irony.37
Comte-Sponville repeats Jankélévitch’s differentiation of irony with
respect to humor.38 However, rather than identifying humor with
 earnestness—which is the human intermediary situation between despair
and  futility—as Jankélévitch does,39 he sees humor as resolutely choosing
both extremes.40 There is tragedy in humor, but it is a tragic that refuses
to take itself seriously41: that which is not tragic is derisory, this is the
lesson that lucidity teaches us.42 Humor is a form of the comical which
makes us laugh especially at that which is not funny.43 It presupposes
determination, effort and creativity. A “joyful disillusion,” it is, or can
be, doubly virtuous: “As disillusion, it adjoins lucidity (thus, good faith);
as joy, it attains to love, and to everything.”44 Thus, humor is counted
among the virtues in Comte-Sponville’s Small Treatise of Great Virtues.45
To the contrary of humor, irony is not virtuous. Comte-Sponville
completes his uncompromising criticism of irony with a critique of con-
temporary humor, which postmodernism endorse:
[Humor] cannot last or be erected into a system lest it becomes one
defense amongst others and stops being humor. By insisting on cel-
ebrating humor, our epoch perverts it. What can be sadder than to
cultivate humor for itself? To convert it into a means of seduction?
To make it a monument to the glory of narcissism? To turn it into a
profession is justifiable, as one must earn a living. But a religion? A
pretense? This betrays humor and discloses that one lacks it.
(Comte-Sponville 1995, 281; my translation)
Habit threatens humor. It may become a tic, a stuttering of the spirit. In
the long run, nothing is more annoying, serious and sad than the delib-
erate will to laugh, the determination to be merry, the stubborn effort
to be light! If humor is considered one of the fine arts or a rule of life it
takes itself seriously and ceases to be what it is.
Because our epoch recognizes itself in humor, it is tempted to make
of humor a sense as any other; and, by replacing all other senses by
the sense of humor, it turns humor into a new ethical norm. Comte-
Sponville concedes that an ethics of this kind won’t be too exacting: it
would be an ersatz of religion for difficult times, with its neat, tidy and
funny little god that one would carry within. However, the problem with
this use of humor is as follows: rather than targeting values, the sense of
humor becomes yet another value, an ideal, which intercedes between
life and the real as all ideals do. By becoming systematic, humor alters
its nature: it becomes a sign like all others, a symbol, which in the end
denies (precisely because it is emblematic and pretends to have value)


Concluding Remarks  391
the absence which it notices or indicates. This is how laughter turns into
a new form of fetishism—sense is missing, and this is why we laugh,
but it is missing because we laugh—a postmodern fetishism, if you like,
tainted with bad faith.
This use of humor perverts it: instead of leading to truth or silence,
humor can’t stop leading back to sense, to laugh of it anew. Rather than
the mourning of sense, it becomes its substitute; rather than a shortcut to
the real, it is a discursive diversion. A new form of chatter, it sadly cul-
minates in wordplay: one laughs at language, indeed, but only to avoid
shutting up; when bored in social gatherings, humor fills the silence.
Thus, “luckily, there is humor. A spiritual ruse, it is the last avatar of
chatter and lie: they have inserted laughter, once and for all, between
the true and the real” (Comte-Sponville 1993, 197–8; my translation).
Comte-Sponville’s deadly criticism of contemporary humor is com-
plemented by a criticism of philosophy: it is incapable of embracing
the comical. Comte-Sponville insightfully notes that there is no comic
philosophy; while this undoubtedly sets a limit for laughter (it cannot
replace thought), this also sets a limit for philosophy, which “cannot
replace laughter, joy, and even wisdom.”46
B Nietzschean Philosophers’ Views of Laughter
The rest of the Concluding Remarks present the view of laughter held by
various postmodern philosophers, followers of the laughing  Nietzsche
that I did not address in this study. As noted in previous chapters, the
three philosophers I have studied so far do not represent p ostmodernism.
Only in one of his possible readings is Bataille a postmodern avant- la-
lettre, Rosset defines his thought in opposition to the  poststructuralists
and Deleuze’s postmodernity is a subject of debate: Ronald Bogue raises
the question, answering it in the affirmative, and Gary Gutting, to take
one example, identifies Deleuze as a poststructuralist; however, addi-
tional scholars have different views on the matter. Manuel DeLanda,
for example, maintains that “Deleuze has absolutely nothing in com-
mon” with the postmodern tradition, although “his  experimental style is
bound to create that impression.”47 It should also be noted that Deleuze
was reluctant to use that term.
Nor should the title “postmodern” be easily ascribed to Nietzsche.48
The postmodernists, however, beginning with Foucault considered Ni-
