etzsche the first postmodern:
Nietzsche marks the threshold beyond which contemporary philoso-
phy can begin to start thinking again; and he will no doubt continue
for a long while to dominate its advance.
(Foucault 1970, 353–4)


392  Concluding Remarks
But it is not certain that Nietzsche was the founder of “the uniquely skep-
tical philosophy now called ‘postmodern,’” as Dave Robinson phrases it
in Nietzsche and Postmodernism:
Nietzsche never had any clearly thought-out “genealogical” theory
or systematic method of doing historiography. Nietzsche’s philoso-
phy is an odd mix of scattered, often almost random observations
about history and psychology, based on intuition and personal id-
iosyncrasy, and reveals no sign of the kind of thorough methodical
research practiced by Foucault. Nietzsche is also less skeptical about
individual human identity. He seems to have believed that there are
some essentialist psychological and even physiological qualities that
make people the way they are, and which are therefore the cause of
their core beliefs and values… Nietzsche also maintains, of course,
that it is possible for certain superior and aesthetically developed
individuals to forge their own identities.
(Robinson 1999, 48)
Robinson’s entire study aims at situating Nietzsche’s thought in relation
to postmodernism. He does not hesitate to deem Nietzsche a utopian,
looking forward to the overman, and a reactionary, looking back toward
Greek civilization. And he rightly maintains that Nietzsche would have
despised the postmodern lukewarm relativism, viewing it as a cultural
phenomenon expressive of the last stage of Western liberalism.49
Nietzsche’s views of language and meaning, his genealogical studies
of power and his famous “perspectivism” are among the reasons he has
been deemed by many postmodernists “the first ‘anti-philosopher’.” Ig-
noring the dogmatic visionary he later becomes, postmodern philoso-
phers prefer the early skeptical Nietzsche.50 To claim the kinship with
Nietzsche, these thinkers rely on his critical period and disregard his
mature philosophy,51 of which he was proud. Most importantly, they
endorse a text which he suppressed:
If Nietzsche was a deconstructionist, he didn’t remain one for very
long. He soon abandoned his early theories on language and mean-
ing for more complex and less postmodernist ones, and suppressed
the publication of his early essay “On Truth and Falsity in their
Extra- Moral Sense.” In his later philosopher, Nietzsche became
quite clear in his own mind that some moral and political views are
superior to others.
(Robinson 1999, 55)
Nietzsche does not reject truth, nor can he do so without witnessing the
collapse of his philosophy.52 Unlike Nietzsche, postmodern philosophy
does not seem to have a clear project for the future of civilization.53


Concluding Remarks  393
Moreover, the most conspicuous Nietzschean theses are not postmod-
ern: leaving aside the overman of the later period, his views of the subject
and of the autonomy that crowns it constitute the apex of his philosophy.
At least,
Human beings are determined by the “Will to Power” that govern
all forms of existence. This doctrine finally led him to some “nat-
uralist” or qualified “essentialist” beliefs which, again, aren’t very
postmodernist. He came to believe that there were certain funda-
mental physiological and psychological facts responsible for dif-
ferent human natures. And although he never thought that human
subjects could be explained away wholly by physicalist and reduc-
tionist explanations, neither did he believe that they were no more
than social or linguistic constructs.
(Robinson 1999, 60–1)
The careless and “unspecific abandon” with which Nietzsche uses the
notions of “truth,” “knowledge” and “meaning,”54 combined with the
seductiveness and adaptability of his work, the number of issues his phi-
losophy covers and the variety and changeability of his views certainly
encouraged the postmodernist philosophers “to think differently about
the modern world and its unique problems.”55 Nor were the postmod-
ern philosophers unaware of their approach to Nietzsche’s philosophy,
which emphasized its inspirational nature. Thus, “Foucault’s wise re-
mark” concludes Robinson’s Nietzsche and Postmodernism:
The only valid tribute to thought such as Nietzsche’s is precisely to
use it, deform it, to make it groan and protest. And if the commen-
tators say that I am being unfaithful to Nietzsche, that is absolutely
of no interest.
(Foucault 1977, 33)
It should be noted that Nietzsche himself is a model of such willful ap-
propriation both in his relation to the Pre-Socratic philosophers and to
Schopenhauer and Wagner; and he prided himself on the misuse of the
names of these great Germans.56
In approaching the postmodern philosophers, we should take into ac-
count not only their Nietzschean lineage but also the influence of psy-
chological theories and political ideologies, as mediated by structuralist
views, such as those of Jacques Lacan and Louis Althusser.57 Structur-
alism had a continuing impact on literary and cultural studies as well
as on philosophy, despite the collapse of its scientific claims. As the 60s
began in France, apart from the positivist challenge that structuralism
represented, the traditional claims of philosophy were represented by
phenomenology. Both structuralism and phenomenology shared the


394  Concluding Remarks
assumption that “we could attain deep truths about the human situa-
tion,” which the poststructuralists questioned.58 Especially significant
are the poststructuralists’ relations with Freud and Lacan, whose view
of the subject they seem to endorse.59 Finally, the problematic relation-
ship with Nietzsche may be enlightened by taking into account the years
that elapsed between Nietzsche’s death and the 1968 events, and the
situation of Marxism in the twentieth century to which Nietzsche could
not respond.60 Nancy explains:
Romanticism was the awareness of the desire to moor towards an
unlikely yet necessary port (an “absolute”). It could not and would
not affirm like Nietzsche that we were drifting in the middle of an
unlimited ocean. And Nietzsche himself still wanted to throw a
rope over the abyss… This is why there was 68: because everything
 between Nietzsche and the end of Marxism (not the end of Marx,
especially not of what was romantic in him) had seemed to offer
a possibility of mooring (what can be gathered under the name of
“politics” and whose double spearhead was the overstep of capi-
talism and decolonization), all this turned out to be even more un-
docked. A double bind ensued: romanticism was denounced at the
same time that it was revived; we had to be careful not to get caught
in its trap again and we had to give it another impetus, find an-
other spring for it…. This is how naïve and distrustful of our naivety
we were, and how we knew or rather sensed the pervasive problem
represented.
(Nancy 2012; my translation)
Marxism was seen by twentieth-century French philosophers as the
last systematic attempt to understand the world and find an immanent
order in it. Madan Sarup argues that many denounced it as metaphys-
ics, a belief system that cuts people off reality, and a form of religious
discourse.61 However, if Marxism isn’t true, then nothing is. Nietzsche
best expresses the state of confusion that many poststructuralists believe
we are in.
The double bind that Nancy describes yields the “irony” which defines
the postmodern situation: “The irony is that they need a general theory
to support their assertion as to why there cannot be a general theory. As
they cannot provide grounds for their view, they think of their viewpoint
as being provisional, ‘ironic.’” Rejecting the grand narratives, “these in-
tellectuals focus only on the heterogeneous, the diverse, the subjective,
the spontaneous, the relative and the fragmentary.”62
Within the variety of Nietzschean views that the postmodern philos-
ophers misappropriate or appropriate, their attitude toward Nietzsche’s
laughter stands out. In the thought of the main “French Nietzsche-
ans,” a term that has become synonymous with poststructuralism and


Concluding Remarks  395
postmodernism, we find that laughter, the comical, play, parody and
irony play a significant role.63 Some of these philosophers penned book-
length manuscripts about laughter,64 some relate themselves directly to
Nietzsche’s followers, such as Bataille, and study laughter, rather than
humor or the comical (Foucault, Nancy, Kristeva), others are being as-
sociated with Bataille just because they entrust laughter (and eroticism,
and drunkenness) a prominent role in their thought (Cixous); some share
Deleuze’s concerns about humor and the comical and about the rela-
tions these notions have with philosophy (Kofman, Blondel). Much like
Bataille, and Deleuze, who paired up with a psychoanalyst, Guattari,
the Nietzschean philosophers were influenced by Freud, later by Lacan,
as noted above, and some were trained as psychologists or psychoana-
lysts (Foucault, Irigaray, Kristeva).
The relevance of Freud and Lacan to this study lies in their interest in
humor. As early as 1905, Freud published Jokes and Their Relation to
the Unconscious, which addresses not only jokes, but also wit and hu-
mor.65 More than 20 years later, he published a very sympathetic, albeit
short, text on humor (1928). He did not make much of puns. However,
his main interpreter, Lacan, used puns to exemplify his points, to cast
doubt on Ferdinand de Saussure’s formula that signifier and signified
are bonded together to form a stable, meaning-bearing sign. Not only
are puns signifiers which bond with two or more signifieds at once, they
indicate a particular behavior of the signifier itself: it relates first to other
signifiers rather than to signifieds. As Catherine Bates explains, “in place
of Saussure’s procession of relatively fixed, meaningful signs, Lacan saw
a series of endlessly radiating chains of non-signifying sounds,”66 an
idea that we find again in Derrida.67
The witty and allusive pun undermined meaning, revealed words to
be slippery and unstable, and showed language to have gotten the better
of the writer. But as it proved his point, Lacan always had the last laugh.
He did not choose between jest and earnestness but oscillated to and
from between those not-so-fixed points of sense and nonsense which
made a joke a joke and a pun a pun; he played the most serious game
and played to win.68 Thus, texts cannot have an unambiguous meaning
or original meaning cannot be found in texts; analysts must practice the
language of the unconscious if they want to relate to it, the language of
“poetry, puns, internal rhymes” because “in word play causal links dis-
solve and associations abound.”69
Moreover, Lacan uses the notion of play in explaining the mirror-
stage. Bates explains that “something derisory is going on in front of the
mirror”; the child who looks at his own image between 6 and 18 months
greeting his reflection with signs of “triumphant jubilation and playful
discovery” is being taken in as if there was something substantial, pro-
found and meaningful in what he saw.70 However, it is illusory, a play, a
drama or a spectacle. Thus,


396  Concluding Remarks
From the beginning, the child’s sense of identity rested on a theat-
rical conjuring trick that was quintessentially illusionistic because
it was based on a fraud—on a fracture between real and ideal, be-
tween what was experienced and what was seen. It is based on a fic-
tion, an externalized and objectified self-image, “his identity,” from
which all wannabe follows: all satisfactions of order or complete-
ness, a psychology, a religion, a theory, an ideology, a philosophy of
life, or an over-arching world-view.
(Bates 1999, 165)
The chimpanzee, which is intellectually superior at this point, recognizes
the epistemological void that its image is. However, the theorist and the
child are playing very seriously a play that is both creative and illusory.71
For Lacan, the entire psychoanalytic process may be identified as co-
medic because “psychoanalysis is a change from a state of non-knowing
(repudiation and denial) to one of knowing (acknowledgement and ac-
ceptance).” The latter state Lacan justly referred to as “really and truly
the essence of comedy.”72
Finally, the role of Bataille in the advent of poststructuralism is em-
phasized by Denis Holier in Against Architecture. He argues that the
1929 articles Bataille published in Documents prefigure the attitudes
against structuralism in the writings of Foucault and Derrida.73 These
thinkers renounced the traditional goal of philosophy insofar as it is de-
fined in terms of truth and knowledge and turned to Bataille and Mau-
rice Blanchot as alternative approaches to reflection. With the help of
Philippe Sollers and the Tel Quel group, Foucault revives Bataille’s work
in the 60s.
Now that the origins of postmodernism have been clarified, I complete
this study by introducing the various views of laughter that postmodern
Nietzscheans endorse and the arguments they provide in its defense in
the context of their respective contributions to philosophic reflection.
Many of them use the notion of laughter rather than humor or the com-
ical, and at least in this respect, they remind us of Bataille.
I address below the views of Foucault, Derrida and his followers, no-
tably Kofman and Nancy; Lyotard, Irigaray and other feminist thinkers,
such as Cixous and Kristeva. I generalize these views in order to charac-
terize postmodern laughter and conclude by assessing the irony which is
emblematic of postmodernism.
1 Michel Foucault: A Silent Philosophical Laugh
Following in the footsteps of Nietzsche and Bataille, Michel Foucault
(1926–84) is a philosopher of laughter, “someone who wrote in a laugh-
ing mood.”74 His work is “at root ad hoc, fragmentary and incomplete,”
and the overall interpretations Foucault was prone to give of it changed


Concluding Remarks  397
over the years.75 There is no methodological or theoretical unity in
Foucault’s thought that would support any single comprehensive inter-
pretation, Gutting argues.76 Moreover, although the ethical import of
Foucault’s philosophy can be gathered from his view of philosophy as a
way of life, especially in his later writings, we cannot properly speak of
an ethics in Foucault’s thought.77 Thus, Foucault’s thought could not be
addressed more thoroughly in this study78.
Foucault helps to rekindle the interest in Bataille and acknowledges
the impact he has on his thought, a debt which is amply documented.79
Roland Champagne notes:
Bataille’s work is interspersed throughout Foucault’s work and be-
comes a basic theoretical reference for Foucault’s own writings on
negativity in examining social attitudes toward madness, criminal
discipline, and sexuality. Bataille’s questioning attitude toward the
impositions of arbitrary limitations upon human thought inspires
Foucault to wonder about the possibility of philosophy itself being a
mad discipline in that the parameters of social discourse are proba-
bly found in what Bataille spoke of as the opposition between “the
order of things” and the “intimate order”80 of the human heart.
(Champagne 1998, 90)
There are still notable differences between the two thinkers. Contrary
to Foucault, Bataille does not object to individualism; however, Foucault
ignores Bataille’s revision of Nietzschean sovereignty. While Bataille be-
lieves that Nietzsche’s main notion of the will to power has been errone-
ously interpreted as power, “Foucault is the first post-war philosopher to
take Nietzsche seriously as a political thinker.”81 Deleuze maintains that
Foucault develops beyond Nietzsche the latter’s notion of power, rather
than collapsing it as Martin Heidegger has done.82
For Foucault, power cannot be seized; it does not pertain to the State
because it is not about laws and rights but about domination. Thanks
to Nietzsche, Foucault thinks about power and the individual outside
traditional liberal and Marxist political philosophies, which center on
“legitimacy.” The real purpose of the political agenda which preoccupies
us is to disguise the truth about domination. As power has no essence,
it comes in different forms, some groups monopolizing certain kinds of
power while others have very little power. However, the autonomous
and dehistoricized human being that grants legitimacy to the State and
that inhabits the traditional philosophic discourse does not exist. Beliefs
and values have a history, as have human beings: they are constituted
by loose networks of systems and disciplinary institutions which con-
trol them through “discourses.” Those point to thoughts, beliefs and ac-
tions which are possible and determine the picture that individuals have
of themselves. Rather than possessing a unique identity, human beings


398  Concluding Remarks
are subjects made by systems and networks of power of which they are
unaware.83
Foucault relinquishes the idea of sovereignty, the apex of Nietzsche’s
philosophy, which Bataille endorsed while emptying it of all positive
content. The interest in Nietzsche, following the interest in Bataille
and Blanchot, comes from Nietzsche’s philosophizing in opposition to
the  traditional ideal of absolute philosophical truth, Gutting notes.84
Deleuze argues that Nietzsche snatches thought from the element of truth
and falsity, which I believe is better described as a Shestovian r eading of
Nietzsche rather than an accurate description of Nietzsche’s procedure.
As Deleuze remarks, for the poststructuralists, Nietzsche makes of truth
“an interpretation and an evaluation,” which interprets forces and eval-
uates power.85
For Foucault, the renunciation of truth first means the rejection of the
notion of “man” as claiming absolute knowledge. Rather than the death
of God, he announces the death of His murderer. Foucault’s main ideas
are accompanied by laughter, as we shall see below; thus, the “death
of man” and the genealogical method which Foucault takes from Ni-
etzsche are associated, respectively, with a philosophic laugh and with
the comical.
The “mix of scattered, almost random observations about history and
psychology, based on intuition and personal idiosyncrasy,” which Rob-
inson says form Nietzsche’s genealogy of morality, are an inspiration for
a “genealogical” method for Foucault. With this method he writes “his-
tories” that investigate madness, sexuality and punishment in Western
society. He describes “epistemic institutions that have defined normality
and helped establish prisons and asylums for all those classified as ‘ir-
rational’ or ‘criminal,’” using facts that are now established as false,
and a theory that knowledge equals power, which is used to control:
“Power produces knowledge…knowledge and power directly imply on
another.”86 Foucault’s genealogical histories aim at showing that knowl-
edge and truth are interpretations which involve repression and reduc-
tion. Power elites evolve out of the specifically qualified interpreters and
representatives, which knowledge necessarily requires. Thus, society is a
prison or a “Panopticon” in which we are continually monitored.
The anxiety, which Bataille refuses to own and whose communal
outlet in the sacred he requested, is echoed in Foucault’s view of mad-
ness: the terror and laughter of the insane during the Renaissance were
exchanged in modern times with a “reduced” form of terror, an in-
teriorized anxiety of guilt and shame. In a way that recalls Bataille’s
emphasis on laughter in contradistinction to Heidegger who begins
with anxiety,87 Frederick Dolan answers biographer James Miller. He
points to lived obsessions with various death-related transgressions as
the origin of Foucault’s thought, while Dolan sees its key in Foucault’s
“philosophical laugh.”88


Concluding Remarks  399
In a similar vein, Zwart deems Foucault a laughing philosopher. He
addresses his view of laughter in two studies, one focuses on Foucault’s
view of madness (1955) and the other refers to the entirety of his thought
within a more encompassing study of the ethics of laughter (1996). To
account for Foucault’s laughter, he spans a variety of works, such as
The History of Madness (1961/1972), The Order of Things (1973, 196)
and his essay on Nietzsche (1971). After a decade, Foucault’s attention
to laughter would subside only to reappear in his later writings. Zwart
argues that Foucault’s philosophy of laughter shares various insights
with other theories that he discusses, such as those of Mikhail Bakhtin,
Nietzsche and Bataille; however, he notes that Foucault’s “philosophical
laughter seems to be of a peculiar nature—and quite in accordance with
his remarkable views and methods.” In what follows, I rely on Zwart’s
studies.89
Zwart begins by noticing Foucault’s association of laughter and mad-
ness in The History of Madness. Foucault explains how the Renaissance
experience of madness differs from the “classical” and “modern” expe-
riences.90 Renaissance madness is seen as basically akin to laughter—an
experience which the French word folie expresses through its double
meaning of madness and folly; a distinctive feature of this experience,
considered as omnipresent and inevitable, is its fundamental connection
with truth.
Laughter is lucid and revealing. Madness/folly reveals the futile and
ridiculous nature of that which, according to official established views,
should count as serious and significant. It is a form of wisdom that turns
official knowledge into mere folly, while disclosing a profound insight
and a deeper truth, a revealing and striking view of life. This unusual
experience of madness/folly is brilliantly articulated in Desiderius Eras-
mus’s Praise of Folly, with some ambivalence. Erasmus does not laugh,
according to Foucault, as the Renaissance experience of madness/folly
is in itself ambiguous and unstable, containing both a tragic and a crit-
ical aspect. While Praise of Folly primarily represents laughter’s critical
aspect (“folly”), the tragic aspect (“madness”) emerges notably in the
comical/terrible paintings of Hironimus Bosch. Zwart explains:
The critical aspect indicates that gay laughter reveals certain aspects
of the world that are usually neglected and concealed by more seri-
ous “games of truth”; the tragic aspect entails a somber, threatening
and violent truth which is subdued by gay laughter.
(Zwart 1996, 89)
In the subsequent “classical” and “modern” experiences of madness,
however, this delicate union of the tragic and the gay is lost. According
to Foucault, the modern experience of madness is one-sided because the
basic connection between madness and folly as well as between madness


400  Concluding Remarks
and truth has been obscured.91 And yet Foucault maintains that some
isolated voices in the margins of established discourse manage to retain
this experience of the fundamental connection between madness, folly
and criticism which was omnipresent during the Renaissance—for ex-
ample, authors like Nietzsche and Bataille. Their writings, at odds with
established truth regimes, are grounded in a basic experience of laugh-
ter, which transcend the limits of serious, scientific or philosophical
discourse and contest established morality. They recognize the funda-
mental connection between folly and truth and between the tragic and
the critical aspect of laughter, and their awareness of this connection
constitutes the ground of their philosophies.
It is astonishing that laughter gains a prominent position in a subse-
quent book on the prehistory, or rather the “archaeology” of modern hu-
man science. Laughter is the alpha and omega of The Order of Things:
An Archaeology of Human Sciences92: laughter appears as an experi-
ence of truth, of revelation and contestation, which surpasses the truths
of modern sciences and disclose their limited transient and vulnerable
nature. The first lines of this work describe a revelation, an experience
of laughter, which is evoked again in the final sentence of its penultimate
and decisive chapter, the chapter that announces the death of the mod-
ern human subject.
In the very first lines of The Order of Things, Foucault explains that
the book was written because of a text by Jorge Luis Borges describing a
Chinese encyclopedia. This text conveys a way of perceiving and under-
standing the world which differs from the familiar: a perception and ar-
rangement of things which at first glance is bound to strike us as utterly
absurd and ridiculous. Rather than a mocking laugh, this text elicits
an uneasy laughter, followed by discontent, for it seems to contest the
seemingly solid and self-evident practices of perception. The foundation
of language and knowledge, of words and objects, which we take for
granted proves to be contingent.93 This uneasy laughter reflects the gen-
eral uneasiness that emerges at the beginning of the sixteenth century,
when apparently incontestable structures of knowledge and argumen-
tation were suddenly transformed into something basically ridiculous
and unconvincing. This event is represented by Miguel Cervantes’s novel
Don Quixote.
Foucault notes that we are on the threshold of another fundamental
transformation, which affects the very foundation of knowledge, lan-
guage and perception. The modern human being’s “anthropological
slumber” (i.e. the basic conviction that the Cartesian ego or the Kan-
tian subject is the ground of knowledge) is on the verge of being inter-
rupted by an epistemological dawn: the recognition that “man” as we
have come to understand him is but a temporary fold, a recent invention
which is bound to disappear without leaving a trace.94


Concluding Remarks  401
In the final reference to Nietzsche in The Order of Things, Foucault
couples the Nietzschean death of God with the end of man, an end that
is marked by the laughter of the Übermensh at the going-under of man.
Recalling that in Thus Spoke Zarathustra (“The Ugliest Man”) God is
reported to have died of pity upon encountering the last man, Foucault
writes:
Rather than the death of God—or, rather, in the wake of that death
and in a profound correlation with it—what Nietzsche’s thought
heralds is the end of his murderer; it is the explosion of man’s face in
laughter, and the return of masks; it is the scattering of the profound
stream of time by which he felt himself carried along and whose
pressure he suspected in the very being of things; it is the identity of
the Return of the Same with the absolute dispersion man.
(Foucault 1970, 385)
Foucault’s interpretation of the death of God, which appears at the end
of The Order of Things, may be read as a symbolic manifesto for much
of recent Continental thought, since it really encapsulates the attack on
“man,” humanism and every ordinary account of self-appropriation.95
In this passage, Foucault reads the death of God as a prediction of the
end of our anthropocentric age. Nietzsche is an untimely thinker, be-
cause he envisioned the death of the subject and the dispersion of “the
individual” in the basic regularities of life96:
In our days, and once again Nietzsche indicated the turning-point
from a long way off, it is not so much the absence or the death
of God that is affirmed as the end of man… is it not the last man
who announces that he has killed God, thus situating his language,
his thought, his laughter in the space of that already dead God, yet
positing himself also as he who has killed God and whose existence
includes the freedom and the decision of that murder?
(Foucault 1970, 385)
For Foucault, the final meaning of the death of God is the death of “man,”
in the sense of the final passing of the episteme, or order of things, that
has focused upon the human being, his experience and h istory as the
locus of all meaning and truth:
To all those who still wish to talk about man, about his reign or
his liberation, to all those who still ask themselves questions about
what man is in his essence, to all those who wish to take him as their
starting-point in their attempts to reach the truth, to all those who,
on the other hand, refer all knowledge back to the truths of man


402  Concluding Remarks
himself, to all those who refuse to formalize without anthropologiz-
ing, who refuse to mythologize without demystifying, who refuse to
think without immediately thinking that it is man who is thinking,
to all these warped and twisted forms of reflection we can answer
only with a philosophical laugh—which means, to a certain extent,
a silent one.
(Foucault 1970, 342–3)
This laughter makes us see that there is no ground for the anthropo-
logical discourse of the human sciences, Zwart argues.97 Once God is
removed, every other substantial notion must be challenged as a con-
sequence of the displacement of this central pole. With the death of
God, the self is effectively decentered and the traditional goal of self-
possession becomes entirely problematic as we find ourselves straying
through an infinite void.98
Foucault transforms into a genealogy of power his archeology of med-
ical, psychiatric and psychological knowledge around 1970. The transi-
tional essay on Nietzsche (“Nietzsche, la généalogie, l’histoire”) testifies
to this transformation: genealogy is presented as a kind of laughter, a
form of historical research which laughs at the metaphysical quest for
lofty and divine “origins.”99 Instead of searching for the origin of things
by unraveling their ideal foundations, genealogy points to their origin
by revealing the vile, ridiculous and accidental features of historical be-
ginnings. It degrades the metaphysical, top-down account and replaces
it with bottom-up accounts by drawing attention to bodily and material
forces and the circumstances at work. In On the Genealogy of Morals,
for instance, the ascetic ideal is connected with certain basic, physiologi-
cal instincts. The Herkunft of things is unstable, ridiculous and acciden-
tal, quite different from Ursprung, Zwart argues. Genealogy laughs at
metaphysics, just as the mature Nietzsche laughs at the young Nietzsche,
who still bothered himself with the question whether God should be
considered the origin (Ursprung) of evil. Historical beginnings are vile
and accidental, rather than lofty and divine. When it comes to origins,
true history—genealogy—points to the body, to nutrition and digestion,
to physical constitution rather than to metaphysical ground. Thus, gene-
alogy is a “gay,” “coarse” and “uncivilized” attitude.
Moreover, genealogy is parody: it parodies the attitude toward his-
tory which Nietzsche defines as the “monumentalistic” attitude in the
second of his Untimely Meditations. This attitude sees history as a series
of monumental achievements; for example, the history of philosophy
is presented as a sequence of intellectual highlights without reference
to the circumstances that produced them. Thus, instead of interpreting
the achievements as the accidental outcome of a particular and contin-
gent constellation of forces and conditions, they are transformed into
something whose origin is incomprehensible, maybe also divine. At first,
Nietzsche rejects this attitude, then after 1874 he parodies it, which


Concluding Remarks  403
means that he uses it in a way that defies its original purpose.100 The
monumentalistic attitude is degraded and transformed into its parodical
counterpart.
Furthermore, Foucault presents genealogy as the comic reversal of the
nineteenth-century nostalgic practice of adopting substitute identities.
Instead of feeling at home in historical circumstances long since for-
gotten, one turns history into a fool’s game or a masquerade. Foucault
considers Wagner a perfect personification of such a desperate view of
history, which Nietzsche ridicules. History is repeated but is inadver-
tently transformed into buffoonery. Foucault refers to the famous sec-
tion 223 of Beyond Good and Evil, where Nietzsche claims that only
as history’s buffoons, in a carnivalesque mixture of styles and disguises,
can the modern human being hope to attain to his share of originality.
In The History of Madness, Renaissance laughter, which is satir-
ical and presented as a form of truth, as moral criticism, is followed
by classical or satirical laughter which is presented as a playful device
and instrument of reason. In The Order of Things, however, laughter is
introduced as an epistemological event, as an experience of revelation.
Subsequently, laughter disappears from Foucault’s writings. Although
genealogy is identified with laughter in the 1971 transitional essay on
Nietzsche, Zwart notes that parody and gay science seem to be extin-
guished completely in the genealogical studies that Foucault embarked
upon in the 1970s.101 The mood of Discipline and Punish is serious,
even gloomy. The omnipresence of power overcomes laughter, which is
either powerless or absent. The disquieting transformation of human
bodies into mechanical, machine-like artifacts cannot, as Bergson’s
analysis would imply, be corrected by laughter. Zwart notes:
In Foucault’s impressive account of the massive struggle between
panoptism and disciplinary power on the one hand and popular or
peasant resistance on the other, the outstanding manifestation of
popular resistance (namely parodical laughter) seems absent.
(Zwart 1996, 94)
This twilight of laughter is to last for a decade. In the fall of 1983,
Foucault lectures at Berkeley on “parrhesia” or unrestricted speech.
He introduces modern criticism as a genre whose history has been for
 centuries intimately connected with the history of laughter. Special at-
tention is given to one particular tradition of laughter, cynicism.102 Thus,
criticism is a laughing device whose purpose is to unravel unpopular
truths.
2 Jacques Derrida: Joyous Affirmation of Playful Parody
Jacques Derrida (1930–2004) presents himself as the most assiduous
reader of philosophy rather than its practitioner. His interest in the


404  Concluding Remarks
writings of philosophers and others follows from his understanding of
writing as revealing the essential peculiarities and limitations of human
thought. A written text escapes total clarification and contains irresolv-
able ambivalences that impede the full understanding of what the au-
thor meant. Derrida has been associated with “deconstruction,” which
challenges the characteristic view of structuralists that language is a
fixed system of signs, which generate meanings through difference as de
Saussure argues. Various philosophers, anthropologists, anthropologists
and linguists set out to study the sign systems with the aim of discover-
ing what they reveal about human cultures and about human ways of
perceiving and thinking about the world. These systems, which were
thought to be stable, were also seen as binary, as creating notions of op-
posite meanings, such as Reason and Passion, Male and Female, Nature
and Culture, etc. Derrida pursues de Saussure’s views to their decon-
structive conclusions, as Robinson argues: “If signs are ‘arbitrary,’ then
their meanings cannot possibly be fixed, and will always be inherently
unstable. Derrida is a subversive anti-philosopher whose ‘deconstruc-
tive’ readings of other philosophers reveal semantic instabilities.”103
Rather than engaging in arguments with philosophers, Derrida re-
reads their texts to reveal that the inconstance of language can never
yield one set of meanings. Various meanings may be unintentional,
traces of the sign systems that constitute their thoughts, such as ideas
signified by binary systems; thus, some differences are prioritized while
others are “deferred.” Meanings slip between writer and reader, between
speaker and listener. As there is no stable meaning, a philosopher cannot
make claims about permanent truths lying beyond language. Language
is always metaphorical in the sense defined by Nietzsche:
What, therefore, is truth? A mobile army of metaphors, metonymies,
anthropomorphisms; truths are illusions of which one has forgotten
that they are illusions… coins which have their obverse effaced and
now are no longer of account as coins but merely as metal.
(Nietzsche 1964)
This quote is from an early text, “On Truth and Falsity in their Extra-
Moral Sense,” to which various poststructuralists refer despite its later
suppression by Nietzsche. Language freezes useful but illusory notions
because social beings need them, whether true or not. These valuable fic-
tions, which the pragmatic Nietzsche sees as an inevitable and welcome
necessity, become for Derrida something more contestable.
The metaphorical nature of language means not only that philoso-
phers cannot go beyond language to reach a truth that would transcend
their immediate history and culture, but also that essentialism is to be
abandoned: language can never penetrate the “essences” or meanings of
concepts such as “truth” or “knowledge.” Furthermore, the fundamental


Concluding Remarks  405
belief in identity is no longer guaranteed. “Logocentricity,” the belief
that change can be prevented and ideas can be fixed by language, is as
dangerous as it is misguided. It can work only by excluding “the other,”
by marginalizing the values and beliefs that do not confirm to the hege-
mony, which in itself is just a contingent and limited worldview. Derrida
prefers to celebrate difference, diversity and the marginal. Ethical values
and political doctrines are based on myths about human nature and are
the constructs of authoritarian institutions. Language and reality are the
same thing, as we cannot escape textuality and free-floating signifiers.
Derrida’s interest in the comical can be seen in his interpretation
of Bataille’s laughter (1967/1982), his interpretation of Nietzsche’s
laughter in Éperons: les styles de Nietzsche (Spurs: Nietzsche’s Styles
[1978a/1979]) where the key term is parody, his emphasis on play, and
finally in his work on James Joyce, where he argues that affirmation
cannot be differentiated from laughter.
Derrida’s view of laughter is predicated on his criticism of the meta-
physics of presence, which prefers one of the binary terms it assumes.
The affirmative yes of Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit is the affirma-
tion of identity rather than difference. The Hegelian reconciliation is
nothing but the positive assimilation of otherness. Absolute identity
is the all-inclusive One or the totality that abolishes all novelty, as all
movement is included in the dialectic.104
Derrida attempts to show that islands of resistance or remaining
(“restance”) are not captured by the Hegelian system although they are
in it. The “remaining” introduces play within the closed logic of the sys-
tem through an undecidable, incalculable and unanticipatable element,
whose structure avoids determination. Therein lies laughter, according
to Jérôme Cotte’s study of Derrida.105 Notwithstanding Hegel’s remarks
on humor and the comical in the Lectures on Aesthetics, laughter is ex-
cluded from Hegel’s system. Nor is death present, except theoretically,
when the master fixes it and overcomes it; yet he never risks it. This is
where Bataille laughs, according to Derrida. Death is always mastered
in Hegel’s dialectics; yet the kind of death that Bataille refers to has no
sense in this system. That which is laughable, according to Derrida, is
the submission to sense, to earnestness and truth, the swiftness with
which the system recuperates even death as negativity because it can-
not deal with nonsense. This indicates the submissive self- conservation
of the system and its self-circulation as the circulation of sense. Hegel
cannot deal with radical negativity, which is his “blind spot,” according
to the Derridean Bataille, the place where there is no process and no
system but rather death, sacrifice, suppression, destruction, an expen-
diture without reserve. Thus, Derrida argues that laughter in the way
that Bataille utilizes it hits Hegel at the heart of his system, which is
the master-slave dialectic. Sovereignty is the loss of sense that laughter
represents and this is why Bataille deems it “comical.” It is the loss of


406  Concluding Remarks
principle or ground which neutralizes the discourse of sense and that
which is known by referring it to nonsense and the unknown. However,
this is a repetition, a parody of the Hegelian discourse. Rather than lack
of sense, laughter is for Derrida a relation to the lack of sense, that is,
an openness.
Parody enters Derrida’s thought through his interpretation of Ni-
etzsche, Spurs: Nietzsche’s Styles. In that work, whose key word is par-
ody, he argues that Nietzsche’s thought is an unstable text because there
is no such thing as the truth of Nietzsche or of his text in the same way
that the truth of a woman, if one takes seriously Nietzsche’s analogy of
truth to a woman, does not exist. Deeming Nietzsche’s style “cryptic
and parodying,”106 Derrida asserts that there is no limit to its parodying
play with meaning. The hermeneut cannot but be provoked and discon-
certed by its play.107
For Nietzsche, there are only truths in the plural, never the truth.
Similarly, instead of style we are confronted with styles. In Ecce Homo,
Nietzsche declares that he is capable of a multiplicity of styles and dis-
penses with “style in itself” as “pure folly,” as mere “idealism,” which
is on the same level as the “beautiful in itself,” the “good in itself,” the
“thing in itself.”108 By availing himself of such a multiplicity of styles,
Nietzsche “suspends the decidable opposition of true and non-true, and
inaugurates the epochal regime of quotation mark which is to be en-
forced for every concept belonging to the system of philosophical decid-
ability.”109 Alan Schrift explains:
Reading, in other words, is free to play. Nietzsche’s multiple styles
remove the logocentric imperative of the pathos of truth and replace
this imperative with an invitation to play. The epoch of quotation
marks points to the reader’s predicament of rarely knowing with
certainty “who” is writing in Nietzsche’s text. Utilizing a multiplic-
ity of masks and metaphors, Nietzsche’s styles confront the reader
with the undecidable question: “Who is writing?”
(Schrift 1990, 109)
We may ask whether some masks are identical with “Nietzsche,” while
others are sarcastic or parodic responses of “Nietzsche.” For Derrida,
“Nietzsche himself, as a proper name, falls under the epoch of quota-
tion marks,” and it is for this reason that the Heideggerian question of
the “truth of Nietzsche” of the “totality of Nietzsche’s text” must be
suspended.110 Thus, Derrida argues that we must affirm “the lack of
the unique word or proper name—in the sense that Nietzsche puts affir-
mation into play—with a certain laughter and with a certain dance.”111
Examining Nietzsche’s multiple styles needs these kinds of laughter and
dance, which are part of the Derridean affirmation.112


Concluding Remarks  407
Dance is another name for play. Schrift distinguishes three forms of
play113: Schauspiel or theatrical play, Weltspiel or the play of the world,
and Kinderspiel or the play of the child. The latter is the most significant
sort of play: a serious play, it animates the two other.114 In Derrida’s call
for play, we can hear the echo of Zarathustra’s message to the higher
men in the fourth book of Thus Spoke Zarathustra, in which the re-
curring theme is the invitation to dance and laugh.115 Derrida himself
acknowledges Nietzsche for pointing the way to affirmation of the de-
centered play of writing that disrupts the metaphysics of presence which
guides the logocentric tradition. Nietzschean affirmation is
The joyous affirmation of the play of the world and of the inno-
cence of becoming, the affirmation of a world of signs without fault,
without truth, and without origin which is offered to an active
interpretation.
(Derrida 1978b, 292)
Finally, Derrida notes the laughter that signs Joyce’s affirmative stance
in the novels, Ulysses and Finnegan’s Wake.116 In a lecture on Joyce,
Derrida said “I am not sure I like Joyce… except when he laughs—and
you will tell me that he is always laughing.”117 Exploring the relations
between Joyce’s signature (“who signs? Who signs what in Joyce’s
name?”) and his affirmation, laughter comes about in a singular way in
Joyce since Ulysses.118 Playing on the verb “ouï-dire” (hearsay), Derrida
coins “oui-rire” (yes-laugh) to describe the way laughter and affirmation
are associated in Joyce. This yes-laughter is for Derrida the tonality in
Joyce, the Heideggerian dominant mood or tune (Stimmung), the pathos
that marks everything in Joyce’s text without being reducible to just one
element in the whole. The hypothesis is that yes-laughter signs the length
and breadth of Joyce’s text, like the final “Yes” in Ulysses, Molly’s yes,
thus constituting Joyce’s “signature” (1992, 116).
However, there is more than one kind of laughter. There is a “typol-
ogy” of yes-laughter in Joyce, turning on two distinguishable, domi-
nant types or keys (at least) in which yes (oui) can be heard (ouï); two
different yeses heard in Joyce, one is negative and the other affirmative
and repetitive. Nietzsche helps Derrida recognize both kinds of laughter;
the first is related to the donkey’s “ja, ja,” and the second is related to
the eternal return and to Joyce’s last word in Ulysses. Molly’s “yes” is
a capitalized “Yes” followed by a full stop. It is the perfect way to end
the novel, although, as Parvulescu notes, yes calls for confirmation and
repetition and thus cannot be an ending in any strict sense.119 Thus,
laughter and yes-saying are both an answer and a call which implicate
us in relation to the other. Affirmation and laughter are associated with
responsibility, which Derrida explores in Donner la mort, when writing


408  Concluding Remarks
about Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice Isaac. Laughing and affirming
exemplify the ethical impetus that is driving Derrida’s work.120
We have seen that Derrida writes about laughter in relation to Bataille,
about parody and play in relation of Nietzsche and about the laughter
of affirmation in relation to Joyce. As Derrida comments on the texts of
others rather than writing his own text, we should not expect to find a
Derridean laughter, a humor or irony that is properly “his.” However,
in the interview Derrida gave shortly before his death, Jean Birnbaum
detects “a laughing voice,” and Cotte notes in Derrida’s work a laughter
that makes us reflect, a laughter yet to come and full of promise.121
Cotte also identifies a Derridean irony of différance and deconstruc-
tion which opens the Hegelian dialectic to the laughter of the remain-
der.122 Cotte maintains that the same relation holds between Derrida’s
irony and the Hegelian system as diagnosed by Derrida when addressing
Bataille’s laughter and the system: the Bataillean laughter of sovereignty
only troubles the discourse by disclosing the nonsense which submerges
it; the system acknowledges that it cannot encompass everything; rather
than abolished, it is redynamized by Bataille. In the same way, the Der-
ridean irony of différance does not stop the movement of the Hegelian
system. Derrida resisted the attribution of irony, which was ascribed
to him by some commentators and denied by others. Let me detail this
controversy.
Jacques Bouveresse argues that the strangeness of Derrida’s position
is the result of a combination of satire, on the one hand, which is in
principle pitiless toward the philosophic tradition and its significance
in Western civilization; and, on the other hand, an intrinsically positive
and completely traditional conception of that which we can still hope,
expect and demand of philosophy, regardless of the form it will have to
take from now on.123 Ernst Behler makes the same point in relation to
the criticism of philosophy undertaken by postmodernists; however, he
finds a “post-Nietzschean irony,” which “is perhaps best accomplished
in the writings of Jacques Derrida.” He claims that “from this formal
point of view,” Derrida’s texts appear as a congenial contemporary cor-
respondence to the tradition of irony in the modern period”; he never-
theless admits that Derrida “avoids the word irony, at least he does not
accord any prominence to it in its writings.”124
Richard Rorty notes that “Derrida found again…the slaphappy je-
m’en-foutisme of Nietzsche,” his refusal of being “serious, concentrated
and thoughtful.”125 To the contrary, Bouveresse argues that the task
that Derrida set for himself should imply a good dose of irony and
skepticism toward this enterprise. But there is no trace of that in the
most characteristic productions of the deconstruction school. Their de-
rision strangely lacks any reflexive dimension and ignores completely
the kind of redoubling which characterizes the attitude of the genuine
je-m’en-foutisme.126 It is true that Nietzsche himself is far from having
entirely escaped from the fatal contamination of the spirit of seriousness.


Concluding Remarks  409
Yet for most of his disciples, it should not be possible to fall prey to
the very mistake they believe they are the only ones to have overcome.
Contemporary forms of thought that consider themselves, directly or
indirectly, Nietzschean often preach to serious people a form of ironic
jubilation which they are incapable of practicing with a minimum of
spontaneity, naturalness and conviction.127 In Deconstruction in a Nut-
shell, John Caputo titles a section, “Deconstruction Is Serious Business.”
He maintains that “Derrida is perfectly serious… Deconstruction, after
all, is serious business. It is gravity itself, if it has an itself.”128
Thus, a controversy surrounds the need for self-referential laugh-
ter, for lightness or irony in Derrida’s project; the very presence of any
self-referential skeptical attitude, lightness or irony in Derrida’s writings
is also a matter of dispute, as it is in the writings of his followers in the
school of deconstruction.
Among Derrida’s numerous followers, Bernard Pautrat, Jean-Michel
Rey, Sarah Kofman and Jean-Luc Nancy reflect on laughter. I focus on
Kofman because her views are significant both for philosophy and for
the comical, and on Nancy, who writes in the wake of Bataille yet in-
troduces a view of transcendent laughter that fits his own transcendent
philosophy.
3  Sarah Kofman: The Comical—The Proper Talent of
Philosophical Genius
Sarah Kofman (1934–94) positioned herself as a woman philosopher of
deconstruction. She collaborated first with Jean Hippolyte and later with
Deleuze, yet it was Derrida who was decisive for her thought. Her Ni-
etzsche et la métaphore (1972), where she pays attention to Nietzsche’s
style and to Nietzsche’s figurative language in particular is heavily in-
debted to Derrida.129 She was renowned for her work on Freud’s attitude
toward women130; for this study, however, her work on Freud’s theories
of the comical is of greater significance.131
Given Kofman’s interest in Freud, her attitude toward Nietzsche be-
comes a distinctly powerful analytical method, “a Derridean-Freudian ap-
proach, at once semiotic and symptomatic,”132 which is enlightened by her
interest in the comical. While her reading of Nietzsche through Freud was
typical of the 1960s and 1970s in France, she is particularly methodical in
that approach. Critical of Deleuze’s view of Nietzsche,133 she defends the
latter’s reputation as a philosopher in Nietzsche et la scène philosophique
at the same time that she “underscores the comic talent Nietzsche displays
in the course of Nietzsche’s parodic critiques,” as Duncan Large notes.134
Most importantly in relation to this study, she maintains:
To read Nietzsche on “the great philosophers” is to attend a com-
ical show, a “primitive scene” where the smallest mistakes, and
the smallest missteps of those who present themselves as masters


410  Concluding Remarks
of thought are watched with pitiless vigilance. It is to denounce the
childishness of the old philosophers, strip them of their earnestness
and senility and make them laughable.
With Nietzsche, philosophy enters the domain of comedy, and it
appears that the most proper talent—the most hidden as well—of
the philosophical genius is the comical talent. The philosopher is a
comedian who hides behind the speculative mask the pharmaceu-
tical function of philosophy, its most persistent will: to make the
intolerable tolerable. This is a cathartic will, which in its way repeats
the will of tragedy, a will denied by the philosophers, whose most
tenacious phantasm has always been the will to autonomy, to inde-
pendence from impulsive, Dionysiac forces.135
This view of philosophy is embodied by Baubô—the servant who made
Demeter laugh by showing her private parts. Nietzsche relates to this
myth in the Gay Science and makes it a symbol of the truth. Baubô in
Greek mythology is the figure of laughter, affirmation, rebirth and re-
newal. For Kofman, she is the counterbalance of Dionysus because she
represents the fecundity of laughter—the emblem of her own affirmative
philosophy.
Kofman championed the cause of women in both Nietzsche and Freud,
showing how their respective views derived from the former’s ambiva-
lent love and the latter’s fear of women. In Explosions, parts I and II
(1992, 1993), she explains every word of Nietzsche’s Ecce Homo, reject-
ing the received opinions that it is a “mad” and straight autobiographic
text. Her last engagement with Nietzsche addresses his relation to the
Jews, Le mépris des Juifs: Nietzsche, les Juifs, l’antisémitisme ([1994];
Scorning Jews: Nietzsche, the Jews, and Anti-Semitism), where she de-
fends him against the Nazi appropriation of his texts. She did not read
Nietzsche with Marx or with Heidegger; rather, she emphasized the
ludic and autobiographical character of his text, deeming him both a
woman and a Jew.136
Among other scholars, Tina Chanter and Pleshette DeArmitt com-
ment on the affirmative stance of Kofman’s philosophy.137 Notable in
their anthology is Ann Smock’s essay about Kofman’s wit (2008). Smock
argues that Kofman liked “to play the role of a mocking girl whose
laughter interrupts the philosopher at his desk, scatters grave truths
the better to greet in their stead beautiful fictions, uncanny signs, and
figures ‘devilishly deceptive.’”138 Approaching the great thinkers of the
Western intellectual tradition with child-like irreverence, she played
with their ideas, laughed at their poses and put her finger on their blind
spots. Deemed a “laughing and dancing philosopher in the Nietzschean
vein” by Verena Andermatt Conley,139 Kofman shows in L’Enigme de la
femme: La femme dans les textes de Freud (1980) how Freud’s theory of
feminine sexuality continues the masculine and metaphysical tradition,


Concluding Remarks  411
which excludes women at the same time that it deconstructs this very
same tradition with its hierarchical binary oppositions.
Kofman’s study of Freud’s book on Witz (Joke/Wit) transforms it into
a philosophic text. She deems, why do we laugh? “a very important ques-
tion.” Witz in her reading becomes a Janus double-faced rogue, whose
magical moves, worthy of the greatest hypnotizer, force laughter yet
without one’s knowledge of why one is laughing or what one is laughing
at. It is Freud’s ambivalence toward his Jewishness that Kofman reveals
through this study,140 as well as the necessary play of truth with illusion
that the study of Witz imposes: “One” laughs neutrally and anonymously
while communicating through the contagious propagation of this laugh-
ter with the entirety of the fraternal assembly which spread from mouth
to mouth the word, the annunciation of a terrible victory: “the victory
on society and its taboos, which for the length of a (totemic) feast, of one
word, are lifted in euphoria for the greatest general relief.”141
Few are capable of humor,142 because few are capable of living with
no illusions without sinking under life’s injustices. In “Sarah Kofman’s
Wit,” Smock notes the “buoyant clear-headedness” as evoked in
Kofman’s quatre romans analytiques.143 To recognize that the more dif-
ficult task is not different from a child’s play, that frivolity can be found
in the most profound matters, that science and fiction are not opposites
and that truth and illusion are interwoven requires a vitality which is not
given to all. The triumph of humor implies an unassailable narcissism,
Smock argues, as that of beautiful unapproachable women.144 However,
there is no such thing,
no perfect self-sufficiency… no such simple, happy mastery that a
servile double has not edged aside, as it were and cause to differ
from itself, granting it in this contradictory way alone its carefree
self-assurance.
(Smock 2008, 37)
Much like Bataille, Kofman maintains that the humorist loses and at-
tains his happy position simultaneously. His identity both withdraws
from him and crowns him. Thus, “Humor muddles the clear distinction
between triumph and defeat, mastery and abjection; it shows that gaiety
dwells in despair.”145
In her study of Shakespeare, Conversions, Kofman argues that the
playwright shows the vanity both of human life and of simple oppo-
sitions. “Lodging madness inside wisdom and comedy with tragedy,
he shows the interdependence of time’s two faces, mania and melan-
choly.”146 Indeed, this is the very way Smock characterizes the entirety
of Kofman’s work: “That hilarity and desperation are double, that tri-
umph and humiliation cannot be disentangled, is what Kofman demon-
strates regularly in her work,” but nowhere more poignantly than in the


412  Concluding Remarks
essay “Le battu imbattable,” Smock argues, where “utter degradation
is exhilarating.” In the story that Kofman relates in the latter work, a
clown manages to change tragedy into comedy by switching from a pas-
sive to an active position in relation to his disgrace.147 Such contempt for
self and others is not suited for everyone; if one has not felt the sting of
one’s scorn, one may be trapped in self-satisfaction. Thinking highly of
oneself yet also scorning oneself is the precondition for telling jokes; it
is the expression of the double character of the Jews, she has Freud say.
Her own predilection for double-edged instruments is exemplified in her
study of Nietzsche and the Jews.
Jokes have a collective structure and are a social product, she a rgues,
as do Nancy and Philippe Lacoue-Labarthe. However, by having
 simultaneous conscious as well as unconscious content, and thus daz-
zling the censor, they are Janus-faced much like laughter and art. That
is, their essence is that of the double, “diabolically unidentifiable, wreak-
ing havoc in the system that opposes appearance to reality, surface to
depth,” like laughter, which “wrings meaning’s neck and opens a place
of indetermination.”148
Kofman was eulogized posthumously by Derrida as the best reader of
both Freud and Nietzsche, which she claimed as identificatory figures:
She loved them pitilessly and was implacable toward them (not to
mention a few others) at the very moment when, giving them with-
out mercy all that she could, and all that she had, she was inheriting
from them and was keeping watch over what they had—what they
still have—to tell us, especially regarding art and laughter.
(Derrida 2007, 7)
He stresses the place of laughter in her studies, and notes her “irresist-
ible joy of uncontrollable laughter on the verge of tears,” which others
emphasized along with her joy.149 Renowned for her self- deprecating
laughter, Kofman committed suicide. Thus, Derrida adds, “I want to
believe that she laughed right up to the end, right up to the very last
second.”150
The most striking affirmations of Kofman in relation to the comical
are, to my mind, that the proper talent of philosophical genius, also the
most hidden, is the comical talent, and that utter degradation is exhilarat-
ing. The former view she shares with Deleuze and the latter with Bataille.
However, she made these views her own by transforming them into an
affirmative philosophy which she practiced till she ended her own life.
4 Jean-Luc Nancy: Transcendental Laughter and Critical Witz
Jean-Luc Nancy (1940–) maintains in several interviews that after Jean-
Paul Sartre, Derrida brought something new to philosophy. Inspired by the
latter’s work, he organized in 1980 with his long-life friend and colleague,


Concluding Remarks  413
Philippe Lacoue-Labarthe, a conference in Cerisy-la-Salle on Derrida and
politics, Les fins de l’homme. This conference helped to consolidate Derrida’s
place at the apex of current philosophy. The only contemporary philosopher
on whose thought Derrida penned a book (Derrida 2000), Nancy continues
Derrida’s work with deconstruction by reading and thinking mostly about
other authors and developing his own thesis out of this commentary.
While Nancy contributed to Nietzsche’s scholarship,151 it is his com-
mentary on Bataille, “La communauté désoeuvrée” (1983), that made
him famous. This work led Blanchot to tackle the question of commu-
nity and to address Nancy’s comments on Bataille in La Communauté
inavouable (1983). Nancy answers with two books of his own.152
Nancy’s interest in laughter spans the entirety of his work. He trans-
lated Jean Paul Richter’s Vorschule der Aesthetik, published an article
on Witz and edited with Lacoue-Labarthe an anthology of Romantic
literature in which he addresses Romantic irony. Nancy’s view of laugh-
ter is presented as a commentary on a poem by Charles Baudelaire,153 in
which he disregards his theory of laughter (1968) but comments in the
wake of Bataille on the meaning of Nietzsche’s aphorism, “To see higher
natures perish and to laugh at it…this belongs to greatness!”154
Nancy explains how laughter and death are related and what is their
association with the divine. His explanation differs from Bataille’s:
Nancy believes that the Romantic movement was right in asserting our
yearning for the Absolute,155 and he develops a transcendent philosophy,
which was close at first to Catholicism. Because for Nancy immortality
does exist, the role of laughter differs: laughter “knows” that we are
immortal and indicates the way beyond death. Nancy’s understanding
of Bataille’s ecstasy, which is enabled by laughter, is transformed by his
transcendent philosophy. He sees in it “the ontological as well as the
epistemological impossibility of an absolute immanence,”156 a release
from the self’s lack of place.
Nancy notes that laughter symbolizes the limits of meaning and some-
times its absence, as there is no origin to meaning and no accessible
truth. Laughter symbolizes the point at which it becomes evident that
there is no full meaning, and is, therefore, best accounted of as a tran-
scendental laugh. Divorced from the comic, laughter reflects “the flaw
at the heart of all attempts to create meaning,” the ultimate inability to
square systems with ultimate meanings. Andrew Stott sees in Nancy’s
laughter “a fundamental contradiction that affronts modes of under-
standing that are grounded in reason,” a kind of “metaphysical contra-
diction encountered at the boundary of reason.”157
Rather than laughter, it is Witz, the wit that the German Roman-
tics elevated to the rank of worldview or life’s aesthetic that fulfills for
Nancy the role of critical perception of our world. It perfectly exempli-
fies the dissonant complementarity of literature and philosophy. Actual
today as it was in the past, wit is knowledge—Wissen—which sees and
immediately grasps the idea and distinguishes with lucidity.158


414  Concluding Remarks
5  Jean-François Lyotard: Humor—An Essential
Tone of the Postmodern
Jean-François Lyotard (1928–98), a key intellectual contemporary fi gure,
left a work which is heterogeneous, as it spans various disciplines, and is
marked by abrupt shifts in tone, style, form and thematic concerns. His
highly inventive style has earned him the title of “writer-philosopher,”
a literary creator rather than a purely technical or academic thinker.159
Truth cannot be separated from style in Lyotard, and two of the “most
important tones” in reading him are directly relevant to this study, ac-
cording to editors Keith Crome and James Williams: laughter and irony
(the remaining two are fear and passion).160 However, fear is also of
interest because laughter is associated with fear in Lyotard’s thought,
“as if joy were not full until it had risen out of despair and out of the fear
of a final nihilistic absence of will.”161 His deepest fear is of the ways
in which the body can fail us; yet he recognizes the revelatory power of
these failures, which bring along new capacities to affirm and to create.
In the same way,
Lyotard’s irony, though stylistically light, has the high ethical role
of testifying to that which we can never know, but only sense as
unknowable. It is, then, not an irony of contradictory propositions
or positions, but one of paradoxical obligations without release. The
irony is not one of sneering asides or clever mind-games, it is one of
profound ethical lessons, where we learn of the limitations of even
pour most powerful and valuable ideas in the face of feelings and
demands that we can only testify to and fully articulate.
(Crome and Williams 2006, 17)
Lyotard has been writing about postmodernism long before he settled
for a name for it.162 According to the notion of the postmodern in Just
Gaming,163 to be postmodern is to be in the realm of the “pagan.” The
pagan is a space outside received law. It is an affirmative, rather than a
nihilistic, stance: to be pagan is to accept the fact that there is no univer-
sal language game and that the best that one can do is to play one’s game
well, with imagination and cunning; it is to judge without criteria. As a
result, Lyotard claims that “humor is an essential tone” of the postmod-
ern. However, the laughter that closes the conversation with Jean-Loup
Thébaud, which constitutes Just Gaming, seems to acknowledge the un-
tenability of his position.164 Schrift argues that:
This universal proclamation of the justice of multiplicity is, how-
ever, difficult to maintain from within a Nietzschean perspective, as
both Lyotard and Thébaud realize when they laugh in response to
Thébaud’s closing observation that Lyotard here “is talking like the
great prescriber himself.”165


Concluding Remarks  415
Given Lyotard’s understanding of politics and evil, “politicians cannot
have the good at stake, but they ought to have the lesser evil.” As the
lesser evil ought to be the political good,166 it is impossible to take en-
tirely seriously the law established by political sovereignty since it will
always create victims, those whose voices are silenced by the law. Ly-
otard sees humor as “the locus of opposition to the inadequacies of the
law: the law should always be respected with humor because it cannot
be completely respected.” The people must always to some extent laugh
at the law: “The people is not the sovereign; it is the defender of the dif-
ferend against the sovereign. It is full of laughter. Politics is tragedy for
the authorities, comedy for the people.”167
Lyotard’s predilection for problems and paradoxes, “for irony and hu-
mor, over solutions and settled positions… is the sign of a philosopher
wary of making claims to truth or commitments to methods that curtail
thought and stunt our capacity to feel and think differently,” Crome and
Williams affirm.168 This view may not be without dissidents, as irony
and humor as well as the comical and laughter are not part of The Ly-
otard’s Reader and Guide (2006).169
We turn now to additional thinkers that work in Nietzsche’s wake.
The interest that feminists have in Nietzsche may seem out of place
given the latter’s misogyny. However, many of them have found in his
thought the tools for an effective critique of the existing order; some
have also found the tools for creating an autonomous woman. I ad-
dress three feminists that work in Nietzsche’s wake, Irigaray, Cixous
and Kristeva.
6 Luce Irigaray: Feminist Humor Is Inauthentic
The French feminist philosopher, Luce Irigaray (1930–) wrote a book
on and for Nietzsche, translated as Marine Lover of Friedrich Nietzsche
(1991), where she represents a female voice, a lover, who responds to
Nietzsche.
Irigaray is concerned about the erasure of women in the discourse of
men. She indicates that laughter can be liberating for women. She states
that her first impulse when she envisions possibilities for women outside
of the masculine imaginary is to laugh. She notes that laughter can be
the first stage of liberation from subjugation because it can be opposed to
the masculine “seriousness of meaning,” and laughter can help maintain
a sense of humor among women. Women’s sense of humor is important
insofar as it impedes the operation of a “simple reversal of the masculine
position,” which would replace the hegemony of men with a hegemony
of women, that would still involve problematic power relations:
Isn’t laughter the first form of liberation from a secular oppression?
Isn’t the phallic tantamount to the seriousness meaning? Perhaps
woman, and the sexual relation, transcend it “first” in laughter?


416  Concluding Remarks
Besides, women among themselves begin by laughing. Escape
from a pure and simple reversal of the masculine position means
in any case not to forget to laugh. Not to forget that the dimen-
sion of pleasure, is untranslatable, unrepresentable, irrecuperable,
in the  “seriousness”—the adequacy, the truth…—of a discourse
that claims to state its meaning. Whether it is produced by men or
women. Which is not to assert that one has to give in to saying just
anything at all, but that speaking the truth constitutes the prohi-
bition on woman’s pleasure, and thus on the sexual relation. The
covering-up of its forcefulness, of force itself, under the lawmaking
power of discourse. Moreover, it is right here that the most virulent
issue at stake in the oppression of women is located today: men want
to hold onto the initiative of discourse about sexual pleasure, and
thus also about her pleas.
(Irigaray 1985, 163)
Irigaray gives us a picture of laughter as a crucial stage in the process of
women asserting their speech outside the totalizing limits of men, out-
side of phallogocentrism.170
However, she argues in Sexes et parentés (1987) that as yet no female
values exist. Thus, feminist humor is inauthentic in that it merely apes
the power-structures of phallocracy and the assumptions of phallocen-
trism. Thus, although Irigaray advocates for the power of laughter in
relation to women who talk on their own terms, she does not explain
how this will happen or even can happen independently from a social
change that would help create a new form of humor. A similar case for
the liberating power of laughter is made by Cixous, yet also here no way
is indicated as to how it can be so, except in the “text,” in writing.
7 Hélène Cixous: The Feminine Laughter of Hysteria
The author and philosopher Hélène Cixous (1937–) has been associated
with Bataille because she “writes of excess as effusion, eros, poetry,
drunkenness, and laughter.”171 She wrote an influential text called The
Laughter of the Medusa (1976 [1975]).172 As much a novelist and dra-
matist as a theoretician, her theory of humor is coextensive with her
comic writing. Her work has been characterized as “full of humour.”173
She writes of a nouvel art de rire as if it were coterminous with a nouvel
art de vivre yet she does not theorize it.174
Cixous’s novels end with paradoxical and inexplicable gales of laugh-
ter, which may be condemned as hysterical by those who distance them-
selves from it. According to Cixous, Freudian psychology focused its
entire energy against hysteria and therefore against femininity, while she
claims solidarity with hysterics—they are her “sisters”175—and one of


Concluding Remarks  417
the most obvious, striking and perhaps disturbing features of hysteria
is the uncontrolled and unexplained laughter. For Cixous it is signifi-
cant and appropriate that this laughter disturbs, for it is “the moment
at which the woman crosses a dangerous line—the cultural demarcation
beyond which she will find herself excluded.”176
This laughter is joyful rather than humorous, final, freeing, illogical,
redeeming and intentionally therapeutic. Cixous’s La Jeune née has been
praised for favoring monstrosity and excess as characteristics of those
new forms of laughter that will help undo socio-cultural constructs.
Like Joyce, on whom she wrote her doctoral dissertation, she holds com-
edy to be the superior genre,177 as “the secret of tragedy” is that “it is
always two steps away from the ridiculous.”178
Cixous outlines a future feminine writing which should aim at sub-
verting the status quo while rehabilitating the dominant symbols under
whose shadow woman has been marginalized. These symbols include
the abyss, with its connotations of swallowing, smothering, the body
and the vulva, and the Medusa with her attributes of danger, horror and
evil. Cixous’s voice will be a voice from the ovaries, situated as deep as
possible in the abîme,179 and her redeemed medusa will be recognized as
a beautiful and “laughing creature.”180
8  Julia Kristeva: Laughter—Participating in the
Mother-Infant Initial Bond
Julia Kristeva (1941–) is a linguist and psychoanalyst, the wife of Philippe
Sollers and an editorial member of the journal he founded, Tel Quel.
Kristeva derides the masculine fear of women and mocks Nietzsche’s
fear of the body, both his own and the body of women. She argues that
subtending the rational subject is a sexuate subject governed by uncon-
scious desires, and subtending philosophy itself is a male imaginary. The
male replica, which women are supposed to be is the target of feminist
and deconstructive attacks. She points to the passional foundations of
the male reason and the male subject and comes to see women as their
interlocutors in philosophy.
She uses the mother-child relation, which is obscured in the thought
of Freud and Lacan, to explain laughter. Kristeva contributes to laughter
theory by showing the significant role laughter plays in the concept of
chora that she reclaimed from Plato:
Every practice that produces something new (a new device) is a prac-
tice of laughter. It obeys laughter’s logic and provides the subject with
laughter’s advantages. When practice is not laughter, there is nothing
new, practice cannot be provoking: it is at best a repeated, empty act.
(Kristeva 1984, 225)


418  Concluding Remarks
At the beginning was laughter, as many cosmologies tell us. Kristeva
notes that laughter remains the privileged experience of the artist. Gloss-
ing Bataille, she explains that it is “a sovereignty (of the subject and
of meaning, but also of history) that is simultaneously assumed and
undermined.”181
Chora, to which Plato refers in the Timaeus, is the nonplace needed
to think the relation of the two categories of creation, the visible and
the intelligible.182 Kristeva draws on the metaphors Plato uses for chora,
such as mother or “imprint bearer,” to conceptualize the relationship
between the mother and the infant, which she sees as an ungendered an-
imate “it.” The mother becomes a mother through an invocation, a voice
that is not a demand; more specifically, she receives a laugh: the dual “it”
that the mother and the child form laughs. This “it” is the space-time of
a laughing voice, Parvulescu argues, the voice “scores a point: laughter.”
“It” laughs.183
This is something that escapes language but remains in the realm of
affect. The unarticulated sounds, rhythms and flashes of colors of that
maternal receptacle is part of a feminine, prelinguistic semiotic which
striates the symbolic order and prevents its closure. As we have seen,
laughter holds an important role in this semiotic, as the contact or the
relation between the mother and the infant, where “it” laughs.
In laughter, the subject is not the agent of an external action but has
an “interest” in the action. “Through the action, the subject achieves
something which is being achieved in him and—being born, lying [help-
less or dead], imagining, growing, etc. The subject is somewhat ‘inside’
the process of which he is the agent.” The subject participates in the ac-
tion without predicating it. This is the relationship between the subject
of laughter and the action of laughing. The laugher is “interested” in the
laughter and “participates” in it.184
We access laughter synchronically through laughter. The mother in
us laughs again: our bursts of laughter are a memorial of the mother-
infant initial bond through chora. This is what the Roman poet, Virgil,
attempts to capture when he writes, “Begin, young child, by recognizing
your mother by your laughter.”185
Kristeva acknowledges the significant role that the comic plays in
postmodernism. She actually differentiates between modernity and
postmodernity according to their relationship with the comical: while
“the modern essentially focuses on the ‘malady of pain,’” the postmod-
ern “lies closer to the human comedy than to abysmal malaise.”186
It is time to find out if she is right. The account I have given of the
main French Nietzscheans’ views of laughter is by no means exhaus-
tive: focusing on philosophers, I have deliberately left out psychoana-
lysts, like Lacan, and sociologists, like Jean Baudrillard.187 I would like
now to generalize the findings of the specific theories and probe post-
modern laughter in its various declinations as the comical, parody and


Concluding Remarks  419
pastiche, play, cynicism and sarcasm, humor and irony. A criticism of
postmodern irony ends the Concluding Remarks.
C Postmodern Laughter
David Michael Levin defines the postmodern situation as an awareness
of the impossibly to trust “in the old vision of reason—and in the ‘Man’
of its humanism.” Finding it difficult to live in the light of the modern
or traditional paradigm of knowledge, truth and reality, postmodernism
describes a crisis, which it sees as our “present plight.”188 This crisis is
variously defined in relation to laughter, the comic, play, parody and
pastiche, cynicism and sarcasm, and finally humor and irony, as we shall
shortly see. The reason for the association of postmodernism with a cog-
nate of the comical lies, I believe, in Rorty’s assertion, that it is comical
to think that there is something called Truth.189
1 The Comical
Postmodernity has been associated with the comical by various authors.
To take a few examples, Mark Weeks notes that in the latter decades of
the twentieth century philosophical, literary and cultural studies were
imbued with something of a comic spirit. Postmodernism was identified
with and through images of play, energy and movement that sought to
ceaselessly and joyfully throw into crisis our faith in the permanence
of structures.190 Targeting more specifically twentieth-century philoso-
phers, Lisa Trahair notes:
Comedy, the comic, the ludic, the joke, play and laughter are terms
which pervade the works of Derrida, Baudrillard, Lyotard and
 Weber—they are but better-known examples of what might consid-
ered a more general phenomenon of incorporating the tenets of the
comic into contemporary philosophical thinking.191
To the philosophers she lists, we can add Foucault, Deleuze, Guattari,
Pautrat, Cixous, and Derrida’s followers, Kofman and Rey, in France as
well as many outside of France.192
Levin associates the crisis that postmodernism represents with
 Nietzsche, without addressing laughter or play as one of the German
philosopher’s influence:
