Drawing on insights of Nietzsche, whose extraordinary foresight
positioned him almost a century ahead of his time, the discourse of
postmodern thinking begins with a consciousness of deepening cri-
sis…it is this consciousness of this situation which separates us from
modernity; but postmodern discourse is not only a discourse which


420  Concluding Remarks
takes as its problem the experience of a crisis; it is also a discourse
which is itself in crisis: a discourse without grounds, without sub-
ject, without an origin, without any absolute center, without reason.
This sense of crisis, and of being irremediably separated, by this
crisis, from the questions and answers that have challenged us in the
past, figures in the thinking of all those who have let themselves be
guided by Nietzsche’s vision.
(Levin 1988, 5)
Various authors relate the postmodern propensity to the comical to
Nietzsche. Bates opens Play in a Godless World with the argument,
“Nietzsche, the arch-philosopher of play…anticipates the playful philos-
ophy which has become the hallmark of postmodern times.”193 Daniel
O’Hara notes in the preface to Why Nietzsche Now:
Friedrich Nietzsche is not a serious writer…Nietzsche can only be
seen as the prophet of our laughter…it is as the prophet of an ironic
perception of the worthlessness at the heart of culture alone that we
laugh at and with him.194
These evaluations are significant for characterizing English-speaking
contemporary philosophy; as noted by Alan Schrift already in 1995, “It
bears notice that, at this historical moment, Nietzsche’s French legacy is
playing itself out more than anywhere else in the English-speaking phil-
osophical and critical worlds.”195 Schrift does not address the comical.
As the French legacy has incorporated the comical, its impact on the
English-speaking philosophical and critical world should be felt.
How is the postmodern related to the comical? According to Lance
Olsen’s Circus of the Mind in Motion: Postmodernism and the Comic
Vision, postmodernity “is a radical skeptical state of mind whose im-
pulse is to decenter, detotalize, and deconstruct while taking nothing,
including its own (non)premises—very seriously.”196 We have seen that
Kristeva differentiates between modernity and postmodernity according
to their association with the comical, the former focusing on “the ‘mal-
ady of pain,’” whereas the latter lies “closer to the human comedy than
to abysmal malaise.”197 This differentiation is deemed by Olsen “too
simplistic an opposition,”198 as the comical and the postmodern tend to
complement each other. He argues that
Both attempt to subvert all centers of authority—including their
own—and because they both ultimately deride univocal visions,
toppling bigots, cranks, and pompous idiots as they go… Both
seek through radical incongruity of form to short-circuit the domi-
nant culture’s repressive impulses. Hence, both are simultaneously
destructive and constructive. Both represent a survivalist aesthet-
ics…. Both focus on process rather than conclusion. Both embrace


Concluding Remarks  421
plurality, an abundance of language games, and the idea that the
universe is a text that may be rewritten in a host of equally accept-
able ways. And both therefore understand, along with Johan Huiz-
inga, that “pure play is one of the main bases of civilization.”
(Huizinga 1970, 5; Olsen 1990, 31–2)
The comical and postmodernism have much in common, according to
Olsen. Notably, they share a predilection for pure play.
2 Play
In Play in a Godless World, Bates argues that deconstruction leads to
hyper-awareness rather than mindlessness. Mastery and identity are
 illusions, and while we know as much, we still follow them. In the the-
ater, we are captivated by what we know is a “play,” a fiction we like
to believe in. The self-cancelling rhetoric of deconstruction is akin to
play: “Order may be illusory and the scramble for it frankly neurotic
and that doesn’t mean that people want it any less, including those who
call themselves enlightened,” Bates argues. Jokes, which involve tension
and release, are the developed play of adults; laughter is the release but
joke is the play. The tension that can be found in play is a particular
one because it “can be either pleasurable or unpleasurable,” both tensed
and relaxed, meaningful and meaningless, reasonable and mad, both
creative and illusory. This kind of tension wishes to prolong itself to no
good end. To write out a play is itself a form of play.199
Humorous play resists certainties and conclusions, it is continually
creative, inventing new ways of seeing and thinking. By keeping poten-
tially oppressive authorities in check, these authorities are not destroyed
but valued. Thus, Olsen argues that there is much optimism in postmod-
ern play.200 However, the relationship to past authority is not simply
humorous; it is also parodic.
3 Parody
In the later 1980s, theorists of postmodern fiction such as Linda Hutch-
eon defined postmodernism “as a contradictory phenomenon, one that
uses and abuses, installs and then subverts, the very concepts it chal-
lenges.”201 It does not unconditionally reject, as does the purely self-
reflective text—which Hutcheon sees as late modern—but it ironizes,
through “parody (the perfect postmodern form)” and other strategies.202
Thus, parody, which Frederick Jameson deems “pastiche” or the imita-
tion of dead styles, characterizes postmodernity.203 Sarup explains,
…the great modernisms were predicated on the invention of a per-
sonal, private style. The modernist aesthetic was organically linked
to the conception of an authentic self and a private identity which


422  Concluding Remarks
can be expected to generate its own unique vision of the world and
to forge its own unmistakable style. The poststructuralists argue
against this; in their view the concept of the unique individual and
the theoretical basis of individualism are ideological. Not only is the
bourgeois individual subject a thing of the past, it is also a myth, it
never really existed in the first place… And so, in a world in which
stylistic innovation is no longer possible all is left… is pastiche…the
imitation of dead styles…
(Sarup 1999, 146)
However, the parodying of the past is not without mockery. Thus, post-
modernism has been considered akin to cynicism, and recently also to
sarcasm.
4 Cynicism and Sarcasm
Hostage to their knowledge, postmodernists cannot help knowing
what they know. Thus, Bates argues, they make a virtue of necessity as
 “ratiocinative thought, deceptive as it is, stills allows them to see and to
articulate more clearly than anything else does the tragi-comic paradox
of their situation.”204
Bates notes the playful cynicism of Slavoj Žižek, who maintains that
“cynical distance, laughter, irony, are, so to speak, part of the game.”205
Žižek relies on Peter Sloterdijk’s description of the modern cynical atti-
tude, which differs from the ancient Cynics’ positive view of virtue and
the good life (1983).
Along the same lines, Timothy Bewes identifies postmodern irony as
cynicism (1997). While cynicism has been long considered part of post-
modern irony, Roger Kreutz has recently argued that it is sarcasm that is
irony’s “evil twin.”206 It is important to take into account this dark side
of postmodernism, either its cynicism or its sarcasm, when we evaluate
the proposal to associate it with humor rather than with irony.
5 Humor
In “Toward a Theory of Postmodern Humor,” Olsen argues that there is
nothing new in postmodern humor. His stance is that of someone who
is not a postmodern theorist and recognizes it in various epochs in the
past207: “Postmodern humor is an attitude that has arisen at various
times in various places but which has gained a striking prominence in
our contemporary culture both in ‘high’ and ‘low’ art.” Most impor-
tantly, rather than simply representing either a destructive or a construc-
tive thrust, it represents paradoxically both at once.208
There is a dark impetus in postmodern humor alongside an essentially
light one. The absences this kind of humor notes may signal the possibility


Concluding Remarks  423
of destruction, they also signal the possibility of construction, that is, a
radical freedom, a renewed sense of potential. Thus, postmodern humor re-
fuses to see truth as something that always exists along an either-or axis. It
becomes both a negative and a positive perspective on the world, simultane-
ously holding “within itself the destructive and nihilistic force of absurdist
black humor… and the constructive and affirmative force of creative free
play…. Postmodern humor delights in its own sense of liberty.”209
Olsen’s point is that postmodern existence has metamorphosed from
the ironic into the humorous. While humans once confronted a reality
that was basically sincere, interpretable and filled with indications of
how it should be read, we now face an unreality that is disingenuous,
against interpretation and unreadable. Ironists perceive such a postmod-
ern pluriverse as tragic because no truth is discoverable in it. Humorists
perceive such a postmodern pluriverse as comic for the same reason.
Texts produced by a humorous culture are of course themselves humor-
ous, and the humorous text, as Candace Lang acknowledges,
does not express meaning in the traditional, etymological sense of
exteriorizing what was interior to the authorial psyche …; it orga-
nizes a number of linguistic elements into systems offering a variety
of potential meanings to be actualized by the reader.210
Olsen relies on Lang’s distinction between irony and humor:
Irony is a state of mind that assumes the presence of meaning behind
or under a given text. In other words, truth is envisioned as the gold
that can and should be mined. Such a vision goes back at least as far
as Plato, who suggests that a “truer” reality exists behind this one.
Humor, on the other hand, is a state of mind that believes primarily
in surface, in a positive content. In other words, there is no “truth”
to humor, rather, an incessant questioning that yields no ultimate
answer. Such a vision goes at least as far as Socrates whose thought,
as Kierkegaard points out, is not subject to interpretation, in the
traditional sense, since there is no underlying message.
(Lang 1988, 3)
The modern text is primarily ironic, for it believes that its intent is to
communicate a message (although it chooses to do so in a less “sincere”
or direct way than a pre-modern non-ironic text). Thus, Olsen argues
that the postmodern text is primarily humorous because it believes its in-
tent is inconclusive, polyvalent, and unreadable through an ironic optic
because there is no meaning tucked under its surface. The ultimate dif-
ference between the ironic and the humorous attitude is as follows: “The
humorous, which needn’t necessarily be funny, delights in discontinuity;
the ironic, which needn’t necessarily be sad, mourns it.”211


424  Concluding Remarks
Bakhtin’s work can help us explain the difference between humor
and irony in terms of views of the world that suit postmodernism. In
Problems of Dostoevsky’s Poetics (1984), he differentiates between two
visions of the world. The first is monologic, the other is dialogic or poly-
phonic, the novels of Tolstoy exemplify the former, those of Dostoevsky
the latter. In the first case, all the voices in the work are subordinated
to the author’s univocal sense of truth. In the second case, no attempt
is made at univocal truth since each voice represents a unique point of
view and is allowed to speak for itself. The author pits one idea against
the other. Bakhtin states that an idea truly “begins to live, that is, to take
shape, to develop, to find and renew its verbal expression, to give birth
to new ideas, with the ideas of others.”212 The power of polyphonics is
that it forces “to quarrel” and it generates “new linkages of ideas… new
voice-ideas and changes in the arrangement of all the voice-ideas in the
worldwide dialogue.”213
Bakhtin finds the roots of polyphony in the carnival and “carnivalized”
genres as Menippean satire, a heterogeneous mode of discourse com-
posed of mixed prose forms interspersed with verse that foregrounds di-
alogues among various mental attitudes while backgrounding traditional
concerns of character and plot. Northrop Frye calls such a structure an
“encyclopedic farrago,” and Brian McHale refers to it as a “stylistic het-
eroglossia.”214 Clearly, the comic postmodern, who romps in polyphony,
plurality and the maximum freedom in a joyous relativity where all that
is rigid is overturned, is a descendant of such a mode, a radical intensifi-
cation of it rather than simply an extension of it. Indeed, as if to under-
score the point, images of carnivals pervade the comic postmodern text,
“from the weird winding hallways of Borges’s fiction to the funhouse
in John Barth’s famous creation, from the Schweinheldfest in Gravity’s
Rainbow to the grotesque country fairs in Ed McClanavan’s work.”215
Although postmodernism can be defined in terms of modes of con-
sciousness rather than historical periods, in terms of perspective rather
than chronology, it came to dominance since World War II. However, Ol-
sen and others note that postmodern atonality and hyper-self- reflexivity
can be read back in works by writers as varied as Miguel de Cervantes,
Laurence Sterne, Herman Melville and Franz Kafka.216
6 Irony
The case for the association of humor with postmodernism is made on
the plurivocal nature of humor as well as on the assumption, formulated
by Paul McDonald, that “humorous narrative can avoid becoming au-
thoritarian and absolutist because it can form assertions and simulta-
neously undermine them.”217 However, this is not the common way to
address postmodernism’s contradictory position. It is usually described
in terms of irony. For example, Gutting focuses on the differences


Concluding Remarks  425
between poststructuralism and structuralism to argue that the former
is inevitably ironic:
Poststructuralism combines the structuralist style of objective, tech-
nical, and even formal discourse about the human world with a re-
jection of the structuralist claim that there is any deep or final truth
that such discourse can uncover. The poststructuralist project need
not be self-contradictory, but it is inevitably ironic, since it sees its
method of analysis as both necessary and given traditional goals,
doomed to failure.218
The postmodern individual is defined by his understanding that he is
prone to mystification at every turn. However, as he has little choice, he
lives in a state of paradoxically enlightened mystification. Even if reality
is a colossal joke, as he believes, and all man-made orders are simply
myths designed to dupe, even if no illusion is left to him, in realizing this
he still remains a thinking, ordering and image-making creature, whether
he likes it or not. The best he can do is to set up ever more distant frames
of ironic detachment, raise himself on platforms from which to survey
everything—including his act of surveying—as pointless, empty and ab-
surd. Bates argues that as so long as he is doing this, “he’s still got his feet
firmly on the scaffolding. There is no escape from the mind…”219
Along similar lines, Claire Colebrook notes that many have argued
that our entire epoch, being postmodern, is ironic,220 which makes its
definition elusive:
Our very historical context is ironic because today nothing really
means what it says. We live in a world of quotation, pastiche, sim-
ulation and cynicism: a general and all-encompassing irony. Irony,
then, by the very simplicity of its definition [saying what is contrary
to what is meant] becomes curiously indefinable.
(Colebrook 2004, 1)
It is also widespread: irony is found in painting and architecture, in fic-
tion and is construed as a political attitude by Rorty.221 Let me elaborate
on each of these fields.
Postmodern architecture emerged as a reaction to Modernism and the
Modern Movement in architecture, which seemed elitist and exclusive
despite its democratic intentions. A colorful and eclectic style of archi-
tecture and the decorative arts that appeared from the late 1970s contin-
ues in some form today.
Like postmodern architecture, postmodernist painting combines his-
toricist awareness, a new representational impulse and an ironic self-
reflexivity. In his study of the history of postmodernism, Hans Bertens
notes that in America more and more critics in the early 1980s came to


426  Concluding Remarks
accept this view of the postmodern in painting.”222 Achille Bonito Olivo
notes similar developments in Europe. Its “international trans- avantgarde”
is ironical, it gives in to whims, and it deliberately avoids the heroic stances
of the modernists: “The work…presents small events related to individual
sensibility and circumscribed by adventures laced with irony and subtle
detachment.”223 Kim Levin notes how the 1970s innovations were dis-
guised as revivals; postmodern art reintroduces representation, illusion
and narration, but it does so “with irony, whimsy, and disbelief.”224
From a political point of view, irony offers the postmodernist a sem-
blance of freedom. However, as John McGowan remarks, irony is “un-
profitably close to the modernist goal of autonomy.”225 Significantly,
autonomy is the term that Rorty uses to describe the objective of his
postmodern “ironist,” who
is not in the business of supplying himself and his fellow ironists
with a method, a platform, or a rationale. He is just doing the same
thing that all ironists do—attempting autonomy. He is trying to get
out from under inherited contingencies and make his own contin-
gencies, get out from under an old final vocabulary and fashion one
which will be all his own. The generic trait of ironists is that they do
not hope to have their doubts about their final vocabularies settled
by something larger than themselves. This means that their criterion
for resolving doubts, their criterion of private perfection, is auton-
omy rather than affiliation to a power other than themselves.
(Rorty 1989, 97)
Rorty’s ironist attempts to retreat to a separate space, far from the po-
litical crowd. In postmodern texts, the use of the term “irony” or “iro-
nist” is lax; it has not much to with its original meaning. It seems that
to qualify something as “ironic” does not clarify much its nature. Rorty
uses it as a “definition of the contemporary intellectual,” who is for him
the same as the postmodern intellectual. He opposes the “ironist” to the
metaphysician and tells us that he favors redescription; interested in his
personal autonomy, the ironist uses philosophy for his own purposes—
on the condition that it will be called “theory” and does not bother with
the way others see him.
The concept of irony evolves in the realm of literary criticism, Kreutz
notes. Paul de Man, notably, used it in a way that “practically coincides
with the notion of deconstruction.”226 The “wisdom of uncertainty” that
Milan Kundera introduces in his art of the novel serves the postmodern
agenda in offering a kind of qualified debate that postmodenists need.
McDonald explains that the purpose is to create an arena where it is pos-
sible to present a debate in a qualified way with an implicit reservation
that uncertainty must be acknowledged. Hence the need for literature,
especially comical, and for humor and irony in a text.227 Postmodern
irony follows in the steps of Romantic irony. Both include the notions of


Concluding Remarks  427
self-awareness and skepticism, “which in literature can manifest in the
intrusion of the creator into the work itself.” Romantic irony “has also
become a fixture in postmodern writing”; the trope of self-awareness
can also be found in the cinema and on radio and television and is being
referred to as “breaking the fourth wall.”228
In a recent book on irony, Kreutz’s Irony and Sarcasm (2020), the au-
thor has very little to say about postmodern irony. The sitcom Seinfeld may
be “considered the apotheosis of the ironic sensibility,” he writes, describ-
ing the program’s characters as “detached, apathetic, jaded, flippant, self-
absorbed, and superficial.”229 Indeed, a show about nothing, it reflected
the wider postmodern sensibility “that had been part of the American cul-
ture since World War II, infusing the arts in general with a self-referential
and relativistic ethos.”230 After 9/11, there were many claims about the
death of irony, whose ambiguity as a term came to be seen as synonymous
with a sardonic, flippant or facetious worldview. Rather than verbal or
situation irony, “for many, irony now refers first and foremost to the ironic
attitude.”231 And the ironic attitude became a fixture in popular culture.
Kreutz notes that this attitude has been criticized before 9/11 and
that “pronouncements of irony’s death have been made on a regular
basis.”232 However, those who write irony’s obituary have exaggerated
once again. He argues that the ironic attitude has played an important
role throughout the US history, as a way of “speaking truth to power,” a
powerful tool for non-violent protest.233
Thus, one contradiction in relation to irony is that being associated
with the young, it is criticized by the elders, and may be “both alive and
dead at the same time.” Another contradiction is noted by Colebrook in
concluding Irony: postmodern irony can neither be achieved nor over-
come; while one way to understand postmodernity is to see it as a radical
rejection or redefinition of irony, another is to see it as the impossibility
of overcoming irony.234
While the future of the ironic attitude may be assured, the future of
irony as a coherent concept is less certain.235 This study, then, culminates
in the demise of postmodern irony and of irony tout court as Bataille,
Deleuze and Rosset, as well as Jankélévitch and Comte- Sponville, and
also Lyotard and Derrida either object to irony or transcend it, following
a long tradition of philosophers who did the same, or as is the case with
Derrida, simply ignore it.
III Conclusion
The Concluding Remarks of this study addressed French laughter in
the twentieth century as conceptualized by non-Nietzscheans, such as
Jankélévitch and Comte-Sponville, and by various Nietzscheans, such as
Foucault, Derrida and his followers, Kofman and Nancy, but also Ly-
otard, Irigaray, Cixous and Kristeva. This study could not have been
completed without engaging with the thought of the philosophers addressed


428 Concluding Remarks
above. In order to understand the impact of Nietzschean laughter on phi-
losophy, its fate in France had to be followed into its postmodern forms.
Thus, the Concluding Remarks led to analyzing postmodern laughter
into its constituents, spanning the comical as well as the play, parody,
cynicism and sarcasm, humor and irony that make it what it is. And, in
the process of this analysis, the notion of postmodern irony disintegrated
along with the opinion that Bataille, Deleuze and Rosset, or Jankélévitch
and Comte- Sponville, or again Lyotard and Derrida endorsed irony. Not
only is irony not definable or viable in the present; but contrary to com-
mon belief, irony has been repeatedly rejected in the past from Aristotle
on and indeed endorsed in philosophy only by the German Romantics.236
Nietzsche claims that “we should call every truth false which was not
accompanied by at least one laugh”237; he yearns “to laugh at oneself as
one would have to laugh in order to laugh out of the whole truth.”238
He notes that:
To do that even the best so far lacked sufficient sense for the truth,
and the most gifted had too little genius for that. Even laughter may
yet have a future. I mean, when the proposition “the species is ev-
erything, one is always none” has become part of humanity, and this
ultimate liberation and irresponsibility has become accessible to all
at all times. Perhaps laughter will then have formed an alliance with
wisdom, perhaps only “gay science” will then be left.
(GS, 1; emphasis added)
The yearning for laughter’s future is voiced again in Beyond Good and
Evil, “Perhaps, even if nothing else today has any future, our laughter
may yet have a future” (223).
Given Nietzsche’s meager theoretical output on laughter and the lib-
erties the French have taken with his views, his worry, as expressed in
Thus Spoke Zarathustra, “If they learned to laugh from me, it still is not
my laughter that they have learned”239 may be warranted. I believe that
the problematization of Nietzsche’s laughter undertaken in this study
has shown that this worry may be justified. At the same time, owing to
the very liberties the French took with Nietzsche’s thought in general
and with his laughter in particular, Nietzsche’s yearning for the future
of laughter seems to have materialized. I hope that this study has shown
how the laughing Nietzsche has changed the face of philosophy more
deeply than any other laughing philosopher, and may be also more thor-
oughly than any other “Nietzsche.”

 46 Comte-Sponville 1995, 283; my translation; also 1994, 16. This section
should also refer to Eric Blondel’s view of laughter. Blondel is not easily
characterized as Nietzschean or not; he is a translator of Nietzsche’s late
work and a reputed Nietzsche scholar, who has published, aside from many
articles, two books on Nietzsche (1980, 1986); however, his references
to “the catch-all fashion called poststructuralism” and “the pretentious
young men of the signifier” (“La mode fourre-tout dite poststructuraliste”;
“les précieuses ridicules du signifiant” [Blondel 2019]) leave little doubt
about his allegiance. Blondel emphasizes Nietzsche’s “medicynism” which
leads back from morality to its bodily origin, and refreshingly notes his
lack of humor:
Nietzsche has no sense of humor, in the sense of showing an ability to
look at oneself critically, tongue-in-cheek, or more simply to be able to
laugh at oneself in the most serious contexts or dangerous situations.
On the one hand Nietzsche is endowed with a brilliant sense of irony,
but on the other hand as a person and in his settings, he never mocks
himself or laughs at his own self, never looks at himself with this par-
ticular critical and humorous detachment that characterized properly
humor… Nietzsche only laughs at others, never at himself.
(Blondel 1999, 171–2)
Blondel penned a book on the laughable and the derisory (Le Risible et le
dérisoire [1988]), which does not refer to Bataille, Deleuze, Rosset, Nancy,
Kofman, or anyone else this study addresses, but rather to Plato, the Cyn-
ics, Descartes, Pascal, Spinoza, Hume, Bergson, André Gide, Søren Kier-
kegaard, and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. Somehow, however, this book sums
up the concerns of his generation. Blondel dedicates it to “grave and humor-
ous philosophers,” who taught him “to live, that is, to laugh”; he explains
the association of philosophy and laughter, and exemplifies this association
with 30 pages of verbal and pictural examples both literary and philosoph-
ical. Laughter is serious because to laugh at certain things is more serious
than to lament them, be indifferent to them or abstain from doing anything


Concluding Remarks 431
about them. Laughter is too serious to be left in the hands of earnest people
or buffoons, as the laughable is not necessarily funny. In accordance with the
law of Janus, the other face of laughter is the tragic. Philosophy, which is at
equidistance between the respectable and the ridiculous, is not meant to be
funny. However, it can enlighten laughter with a “philosophical laugh,” ei-
ther earnestness mitigated with irony or the laughter of seriousness. Not only
are the habitual questions about laughter asked in Blondel’s study (“why do
we laugh?” etc.), but also the question of laughter’s optimism or pessimism
and the question of the tragedy or comedy of the world, life and the human
condition: life is comical and immensely sad at the same time.
 47 DeLanda 2002, 1; Gutting 2001, 331; Bogue 2004, chapter 2. Ronald
Bogue asks whether Gilles Deleuze can be characterized as a postmodern
philosopher. He answers that question mostly in the positive, noting that
Deleuze, particularly in his later work with Félix Guattari, resists the temp-
tation to offer grand narratives and writes instead in more specific areas,
jettisoning earlier discussions of Being as difference for multiple and inter-
secting discussions that resist packaging into a coherent whole. One thinks
here particularly of A Thousand Plateaus. Bogue’s claim is interesting, al-
though I don’t know how compelling. The concept of the postmodern is
elusive, if indeed at all coherent, and Deleuze’s reluctance to appeal to the
term (a reluctance Bogue notes) is an indication that perhaps should be fol-
lowed. Not that nothing can be characterized as postmodern in Deleuze’s
work. But rather, the term itself does not bring us closer to understanding
Deleuze’s work. For Gary Gutting, Deleuze remains a poststructuralist in
rejecting the unifying devices of mainstream philosophy (subject, object,
representation, cause, etc.), and his sympathy with projects of systematic
philosophy is based on their construal not as searches for truth in the tra-
ditional sense of representation but as creations of new concepts (Deleuze
and Guattari WP, 1).

 59 For Freud, the ego is never illusory, whether connected with the reality
principle, as in his early work, or formed through an identification with
parental figures. To the contrary, Lacan argues that intersubjectivity is


432 Concluding Remarks
there right from the beginning. While the unconscious threatens Freud, it
is the locus of authenticity or truth for Lacan, it is implicit in everything
we say and do. As we can never know it, self-knowledge is impossible for
Lacan. The dream is a text for Lacan, a kind of writing, and its processes of
condensation and displacement are redefined as metaphor and metonymy,
respectively. Additional differences with Freud are enumerated in Sarup’s
first chapter (1993, 16) and the influence of Hegel on Lacan is addressed.
Sarup notes there that Alexandre Kojève’s lectures on Hegel shaped Lacan’s
view of desire, which is ontological, a struggle for wholeness, rather than
a sexual force as in Freud. The Phallus refers to plenitude, and stands for
this yearning for completion in both men and women. Lacan introduces the
symbolic order as the level in which all Oedipal struggle occurs. Lacan’s
work is implacably anti-biological (madness is a discourse; as an attempt at
communication, it must be interpreted) and social: his thought emphasizes
the work of culture and society and allows for no separation between self
and society: “Human beings become social with the appropriation of lan-
guage; and it is language that constitutes us as a subject… Society inhabits
each individual” and “Knowledge of the world, of others and of self is de-
termined by language. Language is a precondition for the act of becoming
aware of oneself as a distinct entity” (Sarup 1993, 6, 8). However, language
is autonomous from meaning as the signifier is freed from the signified. La-
can’s hermeneutics comes to the fore when he states that social phenomena
always have a meaning, which we should understand rather than explain.
Instead of the rational, conscious actor who can understand the basis for
his action, which existentialism offers in its philosophy of individual auton-
omy and rational choice, Lacan decenters the rational, conscious subject,
which Freud identified with the ego. Not only “I think, therefore I am” is
not true, but “I think where I am not, therefore I am where I do not think”
(Lemaire 1977, 166; quoted is Sarup 1999, 10). The Lacanian subject, a
fragment of something larger and primordial, which demarcates itself from
both Freud and Sartre as representative of the Enlightenment ideal of the
rational self, has been embraced by the French Nietzscheans.

socialism.
